1.title: Shabu'ot, Torah Study and Dairy
1.text:
Pesah, Shabu'ot, Sukkot, three holidays that are mentioned together in the Torah time and again. Pesah everybody associates with the Haggadah, Sukkot everybody associates with Sukkah as well as Lulab and Etrog. That leaves us with our holiday of Hag HaShabu'ot. What is the ritual associated with Hag HaShabu'ot? What is Hag HaShabu'ot? Hag HaShabu'ot is the commemoration of Mattan Torah, of HaShem giving the Torah to 'Am Yisrael and 'Am Yisrael accepting the Torah.

To that effect, we have a centuries-old custom where the men go to Kenis on the first night of Shabu'ot or they gather in private homes on that first night to reacquaint themselves with the Torah, to study the Torah, to read the Torah. But it's not done in the studying method that people think of today as studying, but in the sense of reading. In fact, there is a prescribed way of studying Torah. There is an old book called Sefer Keri'e Mo'ed, and in this Sefer Keri'e Mo'ed we have something called Tikkun Lel Shabu'ot. This Tikkun Lel Shabu'ot is the beginning and end of each Parashah, each of the Nebi'im, each of the Ketubim, each of the Megillot. It's a way that we reconnect with the Torah and what's written in it, and we reacquaint ourselves with it and re-energize ourselves with it so we get carried through with it through the entire year.

This is a marriage between 'Am Yisrael and the Torah. It's a marriage that has been noted as such by the Hakhamim, and in fact, Rabbi Yisrael Najara, the famed poet from Damascus as well as Gaza, wrote a special Ketubah, a marriage contract, for that instance, for this commemoration, and for that holiday. This is something that is said at Petihat HaHekhal on the morning of Hag HaShabu'ot. In the old days, this was common in many countries. In fact, in Halab, it was recited. In fact, there's a special tune for it. And even though today we don't find it in our Mahzorim, it's clearly noticeable in the old Mahzorim that you see Ketubah for Hag HaShabu'ot.

Another thing associated with Hag HaShabu'ot also has to do with Torah and Missvot, and that are the Azharot. The Azharot, not meaning warnings, but Azharot meaning a reminder, a reminder of each one of the 613 Missvot. So we say these Azharot in poetic stanzas with a special tune. People generally gather at home with friends and family to recite them, and we say the 248 positive commandments on the first day and the 365 negative commandments on the second day. Those also appear in the Mahzorim, and they were written by Rabbi Shelomo Ibn Gabirol in Granada, Spain.

We also read the Megillah of Rut. Megillah of Rut is very important to us because that also shows us the ethical side of Torah, how people are to conduct themselves with one another in a social setting, how people need to learn how to get along and help one another out. These are all aspects of the Torah that the Torah cannot see itself going ahead without. So these are all the main things that come together with Hag HaShabu'ot.

On another note, there are those that think of Hag HaShabu'ot as a dairy holiday. I would just like to dispel that myth. These three holidays, Pesah, Shabu'ot, and Sukkot, all prescribed by the Torah as 'Aliyah LaRegel, going up to the Bet HaMikdash in order to bring the holiday sacrifice. The sacrifice was meat, and therefore on the holidays we are told in the Halakhah, specifically by HaRambam, to eat meat. Now as far as eating dairy, there are those that eat dairy on the first night of Shabu'ot, and that was the most common Minhag in Halab, and that was to facilitate staying up all night, reading all night, and partaking of dairy sweets throughout the night. And many other Sefaradim would have dairy as a festive breakfast on the first morning of the holiday in order to partake of the dairy and have a meal after staying up all night.

That's basically what Hag HaShabu'ot is about. It's the Torah, it's the sweetness of the Torah, it's reconnecting with the Torah. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

2.title: Dairy on Shabu'ot in Syria
2.text:
So there's a popular custom of serving dairy in honor of the holiday of Shabu'ot. What is the origin of this custom, and to what extent was it practiced in the Middle East in general, and in Halab, Aleppo, Syria, in particular?

So the earliest record of serving dairy for Shabu'ot is in the 13th century. We find it documented in both France and Germany. The Kol Bo was an authority who lived in France in the 13th century, wrote that it's customary to eat honey and milk on Shabu'ot because of a verse that we find in Shir HaShirim, the famous verse, "Debash VeHalab Tahat Leshonekh," honey and milk under your tongue. So it's understood by commentators to allegorically be referring to one speaking words of Torah.

Another source from 13th century France is Rabbi Abigdor Sarfati, and he writes that the Torah itself alluded to the custom of eating dairy on Shabu'ot. There's a verse that says "Minhah Hadashah LaAd-onai BeShabu'otekhem," a new offering to God on your holiday of Shabu'ot. This is referring to the two wheat loaves of bread that were brought and waved in the Bet HaMikdash on the day of Shabu'ot, is described as a new offering, and the acronym of the Pasuk, "Hadashah," Het, "LaHaShem," Lamed, "BeShabu'otekhem," Bet, spells out Halab, which is milk. The custom is also documented by the Rokeah, who was an authority in Germany also in the 13th century.

Now what's interesting is that the more popular reason for dairy on Shabu'ot, which was that they ate dairy after they received the Torah because their dishes weren't Kasher, they weren't able to slaughter, they didn't have a knife, they didn't have everything necessary to do it properly according to Halakhah, this reason was first documented in the 19th century, we find it in a Hasidic source, but there's no earlier source to support that narrative.

Now the earliest documentation for serving dairy on Shabu'ot amongst Middle Eastern authorities begins in the 17th century. It was documented by Rabbi Hayyim Benveniste in Shiyare Keneset HaGedolah. He lived in Turkey. The Peri Hadash, also 17th century, who is originally from Italy, but he lived and taught in Yerushalayim, also documents the custom. But what we find in many sources is that they ate dairy foods before their meat lunch on the first day of Shabu'ot. This is what's written by the Rema, Rabbi Moshe Isserles, who was an authority in Poland in the 16th century. This was also the practice of Rabbi Hayyim Benveniste, whom we mentioned previously, and of Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, who was the chief rabbi of the Turkish Empire in the 19th century. Rabbi Abraham Hamwey, who was born in Halab in the 19th century, also emphasized the importance of eating meat on Shabu'ot. He wrote, after you eat dairy, make Birkat HaMazon and then eat meat in honor of Yom Tob. And this was also the practice of Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alav HaShalom.

So we also find some communities that did not even serve dairy as a prelude to a meat meal, but rather it was just the breakfast after they stayed up and learned and studied Torah all night, when they came home, they ate breakfast, they served dairy foods, foods with honey, in honor of "Debash VeHalab Tahat Leshonekh." In Yemen, they didn't serve dairy at all on Shabu'ot.

So what about the Syrian custom? So in Syria, it was customary to serve a dairy meal on Shabu'ot. The prevalent custom was the first night. Many had the custom to serve it on the first day instead. And although HaRambam requires meat for all of the Yom Tob meals, Maran did not agree with HaRambam on this point. He ruled that the meat was a requirement of the times of the Bet HaMikdash, when they had the Korbanot, the Shelamim, in honor of Yom Tob. But in our times that we don't have the Korbanot, we can fulfill our obligation of Simhat Yom Tob by drinking wine.

So yes, there are customary dairy foods amongst the Syrian community for Shabu'ot: Ishta B'asal, the Sambusak, the dairy Sambusak. Furthermore it was also customary to serve Rizz B'haleeb, which is rice with milk, and Rizz B'asal, which is rice with honey, again with the based on the Pasuk "Debash VeHalab Tahat Leshonekh." Many also have the custom to serve Qarabeej, which is a pastry with a marshmallow fluff. So the marshmallow fluff in Arabic is known as Natef, and it's reminiscent of a verse that we read in the Mizmor in honor of Shabu'ot, the Pasuk in Tehillim says, "Af Shamayim Natefu, Zeh Sinai." Natefu is reminiscent of Natef.

So while it was customary to have one dairy meal, and if you drink wine with your meal, as we said, you fulfill your obligation of Simhat Yom Tob, of being happy on Yom Tob according to Maran HaShulhan 'Arukh. We also see that according to most of the sources, dairy on Shabu'ot was not intended to replace an actual meal. It was either a prelude to a meat lunch, or it was just a breakfast, so it wasn't even together with a meal, and therefore, the other three meals should be all be meat meals. And that way, we fulfill our obligation, at least with the other meals, according to all the opinions, including HaRambam, who, as we said, requires meat for all of the Yom Tob meals.

3.title: Introduction to Tefilah BeSibbur
3.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. My name is Joey Harari. I am a Brooklyn-born community member who, together with my wife Katie, had the Zekhut of coming to Israel, making 'Aliyah to Yerushalayim about 20 years ago. In this series of Minhag of the Week, you'll be hearing from me, BeEzrat HaShem, about Minhagim dealing with Tefilah BeSibbur, the daily prayers in our synagogue. The playlist to begin with the weekdays, go on to Shabbat, and the rest of the holidays.

Before I begin actual content, we're going to have a little bit of an introduction I feel is necessary. In our joint introductory remarks when we started this project, Joey, Morris, and I spoke about the importance of the Minhagim, the halakhic obligation to maintain them, the social, the cultural, even the emotional benefits of knowing that we belong to a global community of Halabiyeh who, for over a thousand years, developed customs that were meticulously and zealously maintained by our Hakhamim, our Gabba'im, our laymen.

You know, it's amazing. I'm sitting here in Kenis Ades in Yerushalayim, and when we made 'Aliyah, we came to Yerushalayim, we sought Kenis Halabiyeh, and because of our the importance we put on keeping our Minhagim, I could come here, and after 40 years of being in Brooklyn, I come to a new synagogue, seamless transition, instantly feel at home, and pray exactly the same way I was praying all my prior life.

Customs evolve. No community is 100% homogeneous in their practices. The Halab community in particular went through a couple of events in their history, went through many events in their history, but a couple in particular that had a very big impact on our customs. Two major factors changed our Siddur forever. One was the influx in the late 15th century of significant amount of Jews who were expelled from Spain and came to Halab armed with a rich and proud tradition and Piyyutim and prayers, and they weren't so keen on letting go of those customs so quickly, and that was one of the reasons. The other factor that changed our Siddur was in the 16th century the rise and the spreading of the Kabbalistic thought, which was which began in Sefat by Rabbi Yisshak Luria Ashkenazi, Zikhrono LiBerakhah, the Ari, and this spread of this Kabbalah spread to many, many communities, altered the practices and the Nushaot and the Tefilot, and that's something we have to keep in mind.

I'm holding in my hand Mahzor Aram Soba, published originally in Venice in 1527. We go through the Siddur and Mahzor, and it hardly resembles the Siddurim that we use today. This was generally the Nusah, the prayers of the Musta'arabim, the local Halabiyeh before the Sefaradim came. Besides being very interesting, rich in content and Piyyutim, it's a valuable reference tool, and it helps us understand some of the Minhagim that we have today.

The purpose of this series will be simply to let you know our community's customs. I remember when I was growing up, as long as I remember about 50 years ago, going to the synagogues, and when I mention a Minhag, when I go through Minhagim, if I mention a specific Minhag, it's only because other communities do it differently. Now, a lot of what I say may be obvious, and you're going to say, react and say, "Well, what's the Hiddush?" But that's precisely the point. It may be common practice today. Our hope is to preserve them so 50 years, 100 years from now, things won't be changing and we won't be having outside influences alter what we do, and we can always go back and see how it was done. And the reason I'm saying that is because we see practices today, I see things today in Brooklyn which are different than how they were done 50 years ago. So that's why we are here. See you next time. Shalom.

4.title: Candle Lighting and Facing the Hekhal
4.text:
Friday night, Lel Shabbat, beautiful time, time when the family is getting ready to enjoy Shabbat together. The women of our homes, of our households, of our families, they light candles. But it should be known that they didn't light candles in the past. They actually lit floating wicks in bowls of oil, and only in modern days do they light candles because of convenience and easy accessibility to get candles. But there are still women who light oil, and that is the true Minhag.

Now the question really comes to a head as to what is the Minhag, how to light? In other words, do they light first and then make Berakhah, or do they make a Berakhah prior to lighting? Now this was an arena that men weren't really involved in, and it was strictly something that was transmitted over the course of many generations from mother to daughter and to their daughters and their daughters after them. And in most cases, and this was the case not only in Halab, or Sham, or Cairo, or Alexandria, or Lebanon, but this was the Minhag in almost every Sephardic community, that the women actually lit first and then made the Berakhah.

Now this is different than our standard rule of "Berakhot 'Ober La'Asiyatan," that we make Berakhot prior to doing the action. For some reason, the Minhag developed over here where candle lighting preceded the Berakhah, and this Minhag has many, many sources to rely upon, Hakhamim through running the gamut over the course of centuries explaining it and defending it, and in fact telling you that it's even better than making the Berakhah first. So women should not feel today that their custom of lighting or that their mothers before them lit, or their grandmothers would light before making the Berakhah, that it was a negative custom or something that's not well-grounded or based in Halakhah or Minhag. They should know that they should hold onto their Minhag and they should do such a thing.

And as I mentioned, this is something that we have documented sources, both written and oral sources telling us that this was the Minhag of most women. And obviously, if that was the Minhag of your family, of your mother and her mother before her, you should continue the same way of lighting and then making the Berakhah. But if your Minhag is otherwise, to make the Berakhah and then to light, that's the way you should continue. But do not feel forced to forgo your Minhag because somebody is telling you otherwise. There was no one Minhag for any one city, but in the majority of households, because this was a specific household Minhag, the Minhag was to light prior to making Berakhah.

Another thing I'd like to mention is Lel Shabbat in the Bet Keneset. During Kabbalat Shabbat, like at any other time, the Minhag has always been to face forward, facing the Hekhal, not to turn around, not to spin around. And unfortunately, in recent years, we're seeing a new phenomenon where people come to the Bet Keneset, and when they get to Mizmor LeDavid, or Lekha Dodi, or Bo'i BeShalom, they all of a sudden spin around, their backs face the Hekhal, and their fronts face the west side of the Bet Keneset. This has never been our Minhag. It was not a Minhag in any of our countries of origin, not in Syria, not in Egypt, not in Lebanon, not in Iraq, not in Turkey, and this was never the Minhag here in the United States from the time that Sefaradim started coming here circa 1900 till today. Our Minhag is to face forward, to pray to HaShem facing forward, giving the proper Kabod to the Hekhal, and not to face westward or to turn around at any one point.

Always be proud to hold onto your Minhagim, to our Minhagim, and not feel forced because somebody came from another country or another community telling you that this is better and this is the way you should be doing things and you should change things to do that. Always look for your true Minhag, and adhere to your Minhag, and be proud of your Minhagim.

5.title: Friday Night Kiddush Customs
5.text:
So on Friday night, many have the custom when they begin Kiddush, they start by first singing the song Shalom 'Alekhem. They sing each stanza three times, and then they followed by Eshet Hayil, and then there's more pieces that they say: Atkinu Se'udata, some sing Azamer BiShbahin, VeHa'Arabah, and then after all the pieces, they begin with "Yom HaShishi." However, there are many Halabi families that don't have the custom to read all the preliminary pieces. They start off right away with "Yom HaShishi."

Now with regards to the song of Shalom 'Alekhem, it's not known who wrote the song, but it dates back to the late 16th century, and there are halakhic authorities who objected to the song. Why? Because the song has a stanza, has a verse: "Barekhuni." They're asking the angels to bless them. According to HaRambam, you're not only is allowed to pray directly to HaShem, you're not allowed to ask an angel to bless you. This is one of his 13 principles of Judaism, so therefore there was objections, and on the other hand, the Mekubbalim, the mystical authorities, promoted the song along with the other pieces before you get to "Yom HaShishi."

So as we said, that there were some families that did not recite any of the pieces, they began only with "Yom HaShishi," and this is based on the concept that people that are not knowledgeable in Kabbalah and they're not they don't have an understanding of the teachings don't necessarily adopt kabbalistic practices. So there were some families that adopted it, and other families that didn't. So in this case, as we said, some did and some didn't.

In Halab, it was also customary to drink the Kiddush wine standing up, even though the Arizal, who was the master of Kabbalah, his own personal custom was after he finished the Kiddush that he recited standing up, he would sit down to drink the wine. However, we're not Mekubbalim, and we don't do everything that's taught in the Kabbalah, and therefore our custom was to stand when we drink the wine. There's others that said that taught that it's always proper, whenever you eat or drink, to sit down. However, since we don't always make a point to sit down before we drink anything, therefore even our rabbis, many rabbis in Halab had the custom then when they drank the Kiddush wine to remain standing.

So now, another custom that's associated with Kiddush is after we make Kiddush, it's customary for the children to kiss their father's hand, to kiss their mother's hand, and to receive a blessing. And usually the parent puts their hand over the child's head after the child kisses the hand. And if it's a boy: "Yesimkha Elokim KeEfrayim VeKhiMnasheh," followed by the Birkat Kohanim. If it's a girl, they say: "Yesimekh Elokim KeSarah, Ribkah, Rahel, VeLe'ah," also followed by the Birkat Kohanim.

One last point. As we said, although many times the kabbalistic practice was not customary in Halab, in other cases it was, and therefore many had the custom to add three drops of water to the wine prior to making Kiddush. This would be both on Friday night and on Shabbat day. The exception is the Habdalah cup. It's not customary to put to add any water to the Habdalah cup. All this is based on the teachings of the Mekubbalim, and as we said, in some cases the kabbalistic practice became widely accepted, in other cases was only practiced by those that were knowledgeable in kabbalistic teachings.

6.title: Entering Kenis, Talet and Tefillin
6.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will be continuing our discussion with Minhagim relating to Tefilah BeSibbur, and as I mentioned, generally I will discuss Minhagim which are either unique to the Halabi community or Minhagim which are practiced differently in other communities, in some other communities.

So we come to Kenis in the morning, having already recited Birkot HaShahar at home. That is our custom. In addition, note that Birkat HaMappil Hable Shenah and the subsequent Yehi Rassons are said in the plural: "HaMappil Hable Shenah Me'enenu."

Now we're going to go into the Kenis. As we enter the Kenis, we pause and we say the Pasuk from Tehillim: "VaAni BeRob Hasdekha Abo Betekha Eshtahaveh El Hekhal Kodshekha BeYir'atekha." It's an old custom, it's even found in the Mahzor Aram Soba.

So now we proceed to put on our Talet. And there are a number of ways to put on the Talet, all are valid. Those who are particular to follow the instructions of the Kabbalah to put it over the head and move all the Sissiyot to one side, will make the Berakhah, put it over the head, and then in the ensuing few seconds, some say, some have the custom to say the Pasuk, the Pesukim: "Mah Yakar Hasdekha Elokim," and there's four Pesukim total. The more prevalent way to put on the Talet, which we grew up seeing everybody put it on in this fashion, simply make the Berakhah, kiss it, put on the shoulders, either like this or over the shoulders. Over the shoulders really started when the wool Taletot started appearing in the '70s. Before then we used to use, all the shuls, all the synagogues had the silk Taletot, which weren't really silk, they were probably rayon, and they used to simply put them on like that. Some people, after they put it on their shoulders, go over the head, kiss it, and put it back. Some do that initially, say the Berakhah, shoulders, and back. Those are the different ways which we put on Talet. They're all fine, they're all halakhically viable. Again, the prevalent custom was simply over the shoulders.

Now, we will talk about how we put on Tefillin. Our custom, as the custom in many Sephardic communities, is 'Al Pi HaKabbalah to put the Tefillin Shel Yad Meyushab, in a sitting position. We say the Berakhah and put on the Tefillin sitting down. I've noticed, I used to see often that some people, when they say the Berakhah, get up a little bit. Not all, not everybody, but I've seen it. And then we put on Tefillin Shel Rosh, and after we tuck in the Ressu'ot, we say the Pasuk: "VeRa'u Kol 'Amme HaAress Ki Shem Ad-onai Nikra 'Alekha VeYare'u Mimmekka."

Immediately after we put on the Tefillin, we say the Parashiyot "Kadesh Li Kol Bekhor," "VeHayah Ki Yebi'akha." The reason we say these Parashiyot, now this is a custom, it's an old custom, the earliest attribution I've seen was from Ramban in the name of Ramban Nahmani, and the reason we say this is because now that we have our Tefillin on, we want to recite the Parashiyot which are actually written in the Batim of the Tefillin Shel Yad and Tefillin Shel Rosh. So the four Parashiyot of course: Kadesh Li, VeHayah Ki Yebi'akha, Parashat Shema, and VeHayah Im Shamoa'. Now VeHayah, Shema and VeHayah Im Shamoa' we're going to say in the Tefilah. So we want to say immediately Kadesh Li and VeHayah Ki Yebi'akha so that we recite the four Parashiyot as, in the same order which they are written in the Torah.

Obviously if somebody's running late and wants to make sure he catches the 'Amidah with the Sibbur, and follows the Maran and how to skip appropriately in order to catch up properly, of course he could say Kadesh Li after 'Alenu LeShabbeah, but it's preferable to say it before, immediately when we put on the Tefillin, before we begin. Some have the custom to say it right before Barukh SheAmar, we'll discuss a little bit about that next week. Regarding Tefillin of Rabbenu Tam, I'm not going to get into it since this was a rare occurrence, practice only by very unique individuals. Kol Tub.

7.title: Berakhot Between Kiddush and HaMossi
7.text:
Every Friday night and holiday night, every Shabbat lunch or holiday lunch, we know we have Kiddush. After Kiddush, people generally run to do Netilat Yadayim for HaMossi. But there is a custom, a custom that was still in vogue until not too long ago, that between the Kiddush and the Netilat Yadayim, people would stop to make Berakhot on individual items, maybe have a Kibbeh and say Mezonot, have an olive, say Ha'Ess, have a cucumber, say HaAdamah, and say all different types of Berakhot prior to doing Netilat Yadayim for HaMossi.

This is a very old custom. It's a well-established custom. It seems to be based upon the idea that a person is obligated, as HaRambam tells us, a person is obligated to make 100 Berakhot each day. And these Berakhot were not considered a interruption, a Hefsek, between the Kiddush and the meal, because these are appetizers. This is a way to open up the appetite, to get you to enjoy the meal better.

And the source of not having these appetizers or saying Berakhot between the Kiddush and Netilat Yadayim seems to stem from a saying by Muram. Muram is Rabbi Moshe Isserles who wrote his commentary on the Shulhan 'Arukh, which is published in every version of the Shulhan 'Arukh that we presently have, and it's become standard practice to read it and study it along with Shulhan 'Arukh. And he writes over there, "VeSarikh LeEkhol BiMkom Kiddush LeAltar," and you must eat in the place of Kiddush immediately. And on that line, the Magen Abraham quotes the Maharil, says that you cannot have any sort of interruption, you cannot have any break, and it must be done immediately.

And we don't have any Sephardic Hakhamim that say the same thing. In fact, we have the famous Rabbi Abraham HaLevi in his Ginat Veradim, who tells us, "I don't know where Maharil or Muram or Magen Abraham came up with this. This is not something that appears in our Gemara at all. It's not something that appears in any of the Rishonim prior to Maharil, and there is no such law. There is nothing that says that you cannot have a break." And in fact, having a break is something that seems to be done among many Sephardic communities, many Sephardic households. As I said, I know that it was done in Syria, I know it was done in Egypt, I know it was done in Yemen. We even have the Hida, the famous Rabbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, who was born and raised in Yerushalayim, and was an emissary and traveled the world. And he even writes in his Kunteres Aharon of Mahzik Berakhah that he grew up in Yerushalayim, and they made Berakhot. They made Berakhot on fish, they made Berakhot on hard liquor prior to going to do Netilat Yadayim for HaMossi.

So this is a beautiful custom. It's a custom that helps enhance the Shabbat, helps to enhance the holiday. It enhances the meal, enhances the setting of the table, brings back the custom that our forefathers did, and it helps us to get those Berakhot that we need each and every day. So I think it's a Minhag that we need to perpetuate. It's a Minhag that we need to embrace, Minhag that we need to bring back.

8.title: HaMossi, Salt and Passing the Bread
8.text:
So on Friday night and Shabbat day, as well as on the nights and days of Yom Tob, it's customary to dip the bread after you make HaMossi, to dip it in salt after reciting the Berakhah. However, it was not customary to dip the bread in salt on ordinary weekday meals.

Prior to reciting the Berakhah of HaMossi on Shabbat and Yom Tob, it's customary to recite the following Pesukim: "'Ene Khol Elekha Yesabberu VeAttah Noten Lahem Et Okhlam Be'itto," followed by the next Pasuk of "Poteah Et Yadekha UMasbia' LeKhol Hai Rasson," followed by "Barukh Mekaddesh HaShabbat" without HaShem's Name. If it was Yom Tob, "Barukh Mekaddesh Yisrael VeHaZemanim." If it's Shabbat and Yom Tob, "Barukh Mekaddesh HaShabbat VeYisrael VeHaZemanim." And then you recite the Berakhah of HaMossi.

So now, when you're reciting the Pesukim and the Berakhah, you hold two loaves of bread in both hands, and it's customary when you get to the word "HaMossi" to lift the bread up. And then, as we said, after you complete the blessing, you it was customary to break the bread with your hands, as we never had the custom to cut the bread with a knife. And then, as we said, you dip it in salt. Those that follow the kabbalistic teachings are careful to dip each bread of each piece of bread in salt three times, and then it's after you taste your piece, you distribute it to the other people.

So the custom in Halab was, when they distributed the bread to others, that they would throw it, meaning in a gentle way, to each person at the table. So as long as the bread is not being thrown in a disrespectful manner, it's not a halakhic problem. This was the custom of Hakham Moshe Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, he was the Chief Rabbi in Halab, as well as his student, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, who went on to be the Chief Rabbi in Argentina. According to Hakham David Yosef, the son of Hakham 'Obadia, his father, Hakham 'Obadia, would also gently throw the bread to people that were sitting a little bit further away, in a manner that he was careful that it wouldn't fall on the floor. This is if somebody was sitting a little further away from him. And as we said, it's not a halakhic problem, since you're not throwing it in a disrespectful manner, but you're just being careful not to put it in someone's hand.

Why don't you want to put the bread in someone's hand? HaRambam writes in Hilkhot Berakhot that when you're distributing bread to people, that you put it in front of them, and you don't put it in their hand unless they're a mourner. So therefore, the custom came to be, if they're not sitting next to you and you can't put it directly in front of them, you throw it gently.

Just one last custom, and that's after the person who makes HaMossi tastes the bread and he's distributing it to others, the custom, also interestingly based on the Mekubbalim, is to always give your wife right after you. After you taste it, the first person that gets is your wife, before anyone else at the table.

9.title: Where Shahrit Begins and the Hazzan
9.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will be continuing with the Minhagim of Tefilah BeSibbur. Now we left off last time having recited the Kadesh Li and VeHayah with our Tefillin on, and now we're ready to begin the prayer.

Simple question, where do we start from? So you're going to say, "What's the big deal?" Open the Siddur, we see the beginning of Tefilat Hannah, begins with the section of the prayer which is known as the Korbanot, start from there. Well, it's not that simple. A custom has developed not only in our community, but in other Syrian communities throughout the world, that only the first Minyan begins with the Korbanot, subsequent Minyanim start from HaShem Melekh. Now this could be for a number of reasons. Maybe just the people that frequent the first Minyan were the more pious, Anshe Ma'aseh, they don't want to skip over the Korbanot. Maybe time constraints for later Minyanim. Maybe people used to say the Korbanot on the way to the to second Minyanim, all possibilities. At any rate, we know that first Minyan begins Tefilat Hannah or Elokai. Second Minyan, if they announce 7:00 second Minyan, we know 7:00, HaShem Melekh. That's the way it developed, and it's very interesting.

So we begin with the Korbanot, which include many passages from Torah SheBe'al Peh: Ketoret, Ezehu Mekoman. So when we conclude the Korbanot, we say Kaddish 'Al Yisrael. This is a Kaddish which mourners also participate in, as well as people who have the yahrzeits for their parents. Now, we're going to be dedicating an entire video to Kaddishim, so we're not going to dwell on it. However, if you start from HaShem Melekh, you say HaShem Melekh, "VeHayah HaShem LeMelekh 'Al Kol HaAress," LaMnasseah, you can't really say Kaddish 'Al Yisrael because we didn't say anything from Torah SheBe'al Peh. Therefore, we add Rabbi Hananya so as to not the people who have to obligate to say Kaddish, they don't miss out, and we say that Kaddish.

Regarding Kadesh Li, so again, if you finished putting on the Tefillin, you'll say Kadesh Li before HaShem Melekh or right before Barukh SheAmar. Now, before Barukh SheAmar, like we said in the last video, if you have to catch up or so you could always put it off, and if you can't make it before Barukh SheAmar, you could always say it after the prayer. However, don't get the impression that saying it before HaShem Melekh is the proper time for Kadesh Li. In other words, if you of course, if you start by HaShem Melekh, that's the proper time, but if you start at saying the Korbanot or Hodu, you don't stop after Le'Olam Odekha before HaShem Melekh to put on this to say Kadesh Li. You'll say it either before you put on before you start praying, or again, before Barukh SheAmar.

Now, we're ready to say Barukh SheAmar, but I want to say a few words introduction about our style of Tefilah. Our Tefilah is very focused on the Hazzan. Now this leads to a few customs which have developed. Number one, because everybody's focused on the Hazzan and they pray following the Hazzan, the Hazzan from HaShem Melekh has to stand at the Tebah. Korbanot, you could say from your seat, but HaShem Melekh, starting HaShem Melekh, they stand at the Tebah. So this way it's Kebod Sibbur and the Sibbur could be focused on the Hazzan.

Secondly, everybody prays quietly. There's no din coming up from the Kahal like in other communities. Even the person next to you doesn't hear your doesn't hear you pray. Very, very important. There are parts of prayer where we have to answer out loud, we'll get to those when we get to them in the Tefilah.

The third development as a result of our Hazzan-centric prayer is that we choose Hazzanim who know how to read properly, clearly, nice loud voice, they don't swallow, and especially they know how to read properly grammatically. And this is very, very important. And to our credit, our community is not tolerant of Hazzanim who don't pronounce the words properly, and very often will let him know it in real time. And to our credit, like I said, we've developed Hazzanim because of this, Hazzanim that are very particular with the 'Ayin and the Alef, with the Het and the Khaf, Mil'el, Milra', Degeshim. And it's very important to select a Hazzan based on these criteria. Shalom UBerakhah, next week: Barukh SheAmar.

10.title: Tish'ah BeAb Customs of Halab
10.text:
Tish'ah BeAb, very solemn day, national day of mourning, crying over the destruction of the Bet HaMikdash and so many other calamities that befell 'Am Yisrael. This is a day that has so many different types of Minhagim associated with it. Many of these Minhagim are related to the way we conduct ourselves on the day itself. And even though many of them are the same from community to community, so many more are different as well, as mourning customs developed differently in each community. I'd like to focus on Minhagim strictly of Halab, Aleppo, Syria, and once in a while I may mention how they compare and/or contrast with Minhagim of other communities, but for the most part many of these Minhagim are the same.

First and foremost, it's not a happy time. It's a very sad time. It's a day that we do not greet one another. It's a time that we just lower our heads, walk into Kenis quietly without saying anything to anyone. We sit on the floor from the night until at least midday. We don't even sit in our same spots. We sit in a different spot in the Kenis. If we usually sit in the front, we sit in the back, we sit on the side, we sit in a different row, we sit some place else. At night, we actually count down the years since the destruction of the Second Temple, the second Bet HaMikdash, which according to our Minhag, our tradition, occurred in the year 68 CE.

The Torah is not taken out of the Hekhal on the day of Tish'ah BeAb with the same fanfare that we normally would even on a regular weekday, but it's taken out with sadness. It's taken out while saying special prayers, not really a prayer, but more of a lamentation, a dirge. We're crying when we're taking out the Sefer Torah because even the Sefer Torah is mourning. We don't lift up the Sefer Torah to show it to the people. We just take it out quietly and place it on the Tebah.

At night we open up the prayers with the reading of Parashat Ha'azinu. In the morning, we say Ha'azinu in place of Az Yashir. At night and during the day, we say Kinot. Kinot are lamentations, elegies, dirges, very, very sad things, things that we would normally say at a funeral. That's what we're saying. We read Megillat Ekhah both at night and during the day.

We Again, I said, we do not greet people, but it's not only that we do not greet people, we don't laugh, we don't joke, we don't say, "How you doing?" We don't gather. We don't go for strolls. We don't go for we go we don't watch movies. We just try to focus on the events, the tragedies of the day. Instead of saying "Shalom 'Alekhem," if you must say hello, the way to greet people is you say, "Tizkeh BeNehamat Siyyon," and the response is, "Tizkeh BeBinyanah." At night, we dim the lights in the Kenis.

There is a prayer called Nahem. According to the Halabi tradition, it's only said during Minhah. So, one 'Amidah the entire year that Nahem is added, Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb. Other communities also only do it during Minhah. Some other communities do it in 'Arbit and Shahrit, as well as Minhah.

It's forbidden to study Torah. We don't study any Torah. We just read certain sad pieces, like we said Megillat Ekhah we would read, certain sad pieces from the book of Yirmeyah. We also focus on sections in the Gemara that deal with the destruction of the Bet HaMikdash and the tragedies that led up to it. We don't publicly wear Tefillin on Tish'ah BeAb until Minhah. We don't do Birkat Kohanim during Shahrit at all, but we do it during Minhah. As far as work is concerned, it's not the proper day to be working. You're supposed to be focusing on this national mourning, but if there's a great necessity to do work, you do work so you don't lose out on so you don't have a major financial loss. As far as preparing for after the fast, that is not done until after Minhah as well.

There is a Haftarah that we read on the morning of the fast. We don't have a Haftarah on the morning of any of the other fasts, except for Kippur, of course. Kippur is a different story, and we're not comparing Tish'ah BeAb to Kippur or any Kippur is in a class by itself, but as far as Haftarah, Haftarah is said on Tish'ah BeAb morning, but in the Halabi tradition according to the Rambam, there is no Haftarah during Minhah, as opposed to most other Sephardic communities, which, in fact, do say Haftarah in Minhah.

There are other changes in the 'Amidah. You would have to see the special Siddurim for Tish'ah BeAb for those, especially the older Siddurim. They have more of those changes, whereas in the more modern books for Tish'ah BeAb, a lot of those changes have been left out.

Not only everything that we said, but this was a day that was for the entire people. There were special pieces that were translated into Judeo-Arabic, so all men, women, and children would understand what's going on. So, the Haftarah of the morning from Sefer Yirmeyah would be translated into Judeo-Arabic. There were special Kinot that would be said in Judeo-Arabic as well: 'Eset Hannah, 'Eset Yirmeyah, 'Eset Zekharyah, they even had 'Eset al-Zalzalah, so many different things that were said to really get all of the people into the sadness and into the mode and the mood and the focus of the day.

This is what Tish'ah BeAb is about. It's a day full of Minhagim, Minhagim that cause us to think together, come together, and channel our thoughts together in the hopes and the aspirations that this will finally be the end and we'll finally see the rebuilding of the Bet HaMikdash BiMherah.

11.title: Tefillin on Tish'ah BeAb Morning
11.text:
So what about wearing Tefillin on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb? So according to some authorities, Tefillin is not worn at all. These authorities include the Ra'abad, the Maharam MiRothenburg, the Shibbole HaLeket, the Meiri, the Semag, and the Rokeah. And their reasoning is that Tish'ah BeAb is a national day of mourning, so it's comparable to the first day of mourning for a person who lost a close relative. Now if the death and the burial occur on the same day, the mourners do not wear Tefillin on that first day. So they compared Tish'ah BeAb to such a case. So, interestingly, HaRambam writes that there were some Hakhamim that didn't wear the Tefillin Shel Rosh on Tish'ah BeAb.

On the other hand, we have other authorities that don't compare Tish'ah BeAb to the first day of mourning, but rather to the subsequent days of mourning when the mourners do wear Tefillin, and therefore, they do require Tefillin on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb. Amongst those authorities are many Geonim, the Ramban, the Ritba, the Ran, and the Nimmuke Yosef. Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh requires Tefillin on Tish'ah BeAb, but he says that we can fulfill our obligation of Tefillin in Minhah, and therefore he says the custom is not to wear Talet and Tefillin at all for Shahrit, just wear a Talet Katan, and then in Minhah you wear Talet and Tefillin.

But this is an exceptional rule. Normally the rule is to follow the rulings of Maran, but in this case, different customs developed in various Middle Eastern communities. So Ribbi Moshe Galante, he was a rabbi in Yerushalayim in the 17th century, so his custom was to wear Talet and Tefillin at home, read Keri'at Shema with the Talet and Tefillin, and then go to the Bet Keneset afterwards and pray without Talet and Tefillin. And this because he wanted to have Keri'at Shema with Tefillin, Keri'at Shema of Shahrit with Tefillin, and therefore that was his custom.

There were others that wore Talet and Tefillin at home, but they prayed from the beginning of the prayers up until and including the silent 'Amidah. And the reason they did this is because they wanted to have not only Shema with Tefillin, but the 'Amidah with Tefillin as well. And then they took off the Tefillin, they went to the Bet Keneset, they said the Kinot in the Bet Keneset, they heard Sefer Torah, they read Ekhah, and the end of the prayers. So the authorities that record this custom is Ribbi Hayyim Palachi. It's also recorded in a famous Siddur known as Bet 'Obed, which contains many Halakhot. It was a very popular and considered an authoritative Siddur in the 19th century. Ribbi Hayyim Ben Asher Sethon, who wrote a book of the customs of Eress Yisrael known as Eress Hayyim, he also included this as the custom in Eress Yisrael. Ribbi Shem Tob Gagin in his book on customs entitled Keter Shem Tob, also described this as the custom. It was also the custom in Djerba.

What was the custom in Halab? In Halab, most prayed at home with Talet and Tefillin up until and including the silent 'Amidah, and came to the Bet Keneset afterwards for Kinot, as we said, Sefer Torah, Ekhah, and the end of the prayers. But there were those that wore the Tefillin at home only to recite conditionally and Keri'at Shema, and then they came to the Bet Keneset, and they recited the prayers with a Minyan, but without Talet and Tefillin. Nobody wore Talet and Tefillin in the Bet Keneset in Shahrit of Tish'ah BeAb in Halab.

So what about those that do wear Talet and Tefillin in the Bet Keneset? This was the custom of the Kenis known as Bet El, which was a Kenis of Mekubbalim in Yerushalayim, and eventually this spread to other Batte Keneset in Yerushalayim. Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alav HaShalom, promoted this custom, so it really became a prevalent custom in Eress Yisrael. But our tradition is no Talet and Tefillin in the Kenis in Shahrit, only in Minhah.

12.title: From LaMnasseah to Barekhu
12.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. Before we begin, I was informed that a few weeks ago in one of my earlier videos I misspoke and when discussing Birkot HaShahar, inadvertently said Birkat HaMappil when I was when I meant to say Birkat HaMa'abir.

Now, we're going to begin. And before Barukh SheAmar the Hazzan the people say LaMnasseah. Just to point out that we do not say the Pesukim beforehand, we just start with LaMnasseah, we don't say Shiviti. There are those who say that read the LaMnasseah from the shape of a Menorah.

Now, we begin Barukh SheAmar, and it's interesting that most of the time the Hazzanim will pray the Zemirot and Shahrit in Maqam Sigah. Now, while this is not a strong recorded custom such as Minhah of Shabbat where we do Rast and Bayat in Mossa'e Shabbat and so on, it is interesting that most of the Hazzanim do Sigah. And as a matter of fact, when Gabriel Shrem, 'Alav HaShalom, our esteemed late Hazzan who had a lecture series in Yeshiva University recorded our liturgical customs, he did actually demonstrate how to pray the Zemirot in Maqam Sigah, so that would be an indication that that indeed was the prevailing custom.

Now, we begin with Barukh SheAmar, and we stand up for Barukh SheAmar. There are those who have the custom to hold the Sissiyot, two Sissiyot in front of them, and then when they say "Melekh Mehullal BaTishbahot," they'll kiss them and sit down. And of course, there are those who do not say who do not hold the Sissiyot, so it's not a definitive custom one way or the other, it's 'Al Pi HaKabbalah.

We sit down, we're saying the Zemirot, the Hazzan, and the people when they say Ashre, when they say "Poteah Et Yadekha," a lot of them demonstrate, this you see often, not everybody, but most people do that, and it's similar in other Kehillot as well.

Now, we get to VaYebarekh. VaYebarekh David, we stand up at VaYebarekh David, and when we get to the words "VeAttah Moshel BaKol," we have the custom, 'Al Pi HaKabbalah, to give Sedakah. And I long for the days where the Shamash of the Bet Keneset would go around with the Kuppot and the people used to put it in. The diminishing role of the Shamash of the Bet Keneset is a little sad, and we'll discuss it maybe in another video.

We sit down when we say "Attah Hu Ad-onai HaElokim," we sit down, "Asher Baharta BeAbram." Now, we continue with the Shirah. Very important, the Shirah we say the Hazzan says it with Ta'amim, very important. We continue, "Ki LaHaShem HaMelukhah." It's at this point where if there's going to be a switch of Hazzanim, this is where we make the Hazzan for Shahrit gets up and then the Hazzan for the Zemirot sits down. I've seen in one Kenis where they decided to do it at Yosser after the Kaddish, I'm not sure where they got that from, I understand the logic, though that's not our custom. Our custom is "Ki LaHaShem HaMelukhah," that's where we make the switch of the Hazzanim.

Now, we get to the Kaddish, and truth is I'm going to have to dedicate a separate video to the this very special and unique prayer of the Kaddish and all the customs associated with it. Just one point I have to make here, that in our community there is a custom where the Abelim and those who have to say Kaddish in commemoration of a loved one, not only say the Kaddishim which is considered the Kaddishim of the Abelim, Yehe Shelama and 'Al Yisrael, but in addition, they say in Shahrit the two Hassi Kaddishim: the one after Yishtabbah and the one before Ashre after Hazarah. This is the custom. However, it's important that the Hazzan also says the Kaddish. The fact that other people say the Kaddish does not absolve him of his responsibility to say the Kaddish, because he is the Hazzan, he understands what it means to be Mossi Anashim Yede Hobah, and he has that Kavvanah, and so even if there are others, he also must say the Kaddish.

Finally, in Barekhu, we sit down. Our custom is not to make the half-bow, certainly not to stand up, it is found in other communities. In our community Barekhu, we sit, we sit as usual. Shalom.

13.title: Hatarat Nedarim Before the High Holidays
13.text:
Hatarat Nedarim UKelalot, or just Hatarat Nedarim, or more commonly known as Hatarah. Hatarah is the annulment of promises, swears, vows, and something that we customarily do every year before the High Holidays. So what exactly is a Neder? What is Hatarah? When is it done? Who is it done by, and how is it done?

So, a Neder is a promise, it's a swear, it's a vow. It's something that a person generally tells himself he is going to enact to either do something, or more likely, to prevent himself or herself from doing something. That's number one. The Hatarah is the annulment of that vow because that vow basically hinders ourselves from being part and parcel of society, and we do this prior to the High Holidays because we cannot enter the High Holidays and come before God and request forgiveness and request all types of things that we want and need, while our at the same moment, we have basically put up this wall, a stumbling block, to prevent us from being involved wholeheartedly with the world around us and the world of which we live in.

So what would be done? Hakhamim would get together, generally either three or 10 Hakhamim, 10 preferably, if possible, would set up themselves as a tribunal, as a court, and they would appoint one person from the congregants to represent them. This congregant, or Hazzan, or Sheliah Sibbur, or a Hakham himself, would stand with his back to the congregants while facing the tribunal of Hakhamim, like I said, either three or 10, and he would recite the words of the Hatarah, of this annulment. And everybody would just listen silently. The Bet Din, the tribunal, would listen to his words to see what he wants to say and if they're sincere. And the congregants behind him would also have to be silent, because if you have so many people reciting the same words at the same time, some are high, some are low, some are fast, some are slow, the Bet Din, the tribunal, cannot really hear and pay attention. So one person recites on behalf of the entire Kahal. And at the end, the tribunal annul the vow, allow the person to move on.

This is something that is done at three intervals. We do it 40 days prior to Rosh HaShanah, we do it 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah, and we do it 'Ereb Kippur. And in days of old, it was done on those exact dates, but due to societal norms today, it has been changed, and it is done now on the Saturday night prior to each one of those dates. So it would be done the Saturday night prior to 40 days, the Saturday night prior to 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah, and the Saturday night prior to 'Ereb Kippur. And this is done to bring the people together, because it's very hard for people to gather in the mornings, but at night, especially on a Saturday night right after Shabbat, it becomes very, very easy to get together men, women, and children.

In days of old, it was even more difficult for women to be involved, and they, of course, like men and anybody else, have to annul their vows for their prayers to be accepted on the High Holidays. The Hakhamim would actually go to the homes, to the courtyards of the people. Four Hakhamim would go, three would sit as a Bet Din, the fourth Hakham would read the annulment service on behalf of the women, and they would go around from courtyard to courtyard, from house to house, until all the women of the community had the Hatarah done for them.

And this is something that is very, very important that we do it, not just once, okay, or not at all as I'm hearing people today might want to do, but this is something that's important that it's done all three times. It basically sets the tone and gets us to really come to terms with things that we may have promised ourselves out of anger that we should not have promised, and to break down and to finally give in so we could become part and parcel of the society of everybody around us, and hopefully that way, Bore 'Olam could accept our prayers. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

14.title: Shir HaShirim and Facing West at Kabbalat Shabbat
14.text:
So on Friday night, it's customary to read Shir HaShirim, and there are various customs as to when to read Shir HaShirim. Even in Halab, there were various customs of exactly what point in the prayers it was read. Some read Shir HaShirim before Kabbalat Shabbat, right after Minhah, Shir HaShirim, and then they began Kabbalat Shabbat. Others would wait until after Kabbalat Shabbat and recite it before 'Arbit, and yet others recited it after 'Arbit.

So the custom of reciting it right after Minhah, before Kabbalat Shabbat, this custom was recorded by Hakham Moshe Dayan. Hakham Moshe Dayan was a rabbi in Halab in the 19th century. He wrote a commentary on Shir HaShirim, which is called Yashir Moshe, and there he has many Halakhot and customs, and he records the proper custom as to recite Shir HaShirim prior to Kabbalat Shabbat. This is also what is instructed in the Siddur Bet Menuhah. Bet Menuhah was a very famous Siddur in the Middle East. It was very commonly used. It has many Halakhot and Minhagim, and it was popular in Halab as well. Furthermore, the Ben Ish Hai instructs one to recite Shir HaShirim prior to Kabbalat Shabbat.

The custom of reciting it after 'Arbit was very common in Halab because they had many Minyanim on Friday night, because they would start praying from before sunset, and one Minyan after another as the people came, they would form another Minyan. And then when they prayed in the Great Synagogue of Halab, afterwards they would come out and go into a cave known as the cave of Eliyahu HaNabi. They had a tradition that Eliyahu HaNabi had appeared in that cave, and one Minyan after another would go into the cave to read Shir HaShirim together as a Minyan.

Growing up in the community here in Brooklyn, we would read it before Kabbalat Shabbat, like the Ben Ish Hai and Rabbi Dayan, in the wintertime, but in the summertime, we would usually read it before Minhah.

Now reciting Kabbalat Shabbat was instituted by the Mekubbalim. From Maran, all you would say is the Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. Just like every time you have a holiday or Rosh Hodesh, you have a Mizmor, so the Mizmor every Friday night was Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. But the Mekubbalim added those extra pieces in approximately the 16th century. And according to the Mekubbalim, you begin Mizmor LeDavid, the first Mizmor of the Kabbalat Shabbat, at the moment of sunset, not before sunset, meaning even though we have an obligation to have Tosefet Shabbat, to start Shabbat prior to sunset, this Tosefet, this additional time that we have to add is not necessarily does not necessarily have to be accepted verbally. And therefore, if you are not engaging in Melakhah, you're not going to engage in anything that violates Shabbat already from a few minutes before sunset, you don't have to say anything verbally, and therefore you can start Kabbalat Shabbat at sunset. It's not necessary to recite it a few minutes before.

Now the Mekubbalim when they went when they recited and when they recite Kabbalat Shabbat, they go out to the field to recite Kabbalat Shabbat. And when they went out to the field, they faced the west where the sun was setting. So when you recite Kabbalat Shabbat in the Kenis, it was never customary to turn around and face the west. Those that wanted to face the west, if they didn't go out to the field, they went outside of the Bet Keneset into the courtyard in order to face west. In the Kenis, the custom was always to face whatever direction you normally face. This was not only the custom in Halab, it was the custom in other Middle Eastern communities as well: in Morocco, in Yemen, in Tunisia. Even for "Bo'i Khallah," nobody turned around. You face whichever way you were facing. Those that wanted to face west 'Al Pi HaKabbalah, at the very least, went outside of the Bet Keneset to do so.

Now recently, the Hazzan Isaac Cabasso, HaShem Yebarekhehu VeYishmerehu, contacted me, and he was telling me that till today, he still does not turn around for Kabbalat Shabbat, since this was never the custom in our community. When he grew up, nobody turned around, and until today, he doesn't turn around. So he told me that one time he was in a Kenis in the Deal area, and Rabbi Meyer Yedid was also there, and it turned out that the Hazzan Isaac Cabasso and Rabbi Meyer Yedid were the only two people in the Kenis that didn't face west for Kabbalat Shabbat. So after the Salah, somebody went over to Rabbi Yedid and asked him how come he didn't turn around to face west, and his answer was, "Because my father, 'Alav HaShalom, Hakham Yom Tob Yedid, never turned around, and his father never turned around, and I continue the custom of my forefathers."

We also have a report from Hakham Yisshak Tawil. Hakham Yisshak Tawil is alive, HaShem Yebarekhehu VeYishmerehu. His father was Hakham Moshe Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, he was the chief rabbi of Halab, he was the teacher of Rabbi Yedid, he also reported that in Halab nobody turned around for Kabbalat Shabbat.

So between the fact that we're not Mekubbalim, that we don't go out to the field or even to the courtyard, that we don't necessarily recite Kabbalat Shabbat at the moment of sunset—in the winter sometimes we pray, in the summer sometimes we pray earlier, in the winter sometimes till we say Minhah and Shir HaShirim, it's already after sunset, and so on and so forth—so we should continue the established custom of our forefathers, which is not to turn around during Kabbalat Shabbat. Those that wish to face west, they want to do it 'Al Pi HaSod, they should walk out, walk outside into the courtyard, into the outdoors, and face west. And in fact, in some synagogues in our community, the Hekhal is not even in the east, so when they're turning around, they're not even facing west. So all the more so that we should be Mahzir 'Atarah LeYoshnah, to follow Minhag Abotenu.

15.title: From Yosser Or to Yahad Kullam
15.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We're continuing with the Tefilah. We are up to Yosser Or. There are those who have the custom 'Al Pi HaKabbalah when they say the words "Yosser Or" and, in addition, when they say the words "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh," to touch the Tefillin Shel Yad. It's 'Al Pi HaKabbalah. Not everybody has the custom, but we do see it sometimes in our community as well.

For some reason, I was taught and even observed when I was younger that in when they say "Yosser HaMe'orot," they would touch the Tefillin Shel Rosh. And I was looking back at the custom, I couldn't find any source for it. As a matter of fact, I found a reverse source 'Al Pi HaKabbalah where you're not supposed to touch Tefillin Shel Rosh during Shahrit. And I haven't really seen it a lot lately. So, it's a I wouldn't call it a custom, it may have been a mistaken custom. I don't know what to make of it exactly, just wanted to point that out.

When you get to "Me'arba' Kanfot HaAress," there are those who hold up the two Sissiyot that are in front of them. There are those who will take all the four Sissiyot and hold them together. There are those who don't hold them at all. These customs, they run the spectrum, and I don't know if there's any definitive one custom that is found in our community.

The Hazzan recites Keri'at Shema with Ta'amim. When he gets to the Pasuk "VeHarah Af HaShem Bakhem," he says the word "VeHarah" out loud, says the rest of the Pasuk in a whisper, and resumes when he says the words the word "VeSamtem." Recently, I've seen some people begin saying out loud from, and in fact that's how the way it's written in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, after "HaAress HaTobah," will say "Asher HaShem Noten Lakhem." The truth is, when I was growing up, it was always "VeSamtem."

When he completes "Ani HaShem Elokekhem," the Kahal answers "Emet," and the Hazzan says out loud "HaShem Elokekhem Emet." The question came up of whether the Hazzan actually says "Emet" or not, and I've seen it done both ways. But regardless, most of the times they don't even say it, which probably makes more sense. But even when he does say it, he says it very very low, nobody hears it. Never did I hear anybody saying it out loud, although I'm hearing now that there are those that say it out loud. I've personally never heard it. The custom was always to either not say it at all or say it very, very in a very low voice.

Now we get to the 'Amidah. We stand up in, generally, "Tehillot LaEl 'Elyon," "Go'alam." And we turn our to say when we face to say the 'Amidah, if you come with me and bring the camera around here, we face the Hekhal to say the 'Amidah. When we get to the words "Yahad Kullam," we see people going like this to the Kahal. This is a very uniquely Halabi custom. Not I wouldn't say exclusively. I've seen it mentioned also in some Iraqi circles. And it's a very interesting custom, and there's a few reasons given for it.

First of all, when we, when the Halabiyeen do it, we do it while we're going back for the Shalosh Pesi'ot. And the reasons I've seen for this custom: number one, we want to emulate the Mal'akhim when they're Mekabbelim Reshut Zeh MiZeh. So, we emulate the Mal'akhim, the angels, when they're praising Bore 'Olam, so we do the same. A more practical reason is that, you know, sometimes you're sitting when you're praying the 'Amidah, you look behind you, there's somebody behind you, and you I'm not right, I know. I don't know, whatever it is. Here, it's as if we're asking permission from the person behind us to stand in front of him. A third and final reason, which I think is a beautiful reason, is to get the Kahal all BeLeb Ehad with Ahabah, with Ahvah, where we're greeting each other. This way we're praying Tefilah BeSibbur, BeLeb Ehad, and, inshallah, "Titkabbal Tefillatenu BeRasson."

A lot of people, after "Ga'al Yisrael," you'll hear every now and then a few will say "HaShem" out loud, again, an illustration of connecting the Ge'ulah to the Tefilah. Not essential, not required, but something I wanted to point out, we do hear it. Kol Tub.

16.title: The Rosh HaShanah Night Table
16.text:
Rosh HaShanah, the Jewish New Year. As families gather at home on the night of Rosh HaShanah around the table, we begin with Kiddush, commonly known as 'Edut. And 'Edut would be said on the night of Rosh HaShanah, even if on Friday night we would not preempt the Kiddush with Shalom 'Alekhem or Eshet Hayil, rather we would begin immediately with Yom HaShishi if on Shabbat night as I mentioned, or with UBeYom Simhatkhem if on a weeknight.

After Kiddush is where symbolic foods are generally partaken. And in all Sephardic communities, except one, all these symbolic foods are partaken of on both nights of Rosh HaShanah, night one and night two, except for the city of Aleppo, Syria, the city of Halab. In Halab, the Minhag was to only partake of these symbolic food items on the first night.

Now, what are these food items and in what order are they eaten? And if you look in the old Mahzorim, the most common old Mahzor was called Zekhor LeAbraham, it was printed in Livorno, Italy, many editions. And there were of course other Mahzorim printed in Italy, as well as in Vienna, Austria, those were the two main printing presses for Sephardic Mahzorim and Siddurim for all Sephardic communities throughout the world. And if you look in those books, you'll see that the order begins with apples. Now, the book does not tell you whether this is done immediately after Kiddush before Netilat Yadayim and HaMossi, or if it was done after HaMossi. And as such, there were two customs. Each family had their own custom as to when they did this, and either custom is fine. As long as you're following your family's Minhag, you're 100% okay.

So, you start with apples as the book lists. And the reason I'm bringing this up is that if you look in more modern Mahzorim, as well as booklets, pamphlets, sheets that are given out for the holiday, you will see that it lists Temarim, dates first, whereas in the old books it lists Tappuhim first, apples. Question is, why apples first, and why is this the Minhag? And there are two reasons that I will give you. The first reason is based upon the Kabbalah, that Tappuhim is a reference to Hakal Tappuhin Kaddishin, the holy apple orchard, which is a reference to the Shekhinah, to God's divine presence. So we want to begin with God's divine presence.

But a simpler meaning, a meaning that makes more sense and fits in with the ideas and the concepts of the night, is that the apple has a certain appeal to it. When you look at it, it has a beautiful appearance. You go to pick it up, you touch it, you feel it, it feels nice. You lift it up to your face, you're ready to bite into it, but then you see, you know, a very very pleasant aroma. And you bite into it, it has a delicious taste. This is the feeling and the message we're trying to convey on the night of Rosh HaShanah. We want to begin the night with everything positive, both, rather, but in all senses of seeing, feeling, touching, tasting, everything that applies, we want that applied to everything that we have going on with us the entire year. And therefore we begin, we begin with the apple.

Now, another thing about the apple, as we know nowadays we hear children singing, "Dip the apple in the honey." So, is it our Minhag to have apples in honey or apples in sugar? So, according to Kabbalah, sugar is white, and therefore you should have the apple in sugar, whereas honey is darker, and you shouldn't have something dark on Rosh HaShanah. Now, there were families who had it this way, families who had it that way. Keep in mind, sugar was much more easily accessible and a lot less expensive, and that's the main reason people had sugar as opposed to honey. Also, many times honey wasn't actual real honey, and the Hakhamim were afraid that the manufacturers of honey or the sellers of honey were mixing in all different types of things into it, and they basically warned the people to generally not have honey unless you were positive that you actually got it from the beekeeper, from the beehive.

Now, other families didn't have apple at all, but they had something in the apple family, and that was quince. And many families have that till today. They take the quince, they cut it up and they actually cook it with sugar, and they have this, we'll call it a quince jelly or as commonly known in traditional circles, Helu Sfarjel, okay? It's a quince jelly, and that's partaken of instead of actually taking an apple and dipping it into sugar or honey.

So, now that we established that apples are first, what is the order? The Zekhor LeAbraham Mahzor has a page with the entire order of the night of these special symbolic foods, which are commonly known as Berakhot or Berakhiyot, or in Ladino communities as Yehi Rassones. And it begins with Tappuhim, with the apple, with the Karti, leek, Salka, Swiss chard, Tamri, dates, Kara, gourd, Rubya, black-eyed peas, Rimmon, pomegranate, Rosh Kebes, the head of the sheep. In between Rimmon and Rosh Kebes, in this book it mentions Dagim, fish, and there were some communities that did partake of fish, and others that did not. In the Halabi community, fish was not partaken of on the night of Rosh HaShanah.

Now, other than these symbolic foods that we enjoy and partake of, we make sure that we have the Minhag to say the Yehi Rasson before eating these foods. When we move on to HaMossi, if we're having HaMossi before or after the symbolic foods, HaMossi in all four meals of Rosh HaShanah, both nights and both days, HaMossi is dipped in sugar, not in salt.

Another very important fact to remember is that on Rosh HaShanah, we do not eat sour foods. Even the Hida mentions it in the name of the Geonim, that sour foods are not partaken of. We do not have things that are lemony, we do not have things that are vinegary. If you look at the traditional table, in traditional households, you will see there are no pickles, no olives, not even any salad on the table, because salad dressing would generally be lemony. And we want this year to be, as we know it, a sweet new year, a year that bodes well for the entire Jewish nation. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

17.title: Sugar Instead of Honey and Salt
17.text:
So the custom of eating an apple and dipping it in something sweet on the night of Rosh HaShanah began as an Ashkenazic custom and later was adopted by Middle Eastern communities as well. So the original Ashkenazic custom was to dip the apple in honey. However, the general custom in our community is to dip the apple and also the bread when we make HaMossi in white sugar.

Now in certain places at certain times, wine or grape juice was added to the honey, making it unkosher. In other places, other times, ground-up animal bones was added to the sugar, making it unkosher. So whether honey or sugar was used often largely depended on which item was free of added prohibited ingredients.

But beyond that, Ribbi Yisshak Palachi, who was a Turkish authority in the 19th century, he wrote that it's preferable to use white sugar instead of honey on Rosh HaShanah, since kabbalistically, white sugar alludes to Hesed, which is kindness, and honey alludes to Geburah, which is bravery, and he thought that Hesed, kindness, is a more appropriate theme for the holiday of Rosh HaShanah.

Now there are some Mekubbalim that taught that we should also dip the bread in salt prior to dipping it into sugar or honey. And in fact, this was the custom of some individuals in Halab. However, the prevalent custom was to dip in sugar only, meaning sugar instead of salt. And in fact, Hakham Abraham Hamwey, who was born in Halab in the 19th century, wrote that sugar is actually comparable to salt, and according to some, it may be used instead of salt when offering a sacrifice. And therefore he concluded, "Yafeh Minhagam Shel Yisrael Litbol BeRosh HaShanah HaMossi BeSukar BiMkom HaMelah." So the Jewish custom of dipping in sugar instead of salt is a nice and proper custom.

Hakham Abraham Hamwey was also a Mekubbal, and he also promoted kabbalistic practices. Yet here, he affirms the common practice of dipping in sugar instead of salt. So therefore, if your family custom was always sugar instead of salt, there's no need to correct your custom and begin dipping it in salt first. As we said, some have that custom, it was the custom of Yehidim, of a few individuals, but as we said, the prevalent and common practice is dipping in sugar instead of salt.

18.title: The Three Steps and the Halabi Nusah of the 'Amidah
18.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. Where we left off our last video, preparing ourselves for the Tefilah BeLahash, and I just wanted to illustrate how we go, take three steps back and three steps forward before we begin the 'Amidah. As we mentioned, this is done before Shahrit when we are greeting everybody during the words "Yahad Kullam," and in 'Arbit we do it during the Kaddish, "Yehe Shemeh Rabba," we'll get to that when we speak about 'Arbit. Basically, our feet are together, and we start with our left foot going back the length of the foot, one step, two steps, and equaling it out on the third step, and then the reverse, going forward: right foot, and now we begin "Ad-onai Sefatai Tiftah UFi Yagid Tehillatekha."

Now, during the Tefilah BeLahash, I wanted to point out some unique Minhagim regarding the wording in the Berakhot. So, maybe grab a Siddur, so we can review it together, and the differences between our Nusah and other Nushaot, the wording.

I guess we could begin with "Teka' BeShofar Gadol LeHerutenu, VeSa Nes LeKabbess Galuyotenu, VeKabbessenu Yahad Meherah Me'arba' Kanfot HaAress," not always found in other Nushaot. We add the word "Meherah," "Kabbessenu Yahad Meherah." It's accurately reflected in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, and maybe it's an opportunity to say that, to give Hazak UBarukh to the editors, 'Alav HaShalom to Sam Cattan, who had the foresight to put together this beautiful Siddur, and they did a lot of extensive research regarding the Nushaot.

So, we continue in "Hashibah Shofetenu KeBarishonah VeYo'assenu KeBatehillah VeHaser Mimmenu Sarah, Yagon VaAnahah." We add the word "Sarah." "LaMinim VeLaMalshinim," we add the word "VeLaMosrim." It's in parentheses in this book, but we do, we do say it. It wasn't really said when we were kids, but when we saw the Nusah in other Siddurim of the Halabiyeh, and then when the influx of the, I think this is what happened, when the in the '80s when the influx of the Halabiyeh came to our community, they sort of rekindled this very, very nice custom.

We are Hotem this Berakhah, "Shober Oyebim UMakhnia' Minim." This is the way it was, I remember from when I was growing up. I know there's Nushaot Minim, there's Nushaot Zedim. I'm not sure if there's a definitive Halabi custom, but even in the Siddur they printed for the Argentinean community that Rabbi Basri printed, the Sukkat David, it says "Minim," and in other books that we used to use, Ahabat Siyyon, it said "Minim." It's a discussion among the Aharonim. We're not going to get into it now.

"'Al HaSaddikim Ve'Al HaHasidim Ve'Al She'erit 'Ammekha Bet Yisrael," we add the words "Ve'Al Ziknehem." Okay? "Et Semah David 'Abdekha Meherah Tassmiah VeKarno Tarum BiShu'atekha Ki LiShu'atekha Kivvinu VeSippinu," we add the word "VeSippinu." "Shema' Kolenu Ad-onai Elokenu Ab HaRahaman Hus VeRahem 'Alenu," we add that word as well.

"Sim Shalom," let's move on to "Sim Shalom." "Tobah UBerakhah, Hayyim Hen VaHesed, Sedakah VeRahamim." And I think that those are the main differences and the main things we have to pay attention to, and again they're all accurately reflected in the Kol Ya'akob.

We finish the 'Amidah with "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav," also going back three steps, starting with the left foot, right, left, and here when we say "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav," we bow down "'Oseh Shalom" to the left side first, which is different than the "Kara Zeh El Zeh VeAmar," we'll get to that. "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav, Hu BeRahamav Ya'aseh Shalom 'Alenu," and then you if there's nobody directly in front of you or directly behind you, then you can sit down at that point and wait for the Hazarah. Okay, we'll begin next week with the Minhagim of the Hazarah. Kol Tub.

19.title: Customs of 'Ereb Yom Kippur
19.text:
Tizku LeShanim Rabbot Ne'imot VeTobot. Moving from Rosh HaShanah to Yom Kippur, there are numerous Minhagim, and we'll discuss or mention a number of Minhagim that are associated with 'Ereb Yom Kippur, Yom Kippur eve.

First and foremost is Kapparot. Kapparot is the custom of taking a chicken, waving it over a person's head, and in essence moving the sins of the person to the chicken, and thus killing the chicken, getting rid of the sins. Now this is an issue that has been debated in rabbinic circles for many centuries, and even in Halab, even though the majority of the community did do Kapparot, there were always those families that did not do it. And this continues still today with more and more people not doing this, and instead of actually killing a chicken, they would take money and give it to Sedakah, and the Zekhut of the Sedakah would stand for a person in place of actually killing a chicken, which at times may or may not have a need or a reason.

Number two is going to the cemetery on 'Ereb Kippur, which in modern days has extended from Rosh HaShanah until Yom Kippur. You go to the cemetery first and foremost to see that this is where a person's fate is sealed in the negative way if they do not repent and change their ways. So this is a wake-up call by going to the cemetery. Also you go to the cemetery to pray there at the graves of the Saddikim and the Hakhamim that possibly in their merit we may have a certain Zekhut to allow us to live a longer, better life.

Another common custom especially related to the deceased on Yom Kippur is the lighting of candles. This was generally done in the synagogues, and each synagogue had a section of a room or an entire room dedicated to tables filled with either oil lamps or candles, where people would come on 'Ereb Kippur and light those candles in memory of the deceased. Some synagogues still do today, and others have abandoned this Minhag.

Also regarding candles, as we light candles for every Shabbat and every Yom Tob, for Yom Kippur, candles was lit as well, but as per HaRambam, a Berakhah is not recited. Again, according to Minhag Halab, you would not say "LeHadlik Ner Shel Yom HaKippurim." You would just light the candle or the oil wicks without making a Berakhah at all. That's, once again, Minhag Halab.

Finally, we have the Minhag of Minhah on 'Ereb Kippur. Minhah on 'Ereb Kippur is a Minhah that it's not a fast day, but all the men wear Talet and Tefillin. Talet and Tefillin are worn during that Minhah to give the person one extra Zekhut, one extra Missvah before going into Yom Kippur, to possibly that Zekhut of that Missvah of Talet and Tefillin, especially for a person that may have missed out on Talet and Tefillin during the course of the year, this time they'll wear it right before Kippur, and that Missvah will help a person going into Yom Kippur, showing Bore 'Olam that we're reattaching ourselves to the covenant and to the Missvot that Bore 'Olam has given us, and thus gaining us a better future. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot Ne'imot VeTobot.
