20.title: Lesheb BaSukkah and the Hosha'not
20.text:
So, on Sukkot, when we're sitting in the Sukkah, we make the Berakhah of "Lesheb BaSukkah." The Posekim, the word is "Lesheb," not "Lisheb." Some Mahzorim have "Lisheb," our custom is to recite "Lesheb." Our custom dates back at least to 1527, where we find in the Mahzor Aram Soba, it's printed "Lesheb."

There are also those that say "Lesheb" is more grammatically correct, that there's two types of verbs that start with the letter Yod, and some of them when they're in the future tense or in the infinitive tense, you say, for instance you would say "Esheb," "Nesheb." So if you say "Esheb," "Nesheb," then when you do the infinitive, it's "Lesheb." You have other types of, other verbs that start with Yod, like "Yashan," since you say "Ishan," "Tishan," so that's why you say "Lishon." But "Lesheb" is "Lesheb." So that's our custom, we say "Lesheb BaSukkah."

So on the first night of Sukkot, when we recite Kiddush, Lesheb comes before Sheheheyanu. So the custom in Halab was right after Lesheb to sit down, upon reciting "Lesheb BaSukkah," and then Sheheheyanu was recited while sitting down. On the second night of Sukkot, so "Lesheb BaSukkah" comes at the end of Kiddush, after Sheheheyanu. So in such a case, after "Lesheb BaSukkah" you sit down, and then you drink the wine. During the day, the custom was that the entire Kiddush was recited sitting down, and Lesheb is recited at the end after Bore Peri HaGefen and before drinking the wine.

So whenever there's Kiddush on the holiday of Sukkot, even on Shabbat Hol HaMo'ed, Lesheb is recited together with Kiddush, whether it's the night Kiddush or the day Kiddush. It's recited at the end of the Kiddush before drinking the wine. But this is only when you're having Kiddush before a meal with Mossi. But if a person, for instance, has breakfast on the, on Sukkot in the Sukkah, but he's not having HaMossi, he's having Mezonot, or fruits, or vegetables, or other foods, so in such a case he makes Kiddush without Lesheb, since the obligation to recite "Lesheb BaSukkah" only comes if you're having at least two ounces of bread or eight ounces of Mezonot.

Now, when you have a weekday Hol HaMo'ed meal where there's no Kiddush, or Se'udah Shelishit on Shabbat Hol HaMo'ed, so now most would recite Lesheb after HaMossi, before tasting the bread. However, there are some that do it the other way: they would make "Lesheb BaSukkah," sit down, and then make HaMossi and eat the bread.

One more custom for Sukkot, and that's taking out the Sefer Torah for the Hosha'not. So the custom in Halab was to take the Sefer Torah out already from Barukh SheAmar, and put it on the Tebah, and leave it there until it's time to encircle the Tebah for Hosha'not. If the congregation forgot to take it out at Barukh SheAmar, so the next time when they're standing in VaYebarekh David, they take the Sefer Torah when everybody is standing in VaYebarekh David. This is done all seven days of Sukkot with the exception of Shabbat.

Now, on Shabbat, even though it's our custom to recite Hosha'not for Shabbat, but since we don't encircle the Tebah on Shabbat, since we don't have our Lulab, not holding the Lulab, so therefore we don't take out the Sefer Torah, and we recite the Hosha'not from our seats.

21.title: Responses During the Hazarah
21.text:
We are up to the Hazarah. Now in the Hazarah, there are certain times during the Hazarah where the Kahal who is sitting quietly, listening to the Hazzan, are prompted to respond in certain ways.

So, first of all, after Shem HaShem and the end of the Berakhah for the Berakhot of the 'Amidah, we say "Barukh Hu UBarukh Shemo" and "Amen." You might hear some people, after the Hazzan says "Eloke Abraham, Eloke Yisshak VeEloke Ya'akob," you may hear some people saying "'Alehem HaShalom." Not our custom. This is not the Halabi custom to respond in this fashion after we hear these words. Be quiet. When the Hazzan says "Morid HaTal" or "Mashib HaRuah," we do answer "LiBerakhah." When the Hazzan says "Memit UMehayeh UMassmiah Yeshu'ah," we hear, we respond "Kerobah HaYeshu'ah" or "Kerobah HaYeshu'ah LeYisrael."

Now we come to the Nakdishakh, where if you have been standing after the Hazarah, you went back the three steps, and now you're waiting for the Hazzan, you didn't sit down, so you'll go back up the three steps to be ready for the Nakdishakh. Or if you were sitting down, you get up and you walk up three steps back to where you were praying the 'Amidah. We say, our custom is 'Al Pi Kabbalah to recite the "Nakdishakh VeNa'arissakh" together with the Hazzan. Obviously in a lower voice, the Hazzan is the only one who has got his voice totally raised. The first two words usually said a little bit louder, "Nakdishakh VeNa'arissakh," and then but it's said all of the words are said.

When we get to "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" and "Barukh Kebod HaShem MiMkomo" and "Yimlokh," we raise our heels three times. Now, "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" is said at the same— The Hazzan will be saying it at the same time that the Kahal is saying it. This is the custom that I was speaking to Rabbi Harold Sutton, and he told me, indeed, the esteemed Hazzan Mr. Isaac Cabasso does it that way, and Hakham Dahouh does it that way. They don't wait for the Kahal to answer for us and then for them to repeat it again. They say "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" with the Sibbur. That's regarding the Nakdishakh.

When we get to "Barekh 'Alenu," again, you may hear some people saying "Amen" after the phrases of "UBerakhah," "Amen," "LiRvayah," "Amen." Not our custom. This is not our custom, even though you may hear it in other communities.

Move forward in the 'Amidah, we get to "Resseh," you hear people saying "Kohanim BeKhabod," prompting the Kohanim to go up. When the Hazzan says "VeTehezenah 'Enenu BeShubekha LeSiyyon BeRahamim," you may hear some people, it is a custom among some members of our community, and it's a very old custom, to say the word "KeMe'az." "LeSiyyon BeRahamim KeMe'az." And there's interesting reasons for that, I won't go into them now.

Modim DeRabbanan. When the Hazzan says "Modim," we say Modim DeRabbanan, the Kahal. And we'll do a little Hishtahavayah, and we don't, we're not required to stand up. It was never our custom to require people to stand up in Modim DeRabbanan. We say it in a lower voice, a quiet voice. The Hazzan is reciting the entire Modim out loud, unlike other communities that you may see the Hazzan lowers his voice in order not to confuse the people. That's not our custom. The people should have a book and read, a Siddur, and read the Modim DeRabbanan from the Siddur. The Hazzan says "Kol HaHayyim Yodukha Selah," the people respond "Barukh Hei Ha'Olamim."

And then we stand up after "HaTob Shimkha ULekha Na'eh LeHodot," we stand up for the Kohanim. And the Hazzan, if there's more than one Kohen, the Hazzan will say the word "Kohanim," and that will prompt the Kohanim to say the Berakhah. And after the Berakhah, you know after everybody says "BeAhabah," they say the first word BeKol Ram, "Yebarekhekha," and then the Hazzan will begin with Shem HaShem. If there's only one Kohen, obviously the Hazzan can't say "Kohanim," you'll have someone in the Sibbur say "Emor," prompting the Kohen to begin the Berakhah. He begins the Berakhah, but he does not say "Yebarekhekha." The Hazzan starts "Yebarekhekha," and the response comes from this Kohen.

There's a very nice custom in other communities, not our community, to gather, father gathers his children around and puts the Talet over their heads. I'm sure at some point Morris Arking will give an interesting perspective on how this custom developed in other communities, the reasons and so on, but it is not our custom. Beautiful custom, not our custom. So better not to modify and change customs, and therefore we shouldn't be doing it. The Kohanim come down from the Tebah, we don't tell them "Hazak UBarukh," we don't shake their hand, like other communities may do. I've seen it in other communities, is not our custom.

A final word regarding Nakdishakh, we never sing Nakdishakh on a weekday unless there's a Farah in the Kenis. If you have or a holiday or 'Ereb, if you're saying, if you're not saying Yehi Shem, there's no business singing the Nakdishakh. If you don't sing Nakdishakh, Torah Sibbur, and then you have the regular Tahanun. It's very important to remember. So, thank you. Kol Tub.

22.title: The Shabbat Morning Kiddush
22.text:
Shabbat mornings, after we finish prayers and we return home, before we eat our meal we make Kiddush. The question is, how different is this Kiddush from the Friday night Kiddush? Friday night Kiddush has two Berakhot and we stand, whereas the Shabbat morning Kiddush only has one Berakhah and we sit down. So the most important thing to know here is our Minhag is Friday night we stand for Kiddush and Shabbat during the day we sit down for Kiddush.

Now, what is the text of the Kiddush? And has this text changed over time? Are there different variations in different families, different words added, different Pesukim added or deleted? So it's interesting that we don't have any direct source from Halab itself as to what the exact Kiddush was over there. But based upon variant Siddurim that were used, we see that different types of Kiddush formulas were made by different families, especially depending if they were more rabbinic families, more kabbalistic families, and that was the Kiddush that was more prevalent within their households.

For example, nowadays, for most of us, if we look at a quote-unquote Kiddush book, we'll see that the Kiddush is comprised of a number of paragraphs, the first one being "Mizmor LeDavid Ad-onai Ro'i Lo Ehsar," followed by "Im Tashib," followed by "VeShameru," and then Pasuk of "'Al Ken Berakh," "Sabri Maranan," and Birkat HaGefen. But if we look at the older Siddurim, we'll see that this "Mizmor LeDavid Ad-onai Ro'i Lo Ehsar" does not appear in every one of the Siddurim. And when it does appear, it appears as a section prior to Kiddush, and even prior to actually holding the Kiddush cup in hand. And after Mizmor LeDavid, other Pesukim and other verses from Zohar and other sources would be recited before actually holding the cup and beginning the Kiddush. So it seems that this addition of Mizmor LeDavid is a later addition.

If we look in a common Siddur that was in our community for many, many years, which was known as Tefilat Yeshurun, Tefilat Yeshurun the Kiddush does not have Mizmor LeDavid whatsoever. Rather, it begins with just "Im Tashib," then "VeShameru," "'Al Ken," and "HaGefen." And that's what many families do till today. There are many, many people that skip Mizmor LeDavid altogether.

Now, as far as saying "Im Tashib," even the older Siddurim, the "Im Tashib" was in a smaller print than "VeShameru." So "VeShameru" seems to be the larger print and the more prevalent item to be said. So there are those that I've heard over the course of time that don't even say "Im Tashib," they say "VeShameru," "'Al Ken Berakh," and "HaGefen."

But there are those families still that add other Pesukim. And if you look in the older Siddurim, you'll find that different Siddurim have different Pesukim added after "VeShameru," before going into "'Al Ken Berakh." You'll have those that begin with "Zakhor Et Yom HaShabbat LeKaddesho, Sheshet Yamim," etc., etc. And there are others that show a Kiddush for, believe it or not, for Se'udah Shelishit, which they use those Pesukim for the regular morning Kiddush, which have to do with the Man: "VaYomer Moshe Ikhluhu HaYom Ki Shabbat Hu LaAd-onai, HaYom Lo Timssa'uhu BaSadeh," etc., etc. And till today I've heard many families that use those Pesukim.

So each person should know what is the Minhag of their family and adhere to that when saying Kiddush for the day. At the very least you know you have to say the Pesukim of "VeShameru," followed by "'Al Ken Berakh," and Bore Peri HaGefen.

Now, there's one more thing that some people do add in the Halabi community, and they'll say, "'Al Ken Berakh Ad-onai Yom HaShabbat VaYkaddeshehu," and then they add two more words: "BiKdusha Rabba." So they say, "'Al Ken Berakh Ad-onai Yom HaShabbat VaYkaddeshehu BiKdusha Rabba," or "BeKiddusha Rabba," with the great Kiddush, which means the Kiddush of the daytime. And those two words are not printed in any of the extant Siddurim, but this is a oral tradition in many families from Halab to add those two words before saying "Sabri Maranan" and going into Bore Peri HaGefen. So once again, in Halab, various Minhagim existed within different homes for Kiddush of Yom Shabbat, and each person should adhere to their Minhag.

23.title: Folding the Talet on Shabbat
23.text:
So in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran prohibits folding on, folding clothing on Shabbat, since it's a form of Metakken, fixing, since it's done to prevent and remove wrinkles. However, Maran allows one to fold clothing if he doesn't fold it on the actual folds, the way it's normally folded. If he folds it not on the folds, Maran allows it.

So based on this, there are those that— They don't fold it on the crease? That they don't fold it on the crease. According to Maran, you shouldn't fold it on the crease. You fold it not on the crease. You could fold it if it's not on the crease. So based on that, there are those that fold their Talet only not on the crease. They won't fold it on the crease on Shabbat.

Now although the general rule is that we follow the ruling of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, in this case, the custom of Halab was to be lenient and to actually fold the Talet on the creases, to fold it the normal way. And this is based on the opinion of the Kol Bo, one of the Rishonim that Maran himself quotes in his longer work known as the Bet Yosef. Now according to the Kol Bo, our folding that we do in our times is different than the folding that they did in the times of the Talmud, because in the times of the Talmud, they would actually actively work to remove the wrinkles. We just fold it. So if you just fold it on the creases and you're not doing anything active to try to remove the wrinkles, then it's permissible. So even though Maran doesn't rule like the Kol Bo, our custom is like the Kol Bo, and we fold the, we fold our Shabbat, we fold our Talet on Shabbat in the normal way.

This custom was recorded by Ribbi Hayyim Attieh. Ribbi Hayyim Attieh lived in the 18th century in Halab, and he wrote a book Orhot HaHayyim, and it's recorded in his book Orhot HaHayyim. It's also recorded by Ribbi Eliyahu Hamwey, who lived in the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century. He records this custom in his book Peh Eliyahu. It's also recorded by Ribbi Hayyim Menasheh Sethon. His book is Eress Hayyim, and it's actually a book of customs of Eress Yisrael. It's not a book of the customs of Halab, but he records it there as the custom of Eress Yisrael. We also find it recorded by Ribbi Yisshak Palachi in his book Yafeh LaLeb. He was an authority from Turkey in the 19th century.

So therefore, our custom of folding our Talet the regular way on Shabbat, on the creases, it's a valid custom, it's based on halakhic sources, and one is not obligated to follow Maran's opinion in this exceptional case.

24.title: Tahanunim, Nefilat Appayim and VaYa'abor
24.text:
Back from Yerushalayim, we have completed the Hazarah and now we are beginning to say the Tahanunim. Now there are days during the year, like Rashe Hodashim, Rosh Hodesh, is a Farah BiKnis, Berit Milah, there's a list in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob where we skip the Tahanunim and go straight to the Yehi Shem.

One point regarding that, there is one day, it's listed, but there is one day that's unique to the Halabi community and that's the 13th day of Sivan, which we commemorate Nes Musan, the miracle of Musan. There are two versions as to what exactly happened, they both involved the famous Rabbi Mordekhai Labaton, 'Alav HaShalom. So that's unique to our community.

Also to note that Bar Missvah is listed on our, on this list. It is the custom in our community to say Yehi Shem if there's a Bar Missvah in the Kenis. Wasn't always the custom. Bar Missvah didn't necessarily prompt the exemption of Tahanunim, but nonetheless that is the custom today.

So if we're skipping Tahanunim or if we say Tahanunim and we go straight to Yehi Shem, I just wanted to note that the Yehi Shem follow the Siddur: "Yehi Shem," "Me'Attah Ve'Ad 'Olam," "MiMizrah Shemesh," "Ad-onai Adonenu," three Pesukim. We do not add the Pasuk "Ram 'Al Kol Goyim," which you find in other Siddurim, that is not our custom.

We begin saying the Tahanunim with Ana, the Viddui, and the Hazzan is saying it out loud. When he gets to "Ashamnu, Bagadnu," the alphabetical order of the 'Avonot, that he says BeLahash, he says quietly. There are other communities which do differently. The custom in our community has always been to say it quietly and resume, the Hazzan resumes saying it loud when he gets to "VeSarnu MiMissvotekha Mishpatekha."

Then we get to El Erekh Appayim. Again, the Nusah in the Siddur is our custom. We don't add the phrase "Tizkor HaYom LeZera' Yedidekha Kemo SheHoda'ta Le'Anav MiKedem," we say straight "Gedullat Rahamekha VaHasadekha Hoda'ta Le'Anav MiKedem," followed by the Yag Middot, VaYa'abor, which we bow down a little bit, we say VaYa'abor.

And now we begin with the portion that's called Nefilat Appayim, "Rahum VeHannun," followed by LeDavid. Now we sit down for this, and I have to say that when I was growing up, I don't remember the Hazzan ever sitting down. He used to stay at the Tebah and say it from the Tebah. The last 25, 30 years or so, the Hazzan, I've seen more often than not the Hazzan sits down. But I just wanted to point out that I don't recall that that was the custom.

Now, there's a big issue regarding LeDavid, because this is called Nefilat Appayim. Nefilat Appayim means we bend down, we put our arm, we put our head in our arm, the left arm, and we recite LeDavid. Now, Nefilat Appayim was Halakhah and it was a widespread custom. It wasn't until the Kabbalists, for their own, for the reasons that they understood that it shouldn't be done putting the head down into the arm. It started early, but the Ben Ish Hai was the one who really pushed the idea that nobody should change what they're doing, they should sit in the regular fashion, and not change, and not fall down on their arm. And I guess that spread, and you don't see it very often, although many Hakhamim and many pious laymen used to make and still make Nefilat Appayim.

'Alav HaShalom, our chief rabbi, Hakham Ya'akob Kassin, which was interesting because he was a Kabbalist and yet nonetheless he did do Nefilat Appayim. Abe Shama, 'Alav HaShalom, Abba Latash, be- Rabbi Shama, and other Anshe Ma'aseh, they do Nefilat Appayim. I heard that in Argentina, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar did Nefilat Appayim. He didn't insist that the whole Kahal do what he does, although he was very particular about doing it, and his children till today do Nefilat Appayim.

The Nefilat Appayim, like we said, is said by the Hazzan quietly. He resumes saying, resumes his regular voice when he says the Pasuk "Ad-onai Eloke Yisrael, Shub MeHaron Appekha VeHinnahem 'Al HaRa'ah Le'Ammekha," "Abinu Malkenu," of course that is said out loud. If it's a regular day, not Sheni VaHamishi, you go to Yehi Shem, then Kaddish.

If we're doing Tahanunim, we get up on Sheni VaHamishi, and the custom in our community is to alternate: Mondays Anshe Emunah, Thursdays Tamahnu MeRa'ot. Now, we're not here looking for shortcuts, this is a very old custom, it's even the Bet 'Obed even mentions it, even though that's not the custom of the Bet 'Obed, but he does mention that the existence of such a custom. I heard that on 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah in Argentina, in the Halabi community, they do both on Mondays and Thursdays, and even the Halabiyeh that came in the '80s, there are those who do both on Mondays and Thursdays, 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah, but that's not the prevailing custom in our community.

At the end of the Tahanunim, we have the final VaYa'abor. Now this wasn't printed in the Siddurim we were using when we were growing up, so you didn't hear it in all the Minyanim. It wasn't until Kol Ya'akob came out and other Siddurim that print this last VaYa'abor. But even if it wasn't printed, always like the first Minyan of Shaare Zion, all the Anshe Ma'aseh, all the people, the Hakhamim, the Gabba'im that were particular about the customs, always said this VaYa'abor. I know there's maybe a couple of Hakhamim in our community which insist not to say it, but nonetheless we do say it.

I don't know the source, but a possibility could be I looked in Mahzor Aram Soba, they don't have Tamahnu MeRa'ot or Anshe Emunah, they have a different system of Tahanunim, but they do have VaYa'abor in the beginning, and right before Kaddish they have another VaYa'abor. Possibly that that's an old custom that kept on, that prevailed till our days.

Following that, like you said, we say, even the days when we say Tahanunim, we say Yehi Shem and then we say Kaddish. Shalom UBerakhah.

25.title: Shir HaShirim on 'Ereb Shabbat
25.text:
Shir HaShirim. Friday night, the Halabi community has a Minhag to recite Shir HaShirim. So we'll delve into a few different points: firstly, why is Shir HaShirim recited, secondly, when is Shir HaShirim recited, and thirdly, who is it recited by and how?

So first let's start with the first thing as to why Shir HaShirim is recited. So initially, the Hakhamim talk about Shir HaShirim in connection to Hag HaPesah. Hag HaPesah has to do with the Ge'ulah, with redemption, and Shir HaShirim talks about that same Ge'ulah. And since the Ge'ulah is mentioned in Shabbat, and we were saved from slavery in Egypt in Hag HaPesah, and Hag HaPesah is mentioned here, so we repeat this Shir HaShirim, or recite rather, Shir HaShirim on Lel Shabbat to remind us if Bene Yisrael observes two Shabbatot, or at least one more Shabbat, because according to tradition one was already observed by all of 'Am Yisrael, if a second one is observed by all of 'Am Yisrael, then the entire nation will be redeemed. That's reason number one.

Reason number two, which is the more commonly heard reason that we hear today, is that Shir HaShirim is Kodesh Kodashim, all right, and which is the most Holy of Holies. As we know, we refer to Shabbat as Shabbat Kodesh, and since this is Kodesh and that is Kodesh, the proper time to recite Shir HaShirim is on Shabbat. For that reason, the Halabi community recites Shir HaShirim every 'Ereb Shabbat.

Now, when on 'Ereb Shabbat is it recited? First let's talk about Halab and what was done over there for centuries. Shir HaShirim was initially recited in Halab after 'Arbit. After 'Arbit was finished, people would enter the Me'arah of the Saddikim, the cave where the Hakhamim were buried, and they had a tradition that Eliyahu HaNabi appeared over there, and they would recite Shir HaShirim over there.

Now, there were other Minhagim that developed in Halab as to what point to recite Shir HaShirim, and those are the other Minhagim that obviously carried forth to America and to the other Halabi diasporas throughout the world, because obviously we do not have this cave of Saddikim to go recite Shir HaShirim in. So there were three Minhagim. There's Minhag number one, that was recited between Minhah and Kabbalat Shabbat, and Minhag number two, that it would be recited towards the end of Kabbalat Shabbat, so technically we would say Mizmor LeDavid, Lekha Dodi, Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat, Bameh Madlikin followed by Kaddish, then Shir HaShirim would be recited, and then the second Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat would be said. So those were the two main Minhagim. The third Minhag, a Minhag that seems to have developed much later, and possibly even outside of Halab, and that is to recite Shir HaShirim prior to Minhah. So you would say Shir HaShirim, and then Minhah, then Kabbalat Shabbat, then 'Arbit. So these are the three Minhagim. All three Minhagim have been practiced in the United States as well, as well as in other Halabi communities.

Now, who says Shir HaShirim? As opposed to other communities where just Hazzanim would individually recite one Perek at a time, in other words one Hazzan would recite one entire Perek, then another Hazzan would recite another Perek, and so on and so forth until all eight Perakim would be completed, the Halabi community has a Minhag for the entire Kahal, the entire congregation, to recite Shir HaShirim with its Ta'amim in unison.

Now, there's another Minhag that you'll see in some synagogues that developed, that they would basically have a give and take with Shir HaShirim, with one side of the Kenis, the people would recite Pasuk A, and the other side of the Kenis would then respond with Pasuk B, followed by the initial side going to C, the next side D, back and forth like that, a give and take. That is not the real Minhag, that's something that was developed in different congregations, it seems, by different Hazzanim or different Hakhamim to get the people more involved cause they may have been slacking off. But the real Minhag, and that Minhag prevalent throughout all our congregations is for the entire congregation, both old and young, to learn the Ta'amim and to recite Shir HaShirim together from beginning to end.

Shir HaShirim is completed, the Hakham or Hazzan would recite the final prayer of the Shir HaShirim, Ribbon Kol Ha'Olamim, and Kaddish would not be recited after that, rather we go straight into either what we talked about before, either Minhah or into Kabbalat Shabbat or either into the Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat, the second one. And that's the Minhag of Shir HaShirim.

26.title: Mourners Reciting All the Kaddishim
26.text:
So there are several questions that come up regarding mourners and the reciting of Kaddish. One of the questions that comes up is which Kaddishim should the mourners say? Now, in most communities the custom is that the mourners only recite Kaddish 'Al Yisrael and Kaddish Yehe Shelama. However, in Halab and in Baghdad as well, the custom was to recite all of the Kaddishim in the prayers except for Titkabbal. Titkabbal was recited by the Hazzan alone, but all the other Kaddishim were recited by the mourners, including Hassi Kaddish.

The Ben Ish Hai in his responsa Rab Pe'alim wrote the following: "In these places, the custom is that the Hazzan only recites Kaddish Titkabbal, and the other Kaddishim, even the Kaddish after Yishtabbah, is recited by the mourners instead of the Hazzan." So from here we learned that not only do the mourners recite all of the Kaddishim except for Titkabbal, but that they recite these Kaddishim instead of the Hazzan, meaning that the Hazzan is not obligated to recite these Kaddishim with them.

And the Ben Ish Hai went on to explain further that even though the only Kaddish that is really for the mourner is the Kaddish before 'Alenu LeShabbeah, in any case, it is customary in all the congregations of Israel that mourners recite all of the Kaddishim that are the obligation of the congregation on behalf of the congregation. And with this, there is benefit and enjoyment to the soul of the deceased, because the mourner is saying Kaddish on behalf of the congregation. And this Missvah that the mourner does by saying Kaddish on behalf of the congregation protects the soul of the deceased and brings the soul great benefit.

This custom was also recorded as the custom of Halab by Hakham Yosef Sha'yo Abadi, 'Alav HaShalom, who was born in Halab in 1895, as he wrote: "The Kaddishim of the whole prayer are recited by the congregation in memory of the deceased, but Kaddish Titkabbal is recited by the Hazzan alone." He also wrote explicitly, "The mourners recite all of the Kaddishim except for Titkabbal."

So all of this is about Kaddish, but what about Barekhu when Barekhu follows Kaddish? So in the early source that records the custom of reciting Kaddish in memory of the deceased, a Midrash is quoted about Rabbi 'Akiba who met a person who already died, but came back to this world. He told Rabbi 'Akiba that he needed his own son to recite Barekhu or Kaddish so that the people will answer "Barukh Ad-onai HaMeborakh Le'Olam Va'Ed" and "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh" in order to save his soul in the next world.

Furthermore, Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin wrote in his work known as Keter Shem Tob that the mourners recite the Kaddishim before 'Alenu LeShabbeah in Shahrit and 'Arbit since those Kaddishim are followed by Barekhu, and by saying these Kaddishim, he will lead the congregation to answer both "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh" and also "Barukh Ad-onai HaMeborakh Le'Olam Va'Ed," which is a tremendous merit, like the Gemara taught that the son brings merit to his father.

So our custom is that the mourners recite all of the Kaddishim except for Titkabbal instead of the Hazzan, and when there is Barekhu, the mourners also lead Barekhu. All of this is based on the sources that we quoted, including the Ben Ish Hai, Hakham Yosef Sha'yo Abadi, the Midrash quoted by the Or Zarua', and the Keter Shem Tob. And this was still the custom in our community when I was growing up in the 1970s and '80s, and it's only recently that there are some that want to change our custom. However, our custom is legitimate, and therefore we should not change it, like our Rabbis taught: "Minhag SheAsu Abotekha, Al Teshanneh Oto."

27.title: Taking Out the Sefer Torah on Weekdays
27.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the Tahanunim, we've said Yehi Shem and Kaddish, and on Monday and Thursday, Sheni VaHamishi, we take out the Sefer Torah. When we take the Sefer Torah out, the Hazzan immediately begins saying the Pasuk, "Gaddelu LaAd-onai Itti UNeromemah Shemo Yahdav." We do not have the custom to say El Erekh Appayim, etc., those two short paragraphs beginning with those words. You'll find them in other Siddurim, they're not printed in Kol Ya'akob because it's not our custom to say it.

The Mesader has invited, honored someone to open the Hekhal, that's called Petihah, and someone else to carry the Sefer, called Gilyan, and as the Hazzan begins and the Kahal joins in, "Romemu," he's opening the Hekhal, and he opens the Sefer Torah a little bit just to make sure it's in the right place, closes the Sefer, and as the Pasuk, "Se'enah URe'enah Benot Siyyon BaMelekh Shelomo," is recited, he takes the Sefer out, gives it to the person carrying it closed. That person will then open it, right hand on the right side, left hand on the bottom, he holds it close to his body, walks down the right side of the— his right, he's facing the Kahal, his right, straight to the Tebah, and while he's walking, the rest of the Pesukim are being said, culminating in the Pasuk, "Ad-onai Hafess LeMa'an Sidko Yagdil Torah VeYa'dir." He puts it straight on the Tebah.

Our custom is not to hold it and then turn around 360 degrees to show everybody. That's not our custom. It's found in other Kehillot, that's not the Halabi custom. We put it straight on to the Tebah.

Now the Ba'al Kore will come up, and it's very important that the person carrying the Sefer does not leave the Tebah until the Ba'al Kore comes up. We never leave the Sefer Torah unattended, not for a second. It's not Kabod. The Ba'al Kore comes up and he says, "Kohen Ha'Oleh Ya'amod BeKhabod." And if there's no Kohen, and even if he knows there's no Kohen, he'll nonetheless turn to the Kahal and say, "Yesh Kan Kohen?"... "En Kan Kohen, Ya'amod Yisrael BiMkom Kohen." Similarly if there's no Levi, he will say "Ya'amod Kohen BiMkom Levi." And then followed by Shelishi: "Shelishi Ha'Oleh Ya'amod BeKhabod," not Yisrael. We say, we call this 'Aliyah, 'Aliyat Shelishi, even though obviously it's a Yisrael that's going up. It's called Shelishi. We know when the Mesader invites somebody, he says "BeKhabod Shelishi," or when you sell the 'Aliyot at the High Holidays you say 'Aliyat Shelishi, that's what we call it.

Before he makes the Berakhah, "Asher Bahar Banu," there are a number of varying customs. Some have the custom to say "Ad-onai 'Immakhem," and the Kahal responds "Yebarekhekha HaShem," and then they say Barekhu. Some have the custom to say "HaShem 'Immakhem." Some have the custom not to say it altogether and to say Barekhu straight. Some have the custom to say "Rabbanan Barekhu." Various customs. I don't know if there's a definitive clear-cut consensus as to what the Minhag was in Halab, or maybe there were multiple Minhagim possibly in Halab as well. There are Aharonim which deal with the different various customs, Hesed LaAlafim, the Kaf HaHayyim brings it. Maybe we'll make a separate video regarding that.

Even in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, differences of opinion. The latest edition doesn't have "HaShem 'Immakhem," starts with "Rabbanan Barekhu." The earliest edition I saw in 1985 has "HaShem 'Immakhem" and no Rabbanan. Joey Mosseri told me that the only Siddur that was printed in the last few hundred years in Syria, was printed in Halab, 1915, 'Olat HaShahar, which indeed has "Ad-onai 'Immakhem," and without Rabbanan, just Barekhu. We'll expand on that at another opportunity.

The Hazzan after the Berakhah, the Ba'al Kore, he says "Amen" a little louder than the Kahal because it also helps him get the right tone to begin the Keri'ah. After Shelishi is finished, he says Kaddish, and immediately the Hazzan begins Ashre, LaMnasseah, UBa LeSiyyon, and Kaddish Titkabbal, and only then do we return the Sefer. That is our custom. You may see differently in other Kehillot, other communities. Our custom is to wait till after Kaddish Titkabbal to return the Sefer.

The same one that brought it out returns it. He goes to the Tebah and now he's going the other direction, right, back to the Hekhal, and he returns it while the Sefer is open. That is our custom. That has been our custom. I've seen, much to my surprise, the last 20 or so years, changes and Kehillot in the Halabi community bringing it back closed. Our custom is bring it open, and it's logical, because we don't do the, like I said, the Hakamah where we show it to everybody. So therefore, the ones who saw the Sefer Torah with the writing open are on this side of the Kenis. And when we take it back, we give the opportunity and the people on the other side of the Kenis to see the writing. Or if women came late, for instance, and they want to see the Sefer Torah open, that is the opportunity. So it's a logical custom.

The reason it was changed probably was the influence of Rabbenu Yosef Hayyim, the Ben Ish Hai, who was much more influential in the last generation in Halab, who gives kabbalistic reasons as to why the Sefer Torah should be closed. But we have ample sources, and it's brought down in Derekh Eress, Sefer Derekh Eress as well. I have other sources which we won't get into now, but we bring back the Sefer open.

After it goes back to the Hekhal, the one who's carrying it closes it right before he gets to the Hekhal, gives it to the one who has Petihah closed, he puts it back in the Hekhal, we close the Hekhal, and the Hazzan begins Tefilah LeDavid. Shalom UBerakhah.

28.title: The Extra Hanukkah Light of the Sefaradim
28.text:
The holiday of Hanukkah. Hanukkah is a time that we all easily recognize as a time for lighting the lights of the Hanukkah. And there's a very interesting and distinct Minhag that was practiced and is still practiced by the Sephardic families of Aleppo, Syria.

Now you may wonder, what do I mean by the Sephardic families? Isn't everybody from Aleppo Sephardic? But in actuality, the answer is no. Every community in the Middle East had indigenous Jews, Jews that were living there going back many, many centuries prior to the expulsion of Jews from Spain in 1492, and those were the indigenous Jews in those cities and countries, and they were known as Musta'arab or Musta'arabim. And when the Sephardic Jews, or the Spanish Jews that is, arrived from Spain, those Jews were known as Sefaradim. And so now Sefaradim and Musta'arabim began to merge into one community, one congregation. But in most places they remained as separate congregations. It took quite a few decades and even centuries for them to merge into one.

Now here's the interesting thing: The Sephardic Jews of Aleppo, Syria, have a very unique custom, and that is a custom of kindling an extra light on each night of Hanukkah. So as we know, while the general Jewish populace will light on the first night of Hanukkah one light for the Missvah plus one light for the Shamash or Shamosh, depending on how you pronounce it, and concluding and or adding each night an extra light for the next night of Hanukkah, concluding on the final night with eight for Hanukkah plus one for the Shamash, the Sephardic Jews, the Spanish Jews specifically of Aleppo, would light an extra light each night. That means on the first night they had actually three lights, and on the final night they had 10 lights. First one would be the light for the Missvah, second one for the Shamash, and then the third, an extra light.

So what's behind this extra light that the Spanish Jews of Aleppo light? Three reasons have been what I've been taught, told, and things that I've researched into to find out. The three reasons go as follows:

Reason number one: When the Jews were expelled from Spain, they didn't know where they would end up, or if they would end up any place at all. And so when they finally got to Aleppo, they felt that this itself was a miracle, and it was Hanukkah time, so they decided to light an extra light to commemorate their personal miracle.

Second reason given is that when these Spanish Jews arrived to Aleppo, they weren't easily accepted into the community. In other words, the Musta'arabi Jews did not want to accept the Sefaradi Jews, and there was a bitter conflict between them whether to let them in or not let them in, and finally they were accepted at Hanukkah time, and because of that they saw this as again a special miracle for them, and they decided to light an extra light.

Third reason being that the Jews that left Spain tended to be very, very wealthy Jews. And keep in mind that in those days, when the sun went down, your day was over, you had no more lights. But since these were wealthy Jews, they had the oil, they had the wax, they had what were necessary to illuminate their homes on those long winter nights when the sun went down early and it was dark outside. So they would always have a light in their house, a light in their window. And so now Hanukkah would come, and what would distinguish them from the rest of the populace? Since everybody else, all the other Jews, would now be lighting lights, how would people know that we are, you know, special Jews, we are wealthy Jews, you know, and this is a custom that we've always followed throughout the year of lighting a light during the winter months or during the long, dark nights? So they decided that on Hanukkah they would continue next to the Hanukkah lights to light an extra light each night to set them apart.

And these are the three reasons given for this particular and peculiar Minhag of the Spanish Jews of Aleppo. Now this is a Minhag that has been followed for centuries by these families, and it seems that unfortunately in recent decades it may have been forgotten by some. So far, I'm very well aware that this Minhag is practiced by the following families, and I'm sure there are many more. And if you haven't followed it, and I mention your name, ask around in your family. Find out if this is your Minhag, and if you should revive it. So I know of the Abadi family, the Attieh family, the Paredes family, the Betesh family, the Braha family, the Cattan or Kattan family, the Dwek family, Haber, Harari, Labaton, Laniado, what else, the Michaans, Sha'yos, Abadis, Suttons, Tawils, and quite a few other families. But these are the ones that easily come to mind right now.

So this is a beautiful custom. It's a custom that sets you apart, shows your children that we know who we are. We know our lineage, our genealogy, and this is something that also shows that within Halab, even though people look at it as one community and one people, there were in fact separate communities and separate people that came from different points of origin. And once again, we keep in mind the miracle of the holiday of Hanukkah, that we as a nation have been able to persevere different persecutions, and even when we were set apart, we still shone through like the lights of Hanukkah.

29.title: Never Skipping a Kaddish
29.text:
So, on the previous video, we quoted from the Ben Ish Hai's responsa about Kaddish in his responsa Rab Pe'alim, where he described the custom in the Middle East that the mourners recite all of the Kaddishim, including Hassi Kaddish instead of the Hazzan. Now, my article that accompanied that video, and that also accompanies this video as well, also refers to what the Ben Ish Hai wrote about this custom in his work known as the Ben Ish Hai.

So, in the Ben Ish Hai, he raised some problems that are caused by mourners who are unaware of the fact that when they're reciting Kaddish instead of the Hazzan, that they're reciting the Kaddish on behalf of the entire congregation. He also raised issues about certain mourners that don't pronounce the words properly. So, he didn't change the entire custom like he did with other customs for various reasons, but here he just changed the custom with regards to Kaddish after Yishtabbah on Shabbat and Yom Tob. Up until then, the mourners also recited that Kaddish instead of the Hazzan in Baghdad, so he instituted that the Hazzan should recite that Kaddish on Shabbat and Yom Tob, but the mourners can recite the other Kaddishim, except for Kaddish Titkabbal, meaning that they still recited Hassi Kaddish, including the Hassi Kaddish after Yishtabbah on weekdays.

In our community, the Hazzan sings that Kaddish on Shabbat and Yom Tob, so the mourners don't recite it anyway, meaning that even though it's customary for mourners to recite Hassi Kaddish, the exceptional case is when the Hazzan is going to sing the Kaddish for any reason. In that case, he's singing the Kaddish in order to enhance and beautify the prayers, so beautifying of the prayers takes precedence over the mourners reciting Hassi Kaddish. If the Hazzan feels that the mourners are not reciting the Kaddish properly, they're not pronouncing it properly, then he should say it along with them so that it's said properly, and that applies to all of the Kaddishim, not only Hassi Kaddish. All of the Kaddishim of the prayers must be recited properly.

So what if there are no mourners present to recite Kaddish? Should we just skip Kaddish? Do we skip 'Al Yisrael? Do we skip Yehe Shelama? So, our custom is that we never skip any of the Kaddishim. This is based on the teachings of the Arizal, who wrote that we have to have a certain amount of Kaddishim every day. According to the Arizal, we must recite 12 Kaddishim every day: six in Shahrit, at least two in Minhah, and four in 'Arbit. The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer mentions our custom of reciting three Kaddishim in Minhah, which would bring us to a total of 13, which, according to the Kaf HaHayyim, corresponds to the 13 attributes of mercy. In any case, our custom in this community was that every Kaddish is always recited, regardless if mourners are present or not.

So, what happens if everyone's parents are living, and no one has permission to say Kaddish? The Bet Yosef quotes the opinion of Rabbi Meir MiRothenburg, who writes that one is obligated to listen to his father if his father objects to his son saying Kaddish during the father's lifetime, and this is based on the fact that one is obligated to honor their father. The Bet Yosef does say that it's customary to say Kaddish for one's mother even if one's father is still alive, meaning that in that case the father is not supposed to object.

But it's important to point out that fathers never have to object, and since our custom is never to skip a Kaddish, parents should give permission to their sons to say Kaddish when they're the Hazzan. It makes more sense to say that since saying Kaddish is a merit to a parent after they pass away, that it's also a merit to, would also be a merit for them during their lifetime. A person doesn't have their life shortened because their son is making the Missvah of being the Hazzan and reciting a beautiful praise of HaShem and leading the entire congregation to answer with that beautiful praise of HaShem. So, just like a deceased parent's soul is benefited from Kaddish in the next world, a living parent is also blessed because of Kaddish in this world, and this also facilitates our tradition of never skipping a Kaddish.

30.title: Honors and 'Aliyot on Sheni VaHamishi
30.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We're going to continue with the Minhagim relating to the Keri'at Sefer Torah Sheni VaHamishi. One point I neglected to mention last time, it was pointed out to me that when after the Sefer Torah is given to the person carrying it, the one who has Petihah closes the entire Hekhal: the Parokhet, and the door, and the outside Parokhet is completely closed, doesn't leave it only the Parokhet closed with the doors open. We don't, that's not our Minhag, we close it, reopens it after Kaddish Titkabbal.

Now the Mesader is responsible for giving out the honors: the Petihah, the Kohen, Levi, Shelishi. And it's important to keep a ledger, keep records even in a small Minyan, and certainly in a bigger Minyan, but it's very important to be fair and equitable. And therefore I've seen this in the first Minyan of Shaare Zion over 50 years ago, and that's made an impression on me where they keep a ledger, all the names of the regulars, and then the time, and the date, and Kohen, Levi, Shelishi, just to be equitable, it's a good, very good practice.

Now, the way we invite is the Mesader himself or designates somebody to go to the person and invite him personally for the honor. He doesn't do it long distance, "hey," you know, does it personally. So now, so the one who he designates to invite, we invite the 'Aliyot using a silver plate. We don't call by name like the other communities, the Ashkenazi communities in particular. We do it with a silver plate, and the one who is being honored, he accepts the 'Aliyah by touching and kissing it. So, "Kohen BeKhabod," you see I'll demonstrate the silver plate. Kabod plate. And this is a custom that when I was growing up in Brooklyn, I did see this custom in Central in particular. Mr. Chabot used to go around and invite like that. I think maybe it's catching on, but this has been the custom from Halab, and we're in Ades, it's 1901.

Anyway, the Kohen comes up to the Sefer. "Kohen 'Aleh BeKhabod." We open the Sefer, I show him the place. Then you put a kerchief over the writing. Right? And we don't close the Sefer, the Sefer is open, the kerchief is on, his hand's on the Sefer, he'll say the Berakhah. Say the Berakhah, if he's someone who knows how to read and he wants to read the Sefer, by all means he can read the Sefer Torah, make sure he knows the Dikduk properly and the Ta'amim.

When he finishes the, when the Ba'al Kore finishes his part, you may hear now and then someone scream out "Emet." When I was growing up, we had, every Kenis has those people which have that custom to say "Emet," some do it quietly, some do it loudly. It's not in my opinion, I couldn't even find a source, I don't know if it's a widespread custom, just thought I'd mention it.

Before, now we finish reading the Sefer, before making the Berakhah, we do not close the Sefer, the Sefer stays open, it's covered with the kerchief, and he will say the Berakhah "Asher Natan Lanu Torato Torat Emet." He finishes, the Ba'al Kore will do if he needs Hashkabah or to do Mi SheBerakh, and then he immediately goes down. He doesn't have to wait for the next 'Oleh to come and finish the way other Kehillot do, he immediately goes down, that's our custom. And he goes in the indirect, he goes back to his seat in the indirect, goes around the Tebah. People will be telling him "Hazak UBarukh," "Hazak UBarukh," and he answers "Hazak VeEmass," shaking the hand or like that.

We don't kiss, it's not our custom to kiss the 'Oleh. We've seen it seep into our community in certain synagogues. Halakhically it's problematic, and we've seen it mainly mostly in the North African, the Moroccan communities. It's not our custom. Shake hands, say "Hazak UBarukh."

The Levi, repeat, the Shelishi, always with the Sefer open and the kerchief either down when he reading or on the writing when he's saying the Berakhot. Only after this he finished the Shelishi is the Sefer closed. And then the one who is reading the, who went up Shelishi proceeds to say the Kaddish. And those are the Minhagim associated with the reading of the Torah Sheni VaHamishi. On Shabbat we will expand it a little bit more. Kol Tub, see you next time.

31.title: Hanukkah in the Traditional Sephardic World
31.text:
Hanukkah. The holiday of Hanukkah in the traditional Sephardic world was very different than the Hanukkah that most people know of today. I'd just like to touch on some points.

Many of the Hanukkah customs that we see today stem from the Ashkenazi tradition, and more specifically from the social mores of Germanic lands. Talking about items like gift-giving, gift-giving did not exist in Sephardic communities on Hanukkah, but on the holiday of Purim, money would be given to the children. Playing with dreidels, or Sebibon, as we call it in Hebrew today, also completely unknown. This is a game from German lands. The eating of jelly doughnuts, once again, a German custom, it did not exist among Sefaradim.

The one thing that was eaten among Sefaradim was a form of fried dough, and this fried dough went by different names in different cities and countries. It was known as zalabiya, it was known as zingol, it was known as awameh or awamat, loukoumades, bimuelos, sfenj. Different countries had different names, but it was invariably some sort of fried dough relating to the issue of oil and the holiday of Hanukkah. But none of these items, of course, were jelly-filled.

Singing of songs, Ma'oz Sur was not known at all. It was not sung after lighting candles, nor at any point during the holiday, nor during the prayers. In fact, the Halabi community, which is well-known for its composition of Pizmonim and Piyyutim, had hardly any songs for Hanukkah. In fact, only two songs, and they were hardly known, as opposed to the holiday of Purim, which is only one day, or two days, in fact, in Halab, and there were 10 very well-known songs.

So we see the holiday of Hanukkah was not as festive as we know it today. It was a much more downplayed holiday, but at the same time, it was the holiday of light. It was a holiday when the family would gather together to light the lights of Hanukkah together.

On that note, the lights of Hanukkah in Hebrew would be Nerot Hanukkah. Nerot Hanukkah shortened would just be Hanukkah, and that's the way the lights were referred to, as Hanukkah, never as Menorah. In some communities, like in Yerushalayim, or in certain Balkan countries, it was referred to as Hanukkiyah, okay, or as Hanukkiyah, depending, some of those who said it with an accent on the first syllable or second syllable, third syllable. The point was that it was never referred to as a Menorah. And in traditional households, still today it's referred to as Hanukkah or Hanukkiyah. And that's what it is, because the Menorah was reserved for a different type of candelabra in the Bet HaMikdash.

But everybody had a chance to light. Even though it was only one Hanukkah for the entire household, the head of the household did not light all the lights. Rather, that individual would light the first light, and then he would hand the candle to the rest of the family members in generally an age order to light the other oil wicks. And that's the way Hanukkah was celebrated. Everybody would gather around the lights, people would sit and talk and enjoy the warmth of the glow, and recall the holiday of Hanukkah and the miracles Bore 'Olam did for us, all without gift-giving, which was only done on Purim, all without playing dreidel, all without singing Ma'oz Sur. We would just say the traditional Berakhot, HaNerot Hallalu, Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid, and that's it.

And it was a simple holiday, but a beautiful holiday, a holiday that gave us the sense of family togetherness and the Berakhah of Bore 'Olam, and all the Berakhot of the holiday of Hanukkah.

32.title: Talet and Tefillin at Minhah of a Fast Day
32.text:
So in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran ruled that one is obligated to recite 100 blessings daily, and in the Bet Yosef, he goes through the calculation of 100 daily blessings. They're found in our prayers beginning with the morning blessings, the various blessings from Shahrit, Minhah, and 'Arbit, including all of the 'Amidot. So in order to get to 100 blessings in one day, we have to eat some meals. So therefore on a fast day, we are short two blessings according to Maran's calculation. So therefore he writes, "VeYesh Lo LeHashliman KeSheYaniah Sissit UTefillin LiTfilat HaMinhah VeYebarekh 'Alehem." So on a fast day, when he's short two blessings, he should complete them when he puts on Talet and Tefillin in Minhah, and he makes Berakhot on the Talet and on the Tefillin.

Although Maran does not write about Talet and Tefillin in Minhah of a fast day in Shulhan 'Arukh, there's documentation of this practice as a custom in Halab. In a Mahzor for Rosh HaShanah, which was entitled Bet Din, that was published in 1858, Hakham Abraham Hamwey wrote in his instructions for Minhah of Som Gedalyah: "BeArssenu Aram Soba Halab Nohagim Lilbosh Sissit UTefillin BeMinhat Ta'anit Sibbur." In our land, Aleppo, it is customary to wear Talet and Tefillin in Minhah of a public fast day.

In another source, Hakham Salim Zafrani, who was born in Halab in 1891 and officiated in the Great Synagogue there until 1930, he wrote in his documentation of the customs of the Great Synagogue of Aleppo regarding the ninth of Ab: "UBaMinhah Mit'attefim BeTalet UManihin Tefillin KeKhol Ta'anit Sibbur." So Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb, he said that they put on Talet and Tefillin like they did on every public fast day.

And yet another source, Hakham Yosef Sha'yo, who was born in Halab in 1894 and moved to Jerusalem in 1935, in his documentation of the customs of Aleppo, he wrote: "UBeArba' Somot BeMinhah Lobshim Talet UTefillin." On the four fasts in Minhah, we wear Talet and Tefillin.

And in a more recent documentation of the customs of Aleppo in a book known as Derekh Eress, he quotes 'Ezra Bawabeh and Nissim Zafrani as attesting to the practice of Talet and Tefillin in Minhah of a fast day.

Beyond that, Ribbi Hayyim Sethon, who wrote a book of the customs of Eress Yisrael known as Eress Hayyim—this book was published in 1908, and in this book he wrote: "SheNohagim BeEress Yisrael LeHit'attef BeTalet ULeHaniah Tefillin BeMinhah DeKhol Ta'anit Sibbur, Kemo SheKatab Maran Zal BeBet Yosef, Kede LeHashlim Me'ah Berakhot SheSarikh LeBarekh BeKhol Yom." So he wrote that it's customary in the land of Israel to wear Talet and Tefillin in Minhah of every fast day, like Maran wrote in the Bet Yosef, in order to complete 100 Berakhot that a person has to say every day.

So we see that this custom that is prevalent in our community today, wearing Talet and Tefillin in Minhah of a fast day, is based on Maran in the Bet Yosef, and was practiced at least since the mid-19th century in Halab, as recorded in several sources.

There are many people in our community who make the false assumption that this custom was adopted here in Brooklyn, New York under the leadership of our former chief rabbi, Hakham Ya'akob Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom. He came from Eress Yisrael, and he became the chief rabbi in the early 1930s. Now, although this custom was also practiced in Eress Yisrael in the beginning of the 20th century, it was also clearly the custom of Halab at that time. Over time, the custom changed in Halab, and by the 1930s, it was no longer practiced there. Likewise in Eress Yisrael, the custom changed, and it's no longer practiced there either. But here in New York and New Jersey, our community has preserved the original custom of wearing Talet and Tefillin in Minhah of a fast day. It's an authentic custom found in the writings of Maran in the Bet Yosef, and in the writings of the rabbis of Aleppo from previous generations.

33.title: Kedushah DeSidra and Kaddish Titkabbal
33.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We left off our last video after we recited the Hassi Kaddish, whether it was from the 'Oleh Shelishi after the Keri'at HaTorah on Monday and Thursday, or on the other days after the Tahanunim. And we come to the portion of the prayer now, which is called Kedushah DeSidra, because in the UBa LeSiyyon, you know, at Attah Kadosh, we have Pesukim resembling the Kedushah that we do in the Hazarah.

So we begin with Perek Kof-Mem-Heh in Tehillim, Tehillah LeDavid, preceded by "Ashre Yoshebe Betekha," "Ashre Ha'Am SheKakhah Lo," the two Pesukim, but we also precede it with a Pasuk which is written in the Kol Ya'akob Siddurim: "Yehi Hasdekha Ad-onai 'Alenu Ka'asher Yihalnu Lakh." This is our custom, and it's widespread. But I just wanted to point out that it wasn't always the custom. I remember growing up, I'm not even sure if it was printed in the Siddurim that we used. I don't remember it being said consistently.

And looking into the development of this custom, it seems that there were always Pesukim said before the Ashre, but not necessarily this Pasuk. This Pasuk is mentioned in one of the Siddurim printed in Italy in the 16th century, but if in Mahzor Aram Soba, you'll see other Pesukim: "Ad-onai Hoshi'ah HaMelekh Ya'anenu BeYom Kor'enu," "Ashre Temime Darekh," again, another Pasuk with the word Ashre. I guess over time Pesukim were added, a few were taken off, and we have today the custom of "Yehi Hasdekha," and that's what we see being done most often.

We finish the Ashre, LaMnasseah, of course, we skip if there is a day where there's no Tahanunim, and then we go to the UBa LeSiyyon that we mentioned. The Hazzan says, "Me'attah Ve'Ad 'Olam," and then he begins the Kedushah DeSidra, which is "VeAttah Kadosh Yosheb Tehillot Yisrael VeKara Zeh El Zeh VeAmar," "Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh, Ad-onai Seba'ot Melo Khol HaAress Kebodo," and then we have an Aramaic translation to that.

So a couple of interesting Minhagim. Even though logic would dictate that the reason it's in Aramaic is because that was the spoken language of the population, and because we wanted them to understand such an important prayer, we did it in Aramaic, so you would think that it was said out loud. No, the custom is, Maran writes in the Bet Yosef, 'Al Pi HaZohar, that kabbalistic custom is to say it BeLahash. So we say this quietly. Also we sit down for this Kedushah, even though you would think that it's similar to the Kedushah of the Hazarah, and indeed this is a discussion amongst the Rishonim and the Aharonim, our custom is to sit down.

There's one other thing I wanted to point out, which to me was very, very interesting, is that when I grew up there was Hazzanim, in particular, I remember Mr. Albert Chreky, 'Alav HaShalom, from that shul, who always prayed Minhah of Shabbat, and he used to say the phrase "UMekabbelin Den Min Den VeAmrin" out loud himself as the Hazzan, and then everybody else would answer BeLahash. "Kaddish BiShme Meroma," everything would be BeLahash. I always wondered why he always said that phrase out loud, I never asked him, but recently I saw in the Siddur of Rab Sa'adya Gaon an instruction that this phrase should be said by the Hazzan. So even though the custom shifted and we say everything BeLahash, 'Al Pi HaBet Yosef, nonetheless it's interesting that this custom to say this phrase out loud, I guess, withstood a thousand years of changes, and I just found that interesting. Although generally, you won't find the Hazzanim saying it, but I wanted to point that out.

Following the end of this section, "Hizku VeYa'amess Lebabkhem Kol HaMeyahalim LaAd-onai," we have Kaddish Titkabbal. Now this, unlike other Kaddishim, which were inserted to differentiate between sections of the prayer, this Kaddish is to complete the entire Shahrit, and that's why it belongs to the Hazzan exclusively, nobody else says it except the Hazzan, and it's called Kaddish Titkabbal. "Titkabbal Selotana UBa'utana," our, the entire prayer is in this Kaddish, and this signifies the end of Shahrit. I know we have Tefilah LeDavid, the Shir Shel Yom, this was a Minhag which was added afterwards. The Ketoret, which we say Kavveh, even a later custom. So this represents the end of the prayer, and that's why—

There's two things interesting to note, that occasionally you'll see that a new Hazzan takes over for the Hazzan of Shahrit, now is the time, because the prayer, the Shahrit prayer, is over. Another thing is interesting is Tefilah LeDavid, when I was growing up, I used to observe all the older guys, and they start taking off the Tefillin at Tefilah LeDavid. Why? Because Shahrit is over, "Titkabbal Selotana UBa'utana," and the rest, of course, our Minhag, no question we say it, and we say it through the end of 'Alenu LeShabbeah, but it didn't have the same status as the Shahrit, that people used to take off the Tefillin.

Now, today, people like to take off the Tefillin later, some people even study Hok LeYisrael after the Tefilah with Tefillin, Tabo 'Alehem Berakhah. But just to make note that the custom was to begin removing the Tefillin in Tefilah LeDavid. Shalom UBerakhah.

34.title: Studying Hok LeYisrael Every Day
34.text:
Limmud Torah. What was the order of learning Torah among our parents, our grandparents, our ancestors, whether here in the United States or back in the old country? Now obviously they learned all types of Torah, but there was one set thing that everybody learned and everybody took pride in learning, and that was Hok LeYisrael, commonly known as Hok. Hok is something that we grew up seeing, grew up reading, grew up studying, something that we witnessed all the time. This was your typical Hok book, printed many, many times. This was the most common one here in the community, printed in Yerushalayim, and this is something that included all the readings from Torah, Nebi'im, Ketubim to Mishnah, Gemara, Zohar, Musar, and Halakhah.

Now this is based upon the teachings of the Ari going back approximately 450 years ago, as handed down to his student Rabbi Hayyim Vital. It was first published only in 1740 in Cairo by Rabbi Yisshak Barukh, and later on added to by the Hida in 1794 in Livorno, Italy. And this is a set standard reading based upon the weekly Parashah, and besides the Parashah there would be a reading from the Haftarah, as well as readings from Tehillim and or Mishle depending on the time of the year, and followed by Mishnayot and the Gemara pertaining to that, a section from the Zohar, Musar, which is ethics, morals, and then Halakhah directly from HaRambam.

And there was a set order for this as well. It wasn't just, "Okay, let's read an 'Aliyah or two," it was a set number of Pesukim for each day of the week, and that went for the Torah portion, the Nebi'im portion, and the Ketubim portion. On Sunday would be six Pesukim, Monday four Pesukim, Tuesday five Pesukim, Wednesday six Pesukim, and Thursday five Pesukim again, totaling 26 Pesukim. On Thursday night, another 26 Pesukim would be read, and on Friday the remainder of the Parashah would be read. So each day of the week you had a set amount of reading. Any place where you ended up in the world, in a Sephardic community, you would find them reading the exact same thing from the exact same book. You'd sit down, you'd join in, you'd know what's going on. Very simple.

The Mishnah would be based upon the Shas DeMishnah. The Mishnah, as we know, has six orders to it, Shishah Sedarim. The first day's reading would be from Zera'im, the next day from Mo'ed, third day from Nashim, fourth day from Nezikin, fifth day from Kodashim, and the sixth day from Teharot. Simple as it was.

And this is something that, as I mentioned, we found everybody doing and everybody learning, and it was something that each person was able to adapt for their own well-being. Some people picked up better reading of Pesukim, some people were able to sharpen their Ta'amim skills, some people were able to understand Aramaic words and apply that to studying of Gemara or Zohar, some people picked up a Halakhah, some people picked up some ethics to take into their business life for the day. Everybody was able to pick up something else. It was considered "Dabar Shaveh LeKhol Nefesh," something that was of equal value to one and all.

And this is something that wasn't just done by the laymen, but it was done by all the Hakhamim. And what's important about that is that we see in the writings of the earlier Hakhamim, they talk about the importance of this for all the rabbis to do it, and anybody who's even a full-time rabbi and has a set learning schedule must do this as well before they begin their day. So this was the common way of learning. After Minyan, people would sit and learn it, read it, some people would do it in a quick 15-20 minutes, some would actually make a class out of it and study it in depth for 45 minutes to an hour.

And this is something that didn't make a difference what country we were dealing with: from Morocco to Tunisia, to Algeria, to Libya, Egypt, to Israel, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran, Turkey, Greece, Bulgaria, any place where there was a Sephardic community, this was being studied on a regular basis. You would walk in, join the Minyan, after Minyan sit down and study what you were studying yesterday and the week before, the week before that someplace else.

Here in the community, I vividly recall it, remember seeing all our rabbis studying it and teaching it, from Chief Rabbi Jacob Kassin to his son Hakham Shaul Kassin, who to his very last days was always seen walking around with his Hok LeYisrael in his hand. He would never let it go. Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim, Hakham Siyyon Maslaton, Hakham Halfon Safdieh, Hakham Yom Tob Yedid, everybody studied Hok and taught Hok. It's a beautiful custom. It's not something that we should forget about. It's something we must really rededicate ourselves to if we've forgotten about it, and embrace the teachings of our Hakhamim and our forefathers.

35.title: A Mourner Serving as Hazzan
35.text:
So in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran writes regarding the house of mourning: "Im En Sham Mi SheYitpallel LeHossi Et HaRabbim Yede Hobatan, Yakhol HaAbel LeHitpallel LeHossian." So, if there's no one else who can be Hazzan in a house of mourning in order that the congregation can fulfill their obligation, the mourner himself may be the Hazzan in order to help the congregation fulfill their obligation. So according to this, if there's someone else to be Hazzan, then the Abel is not Hazzan. Only in that case where there's nobody to be Hazzan does the Abel, that's the mourner himself, go up to be Hazzan.

However, according to Rabbi Moshe Isserles, known as the Rema, the Ashkenazic authority, mourners within the seven days are supposed to be Hazzan if they know how. Many later authorities differentiate between mourning for a parent, where they say a mourner should be the Hazzan, or mourning for other relatives, where the mourner is only Hazzan if nobody else knows how to be the Hazzan. And there are other Aharonim, later authorities, that suggest that a mourner may be Hazzan in our times, since now almost everyone prays on their own, they're not relying on the Hazzan to fulfill their obligation, whereas in former times, many didn't know how to pray and relied on the Hazzan. Hakham 'Obadia Yosef's opinion is that one should be Hazzan during the seven-day period if they're mourning for their parent.

However, the custom in the Syrian community has always been that a mourner is not Hazzan during the seven-day mourning period, based on a straightforward reading of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, who does not differentiate between mourning for a parent or mourning for other relatives. Furthermore, we don't differentiate between our times, where people pray on their own, or former times, where many relied on the Hazzan. So our custom is that only in a case, and it's a rare case, where no one else knows how to be Hazzan in the house of mourning, then the Abel is Hazzan, then the mourner goes up to be Hazzan, otherwise somebody else goes up to be the Hazzan.

So all of this is regarding the seven-day mourning period. But what about during the year, the first year of mourning, or on the anniversary of the passing of a parent? Should the mourner be the Hazzan? Now, if he's normally a Hazzan, of course he could be the Hazzan, but should he be the Hazzan? Meaning, does he automatically receive the privilege of being the Hazzan? Now, according to Maran, if one wants to be Hazzan for that reason, he may do so if the congregation gives permission.

The general custom in the Ashkenazic community is that one automatically has the right to be the Hazzan if it's during the first year of the passing of a parent or on the anniversary of their passing. They refer to this as a Hiyyub, an obligation, an obligation upon the mourner to be the Hazzan. However, the Mishnah Berurah pointed out that some Ashkenazic communities did not allow mourners to be Hazzan because many did not read properly, or because they don't understand the prayers, or they don't pray with the proper Kavvanah. And therefore, even if a mourner was qualified, he wasn't Hazzan because then those that weren't so qualified would insist, and it would lead to arguments. And in fact, sometimes mourners who aren't so observant, and as a result are not permitted to be the Hazzan, would also insist on being the Hazzan. So only regular Hazzanim would be the Hazzan, and mourners would say Kaddish.

Interestingly, that was always the tradition in our community for the exact same reasons. Since many are not so qualified to be the Hazzan, but if it's accepted that someone who knows how to be the Hazzan that he should be the Hazzan, many times those that are not so qualified will insist on being the Hazzan. And that's what's beginning to happen today. Many in our community are going up to be the Hazzan during the year of mourning or on the anniversary of the passing of a parent's, of a parent's passing, even though we never had that custom. Sometimes they're too low, the congregation can't hear them, sometimes they don't really understand the prayers. The Kaf HaHayyim writes that in these cases, not only is it not a benefit to the deceased, but it actually could have the adverse effect. And therefore, it's much better to have regular Hazzanim to be Hazzan, and the mourners say Kaddish.

In some cases, the mourners want to be Hazzan even on Friday night or on Shabbat morning, even though they don't really know Hazzanut, or they're not familiar with all of our musical traditions. That's why our original tradition of leaving Hazzanut to the regular Hazzanim is preferable. It also prevents disagreements when there's more than one mourner who wants to be Hazzan. And of course, in that case, arguing detracts from any benefit there is to the deceased, and more than any benefit that would be gained by being the Hazzan, and this was also pointed out by the Kaf HaHayyim as well.

So all in all, the prayers are better when Hazzanut is reserved for the regular Hazzanim, and the mourners fulfill their obligation by reciting Kaddish. That was always the custom here and in the Syrian community.

36.title: Tefilah LeDavid and the Shir Shel Yom
36.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We ended the last video with the Hazzan following the Ashre, the UBa LeSiyyon, saying Kaddish Titkabbal, which means that our entire prayer should be accepted, and because this really represents the formal end of Tefilat Shahrit. What comes after were Minhagim that were instituted afterwards, and even though today, of course, we pray till the end of 'Alenu LeShabbeah, it's important that we know what the sources are for the Tefilot. And that also explains why, as I mentioned in the last video when I was growing up, this was the custom more often than not, was people begin taking their Tefillin off when they start Tefilah LeDavid.

Now, the Mizmor Tefilah LeDavid, we omit during days that we do not say Tahanun. It's similar to the Mizmor LaMnasseah Mizmor LeDavid which we say after Ashre, but when one was saying when there's a Farah in the Kenis, Hatan, Berit Milah, we don't want to make references to our suffering in our Sarot. So just like in "LaMnasseah Mizmor LeDavid, Ya'ankha HaShem BeYom Sarah, Yesaggebkha Shem Eloke Ya'akob," we don't want to mention the Sarot, also in the Mizmor Tefilah LeDavid, we have "Ki 'Ani VeEbyon Ani," and then "BeYom Sarati Ekra'ekha." Again, we don't want to mention Sarah, so we skip it when there is a happy occasion in the synagogue.

Now, as far as Rosh Hodesh and Hol HaMo'ed, we skip the entire section. There's no Tefilah LeDavid, there's no Bet Ya'akob, no Shir Shel Yom. We will get to those customs when we discuss Rosh Hodesh in the upcoming videos, BeEzrat HaShem. So we say Tefilah LeDavid followed by Bet Ya'akob and Shir HaMa'alot.

Now we come to the section called Shir Shel Yom, where we mention the Mizmorim, the Shirim, songs that the Leviyyim used to sing in the Bet HaMikdash following Korban HaTamid in the morning and in the afternoon. Just as an aside, we didn't institute Shir Shel Yom in the afternoon even though it was sung by the Leviyyim because it wasn't sung every day. It was only sung when there was time permitting it was sung. So very often the ritual of Korban HaTamid on the Mizbeah used to extend, and if it was after sunset, then they didn't say the Shir Shel Yom, and that's why it was instituted only in Shahrit for our prayers.

Now, if you look at the Mahzor Aram Soba, printed in 1527, it makes no mention of Shir Shel Yom. It wasn't the custom. Even in the 16th century in Halab, wasn't the custom. The Siddur of Rab Sa'adya Gaon also wasn't mentioned. HaRambam in Hilkhot Tefilah, at the end he says, "Nahagu Mikssat Ha'Am," it was the custom of some people to say the Shir Shel Yom. So just I'm just pointing out that, you see, it was a custom that evolved over time. There's a reference made to it in the Siddur of Rab 'Amram Gaon, as much as we can ascertain that that's the Siddur of Rab 'Amram Gaon, and it's also a reference made in Masekhet Soferim.

Now, we begin the Shir Shel Yom, and right away we see there's a difference between our custom and the custom of other communities with regards to the introductory sentence that we say before the actual Mizmor. There we start with the mention of the Shir, with the song: "HaShir SheHayu HaLeviyyim Omerim 'Al HaDukhan BeYom Sheni BeShabbat Kodesh." The other custom begins with the day: "HaYom Yom Sheni BeShabbat Kodesh, HaShir SheHayu HaLeviyyim Omerim 'Al HaDukhan." Our custom, like as we mentioned, is to say the Shir first. Indeed, this is the way it's printed in Siddur Kol Ya'akob. If you look at the famous Siddur Bet 'Obed, you're going to find that that's the way it was recorded as well. Predominantly the Ashkenazim and also some 'Edot Mizrah, some Sefaradim also do it "HaYom Yom," but our custom is "HaShir" first, and then "BeYom Sheni BeShabbat Kodesh."

Regarding the word Kodesh, I've been saying it as a matter of fact, but it's not that clear. There are equally as many customs and Siddurim which just say "BeYom Sheni BeShabbat" without the word Kodesh. It is an interesting discussion regarding why that is, which we cannot get to it now, but hopefully at a later date. So if you want—if you have—if you're used to saying just Shabbat, it's fine. If you're saying Shabbat Kodesh, it's fine as well.

We do have a couple of customs that differ from other communities. One of them is when on Sunday, when we say "HaShir SheHayu Omerim 'Al HaDukhan BeYom Rishon BeShabbat Kodesh," we say Rishon. It's also the Lashon of the Mishnah. There are communities who just would say Yom Ehad, but our custom is to say Yom Rishon. As well, on Fridays, the custom developed really in the last few hundred years, instead of "BeYom Shishi BeShabbat Kodesh" to say "HaShishi." This was a later custom, predominantly a kabbalistic custom. Today I would say that the Hazzan would be well served to say "HaShishi," otherwise if he says "Shishi," you're going to have, "Ah!" everybody's going to start yelling, "HaShishi!" So let's save the dramatics and just say "HaShishi."

On Fridays after "HaShem Malakh Ge'ut Labesh, Labesh HaShem 'Oz Hit'azar," that Mizmor, we finish "HaShem Le'Orekh Yamim," we do not say Hoshi'enu. This is also different than other communities which do indeed say Hoshi'enu. Again, the reasons for that are interesting, and hopefully we will get to them at a later date. Kol Tub. See you next time.
