37.title: Tu BiShbat, the Day of Fruits
37.text:
Tu BiShbat, Jewish Arbor Day, Rosh HaShanah LaIlanot, Hamishah 'Asar BiShbat, in Ladino, Frutas, in Arabic, Id esh-Shajar. This is the day of fruits, the day that we partake of and relish in the fruits of Eress Yisrael and of all the bounty of the trees that Bore 'Olam has given us throughout the world. And even though this Rosh HaShanah, this special new year of the trees is mentioned in the Mishnah, there are no special practices, observances, or customs associated with it. It's not until the Mekubbalim of 16th century Safed that we really hear about this Minhag, which seems to have originated among the Ashkenazi communities, and these Mekubbalim raised this Minhag to a greater level by adding a special dimension to the Berakhot that we say before eating the fruits. And in fact, they looked at fruits in different categories: those that can be eaten completely without any sort of outer shell or inner seed, those with just an inner seed, those with just an outer shell.

And regardless of that, the general public looked at this as a way to praise Bore 'Olam, and went out of their way to go to the market already from a week, two weeks before the holiday to buy all the different types of fruits, special fruits, dried fruits, or fresh fruits, and set up their table as lavishly as possible, but not only with fruits, but with different wines as well, to again, once again, praise Bore 'Olam with the Berakhot. We have Bore Peri HaGefen for the wines, they made different sorts of pastries and sweets, Mezonot out of the wheat and barley, and then of course the fruits of Ha'Ess and the fruits of HaAdamah. And everybody would invite their friends and neighbors, you know, and their family members to come and partake of this.

But it wasn't just a spread of fruit and pastries and wine and drink, it was also a night where the mothers and the grandmothers, you know, were very, very proud. They embroidered special little bags for the children and grandchildren, embroidered their names on them. The fathers would have the fruit in front of them, and they would call over each child separately and give them fruits that they would put into their bags, and it would be the first time during the course of the year that somebody may actually even see something as obscure as a cashew nut, which we look at today as what's the big deal? We have everything in plenty. But going back not too long ago, even a few decades ago, things weren't as easily accessible throughout the year. We had actual seasons, and we couldn't partake of everything throughout the year. Nowadays, we take it for granted, but this is a time of year that we learn to appreciate, look back, and see, you know, what HaShem made available to us.

And for this reason, there were special readings. The Mekubbalim that we mentioned earlier created a special reading called Peri 'Ess Hadar. This was first printed in Venice, Italy in 1728. Here's a later printing, this is from 1928, from Livorno, Italy. And this was read in many a home in various Sephardic communities before, after, and during partaking of different types of fruits. Besides that, you had Minhag in other places where let's say, for example, in Damascus, Syria, they would read all of Mishnayot Berakhot, all of Mishnayot Rosh HaShanah before beginning to partake of the fruits.

In Halab, there was a very interesting custom where they didn't read anything having to do with fruits, but they read something called 'Aseret HaDibrot with the sharh, the Perush of Rabbenu Sa'adya Gaon. And this wasn't just a literal translation, but actually an explanation for the men, women, and children to listen and understand. And the reason this was done because the upcoming Parashah always immediately after Tu BiShbat would be Parashat Yitro, the Parashah of 'Aseret HaDibrot. And here's a version of it that was actually printed in Halab, this one from 1924, and this is an earlier version that was handwritten right here on these American shores about 120 years ago, and they would sit and read this together.

And besides that, there was a special song in Halab for Tu BiShbat, a folkloric song in Judeo-Arabic, even though people know the tune today and it's our Tu BiShbat tune for Nakdishakh, most people have forgotten the song. It's called Eshu Khabar Ya Rijal. "Eshu Khabar Ya Rijal, Lela 'an 'Id ash-Shajar," etc. I'm not going to sing the whole song right now. But these are different aspects of Tu BiShbat.

But back to the fruit, that the fruit was the main thing, and the children would gather the fruit in their bags and then want to trade with one another. "Ooh, you got a fig, I got a date, or I got..." Then there was always that piece of Harub, the carob, and most people didn't like it. It was dry, it was smelly, but at the same time it had a connection to the Tanna'im and to Eress Yisrael. So you wanted it, but you didn't want it, and there was always a struggle: trade it, not trade it? Who's going to give me something better for it, you know? "Well, this is something I can hold on to for months, it'll never go bad," you know, and it'll—it's my connection to Eress Yisrael.

So all these different things were things that children enjoyed, and the parents and the grandparents enjoyed sharing with the children. It's this custom that we had among us for at least a few centuries, and it's this custom that unfortunately has been dying out, and it's very important to revive this custom, bring it back to our homes. Happy Tu BiShbat!

38.title: Mourners Reciting All the Kaddishim
38.text:
Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi is a young rabbi currently living in Eress Yisrael. He was born and raised in the Halabi community in Argentina, and he is doing a lot of research and work on the traditions of Halab. And he's currently working on a comprehensive book of all the customs, and periodically sends out excerpts from his upcoming book to rabbis and friends. In a recent excerpt, he wrote the following regarding mourners: "HaAbelim Omerim Kol HaKaddishim Huss MiTitkabbal." The mourners recite all the Kaddishim except for Kaddish Titkabbal. And in his footnote he specifies Hassi Kaddish, 'Al Yisrael, and Yehe Shelama. "VeKhol HaBarekhu": the mourners likewise recite all of the Barekhu in the prayers, meaning after Yishtabbah, before 'Arbit, as well as before 'Alenu. This was the custom in the Halabi community in Argentina.

But he has another very interesting source. There was an important Mekubbal in Halab in the beginning of the 19th century. His name was Hakham Eliyahu Mishan, and he received questions from other Mekubbalim, and the answers that he provided to these questions were printed in his book entitled Sedek VeShalom. Sedek VeShalom was printed in Yerushalayim in 1961, together with some other books by Rabbi Yosef Abadi Sha'yo. Rabbi Yosef Abadi Sha'yo was also born in Halab at the end of the 19th century. And Sedek VeShalom is printed with this book that he printed, and it contains the questions and the answers, among which we are going to be referring to now.

So Hakham Abraham Galante was an important Mekubbal in Damascus, and he posed the following question to Rabbi Mishan. Now, before we get to his question, we must note that originally, only the last Kaddish in each prayer was recited by the mourners, meaning the last Kaddish before 'Alenu LeShabbeah in Shahrit, Minhah, 'Arbit were for the mourners, and all the other Kaddishim throughout the prayers, including all of the 'Al Yisrael and Yehe Shelama, was recited by the Hazzan.

So Rabbi Galante asked: "VeHinneh 'Akhshav Nahagu SheKol HaKaddishim Shel Tefilah Omerim Otam HaSibbur 'Al HaMetim," now, meaning at the time of the question, the custom in Syria is that all the Kaddishim in the prayers are recited by the congregants in memory of the deceased, "UShliah Sibbur Shotek," and the Hazzan is quiet, "Milbad Kaddish Titkabbal," with the exception of Kaddish Titkabbal, that that is the Kaddish that's recited by the Hazzan by himself. "ULeDa'ati Lo Sarikh LeMe'bad Hakhi." Rabbi Galante is questioning this custom. "DeKhol HaKaddishim Keivan SheHem Le'Illui Ha'Olamot," since all the Kaddishim, the kabbalistic purpose for them is the elevation of the upper worlds, "VeEnam Nog'im LaMetim," they don't pertain to the deceased. And to just put it in simpler terms, all the Kaddishim in the prayers, except for the last Kaddish, belongs to the prayers, they don't have anything to do with the deceased. "Im Ken, Zeh Talui BiShliah Sibbur LeOmro," and therefore all the Kaddishim with the exception of the last one, according to Rabbi Galante, should be recited by the Hazzan, not by the mourners, "O Lefahot SheYomar 'Im HaSibbur VeLo Lishtok," or at the very least, if the mourners are going to say them, the Hazzan should say it along with them and not be quiet, and again, all except for that last Kaddish before 'Alenu.

Ribbi Eliyahu Mishan answered the following: "Ne'emar SheIm Hu MiKlal HaMitpallelim VeEno Sheliah Sibbur," if we're talking about a mourner who's part of the congregation and he's not the Hazzan, "'Im Kol Zeh Yakhol Lihyot 'Aliyot 'Aliyat Ha'Olamot 'Al Yado," still and all, the elevation of the worlds could come through his recitation of Kaddish, or as we explained, he can be the Hazzan for the Kaddish, even though it pertains to the prayers, he could be the Hazzan for the Kaddish, "UBe'Aliyyatam," and at the same time, when the worlds are elevated, so to speak, "Ya'aleh 'Imahem Nishmot HaMetim," this will also elevate the souls of the deceased. So meaning the purpose of the Kaddish for the prayers and for the mourners can be accomplished simultaneously by the mourner.

And then Rabbi Mishan continues, and even though there is a kabbalistic authority that writes that a mourner may only say the last Kaddish, Rabbi Mishan says, I say, with this and everything like this, "Puk Hazi Mai 'Amma Dabar." Go out and see what the people practice, and follow it, mean follow the custom. And the practice, follow practice custom, "UBne Nebi'im Hem," because we are the descendants of prophets, our customs are assumed to be correct.

So Rabbi Mishan did not object to the mourner saying all the Kaddishim instead of the Hazzan. And this is yet another source that both attests to and approves of the Syrian custom of mourners reciting all of the Kaddishim, including the Hassi Kaddish, instead of the Hazzan.

39.title: Ketoret, Halakhot and the End of Shahrit
39.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed Kaddish Yehe Shelama following Shir Shel Yom, and now we are beginning the final section of the prayer, the Kavveh, the Ketoret, followed by Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, Barekhu, and 'Alenu LeShabbeah. As I mentioned, these last two sections were Minhagim that evolved over time. In particular, the Ketoret began about 500 years ago, and while you won't find it in Mahzor Aram Soba printed in 1527, nonetheless it has become part of the prayer. We do not skip it. We say it in its entirety and everything that's printed in the Siddur until after 'Alenu LeShabbeah.

Now, there's a couple of practices I do want to discuss that we've been seeing more frequently in recent years. One is that when the Ketoret begins, a lot of people pull out of their kurachah a Kelaf, and they read Ketoret from a parchment. Now, this is not a custom, certainly not our custom and not a custom of any community. This is an individual Segulah, and I'm certainly not going to speak to the merits of Segulot in general or this Segulah in particular, only to say that it's something we've never seen, not by our fathers, our grandfathers, Hakhamim, Mekubbalim, never have we seen this practice. In fact, the writing of such a Kelaf is a problem halakhically. Those who are interested in reading about it further, Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alav HaShalom, speaks about, writes about it in Yabia' Omer, Helek Tet.

The second practice is a little more important to discuss because it involves the Kahal, and that is when we say Tanna DeBe Eliyahu: "Kol HaShoneh Halakhot BeKhol Yom," more and more Minyanim now you'll see that the Hazzan stops, and a layperson or Hakham will get up and read a few Halakhot and explain a few Halakhot to the Kahal. Now, this is a very, very strange and problematic custom on many levels. I'm not going to get into halakhically whether it's permissible, whether it's considered Torah Sibbur. We'll leave that up to the Hakhamim. I know that even from the Talmud, they're very particular not to even add minutes unnecessarily to the Tefilah. And I'm not going to discuss the kabbalistic ramifications. People who are involved in the study of Kabbalah have told me that it may pose a problem, as the Tefilah is a very structured, structured in a very specific order according to the Kabbalah, and stopping to study Torah may be problematic. Again, beyond the scope of my comprehension.

What I do want to discuss is from the point of view of a worshiper or a Gabbai. Here we're stopping the Tefilah, and we're doing something which easily could be done after 'Alenu LeShabbeah. Now, in fact, I prayed with Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alav HaShalom, many times. Never did he stop the Tefilah in the middle to read Halakhot. After 'Alenu LeShabbeah, he would indeed take out the Rambam and begin reading Halakhot to the Kahal, and we also have Aharonim, other Aharonim, which mention this practice. We've never seen, through a thousand years of the Hakhamim in Halab, and if you just look at all of the Kehillot that we know of in the world, never did we see this Minhag.

And it's odd that you would have a person who chooses a Minyan carefully based on the time it starts, based on the time it ends, because people have to go to work, especially the weekdays, they have to take the kids to school, they have to do errands. People's time is very precious in the mornings. And that's why we make the Tefilot, and it's a Gabbai's job to make sure the Tefilah is consistent and efficient. And here we have a situation where a person is now forced captive audience to sit through Halakhot which he could choose after the Tefilah to do the same thing. It's the same time. In fact, Joey Mosseri gave a very, very important video a few weeks ago about our custom to read Hok LeYisrael after 'Alenu LeShabbeah. We gather at a table, we read: Mikra, Mishnah, Talmud, Halakhot. So this Halakhah, it's just this custom that has been increasingly done is just odd.

I know from a worshiper's point of view, you know, a lot of people even have the obligation to say Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, they have a Hiyyub, they have an obligation. And now they can't leave because they have to say Kaddish. But they can't stay because they have to go to work. So it poses a—I think as Gabba'im have to be sensitive and a Hakham, but have to be sensitive to the needs of all the congregants whether they verbally express it or not. Anything which can be done after 'Alenu LeShabbeah, and by the way I think the same goes for announcements, for raising money for worthy causes, not in the Tefilah. "Zeman Tefilah LeHud." Let's keep the Tefilah consistent and complete. Let's finish the Tefilah and then afterwards we could engage in other issues which are important.

Following the Tanna DeBe Eliyahu, we have Kaddish 'Al Yisrael which is said by someone who has an obligation. If there's nobody, then of course the Hazzan has to say it. Barekhu, which was instituted for those who forgot—who not forgot, who weren't there at the earlier Barekhu, so Hakhamim instituted it here. Again, the Halabiyeh don't necessarily have to do like this when they say Barekhu. They can if they want. 'Alenu LeShabbeah, we're not obligated to stand up. I know it's the custom for many people to stand up. It's fine, but as when I was growing up, I just want to point out that not everybody stood up, and many people—elderly people didn't stand—not elderly, older people did not stand up. And not obligated to.

After 'Alenu LeShabbeah, we have "UBeToratekha Ad-onai Elokenu Katub Lemor, Shema Yisrael Ad-onai Elokenu Ad-onai Ehad." It wasn't printed in many of the Siddurim when I was growing up. It was printed in the Siddur in Halab in 1915, so and not all Hazzanim say it. If you say it, fine. If you don't say it, it's not crucial. After that, we do not say any Mizmorim. It's the custom in Halab not to say any Mizmor after 'Alenu LeShabbeah.

What we do say when we exit the synagogue, just as there was a Pasuk when we enter, "VaAni BeRob Hasdekha," the following Pasuk in Tehillim Perek Heh we say when we exit: "Ad-onai Neheni BeSidkatekha LeMa'an Shorerai, Hayshar Lefanai Darkekha," meaning Bore 'Olam, beseeching Bore 'Olam to guide us in his just ways, with the Zekhut "LeMa'an Shorerai," the Zekhut of the prayer which I have just recited. "Hayshar Lefanai Darkekha," keep me on the straight and narrow. BeEzrat HaShem, we'll see you in a few weeks. Kol Tub.

40.title: Adar, Shabbat Zakhor and Purim
40.text:
"Mishenikhnas Adar Marbim BeSimhah." The month of Adar, the happiest month in the Jewish calendar, the month of the holiday of Purim. Prior to Purim, we give Zekher LeMahassit HaShekel. This is a custom that we give a half of the local coin in remembrance of what Bene Yisrael used to do to count the census, and this money would go for the upkeep of the Mishkan, later on for the Bet HaMikdash. We give this money today, and it goes for 'Aniyim, for Talmide Hakhamim, for synagogues, for Batte Midrash, holy institutions, and what have you. And in most places, half of the local coin would be the custom to give per family member. In other places, they would actually give the value of what a half a silver Shekel used to be. But as I said, in most locales, most cities, most communities, it was half the local coin, and this was in fact the Minhag in Halab as well. So in Halab, they would give half a majidi.

Here in New York, we've always given half of a dollar. As a child, I recall that in the Kenis, they would have before Purim, they would have a tray with actual silver half dollars on it, and when you would come to give your Zekher LeMahassit HaShekel, you would put your donation onto the tray. Let's say your family of six, so you're giving 50 cents a person, so it's a total of three dollars, you'd put three dollars onto the tray, and then you would pick up these silver half dollars and put them down onto the tray as if you're actually giving Zekher LeMahassit HaShekel.

Now, we have the Shabbat prior to Purim, known as Shabbat Zakhor. Shabbat Zakhor, besides reading the regular Parashah, we also read a special Parashah called Parashat Zakhor. It has never been our custom for the women to attend this reading. Just the people who generally go to Kenis, the men, you know, obviously make it their business as an obligation to hear Parashat Zakhor. And if there are women that normally attend, so they would normally attend on this Shabbat as well, but women would not come specially to hear the reading of Zakhor.

What was special about this Shabbat, it was also known as Shabbat Mi Khamokha, that we had a special Piyyut written by Ribbi Yehudah HaLevi, all about the holiday of Purim, the entire story of Megillat Ester in poetic form. And in most Sephardic communities, this would be read in its entirety, it would be sung in a special tune in its entirety after the reading of the Haftarah. In the Halabi tradition, only the first three and last three verses would be sung in the Bet Kenis, and that was to avoid Torah Sibbur, to avoid burdening the people by stretching out the prayers. Instead, in Halab, they would go home after the prayers and sing the Mi Khamokha with family members, especially with the children, either before or after lunch.

Then we get to the holiday of Purim itself. We all know Megillat Ester, and there are many customs associated with Megillat Ester, too numerous for us to get into at this point. But one thing that's important to remember is that when we're coming to the Kenis for a holiday, we have to dress like it's a holiday. We don't dress in a funny or silly manner, not in a frivolous manner, we don't put on costumes to come to Kenis, but we dress like we normally would come in a dignified manner to attend prayers and Megillah reading in the Bet Kenis. You would never have seen adults dressed in costumes, and if children would wear costumes, and that's based upon outside influences, it would always be outside of the Bet Kenis, never inside, and definitely never during the prayers or during the reading of the Megillah.

What else do we have on the holiday of Purim? We have Mattanot LaEbyonim. Mattanot LaEbyonim, giving of alms to the poor. This was given to everybody. It didn't make a difference if the person was Jewish or non-Jewish. We wouldn't investigate to find out the person's situation, just they would put out their hand and they would be given money generously.

We have Mishloah Manot next, which was the highlight for the children especially. Mothers and grandmothers would be preparing Middle Eastern pastries for weeks before the holiday, and pile them high onto trays. The children would be entrusted to take these trays to family members. They would be taken from family to family, not individual to individual, but rather family to family. So they would take things to grandparents, to aunts, to uncles, to cousins, to neighbors, and as they would enter to give these trays of Mishloah Manot, they would in return receive trays of Mishloah Manot to take back to their families.

But more importantly than that is the children would receive Furieh. Furieh was special money just for them for Yom Purim. They would look forward to it year-round, instead of the custom that we've heard of today where people go around, you know, and wait for eight nights of... Hanukkah to get presents, custom that we've never had and never known of, we had Purim, and we had the Purim money known as Furieh, and they would look forward to it, the children, and the adults would look forward to giving it to the children as well. So they wouldn't just be getting it from parents or grandparents, they would be getting it from aunts, from uncles, from neighbors, from cousins, from all different people that they would visit that day to bring Mishloah Manot, they would get money in return. And it was a real highlight and a real treat for the children and for the adults that were giving it to them.

Now we have Se'udat Purim. Se'udat Purim was always a very, very festive meal. In the Halabi tradition, there are so many beautiful Pizmonim for Yom Purim, and these Purim songs would be sung while eating, while drinking. As we're talking about drinking, we're talking about drinking, but not to the point of intoxication, not to the point of getting so drunk that we would do things that we would regret later on. We would never, ever start vomiting or have to call Hatzalah to come save us or anything to that manner. Rather, we would drink to a point where we would feel happy, feel giddy, but to the point where we were still sober enough to understand where we are and what's the point of the day. This is something that is lacking today, and it's very, very important to understand.

In fact, some of the Hakhamim of Halab, especially Hakham Eliyahu Hamwey, wrote, if you want to get drunk and you feel you want to drink more after you already drank, go and study Torah. Study Torah and get drunk on Torah. That was the attitude of our Hakhamim towards drinking. Once again, the holiday of Purim is very, very important. It has a serious note while being very, very happy. Enjoy it, have a...

41.title: Unrolling the Megillah As You Read
41.text:
So in some communities it's customary to unroll the entire Megillah prior to the reading. And in some communities it's only the reader for the congregation that unrolls the entire Megillah. In some communities the congregants do it as well. I'm demonstrating how they unroll the entire Megillah. So now this opinion of unrolling the entire Megillah prior to the reading is based on the opinions of the Tosafot, of the Tur, of the Bayit Hadash, of the Maharil, and there are Sephardic authorities that write this opinion as well, and it should be practiced according to the Peri Hadash, according to the Keneset HaGedolah, the Ben Ish Hai, the Kaf HaHayyim, Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, all write that this is how you read the Megillah. Prior to reading it, you unroll the entire Megillah.

This is not our custom. The custom that was practiced in Halab was that the Megillah is unrolled as you read it. And the reader, the Hazzan for the reader for the congregation does not roll what he read already like this, like a Sefer Torah, but rather he leaves unrolled what he read, and he's unrolling as he reads, and leaving unrolled what he read. However the congregants do roll their Megillot like a Sefer Torah so that it won't fall on the floor. And this opinion of unrolling it as you read it as opposed to unrolling the entire Megillah before you read it is based on the common understanding of the Halakhah, "Koreh UFoshet Ke'Iggeret," which means read and unroll like a scroll. So like a scroll means that you leave unrolled what you already read as opposed to a Sefer Torah. If you read and unroll like a Sefer Torah, then you roll what you read already on the other side.

Our custom was documented by Hakham Abraham Antebi who was the chief rabbi of Halab in the first part of the 19th century, was also documented by Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo who was born in Halab in 1894 and he lived there until he moved to Yerushalayim in 1935. The book Derekh Eress, which is a compendium of the customs of Halab, wrote the following: that the Hazzan unrolls the Megillah as he reads, and he does not roll it like a Sefer Torah, however the listeners roll it like a Sefer Torah so that it won't fall on the floor.

Now this was not only the custom in Halab, it was also the custom in Egypt. It's documented in the book of Egyptian customs known as Nehar Missrayim, which was published in 1908. Another compendium of customs known as Keter Shem Tob wrote the following: "The custom of the Land of Israel, Syria, Turkey, and Egypt is to read and unroll, and to leave unrolled what was already read." And then he added, "And I saw some men in the Land of Israel that unroll what they read, and before unrolling the next section, roll what they already read exactly like we do with the reading of the Sefer Torah." This book Keter Shem Tob was published in 1934.

Now it's important to note that our custom to unroll as you read is based on the writings of the Rif, of HaRambam, of the Rosh, of the Ritba, and Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. And it's also the opinion of the Shulhan Gaboah who is an important authority from Greece in the 18th century.

In our community, the custom of unrolling as we read was taught by Dayan Estrucha, 'Alav HaShalom, and it was maintained by our esteemed Hazzan, Isaac Cabasso, HaShem Ya'arikh Yamav UShnotav. In fact, Mr. Cabasso related to me that he was in Florida one year for Purim, and the Hazzan started to unroll the entire Megillah prior to reading, and he made a point to go up to the Tebah to stop him, and he explained to him that our custom is that we unroll the Megillah as we read it.

So therefore readers in our community should maintain our tradition. It's based, as we said, on Maran and HaRambam. It was documented by the rabbis of Aleppo, and it was maintained by our elders. This is our custom to unroll as we read as opposed to unrolling the entire Megillah prior to the reading, which is not our custom.

42.title: Introduction to the Kaddish
42.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed Tefilat Shahrit, and as I promised, we want to dedicate a few segments specifically to the important prayer of the Kaddish and the Minhagim in our community relating to this prayer. Now the Kaddish in its present form and wording and structure is not found in the Talmud, and it's something which evolved over time. As a matter of fact, even if you look at Mahzor Aram Soba, you'll see that the Nusah, the wording of the Kaddish from 500 years ago was much different than the wording that we have today.

The Kaddish, before we begin, I want to just give a few words of introduction regarding the Kaddish that will help us understand some of the Minhagim that will follow. This prayer is a prayer beseeching for the magnification, "Yitgaddal," and the sanctification, "Yitkaddash," of God's exalted name, "Shemeh Rabba," in this world that He created, "Be'Alma Di Bera Khir'uteh." It continues to speak about the hopes for a speedy redemption, "VeYassmah Purkaneh ViKareb Meshiheh Ba'Agala UBizman Karib," and it goes back to speak about His name, "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya Yitbarakh," until the end of the section.

Now this central phrase in the Kaddish, "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh," is indeed found in the Talmud and in Midrashim, as early as in Masekhet Berakhot, both in Hebrew and in Aramaic. It's unclear if this was a prayer and, if so, how was it used. There's a—an opinion that it was said after a learning session in the Bet HaMidrash. This is a little unclear. It's something which certainly evolved over time.

Now if you look at the words of the Kaddish and the content, there's nothing really to connect it directly to the deceased, which many people have the impression that this is a prayer for the dead. And indeed, certainly Minhagim developed connecting it to the deceased. However, there's nothing in the Kaddish which connects it. There are early references to its usage with regards to the Metim. One would be in the ninth century, the Siddur of Rab 'Amram Gaon, which he compiled for the Kehillot, other Kehillot, and he does say that this prayer should be said by a son on the grave of his father, he writes. Another source is the Ribash from the 14th century, 14th-century Spain, from the Megorashim, and he writes that for 12 months, a son should say this prayer for his father. It was really brought to the level of custom that we have it today by the Kabbalah in Sefat by the Ari, Zikhrono LiBerakhah, which mentioned that the saying of Kaddish helps elevate the soul, and then all the customs really developed from that, from those teachings.

However, before its association with the deceased, the Kaddish was a very important part of the prayer, both 'Al Pi HaPeshat and 'Al Pi HaKabbalah. 'Al Pi HaPeshat, we know from the videos, we know that this Shahrit is divided to seven sections. And one would be the Korbanot, second section, the Pesuke DeZimra, the third section is the Kedushah Meyushab, which includes the Keri'at Shema, the fourth and main section is the 'Amidah, which includes the Hazarah and Tahanunim, the fifth section being the Kedushah DeSidra, which includes Ashre and UBa LeSiyyon, followed by the sixth section, which is the Shir Shel Yom, and the last section, which is the Ketoret. And between each section, we have a Kaddish to separate one from the other, each with its appropriate Kaddish, which we'll get to in the customs later on.

According to the Kabbalah, there's different aspects of the world we live in and the prayer ascends to the highest form, which is Assilut, which is the 'Amidah, and then descends through Beri'ah, Yessirah, and 'Asiyah. So we begin with 'Asiyah, Yessirah, Beri'ah, Assilut, the 'Amidah, and go descend. And between each section of these worlds, the Kaddish helps us navigate and elevate and move to the next aspect.

Now the—because of these reasons and its importance in the prayer, that explains the Minhag of not only our community, but all Sefaradim, as opposed to the Minhag of the Ashkenazim, we do not ever skip a Kaddish. Even the Kaddishim which are unique to the Abelim or to those who have a requirement to say a Kaddish, like Yehe Shelama and 'Al Yisrael, if there's nobody in the Bet Keneset, in the Minyan, to say these Kaddishim, they are never skipped. The Hazzan is obligated to say this Kaddish. This is the custom of all Sefaradim. It's only the Ashkenazim that skip the Kaddishim.

What we're going to do in the next video is go through each Kaddish and compare the wording, the Nushaot, and the customs of our community regarding the wording of these Kaddishim. Shalom UBerakhah.

43.title: Rosh Hodesh Nisan, an Ancient Holiday
43.text:
Minhagim. Generally we speak about the Minhagim, Minhagim between Sefaradim and Ashkenazim or the Minhagim of various cities like Aleppo, Damascus, Cairo, Alexandria, Beirut, Baghdad, what have you. But today we're going to talk about a much more ancient custom, a custom that is based upon a Mishnah and the old practices of Eress Yisrael.

So Mishnah Rosh HaShanah, the first Perek, first Halakhah, clearly states: "Arba'ah Rashe Shanim Hem. BeEhad BeNisan Rosh HaShanah LaMelakhim VeLaRegalim." There are four Rosh HaShanahs, the first of Nisan is the Rosh HaShanah of kings as well as holidays. And this is the true Rosh HaShanah of the year, this is the Rosh HaShanah as prescribed by the Torah in Parashat Bo. It says, "Rishon Hu Lakhem LeHodshe HaShanah," it is the first to you for the months of the year, and from that's the point we count the holidays technically, and the holidays of course start with Pesah. And Pesah is of course the holiday of the Ge'ulah, of the redemption.

Now, this is a holiday that this holiday being Rosh Hodesh Nisan, Rosh Hodesh Nisan because it's a Rosh HaShanah, it is a holiday. And for some reason, people have forgotten about it, it has fallen out of use. So let me explain to you what has happened.

There were two ancient Minhagim. There were the Minhagim of Eress Yisrael, and there were the Minhagim of Babel. And they were both flourishing very nicely until the time of the Crusades. The Crusades arrived in Eress Yisrael, in Palestine at the time, in the year 1099. When they got there, they basically decimated the Jewish community. Those that were lucky enough to survive fled. Most seem to have fled to areas south, and more specifically to Egypt. Of course, there were Jews from Eress Yisrael that were already living in Egypt and traveling back and forth to Cairo because they were doing business there.

So in Cairo at the time, we're talking about 1099, you know, let's go from the year 1000, even the year 1100, we didn't have Sefaradim and Ashkenazim, those distinctions didn't exist yet, we had Eress Yisrael and Babel. And they had two distinct synagogues following different Minhagim, styles of prayers, patterns, customs, what have you. Those living in Cairo that came from Eress Yisrael and following that Minhag continued with the practices of Eress Yisrael, and that was to celebrate with much pomp and fanfare Rosh Hodesh Nisan the way it would have actually been celebrated by the Bet Din in Yerushalayim. And this was a old, old custom, obviously as we saw, it goes back to the Mishnah. It's not something that existed in Babel, in Babylonia.

So any custom of such or related to it or similar to it that existed in any other community obviously shows you that it's an ancient community that had old Minhagim. And we have similarities with such a Minhag going on in Tunisia and in Libya, where they gathered in the homes to celebrate the night of Rosh Hodesh.

In Halab, we have the testimony of Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Bet HaBehirah. He writes very clearly on the first page of the book in fact, the third Halakhah, he writes, "UBeArssenu Aram Soba, Zot Omeret Halab, Nahagu LeHarbot Nerot BeBet HaKeneset ULeHarbot BePiyyutim Kemo Yom Tob, UMinhag Nakhon Hu." The Minhag in Halab: to light candles, to sing songs, to get dressed up, all in the style of Yom Tob. So this is obviously an ancient Minhag. It's something that died out in Halab, but it did exist in the past.

Now, where did this Minhag really continue to exist and to exist in a very powerful way? It was in Egypt, in Cairo in fact. Because it landed in Cairo and it flourished there in its own Bet Keneset, it continued to grow and prosper over there. This Minhag became known as Seder El-Tawhid, the order of the Tawhid. Tawhid means the unification, declaring the oneness, the uniqueness of Bore 'Olam.

We speak about His uniqueness on the night of Rosh Hodesh Nisan. Rosh Hodesh Nisan is the time in the Torah that tells us that HaShem told 'Am Yisrael through Moshe Rabbenu that they're going to be redeemed, taken out of Egypt on the 14th of Nisan, celebrate Hag HaPesah, Hag HaMassot as well, and also it's a time to reinstill within our hearts, our souls, our minds the greatness of HaShem, the miracles that He does for us, anytime that we think things are moving in a negative manner and things are looking down, we can never forget that HaShem is there and doing His utmost for us, as long as we rely on HaShem, we pray to Him, we praise Him, we sing His praises, we share His miracles with the rest of our friends and family, He doesn't obviously forget us and He looks favorably upon us. And this is what Rosh Hodesh Nisan, you know, stands for us today.

So this is an ancient Minhag. Rosh Hodesh Nisan is less than a week away, it's a time to reconnect with this ancient holiday of Rosh Hodesh Nisan, whether you're going to do it at home, whether you can do it in a gathering, you know, to do it as it was done in Halab, as the way it was done in Cairo, as the way it was done in Libya, Tunisia, it makes no difference. The point is to celebrate Rosh Hodesh Nisan the way it's meant to be celebrated, and God willing, we'll see that Ge'ulah speedily in our days, Amen.

44.title: Roasted Meat and the Zeroa' on Pesah
44.text:
Eating roasted meats on the first two nights of Pesah is dependent upon local custom. In some places, they had the custom not to eat roasted meats on the first two nights of Pesah, since roasted meats would seem similar to the Pesah offering. And the Pesah offering must be offered in a Bet Mikdash. Since we don't have the Bet HaMikdash in our times, by eating roasted meats it would appear similar to the Pesah sacrifice, and in order to avoid the appearance of that violation of eating an offering that was offered outside of the Bet HaMikdash, they would not serve or eat any roasted meats on the first two nights of Pesah. In other places, the custom was to serve roasted meats on the first two nights of Pesah, and only a whole roasted lamb was prohibited.

The custom of Aleppo was to eat roasted meats on the first two nights of Pesah. This custom was recorded by Hakham Abraham Hamwey in 1875 in his Mahzor for Pesah and Shabu'ot, which was known as Bet HaBehirah. And there he wrote, "A place that has the custom to eat roasted meat on the nights of Pesah, eats it." And then he continued, "And in our land Aram Soba, Halab, it is customary to eat roasted meat." He wrote this with regards to the eating of the Zeroa', the roasted shank bone, as he states in his instructions, "After eating the sandwich, we eat the Zeroa', like it is written in Shulhan 'Arukh: A place that has the custom to eat roasted meat on the nights of Pesah, eats it."

So from here we learn that in Aleppo they roasted the shank bone, and that they did not differentiate between the shank bone and other roasted meats. Meaning that there are some places that even though they had the custom to eat roasted meats, when it came to the roasted shank bone they would refrain. That would seem similar to the prohibition of eating meat that was offered outside of the Bet HaMikdash. But in Aleppo, they ate roasted meats, and they also roasted and ate the shank bone.

This was also the original custom in the Land of Israel. Rabbi Hayyim Menashe Sethon recorded this as the custom of the Land of Israel in his book Eress Hayyim, which was published in 1908. And also Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin wrote this in his book of customs, Keter Shem Tob. The custom, this is what he wrote: "The custom of the Sefaradim in the Land of Israel is to eat the roasted Zeroa' in the middle of the meal." And in his footnote he added, "And from there we learn that they have the custom to eat roasted meat on the nights of Pesah."

Now a more recent tradition that developed in many families was to roast the shank bone and then boil it. Now really the practice of boiling the shank bone originated in the writings of Ashkenazic authorities. There were some Ashkenazic authorities that required one to eat the meat that was in memory of the Pesah offering, but the custom of Ashkenazim was not to eat roasted meats on the first two nights of Pesah, and therefore they came with the solution of boiling it. However, according to Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, the proper way to prepare the meat in memory of the Pesah offering is to roast it, but he doesn't require you to eat it. So in those communities that don't eat roasted meats, they just didn't eat the Zeroa'. In other communities where they ate roasted meats, some didn't eat the Zeroa' because they differentiated between the Zeroa' and other roasted meats.

But as we said, the custom of Aleppo was to eat roasted meats and also to eat the roasted shank bone, and therefore it's not necessary to boil it. This custom is in accordance with the actual law that was recorded by Maran and HaRambam that only prohibits eating a whole roasted lamb. In Halab and among the Sefaradim in the Land of Israel, they did not have the custom to be stringent beyond the actual law, like they had in other communities in different

45.title: The Different Kaddishim and Their Nusah
45.text:
Shalom UBerakhah MiYerushalayim. We gave a brief introduction to the Kaddish in our last video, and now we want to go through the different Kaddishim and the Nushaot, the wording which may have different customs for different communities.

We have a number of Kaddishim that we say. The one we're all familiar with, the one which is common to all the Kaddishim, is the from "Yitgaddal VeYitkaddash" until "DaAmiran Be'Alma VeImru Amen." When we say this alone, like before Yosser or after or before Ashre, this is called Hassi Kaddish. Once every prayer, the Hazzan will say Kaddish Titkabbal, accepting our prayers after the prayer is over, "Titkabbal Selotana UBa'utana." We have, in addition, Kaddish Yehe Shelama Rabba, which is said following recitation of Torah SheBikhtab, and that's why we say after the Shir Shel Yom, or if we have a group that's reading Tehillim on Shabbat, we'll say this Kaddish. And then we have Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, which is said after we recite Torah SheBe'al Peh, and that's why this is a Kaddish that you will find after the Korbanot before Hodu, after Ketoret, after let's say an Azkarah that we read Mishnayot, they'll say Kaddish 'Al Yisrael.

There are a number of other Kaddishim which we won't go into, but I'll mention them: you have Kaddish Targum, "De'Atid LeHadata 'Alma," which we'll say on Tish'ah BeAb, or when I was growing up they used to say it at funerals, il-ba'id. It's said when we do a Siyum, Siyum Masekhet, we have also a Kaddish Targum. We also have Kaddish 'Al Hayye HaAress, Kaddish "Te'anu VeTe'atru BeRahamim Min HaShamayim," so there's a number of the Kaddishim.

But let's go right to the Kaddish and look and see if there's any differences in Nusah and what is the custom of our community. As I said, this Kaddish that we have today is much different than the Kaddish of Mahzor Aram Soba, the Kaddishim that evolved over time.

So now we have in the—Let's start with the main section of the Kaddish: "Yitgaddal VeYitkaddash." We say "Be'Alma Di Bera Khir'uteh" with a Khaf, as opposed to some grammarians that want to insist it's "Kir'uteh," and which is fine, except our custom is "Be'Alma Di Bera Khir'uteh."

We have "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya." You have some Nushaot which have "Le'Alme 'Almaya." Growing up, I always heard "ULe'Alme 'Almaya," and indeed that's how it's printed in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob. This is the Siddurim I'm using now, the Kol Ya'akob.

Finally, in the Hassi Kaddish, we have "Le'Ela Min Kol Birkhata Shirata Tushbehata." Now, you're going to say that's not Kol Ya'akob. Well, I'm looking at the original Kol Ya'akob from 1985. It said "Tushbehata." Since then, it's been changed to "Tishbehata." The Kabbalists insist that we say "Tishbehata." I'm not Baki, but it seems that grammatically "Tushbehata" may be more appropriate, and 'Al Pi HaKabbalah they insist on "Tishbehata." So, just pointing that out. That's the Hassi Kaddish.

Now we go to the Kaddish Titkabbal, which is said once every prayer by the Hazzan. So you have "Titkabbal Selotana UBa'utana 'Im Selothon UBa'uthon DeKhol Bet Yisrael." What's written what's printed in the books is "Kodam Abuna Di Bishmaya VeAr'a," right, in front of our Father of the heavens and the earth. Now, many modern Siddurim, not the Halabi Siddurim, other Sefaradi communities will have "Kodam Abuna Di Bishmaya" without "VeAr'a" because we say "Abinu SheBashamayim," not "Abinu SheBashama... VaAress." Our custom is to always say "Shamaya VeAr'a." However, there is a change which is indeed a custom that I heard a lot growing up, and it does solve the problem in addition: you'll hear many people say "Kodam Abuna Elahana Mare Shamaya VeAr'a." So that's another custom which you may find.

Continuing on, in the 'Oseh Shalom, it's printed "Hu BeRahamav Ya'aseh Shalom 'Alenu." I've heard many, many times, and even in Ades, most of the Zekenim will say "Hu BeRaham... HaRabbim Ya'aseh Shalom 'Alenu."

Now let's move on to Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, because here is also a couple changes. So "'Al Yisrael Ve'Al Rabbanan Ve'Al Talmidehon," again this is because we just read Torah SheBe'al Peh, "Ve'Al Kol Talmide Talmidehon De'Askin BeOraita Kaddishta." I hear many people that say instead of "De'Askin BeOraita Kaddishta," they add "DeYatbin Ve'Askin BeOraita Kaddishta." It's a legitimate Nusah that you may be hearing.

"Yehe Lana," we'll continue with that same section of 'Al Yisrael, "Yehe Lana ULehon ULekhon." There are Nushaot, there are there is a custom amongst the Halabiyim, and it's brought down in the Sefer Derekh Eress, which says "Yehe Lana ULekhon ULehon."

Continuing on, it says "Hinna VeHisda VeRahame Min Kodam Mare Shemaya VeAr'a." Here also you'll find an addition. You'll have some people saying the Kaddish, you'll say, "Oh what is he saying, he's saying adding a few words." After "Hinna VeHisda," before "Rahame," he'll say "VeHayye Arikhe UMzone Tabe." Actually it's after "Rahame": "ULekhon Hinna VeHisda VeRahame VeHayye Arikhe UMzone Tabe," some say "UMzone Revihe," "Min Kodam Mare Shemaya VeAr'a VeImru Amen." And this is another change that you may be hearing. It's a legitimate custom as well. There's no definitive custom. Most people don't add it, but it's there. Shalom UBerakhah.

46.title: Mish'arotam and Its Many Variations
46.text:
The holiday of Pesah automatically makes one think of the Haggadah. And the Haggadah obviously invokes so much memory and ritual. But there's one thing that until very recently wasn't printed in the Haggadah, but we had a tradition of doing. And this existed throughout the Jewish world, and this is Mish'arotam.

Because it wasn't printed, I think it was forgotten in certain communities. But based upon ancient sources, this tradition of Mish'arotam and variations on it existed among Ashkenazim as well as Sefaradim, and existed in different communities in different ways. In some communities, it would just be one person that would do it and actually walk around the house. In some places, it would just be the children. In some places, it would just be the males. But a variation of Mish'arotam definitely existed in different communities at different times. Within our community, the communities of the Middle East, specifically we're talking now about Syria, Lebanon, Egypt, and even Iraq, this custom of Mish'arotam grew, flourished, and developed, and on these shores in America changed once again.

How is that? So, Mish'arotam, people think Mish'arotam, "Oh, I learned that in school, I learned that in school." So, prior to 1975, nobody learned it in school. In 1975, the Young Shaare Zion Haggadah came out, and this was made in conjunction with the Yeshivah of Flatbush. And many people were called upon to make this particular work. And this is the first time that we have a Sephardic Haggadah printed in the United States that actually has Mish'arotam in it. And in this version of Mish'arotam, it tells you the Mish'arotam, and "Min Wen Jaye," "Min Missrayim," "Wen Rayeh," "Yerushalayim," "Eshu Zawattak," "Massah UMaror." And at the end, it says, "Variations on this theme are followed in many homes." And that's the crucial point: variations. What happened is, by printing it here, from this point on, and especially since 1978, it became part of the curriculum in Magen David and in other community schools, this became the format, and particular versions and variations in different homes have been forgotten.

So let's run through some of these variations very quickly. First and foremost, we know we take the middle Massah, we break it into two portions: a larger portion and a smaller portion. There are some that'll have a Minhag to just break it into larger and smaller, some that break it into two different letters of the Hebrew alphabet. In any case, the larger portion is the one that gets put on the side for the Afikomin, and generally on the side meant it went into a white towel. And that white towel with the Afikomin piece in it was used for Mish'arotam.

So the head of the household would start holding it in his right hand, placing it over his left shoulder as such, and reciting the Pasuk of Mish'arotam, which is really two half Pesukim: "Mish'arotam Serurot BeSimlotam 'Al Shikhmam UBne Yisrael 'Asu KiDbar Moshe." And then the question and answer would proceed: "Min Wen Jaye?" Where are you coming from? He would respond: "Min Missrayim." Next question: "Wen Rayeh?" Where are you going? He would respond: "Yerushalayim."

From that point on is where things change. According to this Haggadah that I showed you, it showed another set of questions: "Eshu Zawattak?" "Massah UMaror." Now that is not something done among all Middle Easterners, not even among all Halabiyeh, and in certain communities of Halabiyeh, for example in Argentina, they practically don't know of it at all. They just end at that point. If we look at Mahzor Bet HaBehirah of Hakham Abraham Hamwey, printed in Livorno, Italy, but he was from Halab, writing about Halab, he doesn't mention that last set of questions. The first place we find those set of questions, and it's only the first part of it, is in a Baghdadian Haggadah that was printed in 1887 in Livorno, and it says the last question of "Eshu Zawattak?" and instead of answering "Massah UMaror," the person would just answer "Mah Nishtanah."

So again, this is just a show of the variations. In many homes after reciting "LiYrushalayim," and then after they go around the entire table, they would just answer "LaShanah HaBa'ah BiYerushalayim HaBenuyah." In some families, or some homes, some communities, after saying "LiYrushalayim," then each person, before passing it to the next person, would say "Ba'Agala UBizman Karib VeImru Amen." So there were different variations, and unfortunately, the good part of printing it is that it wasn't forgotten, and the bad part of printing it is that the variations were forgotten.

So once again, hold the towel that has the Afikomin in it with the right hand over the left shoulder, you say the Mish'alotam, the questions are asked, and then it's passed to the next person to the right. In some families, the entire set of people around the table will do it, meaning men, women, and children. In some families, it's just the men, some it's just the men and the children. Everybody should adhere to the Minhagim of their families.

Most important part in all of this is we say "Bene Yisrael 'Asu KiDbar Moshe," and as Hakham Yisshak Alfiah has pointed out in his Siah Yisshak, we're saying this to remind us that everything we've done until this point is that we are following all the Halakhot that Moshe Rabbenu gave to us, and we're continuing this tradition from generation to generation. Let's continue with our Minhagim, let's not forget about them, let's not make fun of them. They are beautiful traditions that we should really pass on from generation to generation. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot.

47.title: Shaving During the 'Omer
47.text:
What about shaving during the 'Omer? Is it prohibited? Is there a suggested stringency to refrain from shaving? What's our custom regarding shaving and taking haircuts during the 'Omer?

Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, who was born and educated in Halab, and then went on to become the Chief Rabbi of Argentina, wrote in a responsa in his book known as Yisshak Yeranen: in Halab, they did not have the custom to refrain from shaving on the 'Omer, except for one person out of a thousand. And the rabbis also used to shave. Perhaps this was the custom from before the times of Maran, since we know from the Tur that only some places did not take haircuts and shave during the 'Omer. From the words of Rabbi Chehebar, we see that it is referring both to taking haircuts as well as shaving.

Hakham 'Obadia Yosef wrote the following in his book Hazon 'Obadia: "VeHaHaredim LiDbar HaShem Nizharim Gam LeGabe Giluah HaZakan." Those that are more pious in their observance also refrain from shaving. Meaning, even in those places that have the custom to refrain from taking haircuts during the 'Omer, only those that wish to be more stringent extend the custom to refraining from shaving as well. But it's not part of the original custom. As Hakham 'Obadia explained, the halakhic authorities never spoke about shaving one's beard at all in their times. This is based on the fact that Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, when he mentions the custom of refraining from taking haircuts, he uses the word "LeHistapper," which means to take a haircut, as opposed to the word "LeGalleah," which usually includes shaving as well.

Furthermore, if one finds it very uncomfortable to refrain from shaving during the 'Omer, and all the more so if it would affect one's livelihood, he is exempt from the custom, as Hakham 'Obadia Yosef wrote in Yabia' Omer: when one is uncomfortable, he may be lenient with the custom.

So, to summarize, the custom of refraining from haircuts during the 'Omer was not accepted in all places. And according to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, the custom, even among the rabbis of Halab, was to be lenient. And even in those places that do refrain from haircuts, haircuts does not necessarily include shaving as well. It's an optional stringency that one could choose to accept upon himself. When I was growing up in the community, the prevalent custom was to refrain from haircuts until the 34th day of the 'Omer, but only a few individuals refrained from shaving as well. Like we explained, shaving is not part of the original custom. It's an added stringency that some might want to voluntarily accept upon themselves.

48.title: Bowing and Answering During Kaddish
48.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are filming today in our home due to the situation, not permitted to be in the Kenis, so hopefully by next time we will be back in Kenis Ades, and Bore 'Olam should send Refu'ah Shelemah to all of those who have been affected, inshallah, very, very soon.

In our last couple of videos, we have been discussing the Kaddish, and the structure, and the Nusah, and we are going to conclude this mini-series of the Kaddish with the Minhagim of the person saying the Kaddish, and the Minhagim of the people who are listening and answering the Kaddish.

Regarding the person saying the Kaddish, there are two different approaches as to when he bows down. First, I will tell you our Minhag, and the Minhag I have seen growing up, and it is also based largely on Maran and then the Bet Yosef as well, based on the Kol Bo, where there are five times that we make a Keri'ah. The first is when we say "Yitgaddal VeYitkaddash Shemeh Rabba." In the next phrase, "Be'Alma Di" and "BeHayyekhon," there are no Keri'ot. When we say "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh," we are Kore'a. "Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya Yitbarakh" is the third time. "VeYishtabbah," and so on, until "Shemeh DeKudsha Berikh Hu" is the fourth time. "Le'Ela Min Kol Birkhata Shirata Tishbehata VeNehamata DaAmiran Be'Alma VeImru Amen" is the fifth and last time we do a Keri'ah in the Kaddish. This is the obligatory Keri'ot of the Hazzan.

There is another approach brought by some Aharonim: Kaf HaHayyim, Palachi, Hesed LaAlafim, Shalme Sibbur, who say to bow down simply before, right before the Kahal answers the Amenim. So the five times before the Amen: "Yehe Shemeh Rabba," "Meshiheh," and so on. That is not the custom that I have observed in our community throughout the years.

You will also find occasionally when the words are uttered "BeHayyekhon UBYomekhon," in your lives and in your days, we are talking about the Ge'ulah, you will see the Hazzanim sometimes will do "BeHayyekhon UBYomekhon." It is not required, but just you may notice it, I did want to point it out. Similarly, like the Keri'at Shema when you have "LeMa'an Yirbu Yemekhem VeYeme Benekhem," you may notice it, so I did want to point it out.

Finally, I want to discuss when we say "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav" in the Kaddishim, like Kaddish Titkabbal, or Yehe Shelama, or 'Al Yisrael, where you have at the end "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav." There is a debate going back to the early Rishonim as to whether we go back "'Oseh," first we go back three steps starting with the left, "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav Hu BeRahamav Ya'aseh Shalom 'Alenu Ve'Al Kol 'Ammo Yisrael VeImru Amen," whether we do that on every Kaddish or only in Kaddish Titkabbal. Because Kaddish Titkabbal, the perception is that it is for the Hazzan, and it corresponds to the Hazarah, and being that in the Hazarah he did not say 'Oseh Shalom, he stops at "Yihyu LeRasson," so this is the completion of the 'Oseh Shalom in the 'Amidah and the Hazarah that he didn't go back three steps. There is a debate amongst the Rishonim and the Aharonim.

Our custom in our community, from what I have observed throughout the decades, is that on every Kaddish where there is "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav," the one saying it will go back the three steps and then say "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav Hu BeRahamav Ya'aseh Shalom." It is actually written BeFerush in a couple of the latter Hakhme Aram Soba: Rabbi Eliyahu Hamwey in Pe'er Eliyahu, the Helek Bet, towards the very end when he comments on, he made commentaries on Maran, he deals extensively with this discussion, and he concludes that we do go back every time we say "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav." Also, Rabbi Moshe Attieh in his book Me'at Mayim also mentions it. So that is the custom in our community.

Now, regarding the people who are listening and answering the Kaddish: First of all, our custom in our community and most Sefaradim, we are not required to stand up for every Kaddish like we find amongst many Ashkenazim. However, if we are caught standing and the Kaddish is beginning, we do not sit down. It is based on the writings of Maharhu, based on the Ari. We do not sit down, we remain standing until the person who is listening to the Kaddish, the person standing responds "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh" until "Be'Alma," then he can sit down. That is the custom.

Now, very interestingly, interesting enough in our community, if a person is in that position, he comes into the Kenis and the Hazzan is starting to sing the Kaddishim that we sing either Shahrit of Shabbat in the morning or Lel Shabbat or before 'Arbit, we do not require the person to remain standing throughout the Kaddish if the Hazzan is singing it. It's too much of a Torah, and that's what I've observed also in our community. For those people who don't know where they are or they're not paying attention and they do sit down, rest assured there will be someone in the Kehillah saying, "Hey!" stand up, reminding them. That's also part of the flavor of praying in the Kenis.

Regarding answering "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh," there are a number of different Minhagim. The Minhag which I've seen the most is, like I mentioned earlier, is to say "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya Yitbarakh," entire segment until "DaAmiran Be'Alma," as we continue "Le'Ela 'Al Kol Birkhata, Shirata, Tushbehata, VeNehamata, DaAmiran Be'Alma," and that's one approach, and that's the prevailing custom. There are those that answer only until "Yishtabbah," excuse me, "Yitbarakh": "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya Yitbarakh," and there are still a small minority which go until "Shemeh DeKudsha Berikh Hu." Those are the three possibilities. Again, the main custom is to read all the way until "Be'Alma."

Finally, we have a custom in our community that when you have the Kaddishim which have "VeRevah VeHassalah," when the Hazzan says "VeRevah VeHassalah," you hear the people will yell out, "VeRevah!" Again, not obligatory, but it's a custom which is well known. And Be'Ezrat HaShem, "Revah VeHassalah Yabo LeKhol 'Am Yisrael BiMherah BeYamenu, Amen." Shalom UBerakhah.

49.title: Our Pronunciation of the Alef-Bet
49.text:
Alef-Bet, the Hebrew alphabet. It seems in the last few decades, something that was so simple, so commonly known as the Hebrew alphabet, the way we pronounce it, we being the Jews of the Middle East, and more specifically Syria, Lebanon, and Egypt, there was a specific way that we pronounced it. It was a very easy way that we pronounced it. We knew the letters, we know the sounds of the letters, but in recent decades, especially with the influence of teachers from other communities or based upon modern Israeli pronunciation, a lot of that seems to be being attacked, and it's important that we know our pronunciation because it's still the pronunciation that invariably we use in our prayers, and it's something that should be used in all our reading, all of our learning, and something that we have to make sure that we continue with it in our prayers as well.

So, I'm going to review the letters of the Hebrew alphabet the way we pronounce them. So, as we know, these are the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, it's called the Alef-Bet, and we'll go through them one by one.

First is Alef. Alef, very easy, A sound. Next letter, Bet. Bet, whether it has Dagesh or no Dagesh, meaning whether it has a dot or not or no dot in it, that second letter Bet is pronounced as a B sound. It's never pronounced as a V, as nowadays it's become common to become with a dot it's a Bet and without a dot it's a Vet, so it's B and V, but we don't have that tradition, we pronounce it as a B.

The third letter is a Gimmel. Gimmel has two different sounds: with a dot it's a Gimmel, a hard G sound, and without a dot, without a Dagesh, it's called a Ghimel, so it's a GH sound. Fourth letter is a Dalet. Dalet, whether it has a Dagesh or no Dagesh, with the dot, without the dot, it's a D sound. Next letter is a Heh, regular H sound. Sixth letter is a Vav, that's our V sound. Seventh letter, Zayin, Z.

Eighth letter is a Het. The Het is a distinct sound that is a guttural sound from the back of the throat. It's not a H sound, and it's not a ch sound, it's a ch sound, Het.

The ninth letter is a Tet. Tet is a different sound than a regular T, it's a much harder T. Later on we'll have a regular T sound, the last letter of the alphabet, called the Tav, and that's a T sound. But right now we're dealing with the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and it's called the Tet, so it's a T sound.

Tenth letter is a Yod, Y. Then we have the eleventh letter is a Kaf. The Kaf would have a Dagesh, it would have a dot, and if the Dagesh is removed, if there's no Dagesh, it's called a Khaf, and that's your KH sound. So now we had a Heh, the fifth letter, Heh sound, H sound, Het, the eighth letter, and now we had the Khaf, which was the eleventh letter without a dot, as a ch sound.

Then you have the twelfth letter is a Lamed, L sound. Then we have the Mim, it's an M sound, it's Mim, not a Mem. Then you have the Nun, which is the N sound. Samekh, it's a regular S. 'Ayin. 'Ayin is not an Alef, Alef is the first letter, and this is the 'Ayin, so it's two different sounds: Alef is a plain A sound, and this is 'Ayin, a deep guttural A sound, 'a. Then we have Peh. Peh is the sound of a P that has a Dagesh in it, and Feh, the F sound, without a Dagesh.

Now we get to the Sadi. Sadi is a very, very important letter. It's a double S sound coming also again from deep within the mouth, and this is a sound that does not exist in Western languages, it does not exist in European languages, and therefore there's such a confusion because most of those people that came and modernized the Hebrew language today in Israel came from Germany or Russia or Poland, and they brought a sound with them called this sound of Tzadi, which is a TS sound or a TZ sound, and that's not something that we ever had. Hebrew is a Semitic language, and therefore it has to have a Semitic sound, and this Sadi is that sound. It's a double S sound. We find it in last names like my own last name, Mosseri, it's Mosseri, or Kassin, Qassin, or Kessab, Qassab, you have that S sound, that double S sound is there, and that's a Tzadi.

Then you have a Kof. A Kof is not a Kaf. The Kaf, as we mentioned, is the eleventh letter with a dot in it, and that's a Kaf, but this is a Kof. It's a deeper sound. Then you have Resh, R, Shin is a SH sound, Sin is a S sound identical to the Samekh, and then we have Tav, the final letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which with or without a Dagesh, that's with or without the dot, it remains a regular, plain T sound.

So, to review: Alef, Bet, Gimmel, Ghimel, Dalet, Heh, Vav, Zayin, Het, Tet, Yod, Kaf, Khaf, Lamed, Mem, Nun, Samekh, 'Ayin, Peh, Feh, Tzadi, Kof, Resh, Shin, Sin, Tav.

50.title: Celebrating Lag La'Omer
50.text:
As you know, it's customary to refrain from reciting Tahanunim, 'Anenu, LeDavid on the holiday of Lag La'Omer. Already beginning from Minhah prior to Lag La'Omer, we say Yehi Shem. But beyond that, what is the traditional way to celebrate Lag La'Omer, and what exactly is the celebration for?

First of all, since every night when we count the 'Omer, our tradition is to count with "La'Omer," as opposed to the Ashkenazim, who when they count, they say "Ba'Omer," therefore our tradition is to refer to the holiday as Lag La'Omer, as opposed to the Ashkenazim, who refer to the holiday as Lag Ba'Omer. Furthermore, even though we wait until the 34th day of the 'Omer to take a haircut, the celebration of Lag La'Omer is on the 33rd night of the 'Omer. This is because that celebration is in honor of Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai, even though the students of Rabbi 'Akiba that passed away didn't stop passing away until the 34th day of the 'Omer.

There are different opinions as to what the significance of Lag La'Omer was in regards to Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai. According to one tradition, Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai passed away on Lag La'Omer, and therefore some want to explain that since Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai was sentenced to death by the Romans, and he escaped, and he miraculously survived, and he went on to live a full life until he died a natural death, therefore we celebrate his miraculous survival by celebrating on the anniversary of his natural death. Others taught that the celebration is due to the fact that Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai revealed great secrets of the Torah to his students on that day just before he passed away.

However, according to the Hida, Rabbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai did not pass away on Lag La'Omer, and therefore he suggested that perhaps Rabbi 'Akiba began teaching Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai and the other outstanding students, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose, on that day, even before the previous students stopped passing away. And this was done in order to perpetuate the oral Torah for the Jewish people.

So Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai was both an important Tanna who continued the tradition of the oral Torah that was subsequently recorded in the Mishnah, along with Rabbi 'Akiba's other students, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose, and also an important teacher of the mystical teachings that were recorded in the Zohar. We honor his memory on Lag La'Omer, either because he revealed important teachings on that day before he passed away, or it's a day that the oral Torah was perpetuated, in spite of the death of 24,000 of Rabbi 'Akiba's previous students.

In Halab, the custom was to gather in the Kenis on the night of Lag La'Omer, and to set up many cups of olive oil, and in front of each cup, there was a small piece of paper with a name written on it: either one of the patriarchs, Abraham, Yisshak, Ya'akob, or one of the matriarchs, Sarah, Ribkah, Rahel, Leah, or one of the prophets, or one of the prophetesses, or one of the great talmudic rabbis. And the privilege to light each candle was auctioned off with the highest prices being paid for the candles in memory of Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai and Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes. And all of this was done with the accompaniment of music, and Pizmonim, and a festive meal in honor of the occasion. This custom was documented in the book Derekh Eress, which is a compendium of the customs of Halab, and with regards to this custom he quoted Rabbi Nissim Zafrani.

Over the years, this custom was forgotten here in Brooklyn, but in recent years it has come back in some synagogues. I just want to point out that it was never our tradition to light bonfires, as is customary among the Hasidim, and became popular in Israel. It's not our tradition to have barbecues in honor of Lag La'Omer. Our custom was always cups of oil, each one in memory of one of our great ancestors. And Be'Ezrat HaShem, with their merit, may we see an end to our troubles, and the Ge'ulah Shelemah BiMherah BeYamenu, Amen.

51.title: Counting the 'Omer in the Kenis
51.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. Today we will be discussing the customs of our community regarding the counting of the 'Omer, the Sefirat Ha'Omer, as it is practiced in the synagogue, in the Kenis.

So, firstly, where in the prayer do we say the Sefirat Ha'Omer? We know we begin the second night of Pesah up until the night before Shabu'ot. It's an obligation on each individual to count, "USfartem Lakhem." It's a Missvah DeRabbanan nowadays according to most Posekim.

Where do we count the 'Omer? The custom in our community has always been, and in Halab as well, as recorded by many, many Hakhamim, that this was indeed the custom, and today is the custom, that we say the 'Omer following Kaddish Titkabbal. There are other communities which recite the 'Omer after 'Alenu LeShabbeah. That is not our custom. Our custom is after Kaddish Titkabbal. A possible reason is that Kaddish Titkabbal, as I mentioned in the videos of Tefilat Shahrit, Titkabbal represents the end of the prayer. What we read after is Minhagim. And therefore, as soon as we finish the prayer, the first opportunity we have to fulfill the Missvah, so we count at that point. Another possible advantage to that custom is that if you wait until after 'Alenu LeShabbeah, it's possible that people will be leaving the synagogue and be missing the Berakhah, and then find it difficult to remember to count the 'Omer that night at home.

Now, everybody counts the 'Omer, and the custom in our community—and again this is testified to by Hakham Yisshak Chehebar in his book and many other Hakhamim—the custom of the Halabi community was always that the Kahal recites the Berakhah and counts the 'Omer first, followed by the Hazzan. Now, many communities do not do it that way. But it seems that this was the prevailing custom in many, many communities going back a long, long time. Even Ribbi Eliyahu Hamwey in Bet HaBehirah, he mentions what the Rashba writes, you know going back 700 years, that in the event that the Hazzan says it first, what does that do for the Kahal? Do they fulfill their obligation, and can they make a Berakhah or not? So we see from that analysis that indeed it was the custom for the Kahal to say it first, lest they have Kavvanah to be Yosse Yede Hobah when the Hazzan makes the Berakhah, which is usually the case in Hallel or Shofar or Megillah, and then they may get into a Safek of whether they have to make a Berakhah or not. To avoid that, the Kahal says it first.

Growing up always, in all the synagogues I prayed in in Brooklyn, always the Kahal said the Berakhah first. If it changed today, I'm not familiar with all the synagogues. It's possible that Hakhamim came in from other communities or other backgrounds and weren't familiar with our custom. But that is the custom.

Finally, what do we say? How do we say the 'Omer? If you look in the Siddur, it just begins with the Berakhah. And indeed, also Hakham Yisshak Chehebar writes that in our communities, in our custom in Halab, was not to say the LeShem Yihud followed by the Pesukim. We begin with the Berakhah.

Now I know some I've heard from people who used to pray in Shaare Zion many decades ago that Hakham Ya'akob Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom, our chief rabbi, the first night of the holiday on the first night of the Berakhah, the second night of the holiday, would get up and say the LeShem Yihud and all the Pesukim, and say the entire Seder of the Kessirat Ha'Omer, which is not found in our Mahzorim or our Siddurim, but is found in other Mahzorim. It's possible that this was a custom he brought with him from the Kabbalists of Yerushalayim, or other communities which say the Seder Kessirat Ha'Omer. I understand there are maybe one or two other congregations which say the Seder Kessirat Ha'Omer, which is fine, except Hakham Yisshak Chehebar was very insistent that we do not say the LeShem Yihud beforehand.

Indeed, even in Ades, Hakham Yosef Sha'yo, Yizkerehu LeTob, told me that his father, Hakham 'Ezra Sha'yo, never said the LeShem Yihud. And indeed we don't say we don't have our Hazzanim say LeShem Yihud or Hakhamim before all the Missvot, Megillah, Shofar, Lulab. The Hazzanim were not have did not have the custom to do so.

Following the counting of the 'Omer, we say HaRahaman, which is mentioning the Bet HaMikdash, followed by LaMnasseah, Ana BeKhoah, and then we continue Shir LaMa'alot, and the end of 'Arbit as usual. Shalom UBerakhah.
