52.title: Azharot and Sweets on Shabu'ot
52.text:
The holiday of Shabu'ot. Shabu'ot is our yearly commemoration of 'Am Yisrael receiving the Torah from Bore 'Olam at Har Sinai. The holiday of Shabu'ot has many beautiful Minhagim associated with it. The most beautiful of all is the recitation of the Azharot.

Azharot is a poetic form of all 613 Missvot of the Torah. And this endears the Missvot to us. We get to enjoy them. We get to really see the beauty of the Missvot. And so many of our Hakhamim over the course of centuries have turned the Missvot of the Torah into poetic form, but the grandest of all are the Azharot of Rabbenu Shelomo Ibn Gabirol of 10th-century Spain. He took the Azharot and he really raised them to a higher level, so much so that this has become a custom among all Sephardic Jews. Jews that were exiled from Spain have carried this Minhag with them, and we've been doing this for close to a thousand years now.

So no matter whether you're from Syria, Egypt, Lebanon, Iraq, Turkey, Greece, Eress Yisrael, and so many other places, you know, the holiday of Shabu'ot comes, the family gets together, sits around the table laden with beautiful sweets for the holiday, and the Azharot are recited. They are sung together. There is each person will take a piece, and it's a fantastic Minhag. It's Minhag that's been going on for so long and has become so dear.

For example, we have a Azharot that was translated into Judeo-Arabic printed in 1912 in Halab, and it says on the cover that this was done to endear them to the children, teach the children the Missvot, teach them the Azharot. Therefore, when they grow up, they will know the Missvot and they'll be able to follow them properly, and they will look at it as something pleasant and not as a chore, not as something that, you know, is beleaguered on them, but rather a labor of love.

Later on, within our own community, the famed principal and educator Rabbi David Bitton was so enamored by the Azharot, especially when he got to New York and he saw year after year on the holiday of Shabu'ot in Shaare Zion, Mr. Selim Sutton, 'Alav HaShalom, teaching the Azharot, explaining the Azharot, it gave him, you know, that feeling that he had to write a commentary on Azharot, and he wrote a fantastic commentary that we know and, you know, we've been using already since 1980 when he first put it out. It's called Ta'am VaDa'at, and it's a fantastic explanation of the Azharot, of the Missvot.

As it was written in Hebrew, it became difficult for people to understand. And about a dozen or so years ago, the Sephardic Heritage Foundation decided to issue a book of Azharot specifically for Shabu'ot with a Hebrew explanation by Rabbi Alouf and an English explanation by Rabbi Labaton, 'Alav HaShalom. And this is a fantastic, fantastic item for the family to sit, read, get together to enjoy the Azharot, to understand the meaning of the Missvot, and to cherish them.

And this is something that was always done on the days of Shabu'ot, usually prior to Minhah, as you had plenty of time after you took a nap, after you had lunch, you'd sit around with the family, with friends, and you'd read the Azharot, you'd sing the Azharot, you'd explain them, you know, to one another, to really enjoy them. And on the first day, the Missvot 'Aseh would be done. On the second day, the Missvot Lo Ta'aseh would be done. Followed by the reading of Azharot, we would also read the first half of Megillat Rut on the first day and the second half on the second day, to instill within us not just putting the Missvot into action, but seeing how the Missvot worked within society, especially Missvot Ben Adam LaMakom and Ben Adam LaHabero, how they intertwined, intermingled with one another so we could really take it to heart and carry that lesson throughout the year.

Now, as I said, this was the sweetness of the Missvot. The sweetness also carried through to the palate as well, and while the Azharot were read, there were special sweets on the table specifically for Shabu'ot, not that they weren't partaken of throughout the year, but specifically on Shabu'ot these sweets, these halwiyat were known to have been on the table. Things like Qarabeej, Qarabeej you had to have because of the natef that goes on top, the white, what we know today in America as marshmallow fluff, but that natef, you know, was homemade in the past, and the reason was used was a play on words because of the holiday Mizmor. The holiday Mizmor of Shabu'ot, there's a Pasuk that says, "Eress Ra'ashah Af Shamayim Natfu." So "Natfu," natef, they would have that. Other things that would be had, you'd have Riz b'Haleeb, you'd have Riz b'Asal, you'd have el Masieh, all types of sweet, golden, honeyish things, things that would be extra sweet on the palate to connect the sweetness that is both going into your mouth from what you're eating as well as what's going out of your mouth from reading and reciting the Mizmor.

I'd also like to mention that this year is the one-year commemoration of Minhag of the Week. The SCA put together this idea of having a weekly Minhag, and we started it last year on Shabu'ot, and this is our commemoration, Shabu'ot, from year to year. The same way we accept the Torah upon us from year to year, and we relive the Torah, and we give over the ideas of the Torah from father to son and from mother to daughter, and we transmit our traditions, you know, from the Torah, as we've been doing now for thousands of years, this is now a Minhag within our community that we've started, Minhag of the Week, through the auspices of the SCA to transmit our traditions, our heritage, our Minhagim. And hopefully, this'll be an ongoing thing for many years to come. Tizku LeMissvot to all those involved. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

53.title: Kiddush Before Nightfall on Shabu'ot
53.text:
Is there a requirement to wait until nightfall before reciting Kiddush on the first night of Shabu'ot? In New York and New Jersey, nightfall is usually around 9:00 p.m. on the first night of Shabu'ot, and many Ashkenazim and Sefaradim have the custom to wait until nightfall before reciting Kiddush. And some even have the custom to wait until nightfall before reciting 'Arbit, and then afterwards they go home to recite Kiddush.

The earliest record of this custom was by Rabbi Abraham HaLevi Horowitz, who lived in the 16th century in Poland, and he had a tradition that dated back to Rabbi Ya'akob Pollak, who lived in the 15th century and was also from Poland. And their tradition was to wait until the stars come out before reciting Kiddush on the first night of Shabu'ot. And he wrote that they waited for Kiddush even though they didn't wait for 'Arbit. Other later authorities that record this custom include the Magen Abraham and the Ture Zahab, and there were also Sephardic authorities that record this custom as well, including the Peri Hadash, the Shulhan Gaboah, the Ben Ish Hai, and the Kaf HaHayyim.

What was the custom in Halab? Did they recite Kiddush early on the first night of Shabu'ot, or did they wait until nightfall? Rabbi Efrayim Laniado, who was the chief rabbi of Halab from 1794 until 1805, addressed this question in his book Degel Mahaneh Efrayim. At first, he explained the reasoning of those that had the tradition to wait: the Torah commands us to count seven complete weeks, and then we observe the holiday of Shabu'ot. If we start Shabu'ot a little bit early, then the seventh and final week will not be complete.

However, Rabbi Laniado raised some questions regarding this opinion. One is that the requirement to wait until nightfall in order to recite Kiddush on the first night of Shabu'ot is not found in the Gemara or in any of the early authorities. And in fact, the Gemara only requires one to wait until nightfall on the first two nights of Pesah, and they excluded other holiday nights. This is an indication that according to the Gemara, we could start early on the first night of Shabu'ot. Furthermore, some early authorities, like the Tosafot and the Rosh, wrote that because the weeks have to be complete, one should make sure to count the 'Omer before nightfall on the first night of the counting, without mentioning any requirement whatsoever about waiting until nightfall in order to recite Kiddush on the first night of Shabu'ot.

So Rabbi Laniado reasoned, perhaps this is because it's more important for us to add Kodesh to Hol by starting the holiday a little earlier, or because once the sun sets, the holiday has begun, so waiting until nightfall in order to recite Kiddush won't make a difference anyway. Also, according to the law, one may count the 'Omer every night after sunset, so once the sun sets, the weeks are complete. Furthermore, since Maran considers the entire requirement of counting the 'Omer to be rabbinical in our times, so too, having complete weeks is rabbinical. So it would not be necessary to be stringent and wait until nightfall in order to complete the weeks. Therefore, Rabbi Laniado concluded, "The true law is that it is not necessary to wait for Kiddush on the night of Shabu'ot until dark," and then he added, "This is simple." It is also clear from Rabbi Laniado's writing that when he wrote this responsa, the custom of waiting until nightfall was not customary in Halab at that time.

Dennis Dweck, 'Alav HaShalom, related a conversation that some men from our community had with Hakham Matloub Abadi on this subject. They asked Hakham Matloub, "Is it okay to eat to pray early and eat early on the first night of Shabu'ot?" So Hakham Matloub asked them, "Does the Rambam prohibit this?" They answered, "No." Then Hakham Matloub asked them, "Does Maran prohibit this?" They answered, "No." So Hakham Matloub looked at them, "So then what's your question?"

It is also known that Hakham Barukh, 'Alav HaShalom, prayed early and ate early on the first night of Shabu'ot. This was also the custom of Hakham Yom Tob Yedid, who was the former chief rabbi of Halab. So while other communities have the custom to wait until nightfall for Kiddush on the first night of Shabu'ot, the custom of the rabbis of Halab was based on the Rambam and Maran, that do not require one to wait for 'Arbit or for Kiddush on the first night of Shabu'ot, and therefore we can begin early like we do on other Friday nights and holidays. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

54.title: Minhah and No Nefilat Appayim
54.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the Minhagim relating to Tefilat Shahrit, and today we will do the Minhagim related to Tefilat Minhah.

Minhah, as you know, begins with LaMnasseah, followed by VaYedabber, and the Ketoret. Prior to saying, to beginning LaMnasseah, we say a Pasuk. We open up Minhah with a Pasuk: "Vihi No'am Ad-onai Elokenu 'Alenu UMa'aseh Yadenu Konenah 'Alenu UMa'aseh Yadenu Konenehu." Similarly in Shahrit, we also opened with a Pasuk before the 'Akedah, the same Pasuk. So the custom in our community, you'll see the Hazzan when he gets up and he says "Vihi No'am," is to say this Pasuk once. There are other communities which say, or recite it twice. The Syrian custom is to recite this Pasuk only once.

Prior to the "Vihi No'am," we do not have the custom to say "LeShem Yihud Kudsha Berikh Hu." As I mentioned in a prior video, I think it was episode 51 that spoke about the 'Omer, I brought the writings of Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, Zikhrono LiBerakhah, the chief rabbi of Argentina, who wrote very specifically that the Syrian custom was never to begin, to precede the Missvot with the saying of LeShem Yihud, as you may find in other communities. That is not our custom. So similarly in the Tefilot, we do not begin with LeShem Yihud.

Vihi No'am, LaMnasseah, VaYedabber, Ketoret. Following the Ketoret, we say Ashre. Now, unlike the Ashre which we said in Shahrit following the 'Amidah, which I mentioned it was episode 33, where we precede that Perek of Ashre with the Pasuk "Yehi Hasdekha Ad-onai 'Alenu Ka'asher Yihalnu Lakh," that is particular for the Ashre prior to UBa LeSiyyon, which comes after the 'Amidah in Shahrit. However, here we do not precede Ashre with any Pasuk. We complete the Ketoret, "KeShanim Kadmoniyot," "Ashre Yoshebe Betekha." It's followed by Tikkon Tefillati, Kaddish, Hassi Kaddish, the 'Amidah, and the Hazarah.

After the Hazarah, if it's a day where there's no Tahanunim, we go straight to Yehi Shem and Kaddish Titkabbal. If it's a normal day where we say Tahanunim, we will say the Viddui, the Ana and the Ashamnu, followed by "El Erekh Appayim Attah" and the Yod-Gimmel Middot, VaYa'abor.

It is not the custom in our community to do Nefilat Appayim during Minhah, meaning LeDavid and Abinu Malkenu. There has never been the custom in the Brooklyn community, as far as I can remember, upwards of about 50 years that I've been praying, remember myself praying in synagogues, never was there Nefilat Appayim during Minhah.

Now, if you look at the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, you'll find a notation which says Syrian custom is to say when praying before Pelag HaMinhah. Brief description: Pelag HaMinhah refers to the midpoint of the Minhah Ketanah section of the day, which is, in Sha'ot Zemaniyot, two and a half hours roughly before sunset is a period called Minhah Ketanah, which is generally when we pray Minhah, closer to sunset. If the, according to this notation, if we are praying before an hour and a quarter before sunset, then we would say indeed Nefilat Appayim.

Now, while it is noted in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, and it may have been the custom in Aleppo a hundred years ago to say Nefilat Appayim when there's, you know, a long time before sunset, this has never been the custom in our community. Even a few of the elders that I consulted with testified that they have never seen it in our community and it is not said. Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, Yizkero BeTob, is quoted in the book Derekh Eress that it indeed was the custom in Halab, but being that it's a Minhag, and so if someone is playing praying close to sunset they do not say it. Also Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, 'Alav HaShalom, writes that when he came to Argentina, some of the Zekenim used to say it if they were praying early enough, but then it fell into disuse. And being that it's a Minhag, so they didn't, they weren't particular about it.

So the bottom line is, I've never seen it, the elders I've consulted with have never told me, they've never said it in our community, and so we do not say Nefilat Appayim during Minhah, even if we're praying before Pelag HaMinhah.

It's followed by Yehi Shem, Kaddish Titkabbal, said by the Hazzan only, followed by the Perek of Tehillim "LaMnasseah BiNginot Mizmor Shir." During the weekdays, on Friday we say "Ad-onai Malakh Ge'ut Labesh." It is our custom in the community not to add Mizmorim, like you may find in other communities, in Ta'anit Sibbur they'll add a Mizmor, and we do not add Mizmorim. We say one Mizmor. If it's Hol HaMo'ed Pesah, Hol HaMo'ed Sukkot, Purim, we will replace the LaMnasseah with the appropriate Mizmor, but we will never say two Mizmorim. That is our custom. It's followed by the Kaddish Yehe Shelama and 'Alenu LeShabbeah. Kol Tub.

55.title: Dictating the First Word of Birkat Kohanim
55.text:
There is a difference of opinion among the halakhic authorities whether the Hazzan begins dictating the blessing to the Kohanim with the first word of "Yebarekh-kha," or if the Kohanim say that first word by themselves, and then the Hazzan begins dictating the words to them with the second word, which is HaShem's name.

But before we discuss that difference of opinion, I just want to note that the Halabi tradition is to pronounce that first word "Yebarekh-kha," which is not like most other communities do. Other communities pronounce that word "Yebarekhekha." Our tradition is based on the opinion of ancient grammarians. In this case, and in other cases in the Mikra, the Sheva under the first Khaf is a Sheva Nah, a resting Sheva, even though it's followed immediately by another Khaf. So we accentuate the Bet, and we rest the Sheva under the first Khaf, and it's pronounced "Yebarekh-kha," not "Yebarekhekha."

With regards to whether that first word is dictated or not, Maran wrote the following in Shulhan 'Arukh: "The Kohanim begin by saying 'Yebarekh-kha,' and afterwards the Hazzan dictates to them word by word, and they repeat each word." This is based on the opinion of HaRambam. However, Rabbi Moshe Isserles, an Ashkenazic authority who appended notes to Shulhan 'Arukh, wrote the following: That some say that the Hazzan also dictates the word "Yebarekh-kha" first, and that's the custom in Ashkenazic communities.

According to Maran, the custom of the land of Israel and Egypt was that the Kohanim begin with the word "Yebarekh-kha" on their own. Maran explains that even though there is a requirement to dictate the words to the Kohanim, when the Hazzan says "Kohanim," that's a call for them to bless, so it's not necessary to start them with the first word. And according to the Bet Menuhah, which was an important Siddur that was commonly used in the Middle East in the 19th century, it is customary for the Hazzan to dictate the word "Yebarekh-kha" if there's only one Kohen, since when there's only one Kohen, the Hazzan does not say the word "Kohanim" before the Kohen starts to bless.

Now, even though Maran and HaRambam both wrote that the Kohanim start with the word "Yebarekh-kha" on their own, many Sefaradim have the custom that the Hazzan dictates that word of "Yebarekh-kha" to the Kohanim. This was the custom of the Kabbalists in their famous Kenis known as Bet El in Yerushalayim. This is the opinion of the Ben Ish Hai, of the Kaf HaHayyim, and of Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alehem HaShalom.

But what was the custom in Halab? According to the famous Mahzor, Mahzor Aram Soba, that was published originally in 1527, this is a facsimile of that original publishing, the Kohanim begin with the word "Yebarekh-kha," and then the Hazzan dictates to them. That is what was written in the instructions in the Mahzor Aram Soba. And this custom continued in Halab for centuries, and was recorded again in the book Derekh Eress quoting Hakham Ya'akob Antebi. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote that our custom is like Maran, that the Kohanim say the word "Yebarekh-kha" on their own. And this is the prevalent custom today in our communities in New York and New Jersey, and we should maintain it as it has been our tradition for centuries based on the writings of HaRambam and Maran.

56.title: The Ancient Halabi Custom of Yehi Shem
56.text:
Yehi Shem. Yehi Shem is a very, very unique Minhag to the Halabi community. It's a Minhag that does not exist in any other community that I know of, not in the Shami community, not in the Lebanese community, not in the Egyptian community. It's strictly a Halabi thing.

Now, I'm not referring to the Yehi Shem that we would say if no Tahanunim, that is, no Ana is being said that day, so we scream out Yehi Shem and we're very happy because we shortened the prayers, rather the Yehi Shem that is said after the Tahanunim are said, whether it's a regular weekday, or Monday and Thursday, at the end of the Tahanunim in the Halabi tradition, after you said Ana, and VaYa'abor, and LeDavid, and Abinu Malkenu, you're still saying those three Pesukim of Yehi Shem.

Now, what's going on over here? No other community does it, and when they look at the Halabi community, they think that Halabiyeh are making a mistake. Those Pesukim are there only because on a day that you don't say Tahanunim, you need three Pesukim to say Hassi Kaddish. Over here, we said all the Tahanunim, we had plenty of Pesukim, there's absolutely no reason to say Yehi Shem. This must be a mistaken Minhag, a carryover from somebody who saw it printed in a book and didn't know the correct instructions, and people are doing the wrong thing.

In fact, that's not true, and I'd like to thank Rabbi David Zafrani and the Sephardic Heritage Museum for the research that Rabbi Zafrani has done there in locating the source for this Minhag of the Halabi community to say Yehi Shem. Yehi Shem first and foremost appears in the Mahzor Aram Soba. That's the famed Mahzor of Aleppo, Syria, that was printed in Venice in 1527. Yehi Shem is right there. At the end of the Tahanunim, on page 53b, you see Yehi Shem. So, that's the first indicator that we have that it was actually said in Syria going back at least 500 years ago, and this is obviously no mistake.

So, the question is: What is going on over here, and why is this Minhag done? And why do we see on a regular Kol Ya'akob Siddur, we'll see Yehi Shem in weekday Shahrit printed three times? If it's a day with no Tahanunim, if it's a Monday and Thursday Tahanunim, we have it afterwards; if it's the other days of the week, we have it printed after those Tahanunim to indicate to us not to forget the Minhag that we say Yehi Shem no matter what.

So, why should such a Minhag even exist? And it seems that this is much older than Minhag Aram Soba, and it's something that goes back at the very least to Masekhet Soferim. Masekhet Soferim seems to be a compendium of the Geonim of laws and customs. Some say it came from Babel, some say it reflects the Minhagim of Eress Yisrael from an earlier time period. In either case, it shows that these Pesukim of Yehi Shem were said prior to Kaddish before the 'Amidah with a Barekhu as well or in place of a Barekhu, and that was for people who may not have been there earlier. And then, later on, it got pushed off to after the 'Amidah.

And there in Masekhet Soferim it says, but the people of the West, meaning Eress Yisrael, and the people of the East, meaning Babylonia, have accustomed themselves to say it after 'Oseh Shalom of the three daily prayers of the 'Amidah, and even after reading of the Torah. The words Yehi Shem were said before Kaddish and Barekhu right before the 'Amidah, and that was later changed to be said after each 'Amidah. And that's what we're doing today. After the Tahanunim, we're saying Yehi Shem. If there are no Tahanunim, we just say the Yehi Shem directly.

Now, these sources present to us an understanding of why we say Yehi Shem after the 'Amidah, providing three Pesukim, not just to say Kaddish, but it seems from the sources now that Yehi Shem was said to announce and to initiate the saying of Barekhu and Kaddish. Now we understand it, because we're saying Yehi Shem. What's "Yehi Shem Ad-onai Meborakh Me'attah Ve'Ad 'Olam"? It means let the name of God be blessed from now and forever. So, this is a preamble. This is something to let us know, to prepare ourselves for Kaddish, which is the exalting of God's name, and Barekhu, which is, of course, once again, blessing God's name. So, regardless if other Pesukim were said, Tahanunim or not, you still would need Yehi Shem to introduce the upcoming Kaddish.

And as we said, this is a Minhag that goes back at least 1,500 years based upon this source of Masekhet Soferim. In the 1409 manuscript of Mahzor Aram Soba, we even see Yehi Shem listed after Hallel with a reminder: "Do not forget to say Yehi Shem after Hallel." So once again, Yehi Shem has to be said. When? After the prayers are said, even though there's so many different Pesukim, but prior to the Kaddish.

There's an early source from the Cairo Genizah that seems to show a old Egyptian Siddur that's anywhere from six to 900 years old, and once again we see the Pesukim of Yehi Shem. In the old Romaniote Siddurim that are no longer in use, we see Yehi Shem over there. In the old Persian Siddur that's in manuscript form, once again Yehi Shem is there.

So Yehi Shem is a very, very old custom. It seems to go back to the days of the Geonim, and even though we do not find it in the Siddurim of Rab 'Amram Gaon or Rab Sa'adya Gaon, we know obviously that this is an ancient Minhag. And shouldn't be like people want to dismiss Minhagim and say, "Ah, we don't need this Minhag, other people don't do this Minhag, or we've figured out, quote, unquote, the reason for the Minhag because just we need Pesukim, and we no longer need it, so we could shorten the prayer by these, by expunging these three Pesukim." That's not the case. This is an ancient Minhag. It's there for a reason. It has its sources, and we should be proud to be defenders and upkeepers of our holy Minhagim. And that is Yehi Shem.

So when you hear Yehi Shem even on a day that is not a day that we're cutting out Tahanunim, still be happy. Be happy to know that you're upkeeping the Minhag of "Yehi Shem Ad-onai Meborakh Me'attah Ve'Ad."

57.title: The Minhagim of Tefilat 'Arbit
57.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will be discussing today the Minhagim related to Tefilat 'Arbit.

It is the custom in our community that we pray Minhah and 'Arbit together, one right after the other. We don't, like with some communities, especially in Israel, where they'll wait, they'll pray Minhah like 15 minutes before sunset, and then they'll wait after sunset 15 or 20 minutes until they begin 'Arbit. That is not our custom. Our custom is always to say Minhah, 'Arbit together, even in the summer months. Let's say you'll have the Minyan at 7:00, which could be an hour, hour and a quarter before sunset, we'll pray Minhah, and immediately we will pray 'Arbit, even though it is not sunset yet. That is our custom, even though it's a bit inconsistent with the opinion of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, that has been and was the custom in our community throughout.

So, we begin with the three Pesukim, "Ad-onai Seba'ot 'Imanu," 'Al Pi HaKabbalah. We do not recite any Mizmorim prior to 'Arbit, unless it is Rosh Hodesh or Hol HaMo'ed or Purim. There are other communities which add Mizmore Tehillim. Our custom is not to have any Mizmorim unless on those days I specified.

We say "Ad-onai Seba'ot 'Imanu," followed by Kaddish, Barekhu—excuse me, VeHu Rahum, Barekhu, and the Berakhot of Keri'at Shema: Ma'arib 'Arabim and Ahabat 'Olam. In the Ahabat 'Olam, there's a Nusah which is brought in Siddur Kol Ya'akob: "VeAhabatekha VeHemlatekha Lo Tasur Mimmenu Le'Olamim." This is the custom of the Syrian community. It goes way back. As a matter of fact, it is printed this way in the Mahzor Aram Soba in the 16th century. I got to admit growing up we were using other Siddurim that may not have had that, so the Hazzanim that knew the custom said it. I didn't say it because I didn't know about it until thankfully it's been printed this way in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob.

We say the Keri'at Shema, Emunah, Hashkibenu. In Hashkibenu, there's two things I wanted to point out: we add the Pasuk, our Nusah is to add the Pasuk before the Hatimah, before the final Berakhah, we add the Pasuk "Hinneh Lo Yanum VeLo Yishan Shomer Yisrael." That's the custom in our community, you may not find it in other Siddurim. Also, in the Berakhah we say "Shomer 'Ammo Yisrael MiKol Dabar Ra' La'Ad Amen." That phrase "MiKol Dabar Ra'" is, I wouldn't say it's 100% unique to our community, but we are one of the few communities that have this phrase in the Berakhah, and that's the way it's printed, accurately printed.

Followed by Kaddish and the 'Amidah. After the 'Amidah, you have Yehi Shem, Kaddish Titkabbal, Shir LaMa'alot, and again, the same applies here as applies in Minhah with the LaMnasseah. We do not add Mizmorim after Shir LaMa'alot. If it's again, if it's a holiday or Purim, we will replace the Shir LaMa'alot with the appropriate Mizmor, we will not add or say two Mizmorim on 'Arbit. It's followed by Kaddish Yehe Shelama, Barekhu, and 'Alenu LeShabbeah. Kol Tub.

58.title: Talet and Tefillin at Minhah Around the World
58.text:
We have four minor fast days during the course of the year: Shib'ah 'Asar BeTammuz, Som Gedalyah, 'Asarah BeTebet, and Ta'anit Ester. And each year on these fast days, I'm asked the same question: those who are fasting during Minhah, what is the Minhag? Do we wear Talet and Tefillin or not? So let's understand this Minhag.

This Minhag seems to have been created to fulfill a Halakhah. Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo in his Bet Yosef comments and says that a person has an obligation to make 100 Berakhot every day, and on a fast day it is impossible to make more than 98 Berakhot. The only way to do this is by putting on Talet and Tefillin for Minhah, as such we'll make one Berakhah on the Talet, one Berakhah on Tefillin, thus fulfilling 100 Berakhot. Now, if that's the case, shouldn't everybody be doing this? Shouldn't be this a practice among the entire Jewish nation? What has been the opinion of the Hakhamim in different communities and what is so special and unique about our community? So let's discuss that.

So first and foremost, I'm going to go through different Hakhamim from different cities. We have Hakham Yisrael Ya'akob Algazi who lived in Turkey from 1679 to 1756 and he talks about this Minhag of within Turkey, within specifically the city of Izmir, to put on Talet and Tefillin. So we already know that about 200 years after this was mentioned by Rabbi Yosef Karo, the custom in Izmir was in fact to do such a thing. We have Rabbi Yisshak Ben Walid in Spanish Morocco talking between 1777 and 1870, same thing, it is the custom to do it. Rabbi Ya'akob Rakah in Libya, 1800 to 1891, once again Minhag is to wear Talet and Tefillin for Minhah. Hakham Abraham Adadi, also in Libya, same thing, it is Minhag to wear Talet and Tefillin for Minhah of fast days. Rabbi Rahamim Nissim Yisshak Palachi, also in Turkey, same thing. They all seem to be telling us the same thing.

Finally, we get to Halab, and we have Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Bet Din once again tells us the Minhag in Aram Soba Halab is to wear Talet and Tefillin for fast days. He was born in 1838, passed away in 1886. So this Minhag was obviously the established custom in Halab as well.

We then move to Cairo, Egypt, and we see something very interesting. The chief rabbi at the time, Hakham Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on became chief rabbi of Cairo in 1881. He came from Yerushalayim, and he says, "I see this custom, some people are putting on Talet and Tefillin on the fast Minhah of a fast day, and I do not know why. I don't know where this custom came from. Maybe they're just mimicking putting on Talet and Tefillin for Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb, which everybody seems to do." He obviously, for the moment, didn't think about what Maran wrote in the Bet Yosef. He said though, this is a beautiful custom, and people shouldn't make fun of customs that they don't know what the origin is or what the reason behind it is. In fact, this is a very helpful custom, because we see less and less people fasting, and this now helps us to know who is fasting so we know what prayers we can or cannot say during the Minhah time.

Hakham Hayyim Sethon living in Sefat in Eress Yisrael approximately 1900, once again tells us the Minhag of Eress Yisrael is to put on Talet and Tefillin. Hakham Shelomo Zafrani in Halab, 1891 to 1965, once again, he tells us the Minhag in Halab to put on Talet and Tefillin for Minhah of a fast day.

Interestingly, we move on to French Morocco. Hakham Yosef Messas in Meknes tells us, "I believe that the people made this up on their own so they could look pious," and because of that, he annulled the custom. He stopped it completely.

Back to Yerushalayim, Hakham Abraham Aburabi'a says, yes, the Minhag of Yerushalayim like the Minhag of the entire Eress Yisrael is to put on Talet and Tefillin for Minhah like Maran says. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, also from Halab, 1894 to 1976, in his manuscript work on the customs of Halab, says that everybody wore Talet and Tefillin for Minhah. Rabbi Moshe Malko, Malka, speaking about Morocco, says that was the custom there. Rabbi Shalom Messas tells us the custom there as well, and we saw rabbis from Aden, rabbis from Yemen, so many different rabbis in different communities around the world mentioned that this was the custom in their city.

So, if that's the custom, everybody should be doing it, but nobody's doing it. Outside of the Halabi community of New York and New Jersey, this custom seems to have been forgotten by any community in the world. There may be individuals here and there that do it, but not as a community. People think that our Chief Rabbi Jacob Kassin instituted this Minhag in the community. Obviously, the custom existed before him, and he was upholding the custom, both Halab as well as the custom of Eress Yisrael, where he came from when he came to these shores.

This is a ancient custom. It's a custom to be very proud of. It's a custom that helps bond the people together, and it's something that we should be proud in upholding. So, if you're fasting on a fast day, please, uphold the Minhag, wear Talet and Tefillin for

59.title: Weddings and Engagements in the Three Weeks
59.text:
The fast of the seventeenth of Tammuz brings in a time period known as the three weeks. Even in Halab, this time period was referred to as the Tilat Juma'a, which means the three weeks in Arabic.

Regarding weddings and engagement parties, Maran wrote in Shulhan 'Arukh that we only refrain during the first nine days of the month of Ab. But the Rema, an Ashkenazic authority who appended notes to Shulhan 'Arukh, wrote that with regards to weddings, it is customary to be stringent and refrain during the entire three weeks.

What was our custom in Halab? The book Derekh Eress, which is a compendium of the customs of Halab, was actually compiled in Eress Yisrael in the year 1990, quoted Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, 'Alav HaShalom, who said that the custom was not to perform weddings during the entire three weeks. This was also recorded by Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, 'Alav HaShalom, as well. So even though we usually follow Maran and HaRambam, in this case, we have a custom to be stringent.

This was not only the custom in Aleppo. Other Middle Eastern communities also had the custom to be stringent as well, such as the communities in Turkey, and Morocco, and in Djerba. The Ben Ish Hai wrote that the custom in Baghdad was to be stringent and refrain from weddings during the entire three weeks, but from other sources, it seems that they were lenient in Baghdad.

All of this is with regards to getting married, but what about getting engaged? Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, 'Alav HaShalom, is quoted as saying that they did get engaged during the three weeks. However, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote that they should not have a festive meal in honor of the engagement during the three weeks. And he added that it's preferable not to get engaged during this time, even without a festive meal. All of this is to avoid celebrating a happy occasion during a sad period in the Jewish calendar, when we are focused on the events that led up to and included the destruction of both Batte Mikdash.

The custom of not getting married or engaged during this time period was also recorded by Rabbi Hayyim Benveniste in the 17th century in Turkey, and again by Rabbi Yisshak Palachi in the 19th century, also in Turkey.

Other customs during this three-week period include refraining from wearing a new garment or eating a new fruit that would necessitate the blessing of Sheheheyanu. This is in order to avoid the blessing of Sheheheyanu during the three weeks.

Another custom was to recite the last chapter of the book of Ekhah that began, that begins, "Zekhor Ad-onai Meh Hayah Lanu," and two Mizmorim from Tehillim: "'Al Naharot Babel," and "Mizmor LeAsaf, Elokim Ba'u Goyim BeNahalatekha," both of which are about the destruction of the Bet HaMikdash. These chapters were recited daily between Minhah and 'Arbit while sitting on the floor. In more recent times in Halab, these chapters were only recited during, from the second day of Ab until the fast.

May we see an end to the observance of these customs in our times with the coming of the Mashiah and the rebuilding of the Bet HaMikdash.

60.title: Tish'ah BeAb in Syria and Egypt
60.text:
Tish'ah BeAb and the days leading up to it have many various Minhagim, especially between cities and countries. I'd like to showcase some of the main Minhagim and the similarities and differences between Syria and Egypt for Tish'ah BeAb.

Firstly, regarding no meat during the Nine Days. It's the custom both in Syria and in Egypt to begin these Nine Days not from Rosh Hodesh Ab, but rather on Rosh Hodesh Ab meat is still partaken of, but rather from the second day of the month of Ab. Now, as far as what is eaten or what is not, in Aleppo and in Alexandria, there would be no beef, no lamb, no poultry the entire period of time from the second day of Ab until the fast. In Damascus, it was only during the week of, so not the entire Nine Days. In Cairo, there was no meat for the Nine Days, but in fact in Cairo they ate chicken all Nine Days.

Shabbat Hazon. Shabbat Hazon is the Shabbat during the Nine Days, the Shabbat prior to Tish'ah BeAb. And all agree, even though we're during a sad mourning time, fresh clean clothing is worn for Shabbat Hazon so we do not show any signs of mourning on Shabbat. On that same Shabbat Hazon, no Kinot, no dirges, would be said in the prayers, or before or after, even though they appeared in the old fast day Siddurim. But in Syria, the Maqam of the day, the musical tone for the day, was in Hijaz, which was known as the saddest of all Maqamat, whereas in Egypt they made no distinction and they did not pray in a sad fashion.

Another thing that we need to refer to is regarding Tish'ah BeAb is among Jews from Aleppo, Tish'ah BeAb was known as Tch'abob, whereas in Egypt it was known as Ekhah, based upon the name of the Megillah that we read on Tish'ah BeAb.

Many differences appear in the Tish'ah BeAb prayers between Aleppo and Cairo. The most glaring is that in the Aleppo tradition, the fast begins prior to 'Arbit with the recitation of Megillat Ekhah, whereas in Cairo and in many other communities, Megillat Ekhah is only said after the 'Amidah of 'Arbit. The Nahem prayer, a special prayer that is added to the 'Amidah in Aleppo and Damascus, is only added during Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb day, whereas in Cairo and Alexandria, Nahem is said during all three 'Amidot of Tish'ah BeAb: 'Arbit, Shahrit, and Minhah. In Syria and in Egypt, on Tish'ah BeAb morning, the Berakhah of "SheAsah Li Kol Sorki" is omitted based upon the ruling of the Hida, which is also based upon the Ari.

Another thing on Tish'ah BeAb that comes up every year is the Minhag of Tefillin. The prevalent Minhag in Aleppo was to pray home by oneself with Talet and Tefillin until the end of the 'Amidah, then to go to the Kenis to not pray there, but listen to the Sefer Torah and to read the Kinot. Whereas in Cairo, most people did not wear Talet and Tefillin at all during Shahrit, except for a small percentage of people that would just put it on at home, say Kaddesh Li and Shema, and then go to Kenis to pray without Talet and Tefillin with the entire Kahal, the full prayers from beginning to end. But as far as Minhah is concerned, everybody in Syria and Egypt wore Talet and Tefillin for Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb day.

Another thing that comes up is that in Syria and Egypt, Birkat Kohanim was never said during the Shahrit prayer of Tish'ah BeAb, but in all the cities, Aleppo, Damascus, Cairo, Alexandria, it was said during the Minhah prayer. In Cairo, the three men who had 'Aliyah to Sefer Torah in the morning would be the same three men that would have the 'Aliyot to the Sefer Torah in the afternoon. In Syria, this was not a universal custom, but it was done in some places in Syria at certain times.

In Halab specifically, the people would greet one another on Tish'ah BeAb day by saying "Tizkeh BeNehamat Siyyon," and the reply or the response would be "Tizkeh BeBinyanah," whereas in Cairo they would not greet one another on Tish'ah BeAb, Tish'ah BeAb day, at all, but rather at the end of the fast, people would say to one another, "Tizku Lir'ot BeNehamat Siyyon BeKarob." And there was no specific response to it, rather they would repeat the same line.

Tish'ah BeAb during Minhah, in Aleppo, no Haftarah would be recited. This is a very unique Minhag to Aleppo, whereas in Cairo, Damascus, and Alexandria, a special Haftarah called Shubah Yisrael was said on Tish'ah BeAb day for Minhah, other than the special Haftarah that was said in the morning by everybody called Asof Asifem.

There's an ancient custom, all the women of the Sefaradim, all the different communities, and this custom existed as well in Syria and in Egypt, and that was to start cleaning the home after midday, Tish'ah BeAb day, midday, after midday, in anticipation of the arrival of the Mashiah. Such was the strong faith and belief of our women.

61.title: Shabbat Leftovers During the Nine Days
61.text:
It is customary to refrain from eating meat and poultry, and from drinking wine or grape juice, during the first nine days of the month of Ab. However, it is the custom of the Sefaradim to eat meat and drink wine on Rosh Hodesh Ab in honor of Rosh Hodesh, and it is the custom of both Sefaradim and Ashkenazim to eat meat and drink wine on Shabbat during the nine days, in honor of Shabbat. But what about leftover meat from Rosh Hodesh and Shabbat? Is it permissible to eat those leftovers during the nine days, or are we obligated to put them away until after Tish'ah BeAb?

There were several authorities who were lenient with regards to leftover meat during the nine days. One of the most well-known authorities who was lenient with leftovers during the nine days was Ribbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, otherwise known as the Hida, an important Middle Eastern authority during the 18th century. He authored many books, and one of his books was the Birke Yosef, and in this book Birke Yosef, he discussed this subject.

Other Middle Eastern authorities who were lenient with regards to leftover meat during the nine days include Ribbi Abraham Yisshaki, who was the Rishon LeSiyyon in the beginning of the 18th century, and Ribbi Eliyahu Yisrael, who was the Ab Bet Din of Alexandria in Egypt at the end of the 18th century. Also, Ribbi Hizkiyah Medini, the author of Sede Hemed, who was an important authority from the 19th century. Among those that permit leftovers during the nine days was Ribbi Eliyahu Hamwey, who was appointed to be the Ab Bet Din in Halab in the year 1894.

However, not all of the authorities permit Shabbat leftovers during the nine days. The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer quoted the Shemen HaMa'or, who wrote that eating leftovers avoids the intended suffering of not eating meat during this time. The Hakham Ben Siyyon Abba Shaul was also stringent with regards to meat leftovers during the nine days.

Growing up, I remember Dennis Dwek, 'Alav HaShalom, teaching that our custom is to be lenient with regards to leftovers during the nine days. This is based, of course, on the writing of the Hida and other authorities that I mentioned, including Ribbi Eliyahu Hamwey from Halab.

But what about now that we have freezers? Should we be stringent and freeze the leftovers until after Tish'ah BeAb? If you look at the reasoning for permitting leftovers during the nine days, it's not based on not wasting food. The reasons given are either that Shabbat and Rosh Hodesh leftovers are Shiyure Missvah, leftovers from a Missvah, so they are permitted, or Ho'il VeIshtere Ishtere, since they became permissible for Shabbat, they remain permissible after Shabbat.

Hakham 'Obadia Yosef explained that since refraining from meat and wine during the nine days is a custom, whatever was covered by the original custom is what we can't have, and the original custom did not cover Shabbat and Rosh Hodesh leftovers in some places. In fact, in Hakham 'Obadia's book discussing this topic, he wrote 12 pages on the subject without even mentioning freezers. This is in a book that he published in the year 2007. So our custom of eating Shabbat leftovers during the nine days is a valid custom.

However, the authorities point out that one should not purposely cook extra meat for Shabbat in order to have leftovers after Shabbat, meaning the custom was to have what might reasonably be leftover from Shabbat, but not to be eating Shabbat leftovers all week long. And Ribbi Hayyim Palachi wrote that even one who is stringent with regards to Shabbat leftovers during the nine days should have the Shabbat leftovers for Se'udah Rebi'it, the Saturday night meal after Shabbat, when there is still a spiritual glow of Shabbat, as this fourth meal is also part of honoring Shabbat.

62.title: Barekhi Nafshi on Rosh Hodesh
62.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. The topic today is the Tefilot, the prayers on Rosh Hodesh in the Kenis.

Now, we begin in 'Arbit, when Rosh Hodesh begins, the entire Kahal in unison sing the Mizmor of Tehillim, Mizmor Kof-Dalet, "Barekhi Nafshi Et HaShem." We sing it in the tune of the Tehillim, "Barekhi Nafshi Et HaShem," and the whole Kahal together. And this is an old, old custom, and it's Minhag Eress Yisrael. We're talking about 1,500 plus years ago, where they used to say Mizmorim before 'Arbit. Whenever there was Musaf the next day, they would say the Mizmor of the holiday before 'Arbit the night before.

But why Barekhi Nafshi? So it's interesting, it wasn't always Barekhi Nafshi. Unlike the other holidays and Shir Shel Yom, which we have references in the Mishnah and Tamid, we have references in the Masekhet Soferim, which was a later work, regarding the specific Mizmorim, Barekhi Nafshi is not mentioned. In fact, it's interesting in Mahzor Aram Soba, which we quote often, printed in 1527, which reflects the customs of mainly of the Musta'arabim in Halab, we have Rosh Hodesh, before 'Arbit, they say a different Mizmor: "LaMnasseah 'Al HaGittit Mizmor LeDavid." That's Mizmor Het in Tehillim. And why do we say this Mizmor? Because there is a Pasuk: "Ki Ereh Shamekha Ma'aseh Essbe'otekha, Yareah VeKhokhabim Asher Konanta." We talk about the creation of the Yareah, we see, we look at the heavens, and we see the handiwork of God, and we see the moon and the stars. And of course, Rosh Hodesh is about the renewal of the moon. And so we say, they said that Perek.

It wasn't until much, must have been a later development. We see it mentioned, the earliest that I saw was in the Tur, which was printed around the 1340, where he mentions that in Sefarad, the custom was during the day in Musaf and Minhah to say Barekhi Nafshi, echoed by, some say his student, Rabbi David Abudarham who compiled all the Tefilot and explained them, also mentions it only with regards to Musaf after Tefilat Musaf. And but it's not mentioned in earlier sources.

So why Barekhi Nafshi? Because there is a Pasuk in Barekhi Nafshi: "'Asah Yareah LeMo'adim, Shemesh Yada' Mebo'o." Bore 'Olam created the moon, and they made a Derashah on the Pasuk, LeMo'adim, for the purpose of establishing when the holidays are going to be, because it's all based on the testimony as to when the Rosh Hodesh is. So "'Asah Yareah LeMo'adim, Shemesh Yada' Mebo'o," because of this Pasuk, Barekhi Nafshi became the Mizmor of Rosh Hodesh.

So now we say this Mizmor, we say it all together. When do we say it? Now, what's unique to the Halabi community, which I haven't seen really in other communities, is we say the Mizmor only on the first night of Rosh Hodesh. In the event Rosh Hodesh is two days, we will only say it on the first night of Rosh Hodesh, we will say Barekhi Nafshi, we would not say it on the second night. Why, I don't know. I have yet to hear a satisfactory reason as to why that is, but that's clearly the custom. Other communities, they say Barekhi Nafshi both nights.

The question is, let's say you have two days of Rosh Hodesh, but the first night of Rosh Hodesh is Friday night. Now, our custom, and there are other communities with, that differ, but our custom, and it's also found in other communities as well, that we do not say Barekhi Nafshi Friday night. The reason is not clear. A possible reason is that there's a Pasuk in Barekhi Nafshi which says, "Yesse Adam LeFa'olo VeLa'Abodato 'Ade 'Ereb": a person goes out to work, and it's "VeLa'Abodato 'Ade 'Ereb" on a daily basis, and it's not fitting really to say that on Shabbat. So we don't say it Friday night. And that's our custom in the community, it's clear, and no one dispute it. We don't say it Friday night.

But let's say it's two days of Rosh Hodesh, Friday night and Mossa'e Shabbat. If you didn't say it Friday night, do you say it Mossa'e Shabbat even though it's the second night of Rosh Hodesh, or our custom is not to say it the second night of Rosh Hodesh? That's the question.

Now, growing up it was, to me it was clear. It was like, was almost indisputable. They never said Barekhi Nafshi Mossa'e Shabbat if it was the second night of Rosh Hodesh. I thought it was a very clear and indisputable custom until the last wave of the Aleppian Jews, the Halabiyeh, came in the 80s, and Zikhrono LiBerakhah, the Hakham Bashi, the Chief Rabbi, Hakham Yom Tob Yedid, said, "No, the custom is to indeed to say it on Mossa'e Shabbat if you didn't, if it's the second night of Rosh Hodesh." And was confirmed to him by, to Joe Mosseri by him, and he confirmed it with Hakham Aharon Farhi that this indeed was the custom. I spoke to the younger Hazzanim that came in those days, Edward Ezra and others, they said, "Yes, that was the custom."

So what do we do today? I think most synagogues maintained the custom not to say it the way we grew up, the way it was all my life. I understand that in Shaare Zion, they adopted the custom of Hakham Yom Tob, of the last generation of Halabiyeh, and they do say Barekhi Nafshi the second night. I checked with Argentina, and again, there was both customs were being recorded. So that's LeGabbe Barekhi Nafshi.

We will continue next week with the Tefilot of 'Arbit and Shahrit. Kol Tub.

63.title: Ya'aleh VeYabo on Rosh Hodesh
63.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will continue with the Minhagim pertaining to Rosh Hodesh. We ended up last week with the reciting by the Kahal of Barekhi Nafshi, now we're beginning to say the 'Arbit.

Being that it's Rosh Hodesh, you may find Minyanim, depends on the Minyan, depends on the Kahal, where the Hazzan will sing the Kaddish and sing the Rabbanim, lead the Kahal in the singing of Rabbanim because of the Rosh Hodesh. Generally, from what I remember growing up is that in the weekday Minyanim in Brooklyn, this was never done. People, they want an efficient, quick Minyan, so they didn't sing the Kaddish. I know in Ades, any opportunity we have to sing, we sing, so certainly Rosh Hodesh doesn't go by without the Kaddish being sung, and the Rabbanim being sung.

Be that as it may, we finish with the Keri'at Shema, with the Hashkibenu, Kaddish, and now we're going to say the 'Amidah. In the 'Amidah, we have to say Ya'aleh VeYabo. How do we remind the people so they don't forget the Ya'aleh VeYabo in the 'Amidah? The most common way in our community, and it's even brought down by Rabbi Hayyim Palachi and other Aharonim, that the people, there's either the Shamash starts a little bit earlier so he gets to the Ya'aleh VeYabo clearly before anybody else, and he'll scream out "Ya'aleh VeYabo," and everybody knows that they have to, they'll hear it and they have to say Ya'aleh VeYabo.

Today, what happens mainly in our community is that they don't have to start early, the first one to get to Ya'aleh VeYabo will say "Ya'aleh VeYabo" out loud, and you may hear it a couple of times. After two or three times, it really, it becomes, you know, unnecessary for anybody to scream out "Ya'aleh VeYabo" after most of the Kahal already said it. So it's the first two or three that get there, and everybody knows that to say Ya'aleh VeYabo. I've heard on occasion in 'Arbit at least, where someone will scream out "Ya'aleh VeYabo" even before the 'Amidah starts, because there's no Ge'ulah LiTfilah issue which you have in Shahrit, so he can say that.

Another way is that the Hazzan, when he begins the 'Amidah, will say "Elokenu VeEloke Abotenu" a little bit in a raised voice, hinting to say Ya'aleh VeYabo, to remind the people, because Ya'aleh VeYabo also begins with the words "Elokenu VeEloke Abotenu."

What we do not do, and whoever had the opportunity to pray with the Ashkenazim, they have a custom, a fixed custom in every Ashkenazi Minyan in the world: comes when it's Ya'aleh VeYabo in the 'Amidah, beginning of the 'Amidah before they start, after the Kaddish, the one of the Gabba'im will bang twice loudly on the Tebah, and that's the Siman that everybody knows to say Ya'aleh VeYabo. We don't bang, okay? And I suggest that we don't begin this custom. We have ways to remind the people without banging. Okay.

Now, we get to Ya'aleh VeYabo, and we want to discuss the wording, the Nushaot that we have in Ya'aleh VeYabo. Now if you look at most of the Siddurim of the Sefaradim, even I, there's a very, very nicely done Sefer, I think it's five or six volumes, about all the Tefilot by Rabbi Yisshak Jacobson, called Netib Binah, where he brings all the Nushaot, and then he brings the Nusah of the Ashkenazim, the Nusah of Mahzor Vitry, Nusah Sefarad, and in the Nusah Sefarad it's exactly the way you find it in most Siddurim of the Sefaradim. And that is, we say: "Ya'aleh VeYabo, Yagia', Yera'eh, VeYerasseh, Yishama', Yippaked, VeYizzakher." In other words, we don't put a Vav before each description: "Ya'aleh, VeYabo, VeYagia', VeYera'eh, VeYerasseh." You will find that in some Siddurim, that's not our custom. Our custom is correctly reflected in the printing of Kol Ya'akob in this point, where it says "Ya'aleh VeYabo," then "Yagia', Yera'eh, VeYerasseh, Yishama', Yippaked, VeYizzakher." That's the first Nusah which is important to know.

Now we've seen books printed mainly from the Iraqi communities where you will have "Ya'aleh VeYabo VeYagia' VeYera'eh," that's not our custom. It did spread in our community in the '60s a bit because of the books being printed by, 'Alav HaShalom, by Saleh Mansour, and they were in use in our community so you may come across Siddurim that have that.

The next change that we have, which is consistent with most Sefaradim, is we have "LeHen LeHesed ULeRahamim BeYom." We don't say "LeHen ULeHesed ULeRahamim LeHayyim Tobim ULeShalom." That we will not say. Those "LeHayyim Tobim ULeShalom" is not part of our custom today, nor is it part of most of the Sefaradim. Again, the books, the Siddurim that were printed mainly from the Iraqi community, you'll find "LeHayyim Tobim ULeShalom," as you will in maybe one or two other communities as well. Interestingly enough, in the Mahzor Aram Soba, in the Nusah of Ya'aleh VeYabo, it doesn't have "LeHayyim Tobim," so it has "LeHayyim ULeShalom," but then again, that's no Re'ayah because the entire Ya'aleh VeYabo is quite different than our Ya'aleh VeYabo. So, clearly that's not the Nusah that was adopted for our prayers.

Finally, we are supposed to say "BeYom Rosh HaHodesh HaZeh." When I say we're supposed to say, that's the Minhag, prevalent Minhag, it's brought down by all of the Nushaot of the Sefaradim that we say "BeYom Rosh HaHodesh HaZeh." In Kol Ya'akob, I guess they were influenced by maybe by the other Siddurim that were printed, maybe the Syrian community in Brooklyn got used to saying "BeYom Rosh Hodesh HaZeh." That's the way it's printed here, "BeYom Rosh Hodesh HaZeh," but based on studying the sources and input, and Joey Mosseri did a lot of extensive work on this as well, it seems to be that the proper Nusah should be "BeYom Rosh HaHodesh HaZeh."

It's followed by, we finish the Tefilot the way we finish all of the other Tefilot of 'Arbit on a regular weekday, 'Alenu LeShabbeah. Next video, we will be talking about Tefilat Shahrit of Rosh Hodesh. Kol Tub.

64.title: Yehi Shem, Part Two
64.text:
Yehi Shem, part two. Last time when I spoke about Yehi Shem, I explained how it's an introduction to Kaddish, and in fact, it's an announcement to the people that we will be saying Kaddish. So what exactly is the connection to these Pesukim of Yehi Shem? Which Pesukim do we say as well, and where do they come from?

So the Pesukim that we say all come from Tehillim. First we say, "Yehi Shem Ad-onai Meborakh Me'attah Ve'Ad 'Olam," "MiMizrah Shemesh 'Ad Mebo'o Mehullal Shem Ad-onai." Those are the first two Pesukim. They come from Mizmor Kof-Yod-Gimmel, 113, in Tehillim, and it's the second and third Pesukim over there. Then we go to Mizmor number eight, the second Pasuk: "Ad-onai Adonenu Mah Addir Shimkha BeKhol HaAress."

If you've noticed, all three of these Pesukim have Shem: "Yehi Shem," "MiMizrah Shemesh 'Ad Mebo'o Mehullal Shem," "Mah Addir Shimkha BeKhol HaAress." All three of them have Shem, name. Connection to Kaddish: "Yitgaddal VeYitkaddash Shemeh Rabba." May the name of God be exalted. This is the connection.

Now, a lot of Israeli Siddurim and other Siddurim have another Pasuk, a fourth Pasuk inserted between what we call the first two Pesukim and the last Pasuk, the third Pasuk. There's another Pasuk there: "Ram 'Al Kol Goyim Ad-onai 'Al HaShamayim Kebodo." We do not say that Pasuk. That Pasuk does not have Shem in it, and though that Pasuk comes immediately after the first two Pesukim in the 113th Mizmor of Tehillim, it is not our custom to say it because it has no connection to the name of God.

Now, if you look at that same Mizmor 113, the first Pasuk has a connection. First Pasuk of Mizmor Kof-Yod-Gimmel: "Halleluyah, Hallelu 'Abde Ad-onai, Hallelu Et Shem Ad-onai." So why don't we say that Pasuk, and then followed by "Yehi Shem" and "MiMizrah Shemesh"? Because if we say that, everybody thinks we're saying Hallel, because those are the opening Pesukim of Hallel. Therefore, we omit the first Pasuk, we say the next two Pesukim from 113, and then we say the Pasuk from Mizmor number eight, Pasuk two: "Ad-onai Adonenu Mah Addir Shimkha BeKhol HaAress." All three Pesukim have Shem, nobody will get confused that we're saying Hallel, and everybody understands the connection of Shem to "Shemeh Rabba." And that is our Minhag.

65.title: Viddui HaGadol and No Shofar at Selihot
65.text:
It is customary to recite Selihot every morning in the early morning before Shahrit, from the beginning of the month of Elul, until and including 'Ereb Yom Kippur. However, Selihot are not recited on the days of Rosh Hodesh Elul, or on the Shabbatot during this time period. Furthermore, Selihot are not recited on the days of Rosh HaShanah. On Yom Kippur, Selihot are recited as part of the prayers, but not before Shahrit as we do on the weekdays during the month of Elul and the first ten days of Tishri.

The original custom of Halab was to invite the rabbis to officiate as Hazzanim for the Selihot. Hakham Abraham Hamwey wrote that on the first day of the Selihot, the greatest rabbi would officiate, and on the subsequent days, each one of the other rabbis would take a turn, until they eventually invited laymen to officiate as well. Similarly, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote, on the first day of the Selihot, the chief rabbi would lead the Selihot, with the Hazzan standing next to him. On the second day, the Ab Bet Din led the Selihot, and on all of the days, the Selihot were led by different rabbis.

And both Hakham Abraham Hamwey and Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo specified in their writings that the Viddui HaGadol, the long confession, was recited every day in the Selihot. This is the long Viddui that we recite in the prayers on Yom Kippur. The one that is recited daily in the Selihot is the Viddui for the negative commandments. Likewise, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar printed a Selihot book—here is a copy—with the Viddui HaGadol as the only option to be recited daily.

But reciting the long Viddui every day in the Selihot was not only practiced in Halab. We have a recording of the expert Hazzan Eliyahu Menaged, 'Alav HaShalom, leading the Selihot here in Brooklyn on the first day of Selihot in the year 1952, and he also recited the entire Viddui HaGadol. This custom was revived again in Brooklyn in the 1990s, when rabbis and Hazzanim came to our community from Halab. So this is the authentic Halabi tradition, to recite the long Viddui for the negative commandments every morning in the Selihot.

Now in other Middle Eastern communities, it is customary to blow the Shofar during the Selihot, whenever the Pasuk that begins VaYa'abor is recited. This is done to inspire repentance during the Selihot, and also to invoke divine mercy. However, the Keter Shem Tob, which is a compendium of Middle Eastern customs, notes that while other Middle Eastern communities adopted this practice, in Halab it was not customary to blow the Shofar during the Selihot. The book Derekh Eress, which is a book of Halabi customs, also quoted Hakham Ya'akob Attieh, 'Alav HaShalom, who stated that in Halab, they did not blow the Shofar during the Selihot. So while it's common for Sefaradim in the land of Israel to blow the Shofar during the Selihot, in our community in New York and New Jersey, we don't blow the Shofar during the Selihot. This is in accordance with our traditions from Halab.

One more point: towards the end of the Selihot, we sing a piece that begins "Shomer Yisrael," which has five stanzas. However, it's customary to sing only the first four stanzas during the month of Elul, but after Rosh HaShanah, we sing the fifth stanza as well, the one that begins "Shomer Goy Ehad." This is also documented by Derekh Eress, quoting Dr. Hayim Dahan.

66.title: Shahrit and Musaf of Rosh Hodesh
66.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our discussion of the Minhagim that pertain to Rosh Hodesh and the Tefilah in the Kenis, in the synagogue, and we have completed 'Arbit and now we're going to discuss today Shahrit and Musaf.

The Tefilah is the same, like any other weekday. It may include some singing, depending on the Minyan, "HaShem Melekh" or "Min HaMessar," etc. The Tefilah is the same, except that we say Ya'aleh VeYabo in the 'Amidah, of course. Following the 'Amidah, we say Hallel without a Berakhah, as this is a Minhag on Rosh Hodesh and we don't make a Berakhah on a Minhag, according to the Rambam.

And after the Hallel, we take out the Sefer Torah to read from the Keri'ah of Rosh Hodesh, the four 'Olim. The custom in our community is not to say Berikh Shemeh or this, the special Yehi Rasson for Rosh Hodesh. We take it out as, and as we take out the Sefer during any other weekday. There are other communities which may say Berikh Shemeh, which may say the Yehi Rasson. It's not our custom. We may have one or two synagogues within the community that do say it, depends on the Minyan, but in general we skip those and we take the Sefer Torah out right away.

After the Kaddish of the fourth 'Oleh, the Mashlim, the Hazzan for Musaf will get up and he'll start with Ashre and UBa LeSiyyon. After UBa LeSiyyon is completed, we say Yehalelu and we take the Sefer back. We do not say Bet Ya'akob and the Shir Shel Yom on Rosh Hodesh. This is a very clear and indisputable custom of our communities, and a number of other communities as well, that we do not say the Shir Shel Yom on Rosh Hodesh. There are other communities that do say it. The Ben Ish Hai was insistent that it be said. However, it's not our custom. It's discussed by Rabbi Hayyim Palachi in Kaf HaHayyim. He brings in the name of his grandfather, the famous Rabbi Refael Hazzan, the author of Hikre Leb, where he discusses it, and he says his opinion is also not to say it. So that's a clear difference between our community and some other communities.

Following the UBa LeSiyyon, like I said, we have Yehalelu. We don't say Kaddish yet. We have to take the Sefer back first, and then we'll say Kaddish before the 'Amidah of Musaf.

Now, according to the kabbalists, which is a widespread custom in many communities, in most communities even, we do not keep our Tefillin on for Musaf. We remove our Tefillin before Musaf. The question is, when do we remove the Tefillin? Do we have to wait for the Hassi Kaddish to be over and then we could remove our Tefillin, or during Yehalelu, when they're taking the Sefer back, we could take off our Tefillin? In Kol Ya'akob, they give instructions: "Hassi Kaddish VeAhar Kakh Holssin Tefillin, Et HaTefillin," that first you say the Kaddish, and specifically you take the Tefillin off only after saying the Kaddish. This is brought 'Al Pi HaKabbalah in Sefer Kavvanot, Peri 'Ess Hayyim. It's brought down also in Rabbi Hayyim Palachi in Kaf HaHayyim.

I got to be honest, growing up I don't recall that we were particular about this situation. We used to take off our Tefillin even before the Kaddish. Again, it could be today that the Minhag in our community, as it is reflected by the Siddur, to wait until after the Kaddish.

At any rate, if we are going to wait after the Kaddish, we know we all like to start the 'Amidah together, so we take off the Tefillin, we put them in the Nartik, in the box, but we don't fold the Tefillin and put it back in the Kurachah, because then it would be too much of a delay, and we didn't start the 'Amidah yet, and we already said the Kaddish for the 'Amidah, so we don't want to delay it, so we take off the Tefillin and we leave it on the side, and either before the Hazarah starts, if you finish early enough, or after the Hazarah, you don't want to be folding your Tefillin during the Hazarah, just like a usual weekday, you'll wait until the end of the prayer to fold the Tefillin. Kol Tub.

67.title: The Shofar and Its Sounds
67.text:
Rosh HaShanah, or as the Torah refers to it, Yom Teru'ah. The Pasuk says, "Yom Teru'ah Yihyeh Lakhem," a day of the blowing of the Shofar it shall be unto you.

The Shofar: Most of us, when we think of the Shofar, we think of a ram's horn, somewhat large and curved in different colors. But that wasn't always a typical Shofar. The Shofar could be used from horns of various animals, and doesn't necessarily have to be as curved or as curvy as the ones I just showed you. There is a ram's horn, as the such, that is much flatter, if you will. Notice how thin and flat the Shofar is. Practically no curve in it at all except for this upward curve. Or not from a ram whatsoever, but like this old Shofar from Halab that belonged to Hakham 'Ezra Mash'aniyeh, that is the Shofar of a young gazelle. Very small, very thin, very narrow, practically straight. So the Shofar can come from different animals, it can have different shapes, and of course, each Shofar gives off a different sound. The purpose of the Shofar is to awaken us.

Now, when we go through the Mahzor on Yom Rosh HaShanah, we finish the Sefer Torah, and to introduce the blowing of the Shofar, on the first day, we sing a Piyyut called 'Et Sha'are Rasson, and on the second day, Ad-onai BeKol Shofar. After that, the Hazzan generally will say a number of prayers to get him in the frame of mind to connect with HaShem, with Bore 'Olam, and to allow him to blow the Shofar properly and for it to fulfill its purpose.

What is the purpose of the Shofar? So, according to Rabbenu Sa'adya Gaon, there are numerous purposes: to proclaim the sovereignty of HaShem, to herald the beginning of the 10 days of Teshubah, as a reminder to be faithful to the teachings of the Torah, a reminder of the words of the Nebi'im, a reminder to pray for the rebuilding of the Bet HaMikdash, a reminder of 'Akedat Yisshak, the binding of Yisshak, a reminder of the day of resurrection of the dead, Tehiyyat HaMetim, as a summons to the heavenly court on Rosh HaShanah to be judged by God for our actions, as a reminder for the regathering, the Kibbuss Galuyot, the regathering of the Jewish nation, and finally as a wake-up call to inspire awe, to instill fear of God in the people. This final point was the main point according to HaRambam, to wake up the people to do Teshubah, to reconnect with God.

So when the Hazzan, or when the Tokea' rather, the blower of the Shofar, blows the Shofar, you will generally see him cover himself with his Talet, and you'll see most of the people covering themselves up as well. The reason for this is because you don't want to just be listening to a sound and looking around, seeing what's going on, but rather by closing yourself up, basically creating your own space where you can concentrate without any sort of interruptions. And since you have these 10 various points mentioned by Rabbenu Sa'adya Gaon, it's very important to concentrate and to not be disturbed. That's why you'll see most people covering themselves up when they're listening to the Shofar.

Now, first, we blow 30 sounds while we, the Kahal, are seated. Only the person blowing the Shofar and those standing next to him at the Tebah are standing up. So generally you'll have a maximum of three people standing at the Tebah, and the entire Kahal will be seated for the initial blows, the first 30 blows of the Shofar. Then in the Musaf, we have the custom to blow the Shofar 10 times, 10 times, and 10 times in the silent 'Amidah, and then in the Hazarah, in the repetition of the 'Amidah, we do again 10, 10, and 10. We have the Malkhiyot, Zikhronot, and Shofarot, as they are called. Finally after the 'Amidah, the custom is to blow another 10 blows during Kaddish Titkabbal.

When we get to the end of the prayer, okay, it's right before 'Alenu LeShabbeah, we say the final Kaddish Titk-, Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, and after Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, you'll hear all of a sudden the Hazzan will, you know, say "Barekhu Et Ad-onai HaMeborakh," everybody answer "Barukh Ad-onai HaMeborakh Le'Olam Va'Ed," and then you hear what is known as Teru'ah Gedolah, a long sound of the Teru'ah.

Now, as we mentioned, the Shofar has various sounds, and I'd like to give an example of the sounds so you can see the difference between the sounds that are made in the community by different Hazzanim or within various communities how they are made. So, the Teki'ah, which is the long standard sound, is very simple. Simple, Teki'ah. Then you have the Shebarim. In most communities in the world, it's three sounds. But in the Halabi tradition, it can be anywhere from four to nine, four, from four to seven sounds, and generally in our community here in New York, it's about five short sounds. Then you have the Teru'ah. The Teru'ah is the much shorter sound, and that sound in most communities in the world is referred to as a tu-tu-tu sound. In Syrian communities, in Iraqi communities, in the community of Djerba of Tunisia, it's a different sound called lu-lu-lu. So, your typical tu-tu-tu sound would be more like this: And your lu-lu-lu sound would be somewhat like this: And then finally, as we said, the Teru'ah Gedolah at the end will be that Teru'ah sound, that shorter sound, but for a longer duration of time.

Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

68.title: Short Shebarim and the Lu-Lu-Lu Teru'ah
68.text:
In some communities, the Teru'ah is blown with a tu-tu-tu sound. However, the Syrian custom is to blow with a lu-lu-lu sound. The support for the lu-lu-lu sound is from the Gemara in Masekhet Rosh HaShanah, which describes the Teru'ah sound as "Yelule Yalil," which sounds like lu-lu-lu as opposed to tu-tu-tu.

There's a difference of opinion as to how many sounds are required to make a Teru'ah. According to Rashi, the minimum requirement is just three lu sounds, lu-lu-lu. But the Halakhah is like the Rashba, who requires a minimum of nine lu sounds. Likewise, the length of a Teki'ah must be the equivalent to the amount of time that it takes to blow nine lu sounds, and the Shebarim also must total the amount of time it takes to blow nine lu sounds.

In many communities, only three Shebarim are blown. Each Sheber is of the length of three lu sounds, for a total of nine. But in Halab, they did not want to blow Shebarim that were the length of three lu sounds, since according to Rashi, a Teki'ah only needs to be the length of three lu sounds. So we blow shorter Shebarim. Each Sheber is less than the length of three lu sounds, so that it will be considered a Sheber also according to the opinion of Rashi. But in order to reach the required total length of nine lu sounds between all of the Shebarim, we blow four or five Shebarim, like this:

*demonstration of shofar blowing*

This tradition is based on what Maran wrote in the Bet Yosef, that the custom is to shorten each Sheber as much as possible. By blowing this way, we fulfill the obligation of Shofar according to both opinions that are quoted in Shulhan 'Arukh. Each Sheber is short enough to be considered a Sheber according to both Rashi and the Rashba, but in order to have the required total length of nine lus, we blow four or five Shebarim.

All of this has been documented in the book known as Yisshak Yeranen, which is a collection of letters from Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, 'Alav HaShalom. On this topic, he corresponded with his teacher, Hakham Moshe Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, the former chief rabbi of Halab. This was the custom in Halab. However, in Damascus, they blew three longer Shebarim, like the Ashkenazim.

*demonstration of shofar blowing*

Lastly, the Teki'ah before and after a Shebarim or a Teru'ah must be at least the equivalent of time it takes to blow nine lu sounds, but the Teki'ah before and after Shebarim and Teru'ah must be at least twice as long, or the equivalent of 18 lu sounds.

*demonstration of shofar blowing*

Thank you, Sauly [Haber].

69.title: Overview of Kabbalat Shabbat
69.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. Having completed our videos which dealt with the Minhagim of the prayers in the Sibbur, the prayers in the synagogue for the weekdays and for Rosh Hodesh, we are now going to begin a series of videos on the Tefilot of Shabbat, the prayers in the Sibbur, in the synagogue for Shabbat, and we will begin with Kabbalat Shabbat. We are going to be working off of the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, of course, be easier for everybody to follow. Kabbalat Shabbat, I'll give an overview of the customs of the Halabiyim, of our community, and then in subsequent videos go into greater detail.

We begin with Mizmor LeDavid. As opposed to other communities which either say one Perek of Tehillim, "Lekhu Neranenah," and a Pasuk from the second Perek, "Shiru LaAd-onai Shir Hadash," there are communities which say six Perakim of Tehillim prior to Mizmor LeDavid, corresponding to the six days of the creation prior to Shabbat. Our custom is to begin Mizmor LeDavid.

Following Mizmor LeDavid, which the Kahal standing and singing in unison, we go right into Lekha Dodi. We don't stop and say the prayer Ana BeKhoah, which you will find in other Kehillot, Egyptian community, the Shami community, and the Yerushalmim also. We do not say Ana BeKhoah, we go directly to Lekha Dodi.

Lekha Dodi, the famous poem which is sung by all communities, Sefaradim, Ashkenazim all over the world today Friday nights, written by the great Mekubbal Rabbi Shelomo HaLevi Alkabess in the 16th century in Sefat. We sing that together also, we're all standing up, and of course we're facing the Hekhal. In the video, I think number 14, that my esteemed colleague Morris Arking spoke at length about how we are only to face the Hekhal and we should, were not to turn around, but you can, I'm not going to repeat what he said, you can go look at that very, very interesting video. I think it's number 14.

We say Lekha Dodi. We don't say all of the Battim, all of the stanzas. There are, Lekha Dodi is the refrain, and then you, it's followed by eight stanzas, and then Bo'i BeShalom is the last stanza. The eight stanzas spell out acrostically the name Shelomo HaLevi. We do not say all eight. We say four of them. And the reasons for it we'll discuss in the next video.

Following Lekha Dodi, everybody sits down. The Hazzan will say Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. Of course, we all say it, but it's not sung in unison. The Hazzan alone in Maqam Nawa will say "Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat, Ad-onai Malakh Ge'ut Labesh."

Following that, we have the Perakim of Mishnayot from the second Perek in Masekhet Shabbat, Bameh Madlikin, preceded by the Mishnah from Sanhedrin, "Kol Yisrael Yesh Lahem Helek La'Olam HaBa, SheNe'emar: VeAmmekh Kullam Saddikim, Le'Olam Yirshu Aress, Nesser Mata'ai, Ma'aseh Yadai LeHitpa'er," Bameh Madlikin. Following the series of Mishnayot Bameh Madlikin, we say what the Halabim always typically say following the reading of Mishnayot. We say the Mishnah "Rabbi Hananya Ben 'Akashya Omer" until the ending "Yagdil Torah VeYa'dir." That is our custom. We do not say "Amar Rabbi El'azar Amar Rabbi Hanina." You will find that in many Siddurim, and in other Kehillot, indeed say "Amar Rabbi El'azar Amar Rabbi Hanina." We do not. We say "Rabbi Hananya."

It's followed by Kaddish, and Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, which those who have an obligation to say Kaddish will say this Kaddish. And this is the official end of Kabbalat Shabbat. We will repeat Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat now the second time, but that's connected to the 'Arbit, and I will explain that in the next video.

I did want to speak for a moment on the Shir HaShirim. As you know, it's our custom and the custom of, from Halab many centuries, to say Shir HaShirim on Friday night. Again, there's a video that Joey Mosseri put out, I think video number 25, and video number 14 of Morris Arking, which discussed the customs of when to say Shir HaShirim, why to say it and when to say it. One of the customs is not applicable in the States, that was only done in Halab, but the two customs when I was growing up in the 60s, 70s, 80s, as they mentioned, was to do it before Kabbalat Shabbat, ya'ni after Minhah, or after Kabbalat Shabbat, meaning after Kaddish 'Al Yisrael. Those were the only two customs. Minyanim would decide for themselves whether to say before or after. Every Minyan had their own system. Both customs were legitimate customs, and that was, that's the way it was done.

The upside was everybody knew Shir HaShirim. When I was growing up, every youngster, we sing it every Friday night. So by the time of 13, 14, everyone knows it by heart, with the Ta'amim, with the Dikduk, it was a beautiful thing and it's a beautiful song, a beautiful Megillah.

Unfortunately, I mean I've been here for 20 years, occasionally I go back, and when I go to Kenis Friday night, I'll say, "Okay, I'm ready for Shir HaShirim." "No, we said it before Minhah." And I'm finding it increasingly done in certain Minyanim that they'll do Shir HaShirim before Minhah. And the logic, the reasoning is, well, if somebody going to come late to Kenis, better they miss Shir HaShirim rather than miss Minhah. I don't, I'm not a big fan. The downside is too great, because really before Minhah there's only a handful of people in Kenis, you know, one or two guys saying Shir HaShirim, and basically all of the children, all of the youngsters who come to Kenis Friday night now never heard, I have students here who are 18 years old at the high school, they've never heard Shir HaShirim, because they never hear it Friday night in Kenis and they don't know it, and it's such a haram, it's a shame.

This custom, I would hope, is going to be changed and revert back to the original custom in Halab and in Brooklyn, where we said it before Kabbalat Shabbat, in other words after Minhah, or after Kabbalat Shabbat, before the second Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. It's a beautiful custom, and it really, it's a shame that the kids who grow up today, they won't know Shir HaShirim. Kol Tub.
