70.title: No Berakhah on Yom Kippur Candles
70.text:
According to the Mishnah, Masekhet Pesahim, lighting candles at home on 'Ereb Kippur in honor of Yom Kippur is dependent upon the local custom. In a place where it's customary to light candles, candles are lit; in a place where it's customary not to light candles, candles are not lit.

So since lighting candles on 'Ereb Kippur is a custom as opposed to a rabbinic obligation, some early authorities wrote that in a place where candles are lit, a blessing is not recited before lighting. This is based on the talmudic rule that a blessing is not recited before practicing a custom. These authorities include the Mordekhai, the Orhot Hayyim, the Maharil, and the Radbaz. However, other early authorities disagree, and require a blessing before lighting. These authorities include the Rosh, Rabbenu Yeroham, and the Tur.

Maran discusses this in two places in Shulhan 'Arukh. In Hilkhot Shabbat, Maran writes that when Kippur doesn't fall on Shabbat, there is one who says not to recite the blessing, but then he continues and says, "See what I wrote later in the laws of Yom Kippur." In the laws of Yom Kippur, Maran wrote that there was one who says to recite a blessing upon lighting candles for Yom Kippur. So basically, Maran quoted both opinions in Shulhan 'Arukh. The Shulhan Gaboah understood Maran as meaning that the blessing should not be recited, but Hakham 'Obadia Yosef disagreed, and understood Maran as meaning that the blessing should be recited.

There are later authorities who consider the disagreement about whether or not a blessing is recited before lighting the candles for Kippur as creating a doubt, and they apply the rule of Safek Berakhot LeHakel. When there's a doubt about whether or not a blessing should be recited, we are lenient, and do not recite a blessing. These authorities include the Gra, the Maharikash, the Peri Hadash, the 'Erekh HaShulhan, and Rabbi Hayyim Palachi.

What was the custom in Halab? According to the book Derekh Eress, quoting Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, 'Alav HaShalom, some did not light candles at home for Yom Kippur, but even those that did light candles on 'Ereb Kippur did not recite a blessing before lighting. Furthermore, Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Mahzor Bet HaKapporet also applied the rule of Safek Berakhot LeHakel to candles for Yom Kippur, and concluded that a blessing is not recited before lighting.

But what about when Yom Kippur falls out on Friday night? In that case, should a blessing be recited before lighting because it's Shabbat? Again, even when Kippur falls on Friday night, there is a difference of opinion among the authorities regarding reciting the blessing. According to HaRambam and Maran, you should recite the blessing before lighting when Kippur falls out on Shabbat. But the Radbaz wrote that even when Kippur falls on Shabbat, you don't recite a blessing on the candles since you are not eating with the light of the candles. Based on this consideration, Hakham Abraham Hamwey concluded that even when Kippur falls on Shabbat, a blessing is not recited, as there is still a disagreement regarding the blessing, and the rule of Safek Berakhot LeHakel still applies.

Likewise, our community Siddur Kol Ya'akob also plainly states that the custom of Aram Soba is not to recite a blessing before lighting candles for Yom Kippur, without differentiating whether Kippur falls out on Friday night or a weeknight, which is consistent with what was written by Hakham Abraham Hamwey. So when we light candles for Kippur, we do not recite a blessing, even when Yom Kippur falls on Friday night.

71.title: The Customs of Hosha'na Rabbah
71.text:
Hosha'na Rabbah. Hosha'na Rabbah is the seventh day of the holiday of Sukkot. According to the Mekubbalim, that final day is the day when the judgment that was made for us on the time of Ne'ilah of Yom Kippur is finally sealed, signed, and delivered. As such, the custom is to spend the night of Hosha'na Rabbah steeped in learning Torah. There were those that did that in the Bet Keneset, and there are those that did that learning in private homes.

The order of the learning was to study the entire book of Debarim. After that, a section from the Zohar called the Idra was read, the Idra Zuta, and finally Tehillim. But Tehillim wasn't read straight through, rather Tehillim was separated into seven sections, and between each section of Tehillim, a portion of Selihot would be said. Those same portions of Selihot would also be recited in the morning prayers of Hosha'na Rabbah between each circling of the Tebah while doing the Hosha'not of Hosha'na Rabbah.

In those Selihot, both of the night during Tehillim reading, as well as in the morning, when we would say the Rahamana section, instead of the usual response of "Bedil VeYa'abor," we would answer "Amen" the same way we would answer at the end of Kippur during the Ne'ilah time.

In the Hosha'na Rabbah prayers in the morning, we also mimic Yom Kippur. We say "HaShem Hu HaElokim" before "HaShem Melekh." Also, at the end of Yishtabbah, we add the Mizmor of "Shir HaMa'alot MiMa'amakim Keratikha HaShem," even though it's not found in all the Mahzorim as well as the Shalom Yerushalayim Mahzor that's very popular among us. It is in fact the Minhag of Aleppo, as well as many other cities, to recite that Mizmor on that morning. It may have even been the custom in Halab in earlier days to recite Nishmat on Hosha'na Rabbah as if it was a full-fledged holiday.

As well, on Hosha'na Rabbah, the tunes of the prayers that are used, whether it's for Hoda'ot, or for Kaddish, or Kedushah, are all reminiscent of the High Holidays, and they are High Holiday tunes. The entire day has the flavor of a High Holiday.

And when we finish the prayers and we finish the Hosha'not, we finally go outside to do Habatat 'Arabah, which is an ancient custom of the Nebi'im where five branches of 'Arabot of willow leaves are taken together and banged on the floor, and that has a certain connotation to it, which is explained in the prayer that is said on Hosha'na Rabbah morning.

So that wraps up the entire holiday season so we can move into the next holiday of Shemini 'Asseret and Simhat Torah. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

72.title: Kabbalat Shabbat in the Halabi Custom
72.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. I gave an overview in my last video regarding the customs of the Halabi community regarding Kabbalat Shabbat, what we say and when we say it. I'll go to greater detail now. I'll be using the book, the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, for you to follow.

So we begin with Mizmor LeDavid, and as I mentioned, we don't say Lekhu Neranenah or other chapters from the Tehillim which other communities may say. There are communities which even say up to six Perakim of Tehillim, beginning with Lekhu Neranenah, corresponding to six days of the week, and Mizmor LeDavid corresponds to the Shabbat. That's not our custom. Our custom is to go directly to Mizmor LeDavid. It could be based on a Yerushalmi which is brought down in the Siddur Bet Menuhah that this Mizmor itself corresponds and hints to the seven days of creation with the seven repetitions of the word Kol: "Kol Ad-onai 'Al HaMayim," "BaKhoah," and so on and so forth. So this Perek itself is a hint to the seven days of the creation.

So we go after Mizmor LeDavid, we don't say the prayer Ana BeKhoah like other Kehillot may do. The Halabi custom is to go straight to Lekha Dodi. Now, both Mizmor LeDavid and Lekha Dodi are sung in unison by the Kahal standing up facing the Hekhal, facing the regular way we always face. You will see other Kehillot which turn around. That's not our custom. We don't turn around, not even in Bo'i BeShalom, not even in Bo'i Khallah, Bo'i Khallah. You can look at the video by my esteemed colleague Morris Arking, I think it's video number 14, where he goes into this issue at length. It's very, very informative and very interesting. But we don't turn around.

Following, well, let me talk about Lekha Dodi for a bit. The custom of the Halabiyeh is to say only four of the eight stanzas that precede Bo'i BeShalom. The original poem, written by the famous Mekubbal, Rabbi Shelomo HaLevi Alkabess from Sefat in the 16th century, made up of eight stanzas acrostically spelling out Shelomo HaLevi, we only say four of them which spell out Shelomo: Shamor, Likrat, Mikdash Melekh, Hit'oreri. And there are a number of reasons given for this. Rabbi Abraham Ades brought them down in his book Derekh Eress. It's recorded also one of the reasons by Hakham, two of the reasons by Hakham Yisshak Chehebar in the book that they printed based on his writings.

Basically, there's three reasons. One is just for the sake of brevity. Just like in Mi Khamokha on Shabbat Zakhor, we don't read the whole poem, we read the beginning and the end, so here we don't want to trouble the Kahal, lengthen the prayer unnecessarily, so we read only four out of the eight. Another reason is that the stanzas we omitted not conducive for saying on Shabbat, maybe they arouse some sadness: "Hitna'ari Me'afar Kumi," speaking of Ge'ulah, and our yearning for the Ge'ulah. And the third reason is that they wanted to avoid, this is Hakham Chehebar says that he heard this reason bouncing around in Halab a little bit, that it was the counter-effect of the Shabta'ut, where Shabbetai Sebi, the false Mashiah, "Shem Resha'im Yirkab," which affected in the 17th century, affected greatly the entire Jewish world, but in particular the Halabi community was one of the first to be under the influence of Shabbetai Sebi. And they attributed a lot to the excessive prayers which dealt with the imminent Ge'ulah, and they wanted, you know, that sort of set the stage for the influence of false Mashiah. So they took out those stanzas which dealt with the imminent Ge'ulah that was forthcoming. So that was a reaction to Shabta'ut.

Following that, we say Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. The Kehillah of Halab is known that we say Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat twice. Most Kehillot do not say it twice. Our Kehillah says it twice. And the reason is 'Al Pi HaKabbalah. You'll see that Rabbi 'Obadia Hedaya, Zikhrono LiBerakhah, in Yaskil 'Abdi, he gives reasons 'Al Pi HaKabbalah. But you can also understand it not 'Al Pi HaKabbalah, because both times we say it, there's different reasons why we say it. We know that there's a discussion amongst the Rishonim as to when we accept upon ourselves the Shabbat, also when we're saying if you're saying Kabbalat Shabbat before sunset, so some say it's Lekha Dodi, some say it's Barekhu when you say Barekhu of 'Arbit. Maran writes that we accept LeDidan in Resh Samekh Alef when we say Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. So that's why it belongs in Kabbalat Shabbat, because it's part of our accepting of the Shabbat.

The one that we say after Kabbalat Sh-, after Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, really belongs and it's close, connected to the 'Arbit, just like we have on Rosh Hodesh, on the holidays, we say Mizmor before 'Arbit. Also here, Shabbat, the Mizmor of Shabbat is Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat, we say before 'Arbit, just like we say it on Rosh Hodesh, on Pesah, on Shabu'ot, and so on. So that's the reason for the two times we say Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. And many Kehillot didn't want to impose upon the Kahal to say it twice, so they took out the first one.

We follow that by Bameh Madlikin. Our custom is to say Rabbi Hananya Ben 'Akashya, that standard Mishnah which we say after we read a series of Mishnayot. We do not say Amar Rabbi El'azar Amar Rabbi Hanina, which you will find in other Kehillot. The Halabim do not say that; we say Rabbi Hananya. It's followed by Kaddish 'Al Yisrael for those who have the obligation to say Kaddish. At any rate, if nobody say it, then the Hazzan will say it. And that represents the end of Kabbalat Shabbat, and now we head into Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat, which belongs to the 'Arbit, which we will discuss in our next video. Shalom, and Kol Tub.

73.title: Zimmun and the Cup of Berakhah
73.text:
Birkat HaMazon. There are many laws and customs attached to Birkat HaMazon. In fact, before we even begin saying Birkat HaMazon, we have certain actions that we do, certain things that are connected to Birkat HaMazon. We have firstly, we have Pesukim that we say prior to Birkat HaMazon. If we are three or more men eating together, we say Zimmun, and there is another less common practice of having a cup of wine that we hold from that point of Zimmun, and which we make Kos Shel Berakhah and HaGefen at the end of Birkat HaMazon.

So what are our specific Minhagim? So we have a litany of Pesukim that are said before Birkat HaMazon, sometimes even Mizmorim prior to those Pesukim. The Zimmun is a very, very simple form based upon Shulhan 'Arukh. It's "Nebarekh SheAkhalnu Mishelo," with the response of "Barukh SheAkhalnu Mishelo UBeTubo Hayyinu," and finally, we have that cup of Birkat HaMazon that may or may not be used.

So let's talk about these Minhagim. Let's deal with the cup first, because if you're going to be doing Zimmun, that's generally when the cup comes into play. Even though according to the Gemara in Masekhet Pesahim, it seems that you need a cup of wine to end Birkat HaMazon even if you're just one person by yourself, that is not the practice. According to the Midrash HaNe'elam of Megillat Rut, if you are three or more eating together, you must have a cup of wine, and that is also the practice of the Mekubbalim according to the Ari. But according to the Rif, according to the Rambam, according to the Meiri, and according to the final opinion in Shulhan 'Arukh, even if three or more men are eating together, there is no obligation whatsoever to have a cup of wine. In other words, it's a nice practice, it's a Missvah Min HaMubhar, meaning it's the choicest way to do the Missvah, but it's not obligatory, and therefore the common practice, the common Minhag within community at large and among Sefaradim at large, is not to use a cup of wine to end Birkat HaMazon. That being said, if you are using that cup of wine, you start holding that cup of wine from the beginning of Zimmun.

So what is Zimmun? Zimmun is when we have three or more men together, we would basically have an invitation, a summoning to Birkat HaMazon, and it's an invitation to come together, to join together, to know that we're going to focus and begin Birkat HaMazon. Shulhan 'Arukh clearly says that the wording for Zimmun is very, very short, and sweet, and simple, and this is our custom. The person leading the Zimmun says "Nebarekh SheAkhalnu Mishelo," those there respond "Barukh SheAkhalnu Mishelo UBeTubo Hayyinu," and the person leading then repeats that line "Barukh SheAkhalnu Mishelo UBeTubo Hayyinu." The text is very clear from Shulhan 'Arukh, also from the Rif, from the Rambam, that those are the words: "Barukh SheAkhalnu Mishelo UBeTubo Hayyinu," and not like you find in other Siddurim today, "SheAkhalnu," "MiTubo HaGadol," "Tamid MiTubo HaGadol." We don't add all these extra words. "Barukh SheAkhalnu Mishelo UBeTubo Hayyinu," that is our Minhag.

Now, before we even do the "Nebarekh," there is another Minhag of saying either "BiRshutkhem," or "BiRshut Morai VeRabotai," or "BiRshut Mor Abi," or "BiRshut HaKohanim" prior to that, and the response would be "BiRshut Shamayim" or in short just "Shamayim," and that would be before the "Nebarekh," and that is a very common practice, and you find it in our Siddurim. Unfortunately though, based upon many Siddurim coming from Israel today based upon the teachings of the Ben Ish Hai, there is another introduction that we see there, and it says "Hab Lana VeNebarikh LeMalka 'Ila'ah Kadisha," "BiRshut Malka 'Ila'ah Kadisha UBiRshutkhem." It is not our Minhag to say such a thing. This verbage does not appear in the writings of the Hida, does not appear in the writings of Rabbi Hayyim Palachi. It is not our Minhag to say such a thing.

And even though it would seem from the Zohar that you have to say those three words of "Hab Lana VeNebarikh," we do not do it, and based upon the Ari himself tells us that because we say the Pesukim prior to Birkat HaMazon, and specifically the Pasuk of "Abarekhah Et Ad-onai BeKhol 'Et," "Tamid Tehilato BeFi," which is a Pasuk from Tehillim, Mizmor Lamed-Dalet, Pasuk Bet, and that Pasuk means, "I will come to praise God," that means you've already set yourself up with the proper frame of mind to be saying Birkat HaMazon. That "Abarekhah Et Ad-onai BeKhol 'Et" is a complete replacement for "Hab Lan VeNebarikh," and therefore anybody saying "Abarekhah" does not say "Hab Lan," and that is our Minhag. So we start with "Abarekhah," we go to regular Zimmun of "BiRshutkhem," "BiRshut Shamayim," "Nebarekh SheAkhalnu Mishelo," etc., like I said. And if you are using a cup of wine, you'd be holding a cup of wine from the time of Zimmun.

Next time, we'll talk about other Minhagim connected to Birkat HaMazon.

74.title: Washing the Hands Before Birkat Kohanim
74.text:
Maran in the Bet Yosef cites a disagreement between the early authorities regarding the Kohanim washing their hands before reciting Birkat Kohanim. According to the Tosafot, the Kohanim are required to wash their hands immediately prior to reciting Birkat Kohanim, even though they made Netilat Yadayim when they woke up in the morning. But according to HaRambam, the Netilat Yadayim that they did in the morning that allows them to recite Keri'at Shema and the 'Amidah also allows them to recite Birkat Kohanim, unless the Kohen knows that his hands became impure after he began reciting the 'Amidah. So according to HaRambam, another washing is not normally required before reciting Birkat Kohanim.

HaRambam's son, Ribbi Abraham, was quoted as saying, "The practical law in front of my father and teacher, may his memory be blessed, and the other Torah teachers, is that every Kohen who is involved in prayer goes up to recite Birkat Kohanim and relies on the washing of his hands that he did for Keri'at Shema and the 'Amidah." This means that the same way that every congregant doesn't go and wash his hands again right before Keri'at Shema or right before the 'Amidah, since he made Netilat Yadayim when he woke up in the morning, likewise a Kohen does not have to wash his hands again before reciting Birkat Kohanim.

But Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh ruled according to the custom of Spain that was based on the Zohar, that does require Kohanim to wash their hands again before reciting Birkat Kohanim. However, according to Ribbi Yisshak Tawil, the custom of Halab was not like Maran in this case. They did not wash their hands before reciting Birkat Kohanim. This was based on the opinion of HaRambam that Maran quoted in the Bet Yosef. This was also the custom of Egypt in the 16th century, which is the time period of the Radbaz, Maran, and the Maharikash, all of whom were in Egypt at some point in their lives.

We find HaRambam's opinion quoted by Ribbi Hayyim Benveniste in the 17th century in Turkey, and by the Magen Abraham, who also lived during the 17th century, but in Poland, and he described HaRambam's opinion as a custom in some places. Furthermore, Ribbi Ya'akob 'Emden, a German authority from the 18th century, also ruled in accordance with HaRambam's opinion regarding washing hands for Kohanim.

So the custom of Halab, based on all of these sources, was not to require the Kohanim to wash their hands again before reciting Birkat Kohanim. This was also the custom here in the Syrian community in Brooklyn when I was growing up during the 1970s and 1980s. It is a valid custom, and there is no need to correct it.

75.title: The 'Arbit of Lel Shabbat
75.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the videos dealing with the Minhagim of the Syrian community, the Halabi community for Shir HaShirim and Kabbalat Shabbat. We will now do two videos on the Minhagim of 'Arbit of Shabbat, of Lel Shabbat, the Friday night prayer.

Kabbalat Shabbat either ended with the Kaddish 'Al Yisrael following Bameh Madlikin, or for those who say Shir HaShirim following that Kaddish. So now we are completed Shir HaShirim and we are going to begin 'Arbit. We begin 'Arbit with the second recitation of Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat. I'm going to follow in the Kol Ya'akob Siddur so you could follow with me if you would like.

The first time we said Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat seated was during Kabbalat Shabbat. Now we're saying it a second time, as I explained, it's similar to holidays or Purim where or Rosh Hodesh where we would say a Mizmor prior to 'Arbit, the Mizmor which is particular for that day. The Mizmor of Shabbat is Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat, and therefore we are saying it prior to 'Arbit. The Hazzan will lead the Kahal, the Kahal is seated, people are praying to themselves, and the Hazzan is beginning Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat and "HaShem Malakh Ge'ut Labesh" prior to saying Kaddish, and he will of course be in the musical scale of Nawa, which is widespread among all Halabi communities that this is the scale for Friday nights, just like Rast for Shabbat afternoon and Bayat for Mossa'e Shabbat. We always prayed in this the beautiful scale, very unique, and it gives a feeling of Friday night. We pray in the scale of Nawa.

Unfortunately in the last 20 or so years, when I go back to visit, I see Hazzanim praying in Nahawand, which really it surprised me at first. I mean, I would imagine they're proficient and they know Maqam Nawa. So I don't know why the Gabba'im don't insist that they follow our custom and, you know, they don't have to change the custom to Nahawand. I think it's very, very important. We'll speak about liturgical customs at another time.

We begin Kaddish. Now, in our community we have the custom that this Kaddish, as in all Syrian communities worldwide, we say the people sit down while the Hazzan is singing the Kaddish. There are other Sefaradi communities, of course has to be Sefaradi because the Ashkenazim, they don't even have a Hassi Kaddish on Friday night, but there are other Sefaradi communities where you will see the Kaddish is sung by the Hazzan and the people are standing up. Now this is based on a kabbalistic tradition of the acceptance of the Neshamah Yeterah. It is not our custom to stand up, it's our custom to sit down.

Not only that, we discussed in our earlier videos regarding Kaddish, the hearing of Kaddish in general, if somebody found themselves standing while the Kaddish has begun, he does not sit down, he remain standing. However, if the Kaddish is being sung, we don't trouble that person to stay to remain standing throughout the whole Kaddish. So even if he was caught standing when the Kaddish started by the Hazzan, he is permitted to sit down. This was taught to me by my father-in-law, 'Alav HaShalom, Dennis Dweck. I've heard it from other Hakhamim as well. There may be a synagogue or two in the community which the Zekenim will insist that the people stand throughout, but it's been widespread that for Kaddish BeNiggun we do not require the person to remain standing.

The Hazzan continues with Barekhu, the Berakhot of Keri'at Shema, Keri'at Shema, Emunah Kol Zot, of course they're all BeNiggun, sung. And then we get to Hashkibenu. Hashkibenu is the time when the people begin to stand up in preparation for the Kaddish. We, the Halabi, the Syrian community, do not sing this Hashkibenu in any particular tune like you will find in other communities, even in our neighborhood, the Shwam, or the Egyptian community, I know the Moroccan community, each has their own tune for Hashkibenu and the people sing it in unison. That is not our custom. This is said the same way as the prayer until now, with the Hazzan leading, people saying it to themselves.

Now, this is followed by "Shamru Bene Yisrael Et HaShabbat," and here it's a little bit different. Here you will have the people raising their voices a bit, and saying it in a bit louder voice than they would say the rest of the prayer. It's not sung in any particular tune, and you will still hear the Hazzan's strong voice above the Kahal's voices, but nonetheless I wanted to point out that this is sung in a little bit loud, it's said in a little bit louder voice than the rest of the prayer, followed by the Hassi Kaddish, and we begin the 'Amidah.

Next, in our next video we will discuss the Minhagim following the completion of the 'Amidah of Lel Shabbat. Shabbat Shalom. Kol Tub MiYerushalayim.

76.title: Customs Surrounding Birkat HaMazon
76.text:
Birkat HaMazon. Last time we spoke about Zimmun. Zimmun is when three or more people eat together, and they say a special formula before starting Birkat HaMazon. What else is done or not done prior to Birkat HaMazon?

So, first thing, there is a popular Pizmon called Sur Mishelo Akhalnu, and the general custom in families from Aleppo is not to sing this song. Now, like many other things, this is something that is relegated to the home. Everything surrounding Birkat HaMazon is relegated to the home, so there may be differences within certain families, but for the most part, the Minhag is not to sing this song.

After that, there's something called Mayim Aharonim, the final waters where you wash your fingertips before saying Birkat HaMazon. People in Halab were very scrupulous to do this, and before doing this, would say "Mayim Aharonim Hobah," which is a Halakhah. When saying this Halakhah, you also fulfill your obligation of saying Dibre Torah 'Al HaShulhan, words of Torah at your meal. Now, even though they were scrupulous regarding doing this, and this technically should apply to both men and women, only the men did it, women did not do it.

Following Mayim Aharonim and prior to the recitation of the Pesukim of "Abarekhah Et HaShem BeKhol 'Et" that we spoke about last time, on a weekday, Mizmor Samekh-Zayin, 67, is recited, that's "LaMnasseah BiNginot Mizmor Shir Elokim Yehonenu ViBarekhenu," which we recite every morning. On Shabbat, though, we do not say that Mizmor, we say Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat and "HaShem Malakh." Those are Mizmorim Sadi-Bet and Sadi-Gimmel, 92 and 93.

Once that is completed, we go to "Abarekhah," those five or six Pesukim, then we go into Zimmun if we have three or more eating together. At the conclusion of Zimmun, there is another line that is said, which is "Barukh Hu UBarukh Shemo UBarukh Zikhro Le'Olme 'Ad," and then Birkat HaMazon actually begins. The person who does the Zimmun says the entire Birkat HaMazon out loud with everybody else at the table following along and reciting it in a lower tone voice.

Now, there are many other variations and texts within Birkat HaMazon from the standard Birkat HaMazon that we're used to today from most Siddurim. The ones that I'm going to point out right now are ones that stand out in the Siddur 'Odat HaShahar that was printed in Halab in 1915. This is Siddur 'Odat HaShahar. It's a very rare Siddur, it's not easily found.

The first difference is before the section of Nodeh Lekha, which is generally the second paragraph of Birkat HaMazon, there are a few extra words, which are "'Al Arssenu Ve'Al Nahalat Abotenu." These five words are said before Nodeh Lekha. Also later on in Birkat HaMazon, after the Berakhah of Binyan Yerushalayim, which as per this Siddur is "Barukh Attah HaShem Boneh BeRahamav Binyan Yerushalayim Amen," there are three or so lines that say "BeHayyenu UBeHayye Kol Kehal Bet Yisrael Tibaneh 'Ir Siyyon BeRinah VeTikkon 'Abodat HaKodesh BiYerushalayim VeArmon 'Al Mishpato Yesheb BeKarob KeBarishonah." And then you go into the next Berakhah, "Barukh Attah HaShem Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam La'Ad HaEl Abinu Malkenu," etc. So again you see a difference of words.

There are differences within the HaRahamans, we're not going to get into all of them. And finally upon the conclusion of Birkat HaMazon, after "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav," it is commonly said—again you'd conclude and say "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav Hu BeRahamav HaRabbim Ya'aseh Shalom 'Alenu Ve'Al Kol 'Ammo Yisrael VeImru Amen," and then "Barukh HaZan, Barukh HaShulhan, Barukh Moshe Ben 'Amram." This is a very common addition in families from Aleppo, Syria.

So these are only touching upon some of the additions prior to Birkat HaMazon, and within Birkat HaMazon, and post-Birkat HaMazon. Of course, there are many other additions, and hopefully in a following video, we'll get into the many differences within the text of Birkat HaMazon.

77.title: Removing Shoes for Birkat Kohanim
77.text:
In Masekhet Sotah, the Gemara stated that Rabban Yohanan Ben Zakkai prohibited Kohanim from ascending a platform to recite Birkat Kohanim while wearing their shoes. The Gemara explained that if they wore their shoes, and their shoelaces became untied, that they might leave the platform to tie them, which could lead to a suspicion that they left the platform because they are not valid Kohanim. Rashi explained that it's unbecoming for one to have their shoelaces untied in front of everyone, and people might chide them, because it doesn't look nice.

Therefore, HaRambam ruled that Kohanim may not ascend the platform with their shoes on, that they recite the blessing barefoot. Maran also ruled that Kohanim may not ascend the platform with their shoes on, however he did permit reciting the blessing while wearing socks.

The later authorities addressed the question of whether Kohanim are still obligated to remove their shoes if they recite the blessing without ascending a platform. Since the reason for removing shoes only applies to a Kohen who ascended a platform, making his shoes visible to the congregation, several authorities wrote that the requirement does not apply to those that recite the blessing without ascending a platform. Meaning, that by remaining on ground level, his untied shoelaces would not be noticeable, and he would not feel compelled to tie them before reciting the blessing.

Ribbi Yisshak Palachi, who lived in Turkey in the 19th century, wrote in his book Yafeh LaLeb—this is a copy of that book—that the requirement of removing shoes only applies to Kohanim who ascend a platform. This was also the opinion of Ribbi Yehoshua Perahyah HaKohen in his book VaYikra Yehoshua. He also lived in the 19th century, but he was from Salonika. And it was also the opinion of Ribbi Ya'akob Moshe Toledano in his responsa Yam HaGadol, and the opinion of the former Chief Rabbi of Israel, Ribbi Yisshak Nissim, in his responsa Yen HaTob. They also cited the fact that the Gemara used the term La'alot LaDukhan, to ascend the platform, as opposed to the more common term for Birkat Kohanim of Nesiat Kapayim, to raise their hands, when stipulating the requirement of removing shoes.

Ribbi Yisshak Nissim wrote that in his times, in the beginning of the 20th century, there were Kohanim in Baghdad and Egypt that did not ascend the platform to recite Birkat Kohanim, and therefore they did not remove their shoes. The book Derekh Eress also recorded this as the custom of Halab, and this custom continued here in the community as well, as attested to by Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim, 'Alav HaShalom, in a recorded class from the year 1964. It has also been reported that Hakham Matloub Abadi, 'Alav HaShalom, taught that Kohanim are required to remove their shoes if they ascend a platform that is at least three Tefahim high, which is 9 and 1/2 inches, but they may ascend a platform that is less than three Tefahim high with their shoes on to recite Birkat Kohanim.

So the custom of reciting Birkat Kohanim while wearing shoes is valid, provided the Kohen does not ascend a platform that is at least 9 and 1/2 inches high. This is based on the opinion of several later authorities and was the accepted practice in several Middle Eastern communities, including Halab. This custom also continued here in New York with the approval of the leading community rabbis.

78.title: Completing the Friday Night 'Arbit
78.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. In our last video, we did the Minhagim of the Friday night prayer, the 'Arbit of Lel Shabbat, from Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat until the 'Amidah, and now we will complete the customs of the Syrian community for 'Arbit right as we finish the 'Amidah till the end.

So, the Hazzan begins with the prayer "VaYekhulu HaShamayim VeHaAress VeKhol Seba'am." Now he will say it, and say it straight through till "Bara Elokim La'asot." There will be other communities, not Syrian communities, possibly Yerushalmis, which have the custom where the Hazzan says the first Pasuk, and then all the Kahal recites it, repeats the first Pasuk, and then the Hazzan will continue. It's not our custom. The Hazzan begins, and says it straight through.

Now, an interesting Halakhah regarding VaYekhulu, if a person either came late to Kenis, or spent a longer time in the 'Amidah than the Hazzan, and the Hazzan began VaYekhulu, and he was in the 'Amidah and he didn't hear VaYekhulu from the Hazzan, then he says it, he says it when he finishes the 'Amidah. However, there are many communities which insist that a person cannot say this on his own. It's like a testimony, an 'Edut. So you need two people. So he has to find somebody in the Kenis, go to somebody and say, "Could you say VaYekhulu with me?" and the two of them will say it together. That is not required in our community. The custom is not to have to require somebody to read it together with somebody else. If a person didn't hear VaYekhulu from the Hazzan, and he finishes the 'Amidah a little bit later, or came late to Kenis, he simply says VaYekhulu on his own.

It's followed by the Berakhah called Me'en Sheba', it's a type of an abbreviated Hazarah, where the people are standing up, and the Hazzan will end it "Mekadesh HaShabbat," followed by Kaddish Titkabbal, which he says. After that, it's Mizmor LeDavid, Kaddish Yehe Shelama for those who required or have a yahrzeit and they need to say Kaddish. Obviously, if there's nobody saying that needs to say Kaddish, the Hazzan will say this Kaddish. No Kaddishim are skipped in our custom. Followed by Barekhu, 'Alenu LeShabbeah. After 'Alenu LeShabbeah, the prayer is over.

Now, you'll see in Kol Ya'akob, it says some congregations chant Yigdal. Yigdal is a very famous song, a famous Piyyut, based on the thirteen principles of faith of HaRambam. It is not our custom to sing it Friday night. It is the custom of many Sephardic communities, Moroccan, Egyptian, Shawam, they all sing it. The Halabiyeh community, the custom is not to say Yigdal. In Ades, we don't say Yigdal Friday nights. In fact, I was looking at a book that discusses the Minhagim of Halab, it says there's only a few times a year which we say Yigdal. One is at a Berit Milah, when the grandmother is bringing the baby, the people will sing "Yigdal Elokim Hai." Another time is a couple weeks ago, Simhat Torah, when we take all the Sefarim out, "Yigdal Elokim Hai VeYishtabbah." That's another time. It's brought down that it's said at a wedding, and that obviously is fell into disuse. The Minhag seems to have been discontinued in our community, if indeed it was a, you know, a strong Minhag in Halab. So I don't know when it was said or how it was sung. Joey Mosseri pointed out to me that in the notes of Hakham Moshe Ashear, the famous Hazzan of our community for the first part of our establishment here in the States, first part the first half of the 20th century, he has in his notes that on Rosh HaShanah, following 'Arbit, both nights we sing Yigdal. So I'm not sure if that's been continued, but that is found in his notes.

Now, following 'Alenu LeShabbeah, when everybody's leaving the Kenis, there was a beautiful Minhag when we were kids, where, and you'll find it also in many community many Sephardic communities, but I remember it very clearly, that there was either one of the Gabbayim or a Shamash with Besamim, you know, probably near the doorway at the end, and as people exit, they would make a Berakhah on the Besamim, usually it was Hadasim, where you would make "Bore 'Asse Besamim," or very often, especially in Shaare Zion, 'cause, Barukh HaShem, there was a lot of people, and they used to use the that silver holder that they used to give out the Besamim, I think they still do it on Saturday nights, where it's basically mazahar, rose water diluted with water, and then they would sprinkle it and give it out to the people leaving the Kenis. And they would, you know, splash it on the kids, and it was very memorable and a very beautiful Minhag.

You know, it's a Minhag in order that, you know, on Shabbat we're missing some Berakhot, so it's one of the ways to complete the Me'ah Berakhot on Shabbat. But it's a beautiful custom, and for those synagogues who do not do it, it's very easily instituted. So we could we should restore the old custom of Besamim Mossa'e Shabbat. Kol Tub.

79.title: Textual Variations in Birkat HaMazon
79.text:
In the previous two segments on Birkat HaMazon, I mentioned a third segment where I will discuss Nushaot, Nushaot meaning textual variations. Now, one may wonder, what do you mean textual variations? Isn't Birkat HaMazon Birkat HaMazon? Unfortunately, over the course of time, changes have occurred, words have been added, words have been deleted, things have changed.

Within our very own community here in New York, we've seen many Siddurim that have become commonplace and they have influenced us. From the '30s through the late '70s, the most common Siddur was Tefillat Yeshurun. Tefillat Yeshurun was actually published in New York during those years, between the '30s and the '70s, even early '80s. Then what became commonplace was Tefillat Yesharim that came from an Iraqi Jewish publisher in Yerushalayim. Many of them were made specifically for the community. If you can see down here, it says Yeshivat Magen David. So, this played a extensive role in shaping the way prayers changed in our community between the '50s and the '70s. We had Siddur Ahabat Siyyon, which even had a special printing for our community, thus called Shaare Zion, and on the bottom it says specifically published for Shaare Zion, another one of the common books that you would find in Shaare Zion in the '60s and '70s and early '80s. Then we had a community publication called Bet Yosef VeOhel Abraham, which was based upon the Tefillat Yesharim, so even though it made some changes, it was still heavily influenced by the Iraqi changes. Finally, from the mid-'80s on, we have Siddur Kol Ya'akob, which has been doing its utmost in every edition and subsequent editions through the hard work of the various editors to reintroduce our true Nushaot and our wording the way we have said for countless decades and centuries.

In Birkat HaMazon, we have many, many differences if you compare your modern Siddur today to the way we actually say it. Birkat HaMazon is four Berakhot. The first Berakhah, we have a number of differences. We'll see many Siddurim tell you to say "HaEl Hazan Otanu." We don't say the word "HaEl," we just say "Hazan Otanu." Some individuals and some families add a full word after the Berakhah. They say "Barukh Atah HaShem, Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam, Hazanenu VeLo MiMa'asenu, HaMfarnesenu VeLo MiSidkotenu, HaMa'adif Tubo 'Alenu, Hazan Otanu VeEt Kol Ha'Olam Kulo," etc. But most families in the community have never had that custom. We say "BeHen, BeHesed, BeRevah URahamim." We do not add the word "Rabbim" after that. We say "VeTubo" and not "UBeTubo." We say "Ki Hu Zan UMfarnes HaKol" and not "Ki Hu El Zan UMfarnes HaKol." And finally, we conclude the Berakhah "Barukh Atah Ad-onai, Hazan BeRahamav Et HaKol." All these things are not generally found in other Siddurim.

The next Berakhah, we generally know it as "Nodeh Lekha," but technically there are four words before that: "'Al Arssenu Ve'Al Nahalat Abotenu," and then "Nodeh Lekha." And we continue from thereon, and we have "Ve'Al HaKol Ad-onai Elokenu Anu Modim Lakh." We don't say "Anahnu," we say "Anu." We say "Ve'Al Tassrikhenu" and not like other books that say "VeNa Al Tassrikhenu." We say "VeLo LiDe Halva'atam, SheMatanatam Mu'atah VeHerpatam Merubah, Ela." Other books are missing those words. We say "Ha'Ashirah VeHaPetuhah, SheLo Nebosh." We don't say "Yehi Rasson SheLo Nebosh," we just go into "SheLo Nebosh." When we get to the end of the Berakhah, we say "Boneh BeRahamav Binyan Yerushalayim, Amen."

After the end of that Berakhah, before we start the next Berakhah, we have another bunch of words, "BeHayenu UBeHaye Kol Kehal Bet Yisrael," which I mentioned in a previous video. When we're in the next section, we say "La'Ad HaEl Abinu." In the HaRahaman's, we have a few other changes as well, like "BeHeter VeLo BeIssur, BeNahat VeLo BeSa'ar, VeRevah VeLo VeSimssum."

And there are many other different changes and variations that are not commonly found and we're going to put this together into a list as I mentioned, and the Kol Ya'akob Siddurim are introducing these specific changes to our community and to Sefaradim in general in upcoming editions. Many of them are already there already, and many of them exist within many families of the community who have held strong to our traditions. So take hold of our tradition. Take hold of our heritage. Do not give it up because the Siddur in front of you doesn't have it and think that, oh, we must be making a mistake by adding these words, because these new Siddurim do not have them. Stick to the traditions of the old-timers.

80.title: Birkat Kohanim in a House of Mourning
80.text:
There are different customs regarding reciting Birkat Kohanim in a house of mourning. According to the Shibbole HaLeket, a 13th-century authority from Italy, Birkat Kohanim is not recited at all in a house of mourning. This was also the custom according to Ribbi Hayyim Benveniste, an authority from Izmir, Turkey during the 17th century. According to some, this is because a mourner does not greet people, and therefore he should not bless people with peace, which is similar to greeting people. Also, one does not greet a mourner, which perhaps explains the custom of those that omit Birkat Kohanim altogether in a house of mourning.

However, according to many Mekubbalim, even the mourners themselves can recite Birkat Kohanim if they are Kohanim. This is discussed by Ribbi Ya'akob Sofer in his commentary to Shulhan 'Arukh, which is known as Kaf HaHayyim, and it is based on the writings of Ribbi Shalom Shar'abi, an 18th-century master of Kabbalah who is more commonly known as the Rashash. Now, even according to Halakhah, a mourner may recite Birkat Kohanim. Refraining is a custom, which is not necessarily practiced by all of the Mekubbalim.

There is also a third custom, which is that Birkat Kohanim is recited in the house of mourning, but if the mourners themselves are Kohanim, they walk out of the room before the Kohanim begin to go up. In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote: "After the seven-day mourning period, mourners lift their hands," meaning they recite Birkat Kohanim. Then Maran continued: "But during the seven-day mourning period, a mourner who is a Kohen should leave the synagogue when Kohanim are called." So Maran did accept the custom, but since he only spoke about the mourners themselves, it is understood that other Kohanim do recite Birkat Kohanim in a mourner's house, as Maran did not stipulate any restriction about that case.

So what was the custom in Halab? Did the mourners recite Birkat Kohanim during the seven-day mourning period, or not? And if they didn't, did other Kohanim recite Birkat Kohanim in the house of mourning, or not? Ribbi Eliyahu Mishan, an important Mekubbal in Halab during the 19th century, wrote in his book Sedek VeShalom: "The custom in our city, Aram Soba, is to bless Birkat Kohanim in the mourner's house, the other Kohanim, who are not mourners, but not the mourner himself." So from here we see that the custom in Halab was like Maran. The mourner does not recite Birkat Kohanim during the seven-day mourning period, but only the mourners are restricted. The other Kohanim do recite Birkat Kohanim in the mourner's house.

This was also recorded as the custom of Halab in the book Derekh Eress, and it is also the custom in our community, and was recorded by Meyer Safdieh, 'Alav HaShalom, in his book known as Me'ir Ot. He wrote: "Birkat Kohanim is said in the house of mourning, but if the mourner himself is a Kohen, he should not participate. Rather, he should leave the room before the Hazzan reaches Resseh in the repetition of the 'Amidah."

Now what about when the mourner is in the synagogue on Shabbat? On Shabbat, public displays of mourning are prohibited. Should the mourner recite Birkat Kohanim in the synagogue on Shabbat in order to avoid a public display of mourning? According to Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, if there are other Kohanim in the synagogue, it is not an issue, so he may walk out before Resseh in order to avoid reciting Birkat Kohanim. However, some other authorities do not differentiate between whether other Kohanim are there or not. Some say that mourners recite Birkat Kohanim on Shabbat even if other Kohanim are there, but others say that even if there are no other Kohanim, the mourner should walk out before Resseh, meaning that since the Kohen isn't in the room when it's time for Kohanim, it's not considered a public display of mourning. And this is also the custom in our community, as recorded by Meyer Safdieh in Me'ir Ot.

Even on Shabbat, the mourner does not recite Birkat Kohanim, whether or not other Kohanim are there. This custom was also recorded by Ribbi Hayyim Benveniste in his work known as Keneset HaGedolah, and in the authoritative 18th-century Shabbat Siddur known as Bet Menuhah. According to Ribbi Yehuda Shmuel Ashkenazi, the author of that Siddur, when Maran wrote that mourners do not recite Birkat Kohanim for seven days, Maran did not differentiate between weekdays and Shabbat. Furthermore, the custom of mourners not reciting Birkat Kohanim on Shabbat even when there are no other Kohanim present was recorded by Ribbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on in his work known as Nehar Missrayim on the customs of Egypt.

So we do recite Birkat Kohanim in a house of mourning, but the mourners themselves do not recite Birkat Kohanim during the seven-day mourning period, whether it's a weekday or Shabbat, whether other Kohanim are present or not. In all cases, if the mourners are Kohanim, they leave the room before the Hazzan gets up to Resseh.

81.title: Beginning the Shabbat Morning Prayers
81.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the Minhagim of Friday night prayers in the synagogue, and now we will begin with the Minhagim of the Shabbat morning, the Shahrit prayers in the synagogue.

Now we begin with VaTitpallel Hannah, and that is the widespread custom in all of our synagogues in Brooklyn as well as Argentina and Israel. Now, I'm pointing it out only because that in Halab there was another custom. The custom was by the Sefaradim to start with VaTitpallel Hannah, but the Musta'arabim used did not say VaTitpallel Hannah, they started with Vihi No'am and Elokenu. Just pointing that out, that there was separate custom for Musta'arabim, but again that doesn't apply anymore. In New York, we say we begin with VaTitpallel Hannah.

Now, followed by the 'Akedah, the Korbanot, and Ezehu Mekoman. Now, this section of the prayer, which we say in the weekdays as well, but this section is said by one of the Yehidim, one of the people in the Kahal, from his seat generally. They don't walk up to the Tebah to say this section of the prayer. It's said from his seat, and it's said in its entirety sitting down. The reason I'm pointing this out is because you will find other customs. There is there are other Kehillot which have the custom to stand up at Ana BeKhoah and continue saying the rest from Ana BeKhoah on standing. That is not our custom. Our custom is to be seated throughout until the Kaddish.

Now the Kaddish, provided there's a Minyan, we say Kaddish 'Al Yisrael. If there is no Minyan at this time, we will use the next opportunity to say the Kaddish when the Minyan gets there, usually after HaShem Melekh, before LaMnasseah, or even after "Hodu LeEl HaShamayim Ki Le'Olam Hasdo," before Barukh SheAmar. But if we do say Kaddish not in its proper place, but rather in one of those other places, we have to precede it with the Mishnah of "Rabbi Hananyah Ben 'Akashya Omer." That is our custom.

Now we come to the Zemirot which begin with Hodu. The custom in Brooklyn and in our community growing up was always the Kahal sings it together, the first section, in the well-known tune, "Hodu LaAd-onai Kir'u BiShmo Hodi'u Va'Ammim 'Alilotav," and we continue until "Asher Karat Et Abraham UShvu'ato LeYisshak." Then the Hazzan will continue saying it alone. There are there is another custom, not so much in Brooklyn, but there's a custom in Yerushalayim, and I've heard old recordings from Hazzanim in Argentina which they sing, and this is what we do in Ades, we sing it all the way until "Hodu LaAd-onai Ki Tob Ki Le'Olam Hasdo." And then, the Hazzan will continue, "VeImru Hoshi'enu Eloke Yish'enu." There is another custom that if you're doing it that way, the Pasuk of "Hodu LaHaShem Ki Tob," they will repeat it. They will say it twice. Again, in Brooklyn, that's not custom. We sing until "UShvu'ato LeYisshak," and it's picked up by the Hazzan afterwards.

Now, we get to HaShem Melekh. HaShem Melekh is sung by we say it standing up. A Hazzan will sing it, the Kahal will answer in the same tune. Generally, not an ironclad rule, but generally the Hazzan will sing it in a tune that's in the same scale as the scale of the week, the same Maqam of that Parashah, of that Shabbat. That is the scale which he will choose a tune from to sing HaShem Melekh. Now, the Kahal answers, they're seated, and then the Hazzan at this point will go up to the Tebah and begin the LaMnasseah in the second part of the Zemirot which is the LaMnasseah and so on, and we will pick that up in our next video. Kol Tub.

82.title: Introducing the Life Cycles Series
82.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week presents Life Cycles. Until now, Minhag of the Week has been focusing on holidays as well as prayers of weekdays, Shabbatot, and holidays, and what have you. Many requests come in on a daily basis regarding the Minhagim of life cycles: birth, Berit Milah, Pidyon, naming a baby, Bar Missvah, weddings, and things that come towards the end of a person's life as well. And there are many Minhagim that are associated with all these important life cycles, and we wish to address them as well.

As we know, our community is probably the greatest and largest Sephardic community in a community setting in the world. Even though the greatest concentration of Sefaradim in Eress Yisrael, the Jews in Israel are part of a Jewish nation, a Jewish country, whereas here in the diaspora, we are a very unique community of Jews among other Jews, among Goyim, among all different types of people. Our Sephardic community in New York and New Jersey has been growing steadily over the past 120 years. And obviously, it started with Jews from Syria, then Jews from Egypt, Jews from Lebanon, Jews from Morocco, Jews from Iraq, Jews from Israel, Jews from Turkey, Jews from so many other places have come and joined our community.

And of course, that adds to the flavor of the community, but at the same time, it blurs the differences in the Minhagim. And we wish to preserve the Minhagim because not only people want to know them, but people want to carry on their heritage. So in this series of life cycle Minhagim, I plan on, God willing, addressing not only the Minhagim of the Jews of Aleppo, like we've been doing for the most part till now, but when important Minhagim of Damascus, or Egypt, or Lebanon, or any other country that have played a role within this community, you know, come to play, I'll bring them up and try to show the differences as well.

Again, it's important to be aware of your heritage, be aware of your tradition, know who you are, what you are, where you came from, uphold that with pride. And I'm sure many of you will have questions, and we ask you to please send in your questions to minhag@scaupdates.org. We will, God willing, address them. The first part of the life cycle series will deal with birth, Berit Milah, naming children, and Pidyon. So imagine we'll be doing that for the next six weeks or so. Get in those questions early, that way we can address them. Thank you for enjoying Minhag of the Week and for cherishing your customs.

83.title: Tefillin in Minhah When a Fast Falls on Friday
83.text:
In a previous video, episode number 32, we discussed our custom of wearing Talet and Tefillin in Minhah on a public fast day. That custom was mentioned by Maran in the Bet Yosef, and was also recorded as the custom of Halab by several Halabi rabbis. But what about when a fast falls on a Friday? Do we still wear Talet and Tefillin in Minhah? The only fast day that ever falls out on a Friday is 'Asarah BeTebet, and this year falls out on a Friday.

According to the law, it is permissible to put on Tefillin on Friday afternoon before sunset. We are not permitted to put Tefillin on at night, and we are not permitted to put Tefillin on on Shabbat. But we may put Tefillin on on Friday afternoon if we remove them before sunset. However, there is a disagreement between the Mekubbalim, the authorities on kabbalistic practices, regarding whether or not Tefillin may be worn on Friday afternoon. Interestingly, the Mekubbalim do wear Tefillin every weekday in Minhah, but with regards to Friday afternoon, some do and some do not.

With regards to the custom in our community for 'Asarah BeTebet that falls on a Friday, Rabbi Eliyahu Ashkenazi, a rabbi in our community from Deal, New Jersey, wrote an article discussing our custom. He noted that our custom is to put Tefillin on in Minhah, even when the fast falls on Friday. But in 1994, some of our community rabbis suggested changing that custom, based on the fact that Ribbi Hayyim Palachi, an authority from Turkey in the 19th century, changed the custom in his city Izmir because of those Mekubbalim that taught that Tefillin should not be worn on Friday afternoon when the light of Shabbat's holiness has already begun glowing. This was based on the opinion of many Mekubbalim, including most notably, Ribbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, who is more commonly known as the Hida. And not wearing Tefillin on Friday afternoon in general was recorded as the custom of the Land of Israel by Ribbi Hayyim Ben Menasheh Sethon in his book on the customs of the Land of Israel that's known as Eress Hayyim.

So in 1994, Rabbi Ashkenazi consulted with Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim 'Alav HaShalom, who affirmed our community custom of wearing Tefillin in Minhah, even when 'Asarah BeTebet falls on a Friday. It is also noteworthy that Ribbi Hayyim HaKohen, an important Mekubbal from Halab in the beginning of the 17th century, wore Tefillin in Minhah every Friday afternoon. On the other hand, Ribbi Eliyahu Mishan, an important Mekubbal from Halab in the 19th century, was asked about the proper kabbalistic practice regarding wearing Tefillin in Minhah when 'Asarah BeTebet falls on a Friday. In his book, he answered that it's better to refrain.

That answer was directed to those that always conduct themselves according to kabbalistic teachings, but our community custom to wear Tefillin in Minhah, even when the fast falls on a Friday, is based primarily on the Halakhah, which does not prohibit Tefillin on Friday afternoon before sunset, and it is also proper according to some Mekubbalim. Furthermore, our custom was practiced with the approval of Hakham Ya'akob Kassin and Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim 'Alehem HaShalom. When practicing this custom, make sure to remove your Tefillin and put them away before sunset.

84.title: Dividing the Zemirot and the Shirah
84.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will be continuing in our discussions regarding the Minhagim of the Shabbat morning prayers. We ended up the last video where the Hazzan sang and the Kahal repeated the "HaShem Malakh," and now the Hazzan for this section, until Nishmat, makes his way up to the Tebah, and he will generally, yes, he will say the first Mizmor, the first Perek of Tehillim, "LaMnasseah Mizmor LeDavid," and then he will be responsible for dividing up the Perakim to other members of the Kahal. Each one will take one Perek. Maybe the Shir HaMa'alot, if it's shorter, each one will take two Perakim. And that'll be his job to make sure it's divided properly. It's done in a very specific tune. And I will, in my next video, I will go into more detail regarding the liturgical Minhagim of the Shabbat prayers, because when it comes to Shabbat prayers, the tunes that we use, the scales that are used, these customs are as important as what is said, and when is it said, and by whom is said, which is generally what we discuss when we talk about the Minhagim, because when a person comes to the Kenis, there has to be that feel of Shabbat, and that feel is transmitted through the tunes that we use. So we'll talk about that a little bit more in the next video.

So we go through the Zemirot. The last Perek of Tehillim in the Zemirot is what we call Hallel HaGadol, "Hodu LaAd-onai Ki Tob Ki Le'Olam Hasdo." Here, it is said in the same fashion as all the previous Perakim. In other words, the Hazzan says it from beginning to end. The reason I'm pointing this out is because many other Kehillot throughout the world, Sephardic Kehillot, there is a give and take with the Hazzan and the Kahal. The Hazzan will say, "Hodu LaHaShem Ki Tob," and the Kahal will answer, "Ki Le'Olam Hasdo," and so on, till the end of the Perek. That is not our custom. Our custom is the Hazzan says it from beginning to the end.

And now we go into the Barukh SheAmar. Again, the liturgical aspects we'll talk about in the next video, but Barukh SheAmar in our community is sung to the tune of the Hatikvah, which is an old custom in our community. Again, the Perakim, the song is sung until "Barukh Podeh UMassil Barukh Shemo," and then the Hazzan will pick it up from the Berakhah. And then the Perakim are divided amongst the Hazzanim, until the final Halleluyah, which is sung.

Now, the way it's set up is that we start with the 'Akedah and the Korbanot, which we did last week. That is read very quickly. There's no embellishments, very quickly. The LaMnasseah and the Zemirot is read a bit slower. It's also done rather efficiently, but a bit slower than the Korbanot. And then the Pesuke DeZimra is where you'll find more embellishments and flourishments by the Hazzanim within the scales, until we get to the Nishmat, of course, which is where the Hazzan will sing to his, you know, based on the scale of the week, more than the other sections of the prayer.

When we get to, we've finished the last Halleluyah, we shift from the scale that we've been saying the Pesuke DeZimra into Sigah. So when we get to VaYebarekh David, more specifically the paragraph before, "Barukh Ad-onai Le'Olam Amen VeAmen," you'll hear the Hazzan shift into Sigah, and VaYebarekh David is done in this scale, and as well VaYosha' and Az Yashir, which are done according to the Te'amim, which of course is Sigah.

Now, in the VaYebarekh David, we break it up into four or five smaller paragraphs, which is well-known, the first one ending in "VeKhol Berakhah UTehillah," "VeAttah Moshel BaKhol," where the whole Kahal ends "VeAttah Moshel BaKhol," and then someone else will say "UBeYadkha," until "Berakhah UTehillah," and then the third Hazzan, and then they'll shift around. VaYebarekh David is divided in that fashion.

And then, like I said, the Shirah is done in the Te'amim of the Sefer Torah. It's finished in "BaYabbashah BeTokh HaYam," except two times during the year, the two times that we read the Shirat HaYam, one is Shabbat Shirah, and the other, which is around the Tu BiShbat time, and the other is Shebi'i Shel Pesah when we read the Shirat HaYam. In those two instances, the Hazzan will continue after "Halekhu BaYabbashah BeTokh HaYam," he will continue "VaTikkah Miryam HaNebi'ah" until "Ki Ani HaShem Rofe'ekha." This is an old Musta'arabi custom from Halab. It's recorded by 'Alav HaShalom Hakham Salim Zafrani who was the Hakham of that community, and this custom stayed with us, and it's indeed in, I would say, all the Halabi Kehillot that I've, whether they be in Israel or New York, they continue until "Ki Ani HaShem Rofe'ekha" on these two Shabbatot. Shalom UBerakhah.

85.title: Naming Children After the Living and Deceased
85.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles: Naming the Baby. So, as far as naming a child, that's the first thing that a person will think of before the baby is born. And we have a very clear Minhag, which is different than other communities, definitely different than Ashkenazim. We, in fact, name after both the living as well as the deceased, whereas Ashkenazim will only name after the deceased, and some Sefaradim do the same. So, the general custom in Syria, in Egypt, in Lebanon, and many other places is that the first boy that is born is named for the paternal grandfather, the second boy for the maternal grandfather, the first girl for the paternal grandmother, and the second girl for the maternal grandmother. After that, all names are free, and, you know, any name can be chosen.

Now, some people have questioned this Minhag, you know, is it proper, is it improper, why do we do it? So, in fact, it's a beautiful Minhag. It's done for a number of reasons. One is family pride. You take pride in your family, you take pride in who you came from, and in continuing the legacy through the birth of the child. You give honor, as well, to the grandparents by naming their name. They get to see their namesake carry on their name, carry on their good deeds, carry on the traditions. So, these are beautiful things that we have, as well as identifying the person. Since we have so many people in the community with the same first name, same last name, the only way you can, you know, realize who a person is, is through this family connection. If I tell you the person's name is Isaac, the son of Abe Cohen, "Oh, I know who that is, because his grandfather was Isaac, too, and I know who that, who Abraham was his great-grandfather, I know the family." So, it's a way of honoring, of carrying on, and identifying. So, it's a beautiful Minhag.

Now, also related to naming, there is a misconception, a misnomer that has perpetrated the community, that you cannot name the baby or mention the name of the baby until the baby is quote-unquote officially named, whether for a boy at the Berit Milah or for the girl at Zebed HaBat. We'll get to both things in their proper episodes, but that's not true. Babies are named obviously beforehand, and we know the names, the names are generally known when the child is born, and you could definitely share that name. In fact, as far as boys are concerned, we actually have Berit Milah invitations from Syria, from Egypt, and even here from New York, you know, which have the child's name on it, and obviously the invitations were made prior to the official naming of the baby at the Berit Milah. So, don't worry if you have a name, and you want to share that name with somebody, it's 100% okay, and it is part of our tradition to mention the name of the baby before they are born, and use it with pride.

86.title: Eating Fish with Dairy
86.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that one should be careful not to eat fish with meat, and it is customary to be stringent regarding eating fish with meat. But what about fish with dairy? Is that also dangerous? And what is our custom? Do we also refrain from eating fish with dairy?

The Gemara explicitly wrote that fish may be eaten with a dairy dip known as Kutah. However, in the Bet Yosef, Maran wrote that, in any case, one should not eat fish with milk because it is dangerous, as explained in another section in Shulhan 'Arukh. However, that other section is not discussing fish with dairy; it is actually discussing not eating fish with meat. This led some authorities to the conclusion that there is a misprint in the Bet Yosef, meaning that Maran never actually wrote that eating fish with dairy is dangerous. These authorities include the Ture Zahab from Poland in the 17th century, and the Hida, a Middle Eastern authority from the 18th century. The Peri Hadash, a 17th-century authority from Italy who later resided in Jerusalem, also disagreed with prohibiting fish with dairy.

It's also noteworthy that Maran never wrote anything about eating fish with dairy in Shulhan 'Arukh. If it is not a misprint, it is only discussed in the Bet Yosef. But other authorities have written that doctors have warned that it is dangerous to eat fish with dairy. These authorities included Ribbi Hayyim Benveniste, Ribbi Ya'akob Sahalon, who was also a doctor, and Rabbenu Bahye, a Spanish authority from the first part of the 14th century.

So some authorities say that it is permissible to eat fish with dairy, while others write that it is dangerous. And although Maran writes that it is dangerous, several later authorities questioned the printed textual version in the Bet Yosef, which brings us to our original question: what is the accepted custom?

It is well-known that Ashkenazim are lenient with fish and dairy, as the Rama wrote that he never saw anyone who was careful not to eat fish with dairy. But several Sephardic authorities are stringent with fish and dairy, including Ribbi Yisshak Palachi, the Ben Ish Hai, and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef. Hakham 'Obadia Yosef was more lenient regarding eating fish with butter for those that have the custom of eating fish with butter.

What about Halab? Do we have the custom to refrain from eating fish with dairy, or can we be lenient? Rabbi Yisshak Chehebar was asked about this, and his answer was printed in his book Yisshak Yeranen. He wrote, "There is no clear-cut custom regarding this, and I've never heard of anyone who was careful with this." Furthermore, Hakham David Attieh, the son of the famous Rosh Yeshibah Porat Yosef, Hakham 'Ezra Attieh, was asked if they didn't eat fish with dairy, and he answered that they always ate fish with dairy. This conversation was actually videotaped.

So while some Sefaradim have the custom to be stringent and do not eat fish with dairy, in Halab, there was no binding custom on everyone to prohibit it. While some families may have been stringent, many, including some of the rabbis, were lenient. This is based on the opinions of the Peri Hadash, the Hida, and other later authorities.

87.title: The Tunes of the Shabbat Zemirot
87.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are discussing the Tefillot of Shabbat morning in the synagogue. Last week we discussed the Zemirot until Nishmat, how it's split up and so on, the Minhagim. What I want to discuss today are the liturgical Minhagim, the Hazzanut of these Zemirot, what scale they're sung in. It's very important that a certain atmosphere is created by the way the Hazzan reads the prayers. We know that the holidays are different, and Shabbat, and weekdays, they're all different, and they create a certain atmosphere. I spoke about it a little bit when I discussed Friday night and the Maqam Nawa, which is so important.

"LaMnasseah Mizmor LeDavid," page 237 in Kol Ya'akob, even though these are Pirke Tehillim, we do not read them in the Te'amim of the Tehillim. We actually read them in a Sigah tune, scale. I urge everybody to go to the website pizmonim.com, I think also pizmonim.org, that was set up and established by Mr. Betesh, where he collected all of the liturgical customs, prayers, and Keri'at HaTorah, and Tanakh, from the great Hazzanim of our community. And you can go to prayers, drill down to Zemirot, and you'll find our great Hazzan, Yizakher BeTob, Mr. Isaac Cabasso singing "LaMnasseah Mizmor LeDavid" in the proper way it's sung. He can do a better job than me, but it's something like this: "LaMnasseah Mizmor LeDavid, HaShamayim Mesapperim Kebod El, UMa'aseh Yadav Maggid HaRakia'." So it's a type of a Sigah, and this is how we say for the entire Zemirot throughout "Hodu LaAd-onai Ki Tob Ki Le'Olam Hasdo" up until the very last Pasuk, which is the last Pasuk of the Zemirot, "Hodu LeEl HaShamayim," which I'll come back to.

We begin Barukh SheAmar. Now, Barukh SheAmar is sung in a tune by the entire Kahal. Now, the tune that is sung in New York is the tune of Hatikvah, which was established probably sometime the early part of the century, since the tune was composed around the year 1900. It was written in the notes of 'Alav HaShalom Hakham Moshe Ashear, so it could be that he established it, but it must have been around the years around 1920, 1925, we don't know exactly. Now, this is in Nahawand. Now, this is interesting because most Kehillot of the Halabiyeh around the world sing the Zemirot always in Huseini. Now, this is the way it's been in Ades since its inception 120 years ago.

I think a couple of interesting proofs I have, if you could call them proofs, is that I want to go back to the last Pasuk of "Hodu LeEl HaShamayim Ki Le'Olam Hasdo" which I mentioned. Now if you listen closely to Hazzan Cabasso, everything is done in the same Sigah except the last Pasuk: "Hodu LeEl HaShamayim Ki Le'Olam Hasdo." It goes into a Huseini, which is in the Bayat family. Another interesting point is that if you notice also on the pizmonim.org, we have our great Hazzan, 'Alav HaShalom Gabriel Shrem, when he illustrates how to sing the Barukh SheAmar to the tune of Hatikvah, and he'll sing it in the tune which we're all familiar with, but in the last two words, "Barukh Shemo," he'll switch into Huseini. Another interesting thing to note is that the Reshuyot, the Piyyutim which we sing on the high on Yom Kippur before Barukh SheAmar are both in Huseini.

Interesting anecdote: I was in Hong Kong in 1980, I went to pray in the Kadoorie synagogue on the Hong Kong side, so I spent Shabbat there, and I in the Kenis there was an elderly man saying the Zemirot. Sure enough, it was Huseini. I'm saying to myself, he's got to be a Halabi. So after prayers, I introduced myself, and of course he was Halabi, Mr. Zaki Dwek, 'Alav HaShalom. So it came with the indication that the Halabiyeh always said the Zemirot in Huseini.

Now, because of Hatikvah being the tune of Barukh SheAmar, many Hazzanim, at least in the last 30, 40 years that I can remember in New York, they weren't so careful, particular about saying the Zemirot in Huseini. You hear a lot of Nahawand, sometimes 'Ajam, I have my own theories as to why that is, but Nahawand I can understand because the Hazzan would continue. Now, a Hazzan that's not professional, a professional Hazzan, it's not easy for him to switch, so he would continue in Nahawand, and then the people saying the Zemirot would pick it up in Nahawand. But again, I think the original custom in Halab was to do all these Zemirot in Huseini.

The last Halleluyah we sing all together in Huseini. There is a custom in Argentina that they would say the Zemirot in Huseini, but the last Halleluyah they would switch and sing it in the tune of the Maqam of the week, similar to the "HaShem Malakh" that we sing it in the Maqam of the week. In Ades we sing it generally in Huseini, unless there's maybe a special Saba tune that we like to use, or a holiday that we'll switch to an 'Ajam. So that's the Zemirot.

We go into "Barukh HaShem Le'Olam Amen VeAmen," preceding VaYebarekh David, always switching back into Sigah. We finish VaYebarekh David, dividing it up the way I described in the last video. We get to VaYosha' and Az Yashir, which is sung in the Te'amim of the Sefer Torah, again Sigah. It's divided up generally into two, where the first Hazzan from VaYosha' until "Mi Khamokha," the next Hazzan picking it up until the end, preceding the Nishmat. In Ades we start at, the second Hazzan begins at "Natita" instead of "Mi Khamokha," one Pasuk difference. Shalom UBerakhah, next week we'll begin with the Nishmat. Kol Tub.

88.title: Adding VaTikkah Miryam on Shabbat Shirah
88.text:
The Shabbat that we read Parashat Beshallah is commonly referred to as Shabbat Shirah. This is because Shirat HaYam, the song that begins Az Yashir, is in Parashat Beshallah. On that Shabbat, when we are reciting the Zemirot, the entire congregation sings the Shirah beginning from VaYosha' together with the Te'amim.

In some Middle Eastern communities, it is customary on Shabbat Shirah, and also on the seventh day of Pesah, when we read Shirat HaYam in the Sefer Torah, as the miracle of the splitting of the sea is commemorated on the seventh day of Pesah, to continue reading the next seven verses that begin "VaTikkah Miryam" in unison before the Hazzan begins "Ki LaHaShem HaMelukhah." The custom is to read from "VaTikkah Miryam" until "Ki Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha."

The famous Siddur Bet Menuhah, which was compiled in the beginning of the 19th century by Rabbi Yehudah Shemuel Ashkenazi, includes "VaTikkah Miryam" with the instructions: "On the Shabbat of Beshallah, some have the custom to add." Similarly, Hakham Abraham Hamwey, in his Mahzor for Pesah known as Bet HaBehirah from the middle of the 19th century, writes: "On the seventh day of Pesah, some have the custom to recite until 'Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha' on that Yom Tob." However, he does not specify the custom of Halab, his birthplace, as he does with regards to other customs that he writes about in that Mahzor.

We also find "VaTikkah Miryam" in Siddur Tefillat Yeshurun, which was a very popular Siddur in our community here in Brooklyn from 1935 until approximately the year 1970. The instructions in Tefillat Yeshurun are: "On the Shabbat of Beshallah and on the seventh day of Pesah, it is customary to recite this until 'Rofe'ekha'."

What was the custom of Halab? Did they add "VaTikkah Miryam" on Shabbat Shirah and the seventh day of Pesah or not? If you go all the way back to the 16th century, you will find "VaTikkah Miryam" after Az Yashir as part of the daily prayers in Halab. Mahzor Aram Soba, which was printed in 1527, includes prayers for weekdays, Shabbatot, and holidays, and "VaTikkah Miryam" was part of Az Yashir every day of the year. However, since that time, our prayers have been modified to conform with the teachings of the Mekubbalim, and many changes were implemented. Among those changes is that we no longer continue with "VaTikkah Miryam" after Az Yashir on a daily basis.

But what about on those two special occasions, Shabbat Shirah and the seventh day of Pesah? Did we practice the custom of adding "VaTikkah Miryam"? Hakham Salim Zafrani, 'Alav HaShalom, who was born in Halab in 1891 and officiated in the Great Synagogue of Aleppo, wrote in his notes documenting the customs of the Great Synagogue of Aleppo: "On Shabbat Shirah and on the seventh day of Pesah, after the Shirah, we say 'VaTikkah Miryam' until 'Rofe'ekha', and then the Hazzan recites the Pasuk 'Refa'eni Ad-onai VeErafe', and then 'Ki LaHaShem HaMelukhah'." Similarly, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, who was born in Halab in 1893, wrote in his book on the customs of Aleppo: "And on Shabbat Kodesh, Parashat Beshallah, and also on the seventh day of Pesah, after VaYosha', we say 'VaTikkah Miryam' until 'Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha', and then the verse 'Refa'eni Ad-onai VeErafe' is recited."

So we see that the custom of Halab, even in the beginning of the 20th century, was to add "VaTikkah Miryam" after Az Yashir on Shabbat Shirah and on the seventh day of Pesah. And according to Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi, this was also the original custom of the Halabi community in Argentina until Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, 'Alav HaShalom, came and eliminated the custom. This is most probably based on the fact that some authorities, especially the Mekubbalim, would consider any addition to the Pesuke DeZimra as an interruption.

Similarly, it was not customary to add "VaTikkah Miryam" on those days in most synagogues in Brooklyn, most probably also due to the consideration that it might be considered an interruption of the prayers. However, my father-in-law, Mr. Erwin Dayan, HaShem Yebarekhehu VeYishmerehu, told me that the custom in Ahi'ezer, which follows the customs of Damascus, was to add "VaTikkah Miryam" on those days under the leadership of Hakham Mourad Maslaton, 'Alav HaShalom. And more recently, some of our community synagogues have brought back the original custom of Halab to add "VaTikkah Miryam" on Shabbat Shirah and on the seventh day of Pesah, based on the writings of Hakham Salim Zafrani and Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, in order to return to our original tradition from Halab here in our community.
