89.title: Zebed HaBat and Naming a Baby Girl
89.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles: Zebed HaBat. Zebed HaBat is the birth and naming of a baby girl. On the Shabbat following the birth of a baby girl, the father of the girl will go to the Kenis, to the synagogue, to Bet Keneset, to name his newborn daughter. Generally, he will not go by himself. He will go together with other family members that will be sitting with him. It could be his brothers, brothers-in-law, father, father-in-law, other close family friends and relatives that will sit together with him.

Before the father is given an 'Aliyah to the Torah, a Pizmon will be sung on his behalf in honor of the birth of a baby girl. The most popular two Pizmonim that we generally use in the community are either in Maqam Bayat named "Yefat 'Ayin Lebabtini" or in Maqam Rast, "Yafah Sebiyah," which happened to have been written, that particular song was written in this country by Hazzan Yehezkel Elbag, the author of the famous Shalom Yerushalayim Mahzorim and Shabbat Shalom Siddur. In any case, those two Pizmonim are the most common that would be sung for a baby girl. And before the father goes up to the Sefer, those Pizmonim, or at least one of them, will be sung.

The father will be called up to the Sefer Torah, he'll go up to the Sefer, have an 'Aliyah. At the end of his 'Aliyah, the naming of the baby girl takes place. And the formula for that is called "Yonati BeHagve HaSela'." And we add an additional Pasuk if it's the firstborn. Firstborn girl, we'll add a Pasuk that's also from Shir HaShirim: "Ahat Hi Yonati Tammati, Ahat Hi LeImmah," etc. And it's either said by the Hazzan or by the Hakham of the Bet Keneset.

Now, why is the baby girl named at the Sefer Torah? And what's its connection, and why is a Mi SheBerakh in order as well? And this all stems from a Pasuk from Parashat Lekh Lekha, when HaShem changes the name of Sarah Imenu, when He changes it from Sarai to Sarah. And He says very clearly over here: "VaYomer Elokim LeAbraham, Sarai Ishtekha Lo Tikra Et Shemah Sarai Ki Sarah Shemah, UBerakhti Otah VeGam Natati Mimmennah Lekha Ben UBerakhtiha." So the concept of changing the name, giving a new name to a female together with the concept of Berakhah comes together. So we name when we're at the Sefer Torah, 'cause these are Pesukim from the Torah, plus we are making Berakhot before and after the reading, and after the Yonati Pesukim, a Mi SheBerakh is given, Sheberakh from the same Shoresh, the same root of the concept of Berakhah. And that's how a baby girl is named.

Now, as far as the name of the baby girl, it should be very clearly noted that in the last, I'd say about 60 years in the United States, it has become fashionable, if you will, to make sure the girl has a Hebrew name. Now, this was never done before. It was not done in any of our countries of origin, cities of origin, for hundreds of years. The girls were given names either in Spanish, or Turkish, or Arabic, or even European names. Names that you've all heard of, you know, when you listen to names of your grandmothers or great-grandmothers, names like Oro, or Gracia, or Zakiyeh, or even names like Yvette and Yvonne. So many foreign names to Judaism, but they were accepted as a name for a girl, and the girl didn't have a specific Hebrew name.

It was only here in America, with the advent of Hebrew day school, when girls started going to school, and teachers from outside of our community weren't able to cope with that concept, that they started, you know, forcing upon these girls Hebrew names. "Oh, your name is Bahiya? No, it can't just be Bahiya. Now your name is Batyah also, you know. Your name is Tera? No, what's Tera? Tera sounds like Sarah, so your name is Sarah." And such and so forth. But in the past, girls had foreign names and not necessarily a Hebrew name.

So if you come across somebody who doesn't only, who only has a non-Hebrew name, if you will, it was a very common thing. The Hakhamim were very, you know, at home with it. They have even books written of lists of names of both men and women, acceptable names and how they are spelled in Hebrew lettering, for both men and women, names, like I said, from foreign languages, be they European languages or Islamic languages, and this was the custom of our community, like I said, for hundreds of years, and this is the order of Zebed HaBat. Mabrook.

90.title: Nishmat and the Participation of the Kahal
90.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have been discussing the prayers Shabbat morning in the synagogue. We have completed Pesuke DeZimra, which ends with Shirat HaYam. The Hazzan that's at the Tebah will finish it off with the final Pasuk, ending with "UBene Yisrael Halekhu BaYabbashah BeTokh HaYam." Now the Hazzan for Nishmat, the main Hazzan of the Kenis, will ascend the Tebah, and he will begin the Nishmat. He actually begins it with "Ki LaAd-onai HaMelukhah UMoshel BaGoyim," and he will remain at the Tebah until after Kaddish Titkabbal, which is after the Hazarah and Yehi Shem.

Now, before we begin discussing the specific customs of Tefillat Shahrit, I wanted to speak about the liturgical customs that we have, and I speak about it often because it's central to the experience that we have, the communal experience we have in the synagogue. So we spoke about Friday night Nawa and Shabbat morning Sigah and Huseini with the Zemirot. We know that Minhah is Rast and 'Arbit is Bayat. And we'll speak about that going forward. But Shabbat morning, the Nishmat, the scales change every week depending on the Parashah that is being read.

Now this is a system, it's a highly developed system, it's very sophisticated. It's real one of the great liturgical customs in our community, which is unique to the Halabi community. Now, every community has its own liturgical uniqueness and its cantorial specialties. However, the system of using a different scale corresponding to a specific Parashah is unique to the Halabi community. It's really, in Israel, where we have dozens and dozens of various Sefaradi Kehillot in the country, this is one of our great exports, because many communities have adopted this system and bring in Hazzanim that know how to pray in the various scales depending on the Parashah.

So, what I'm going to be doing in my next video is illustrating with the help of our great, really, this invaluable crown jewel of the creativity of our community, the Sefer Pizmonim, I'm going to go into greater depth and explain how this book is laid out and where we find all of what I'm speaking about now in this great Sefer.

So, the Hazzan will begin with the specific scale, and everybody knows what scale to expect because every Parashah has its own scale. And there is great participation on the part of the Kahal in the Tefillot of Tefillat Shahrit. Now this is not found in all other communities. In many, many other communities, especially Ashkenazi communities, there is a little bit of participation, but not nearly the level that we participate in the prayers, and we do it basically in two ways.

The first way is that at the end of each paragraph, at least, and sometimes if the paragraphs are long, every couple of sentences the Hazzan will, before he ends the sentence, will end it up in a note which invites a response from the Kahal, the Jawab, where the Kahal will respond in the same scale as the Hazzan is singing. And so like "HaShem Ehad," people will answer "UShmo Ehad," he will repeat and begin the Nishmat. And even within that first paragraph: "'Olamo BeHesed," people will answer "UBeriyotav BeRahamim." All the way down, and we'll do "Raglenu Kalot KeAyyalot." You can follow in the book, I'm on page 258 of Kol Ya'akob. So there is constantly a back and forth between the Hazzan and the Kahal, and this is crucial because it keeps the Kahal involved in the prayers.

The second way which the Hazzan involves the people in the Tefillot is that there are pieces, portions of the prayer which are sung, all the Kahal together in unison. Now, it begins the Nishmat, of course, "Shav'at 'Aniyyim," "El HaHoda'ot," "Semehim BeSetam," "MiMissrayim Ge'altanu," and "Nakdishakh." Of course, the Kaddish is sung, but that's sung only by the Hazzan. The Hazzan will initiate the tune, and he has dozens of tunes to choose from within each given scale, and the Kahal will all participate in this portion.

Now it's important, because of this, that the Hazzan knows to select tunes which the Kahal are familiar with, otherwise he ends up singing a solo, and that defeats the purpose of the participation of the Kahal that we're seeking. So he has to know his Kahal, and the Kahal has to insist that he use tunes which are familiar, and the Kahal also has the onus on them to educate themselves and, of course, to educate their children as to these tunes growing up, so that they're always familiar with the customs of our community. We had the privilege in the sixties to have Allah Yerhamo Mickey Kairey come to the Magen David Yeshibah once a week, and we learned literally hundreds of Pizmonim over the course of years. So that was a great education, and I'm sure it's continuing. Kol Tub, next week we will discuss the Pizmonim book in depth. Shalom UBerakhah.

91.title: Female Names and Their Origins
91.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Female Names. My last episode, number 89, provoked a lot of interest, comments, and reactions regarding female names. I mentioned that girls did not always have Hebrew names, and some people were surprised by it, and others recall their grandmothers and great-grandmothers with names that are very, very different, and want to know what they mean and what their origins were. So today's episode is dedicated to female names.

So, firstly, let's say that I did not say that females did not have Hebrew names at all, but rather most females did not have Hebrew names. Some only had Hebrew names. So the most common of names are, of course, biblical names, and from those, the most common would have been Sarah and Rahel, other Hebrew names being Mazal and Simhah. Those are probably the most common four Hebrew names that we find among Jews of the Middle East, and specifically in Syria, and in Halab even more so.

Now, what about other names? So there were two or three different groupings of names and different reasons for names. There were European names. You have to remember, we are Sefaradim, and as Sefaradim, we came from Spain, hailed from Spain, so we already had Spanish names, we had the knowledge of the Spanish and Romance languages, so we carried names like that over with us. We also had Arabic names, because the indigenous Jews of the Middle East prior to the coming of the Jews from Spain, there were Jews there, so they had Arabic names, as well as the proximity of Turkey and the overwhelming reach of the Ottoman Empire throughout Arab lands for a few hundred years, so that, of course, gave us Turkish names as well. Of course, with the influence of the Industrial Revolution and the connection of the mercantile class with France and England, they took upon names from those countries as well, specifically from reigning monarchs and their spouses.

So let's talk about some of these names, because there seems to be a lot of interest. I prepared a chart of some of the most common names, and let's go through them quickly. So we have on the European names, we have Amelia. Amelia coming from the root to work. Elvira, Elvira nobility. Fortune, as the name is very clear, Fortune is good luck. Regine for queen. Yvonne is an archer. Oro, gold. And then we run into names of queens like Marie, Elizabeth, and Victoria.

We have, of course, Arabic names. We have Farida, Farideh, meaning individual. Bahiya, Bahiye is somebody if you want to call them exalted. Latifa, gracious. Jamila, beautiful. We'll skip the next one. We go to Nizha. Nizha is a very interesting name. It means somebody who would wander, wander in the fields. In other words, they were secure, they were away from all sorts of danger. Zakiya, Zakiye, Zakiye was somebody who is pleasant. You have Shafika, Shafika somebody very righteous. Salha, somebody successful. And Teyra is a bird.

We have, of course, Turkish names, like Altun, which is also gold, and Gulsom was a round, beautiful face, like the moon. Now, this name Gracia and Garaz that I left separated and connected with a dotted line: Gracia, of course, grace, charm. Garaz is a nickname for Gracia, specifically from Halab. From there it was used in other places as well, but its origin is in Halab. And although people hear Garaz and they think of cherries, they think of a bell, but really Garaz is a nickname for Gracia. People that originally had the name Gracia became Garaz, and then that name stuck as a regular name by itself.

Now, as you can tell, all these people that had such names, these were names given in regular families, in rabbinic families, and keep in mind that Halab was known as a city of Torah and Hakhamim for hundreds of years, going back to at least the days of HaRambam, okay, until even our most modern times. So in a city like that of Hakhamim and that they gave their daughters names that were not biblical or not quote-unquote Hebrew or Jewish names, tells us that it was the common practice and, of course, was not forbidden and, obviously, permitted. And this was the practice of our mothers, our grandmothers, our great-grandmothers, and when they came here, they carried these names with them and this naming system.

And it's only once they started going to Hebrew school with Jewish teachers, okay, that were from outside our community and weren't familiar with our practices that they started giving them Hebrew names, Jewish names. In fact, until recently, people have told me that when they went to school, you know, I'm talking about not that long time ago, I'm talking about in the 1970s, okay, late '70s, that the Hebrew teachers just said, "Well, what's your name? Oh, your name is Jennifer? Oh, no. Your name can't be Jennifer. Your name is now Hayah." Okay. They took, they, you know, they adopted the name because the school gave them the name, but it was never really their name.

So it's okay if you don't have such a name for your daughters. It's the way of our forefathers, and if they have a biblical Hebrew name like some of our grandparents did, that's also beautiful as well. But we have so many beautiful names, and you could look into the names, you could find out the meaning, you could make a Hebrew cognate for it if you desire to do so. But to just make up a name, it doesn't fall in line with our true practice.

92.title: The Purim Meal on Friday
92.text:
One of the halakhic obligations on Purim day is to eat a festive meal. According to HaRambam, one is obligated to eat meat and drink wine for the Purim meal. And according to Maran, even an Onen, one who lost a close relative who has not been buried yet, and therefore is not normally permitted to eat meat or drink wine until after the burial, may eat meat and drink wine in honor of Purim. However, according to Maran, one is not normally permitted to eat a festive meal on a Friday if it's greater than a meal that one would normally eat on a weekday. This prohibition applies to the entire day of Friday, beginning from the morning. And one should not even eat a meal that one would regularly eat on a weekday on a Friday afternoon after the end of the ninth hour of the day until the Shabbat meal is served. The reason for these restrictions is so that one will have an appetite for the Shabbat meal on Friday night.

So what happens when Purim falls on a Friday like it does this year? When should we eat the festive Purim meal? This question is not discussed by HaRambam or Maran, but it is discussed by other authorities. We should note that although the discussion focuses on the timing of the meal, however, all agree that one does still eat meat and drink wine in honor of Purim, even when Purim falls on a Friday.

Ribbi Moshe Isserles, a 16th-century authority from Poland who appended notes to Shulhan 'Arukh, wrote that it is customary to eat a festive meal that one does not normally eat on a weekday in honor of a Missvah that occurs on a specific day, like a Berit Milah or a Pidyon HaBen, even if it occurs on a Friday. He also wrote that the proper time to eat the Purim meal when Purim falls on a Friday is in the morning. So according to the Rema, since the Purim meal is a Se'udat Missvah that is eaten on a specific day, it is permissible to eat it on a Friday, but one should schedule the meal in the morning in order not to detract from the honor of the Shabbat meal on Friday night.

However, if we go back to the 13th century, we find two well-known authorities that used to start the Purim meal towards the end of the day, even when Purim fell on a Friday. They would recite Kiddush in the middle of the meal, and then continue eating in honor of Shabbat. This practice is described in the Gemara as Pores Mappah UMekaddesh, you spread a cloth and recite Kiddush.

Regarding Pores Mappah UMekaddesh when Purim falls on a Friday, the Meiri, an important 13th-century authority from Provence, wrote, "We and our forefathers have the custom when Purim falls on Friday to begin the meal while it is still daytime until Shabbat begins, and then we spread a cloth and recite Kiddush, and then we finish the meal." Similarly, the Magen Abraham, a 17th-century authority from Poland, quoted a manuscript from the Mordekhai, an important Talmudic authority from Germany in the 13th century, who wrote, "If you are eating the Purim meal on Friday, pray, spread the cloth, and recite Kiddush."

This practice was also recorded by Ribbi Ya'akob Kastro, otherwise known as Maharikash, a 16th-century authority from Egypt. In his book 'Erekh Lehem, he wrote that when Purim falls on Friday, you eat the meal in the afternoon, you recite Kiddush at sunset, and then eat some more, but some eat the meal in the morning; everyone follows their custom.

Furthermore, Ribbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on, who was the chief rabbi of Cairo from 1891 until 1921, wrote that the custom of Egypt and Jerusalem is to Pores Mappah UMekaddesh when Purim falls on Friday. In his book Nehar Missrayim on the customs of Egypt, he wrote that when Purim falls on Friday, the nice and pleasant custom is to eat the meal in the late afternoon after reciting Minhah, and in the middle of the meal, cover the bread, recite Kiddush, and then continue the meal in honor of Shabbat. He writes that you add 'Al HaNissim in Birkat HaMazon, and afterwards, you recite 'Arbit of Shabbat. According to Ribbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on, this is the best way to eat the Purim meal when Purim falls on Friday.

So according to some authorities, you should eat the meal in the morning. According to others, you eat in the late afternoon and recite Kiddush in the middle of the meal. What was the custom in Halab? We have one source from Halab that discusses the Purim meal on Friday. Hakham Ya'akob Dwek, who was born in Aleppo in the 19th century and passed away in 1919, wrote about the Purim meal in his book Sheerit Ya'akob. He wrote, "This year, which is Friday, you must have the meal at midday, and the meal must be with meat." Meat and wine. So we see that Pores Mappah was not mentioned at all, but instead of stipulating the morning, as we found in other authorities, eating at midday is sufficient to preserve the honor of the Shabbat meal, and he also specified that the meal should still be a meat meal, even though it is a Friday.

If one did not eat the meal by midday, they can still, they still can and must eat the meal in the afternoon. If you're eating in the afternoon, you should eat in the early afternoon, but if you didn't, you can still eat the meal in the late afternoon without being Pores Mappah UMekaddesh, as long as you stop eating and drinking before sunset. If you want to Pores Mappah UMekaddesh, you begin the meal in the late afternoon after reciting Minhah. You eat meat and drink wine during the first part of the meal in honor of Purim. Bread is not required during the first part of the meal, but if you do eat bread in the beginning of the meal, you do not repeat HaMossi after Kiddush. Prior to sunset, you light the candles, cover the bread, and recite Kiddush. In Kiddush, you omit the blessing of Bore Peri HaGefen, since you already recited HaGefen when you drank wine in the beginning of the meal. After Kiddush, you must have two ounces or at least one ounce of bread in honor of Shabbat. After the meal, you recite Birkat HaMazon. If you ate an ounce of bread or more before Kiddush, some authorities instruct you to add both 'Al HaNissim and Resseh VeHahalissenu in Birkat HaMazon, but according to Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, you only add Resseh VeHahalissenu, even if you ate bread before Kiddush. And after Birkat HaMazon, when you are no longer intoxicated, you pray 'Arbit of Shabbat.

As we said, the custom of Pores Mappah on a Friday Purim was prevalent in Egypt and Jerusalem approximately 100 years ago. It appears that the prevalent custom in Halab at that time was to eat by midday. Similarly, here in Brooklyn, the custom is to eat the meal early when Purim falls on a Friday, but Pores Mappah UMekaddesh is a viable option halakhically, if you are confident that you will follow all of the required details properly.

93.title: The Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah
93.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim, we are discussing the Nishmat prayer Shabbat morning in the synagogue. And we were talking about liturgical customs and the pieces that the Hazzanim sing in unison with the Kahal. I just want to point out that it was brought to my attention from Mr. Ezra Ashkenazi, Yizakher BeTob, told me that he heard on a number of occasions from our great Hazzan, Isaac Cabasso, HaShem Yishmerehu, that all of the songs were sung, the tunes were hopefully tunes that the Kahal knew and sung together. However, the Nishmat, the rule was the Nishmat belongs to the Hazzan. So if the Hazzan chooses to do a tune that he innovated or something which only he would know, he has the permission, the Hazzan, they say the Nishmat belongs to the Hazzan. It's not the custom in Israel, in Ades, but I think it was important to bring that out and thank Mr. Ezra Ashkenazi for his comment.

I mentioned in my last video I wanted to do a quick review of the Sefer, this famous Sefer Pizmonim which we are so proud of in our community, published by the Sephardic Heritage Foundation, 'Alav HaShalom at the time Mr. Sam Kassin organized the effort, called Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah. I want to speak a few minutes about this Sefer. So it seems like a pretty lengthy name for a title for a book, Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah, but in essence the reason for this is that this is really a combination of two Sefarim of Pizmonim, of songs which were written by our Hakhamim. Shir UShbahah was written by Hakham Refael Antebi Tabbush Ades, one of the great poets and Hazzanim who had many students, one of his students of course being our great Hazzan that we had the merit to have in our community serving in Magen David for 28 years, Hakham Moshe Ashear HaKohen. So Hakham Tabbush wrote Shir UShbahah. Hakham Moshe Ashear wrote Hallel VeZimrah when he was in New York.

This is an original 1928 printing of the Hallel VeZimrah. If you look into your great-grandparents' homes and your grandparents' homes, I'm sure you will find a copy of this Sefer, and it's interesting, I have seen many many copies at homes and there's always at the end handwritten notes of Pizmonim which were added, and the owner of the book would write them handwritten. This actual book also, Hakham Moshe was from Moshe Dwek, which is my father-in-law's grandfather, the father of Albert Dwek. So he has all of his notes in the back of the book.

So what they did when they printed the book is they combined the book of Hakham Tabbush, Shir UShbahah, with the book of Hakham Moshe Ashear, Hallel VeZimrah, making it Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah. And if you notice, we'll talk at length on another occasion, but if we start with where the Maqamat are, in other words skipping the Bakashot in the beginning and the Mossa'e Shabbat and the Petihot, we start with let's say Maqam Rast on page 107. So if you'll notice, it's written here that these songs were from the book of Shir UShbahah, Hakham Tabbush. Now, if we go to page, we continue in the scale of Rast, we go to page 125, you'll see now, from now on these are the songs written by Hakham Moshe Ashear HaKohen from the book Hallel VeZimrah. So this is actually a combination of both books.

Now in later years, as they kept printing more editions, and because more songs were written by Hazzanim in our community, Hakham Refael Nadab, 'Alav HaShalom, wrote a number of songs, Baratashvili, the Hazzan Albert Sabban, Mr. Louis Massry wrote a song, we have many contributions and they were added into the Sefer, but always added at the end of the section of the scale that the song was written in, and always with the page numbers A, B, C in order not to change the original page numbers of the songs, 'cause that's how quickly we, you know, when we were growing up and we were taught by Mickey. So it was very important to remember the page numbers, so in order not to confuse and not to change those numbers, so they put them all at the end of each section.

Now, what I wanted to bring to your attention was page 565, which is important for our discussion. It's a list of every Parashah with the related scale of music which is sung during that Parashah: Bereshit Rast, Noah Sigah, Lekh Lekha Saba, and so on. Now, this list is generally accepted by all the Syrian communities all over the world, but it's not set in stone. There may be differences in two or three Parashiyot between Israel, Argentina, and New York, but the main, I would say, well over 90% are identical.

Now, if you look at pages 567 and 568, A, B, and C, you will have suggestions of which Pizmonim to use for the tunes that we sing in unison. So you'll have, let's say, you have a list: Nishmat, Shav'at, El HaHoda'ot, Kaddish; you have Rast, Mahur, 'Ajam. And then the Hazzan, now, when he goes up, he'll be able to look, and a lot of Hazzanim, they put the book in front of them when they're praying, so if the tune that they planned on slips their mind, they quickly check. That's why it's important to teach our children the Pizmonim, so they're able to follow and be part of the prayers on Shabbat morning. Again, this deserves a lot more time, and hopefully we'll get to it in later videos. Kol Tub.

94.title: The Birth of a Baby Boy
94.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Lifecycles: Pregnancy and Birth. In previous episodes, we began to discuss pregnancy and birth. We spoke about the birth of a baby girl. Now we're moving on to the birth of a baby boy.

Prior to that, I'd like to proceed with a short note that it is customary in many Sephardic communities, not only in Syria, but as well in Egypt and Lebanon, in Turkey, in Eress Yisrael and other places, that during the ninth month, the husband of the woman that has entered her ninth month is given Petihat HaHekhal, especially on Shabbat, and is considered a good sign and a friendly gesture from the Kehillah, from the congregation, to this man and his wife and their family-to-be, wishing them good tidings on an easy birth.

Now, moving forward, we're dealing with the birth of a baby boy, and the birth of a baby boy ushers in the Berit Milah. So prior to the Berit Milah, we have the Shabbat prior to that, and that is considered a very, very special day for the family. The Abi HaBen comes to the Bet Keneset, comes to the Kenis, and he is afforded the honor of carrying the Sefer Torah, but that's not the only Missvah given to him. He also gets an 'Aliyah to the Torah. Prior to his 'Aliyah to the Torah, the Gabbai or the Shamash or the Mesader or the Hazzan or somebody will scream out, "Abi HaBen!" Okay. And if the father, meaning the father of this Abi HaBen, or in other words, the paternal grandfather of the newborn child is alive, then instead of just screaming out "Abi HaBen," they yell out, "Abi HaBen 'Ateret!" In other words, based upon the Pasuk, "'Ateret Banim Bene Banim, 'Ateret Zekenim Bene Banim VeTiferet Banim Abotam." In other words, this is the glory of the family that one generation is seeing the next and seeing the next. And so this is the "'Ateret Zekenim Bene Banim," so they yell out, "Abi HaBen 'Ateret!"

And then they burst into song. The most common songs associated with the birth of a baby boy and Berit Milah are Attah Ahubi and Yehi Shalom BeHelenu. Attah Ahubi: "Attah Ahubi," or Yehi Shalom: "Yehi Shalom BeHelenu." Automatically, any person hears these songs in the community, in the Kenis, they know that there is definitely a baby boy that was born, a Berit Milah will be happening either that day or within the coming few days. These songs are in Maqam Saba. That's the musical mode of Saba that's associated with the Berit Milah. The general association is because the Maqam Saba sounds similar to the word sabi, and sabi is the Arabic word for boy. In any case, they would sing one or two of these Pizmonim, give this gentleman an 'Aliyah to the Torah, and the festivities continue. There may even be a Sebet that day. Sebet, something we'll discuss in another episode as well.

Moving forward, prior to the Berit Milah, we have the night before the Berit Milah or the morning of the Berit Milah, there is something called a special learning, a special Limmud of Zohar. So in different places it has gone by different names. Nowadays in Israel, it's commonly known as Limmud Berit Yisshak, but in places like Egypt, it was known as just Lelet ez-Zohar, the night of the Zohar. In many places, like in Eress Yisrael and Syria, it was known as Limmud LeBerit Milah. And in Halab there was a specific name for it in Arabic called Shidd el-As. Shidd el-As would mean pulling of the pods. Pods are the pods of the as. As is the Hadasim, the myrtle. And there is a special connection in these Hadasim with Eliyahu HaNabi and his chair and the Berit Milah. Some people mistakenly think that the word is Shidd li-Yas, pulling Eliyahu or pulling Eliyahu down to come to the Berit Milah, but really the word is Shidd el-As, pulling of the as. Hadasim.

In any case, this Limmud consists of Zohar, and is generally done the night prior to the Berit Milah, it's done as a protection, if you will, for the mother and the newborn child. And even though we see it as very common today in many families, in Halab, and even here in America, it wasn't so common among Halabi families to be done the night before, rather it was done the morning of the Berit Milah, either in the Kenis or in the house, and usually in the house because most Berit Milah were conducted in the house, and that's something we'll discuss in an upcoming video.

Again, there are many customs associated with Berit Milah, how they're done, when they're done, where they're done, and we'll be getting to each one of them in upcoming

95.title: The Haggadah Plate and Maror
95.text:
It's customary to arrange the Haggadah plate according to the instructions of Rabbi Yisshak Luria, the 16th-century master of Kabbalah, otherwise known as the Arizal. Here's a drawing from the Shalom Yerushalayim Haggadah. The three Massot are placed on the top of the plate. The roasted shank bone is placed on your upper right, and the Haroset is below the shank bone on your lower right. On the left side of the plate, the egg is placed above the Karpas, which is the celery. In the center of the plate, you place the Maror, and below the Maror, on the lower part of the plate, is the Hazeret. Maror is a general term for bitter lettuce, and Hazeret is a specific type of Maror, known in English as romaine lettuce.

According to the Arizal, we use two types of bitter lettuce. This is because the Haggadah plate and everything on it alludes to the ten Sefirot, which is a kabbalistic concept that is best described as the ten emanations from HaShem. The three Massot plus the shank bone, Haroset, egg, and celery add up to seven items, plus the two types of lettuce makes nine, and the plate itself alludes to the 10th Sefirah.

The Mishnah gives us five options for Maror. One is Hazeret, which, as we said, is romaine lettuce. Among the other options are 'Ulshin, which according to the Syrian tradition is either escarole or the curly endive, which is commonly known as chicory. A third option listed in the Mishnah is Tamkha, which according to the Halabi tradition is green butter lettuce. And although the Mishnah gives us two other options, it is not our custom to use them. The Syrian custom is to use romaine lettuce for one of the bitter lettuces, and either escarole, chicory, or green butter lettuce for the other bitter lettuce.

When do we use the romaine lettuce, and when do we use the other bitter lettuce? In Halab, there were various traditions. Rabbi Shemuel Laniado wrote in his book Shulhan HaMelekh, which was completed in the year 1804, that his father-in-law, who was Rabbi Refael Shelomo Laniado and was the chief rabbi of Halab at the end of the 18th century, used Habus, which according to Hakham Leon Gindi is green butter lettuce for Maror, meaning after reciting the blessing of "'Al Akhilat Maror," and then he mixed romaine lettuce together with the green butter lettuce for Korekh, the sandwich. However, Hakham Ezra Attieh wrote that the custom of Halab and Damascus was to take both the romaine lettuce and the other lettuce together for Maror. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote that they use both lettuces together after reciting the blessing of "'Al Akhilat Maror." And Hakham Yisshak Tawil 'Alav HaShalom and Hakham Leon Gindi SheYihyeh both said that they use both lettuces together for Maror and again for Korekh.

But there were some that used romaine lettuce for Maror, which is consistent with the opinion of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. Mr. Leon Sutton reported that his father, Sam Sutton 'Alav HaShalom, used romaine lettuce for both Maror and Korekh. A second type of lettuce was on the plate, but he did not use it for Maror or Korekh. Similarly, Hakham Abraham Hamwey, who was born in Halab in the 18th century, followed Maran and used romaine lettuce for Maror if it was available. He discussed this in his Pesah Mahzor, which is known as Bet HaBehirah.

So some used the other lettuce for Maror, which is based on the opinion of the Arizal, while some used romaine lettuce for Maror, which is Maran's opinion in Shulhan 'Arukh, and yet others mixed both lettuces together for Maror. The prevalent custom for Korekh was to mix both lettuces together in the sandwich.

Now there are also various customs regarding which lettuce goes in the middle of the plate for Maror and which lettuce goes on the bottom of the plate for Hazeret. Many have the custom to put the romaine lettuce at the bottom of the plate, where it says to put Hazeret, because Hazeret is romaine lettuce, and then the other lettuce, which is either escarole, chicory, or green butter lettuce, is placed in the middle of the plate, where it says to put Maror, because Maror is a general name for bitter lettuce. However, others do it the opposite way: romaine lettuce in the middle and the other lettuce on the bottom. According to Hakham Yisshak Tawil 'Alav HaShalom, it could be arranged either way. Each family should follow their custom.

For more information on this topic, and to see samples of the various types of lettuce that we discussed in this video, see the link attached to this video in order to watch another video on this topic.

96.title: Textual Variants in the Nishmat
96.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim, we are continuing our discussion with the Nishmat prayer, Shabbat morning, Shahrit in the synagogue, and in this episode, in this video, I'm going to be speaking about the differences of Nushaot, the different wording that you may find that differ from our community to other communities, and you may find differences in other Siddurim, but I think it's important to point them out.

So in the Nishmat, we have when we're praising Bore 'Olam and telling Him how it's, we don't even have the time to give enough praise for even one of the tens of thousands of goodnesses and miracles and wonders that He does for us, so we break up the sentence as follows: "En Anu Maspikim LeHodot Lekha HaShem Elokenu," "ULeBarekh Et Shimkha Malkenu," I'm on page 258, whoever wants to follow on the bottom, "'Al Ahat MeElef Alfe Alafim VeRob Ribe Rebabot Pe'amim HaTobot," comma, "Nissim VeNiflaot." Many other Siddurim will have "Rob Ribe Rebabot Pe'amim," comma, and then "HaTobot Nissim VeNiflaot." That's not our custom. I'm not here to decide which is more accurate grammatically or stylistically. That is our custom: "Pe'amim HaTobot." Okay, next.

Immediately following that, we have "Nissim VeNiflaot SheAsita 'Immanu Ve'Im Abotenu MiLefanim," period, the way it's in Kol Ya'akob, followed by "MiMissrayim Ge'altanu HaShem Elokenu MiBet 'Abadim Peditanu." Many other Siddurim, you'll have the sentence broken up: "SheAsita 'Immanu Ve'Im Abotenu," period, "MiLefanim," way back, "MiMissrayim Ge'altanu." So that's how they would break up the sentence. But as I said, our custom as it's reflected accurately in the Siddur Kol Ya'akob, "SheAsita 'Immanu Ve'Im Abotenu MiLefanim." It's important because this is one of the, one of those stops I was talking about, that the Hazzan will end up with a note, a higher note in order to invite the response of the Kahal, so it's important that he says that people end with "MiLefanim," because that's the end of the phrase.

Now, it can be logically both ways can be accurate, but why do we say that? Why is that? I was trying to understand why do we end up with "Ve'Im Abotenu MiLefanim"? I found something fascinating. If we look at the Mahzor Aram Soba, we'll have in the Nishmat, the phrase is, where is it? Here. "SheAsita 'Immanu Ve'Im Abotenu MiLefanim Ve'Ad Henah." Now, we don't have the "Ve'Ad Henah" anymore, that fell in disuse over the years, or maybe even in the Sephardic, this is mainly Musta'arabi Siddur, and mainly maybe wasn't even in the Sephardic Siddurim when they came to Halab, but it's an interest-, very interesting that the sentence was "MiLefanim Ve'Ad Henah." And therefore, when the "Ve'Ad Henah" was dropped, we still ended the sentence with "MiLefanim." So it's fascinating that that's something which hasn't been in print for 500 years, a Siddur which was actually probably never used by the Hamonim, we still have that reference in our minds. It just get got passed on from generation to generation and we end up "MiLefanim."

To continue, we have "Kol Lashon Lekha Teshabbeah," "VeKhol 'Ayin," we say "Lekha Tisspeh." Now, other Siddurim from other communities will have "Kol 'Ayin Lekha Tesappeh." Again, not going into which is more accurate, whether they mean the same thing or not, it's a whole discussion, but clearly our custom as it's again printed accurately: "VeKhol 'Ayin Lekha Tisspeh."

Finally, I wanted to point out something really intriguing. If you go to the main synagogues where there's a lot of people singing, you'll find in the "MiMissrayim," where the people will sing, let's take the tune of the holidays, "MiMissrayim Ge'altanu," so we say "VeZedim Tiba'ta ViDidim 'Abru Yam." Say "'Abru Yam." It's "'Abru Yam." If you look at the text, it's printed "'Abru Yam," the way Binyan Kal, you know, "'Abar" in Binyan Kal, Guf Shelishi, that's the way it should read: "'Abru Yam." How come when you go to Shaare Zion, you go to Bene Torah, all the people are, it's ingrained that they say "'Abaru Yam"? Where did they get that from? And it's fascinating because it's not correct grammatically, but yet everybody says it. At least when I was growing up and when I went to all the synagogues in the community, everybody sang, only when they sang it. Interestingly, during the week when they read it, they read it "'Abru Yam." But on Shabbat when they sing it, "'Abaru Yam." It's fascinating.

I saw a Nusah, the early Italian Roman Nusah. Now the Roman Kehilah, of course, predated even Sefaradim, even Ashkenazim. It's from the end of Bayit Sheni. So if you notice in their Siddurim, even till today in Rome, it'll say "BaYam 'Abaru." So the "'Abaru" being that that's the end of the Pasuk, the end of the sentence, so the "'Abru" became "'Abaru" grammatically. Now, I'm not saying that that's the source or that's why, but it's very, very possible that they had the Nusah in Halab "BaYam 'Abaru," and people got used to singing "'Abaru." This is a theory, but I think it very well could be accurate because there's no other explanation as far as I know.

And it's amazing that because things are sung in public, in the Kenis together, it cannot change. It's like the tunes of the High Holidays can never change because people used to come, you know, 100% of the people came to Kenis on the High Holidays, and they sang the same tunes, and these tunes can never change. It's not like every Shabbat we improvise with different... No! So when you have the power of song that even changes a word, it could stick for 1,000 years! And it's just amazing how you see the power of tradition, the power of the transmission of our tradition.

We also see it when we yell out after "'Al Kullam," "Barukh Hai 'Olamim." "Hai 'Olamim," it's not written in any Siddur, or "KimeAz," not written in any Siddur, yet people say it! Where do they get it from? "Well, my father said it, my father said it, my father..." You'll have to go back 600, 700 years to find a Nusah that on Yom Kippur they used to say a prayer called "Hai 'Olamim" in between "'Al Kullam" and "ViHalelu." It's fascinating! Or "KimeAz," which is still the Nusah in the Roman community. So I'm just pointing this out, that we have to be very particular in how we say things, because we are continuing a very old and holy tradition. Kol Tub.

97.title: The Zohar Before the Berit Milah
97.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles. Zohar for Berit Milah. So the night before the Berit Milah, it is customary in many homes, in many communities, to have a reading, and this reading is done from the Zohar, so the reading is simply referred to as Zohar. As we mentioned in the previous video, it also is named specifically in Halab by the name of Shidd el-As, and not all families do it the night before the Milah, some do it on the actual morning of the Milah.

In any case, this is a special reading from the Zohar that talks about Abraham Abinu and his son Yisshak Abinu, and the Berit of Yisshak, and what transpired, and the ideas of the mystics, the mystical Hakhamim, or the Hakhamim that spoke about mystical ideas within the Torah, and more specifically in this case about Eliyahu HaNabi. And this is considered a Segulah for the newborn child. It's a protection for this child. Until the child enters the Berit Milah, he's not considered 100% Jewish yet, and therefore he's vulnerable to all different types of illnesses that may befall him. So this special reading before the Berit Milah is to protect the child.

In any case, this doesn't seem to have been a Minhag in ancient days. It only began, most probably, after Zohar became popular through the Ari. So we're talking about approximately 1520s, 1530s in Safed, Northern Israel, and from there, the study of Zohar, the reading of Zohar, began to spread out from that city in Israel, throughout Israel, and then throughout the rest of the world.

Here is an older printing of this reading. At the time, it was called Mishmeret HaBen, and this is from Livorno, Italy, from 1765. And it has the entire reading for the night. Obviously, over the course of time, it was printed and reprinted many times, and the most common printing that we had viewed in our community over the last number of decades is the book Berit 'Olam, as published in Jerusalem in 1968.

So what does this entail? Is this for everybody? Is it not for everybody? Who comes? What do they do? So generally you have to have at least one Hakham, it's preferable to have three Hakhamim there, and you want to have a Minyan of people. Generally you'll invite very close family members, and they take turns going around the table, each one reading a section of the Zohar until it is complete. In other words, we do not split up the reading from the beginning of the night: "Okay, you read page 1, you read page 2, page 3, page 4, and okay, we'll all read it simultaneously so the whole thing is finished in 15 minutes." Rather, everybody listens to the person, you know, next to him reading, he finishes, then it's his turn, and goes around the table. And the entire thing takes maybe about an hour and a half to two hours.

After the reading, the Kaddish is said, Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, and then songs of the Berit Milah are sung. During the night of the reading, or during that two-hour period, there are all different Berakhot on the table: Mezonot, Ha'Ess, Adamah, SheHakol. And people partake of these sweets usually on the table and make Berakhot, and these Berakhot also work as a Zekhut for the mother and child.

It's considered that if the Milah is in the house, as traditionally was in the past, then Eliyahu HaNabi, his chair is already there, and even his presence is there. So you may begin even that night with lighting candles in honor of Eliyahu HaNabi on the tray for Eliyahu HaNabi, the Siniyet Eliyahu HaNabi. And following that, in many families, there would actually be a complete lavish meal in honor of the baby and the Berit Milah to come.

So again, within each family, within each city, there were different Minhagim, but this is generally the way the Zohar was. It was a section from the Zohar that was read by at least a Minyan of people as a protection for the mother and child prior to the Berit Milah.

98.title: Customs of Counting the 'Omer
98.text:
Last year, in episode 47, we discussed the fact that in Halab, the majority did not refrain from shaving during the 'Omer, as it is not part of the custom of refraining from haircuts. It is an added stringency that individuals may accept upon themselves if they wish. Now I would also like to add that according to Hakham Shalom Cohen, the Rosh Yeshibah of Porat Yosef, when he was a student in Porat Yosef in the 1940s, the students used to shave during the 'Omer, except for Hakham Ben Siyyon Abba Shaul and Hakham Yosef Ades. Then Hakham Yosef Ades got engaged during the 'Omer, and the Rosh Yeshibah at that time, who was Hakham Ezra Attieh, told Hakham Yosef Ades to shave, since the custom in Halab was to shave during the 'Omer.

Another custom, according to the Halabi tradition, it is not customary to refrain from reciting Sheheheyanu during the 'Omer on new fruit or on new clothing. This was recorded in the book Derekh Eress, quoting Rabbi Yisshak Tawil 'Alav HaShalom. Derekh Eress also quoted Hakham Eliyahu Hamwey from his book Peh Eliyahu, who wrote that the custom in many Sephardic communities is to recite Sheheheyanu during the 'Omer.

The general custom of the Syrian community in Brooklyn was not to perform weddings or to take haircuts until the 34th day of the 'Omer. Only some individuals accepted an additional stringency upon themselves with regards to shaving. With regards to Sheheheyanu, the custom is to be lenient for both new fruit and new clothing.

With regards to counting the 'Omer, the custom in Aleppo was that the congregation counts before the Hazzan. This custom was also recorded in the book Derekh Eress, quoting Hakham Yisshak Tawil 'Alav HaShalom, who explained that if people have the intention to fulfill their obligation to count when they hear the Hazzan count, and then they count themselves afterwards, it would be a Berakhah LeBattalah, a blessing said in vain. The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer also mentioned the practice of the congregation counting before the Hazzan, quoting Rabbi Hayyim Benveniste from his book Keneset HaGedolah, who in the 17th century wrote that most congregations count before the Hazzan. The Kaf HaHayyim also quoted Rabbi Yisshak Palachi from his book Yafeh LaLeb, who in the 19th century wrote that some congregations count before the Hazzan. Both Rabbi Hayyim Benveniste and Rabbi Yisshak Palachi lived in Turkey.

What about the concern that if the congregation counts first, some will accidentally count the wrong night? Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi quoted Abraham Dwek, who told him that the congregation formed small groups, who each announced what number they counted the previous night before they all recited the blessing and counted.

One more custom: counting the 'Omer again in Shahrit every morning. Hakham Abraham Antebi, who was the chief rabbi of Halab in the 19th century, wrote in his book Hokhmah UMusar, "And the custom here in Aram Soba is so nice. Immediately after the Hazzan completes the Hazarah, everyone stands and counts the 'Omer out loud without a blessing, and in this way they do not lose the blessing on the other nights if they forgot to count on the previous night." And this custom of counting every morning in Shahrit continued here in the Syrian communities in New York and New Jersey, who count after the first Kaddish after the Hazarah, before we recite Ashre.

99.title: Concluding the Shahrit Variants
99.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim, we are continuing with the Minhagim of Shahrit, Shabbat morning in the Sibbur. We hopefully will conclude it with this video. So we are continuing with the certain variants, the differences of Nushaot, the textual variants that we have in the Nishmat, between our community and other communities.

I'm on page 258 in the Kol Ya'akob Siddur, reading from the Nishmat. We say, and most Hazzanim, if not all, will say, "VaAd-onai Elokim Emet, Lo Yanum VeLo Yishan." That is the Nusah that is presented in our Siddur, in most Siddurim today, in the Mahzor Aram Soba as well, which I have here, and as well as other Siddurim. There is another Nusah, however, is "VaAd-onai 'Er Lo Yanum VeLo Yishan." And what's interesting is that that's the way it appears in the Siddur Bet Menuhah, a very prevalent Siddur used in Halab and in many parts of the Sephardic world.

And in fact, most Hazzanim, I said, say "VaAd-onai Elokim Emet Lo Yanum VeLo Yishan." Our colleague, Joey Mosseri, when he gets up to Hazzan, he still uses the Nusah "VaAd-onai 'Er Lo Yanum VeLo Yishan." He relates a story where once he was in a Sephardic synagogue praying Shahrit and one of a very prominent guest was there, a Hazzan, and he was taken aback and said, "I never heard that before." And Rabbi Shammah told him that indeed this was the custom to say "VaAd-onai 'Er Lo Yanum VeLo Yishan," like in Bet Menuhah. This was the custom in 67th Street in the Magen David. And it wasn't until the mid-'50s or so when the Tefilat Yesharim became more popular in the community that it was changed. And today most Hazzanim say "VaAd-onai Elokim Emet, Lo Yanum VeLo Yishan," but it's important to know the history and the development of that custom.

We continue. We have the custom to say "BaRa'ab BeSaba'," not "BeRa'ab UBeSaba' Kilkaltanu." That's the way it's reflected accurately in Kol Ya'akob. Other Siddurim will have "BeRa'ab Zantanu UBeSaba' Kilkaltanu." We continue, "Hen Hem Yodu ViBarekhu ViShabbehu ViFa'aru ViShoreru." Our custom is to add "ViShoreru." It's not found in Mahzor Aram Soba, but in Bet Menuhah it's found, and it's the custom all over the word, the world amongst the Syrian communities is to add "ViShoreru."

We continue, "BeMikhalot Ribebot." That's the custom amongst all Sephardic communities today to say "BeMikhalot," even though in Mahzor Aram Soba and the older Nushaot will have "BeMakhelot," our custom is "BeMikhalot." In the El Adon, we say "Barukh UMeborakh BeFi Kol Neshamah." You'll find Siddurim, including the Mahzor Aram Soba and other Siddurim that are used today that will say "Kol HaNeshamah." That's not our custom. Our custom, based on the Bet Menuhah and also accurately reflected in the Kol Ya'akob, "BeFi Kol Neshamah."

The end of the El Adon, "Tiferet UGdulah, Serafim VeHayyot VeOfane HaKodesh." This is interesting. This is the way it's found in many Siddurim. However, in the Shalme Hagigah, Rabbi Yisrael Ya'akob Algazi speaks about it. And it's interesting that if you look ahead in the, after the Kedushah, "Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh," in the Titbarakh, it says "VeHaOfannim VeHayyot HaKodesh," which is the reverse. We should say, based on "Serafim VeHayyot VeOfane HaKodesh," we should say "Hayyot VeOfane HaKodesh." And indeed, there is the Nusah in Mahzor Aram Soba, in Bet Menuhah to say "Serafim VeOfannim VeHayyot HaKodesh." Again, there are two Nushaot. The one printed in Kol Ya'akob is what you'll hear today most often by the Hazzanim: "Serafim VeHayyot VeOfane HaKodesh." I thought it was important to point out.

In the Keri'at Shema, there is a custom in our community and many Syrian communities, including in Ades, where the Hazzan will honor one of the other Paytanim or Hazzanim in the Kahal to say the Pasuk, not the Pasuk, the words "VeKerabtanu Malkenu LeShimkha HaGadol BeEmet LeHodot Lekha ULeYahedkha BeAhabah, LeShimkha," and he will honor somebody to say that in the Maqam that is being sung, and that person will usually go and continue the Keri'at Shema. It's up to the Hazzan, it's not mandatory, but we see it done often. We say "VeAhabah Et Shimkha." Many other Siddurim will have "Shemekha," that's not our custom. Our custom is "Ahabah Et Shimkha."

In the 'Amidah, "Yismehu BeMalkhutakh," that paragraph, it ends "Hemdat Yamim Oto Karata," and that's it. In 'Arbit and in Musaf, a similar paragraph ends "Zekher LeMa'aseh Bereshit," we do not say it in Shahrit based on the Ari, the writings of the Kabbalah. It's interesting that in Mahzor Aram Soba the entire paragraph is not mentioned in Shahrit. However, we do say it, but we do not say the ending "Zekher LeMa'aseh Bereshit," that's reserved for 'Arbit and Musaf.

Regarding the customs of the Hazarah, the Nakdishakh, the Kohanim, you can refer back to my videos in Shahrit, number 21, number 48, also the Minhagim of the Kaddish. It's the same Minhagim. Finally, the Hazzan will read the Kohanim, generally expanding on the words, a little slower. But he's got to take into account that the Kohanim, they're with their hands up so he shouldn't go too slow. Generally, they, I know in Ades at least and many times in New York, you'll see every word will be a different Maqam, will show how they can maneuver from one Maqam to the next. The Hazzan very often will invite somebody else to say the Kohanim, that's been done, that's how they do it in Ades.

And that wraps up Shahrit. Beginning next week, we will, the next video we will discuss the Hossa'at Sefer Torah, the Keri'at Sefer Torah, the Minhagim of the 'Aliyot, and the honors, and so on. Kol Tub.

100.title: Where and When Berit Milah Takes Place
100.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles. Milestone episode number 100, and how befitting it is to begin this episode number 100 with the Minhagim of Berit Milah. Berit Milah, or as it was commonly known, abbreviated as Milah, or in Arabic as tahur, but never as bris, and till today most people traditionally refer to it as Milah.

Now, when and where should the Berit Milah take place? We as Sefaradim look back to Spain, what they were doing in Spain, and we have the book Abudarham written by Hakham David Abudarham, who lived in Seville, Spain in the 14th century, and it tells us the Minhag in Spain was that both Shahrit prayers and the Berit Milah would be held in the home of the Abi HaBen, the father of the newborn child. So Shahrit prayers there in the house, and immediately thereafter the Berit Milah.

Now, did that Minhag trickle down to our communities in the Middle East, or was it different? So we look at the writings of Hakham Abraham Antebi. Hakham Abraham Antebi was the chief rabbi of Halab from 1818 to 1858, a 40-year span, and in his book Hokhmah UMusar he talks about the Berit Milah. And not only does he talk about the importance of Berit Milah, he talked about the importance of Eliyahu HaNabi attending the Berit Milah. And he says like this: he says the Berit Milah is attended by Eliyahu HaNabi once he gets permission from God to go there. And Eliyahu turns to Bore 'Olam, he turns to HaShem, asking Him for permission to go to the Milah, and only if HaShem promises him to forgive and atone the sins of all those present. Once he is reassured of that, he goes to the Berit Milah.

What does Rabbi Abraham Antebi then tell us? He bemoans the fact that most people in Halab in his day were doing the Berit Milah at home and later in the day, in other words in the afternoon or late afternoon, evening, and he said it's a terrible circumstance because when that happens we have barely a Minyan of people in attendance, and you were only benefiting those few people that are in the home. He wanted everybody to have the Berit Milah in the Bet Keneset in the morning, therefore you avail this Zekhut, this merit, this privilege of having people come to pray and having their sins atoned by listening to the Berakhot of Berit Milah and answering "Amen." And he wanted to really push that agenda, and he did his utmost, but unfortunately it doesn't seem like he was able to, because even until the later part of the century and the early 20th century, and well into the 20th century, the common custom remained to do the Berit Milah in Halab in the home, and not in the Bet Keneset except for a few cases, but it wasn't commonly done in the Bet Keneset.

Now what was going on in Cairo, Egypt? Cairo, Egypt also presented a very interesting issue. Chief rabbi there, Hakham Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on, chief rabbi from 1881 to 1921, tells us that there was a Minhag in the city that anybody who would have a Berit Milah at home, there was a Minhag established that he would have to serve a very lavish feast to all those in attendance. Because of that, people were not doing the Milah in the morning, they were purposely pushing off the Milah to the afternoon, therefore avoiding the Minhag of serving a feast. Even though he wasn't happy about this, because he wanted people to follow the dictate of Shulhan 'Arukh of Zerizin Makdimin, those who are scrupulous do the Missvah early, he understood the concept of financial constraint upon the people, and he realized that it's very difficult, but since this was a community Minhag, even as chief rabbi he could not change it, only the community themselves could change a community Minhag, and he would have liked to have seen it change, but even there as well, into the 1940s, '50s, and '60s, the Minhag remained that most Milot were held at home, but in the afternoon.

Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin, who compiled Minhagim of so many Sephardic communities, wrote that the Minhag of Sefaradim in London and Amsterdam was to do the Milah at home, but the general Minhag in Eress Yisrael and Syria and Turkey and Egypt was generally to do the Minhag of the Berit Milah in the Bet Keneset. So we see there are different testimonies as to what the Minhag was.

Now what's the Minhag of our Syrian community of Brooklyn? So in the '40s and '50s and even the early '60s, because a mother who gave birth was left in the hospital with the newborn child well past eight days, so the Berit Milah was generally done in the hospital. Later on, in the later part of the '60s, in the '70s, in the '80s, most Berit Milah were done at home, and from the '90s on, it became very, very popular, and still is till today, to do the Berit Milah in the morning, in the Bet Keneset after the prayers. So we see we go back and revert to the request of Hakham Abraham Antebi of Halab, who wanted the Milah to be in the Bet Keneset at the Shahrit time after the prayers, to atone for the sins of the people, and that is the current Minhag of our community today as per the wishes of Hakham Abraham Antebi in Hokhmah UMusar.

101.title: Traveling to Meron for Lag Ba'Omer
101.text:
Last year, in episode 50, we discussed the Halabi tradition of celebrating the night of Lag Ba'Omer in the Kenis, auctioning off the privilege to light cups of oil in memory of our patriarchs and matriarchs, prophets and prophetesses, and great talmudic rabbis. This custom was practiced along with music, singing, and a festive meal. But what about traveling to Meron to visit the grave of Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai on Lag Ba'Omer?

Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca found several accounts of Jews from Halab traveling to Meron for Lag Ba'Omer in the 19th century. Prior to 1865, Rabbi Yehosef Schwartz wrote that in addition to the Jews from Jerusalem and other parts of Israel, many Jews from Damascus, Aleppo, Baghdad, Cairo, Constantinople, and many other cities traveled every year on Lag Ba'Omer to gather at the tomb of Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai to celebrate the holiday. Many times, several thousand Jews could be found there, lighting many candles like the stars of the sky, and singing and dancing and celebrating. And they called this holiday the Hillula of Rabbi Shim'on Ben Yohai. It's noteworthy that even in Meron, the Middle Eastern Jews did not light bonfires. Our custom was to light candles on Lag Ba'Omer in Meron, just like we do today when we celebrate Lag Ba'Omer in the synagogue.

Similarly, in a book published in 1844, Rabbi Hayyim HaLevi Horowitz reports that Jews from Sefat, Akko, Damascus, Aleppo, and other places traveled to Meron on Lag Ba'Omer, and they would donate money to light oil cups above the gravestones. The Shamash would announce the donations. They would pay their donations, and a Mi SheBerakh was recited. Rabbi Horowitz was also there himself in the year 1836.

There are also newspaper articles from a Jerusalem newspaper in 1888 and in 1904 that report that Jews from various Middle Eastern cities, including Baghdad, Aleppo, Damascus, and Alexandria, would come to visit Jerusalem after being in Meron for Lag Ba'Omer and visiting Sefat and Tiberias, and they would stay in Jerusalem to celebrate the holiday of Shabu'ot before returning to their respective cities. The article also reported that during their visit in Israel, they would go to pray at the Me'arat HaMakhpelah in Hebron.

So from all these accounts, we see that it was common for Middle Eastern Jews in general, including Syrian Jews in particular, at least since the 19th century, to travel to Meron on Lag Ba'Omer and light candles and celebrate there, as well as visiting the other holy places in Eress Yisrael as part of their visit.

Rabbi Antebi Sacca also quoted Rabbi Abraham Ades, who wrote that in Halab, they never had the custom of waiting until a boy was three years old to give him his first haircut. So the custom of giving three-year-old boys their first haircut on Lag Ba'Omer was never practiced in Halab. The holiday was observed by lighting candles in memory of our esteemed ancestors, with music, singing, and dancing, either in the Kenis or at the gravesite of Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai in Meron.

102.title: Tunes and the Accentuation of Words
102.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. In our past videos, we discussed the Tefillat Shahrit of Shabbat, the liturgical customs, the textual variants. We concluded and we're ready for the next part of the prayer, which is the taking out of the and the reading of the Sefer Torah. However, I did want to make one final, though very important point regarding the tunes in general and their application in our prayers.

We know there are parts of the prayer which we sing, Nishmat, El Hoda'ot, Kaddish, and so on. And when we match a tune to these parts of the prayers, you'll notice many, many times that we're not loyal 100% to the proper reading of the word. Now, we're not talking about deviating from punctuation or Dageshim or Nekudot, obviously, but we're talking about the accentuating either the first part of the word or the last part of the word. The accentuating the first syllables except for the last is called Mil'el, and accentuating the final syllable of a word is called Milra'. Now, very often we will transpose Mil'el and Milra' in order to fit the tune properly.

Now, there was a very, very interesting discussion that Joey Mosseri recounted to me of a discussion between members of the great Tawil family in our community, Hazzanim, Paytanim, Hakhamim. And 'Alav HaShalom, Mr. Mo Tawil, a great Hazzan and Paytan beloved by all, he was of the opinion that wherever possible the Hazzan should be loyal to the accentuation, even you know, even if it's pushing a little bit the boundaries of the tune, but you should be loyal to the accentuation of the word wherever possible. Some tunes it's impossible.

However, his brother, sort of a familial dispute here, so his brother Hakham David, 'Alav HaShalom, said, "Absolutely not." There is a poetic license, a musical license if you will, where when the Kahal is singing in unison, it should be sung the best way to maximize the tune, to the point where if a Hazzan in his presence would try and shift the Mil'el and Milra' in order to say it properly at the expense of the tune a bit, he would draw the ire, the scornful look of Hakham David, with some other disapproving gesture, because he was to him, it was important that the feel of the music take precedent over the reading of the word.

Now, if you look at most tunes, I would say, especially the older ones, most tunes naturally involve the transposing of Mil'el and Milra'. And that's the way actually practically that's how it's applied, so I guess Hakham David, 'Alav HaShalom, won the day in this argument. I just I'll give you a few examples and you'll notice if you pay attention, you'll notice it in almost all of the tunes.

So let's take the Maqam Sigah, Elyasirani Li'Amal, a common tune that's used for Kaddish and Nishmat, especially on the first day of the holidays. So I'll pick it up in the middle of the Kaddish, for instance: "VeYissmah Purkaneh ViKareb Meshiheh." So we don't say "VeYissmah Purkaneh," we say "VeYissmah Purkaneh ViKareb Meshiheh." If you pick it up even in the next, in Nishmat where we also say this, so it says: "Tefa'er UTromem." So you'll see that we don't, we're not loyal to the tunes.

And now if you notice on the High Holidays, it's especially obvious. When let's say you'll say "Barekhu," what does the Kahal answer? "Barukh Ad-onai." "Barukh," they don't say "Barukh," they say "Barukh." "Ra'u Banim Et Geburato." So we see that the indeed we are not particular about the Mil'el and Milra' when it comes to fitting the tunes into the pieces.

Now, one final point is that another trademark of Halabi Hazzanim is to sometimes attach the last syllable to the next word. So we'll say, let me see, we could say, like I said, "Tefa'er UTromem," like that, so we'll, the er will be connected to tromem. "Zikhrekha Malkenu Tamid." And that's another, when you hear a Hazzan do that, and many of the old tunes have that nuance, and that's, that talks about how they break up the words. They'll break it up and leave the last syllable to attach it to the next word, and it gives a little Hen, a little grace to the Piyyut, to the tune.

Another point is that very often with Halabi Hazzanim, they'll start the tune and they'll repeat the first syllable. They'll say, like you'll say, "Ni, Nishmat," "Ni, Nishmat Kol Hai." You'll find that occasionally in Nishmat or Nakdishakh, where they'll repeat the words, repeat the first syllable again. When a Hazzan does that, you know that either he's a Halabi Hazzan or he studied from the, from a Halabi Hazzan. So that wraps up the liturgical customs of our

103.title: Prayers on the Day of Berit Milah
103.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: lifecycles, Shahrit prayers on the day of the Berit Milah. On the day of the Berit Milah, Tahanunim, supplications, are not recited. Rather, everybody in the Minyan, in place of supplications, joyously scream out Yehi Shem, an indication that we have a very happy occasion today.

What else is going on other than that being a happy occasion? We sing the prayers. So if it's a special Minyan just for the Milah, then the entire prayers will be conducted in Maqam Saba. Maqam Saba is used for a Berit Milah, because Saba sounds like sabi, sabi the Arabic word for boy. Now, we're saying only when it's a special Minyan for the Berit Milah, because if it's the regular Minyan of the Kenis, and the Abi HaBen happens to be there praying with them, we don't want to hold them back by stretching out the prayer while singing in Maqam Saba. Rather, we will only sing the section of Nakdishakh to the tune of Attah Ahubi.

Now what about Shabbat? What happens to the prayers on Shabbat? Do we change the Maqam to Saba because we're not rushing anyplace? So, in some Halabi communities, they will do the entire Shabbat prayer in Maqam Saba. But the Minhag of our communities in the United States is we never change the Maqam of the Shabbat because of Berit Milah. The Maqam of the Shabbat has to remain connected to either the Parashah of the week, or the holiday, or the time of the year. And only once again the Nakdishakh will switch to Saba to be sung in honor of the Berit Milah.

Now, as we said, the Berit Milah, Attah Ahubi. Now, what else is going on? So if the Berit Milah is being held in that synagogue that day, even if the Abi HaBen, the father of the child, is not there, also we will switch from supplications to Yehi Shem, and we will also sing the Nakdishakh to Attah Ahubi. This also goes into play not only if the Abi HaBen is there, or not there, being in the case if the Milah is there, also if the Sandak, the person that holds the child while sitting on the chair, or the Mohel, the ritual circumciser. So if any of these three personages are there, or the Berit Milah is being held in that place, so Yehi Shem is said instead of Tahanunim, and Nakdishakh is sung in Maqam Saba to the tune of Attah Ahubi.

What about on Shabbat? What else is done? So the Abi HaBen will generally get the honor of Jilyan, of carrying the Sefer Torah, and he'll also be accorded an 'Aliyah to the Sefer Torah. But he's not just told, "Okay, Kabod, go up to the Sefer Torah." Rather, person inviting or the Hazzan or one of the Gabba'im will scream out: "Abi HaBen!" If the Abi HaBen's father is alive, in other words the grandfather of the newborn child is alive, instead of just screaming out "Abi HaBen," they'll yell out, "Abi HaBen 'Ateret!" And if the Milah actually is occurring on Yom Shabbat, then they'll say, "Abi HaBen 'Ateret, HaYom Shabbat UMilah!" So we have all different sayings that are said depending on the situation at hand, and these give an indication to the entire congregation of what's going on: who's there, who's present, who's alive, when is the Milah, you know.

And if the, obviously if the Milah is there, people are excited, as we've said in previous videos, they want to find out, they want to attend the Milah as well. And of course, before the Abi HaBen goes up to the Torah, the Hazzanim and the Mezammerim will break out into one or two Pizmonim in his honor before inviting him up to the Sefer Torah. So once again, the whole idea of Berit Milah is a very joyous one, not only for the people involved, but for the entire congregation and all of 'Am Yisrael.

104.title: Nes Musan and the Thirteenth of Sivan
104.text:
The general custom of Middle Eastern Jews is to refrain from reciting Tahanunim until and including the twelfth of Sivan, since during the times of the Bet HaMikdash, one could still bring his holiday offering to the Bet HaMikdash until the twelfth of Sivan if he did not bring it on the day of Shabu'ot. But in Halab, it was customary to say Yehi Shem on the following day as well, on the thirteenth of Sivan.

However, the custom of reciting Yehi Shem on the thirteenth of Sivan was not related to the holiday of Shabu'ot. It was in honor of a miracle that occurred in Halab in the year 1853. This miracle is referred to as Nes Musan. Now, there are several versions of what actually happened with the miracle of Nes Musan. The version that I am presenting here is based on a manuscript from the collection of Hakham Moshe Sethon. Hakham Moshe Sethon was a rabbi in Aleppo in the nineteenth century and was approximately 56 years old when the miracle occurred. He passed away 25 years after Nes Musan in 1878. This manuscript was made available by Rabbi Abraham Ades, who currently lives in Israel. Since this is based on a written account by a rabbi who lived in Aleppo at the time of the miracle, it is clearly the most reliable account of Nes Musan.

The story began on the twelfth of Sivan on a Shabbat afternoon when a Christian woman accused Moshe Musan's son, Yisshak, who was Jewish, of being the last person to be with her son, who was now missing. And then she accused the Jews of murdering her son like they did with other children in Damascus and other places. She also reported this to the local Muslim authorities, who arrested Yisshak Musan and put him in jail. The incident was reported to the Turkish authorities as well, and a complaint was filed by the Christian clergy stating that they cannot live in the same city as the Jews because the Jews commonly kill non-Jewish children. The Jews were very afraid about the trouble that they were expected to endure from this accusation.

But on the following day, the thirteenth of Sivan, a Protestant informed a Jew that the Christians were hiding the boy in order to incriminate the Jewish community. The Jews then went to the woman's home, and they found the boy in a hidden room under a pile of laundry. They took the boy to the Muslim authorities, who got a confession about the plot against the Jews. Yisshak Musan was freed from prison, and the complaints against the Jews were dismissed.

Then the rabbis of Halab declared that the thirteenth of Sivan should be observed every year by eliminating Tahanunim on that day. And until today, Halabi communities around the world continue to say Yehi Shem on the thirteenth of Sivan in honor of Nes Musan, a miracle that occurred for the Jewish community in Halab in the year 1853.

105.title: The Role of the Mesader
105.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. In our previous video, we concluded the Minhagim relating to the morning prayers, the Shahrit of Shabbat, and before we begin the next part of the prayers, which is the Keri'ah from the Torah, we want to discuss and really dedicate at least two videos, possibly three, to the role, the very important role, the crucial role of the person who is tasked with distributing and giving out the honors for the Sefer Torah. In other words, the Petihah, opening up the Hekhal, who carries the Sefer, which we call Jilyan, and of course the 'Aliyot. This role is performed by the person we call in our Kahal, we call him the Mesader. Other, and I know the Ashkenazim may call him Gabbai, we call him the Mesader.

Now, in order for the Mesader to do his job professionally, equitably, which is a key thing, he has to be very, very familiar and proficient in the following areas. Number one, he has to know the Halakhot, the Halakhot of the 'Aliyot, who's allowed to go up, who's not allowed to go up, when they go up, two brothers, and so on. As you can look at Shulhan 'Arukh, Siman Kof-Lamed-Heh and on, the subsequent Simanim, to discuss all of the Halakhot of the 'Aliyot of the Sefer Torah. Very important to follow the Halakhah.

Secondly, he has to know the Minhagim of our community when it comes to the 'Aliyot and to the Petihah. There are instances where there are Semahot, occasions, in the synagogue. So what does the, what do the family of the, of this, of the person who has a Simhah receive? Do they get Petihah? Does he carry the Sefer? Do they get 'Aliyot? How many 'Aliyot? What if there's multiple Semahot? There's, which occasions, like you have baby boy, baby girl, Bar Missvah, engagement, which we call Arus, just married, which we call Hatan, two very different things which have different customs. How do you prioritize them? Who gets what? These are all part of the customs which we will be discussing.

He has to know that there are certain 'Aliyot which are earmarked for certain individuals: 'Aseret HaDibrot, the Ten Commandments, which we read in Yitro and VaEthannan, generally go to the Hakham. We have the Shirah, we have the certain 'Aliyot which are considered, again, everything is Torah and everything is Kadosh, but there's a certain protocol. Shishi is considered, 'Al Pi Kabbalah, the most important 'Aliyah, and that's why we reserve it for a person who has Hashibut. And so we have he has to know exactly which 'Aliyot he's giving to whom based on our customs.

Thirdly, he has to know the congregation. He has to know the people who come to the Kenis regularly. He has to know, keep a record, who went up when. Most Kehillot, if not all, keep records, so a Mesader can go back and look and see who, whose turn it comes for an 'Aliyah. He also has to know the status. Who has Semahot? Who has occasions? Who, God forbid, needs to say Kaddish? All of these things has to be he has to be very, very familiar with the Kahal. Who needs to say HaGomel, the Berakhah that we say when someone, God forbid, was in the hospital for a few days, or so on, or came from a trip.

Finally, he has to know the Parashah. He has to have an intimate knowledge of the Parashah that's going to be read that Shabbat. He has to know how it's divided up. He has to know how many 'Aliyot he can fit after the Shishi, what we call Rekeb, the extras. He has to know the content of the 'Aliyot in order to properly pair up and not to make a Fadihah, which means making put somebody in an embarrassing position. As an example, you have a Hatan, someone who just got married, it's Parashat Ki Tesse, don't send them up the 'Aliyah that speak, speaking about divorce. Again, common sense, but he has to know that, he has to prepare it beforehand.

Therefore, you look at all of these four areas, not one, and they're all of equal importance. One doesn't work without the other. He has to know Halakhot, Minhagim, the Kahal, and the Parashah. And when he does his preparation properly, which should be done a few days before the Shabbat, he has to have a very good idea of who exactly is going up, and not thinking on the fly, because then you're going to make mistakes. And there's always changes. You have to have it you have to be prepared, also prepared for changes: a Hashub person comes to the Kenis, you have to give him an 'Aliyah, then all of a sudden his whole Seder is mixed. He has to be able to be prepared, he has to be flexible.

Therefore, the Mesader really is probably the most important person in the Kehillah on Shabbat morning. He ensures goodwill and harmony and a good feeling and comfortable feeling for the people in the Kahal, because God forbid he makes a mistake, there could be ill will and Mahlokot, and anger, God forbid, we don't want to see that. So therefore, the Mesader has to understand all of these areas very well, and we'll go into greater detail regarding these areas in future videos. Kol Tub.
