106.title: The Tray of Eliyahu HaNabi
106.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles: Berit Milah, Siniyet Eliyahu HaNabi, the tray of Eliyahu HaNabi. We have a beautiful Minhag associated with Berit Milah, and that's the Siniyet Eliyahu HaNabi. And this is a tray that is bedecked with flowers and candles that is taken around by a young unmarried female, giving everybody the opportunity to light a candle and give Sedakah.

What does this tray look like? Here's an example of one of these trays, this one courtesy of the Edmond J. Safra Hathaway Synagogue. Here's another one of the trays, this one from Congregation Magen David of West Deal. These trays are very common in our community. Almost every one of our synagogues have one. Anytime you have a Berit Milah, they know to bring it out to give you the opportunity to use the tray.

We're going to discuss the tray, the Minhagim associated with the tray, what goes on with the candles, with the money, as well as the reasons for this tray. So, this multi-leveled tray, as I mentioned, everybody gets the opportunity to light a candle and give Sedakah. How does it go? Very, very simple. The young lady carrying the tray has a candle, she'll offer you that candle. You will light one of those candles that are on the tray, and give Sedakah, place it on any one of the tiers. You may, as well, at the same time take a coin that's on the tray of a smaller denomination than you contributed, whether it be a penny, a nickel, dime, quarter, whatever it may be, and you can keep that coin for good luck, or you could give it for Sedakah elsewhere as well.

Now, once everybody has had a chance to light a candle and give Sedakah, the tray is auctioned off. Not the actual tray, but the Zekhut, the Kabod of offering even more Sedakah and being further involved. So what goes on over here, generally the Shamash or somebody else involved in the situation will auction off the tray. For example, the greatest amount of money that you would find on one of these trays after everybody has had a chance to give Sedakah is about $200, $300, but it could go, auction off for a few thousand dollars. So let's say you now won the bidding on the tray, you got it for $8,000, you give this $8,000 to Sedakah.

What about the money that's on the tray? So the money that's on the tray, you can either give it to Sedakah as well, you could give a portion of it to Sedakah, you can keep the whole amount, you could do keep part, give away part. Usually, people will keep that money. What do they keep that money for? So you have a few different factions over here. You have item number one, they'll keep the bulk of the bills, and they'll use that as part of the money they use for starting a new business, or putting a down payment on a home, to bring Berakhah to that endeavor. The coins that are on the tray, they'll take and give them out to friends and relatives, once again as a Siman Berakhah, as a positive omen to bring Berakhah to any sort of monetary concerns.

I clearly recall, and I've heard many times over, that in the '40s, the '50s, '60s, '70s, '80s, and probably continues still today, the older women would love to take the coins, they'd put a drop of red nail polish on it to indicate that this came from the tray of Eliyahu HaNabi, and they would mix it in their change purse, or they would take it and tape, let's say a dime, into the billfold section of a wallet, again, to mix in Berakhah into the money a person already has.

Now, other than that, what else is going on over here, and what is the purpose of these candles, where did it originate, why did it originate? It seems to be that this is a very, very ancient custom. Now, this is a custom where even though we're not making any sort of Berakhah or prayer when we're lighting the candle, or when we're giving the Sedakah, it's a custom that goes back and is connected to Eliyahu HaNabi. How so? Hakham Shem Tob Gagin in his Keter Shem Tob brings a very interesting explanation based upon two sections of Gemara, one in the Talmud Babli Sanhedrin and one in the Talmud Yerushalmi Ketubot. And he talks about Yeme HaShemad, the days of persecution.

Close to 2,000 years ago, there was a time in history where the foreign governments were not allowing 'Am Yisrael to do the Missvah of Berit Milah. Bene Yisrael, of course, could not forego this most important commandment, and they had to create a way to signal to friends, relatives, neighbors that we are still going to do the Milah. So they devised a signal: place a candle in the window, candle at the door, some way of indicating through that light that we are continuing the light of the Torah. The light that comes with the Berit Milah, because the Berit is a covenant, same way the Torah is a covenant, it's a Berit. So it's an indication to the people, we are continuing. Watch out, watch that we're doing it, come and join us, watch that others are not around, and the same way Eliyahu HaNabi comes to every Berit Milah to watch that we're doing it and go back to Bore 'Olam and say that 'Am Yisrael upholds this Missvah that you've given to them so dearly, we too are watching and we're telling one another to uphold the Missvah.

This is an ancient custom. It exists among many Sephardic communities, not only among the Halabi community, simply among us, we know of course it's among the Halabis, the Shamis, the Egyptians, the Lebanese, but there are many other Sephardic communities that uphold this custom, and it's a very dear and special custom, and it's something that we need to cherish, and we need to uphold, and we need to pass on to future generations.

107.title: The Custom of Throwing the Bread
107.text:
In a previous video regarding the customs of HaMossi, which was episode number eight, we discussed the custom of throwing the bread to each person at the table. We cited the practice of several rabbis who would throw the bread gently, including Hakham Moshe Tawil, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef 'Alehem HaShalom. And we mentioned that the custom is based on a Halakhah that HaRambam wrote in Mishneh Torah. In the seventh chapter of the laws of Berakhot, Halakhah Heh, HaRambam wrote that the one distributing the bread does not place the bread in the hand of the one that he is giving it to, unless the person receiving the bread is a mourner.

But what about the prohibition of throwing bread? The Gemara, Masekhet Berakhot, taught that we may not throw bread. And in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran ruled in accordance with the understanding of the Tosafot that throwing bread is disrespectful, even if the bread does not become inedible as a result of being thrown, whereas other foods may be thrown unless they become undesirable after they are thrown. However, the rabbis in Halab were careful to throw the bread gently so that it would not be disrespectful to the bread. According to their understanding, full-fledged throwing is disrespectful, and is what was prohibited according to Maran based on the Tosafot. But gentle throwing is not disrespectful, and is not included in the prohibition of throwing bread even according to Maran and the Tosafot.

It is noteworthy that other authorities did not differentiate between bread and other foods, and explained that the Gemara only prohibited throwing bread if throwing it would cause the bread to become inedible. These authorities include Rab Hai Gaon, Rashi, and it also appears to be the opinion of the Rif and HaRambam. And therefore, those that are not careful to throw the bread gently have several prominent authorities to rely upon.

Interestingly, there are also Ashkenazim that had the custom of throwing the bread when distributing it to everyone at the table. Rabbi Hayyim Tzanzer, an 18th-century authority from Ukraine, wrote that throwing the bread is the custom, and he legitimized the custom since it is permitted according to several authorities, including the Ba'al Halakhot Gedolot and the Rashba. And when there is a question of a rabbinic prohibition, such as throwing bread, one may rely upon the lenient authorities when there is a custom to do so. The Hatam Sofer's son, Rabbi Abraham Sofer, who was an authority in Hungary in the 19th century, also used to throw the bread when distributing it to everyone at his table.

So the custom of throwing the bread is based on a Halakhah that HaRambam wrote in Mishneh Torah. In Halab, the rabbis were careful to throw it gently in order to conform to Maran's ruling based on the Tosafot, who considered throwing bread to be disrespectful even when throwing it did not cause the bread to become inedible. But even those that don't throw it so gently are relying upon the opinion of the other authorities that we mentioned, that explain the Talmud's prohibition of throwing bread as only applying to throwing that causes the bread to become inedible, and therefore they allow one to throw bread if the bread is still going to be edible after it was thrown. And this was also the custom in some Ashkenazic communities as well.

108.title: Prioritizing Honors for the Semahot
108.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will pick up where we left off in our last video, discussing the customs of the person who is empowered, is in charge of distributing the honors in the synagogue on Shabbat morning, the Missvot, as we call them, namely the Petihat HaHekhal, opening up the Hekhal, carrying the Sefer, which we call Gilyan, and the, of course, the 'Aliyot.

Now, in many synagogues, it's the Mesader himself who decides and actually does the inviting, and in some cases, he will decide, usually in the bigger synagogues, and there will be somebody in charge of actually going to the people and inviting them. In some cases that was the Shamash, that was the job of the Shamash. That's the way it was I remember in the '60s and '70s in when I used to pray as a youngster in Bene Yosef, it was the job of the Shamash to go actually invite the people. When somebody invites somebody else for an honor, he does so personally. He goes up to them, "Kabod Petihah, Kabod Sefer." You don't invite somebody from a distance. It's not Kabod.

Now we want to talk about our traditions regarding occasions in the synagogue. Generally, when there's an occasion, there's a policy in the Kenis as to which honors the Ba'al HaSimhah, the one who has the occasion, will receive. Usually it's Petihah and/or Sefer, three 'Aliyot, every Kenis has their own policy, and it's very important to have these policies in place so that there's no unreasonable expectations and nobody is disappointed.

What happens when there are multiple occasions in the synagogue, Ken Yirbu? So we have a pecking order, if you will. We have a whatever way which we prioritize them. Semahot, generally you'll have Hatan, someone who got married within the week and he's in the seven days of the Huppah. We have Abi HaBen, obviously the father of a baby boy, Abi HaBat, a baby girl, we have a Bar Missvah, and we have Arus, someone who got engaged. Now, in all of these cases, the Ba'al HaSimhah will get an 'Aliyah, they will sing for him. In the case of the Hatan, they will say "VeAbraham Zaken" after his 'Aliyah, we'll get to that in later videos.

But when there are multiple Semahot, the way we prioritize them is as follows: Generally, the Hatan, because a Hatan is Domeh LeMelekh, he's compared to a king, the Hatan will take precedent over any other Simhah. And then you'll have the Abi HaBen, followed by Abi HaBat, followed by Bar Missvah, and lastly, the Arus, the engaged, because engagement, there's really no halakhic ramifications, it's not Kiddushin, it's simply an engagement. So we will give him an 'Aliyah, we will sing generally "Ani Likrat Dodi Arus," and however, that's at the bottom of the priority list. Where this comes into play is who to give Petihah to, who to give the Sefer to, and so on.

Now there is some congregations have the custom to prioritize Abi HaBen over the Hatan. Both customs are legitimate. As a matter of fact, Maran HaHida, the famous Aharon from the late 18th century, Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, he writes in his Sefer LeDavid Emet that indeed the Abi HaBen is prioritized over the Hatan, but generally the Minhag that I have seen is that the Hatan is prioritized over the Abi HaBen. Now what this means is that Petihah will go to the family of that Ba'al HaSimhah. Generally, Petihah, which is considered in the Halabi tradition to be a very high honor, and therefore, even on regular Shabbat, you'll see the elders and more respectable people who will be getting the Petihah, you know the older people in the community, whereas the Sefer is generally carried by a younger person, especially since they're heavy these days.

Now that's not the case in other communities. You'll find by the Ashkenazim that Petihah is not a high honor at all, it's not a big deal. But by us it is, and therefore, when we have a Simhah, we'll generally give it to the oldest person of the family. For instance, if it's a Hatan, either the father or the father-in-law, depending on again, there are other factors, who's a Yahid in the Bet Keneset, a guest, there are other factors which we have to that come into play that are, let's call them, common sense. Like even if you prioritize generally the Hatan, if you have a Abi HaBen, let's say, that had a child after many, many years, and you have a father that married off already four, five children, Ben Porat Yosef, so generally favor the father of the Abi HaBen in this case. And then, there's a lot of common sense involved, but there are general rules that we'd like to adhere to.

So again, you have Hatan, Abi HaBen, sometimes the custom is Abi HaBen or Hatan, legitimate, followed by Abi HaBat, Bar Missvah, and Arus. Now, I've seen many times, if there are multiple Bar Missvahs, we'll tell one of the Hatan Bar Missvah to take the Sefer out, and the other Hatan to take the Sefer in. Occasionally, some synagogues use a Sefer Haftarot. It's not required, but many synagogues do will have Sefer Haftarot, so you could give one the Torah, the other one the Haftarot, maybe switch it on the way back. Again, with the mindset always of being equitable and being able to explain yourself in case anybody has some comments after. So that's with regards to the Semahot.

In our next video, we will talk about various Minhagim regarding the Petihah, and we will focus more on the 'Aliyot. Kol Tub.

109.title: Bringing In the Child
109.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Life cycles, Berit Milah. As we continue speaking about the Berit Milah ceremony, last time we spoke about Siniyet Eliyahu HaNabi, the Pizmonim that are being sung while it's being passed around, the auctioning off of this tray, but what else is going on? What's going on outside this room where the Berit Milah is going to take place?

We move into the room where the mother is, the mother of the newborn child, with her newborn son. The grandmothers are there, some aunts are there, some other elderly female relatives may be there with her as well. They're waiting, waiting for that moment where they're told it's time for the Berit Milah ceremony to begin and to bring in the baby.

Now, you would expect the mother to be bringing in her own child, but that's not our custom. The mother stays put. In the old days, the mother was still considered weak and regaining her strength. She was probably even in bed and she wouldn't even be standing up. Nowadays, the women are much more agile and much more energetic and they can get up and be there, but it's also possibly emotionally disturbing to have the mother of the child there witnessing her son going through the procedure of a Berit Milah, so the custom has remained that the mother of the child is not there.

Rather, it's the grandmother that is given this job. The grandmothers, both the paternal grandmother and the maternal grandmother, are honored with the job, if you will, of bringing in the newborn child to present him for the Berit Milah. So for the first baby boy, it's usually the paternal grandmother; second baby boy, the maternal grandmother; then it could switch off like that, or it could be honored and given to other elderly women or other women as well, as the need may call for.

In any case, what happens? So the women have been preparing the child, making sure that he's dressed properly and he's laid carefully on a very, very soft, high, white pillow usually, to bring him in, makes it much more comfortable when the Milah is going on. When they're given the signal, the baby comes in, the grandmother will put on a white lace scarf over her head and draped down onto her shoulders, and this is a very old custom going back to Spain. This white lace scarf is called the mantilla, and it's an ancient custom in Spain, not only among the Jews, but among people in Spain among other religions as well.

And this is probably the only vestige of this Minhag that remains from Spain that women did over there for religious ceremonies that we still have among us, that the women are doing a custom, following a practice that was done in Spain and they're still doing it today, specifically with this white lace scarf, the mantilla, for a religious ceremony, in our case, for the Berit Milah.

The grandmother wears this, she comes in carefully. As she enters, the Kahal is singing Yigdal Elokim Hai, which represents the 13 tenets of faith as per HaRambam, Maimonides. We're bringing the boy to enter the faith and that's why it's appropriate to sing this. As that finishes off, everybody rises and starts singing together, "Barukh HaBa BeShem Ad-onai," welcome in the name of God, and the grandmother walks in all the way to the place of the Berit Milah and hands the child on the pillow, pillow and all, to the father of the child, the Abi HaBen, to begin the Berit Milah ceremony.

110.title: Saying VeHarah Af in a Whisper
110.text:
When the Hazzan recites Keri'at Shema, the custom is to recite the verse that begins VeHarah Af in a whisper. Hakham Shalom Hedaya, who was born in Halab in 1862, discussed this custom in his book of responsa that is entitled VeDibber Shalom. Here is a picture of the rabbi. He was responding to an anonymous rabbi who wanted to change this custom. The rabbi whom he was responding to suggested that the Hazzan should read that verse out loud as well. His reasoning was that everyone should hear the words of rebuke in this verse, which states that if we were to engage in idol worship, that HaShem would become angry with us, so rain would not fall, and the land would not give produce, and we would be forced to leave the Land of Israel.

Hakham Shalom disagreed with the idea of changing this custom. He explained that we should always make an effort to reconcile customs that were accepted by previous rabbis, even those customs that seem to contradict the law or are surprising in some way. And he cited sources, such as the Maharam Padua from Italy in the 16th century, and the Sedeh Hemed from Jerusalem and Hebron in the 19th century, who emphasized the importance of investigating the origins of customs and finding support to justify customs that were accepted by a community.

In this case, Hakham Shalom said that the Hazzan says this verse in a whisper, so it won't appear as if he is wishing bad upon his enemies, and that if he says it quietly, it will be less likely for him to intend it as a curse against specific people. He also cited another reason, based on concerns raised by the Gemara in Masekhet Megillah regarding the reading and translating of curses, warnings, and punishments. There, the Gemara said it could possibly cause the people to lose heart, since the punishments are so harsh, or to only observe the Missvot out of fear, as opposed to truly appreciating the Missvot as something that is good.

The Gemara did not consider it a concern when reading the Torah. Hakham Shalom explained that it is not a concern with regards to Torah portions that are only read once a year, but it is a concern with regards to Keri'at Shema that is read every morning and evening.

At the end of the responsa, Hakham Shalom pointed out that on Tish'ah BeAb, it is customary to read the verse that begins VeHarah Af out loud, since that is an exceptional case, one day a year, when we want to acknowledge the justification of HaShem's judgment of our sins. So our custom of saying VeHarah Af in a whisper all year round, except on the night and morning of Tish'ah BeAb, was documented by Hakham Shalom Hedaya in his book of responsa VeDibber Shalom.

Interestingly, Hakham Shalom Hedaya's son-in-law was Rabbi Jacob Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom, who was the chief rabbi of the Syrian community in Brooklyn from 1933 until he passed away in 1994.

111.title: Customs of the 'Aliyot
111.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are going to continue with our discussions dealing with the Mesader, this is part three, the one empowered to giving out the honors and the Missvot in the synagogue, the 'Aliyot, and the Petihah, and the Gilyan. We mentioned the Petihah and the Gilyan, and before I begin the discussion of the 'Aliyot, I did want to mention a custom which is not practiced today, certainly not in Brooklyn as far as I know, in the other Halabi communities there also is also not practiced, but it was practiced in Halab and in 67th Street at the Magen David.

This is an honor that is called Menawaleh. Menawaleh comes from the Arabic root Nawala, which means to hand over. Now what this honor was, as I mentioned previously, the one who is honored with opening the Hekhal with the Petihah is also responsible for taking out the proper Sefer Torah and handing it to the person who has the honor of the Gilyan, of carrying the Sefer. There was another honor that was called Menawaleh, where the person who was given this honor is the one not the one who opens the Hekhal, someone who has the Petihah, and then this person who gets the Menawaleh is in charge of taking the Sefer Torah out and giving it to the one who is carrying the Sefer.

Now, this was probably only done on the high holidays, when they sold the Missvot, maybe in the they also sold them in the Shalosh Regalim, I'm not sure, but we know that this was done in Halab in certain synagogues, and only during certain times of the year, usually the high holidays. We know because we have this the records from 67th Street for the Magen David, and you have the honor of Menawaleh. It's not practiced today, but I think it's important to know our history.

Now we're going to continue talking about the 'Aliyot and the customs of our customs regarding the 'Aliyot, and we'll begin with that we follow Maran in Siman Kof-Lamed-Heh, where he speaks about that the Kohen goes up first, then the Levi, then the Yisrael, MiPene Darkhe Shalom. The first 'Aliyah, first of anything, always was the most important. So there is a discussion and there are other opinions that the biggest Hakham, the most important person in the Kahal would be the one to get the first 'Aliyah, but we follow the custom that it's Kohen, Levi, Yisrael.

The most important 'Aliyah for the Kahal, based on the kabbalistic tradition and the Sefirot, is 'Aliyat Shishi. Now this 'Aliyah is usually reserved for a Talmid Hakham, or the Hakham of the Kehillah, or someone who is learned. A very important person that's learned is the one who goes up 'Aliyat Shishi. You don't give Shishi to anybody in the Kahal, it's reserved for the learned people.

The 'Aliyah of Maftir, based on the Kabbalah, which we follow in this case, is the most important 'Aliyah for someone who has to make the prayer for the deceased, what the Ashkenazim call yahrzeit, what we call Ma'ad, he has to make the Hashkabah. And here again, it's up to the Mesader to understand that there are even when it comes to Azkarot, there are priorities. Someone is within 30 days, okay, that's takes precedence over someone who's within a year. If someone is within a year and there's somebody who's today they had a parent passed away many, many years ago, so obviously someone within the year would take priority. Again, but it's all Shikul HaDa'at, it's all up to the discretion of the Mesader, but he has to have a logic behind his actions.

It's important that the one going up Maftir reads the Haftarah. It's very important. I'm not going to get into the halakhic issues, that's beyond the scope of this video, of this series, but it's important that he read the Haftarah. Similarly, it's important that the one going up Mashlim says the Kaddish. If somebody doesn't want to say the Kaddish, for whatever reason, his parents are Makpid, superstitious, whatever you want for whatever reason he doesn't want to say the Kaddish, he shouldn't go up Mashlim. He should go for another 'Aliyah.

Following Shishi on Shabbat, we add 'Aliyot. It's called Rake. Rake means Gam 'Oleh, Gam 'Oleh. The reason we do this, because there are Semahot, Ken Yirbu, in the synagogue and we have to, we need extra 'Aliyot. So we try, if there's room, to have a new reading for every 'Oleh, but if it's not possible then you could, custom is to repeat a very short piece after Shishi. So you have Shishi, then Rake, Gam 'Oleh, Gam 'Oleh as many as needed, followed by the Samukh, which is also an 'Aliyah which we sell on the High Holidays. And usually when it's Samukh, so the someone, the Karoz HaMesader will say, "Samukh!" So for two reasons: number one, so if there's many 'Aliyot and people are, maybe they go outside for a period, they can they know they have to come back for the new reading. And also because the Somekh, which we will discuss in a later video, the one standing next to the Kore, instructing him to the stops, he knows that this is the last 'Aliyah before the Mashlim. That's what it means Samukh. Samukh means close by to the Mashlim, Samukh LaMashlim. We call it 'Aliyat Samukh. On the High Holidays, we want to add 'Aliyot, so with sales, so we'll say Somekh and Samukh, but generally on Shabbat we only have Samukh.

Now, the it's important for the Mesader to understand, if you recall in our last video, we spoke about the how to prioritize the Semahot: Hatan, Abi HaBen, Abi HaBat, Bar Missvah, Arus. And the same thing applies not only when it comes to Petihah, but it comes to the 'Aliyot. So the 'Aliyot also: Hatan would go before a Abi HaBat or a Bar Missvah, and that's generally how it's broken up based on the priority of the type of occasion. So we will continue in our next video discussing customs of the 'Olim LaTorah. Kol Tub.

112.title: The Two Chairs of the Milah
112.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles. Berit Milah ceremony. So, in our last episode, we spoke about the grandmother bringing in the child, handing it to the Abi HaBen, the father of the newborn boy. So, the father of the newborn boy is standing there, wearing a Talet, not Tefillin, only Talet is our Minhag, as well as the Mohel is there, he does not wear a Talet or Tefillin, and the Sandak, we'll translate as the godfather, if you will, and he is the person that sits on the chair.

Okay, there are two chairs if you notice. There's one chair over here, and another chair over here. This larger, more ornate chair, particularly this particular one over here is part of the display of the Sephardic Heritage Museum that is housed in the Bet Yosef synagogue in Deal, and this is an older chair that comes from Cairo, Egypt. This is a simpler chair, and in the Halabi tradition, there are two chairs. There is one chair designated for Eliyahu HaNabi, and one chair that is designated for the Sandak. The chair that is designated for Eliyahu HaNabi, nobody sits on, based upon tradition. Eliyahu HaNabi himself arrives for every Milah, and this is where he would be sitting to the right of the Sandak.

The Sandak is the godfather who sits in this special chair, and he holds the newborn when the Mohel does the circumcision. So the Sandak is wearing a Talet, the Abi HaBen, the father of the child, is wearing a Talet, and the Mohel is not wearing a Talet. And of course, it's not our Minhag for any of these three individuals to be wearing Tefillin.

When the father of the child accepts his son in his arms from the grandmother, he says a number of Pesukim which appear in the Siddurim. And when we get up to the actual text of the Milah, we'll discuss all the Pesukim as well, which are, which Pesukim we do say, which we do not say, which have been introduced at a later date, and by whom and why. And after the general Pesukim, the father of the son will say "Shema Yisrael Ad-onai Elokenu Ad-onai Ehad," which everybody will repeat, followed by, in traditional, a traditional tune of Attah Ahubi, which everybody repeats, Pesukim of "Ana Ad-onai Hoshi'ah Na," "Ana Ad-onai Hasslihah Na," and some more verses.

After those verses, the father of the child will say the Berakhah of the Milah, which is: "Asher Kiddeshanu BeMissvotav VeSivvanu LeHakhniso BiBrito Shel Abraham Abinu." At that point, everybody responds: "Keshem SheNikhnas LaBerit Kakh Yikanes LeTorah ULeMissvot ULeHuppah ULeMa'asim Tobim VeKhen Yehi Rasson VeNomar Amen."

Then they carry the baby, okay, generally they will appoint the father to be doing that, together with the Mohel inside, bring the baby, place it down on this particular chair over here for Eliyahu HaNabi and say, "Zeh Kisse Shel Eliyahu HaNabi Malakh HaBerit Zakhur LeTob." According to some traditions, a Humash open to Parashat Pinhas would be placed on this chair. It seems that there were two specific, two customs in Halab itself: some of those who put a Humash open to Pinhas on the chair, others who did not. And there were obviously various traditions based upon which synagogue you were in and which Hakhamim were there. Some remember it this way, some remember it another way. In either case, it's not incumbent if a person does it or not.

The main thing is that in Halab, they were specific and particular to have two separate chairs, as opposed to other communities outside of Syria, who would only have one chair, which would be designated as Kisse Shel Eliyahu HaNabi and also the same chair that the Sandak would sit on. So, to recap: Halab, two chairs, and the Abi HaBen and the Sandak would be wearing Taletot, and Lo Tefillin.

113.title: Counting the 248 Words of Shema
113.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that since there are only 245 words in Keri'at Shema, we repeat the words "HaShem Elokekhem Emet" at the end for a total of 248 words, which correspond with the 248 limbs that a person has. However, Maran actually wrote that the Hazzan concludes Shema with "HaShem Elokekhem Emet," and then repeats "HaShem Elokekhem Emet." Adding the word Emet before repeating "HaShem Elokekhem Emet" led to some confusion as to how to count the 248 words.

According to the Radbaz, an authority who was born in Spain at the end of the 15th century, and eventually became the chief rabbi of Egypt, and according to the Maharikash, who was a student of the Radbaz, and also became the chief rabbi of Egypt, the Hazzan recites the first Emet in a whisper, so it's not part of the count of 248. It's actually part of the continuation with VeYassib, or with VeEmunah in 'Arbit. The Hida, in his book Mahzik Berakhah, cites an opinion that the Hazzan doesn't say the first Emet at all. Only the congregants answer "Emet" when the Hazzan finishes Shema, and then only the Hazzan repeats the words "HaShem Elokekhem Emet."

This custom was also recorded by the Shalme Sibbur, by the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer, and by Ribbi Hayyim, in a Shitah of his own, in his book on the customs of the Land of Israel, entitled Eress Hayyim. But according to Maran, it seems that the Hazzan does say the first Emet out loud. Some explain that having 249 words is fine, as long as it's not less than 248, while others explain that the last Emet is not part of the count; it goes with the continuation of VeYassib in Shahrit, or with VeEmunah in 'Arbit. And according to the Zibhe Sedek, and the Ben Ish Hai, who are both authorities from Baghdad in the 19th century, the Hazzan does recite the first Emet out loud.

Growing up in the community in the 1970s and '80s, no Hazzan ever said the first Emet out loud. Either they said it quietly, like the Radbaz and the Maharikash, or not at all, like the Hida and the Kaf HaHayyim. In fact, Ribbi Hayyim, in a Shitah of his own, suggested that the custom of not saying it at all is actually a custom that predates the rulings of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. He also wrote that the congregants should wait for the Hazzan to finish Shema and answer "Emet" out loud together. He specified that waiting quietly before the word Emet is not an interruption. The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer wrote this as well.

If the Hazzan finishes Shema before you, or you are not praying with a Minyan, you still say "Emet," and then repeat the words "HaShem Elokekhem Emet." And according to Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alav HaShalom, if the Hazzan is not so knowledgeable, and he doesn't realize that he is repeating the words "HaShem Elokekhem Emet" on behalf of the congregation, the congregants should repeat the words "HaShem Elokekhem Emet" to themselves, before continuing with VeYassib in Shahrit, or with VeEmunah in 'Arbit.

114.title: Customs of Petihat HaHekhal
114.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed in our recent videos the Minhagim concerning the Mesader. We will now proceed and discuss the Minhagim about the Petihat HaHekhal. We have completed Tefillat Shahrit with the Kaddish Titkabbal. By this time, the Mesader has invited someone to be to open the Hekhal, the Petihah, someone to carry, a young youngster to put on the Rimmonim. Everything is in place. The Kahal, after Kaddish Titkabbal, will begin Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at, and the one who is honored with Petihah will open the Hekhal. Please note that he always opens from left to right the Parokhet. It's very important.

Now, he opens the Hekhal, and the one who has Gilyan will be standing next to the open Hekhal. He will take the Rimmonim off, give them to the young man who will be putting on the Rimmonim. Okay, now we'll step to this. He'll open the Sefer to make sure that this is the Sefer that's correctly designated to be read this Shabbat, and he'll step to the side. Now, the Hakham or the Hazzan will begin saying the Berikh Shemeh and the prayer for the Israeli Defense Forces. The Berikh Shemeh is said while the Sefer Torah is open, as to my recollection of the custom growing up. There may be other communities which insist that the Sefer Torah is closed while saying Berikh Shemeh. As far as I remember all my life, it was always open a little bit, and that's how we do it in Ades as well.

So, he will say Berikh Shemeh, followed by the prayer for the Hayyale Seba HaHaganah LeYisrael, which is generally said amongst all Kehillot. And following that, a custom which really, I would say, is relatively recent, maybe 30 years or so, COVID obviously, but there's a prayer for sick people. We're asking for Refuah Shelemah during the Petihat HaHekhal. This is a recent custom. Growing up, I never recalled that they had people with lists, people would come forward to the Hekhal and tell the Hakham Peloni Bat Pelonit or Ben Pelonit. We never had that. I don't recall it. Maybe if there was a Hakham that was in the hospital that our whole Kahal would pray for him at this time, but to do it for the Hamon 'Am, and then afterwards read all the names, and say "Shabbat Hi MiLiz'ok URefuah Kerobah Labo," being that it's Shabbat, we shouldn't be praying or ask for the Refuah, but Refuah Kerobah Labo. There'll be a Refuah Shelemah soon. So again, I spoke to my friends in Argentina who are Gabba'im, and also agreed that this was not done 20, 30, 40 years ago. It's a recent development.

At anyway, the they finished saying the Berikh Shemeh. The one who has Petihah will close the Sefer and give it to the one who has Gilyan. Always when you're transferring a Sefer from one to the other, it's always closed. It's just much easier to transfer when it's closed. And the one who has the Rimmonim will come put the Rimmonim on. Generally, they try to take it out from the Hekhal when we say "Se'enah URe'enah Benot Siyyon BaMelekh Shelomoh Ba'Atarah." Put the Rimmonim. And we never lower the Torah if the child is short. We never lower the Torah so he could be able to put the Rimmonim. If anything, we have to pick him up, and he has to come and put the Rimmonim on.

Now, at this point, the Kahal has already said Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at until the Petihat HaHekhal, and it is customary Ashre Ha'Am. In many Kehillot, and that's the way it was in Halab from my conversation with the elder statesmen, and in Israel and in Argentina, they would the whole Kahal will begin "Ashre Ha'Am SheKakhah Lo," and the one who has Gilyan will start moving with the Sefer Torah open. If you notice, his right hand is on the right side of the Sefer, and his left hand is on the bottom of the Sefer. That's the correct way to carry a Sefer Torah. And they will sing Ashre Ha'Am. Sometimes there'll be a Pizmon, and they'll wait until the Pizmon is over, then they'll put the Sefer Torah on the Tebah.

In the 1960s, we had the privilege of having an esteemed Hazzan, a Hakham, Hakham Refael Nadaf, an illustrious Hazzan, who introduced a new liturgical custom where Ashre Ha'Am and Gadelu, these two Pesukim, are sung in a beautiful melody by the Hazzan. The Kahal will answer in like, both Pesukim. And following those two Pesukim, the whole Kahal will begin Romemu, Romemu. Start to walk down the Sefer Torah. By the way, if you notice the what's happening there, Rabbi, if you noticed the Hekhal after the Torah leaves, he closes the Hekhal completely. That's our custom, not to leave it half-open. He closes it and now the one who has the 'Inyan is walking, someone will be walking before the Sefer with the Yad pointing the place and he will be singing the appropriate melody, the appropriate text which we'll deal with next week. He will get to the Hekhal, will close the Sefer, put it on the Tebah, and that is the end of the ritual of the Petihat HaHekhal. And now we will begin to talk in our next video certain textual differences in the Petihah and about the 'Aliyot. Shalom UBerakhah.

115.title: Pizmonim and the Father's Pesukim
115.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: Life cycles. Until now, we've been talking about the Berit Milah and everything that precedes the actual circumcision ceremony. Now, we can basically break up that circumcision ceremony into a few sections. Section number one will be the songs followed by the bringing in of the child and the introductory Pesukim, verses, that are recited by the Abi HaBen, the father of the child, and as well as the responses by those present. The next section can actually be the Berakhot of the Berit Milah between the father and the Mohel, and then, after the actual circumcision happens, the Berakhot said by the Hakham or the Hakhamim of HaGefen, and Besamim, and Asher Kiddash, and the naming of the child. So we're going to break up the next few videos, each one dealing with one segment. We're going to start with this first segment: Pizmonim, bringing in the child, and the Pesukim said by the father.

So, as we've mentioned in the past, those gathered and present start singing Pizmonim. We know the Pizmonim for the Berit Milah very well, they all appear in our traditional Pizmon book, the red book, Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah. The Pizmonim for Berit Milah are on pages 405 through 413. Generally, the order that we generally use here in Brooklyn: we'll sing Yehi Shalom BeHelenu, followed by E'erokh Mahalal Libbi, followed by Ata Ahubi, and then by Mah Tob UMah Na'im. After we sing those songs a few times, and maybe some of the other songs, we get a signal that the baby is almost ready to come in, we sing Yigdal Elokim Hai. Yigdal Elokim Hai is an old piece of poetry that basically proclaims the 13 principles of faith of Judaism, and when that is finished, the Milah is ready to start.

The grandmother brings in the baby, walks him all the way up to hand him to the father of the child, while everybody sings: "Barukh HaBa BeShem Ad-onai, Berakhnukhem MiBet Ad-onai," "Barukh HaBa BeShem Ad-onai, Berakhnukhem MiBet Ad-onai." Baby is there now. Father, the Abi HaBen, is holding baby in his arms, the Sandak is sitting in his seat, ready to take the baby when it's time, the Mohel is there, ready to do his job, everybody is ready, and the Abi HaBen, the father of the child, starts reciting Pesukim.

Now, before the recitation of those Pesukim, the Minhag in Halab, as well as in Cairo and as well as in other places, was to recite at that point in the very beginning the Mizmor: "Shir HaMa'alot Ashre Kol Yere Ad-onai HaHolekh BiDrakhav Yegia' Kappekha Ki Tokhel Ashrekha VeTob Lakh," etc. In recent decades, we've seen this Mizmor move to the end of the Milah ceremony after the naming of the child, based upon various rabbis and Siddurim that were published in Jerusalem, and rabbis that came from Jerusalem, but our true Minhag is to say it in the very beginning, and hopefully with the dissemination of these videos we'll see a resurgence of our original custom of saying this Mizmor in the beginning.

Now, the father says the Pesukim, we'll see him in the Kol Ya'akob Siddur on page 511, as well as many other Siddurim: "Sas Anokhi 'Al Imratekha," followed by "Zibhe Elokim," then "Hetibah BiRssonekha," "Az Tahposs Zibhe Sedek 'Olah VeKhalil," and then everybody responds: "Az Ya'alu 'Al Mizbahakha Parim." Then the father: "Im Eshkahekh Yerushalayim Tishkah Yemini, Tidbak Leshoni LeHikki Im Lo Ezkerekhi, Im Lo A'aleh Et Yerushalayim," and everybody: "'Al Rosh Simhati." The father then says the Shema' Yisrael Pasuk. He says it, all present respond in kind.

Then he sings HaShem Melekh. HaShem Melekh is sung to the tune of Ata Ahubi, and only to the tune of Ata Ahubi, and not like you'll see some people today want to sing one verse to one song, one verse to another song. The true Minhag is to sing both verses to Ata Ahubi, which is the flagship Halabi Pizmon for Berit Milah. "Amonai Melekh." Says it, Kahal repeats it, he says it again, the Kahal repeats it again, then he says "Ana Amonai Hoshi'ah Na," the people repeat, "Ana Amonai Hoshi'ah Na," they repeat, "Ana Amonai Hasslihah Na," people repeat, "Ana Amonai Hasslihah Na," and the people repeat. Father then says, "Ashre Tibhar UTkareb Yishkon Hasserekha," and everybody responds, "Nisbe'ah BeTub Betekha Kedosh Hekhalekha." We're now ready for the second part of the Berit Milah ceremony.

116.title: Looking Behind Before the 'Amidah
116.text:
The custom of many in our community is to turn to the left and to the right and to look behind us when taking three steps back before the 'Amidah, while waving our hands like this. This custom was common in the Middle East at least since the 17th century. Hakham Abraham Hamwey documented this as the custom of Halab in the 19th century in his Selihot book that he called Bet El. The book also includes the Shahrit prayer, and in the laws before the 'Amidah, he wrote, "That which is customary in our land, Aram Soba, that is flowing with milk," alluding to the common name for the city, Halab, "and in most places, when they stand up to pray before the 'Amidah, they turn behind themselves and motion with their hands to those behind them that they should come in front of them out of respect." And then he continued that he thinks that the reason for this custom is to make peace with each other and to ask forgiveness from one another in order to have love and brotherhood like one person, causing the prayer to be accepted.

And then Hakham Abraham Hamwey cited the 18th-century book Siah Yisshak from Livorno, who cited the 17th-century Me'orot Natan, who documented this custom as the practice of all Middle Eastern Jews, and attributed a mystical purpose to the custom. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, who was born in Halab in 1893 and lived there until he moved to Jerusalem in 1935, also mentioned this custom in his book on the customs of Aleppo. He wrote that when the congregation gets up to pray the 'Amidah, they send a message of peace to each other by moving their head or their hands, and then they begin the 'Amidah. Interestingly, in a footnote appended by his grandson, Hakham Rahamim Sha'yo, he cites the importance of loving your fellow Jews according to the Arizal before the very beginning of Shahrit in the Kenis.

And he also quoted Ribbi Hayyim Palachi, a 19th-century authority from Izmir, Turkey, who also recorded this custom in his book Kaf HaHayyim, where he explained that it's to foster unity in the congregation before the 'Amidah, and he also specified that it was customary before Shahrit, Minhah, and 'Arbit. Derekh Eress, a compendium of the customs of the Jews of Halab that was published in 1990, also quoted Rab Hayyim Dayeh, who understood the custom as asking permission from those behind you to pray in front of them.

We also find this custom by the Ben Ish Hai from Baghdad in the 19th century. He wrote that the custom of the Sefaradim before the 'Amidah is to turn their faces a little behind themselves and motion with their hands to those behind them or next to them. And he says that the reason for this custom is to act like the angels, who give permission to each other to praise God, which shows unity and brotherhood between them, so that we all as one accept God's reign upon us, which is a much greater praise of HaShem, since it's done with unity and with love. The Ben Ish Hai also pointed out that according to the opinion that this custom has a mystical purpose, one should practice it even when no one is next to him or behind him.

So this Middle Eastern custom of looking at those behind us and waving our hands before the 'Amidah dates back to at least the 17th century and continued into the 19th and 20th centuries in Halab, Turkey, and Baghdad. And many continue this custom today in our community in New York and New Jersey. It's meant to show respect and to foster love and unity among the congregants before reciting our personal prayer in front of HaShem. It also has a mystical purpose according to some Mekubbalim. Therefore, we should maintain this well-documented tradition of our forefathers, fulfilling the popular phrase "Minhag Abotenu BeYadenu."

117.title: Mi Lo Yira'akha and Attah Hor'eta
117.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the recent videos about the Mesader, the one in charge of giving out the honors, and last week's, last video we did a demonstration of taking the Sefer Torah out of the Hekhal according to our customs and bringing it to the Tebah. We've had some very interesting feedback and comments, we appreciate it. I did want to convey two of them which I feel are important.

One from a very seasoned Mesader, and he spoke to me and told me, "You know, I was very particular, especially when there's guests in the synagogue, to give very detailed instructions to the one who has the Petihah and the people carrying the Sefer, so there's no confusion, there's no awkwardness, there's no, God forbid, we don't want to see anybody embarrassed. And they're not familiar with the intricacies of the Minhagim. We have to tell them exactly where to stand, when to open the Hekhal, what to take. We tell them in advance so that they're comfortable and know exactly what to do and when to do it. The people carrying the Sefer, where to stand, the one who's giving, putting the Rimmonim on, where to stand. And this way everything is done in a very efficient manner without any confusion."

The second comment regarding the closing of the Hekhal, in our last video we closed the Hekhal, obviously, and the custom is to close the Hekhal and not leave it open after we finished the Petihah. But there is a custom in a couple of Kehillot, namely Shaare Zion, and I was told also in Beth Torah, where the Hekhal, the doors are left open, but the Parokhet is closed. Now, this can be done, certainly in the beautiful Hekhal of Shaare Zion, where the doors slide up and down, so it doesn't interfere, and it looks, it's aesthetically very pleasing, where you have a beautiful Parokhet, and you only close the doors after you bring back the Sefarim. It's done also in Beth Torah, that's what I was told. Now, this can't be done with every Hekhal, because certain Hekhalim, if you leave them open, the doors interfere with the seating maybe of the rabbi, the Hazzan on the platform. Possibly it's just not aesthetically pleasing. Also, it's very important that the Parokhet is behind the doors and you can close the Parokhet. So, it's a custom I did want to bring to your attention, even though it doesn't apply in all cases, but it's important to know.

A couple of points I wanted to make to round out and complete the subject of the Petihah, and hopefully we'll go on to the Sefer Torah in our next video, are textual variants when it comes to Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at, which is found on page 284 in the very, most recent edition of Kol Ya'akob. As you know, after Kaddish Titkabbal, the Kahal breaks out singing, "Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at," these eight Pesukim, which there are reasons why there are eight, we won't go into it now. And as we sing it, we have a Pasuk after "Berikh Shemeh DeMareh 'Alma," "Kumah Ad-onai VeYafussu Oyebekha." Now, that's not the entire Pasuk. In BeMidbar, the Pasuk begins with, "VaYehi BiNsoa' HaAron VaYomer Moshe, Kumah Ad-onai VeYafussu Oyebekha." But that first half of the Pasuk is not printed in Kol Ya'akob and indeed is not said in the community in New York.

Now, it's important when we talk about customs to understand what we say and sometimes you have to understand what we don't say. Because you will encounter it in other Kehillot outside, other Syrian Kehillot outside of Brooklyn. For instance, in Israel, in Argentina, it's a very big Kehillah, they say, "VaYehi BiNsoa' HaAron," and it's reflected also in their Siddur Sukkat David. So, we do say it outside of the community in Brooklyn. For some reason, the Brooklyn community does not say the first half of this Pasuk. I don't have a reason as to why, just want to let you know what is done.

Finally, we sing Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at. It's an old prayer, seems to have come from Sepharad, because we see it quoted even by Abudarham and other Rishonim, which is quite, you know, five, six hundred years ago. But if you look at, and we noticed Sefaradim came to Halab in the 16th century for the most part, if you look at the Siddur, what's called the Mahzor Aram Soba, and if you look at Petihah of Shabbat, taking out the Sefer Torah, it begins with, "Mi Lo Yira'akha Melekh HaGoyim." Completely different prayer. Now, we don't say that today, and in fact in Brooklyn nobody even knows this prayer exists. In Argentina they don't say it. But this was the Musta'arabi, the local Aleppian community before Sefaradim came. This was their prayer. In fact, up until the middle of the 20th century, when the Kenisat HaGdolah was still run with using the Musta'arabi customs, it was recorded, the customs were recorded by the famous Hakham Salim Zafrani, 'Alav HaShalom, he said they used to say Mi Lo Yira'akha. They never said Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at.

Again, it's important that when we're discussing customs we know all the customs of the Syrian community, even from Halab. So you have one custom which said Mi Lo Yira'akha all the time, one custom which said Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at all the time, every Shabbat. And that is what prevailed once they left Halab and went all over the world, that's what we say. But there is a third custom, and that is that we do say Mi Lo Yira'akha on Shabbatot where we take out three Sefarim. Now this happens on Simhat Torah, it possibly happens on Shabbat Hanukkah if it's Rosh Hodesh, or Shabbat HaHodesh if it's Rosh Hodesh before Pesah. And they will, after they sing Attah Hor'eta LaDa'at, when they take all the Sefarim out in the hands of the people who are carrying them, the Hazzan or the Hakham will begin Mi Lo Yira'akha in a beautiful tune, and the Kahal, there are certain places where the Kahal responds. We do that in Ades. They don't do it in Brooklyn and Argentina, but it's recorded in the Sefer Minhagim written by Hakham Abraham Ades, compiled by him, called Derekh Eress. He records that the custom did exist in certain Kehillot to say Mi Lo Yira'akha when we take out three Sefarim. Kol Tub.

118.title: The Berakhot of the Milah
118.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: lifecycles, Berit Milah. In the last video, we discussed the opening of the Berit Milah ceremony and the Pesukim the Abi HaBen, the father, would say. Now we're up to part two: the actual Berakhot for the Milah, the Berakhot said by the Abi HaBen and the Berakhah said by the Mohel himself.

So, first thing is, before they make the Berakhot, we're seeing nowadays that people tell the Mohel, "I hereby appoint you to be the Mohel." This was never our Minhag to publicly make such a statement. If the Mohel is there, obviously he's the only Mohel that's there because the father of the child already told him in advance, "Please be here, this place, this time, with your tools, ready to do the job." Everybody knows he's the Mohel that was appointed by the father. So there's no need for such a public announcement, and as I've mentioned, this was not our custom to do such a thing, and it's not necessary. Number one.

Number two: we now get to the Berakhot. What is the order of the Berakhot? Now, most people will think that since we are generally adherent and loyal to Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo, Shulhan 'Arukh, we would follow the order in Shulhan 'Arukh, and that would mean that first the Mohel would make the Berakhah of 'Al HaMilah, and then the father of the child would make two Berakhot, LeHakhniso and Sheheheyanu. But this is not the case. We have an ancient Minhag, a Minhag that predates the writing of Shulhan 'Arukh, the Minhag of the Musta'arabim, which means the ancient custom or the old custom of the native Jews of the Middle East before the arrival of those who came out of Spain and before the influx of those Jews and the input of the Shulhan 'Arukh. And the Minhag is as such: that the father will make the Berakhah of LeHakhniso, and after that the Mohel will make the Berakhah of 'Al HaMilah, and then the father makes the Berakhah of Sheheheyanu.

And now here is the order. So, first, the father says, "Yodu LaAd-onai Hasdo." He says, "BiRshut Morai VeRabotai." Those present respond, "Shamayim." The father makes the Berakhah: "Barukh Attah Ad-onai Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam, Asher Kiddeshanu BeMissvotav VeSivvanu LeHakhniso BiBrito Shel Abraham Abinu." At that point, everybody present responds: "Keshem SheHikhnasto LaBerit, Kakh Takhnisehu LaTorah VeLaMissvot VeLaHuppah ULeMa'asim Tobim." All this is done while the father is holding on to the child.

At that point, the Mohel takes the child from the father, moves it over to the chair that we mentioned before, that chair that has been set aside for Eliyahu HaNabi. He places the child on that chair, and he says, "Zeh HaKisse Shel Eliyahu HaNabi, Malakh HaBerit Zakhur LeTob." He then lifts the child up from that chair and places the child in the lap of the Sandak, the Sandak who is sitting in the other chair. Now, who is the Sandak? The Sandak, the Minhag in Halab was the Sandak was always the paternal grandfather. Didn't make a difference, it was the first boy, the second boy, the third boy, the fourth boy, it was always the paternal grandfather. In almost every other place outside of Aleppo, the Minhag was the first boy would be the paternal grandfather, the second boy the maternal grandfather, and then either they could switch back and forth like that or they could give it out to others. Generally, it was not given to anybody but a grandfather; it was not given to an uncle, it was not given to a Hakham, generally it remained in the family in that sense, as an honor to the grandfathers.

Now, the Sandak now has the child on his lap, the Mohel is ready to do the Milah. Keep in mind, the child is wrapped up, the Mohel has to unwrap him and prepare the area to do the circumcision ceremony. At that point, the Mohel will recite a few Pesukim while he's preparing. Those Pesukim, which generally do not appear in our Siddurim, they are: "BeMakhelot Barekhu Elokim Ad-onai MiMkor Yisrael," followed by "BiFro'a Pera'ot BeYisrael BeHitnadeb 'Am Barekhu Ad-onai," and finally "Isfu Li Hasiday Korete Beriti 'Ale Zabah." And we know of these Pesukim because they appear in the book Siah Yisshak from Hakham Yisshak Alfiah.

After those Pesukim have been recited and the child is ready for the Milah to happen, immediately the Mohel makes the Berakhah of 'Al HaMilah. He says: "BiRshut Morai VeRabotai," everybody responds "Shamayim," then he says: "Barukh Attah Ad-onai Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam Asher Kiddeshanu BeMissvotav VeSivvanu 'Al HaMilah." He does the Milah, they turn to the father immediately to say the Berakhah of Sheheheyanu, who makes the Berakhah: "Barukh Attah Ad-onai Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam Sheheheyanu VeKiyemanu VeHiggi'anu LaZeman HaZeh."

At that point, break out into song. What is the song? The Minhag Halab, the way we practice it here in New York, and the way it's been practiced in most places in the world, the song is Yahon El Sur: "Yahon El Sur BeHemlato." But there are other Halabi communities as well as the Minhag of Damascus, they sing a different song, it's "HaYeled HaZeh Zakhah LiBrito." Our Minhag here at least in New York is Yahon El Sur. And at that point, of course, the Mohel holds up a piece of gauze with the blood on it for everybody to see, everybody knows the Milah was done, and a drop of blood at the very least came out, usually more than just a drop.

Now, what else goes on at this point? In recent years, we're seeing a few different things. We're seeing either the recitation of Yag Middot, which is "Ad-onai, Ad-onai, El Rahum VeHannun," or somebody blowing the Shofar, or something even newer that they distribute cards like this. "A wonderful prayer and remedy" is what they say in the back in English. And it says this is a prayer to say while the child is crying right after the Milah is done. So, all three of these things: Yag Middot, Shofar, and prayer from the card, none of these things are our Minhag. We've never done them before, we don't do them. The Yag Middot and the Shofar were instituted strictly in the time when there is a great calamity in the city, and only then at the discretion of the Hakhamim for such a thing to happen. As far as the cards, it's a new custom, seems to have crept up in recent years, not based in anything of antiquity or even in an old Minhag of any Sephardic community. And at that point, the Milah ceremony itself is done. We then move into part three, where we get into other Berakhot.

119.title: Seder VeTashlikh and the Fish
119.text:
It is customary to recite Seder VeTashlikh on the first day of Rosh HaShanah, after Minhah, before sunset. The main part of Seder VeTashlikh consists of the last three verses from the book of Mikhah, which we recite three times. The end of the second verse contains the phrase "VeTashlikh BiMessulot Yam Kol Hattotam," which describes HaShem throwing all of our sins into the depths of the sea. The earliest record of this custom is by HaRab Ya'akob ben Moshe Levi Molin, otherwise known as Maharil, who was born in Germany in the 14th century. It was also recorded by Rabbi Hayyim Vital, who was an important authority on Kabbalah in the 16th century. He described it at that time as the custom of the Ashkenazim. He wrote that it was a nice custom and he also explained its mystical significance. Rabbi Hayyim Vital was a very influential Mekubbal who lived in the land of Israel and in Damascus. Since his time, Seder VeTashlikh became an accepted custom throughout the Middle East as well.

And the Maharil associated this custom with a Midrash that taught that when Abraham and Yisshak were on their way to the 'Akedah, the Satan blocked their path with a large river. Abraham and Yisshak entered the river until the water was up to their necks. At that point, Abraham Abinu called out to HaShem for help. HaShem rebuked the Satan, and the Satan let Abraham and Yisshak continue on their way. According to the Zohar, the 'Akedah happened on the day of Rosh HaShanah. Therefore, it's appropriate to recite these verses near a body of water on that day. Rabbi Hayyim Vital taught that when we say the phrase "VeTashlikh BiMessulot Yam Kol Hattotam," we should wish that HaShem will throw all of our sins, together with the Satan or our evil inclination, into the depths of the heavenly sea.

Many have the custom to shake their clothing when they recite VeTashlikh, which is a symbolic gesture expressing one's desire to rid themselves of their sins. Interestingly, Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Mahzor Bet Din was against shaking one's clothing, since it leads many to think that they can rid themselves of sin just by shaking their clothing near a body of water on Rosh HaShanah. Of course, one has to truly repent in order to be forgiven for their sins.

In Rabbi Hayyim Vital's description of the custom, he wrote that it was customary to recite Tashlikh either near the ocean, or a spring, or near a fresh water well. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo in his customs of Aleppo wrote that in Halab, Tashlikh was recited at a well on the premises of the Great Synagogue. According to the Maharil, Tashlikh is recited at the sea or near a river. Some explain that another reason for reciting Tashlikh near a sea or a river is because there are fish there. Rabbi Yeshayah HaLevi Horowitz, a 16th-century authority who was born in Czechoslovakia and is famous for his work Shene Luhot HaBerit, and is often referred to as the Shelah or the Shelah HaKadosh, explained that we are like fish that could be caught in a net at any moment, which should inspire us to repent on Rosh HaShanah, which is the Day of Judgment. Hakham Abraham Hamwey quoted earlier sources that pointed out that on Yom Tob, it is not permissible to feed fish in a river. Since we are not allowed to catch fish on Yom Tob, we are not allowed to feed fish that were not caught before Yom Tob.

According to the book Keter Shem Tob by Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin, the custom of the famous Kabbalistic synagogue Bet El, which is in Jerusalem, was to recite Tashlikh on the first day of Rosh HaShanah, even when the first day of Rosh HaShanah fell on Shabbat. And according to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, this was also the custom in Halab. Hakham 'Obadia Yosef explained that when the first day of Rosh HaShanah falls on Shabbat, Tashlikh is only pushed to the second day of Rosh HaShanah if the water is not in an enclosed area, and the city does not have an 'Erub, and there's a possibility that some might carry their prayer books in a public area in order to recite Tashlikh.

Although the ceremony is often referred to as Tashlikh, many Sephardic sources refer to it as Seder VeTashlikh, which is how the word actually appears in the verse that we recite in the ceremony. The Keter Shem Tob and Hakham Abraham Hamwey both refer to the ceremony as Seder VeTashlikh. After reciting the verses from the book of Mikhah, it's customary to recite a prayer composed by Rabbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, who is commonly referred to as the Hida, an important Middle Eastern authority from the 18th century.

120.title: The Role of the Somekh
120.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have concluded our last video with the Sefer Torah being placed on the Tebah, we're ready to read it for the Kahal and discuss the Minhagim regarding how to break up the Parashah, 'Olim and how to invite the 'Oleh, and so on. But we'll hold off to our next video because I want to dedicate this video to a person who plays a crucial role at this juncture at the services. And I'm speaking about the Somekh.

The Somekh, which means the one who assists, he stands to the left of the Koreh. Koreh being the reader. Our custom is to call him the Koreh, not the Ba'al Koreh, he's a Koreh. The Koreh stands in the middle, the one who gets the 'Aliyah stands to his right, and there is a person called the Somekh who stands to his left. And what is the role of the Somekh? It's a very, very important role. First of all, he is the one who is interacting with the Mesader. As we mentioned, the Mesader knows how many occasions there are, how many people need 'Aliyot. So besides the first six 'Aliyot which it's pretty much predetermined where they begin and where they end, after Shishi until the end of the Parashah is where we add the extra 'Aliyot. We call them Rakkeh. Now, this Mesader knows how many Rakkeh is going to be. It's very important information for the Somekh to know because he has to know how to divide up the Parashah, he has to know the Halakhot, where you can stop, the customs, and how to divide up the Parashiyot for these Rakkeh, and he is the one to inform the reader, when the 'Oleh comes up, we're going to read until here, we're going to read until there. That's the job of the Somekh, so he has to interact with the Mesader.

The second job is to assist the Koreh with the Te'amim. In the event that the Koreh needs assistance or asks for assistance, that's not always the case, but sometimes he'll ask to be reminded, what are the Te'amim at the beginning of each Pasuk, or when is the Sof Pasuk. This is done through hand signals. It's not done verbally. The Halabi have a unique system of signals which they can convey the Te'amim of every Pasuk through these hand signals. We may dedicate a video to describe exactly the system. I know the Egyptians have their own system, a little bit different, the Egyptian Jews. And other communities, I'm sure, have, I've seen it by the Ashkenazim as well, have ways to convey to the reader the Te'amim. That's the job of the Somekh.

Thirdly, he has to be very attentive, and he has to know his Dikduk, because if there's going to be a mistake, he's got to be the first one to catch it and to have the reader go back. Now, I know it's popular sport in Halabi synagogues that, and it's a great thing because everybody's paying attention, and everybody knows their Dikduk, and there's a mistake made, and everybody or a lot of people chime in with the correction, which is very nice. However, the reader, by hearing voices from all over the place, he may not understand exactly what the mistake was. That's the job of the Somekh to tell him very clearly and quickly what the mistake was, and if he has to go back, from where.

Now, the next two responsibilities he has, which are related, it's not set in stone that it's his job, but more often than not, we'll see the Somekh is the one who does the Hashkabot, the prayers for the deceased, and the Mi SheBerakh. The prayers for the deceased on page 289 in Kol Ya'akob, Ashre Ish for men, Eshet Hayil for women, is said when the 'Oleh requests this prayer to be said. Generally, it's the first year of the person passing, when a relative goes up, or subsequent years the week of the passing, or on holidays, or on good occasions, and actually whenever the 'Oleh wants to make the prayer, he's permitted to make this prayer, and the Somekh will do it for him. And here we say the name of the person and, in our tradition, the name of the person and then the name of the person's mother. There is a special prayer for Hakhamim, it's found at the end of the Siddur, HaHokhmah MeAyin Timmasse, for great Hakhamim who serve the community in particular, where when the time of the year comes of their passing, we will make this prayer and the whole Kahal will be asked to stand.

Following the Hashkabot, the Somekh will do a Mi SheBerakh. Mi SheBerakh basically is when the one who gets 'Aliyah wants to donate to the synagogue or to any community organizations, and the Nusah is not printed in the book, but we say, "Mi SheBerakh Abotenu Abraham Yisshak VeYa'akob," He who blessed our forefathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, "Hu Yebarekh HaShem HaTob," He will bless the good name of, and he'll say his name, "SheMitnadeb," who donates X, and then he'll bless him: "LeHayye," bless him with a long, happy, healthy life, and then he'll say "LeHayye" and "Abiv," "LeHayye Immo," and you know, life of his parents, his spouse, children, siblings. And that's the Nusah of the Mi SheBerakh.

Now, it's very, very important that the Somekh knows the details of the person who went up to the Sefer. Like I said before, it's important for the Mesader to know the details who's going up, and if he should tell the Somekh, he should tell the Somekh in case the Somekh doesn't know the name of the person and his family status, so that there's no awkwardness. So, first of all, he has to know his name, because if it's a guest, it's one thing, but if he's a person who comes to the Kenis for 50 years he's praying, and they still have to ask his name, it's a little embarrassing. So, it's important for the Somekh to know the Kahal just as much as the Mesader knows the Kahal, and even more, because he has to know parents, siblings, is he married, does he have children, so that when he blesses him, he blesses him appropriately and there's no awkward moments.

In addition, he has to know his name. In Ashkenazi communities, they'll say the name and the name of the father: "Yosef ben Shelomo," and that's it. That's not our custom. We can mention the name of the father, we could say "Yosef Shelomo Harari" or "Yosef ben Shelomo," that's fine. But we also make sure to say the family name, and not only the family name that's known, we also include the nickname of the family. As you know, many Halabi families have two names: one that's used, and one that is called the Laqab, the nickname of the family. Sometimes the nickname became the primary name and the main family name is the one that's not used, regardless, both have to be mentioned when they go up to the Sefer. It's an old tradition of the Halabi community because we do take great pride in our families. So, if we say the name, let's say, we'll say Dwek, maybe Dwek-Kassab, Dwek-Kassab, Dwek-Khalousi, or Dwek without a Laqab, or you'll say Cabasso Ben Yahya, you'll say, of course, we know the famous Tawil, Mani Elia, Cohen, Khodari-Aboud, Mamiyeh-Dabbah, Levi-Hoha, I mean, there's almost, most families, Hedaya-Abdul-Wahed, most families have nicknames, and we have to know, the Somekh has to know the name and he has to say the name. And it's very, very important that we do the Mi SheBerakh properly, and if the Somekh doesn't know very well the family names and the Laqab of those families, let him do his research. Let him come prepared to the synagogue. It's always a much better experience for the 'Oleh if these details are being paid attention to. Kol Tub, Shanah Tobah UMeborekhet, Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

121.title: HaGefen, Besamim and the Naming
121.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: Lifecycles, the Berit Milah ceremony, part three. So, part one, we talked about the Pesukim that the father says, part two, we talked about the Berakhot of the Milah as said by the Abi HaBen and the Mohel, and now we are up to part three. After the circumcision is finished, we are ready to start with other Berakhot. These Berakhot are namely HaGefen, Besamim, Asher Kiddash Yedid, and the naming of the child.

In Halab as well as in most other places in the Middle East, generally it would be the Hakham, the Hakham present, if it's the Chief Rabbi present, or the greatest Rabbi in the room, he would be the one making all the Berakhot as a general rule. Not that they would never share Berakhot, but that was generally the way things were. Nowadays, as we know, the custom in our community is each one of the Berakhot are given to a different Rabbi, different Hakham to say. So, the Rabbi would start with the Berakhah, he would say "Sabri Maranan," everybody answers "LeHayyim," and he would say Berakhah "Bore Peri HaGefen." Our custom is that he does not yet drink of the wine at that point, though. The Hakham or the Hazzan, whoever is making the Berakhah, like I said though, generally traditionally it was the Hakham, he would wait until all the Berakhot and the naming of the child was completed before actually tasting from that cup.

So, HaGefen, next Berakhah is Besamim, and now we have the special Berakhah for the Milah. And there are a couple of textual differences than what we see in certain Siddurim as well as between our community and other communities. So this Berakhah, "Barukh Attah Ad-onai Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam, Asher Kiddash Yedid MiBeten, VeHok BiShe'ero Sam, VeSe'essa'av Hatam BeOt Berit Kodesh, 'Al Ken, BiSkhar Zo, El Hai Helkenu Surenu Savveh"—our Minhag is we say "Savveh" as opposed to the Minhag of other communities, mainly Moroccans and other North Africans that say "Sivvah." Our custom and that of all the Jews of the Middle East, Syria, Lebanon, Egypt, Eress Yisrael, is "Savveh." "Savveh LeHasil Yedidut She'erenu MiShahat." Now, most of the Siddurim today say "Yedidut Zera' Kodesh She'erenu MiShahat," but we see in the book Makhshire Milah of Hakham Eliyahu Shamma' from Halab that he uses the terminology "Yedidut She'erenu MiShahat." And this seems to have been the Minhag or the original Minhag in Halab. This was also the Minhag in Cairo, this was also the Minhag in Yerushalayim.

Most Siddurim today say "Yedidut Zera' Kodesh," they add those two words, "Zera' Kodesh," which have no source in our Gemara, and it's preferable to omit those words and to adhere to the original Minhag of just saying "Yedidut She'erenu MiShahat, Lema'an Berito Asher Sam BiBsarenu, Barukh Attah Ad-onai Koret HaBerit."

Then we move on to the naming of the child. The naming of the child ceremony is very simple, you would think, just read the words, fill in the blank. So, what blank are you filling in, right? It says "Elokenu VeEloke Abotenu, Kayyem Et HaYeled HaZeh LeAbiv ULeImmo, VeYikkare Shemo BeYisrael." Many of the old books, and this seems to have been the Minhag in Halab, they just name the child. If his name is Yosef, it's Yosef. If his name is Abraham, it's Abraham. In other words, they don't say son of so-and-so. Whereas today books generally will tell you say so-and-so the son of so-and-so. Let's say, so Yosef ben Eliyahu. No, according to the Minhag, it's just Yosef.

Okay, and you would continue, "VeYikkare Shemo BeYisrael," let's say it's Yosef, "Yismah HaIsh BeYosse'e Halasav VeTagel HaIshah BiFri BiTnah, KaAmur, Yismah Abikha VeImmekha VeTagel Yoledetekha. Yoledetekha, VeNe'emar, VaE'ebor 'Alayikh VaEr'ekh Mitboseset BeDamayikh, VaOmar Lakh BeDamayikh Hayi, VaOmar Lakh BeDamayikh Hayi." At that point, when we say "VaOmar Lakh BeDamayikh Hayi," the Mohel will generally dip his fingers, or a piece of gauze to keep it cleaner, into that cup of wine that the Hakham is holding, and give a taste of that wine on the gauze to the baby.

And then the person doing the naming continues, and then they get later on within this text, right, "Hodu LaHaShem Ki Tob Ki Le'Olam Hasdo," and then they say the name of the child, so again, Yosef only, without the name of a father, "Zeh HaKatan," and then everybody responds "Elokim Yegaddelehu." And that is our response, and that is the response of most Sefaradim, "Elokim Yegaddelehu," as opposed to Ashkenazim and some other Sefaradim who say "Gadol Yihyeh." Our Minhag in the text is "Elokim Yegaddelehu." And then we continue and complete it, "Keshem SheNikhnas LaBerit, Kakh Yikanes LaTorah, ULeMissvot, ULeHuppah, ULeMa'asim Tobim, VeKhen Yehi Rasson VeNomar Amen," and at that point it is over, and that's when the wine is drunk by the person who said Birkat HaGefen.

Okay, if it's one person who made all the Berakhot, he drinks at that point. If others said, then the original person who made the Berakhah of HaGefen, he drinks, and if he wants he can give out to other people to drink after that, but nobody is obligated to drink other than him, because he said Birkat HaGefen. At that point Kaddish is said, and the Milah is over.

122.title: Repeating Verses in Hallel
122.text:
Regarding Hallel, the Mishnah in Masekhet Sukkah taught: In a place where it's customary to repeat verses, you repeat them. In a place where it's not customary to repeat verses, you do not repeat them. In a place where it's customary to recite a blessing before the Hallel, recite the blessing. The Mishnah concluded: "HaKol KeMinhag HaMedinah." Everything goes according to the custom of that place. The Gemara specified the custom of Ribbi El'azar ben Perata, who repeated all the verses from "Odekha Ki 'Anitani" until the end of the Hallel.

In the 14th century, the Tur cited the custom of Spain, where they did not repeat the verse of "Barukh HaBa," or the verse of "El Ad-onai VaYa'er Lanu Isru Hag Ba'Abotim." The Tur also cited the custom of Germany, where they did repeat those verses. In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran ruled like the Mishnah: "Kol Makom Kefi Minhago." Every place follows its custom with regards to repeating verses in Hallel.

Interestingly, in the 18th century, the Hida wrote that the custom in Jerusalem and Hebron was only to repeat verses until "Ana Ad-onai Hasslihah Na." They did not repeat any of the verses from "Barukh HaBa" until the end of the Hallel. In the 19th century, the Ben Ish Hai wrote that even though the custom in Jerusalem is not to repeat the verses after "Ana Ad-onai Hasslihah Na," his custom and his father's custom was to repeat them. And then the Ben Ish Hai explained, even if we say it's not necessary to repeat them, repeating those verses is not considered a distraction in any way.

It's noteworthy that in Sha'ar HaKavvanot, it's explicitly written to repeat all the verses until the end of the Hallel, including "Barukh HaBa" and "El HaShem." The Sha'ar HaKavvanot was written by Ribbi Hayyim Vital, based on the teachings of the Arizal, the master of Kabbalah from the 16th century. In the beginning of the 20th century, Ribbi Hayyim ibn Ashish Sethon wrote in his Eress Hayyim that the custom of Safed was to repeat all the verses until the end of the Hallel, based on the opinion of the Arizal that was recorded in Sha'ar HaKavvanot. And that is the accepted custom in our community today.

However, when we sing the end of the Hallel, we are lenient with the verse "El HaShem," and we sing it like this: "El Ad-onai VaYa'er Lanu Isru Hag Ba'Abotim Isru Hag Ba'Abotim 'Ad Karnot HaMizbeah." We don't repeat the entire verse, just part of it. This is to accommodate the melody, especially in this verse where the original custom of Spain and Jerusalem was not to repeat this verse at all, and even the Ben Ish Hai did not consider repeating that verse a requirement. Therefore, our rabbis did not insist that the Hazzanim force the entire repetition into the melody. And even though it's written in Sha'ar HaKavvanot to repeat that verse as well, we are not kabbalists that practice every kabbalistic teaching. Therefore, we should continue the custom of the previous generation, who had sources to rely on, and certainly one should not force a congregation to change their custom in order to conform to the teachings of the Arizal, when the rabbis of our community never did so. We should recite the Hallel with happiness and unity, and BeEzrat HaShem, we'll have the privilege to recite the Hallel together, "BiYerushalayim HaBenuyah BiMherah BeYamenu, Amen."
