123.title: How the 'Aliyot Are Divided
123.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed our discussions regarding the role of the Mesader, the one who invites the congregants for various honors, the Somekh, the one who stands next to the Koreh while reading the Torah, and so now we are ready to proceed into the reading of the Torah and the unique Halabi customs associated with the reading.

There are customs which I discussed in my previous videos when I was talking about taking the Sefer Torah out and reading it on Monday and Thursday, so we covered many topics which are applicable also on Shabbat, so I urge you to look at these videos, numbers 27 and 30, and you will see the discussions of the customs such as inviting the 'Aliyot with the silver plate that has the beginning of the 'Aseret HaDibberot. We discuss the reasons as to why that custom is so beautiful and so important. The customs of what the 'Oleh reads before he makes the Berakhah, "HaShem 'Immakhem" or "Rabbanan" and so on, we discussed that. The Sefer Torah being open with the kerchief covering the writing. So all that you could refer back, they apply also on Shabbat.

Today I wanted to discuss a very unique custom to the Syrian communities all over the world, obviously from Halab, and that is the way we divide up the reading, how we break up the 'Aliyot. Now, if you look at a regular Humash, and I say regular, I mean standard Humash that's printed, it always has the 'Aliyot broken up Sheni, Shelishi, Rebi'i. And for the most part, the entire Sephardi and Ashkenazi world follow these stops more or less. Of course, if you need extras, you always break up and you could add extra 'Aliyot at the end. The only requirement is the Halakhic requirement to not finish three Pesukim before or after the Parashah where you see a Peh or a Samekh in the text, in the Humash, and also we try to end what's called BeKhi Tob and begin BeKhi Tob, which means on a positive note. It's all Toratenu, Kedushah, everything is holy. However, there are some Pesukim which could be Tokhahot, it could be Kelalot, it could be the middle of a story. We try to end on a positive note, a nice wording, and begin with nice wording. And that's also discussed in the Rishonim.

But the way we break up our 'Aliyot are much different than any other community. So let me give you an overview of the system that we use, generally speaking. There's always going to be exceptions on this Parashah or another Parashah, and we may even go through the Parashiyot and discuss where there are exceptions, but generally: What you find in the Humashim, let's say till Sheni, what we read on Monday and Thursday, you'll always in the Humashim it will say Sheni, and on Monday and Thursday we'll divide that into Kohen, Levi, and Shelishi. That's what we do on Shabbat. Shabbat, our Kohen, Levi, and Shelishi, the first three 'Aliyot are generally compressed into the first 'Aliyah that's printed in the books. What's printed in the books till Sheni, we divide that into three. Our 'Aliyat Rebi'i and Hamishi are generally a bit longer, again, not following the stops of the books of the Humashim that are printed. And the Shishi is usually very short, three or four Pesukim, ending with a nice Berakhah. Again, like we mentioned, the Shishi is usually reserved for the Hakhamim or the learned people, the elderly or that go up Shishi. And then following that, we break up as many 'Aliyot as we need depending on the needs of the Kahal, which we call Rakkeh, extras. And the final 'Aliyah before the Mashlim is called Samukh. So we have Samukh, and then Mashlim, and then Maftir. So that's the general way we break up the 'Aliyot.

What is interesting is that even though the system is generally the same throughout all the Syrian communities, the actual 'Aliyot may be a little bit different. You may have different customs between synagogues and between Kehillot. For instance, here we use the Humash that was marked up by 'Alav HaShalom Hakham 'Ezra Sha'yo, and we follow his stops. Now, it's not always consistent with the stops that we used when I was in New York and I prayed in Bene Yisshak, so we had the Humash that was marked up according to the stops of Hakham Ya'akob Kassin 'Alav HaShalom, our chief rabbi. As a matter of fact, he may have actually marked up the Humash, it's still there in Bene Yisshak. And those, and sometimes you'd have differences between the two, let's say the two Shishis. You may have differences. But the system was always the same: first three 'Aliyot was until Sheni in the regular books, and then Hamishi longer, Shishi short, nice Berakhah.

In Argentina, they also have their system, and they probably coincide or agree, let's say, 90% of the cases with New York and Ades, but there are changes. And they actually printed a Humash, Rabbi Basri 'Alav HaShalom printed a Humash called Sukkat David, which is the name of the big Kehillah in Argentina, where he has the stops based on the stops of the community in Argentina. So, we have those Humashim here, and we'll see differences sometimes. And I understand that there's a project in our community to print a Tikkun Sofrim that has all of our actual stops, the customary stops that we use in New York, and also with footnotes, possibly in the end of the Sefer, with the lists of the stops from other Kehillot. It's a beautiful project, and looking forward, very much looking forward to seeing it. So, we'll discuss various other customs about Sefer Torah in our next video. Shalom UBerakhah, Kol Tub.

124.title: Concluding the Berit Milah
124.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Life Cycles, Berit Milah. Part four. We've now ended all the sections of the Berit Milah, including the Berit Milah ceremony, Berakhot, naming of the child. It's all over. We recite Kaddish. The Minhag is to say Kaddish Yehe Shelama. Nowadays you'll see most of the time a number of people will say Kaddish Yehe Shelama together, but at times and in other Halabi communities, only the Hazzan would say Kaddish, because he would actually sing it in Maqam Saba, which is the Maqam of the Berit Milah. The Kaddish is over and everybody is invited to partake of a light festive meal. You know, some Mezonot, some SheHakol to have something considered a light Se'udah, if you will, a snack type of thing to partake in Berakhot and to go on their way. There's nothing else that happens and there's nothing else that ever happened.

In recent years, though, and I would say approximately the last dozen or so years, we've seen a new practice that has crept up. We'll see a long line of people waiting to get a blessing from the Sandak. The Sandak ends up remaining seated in the chair where he was holding the baby when the Mohel performed the circumcision. He stays there and people wait online to see him as if he is the Chief Rabbi, you know, to come and kiss his hand and get a Berakhah from him. This has never been our Minhag, this is not the Minhag of any Sephardic community, this is a foreign concept to us, especially, as we said before, the Sandak is generally the grandfather, and the grandfather may or may not be well-versed, may or may not be well-learned, he may not know the first thing about Berakhot.

But even if he knows something about Berakhot, does he have that piousness, you know, that somebody would go to him to get a Berakhah, other than obviously his children or grandchildren would normally approach him, let's say, around the Shabbat table or holiday table after Kiddush to get a Berakhah from an elder, you know, like a father or a grandfather. But for all the guests to come and wait to get a Berakhah, it's not something we do. It ends up turning Berakhot into a mockery. It basically makes fun of how people will go to a great Hakham who is known for his piousness and his sanctity to get a Berakhah from him, because now you're running to anybody who may be sitting in the chair of the Sandak. So, please, Rabotai, let's give the proper respect where it is due, and let's adhere to the Minhag where the Sandak does not dish out Berakhot to people, and people go to partake of the Mezonot like they're supposed to do and allow the Sandak to do the same. Mabrook.

125.title: The 'Aliyot After Shishi
125.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will continue with our discussion regarding the 'Aliyot to the Torah on Shabbat morning. We discussed in our last video the unique Halabi customs and traditions regarding how we break up the Parashah until the end of Shishi. Now we'll discuss what happens after Shishi.

Now, after Shishi, what's generally the case that there's extra 'Olim. How many extra depends on the requirements of the Kahal and what the Mesader feels is necessary. If, Ken Yirbu, there's many occasions, Semahot in the synagogue, of course we'll have many obligations. If, el-ba'id, there's people who have to go up for Hashkabot, for Azkarah, for the deceased, so those are all obligations, and we fulfill those obligations with these extra 'Olim after Shishi and before the Samukh. If there's no room to break up a new reading for each 'Oleh, then the Minhag, it goes back to Halab as well and other communities as well, it's brought down by Hakham Abraham Ades in his book Derekh Eress, that we'll take a short 'Aliyah and we'll simply repeat it, and repeat it, like we do in Simhat Torah with ULeAsher Amar, we send up everybody to those few Pesukim. So here we'll take a short 'Aliyah and we'll repeat it as necessary. These are called Rakkeh.

It's followed by Samukh. It's called Samukh because it's Samukh to the Mashlim, close to the Mashlim. Usually, the Mesader or somebody will yell out, "Samukh!" This way the Kahal knows that we're proceeding forward. Following the Samukh, we have the Mashlim, which is the 'Aliyah which concludes the Parashah, and it's followed by Kaddish, which should be said by the person going up to the Sefer, not by somebody else. And it's usually, although not exclusively, but usually reserved for somebody who has a Mi'ad, Azkarah, a prayer for the deceased. So they'll usually go Mashlim or Maftir, which is the preferred 'Aliyah according to the Kabbalists for that purpose.

Following the Mashlim, you have the Maftir. The Maftir reads the last few Pesukim from the Parashah, says the Berakhah before and after, and then he says the Berakhah on the Haftarah, and he reads the Haftarah and the Berakhot after the Haftarah. And it should be the one who goes up should be the one who reads the Haftarah. That's why the Mesader should send somebody up who knows how to read the Haftarah with the Te'amim, with the Te'amim of the Haftarah.

126.title: Anshe Emunah and Tamahnu on Monday and Thursday
126.text:
The custom in our community is to recite the paragraph that begins Anshe Emunah in the additional supplications for Monday and Thursday on Monday, and the paragraph that begins Tamahnu on Thursday. In other communities, both paragraphs are recited on Mondays and Thursdays.

One of the earliest sources with our custom is Ribbi Moshe Nigrin, a 16th century Kabbalist who lived in Greece and in the Land of Israel. In his book Rosh Ashmurot, he wrote that the custom developed in his times to recite Anshe Emunah on Mondays and Tamahnu on Thursdays. However, Ribbi Moshe Nigrin disagreed with the custom, and he wrote that the proper practice is to recite both paragraphs on Monday and on Thursday.

In the 17th century Siddur of Ribbi Moshe Zacuto, an Italian Kabbalist known as the Ramaz, the instructions say, on Mondays recite Anshe Emunah, and on Thursdays recite Tamahnu. These instructions are also found in a 17th century Siddur of Ribbi Hayyim HaKohen MeAram Soba, also a famous Kabbalist. In the 18th century, the Italian Kabbalist Ribbi Refael Immanuel Hai Ricchi wrote that it is customary to recite Tamahnu instead of Anshe Emunah on Thursday. This was written in his well-known kabbalistic work Mishnat Hasidim. And in the 19th century, the popular Middle Eastern Siddur Bet 'Obed wrote that some have the custom to recite Anshe Emunah on Mondays and Tamahnu on Thursdays, but that it's proper to recite both paragraphs on both days, which is the custom in the Land of Israel.

This was quoted by Ribbi Hayyim Elisha Sethon as the custom of the Land of Israel in his book Eress Hayyim, and also by Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya in his responsa Yaskil 'Abdi, also noting that it's proper mystically to recite both paragraphs on both days.

Interestingly, Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Selihot book Bet El, wrote, "In our land Aram Soba, Halab, we say Anshe Emunah on Mondays and Tamahnu on Thursdays, but in many other places, they say both paragraphs on both days, and that is correct." This book was published in 1878, so while he documents our custom of Anshe Emunah on Mondays and Tamahnu on Thursdays, he expresses his personal preference for the custom in other places where they recite both paragraphs on both days.

The custom of Halab was also documented by Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo in his Customs of Aleppo, where he wrote that on Thursday we say Tamahnu instead of Anshe Emunah. The book Derekh Eress also records our custom, and includes the practice of adding VaYa'abor at the end of the supplications. Since we only say one paragraph each day, we say one less VaYa'abor than the other communities, which we add at the end of the supplications.

This custom was attested to by Hakham Yisshak Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, and is found in the instructions of the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar that was printed in Halab in the year 1915. Ribbi Shelomo Zaccai Antebi quoted Hakham Yisshak Tawil's teaching that even though our custom is Anshe Emunah on Mondays and Tamahnu on Thursdays all year round, during the 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah, the Mondays and Thursdays between Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur, both paragraphs were recited on both Monday and Thursday in Halab.

There are other Middle Eastern communities that also have the custom of Anshe Emunah on Monday and Tamahnu on Thursday, including Tunisia and the city of Fez in Morocco. The original custom of Baghdad was also like Halab, until it was changed by the Ben Ish Hai towards the end of the 19th century to say both paragraphs on both days.

So the custom of Anshe Emunah on Monday and Tamahnu on Thursday dates back to the 16th century. It was practiced in Halab and in some other Middle Eastern communities. The custom in the Land of Israel and yet other communities was to recite both paragraphs on both Mondays and Thursdays. In Halab, the custom developed to add VaYa'abor at the end of the supplications to make up for the skipped paragraph. This was the custom all year round. However, on the days between Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur, in Halab they recited both Anshe Emunah and Tamahnu on Monday and on Thursday.

127.title: What Pidyon HaBen Is and When
127.text:
Pidyon HaBen, the redemption of the firstborn child. What is Pidyon HaBen? Who is obligated in Pidyon HaBen? What are the moneys used for Pidyon HaBen? And when is the Pidyon HaBen enacted?

So, first of all, the Pidyon HaBen is the redemption of the firstborn male child. And though this is a Missvah which is incumbent upon the father, the mother plays, of course, a critical and crucial role over here. So now, this Missvah is not an easy Missvah in the sense that not everybody can perform it. If either of the parents, the mother or father of this newborn child, are a Kohen, there is no Pidyon. If either one of the parents is a Levi, there is no Pidyon. Only if both parents are Yisrael, then can there be a Pidyon HaBen. But still, wait. If the mother has had a child prior to this son, there is no Pidyon. If the mother had a miscarriage, there is no Pidyon. If the child was born through a Caesarean, there is no Pidyon. This must be a completely natural birth, it must be the firstborn male child of the mother with no other child being born to this woman beforehand.

Now, that is who is obligated. What is the Pidyon money? The Torah clearly tells us in the Pasuk: "UFduyav MiBen Hodesh Tifdeh BeErkekha Kesef Hameshet Shekalim BeShekel HaKodesh 'Esrim Gerah Hu." It has to be five silver Shekalim. We know that five silver Shekalim is the approximate weight of 96 grams of silver, and with our American silver dollars, we have that same 96 grams, and that is generally what we use here in the United States. In the old days, if they didn't have a particular coin that five of them would equal the 96 grams necessary, they would use more coins or less coins depending on what was the size, weight, and value of the coin, or if they didn't have a particular coin, they could use actually a piece of silver or a silver vessel of any sort that has at least that 96 grams of silver to redeem the child.

Now, remember, the child is being redeemed through a Kohen. The Kohen gets the child, and the parents, or technically the father, is redeeming his child back from the Kohen. Now, when is the time of the Pidyon? As the Pasuk tells you, it has to be the child has to be at least 30 days old. So our Minhag is that on the night of the 31st from the time of birth, that is when the Pidyon is held. Now, if this 31st night falls out on the night of Shabbat or the night of a holiday, then we push off the Pidyon to the following free night, let's say to a Saturday night, or if a holiday falls out on Monday night and it's a two-night holiday, so then Wednesday night would be the Pidyon, for example. You can never make the Pidyon prior to the time, but you can make it immediately after the time.

Now, this Pidyon is a very, very joyous occasion, and therefore, they like to do it at night to allow for more people to be able to attend, to partake of this beautiful Missvah, to see the Missvah enacted, to answer "Amen" to the Berakhot, as well as to partake of a special Se'udat Missvah.

So this is our Pidyon: what it is, who's obligated, the money of the Pidyon, the time of the Pidyon, and finally, where is the Pidyon held? The Pidyon can be held any place. It could be held at home, it could be held in Kenis, it could be held in a hall. It makes no difference where it's held. You're looking to accommodate the people that need to be there, the people that you're inviting, you need to have room for the Se'udah, so any place that fits the bill is okay.

128.title: ULeKhapparat Pesha in Musaf of a Leap Year
128.text:
This year is a leap year in the Jewish calendar. The custom has developed in many communities, both Sephardic and Ashkenazic, to add the phrase "ULeKhapparat Pesha'" in the Musaf prayer for Rosh Hodesh in a Jewish leap year.

In his book Kaf HaHayyim, Ribbi Hayyim Palachi, a 19th-century authority from Izmir, Turkey, mentioned three different customs among those communities who add it. Some add it during the entire leap year. Others only add it from the beginning of the leap year until, but not including, Rosh Hodesh Nisan. And yet others only add it in the second Adar. Ribbi Hayyim Palachi's son, Ribbi Yisshak Palachi, also quoted sources for only adding it in the first Adar, in his book Yafeh LaLeb.

The Ben Ish Hai, an authority from Baghdad in the 19th century, also records the custom of adding it. Subsequently, the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer recorded the custom as well. According to Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, it should be added until, but not including, Rosh Hodesh Nisan.

However, many Middle Eastern communities never had the custom of adding the phrase ULeKhapparat Pesha' to the Musaf prayer on Rosh Hodesh at all. It was never the custom in Egypt or Tunisia. Furthermore, it was not customary to add it in Morocco or Algeria.

What about Halab? Ribbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that he was told that the custom of Halab is not to add ULeKhapparat Pesha' to the Musaf prayer on Rosh Hodesh. Furthermore, the phrase is not found in the 16th-century Mahzor, Mahzor Aram Soba, or in later Siddurim, such as the 19th-century Bet 'Obed, or in other Siddurim that were popular at that time, such as Tefillat HaHodesh and Bene Siyyon. Interestingly, in the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar that was printed in Halab in 1915, we do find the phrase ULeKhapparat Pesha', with instructions to add it during a leap year. However, our early community Siddur, Tefillat Yeshurun, does not include it.

So the majority of sources indicate that the prevalent custom of Halab was not to add ULeKhapparat Pesha' to the Musaf prayer on Rosh Hodesh. Perhaps later on, in the 20th century, some decided to add it.

So while the custom developed in Izmir, Baghdad, and Jerusalem, to add ULeKhapparat Pesha' in Musaf of Rosh Hodesh during a leap year, as was recorded by Ribbi Hayyim Palachi, the Ben Ish Hai, Ribbi Ya'akob Sofer, and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, many communities did not add this phrase, including the communities in Egypt, Tunisia, Djerba, Morocco, and Algeria. Similarly, the prevalent custom in Halab was not to add ULeKhapparat Pesha' in Musaf of Rosh Hodesh, as we see it was not added to their Siddurim, except for one that was printed in 1915.

129.title: Standing for an Elder Relative's 'Aliyah
129.text:
The custom, we have a beautiful custom in our community that if somebody has an elder relative, certainly a father or grandfather, but even an uncle, his side or his wife's side makes no difference, an elder sibling, those categories, a person will stand up for the elder relative who's going up to the Sefer. I don't recall we don't have the custom to stand up for cousins. It's elder sibling, uncles, grandparents, parents and grandparents.

And they will stand up from the beginning of the Berakhah till after he comes down from the Sefer Torah, which is immediately after the 'Oleh. We don't have the custom to stay like other communities do, to stand until the next 'Oleh finishes. No, when he's finished the 'Aliyah, Hazak UBarukh, Mi SheBerakh, he goes down. And the person, the younger relative or the son or grandson will be standing, and then they'll if it's a case of a parent or a grandparent they will kiss his hand, get a Berakhah from the parent, and it's a beautiful, beautiful custom.

When it comes to the Maftir, he's not required to stand up till the end of the reading of the Haftarah and the Berakhot. He stands up for the Berakhot and the reading of the Torah, then he could sit down. He resumes standing after the Berakhot of the Haftarah, when they're doing the Mi SheBerakh, or if there's Hashkabah. This way, when the relative comes down from the Torah, he sees his family standing for him. It's a great honor, and it's a very important custom.

Now a question came up as to whether women should stand up as well for the same elder relatives as a man does. Now, I tried to research with the Halabi Hakhamim from Halab, I'm saying, in the old days, and really I haven't found anything that speaks to the subject, probably because women in general didn't regularly attend a synagogue on Shabbat, but nowadays they do, and the question is whether they have to stand up.

So I'm not I mean when I was younger, I don't recall it. I mean I don't know if they stood if I would have noticed, but I don't recall it being a custom, and because it's not something which is spoken about beforehand, I wouldn't put in the category of a custom, although there are some elder, respectable people in the community which told me that, no, our custom is that women do not stand up. For what particular reason, I don't know, but they didn't stand up.

But I noticed in the last 30, 40 years, is that women do stand up, and the truth is, I haven't really found a good reason for them not to stand up. On the contrary, I find a very good reason for them to stand up and show the same respect and honor to their elder relatives as the men do. So I think it's a proper practice. Again, I don't think there's a particular custom one way or the other, but especially today where many, many women come to synagogue and they, and, you know, they're aware, they're engaged in the prayers, they see who's going up, if somebody doesn't stand up for their husband or their parent or uncle, it may seem a bit disrespectful, so in that case certainly they would stand up and it would be proper to do so. Kol Tub.

130.title: The Pidyon HaBen Ceremony
130.text:
The Pidyon HaBen ceremony. What exactly is the ceremony for Pidyon HaBen? Who is involved in this ceremony, and what is done? So, obviously the main people involved are the newborn child, the parents of that newborn child, and the Kohen. These are the only people necessary for the ceremony. Nowadays, you may see that they bring up to the dais a rabbi or two, grandparents, others, but all the extras are not necessary. The necessary people for the ceremony are the child, the parents, and the Kohen.

Generally, and for generations, the Kohen would be a Kohen that they knew was from a well-established line of Kohanim, there was no question as to the heritage of this Kohen, and usually they chose a Kohen who was a Hakham as well, a rabbi, so he was familiar with the entire ceremony from A to Z, he knew all the Halakhot necessary, he knew the Pesukim that need to be recited, and he had a tradition of doing Pidyon HaBen.

Now, in walk in the parents with the child. The Kohen is already seated and waiting for them, and the mother is dressed in her wedding gown. Yes, the tradition of Syria, of Egypt, of Turkey, of many other places was that the mother of this child that is coming in for the redemption wears her wedding gown. And this is to show to the people that, "Yes, he is really my firstborn." You understand what I mean.

The Kohen is there, the people break out into song, we have a special Pizmon for Pidyon HaBen, it's called Ani LiShmekha Ahallel: "Ani LiShmekha Ahallel VeAshir Lakh Yom VaLel," etc., the final verse referring to the Pidyon, "Pedeh Binkha HaBekhor."

After the song is over, the ceremony starts with these important people sitting down. The Kohen turns to the father of the child, says, "Is this your firstborn son?" Father answers in the affirmative, "Of course he is." "Do you want your son? If you want him, you know technically right now he belongs to me as I'm the Kohen, and if you want him you're going to have to redeem him for five silver coins." Says, "Yes, absolutely, I want my son back, and I'm ready to do the redemption process." He then turns to the mother and asks the mother, "This is your son, this is your firstborn son, maybe you had another son or another child before him? Maybe you had a miscarriage? Maybe he was born through a Caesarean section?" She answers, "No, this is definitely my firstborn son, I have had no other children before, I've had no miscarriage, he wasn't born through Caesarean, he was born naturally."

At that point, it's well established that this child must go to the Kohen. The child is then handed over to the Kohen, the Kohen recites some verses saying that this is a firstborn son that needs to go to the Kohen until the parents do in fact redeem him. Then father says, "Yes, I'm ready to redeem him, and I have the silver coins, I'm ready to do what I need to do." The father then says two Berakhot: the first one of "Barukh Attah Ad-onai Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam Asher Kiddeshanu BeMissvotav VeSivvanu 'Al Pidyon HaBen," followed by the Berakhah of Sheheheyanu.

Once he completes both Berakhot, he then hands over the silver coins to the Kohen. Generally it's done one by one: one coin, two coins, three coins, four coins, five coins handed over to the Kohen, and he says, "Zeh Pidyon Beni Bekhori. This is the redemption for my firstborn son." Then the Kohen, who now has the money in his hand, says, "Kibbalti Mimmekha Hamesh Sela'im Ellu BeFidyon Binkha Zeh VaHare Hu Padui Bahen KeDat Moshe VeYisrael." Yes, I have received the money from you for the redemption, and he is now redeemed according to the laws of Moshe and Yisrael.

That point, before the Kohen returns the child to the parents, generally say a number of Pesukim, among them is Birkat Kohanim, as he is a Kohen. He puts his right hand on the head of the child, and he recites, "VaYedabber Ad-onai El Moshe Lemor, Dabber El Aharon VeEl Banav Lemor, Koh Tebarekhu Bene Yisrael Amor Lahem: Yebarekhekha Ad-onai VeYishmerekha, Ya'er Ad-onai Panav Elekha ViHunneka, Yissa Ad-onai Panav Elekha VeYasem Lekha Shalom, VeSamu Et Shemi 'Al Bene Yisrael VaAni Abarekhem." Everybody answers "Amen."

The child is then returned to the parents. Everybody's happy, of course. And at that point, the Kohen can continue, or there can be a rabbi, or two rabbis there. We say Berakhah, Birkat HaGefen, Bore Peri HaGefen on a cup of wine, and that's according to almost everybody's tradition. In the Halabi tradition, there is no Berakhah Besamim, but in the Damascus tradition, as well as other traditions, they do say Besamim after HaGefen, and generally here in New York, at every Pidyon HaBen, we do both Birkat HaGefen followed by Birkat Bore Mine Besamim.

After that, there is another Berakhah. And that Berakhah was established by the Geonim, it's known to us by the Rashba, and it's a Berakhah of "Asher Kiddesh 'Ubar BeMe'e Immo." And it is not the Syrian custom to recite that Berakhah whatsoever. It is recited by other communities, and it's usually said without Shem UMalkhut, without reciting HaShem's name, because it's not an established Berakhah from the Gemara, and it's only from the Geonim, and it's known to us from the Rashba. And in the Halabi tradition, and in the Shami tradition, it is definitely not said whatsoever.

So technically, at that point, the Pidyon HaBen ceremony is over. Just finally, before it ends, the Kohen gives a short, one-line Berakhah to the parents of the child, and he tells them, "Yehi Rasson MiLifne Elokenu SheBaShamayim, KeShem SheZakhita LeFidyon HaBen, Kakh Tizkeh LeKayyem Et Kol HaMissvot SheBaTorah." The same way that you were able to merit to redeem your firstborn, you may merit to fulfill all the Missvot of the Torah.

At that point, the Pidyon is over. Now, everybody's wondering about the coins. Coming up in the next episode.

131.title: The Wording and Timing of the Hanukkah Blessings
131.text:
There is a difference of opinion regarding the exact wording of the first blessing that we recite upon lighting Hanukkah candles. The printed versions of the Talmud all say "LeHadlik Ner Shel Hanukkah." However, there is one Spanish manuscript of the Talmud from approximately the 14th century that says "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah," without the word Shel.

We also find this difference of opinion among both earlier and later post-Talmudic authorities. According to Rab 'Amram Gaon, the Rif, Rambam, and the Rosh, the blessing is "LeHadlik Ner Shel Hanukkah," but Rab Sa'adya Gaon, the Ran, and Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, all write "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah." Among the later authorities, the Peri Hadash and the Hida both wrote that "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah" is the correct version, whereas the custom of most Ashkenazim is to say Shel Hanukkah, and yet other authorities say SheLHanukkah as one word. It's noteworthy that according to the Arizal, the correct version kabbalistically is "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah."

What was the custom in Halab? Mahzor Aram Soba, which was printed in 1527 for the Musta'arabi community, the Middle Eastern Jews who were already living in Halab for centuries prior to the arrival of Jews from Spain after the expulsion in 1492, has "LeHadlik Ner Shel Hanukkah." Even the popular 19th-century Siddur Bet 'Obed has the word Shel in parentheses. But other sources, such as Shulhan HaMelekh, that was written in Halab in 1804 by Ribbi Shemuel Laniado, has "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah." The Siddur 'Olat HaShahar, that was printed in Halab in 1915, also has "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah." And the book Derekh Eress records the custom of Halab in the 20th century as saying "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah."

However, Ribbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that even in the 20th century, there were still some families that maintained their earlier Musta'arabi tradition of Shel Hanukkah. And in fact, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, who was born in Halab in 1893, was quoted as having said that in Halab, some added the word Shel to the first blessing, but according to the Kabbalah, it should not be said. And therefore, Hakham Yosef himself, who was proficient in kabbalistic teachings, used to say "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah."

So in our times, the prevalent custom in the Syrian community is to say "LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah," based primarily on Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh and the Arizal. But there are still some families who have maintained the earlier tradition of the Musta'arabim and recite "LeHadlik Ner Shel Hanukkah," which is based primarily on the opinions of the Rif, Rambam, and the Rosh. Therefore, each family should follow their custom, as both customs are supported by prominent halakhic authorities.

There's another difference of opinion regarding when to begin lighting: either immediately after reciting the first blessing, or after reciting both blessings, and on the first night, after all three. Beginning to light right after the first blessing, before reciting the second blessing of She'asah Nissim, is the opinion of the Meiri and the Terumat HaDeshen. It was the custom in Algeria, and also the custom of the kabbalists in the famous synagogue Bet El in Jerusalem. According to the book of customs known as Keter Shem Tob, the common custom of the Middle East was to begin lighting immediately after reciting the first blessing.

However, according to the Ben Ish Hai and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, both blessings, and on the first night all three blessings, are recited before beginning to light. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote that all of the blessings are recited before lighting. This was reprinted in the book Ro'eh Ne'eman. Similarly, the custom of the Ashkenazim is to recite all of the blessings before lighting. This was specified by the Maharil, Muram, and the Ture Zahab.

So while the prevalent custom in the community is to recite all of the blessings prior to lighting, I remember Dennis Toueg, 'Alav HaShalom, teaching to begin lighting immediately after the first blessing. Therefore, once again, both customs are valid, and each family should follow their custom.

132.title: Reading the Haftarah and Its Berakhot
132.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim, we are still continuing with our customs surrounding the reading of the Torah in the Sibbur. Actually, today we're going to talk about the reading of the Haftarah. The Haftarah is the portion of the Nebi'im which we read following the reading of the Torah. It's the Maftir, the one who goes up for 'Aliyat Maftir, which will actually be the one to read the Haftarah. He will make the Berakhah before, the Berakhot after, and it's important that he himself read the Haftarah.

Now he begins with a Berakhah, "Asher Bahar BiNebi'im Tobim." What's interesting about this Berakhah is that we read it with the, using the Te'amim of the Nebi'im. The way we read the Nebi'im in Haftarah is how we read the Berakhah. Even in some Humashim they print it with Te'amim, even though obviously it's a Berakhah without Te'amim, but they added the Te'amim. So "Asher Bahar BiNebi'im Tobim, VeRasah BeDibrehem HaNe'emarim BeEmet, Barukh Attah." So we have the Te'amim of the Nebi'im in the Berakhah beforehand.

Then he begins the reading the Maftir, and he reads it usually from the Humash, or there's a book of Haftarot on the Tebah. Even we don't have a required custom to take out a Sefer Haftarot. Some Kehillot will do it, some won't do it, a special Sefer Haftarot. But even if we take out a Sefer Haftarot, the one is not required to read from the Sefer Haftarot. Many times you'll just see them it's easier for them to read it from the Humash.

Now he will read the Haftarah out loud. Now unlike the reading of the Torah, where all the Kahal is quiet and attentive to every word of the reading, here the Kahal will actually read it each one to themselves. They all have Sefarim, they all have Humashim, and they read it to themselves while the Maftir is reading it out loud. This goes a custom that goes back a number, a couple hundred years, it's brought down in the Teshubot of Rabbi Shelomo Laniado, 'Alav HaShalom, Bet Dino Shel Shelomo. His discussion about what they did in Halab is brought down in the book of Hakham Abraham Ades in Derekh Eress. And that's the custom today, BeEmet. You see everybody reading the Maftir to themselves.

Following the reading of the Haftarah, there are two Pesukim which are added at the end: "Go'alenu Ad-onai Seba'ot Shemo, Kedosh Yisrael. Barukh Ad-onai Le'Olam, Amen VeAmen." Very interesting. Now the Go'alenu, Pasuk in Yesha'yah, is said by everybody, and even the Kahal all join in. The second Pasuk, "Barukh Ad-onai Le'Olam Amen VeAmen," was the custom, and we hear it a little less often today than I used to growing up, but certainly it is a custom.

As a matter of fact, it's interesting, there's a Kehillah in Argentina which really they take care of the Minhagim very, very closely, it's called Sha'are Siyyon in Argentina, and they actually say these two Pesukim in Hebrew and in the Sharh, in the Arabic. So that's an interesting custom which obviously we I haven't seen it in New York, but could have been that was the Minhag in Halab, obviously they got it from somewhere. That's interesting.

Following those two Pesukim, he says the Berakhot after, there's a number of Berakhot, following four Berakhot following the reading of the Haftarah. Now here he does not read it in the same tune of the Nabi, not the same scale at all. As a matter of fact, he will read it in, for the most part, Maqam Saba. This is a custom that we have that the Berakhot of Haftarot, for the most part, were in Maqam Saba. I'll try to find a link of Hakham Yosef Gozlan and attach it to this video so you can hear it for yourselves. It's very, very interesting.

Following the last Berakhah, "Barukh Attah HaShem, Mekaddesh HaShabbat," many books print Amen. Now based on Maran in Resh-Tet-Vav, where if a person has a say saying a series of Berakhot and following the last Berakhah he will say himself say Amen, it's Amen to his whole, to his own series of Berakhot. There's a Halakhah in Resh-Tet-Vav. Maran cites Hallel and Yishtabah, where we know "Melekh Hai Ha'Olamim, Amen" or "Melekh Mehullal BaTishbahot, Amen." He doesn't mention the Haftarot.

Now Maran HaHida in Birke Yosef says based on this reading, based on this Halakhah that Maran brings, it should also apply to the Haftarah, to the Berakhot of the Haftarah, and indeed some Kehillot have this custom. Also brought down in Derekh Eress, it's a discussion that we never, we didn't have this custom in Halab. He just ends "Mekaddesh HaShabbat," and the Kahal will answer "Amen." Kol Tub, Shalom UBerakhah.

133.title: The Coins of the Pidyon HaBen
133.text:
Pidyon HaBen, the coins. Everybody wants to know about the coins. What happens with those coins? What are these coins and why does everybody want them so much? So, to be honest with you, the coins belong to the Kohen. When the father of child redeems his child from the Kohen and pays him those five silver dollars, those five silver dollars belong to the Kohen.

So, what's going on? We have a very unique practice here in our New York, New Jersey, Syrian, Sephardic community, where at almost every Pidyon, we see that these coins are auctioned off and they are sold to the highest bidder. Where did this custom come from? What's going on? So, this custom did not exist in Syria, nor did it exist any place else in the Middle East or any other Sephardic community. It's a new practice that was established here in New York.

What's behind it? Hakham Murad Maslaton, who was founder and first chief rabbi of the Ahi 'Ezer congregation, was a very beloved Hakham and Kohen, and he was called upon at almost every Pidyon HaBen to be the Kohen. After a while, he had so many silver coins, he said, "What am I doing with all these coins? I'm collecting coins. There must be something I can do cuz I don't need all of them." He saw the plight of the people. There were people that were out of work, people that were hungry, people that couldn't pay their rent. He saw there was a need for more Sedakah in the community, and he realized that people have something called Hibbub Missvah, love of Missvah, and they want to attach themselves to a Missvah.

So, he came up with this very unique idea at the end of the Pidyon to auction off these coins, to sell them to the highest bidder to raise money for Sedakah, which he then collected, and he personally gave out to people that he knew needed that money, or if he needed to buy them food, or if he needed to buy them clothing, or he needed to pay their rent. He found a way to do things in a very respectable manner, in a dignified manner. And this was his way of doing things. So, he started this practice, and this is as told to me by his son, Hakham Siyyon Maslaton, 'Alav HaShalom, who continued his father's practice.

So, this is a practice has been going on in the Syrian community in New York for at least the last 75 years, and it's something that people love. Nowadays, it's taken on a life of its own, where the rabbis involved decide, you know, we'll give the money to this Sedakah for the first coin, and a different Sedakah for the second coin, etc., etc. Or the parents of the child decide they want this Sedakah, or the grandparents decide, well, we want this Sedakah and that Sedakah. It used to be plain and simple. Hakham Maslaton, he was a Hakham and Kohen, he took whatever money was made through the sales, and he personally gave it out, distributed it.

Now, mashallah, we have so many different organizations, so many worthy causes, and everybody wants to get their fair share, and so many people want to help out these causes. But this is Hibbub Missvah. But now, okay, let's say you went and you spent $1,000, and you bought one of these coins that was used for the Missvah of Pidyon HaBen. What are you doing with it? Some people just like to save it, to know that they have a portion of this Missvah, some way of connecting themselves with the Pidyon HaBen, because they could never have gotten to do a Pidyon because they had, you know, a circumstance where they wouldn't be able to have a firstborn boy, or they're a Kohen, or they're a Levi, or whatever the case may be. Some people use it as a coin that they give to their son or their grandson to use when they get married, when they need to use a coin, which we'll talk about once we get to the episodes dealing with marriage. Some people will use it as a positive omen to start a fund to buy a home. Everybody does something else with it.

But the bottom line is this is Hibbub Missvah. It's a Missvah that brings you to do another Missvah that endears the Missvah to you. And this is a very unique practice that Rabbi Maslaton established in the Syrian Sephardic community of New York, and everybody in the community does it now, and everybody really enjoys it and looks forward to this as the highlight and the ending of the Pidyon HaBen ceremony. Mabrook.

134.title: Washing the Hands for a Wet Food
134.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran requires one to wash their hands with a cup, each hand three times, like one would wash before eating bread, for a wet food. If the food is wet from water, or wine, or bee honey, or olive oil, or milk, according to Maran, one must wash their hands with a cup without reciting the blessing of 'Al Netilat Yadayim before eating the wet food, unless they dry the food, in which case they may eat it without washing their hands first. A common example would be a rinsed fruit or vegetable.

There are some authorities that do not require washing for a wet food in our times because there are certain laws of purity that we do not observe now, since they apply to the Bet HaMikdash. These authorities include the Ba'al Ha'Ittur, a 12th-century authority from southern France, the Tosafot, and the Maharam MiRothenburg, a 13th-century authority from Germany. Maran did not rule like those authorities, but rather like HaRambam, the Rosh, and most of the other authorities who do require washing before a wet food, even in our times.

However, the Magen Abraham, an important 17th-century authority from Poland, quoted the Lehem Hamudot, who also lived in Poland in the 17th century, who wrote that the custom of the world is not to wash for wet foods, and they have authorities to rely upon. And therefore, many Ashkenazim are lenient and do not wash their hands before eating a wet food.

What was the custom in Syria? The general rule among Syrian Jews is to follow the rulings of Maran and HaRambam, both of whom require washing before a wet food. However, Hakham Yosef Sethon, who was born in Halab in 1813, wrote in his book, VaYimssa Yosef: "Wash your hands for wet foods like Maran wrote in Shulhan 'Arukh, but now we are lenient with this, as was written by the Lehem Hamudot, based on the Tosafot, and quoted by the Magen Abraham, and this was also written by the Maharam MiRothenburg. But we are careful with this when we dip the Karpas on the night of Pesah. And one who is always careful with this is holy and should be praised, but one should not appear arrogant as a result of this stringency."

So we see from here that the general custom in Halab was to be lenient with regards to washing before a wet food, except for Karpas on the night of Pesah, when the custom was to be stringent. And while Hakham Yosef Sethon praises one who is stringent upon themselves, he cautions them to be careful about being stringent in front of others who follow the general custom, since it is not appropriate to appear as if you are better than others who observe the accepted practice.

Similarly, in Damascus they were lenient as well. In a manuscript quoted in the Sha'ar Binyamin HaGadol, Hakham Ya'akob Antebi wrote regarding the custom of Damascus: "The Tosafot wrote that the custom of the world is not to wash for a wet food, and this was our custom since that time, before the ruling of Maran, and the custom never changed. However, on the night of Pesah, which is a special night of many Missvot, our custom is to wash our hands before the Karpas, because on the night of Pesah, it is appropriate to be stringent."

So both the custom of Aleppo and Damascus was to be lenient regarding washing before a wet food, like many Ashkenazim who do not wash their hands before eating a wet food. In a short video clip that is attached to this video, Hakham Yisshak Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, who is the son of the former chief rabbi of Halab, Hakham Moshe Tawil, said that they never washed before a wet food because they relied on the lenient authorities.

Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca also asked Rabbi Yosef Hayyim Chehebar, who said that his father, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, 'Alav HaShalom, did not wash his hands before eating a wet food. Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca also asked Rabbi Meir Yedid, who also remembered that his father, Hakham Yom Tob Yedid, 'Alav HaShalom, did not wash before eating a wet food.

So while the general rule in Syria was to follow the rulings of Maran and HaRambam, with regards to washing hands before eating a wet food, the custom was not to wash, based on the opinion of the Tosafot and a few other authorities who do not require washing before wet foods in our times.

135.title: The Text of the Hashkabot
135.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with the Minhagim surrounding the reading of the Sefer Torah and the 'Aliyot. Today, we are going to focus on the text, the Nusah of the Hashkabot.

Now, Hashkabah is a prayer for the deceased, beseeching Bore 'Olam to have compassion, to show compassion and mercy on the soul of the deceased. This prayer is said after the Berakhah for the Sefer Torah, before the Mi SheBerakh. The one who has the 'Oleh will request that Hashkabah be said.

Now, when is the Hashkabah said? It's said the entire year, the first year of the passing. Whenever a relative goes up to the Sefer, he will make the Hashkabah. And in subsequent years, someone from the family will go up to the Sefer on the Shabbat prior to the anniversary of the passing, which we call the Ma'amad, or the Ashkenazim in Yiddish they call it the yahrzeit. So that Shabbat, they will get an 'Aliyah, and they will say request this prayer be said.

Now, the Somekh or the Kore generally will say the prayer. It's not required. I've seen it's rare, but I've seen sometimes that the person himself will make the Hashkabah for the deceased in his family, and then the Somekh will do the Mi SheBerakh. But generally, the Somekh or the Kore will do both the Hashkabot, and the Refuah Shelemah, and the Mi SheBerakh.

The Nusah, I'm looking at Kol Ya'akob, page 289. The prayer is "HaMerahem 'Al Kol Beriyotav," right? One who has mercy on all of His creations. "Hu Yahos VeYahmol VeYerahem 'Al Nefesh, Ruah, UNeshamah Shel," and then they'll add "HaIsh HaKasher, HaNiftar LeBet 'Olamo," Kahar and they'll say his name, and the name of his mother.

Before we say this prayer, there for a man we say a couple of Pesukim, and for a woman, we say different Pesukim. Now, there may be varying customs. I'll read what's in Kol Ya'akob, and there's other Siddurim which are printed even in our community which have differing Pesukim. I've seen them, I've seen it done in many different ways. Again, there's no set Minhag when it comes to the Pesukim we say before the Hashkabah. In Kol Ya'akob, it says, "Ashre Ish Yare Et HaShem BeMissvotav Hafess Me'od, Ya'alezu Hasidim BeKhabod Yeranenu 'Al Mishkebotam." In other Siddurim, after the Ashre Ish Pasuk, there will, there'll be a Pasuk: "Tob Shem MiShemen Tob VeYom HaMavet MiYom Hivaldo, Sof Dabar HaKol Nishma' Et HaElokim Yare VeEt Missvotav Shemor Ki Zeh Kol HaAdam," followed by "Ya'alezu," and then "HaMerahem."

For a woman, it's "Eshet Hayil Mi Yimssa VeRahok MiPeninim Mikhrah, Sheker HaHen VeHebel HaYofi Ishah Yirat HaShem Hi Tithallal"—I'm reading from the Siddur—"Tenu Lah MiPeri Yadeha ViHaleluha VaShe'arim Ma'aseha," and then "HaMerahem." The what I've seen and also what's been told to me by other Gabba'im of various synagogues in Brooklyn is that these few Pesukim that they say before the actual Hashkabah, they'll say usually once. The first time an 'Oleh asks for to say Hashkabah, they'll say these Pesukim, and then subsequent requests for Hashkabah, they will begin directly with "HaMerahem."

When we say "HaMerahem," when we get to the name, the custom in our community is based on the Kabbalah that we say the name and the name of the mother, "Yisshak Ben Sarah." And if there's additional names, you don't have to repeat the whole prayer, just say "Ve'Al Nefesh," "VeGam Nefesh," again, "Peloni Ben Pelonit," until we finish the prayer. Now, there are those, it's not common, but there are those who insist on saying the name, it's only the given name, not the family name, the name and the name of the father and the mother. So they may say "Yisshak Ben Abraham VeSarah." Not common to hear, but occasionally I've seen it where people want to mention the name of the father and the mother. And the same applies to the woman, it's the woman and her mother's name.

That's the Hashkabah, and we say, we, if it's multiple names, obviously you'll say "Ruah HaShem Tenihem BeGan 'Eden, Hem VeKhol Bene Yisrael HaShokhebim 'Immam." If it's one person, you'll see what it says in the book, "Tenihenu BeGan 'Eden, Hu VeKhol Bene Yisrael HaShokhebim 'Immo." For woman: "Hi VeKhol Benot Yisrael HaShokhebot 'Immah." "Bikhlal HaRahamim VeHaSelihot, VeKhen Yehi Rasson, VeNomar Amen."

Occasionally, il-ba'id, there's someone ill in the family, seriously ill, and the one who gets an 'Oleh, who gets an 'Aliyah, the 'Oleh will ask for a prayer for Refuah Shelemah, and that begins "Mi SheBerakh Abotenu Abraham Yisshak VeYa'akob," or for a woman, "Mi SheBerakh Immotenu Sarah Ribkah Rahel VeLeah," "Hu Yishlah Refuah Shelemah LeKhol Hole 'Ammo Bet Yisrael," requesting for everybody, and among them, "UBikhlalam," and the name and the name of the mother, "El Na Refa Na Lo," or "El Na Refa Na Lah," "VeKhen Yehi Rasson VeNomar Amen." If it's Shabbat, which we're talking about Shabbat, often you'll hear the added phrase, "Shabbat Hi MiLiz'ok URefuah Kerobah Labo." And in addition, you may have an extended Berakhah, a prayer for the ill, when they say the name Ben or Bat, "El Na Refa Na Lo," "Yishlah Bore 'Olam Yishlah Lo Refuah Shelemah BeRemah Ebarav VeShasah Gidav," or for a woman, "BeRemah Ebareha VeShasah Gideha," "VeKhen Yehi Rasson VeNomar Amen."

Now, I didn't mention, but for a Hashkabah, for a great scholar or rabbi, but one generally it's one affiliated with the community, there'll be an extended Hashkabah, "Hokhmah MeAyin Timmasse." It's printed in the back of the Siddurim, and when you do Hashkabah for a great Hakham, generally the Kahal will be requested to stand up for that Hashkabah. Kol Tub, Shalom UBerakhah.

136.title: The Age of the Bar Missvah
136.text:
SCA Minhag of the week, life cycles: Bar Missvah. Already from the birth of a child, from his Berit Milah, friends and relatives would be blessing the parents: "'Okbal Tifilino! 'Okbal Tifilino!" Looking forward to the occasion of his Tefillin, of his Bar Missvah, in other words. Commonly known today as Bar Missvah, back in Halab, back in Sham, in Egypt, in Lebanon, and so many other places, Bar Missvah or bar missvah was known as Tefillin, or more commonly by the masses as Tiflin.

What was this? At what age did they do it? What were the ceremonies involved, what were the rituals, what were the functions, what were the customs, what peculiarities? That's what we're going to discuss in the next few series of videos on Minhagim of Bar Missvah.

So for this opening video, I'd like to mention the age. So it's commonly thought of 13, 13, 13. Were they rigid about it? Was it done at exactly 13 years of age, or was it done even prior to that? And if it was prior to that, how much before? So it's known that in North African communities, like in Morocco or in Tunisia, it was already celebrated from the age of 11, and possibly even before. But in Syria, it was generally celebrated sometime after 12 years, and most commonly about the age of 12 and a half. And that's the way it was commonly celebrated in Syria for decades and generations, I'd say at least from the records that we have, from about the 1850s till the Jews left Syria. And here in America, that custom continued and prevailed, that the common Minhag was to have the Bar Missvah ceremony from approximately the age of 12 and a half.

Why that age? Basically, to prepare the lad. In other words, the Minh- the Halakhot fall upon the boy who reaches the age of 13, when he reaches 13 years and one day. If you only begin to teach him and indoctrinate him into them when he reaches that exact day, it may not be enough time for him to become familiar with the rituals and to do them properly. So they start approximately six months before. It could be three months before, four months before, whatever it may be, but approximately six months before, to get him familiar with things, with the prayers, with how to put on Talet and Tefillin in a regular fashion, in the extra prayers to say, in the practice of Missvot, in the reading of the Torah. That way, by the time he reaches 13 years and one day, he'll be proficient and will be able to fulfill the Missvot properly.

And that's the way the Minhag was when I was growing up, that's the way it continues to be. And not only were they doing it, but they actually considered the boy, for the most part, and I mean for the most part, as a Bar Missvah, as 13. Fully 13? Not fully 13, we'll get to that. But he already was allowed to have 'Aliyah to the Torah, whether it be on a Monday or Thursday, on a Rosh Hodesh, on a Shabbat. He had 'Aliyah, he made the Berakhot, and that was considered a full and proper 'Aliyah to the Torah based upon a Halakhah known as "Katan 'Oleh LeMinyan Shib'ah" or "Katan 'Oleh LeMinyan Sheloshah." It's a concept that the Hakhamim discuss.

Now, there are many Halakhot and Minhagim that are integrated when it comes to Bar Missvah. People have already anticipated that I'm going to be discussing in this life cycles episodes the Minhagim of Bar Missvah. They've already started sending in their questions: what are the various Minhagim for the Tefillin? What about speeches? What about parties? What about the winding of the Ressu'ot, the straps around the boy's arms? What other Minhagim? What peculiar to our community? When did they start going away? What kind of Pizmonim? What about saying Tahanunim, not Tahanunim? We're going to get to all these various Minhagim in upcoming episodes.

But please, don't wait for me to say something, or for me to possibly leave out something that you're waiting for. Write in your questions: minhag@scaupdates.org. Address them to me, Joey Mosseri, regarding Bar Missvah Minhagim, and BeEzrat HaShem, I'll be sure to get to them. Thank you.

137.title: Customs of Tu BiShbat
137.text:
According to the Talmud, the 15th of Shebat is a cutoff date regarding the laws of Ma'aser, tithes that are given from fruit that grows in the land of Israel, and for 'Orlah, laws regarding fruit that grows from a tree within the first several years from when it was planted. However, in later times, a custom developed, originally by the Ashkenazim, to eat fruits on that day that is commonly referred to as Tu BiShbat.

In the 16th century, Ribbi Yissakhar ben Susan HaMa'arabi, who was originally from North Africa and later moved to the city of Safed in the land of Israel, documented the custom of the Ashkenazim to eat fruit on Tu BiShbat in his book Tikkun Yissakhar. The custom was eventually accepted by the Sefaradim as well, after it was endorsed and promoted by the Mekubbalim, the authorities on mystical teachings.

By the 19th century, Ribbi Hayyim Palachi, the chief rabbi of Izmir, Turkey, wrote that serving fruit on the night of Tu BiShbat is the custom in the majority of Jewish communities. He wrote this in his book Mo'ed LeKhol Hai.

The book Derekh Eress recorded the custom of Halab, which was to make an effort to acquire all of the fruits that are available on the market at that time of the year, with a special emphasis on having the seven species that are associated with the land of Israel, namely: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates.

In the Middle East, it was customary to conduct a reading prior to enjoying the pastries, fruits, and nuts. In Halab, it was customary to read the Asher Kalamat, an Arabic translation and explanation of the Ten Commandments. They read that because Tu BiShbat always falls out one week or less before the reading of the Ten Commandments in Parashat Yitro. In Damascus, they read Mishnayot. They would read Masekhet Rosh HaShanah that mentions Tu BiShbat, and Masekhet Berakhot that discusses blessings, including blessings that are recited before eating fruits. Other Middle Eastern communities read from a book called Peri 'Ess Hadar that was originally composed in the beginning of the 18th century. It includes passages from the Tanakh, the Mishnah, and the Zohar that are related to fruit.

In Aleppo, it was customary to sing an Arabic folk song in honor of Tu BiShbat that mentioned the various foods and drinks that were served and the humorous reactions of the guests. They the song mentions slia, atayef, arak, and some of the fruits that were served as well.

In Halab, the holiday was called Eid al-Shajar, the holiday of the trees. The women would prepare special bags for the children, with each child's name embroidered on their bag. The bag was then filled with fruit and other treats from the Tu BiShbat table.

The night of the holiday was very festive in Halab, with family and friends gathering together around the table, reading, singing, and reciting Berakhot upon the large array of pastries, fruits, nuts, and drinks: Mezonot on the pastries, HaGefen on the wine, Ha'Ess and HaAdamah on the fruit and nuts, and many try to find a new fruit for the night of Tu BiShbat in order to be able to recite Sheheheyanu. Wishing you all a happy and healthy Tu BiShbat.

138.title: Mi SheBerakh and Hashkabot Customs
138.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. And we want to continue with the Minhagim surrounding the Mi SheBerakh prayer, the prayer that and the blessing that someone receives when they after they're getting 'Aliyah. Before that, I want to revisit my last video about the Hashkabot, being that some of you sent in some questions, and we appreciate the comments and the questions, and we encourage all those if they want clarification or they want us to cover other topics, please let us know. Tizku LeMissvot.

So, going back to the Hashkabot, the prayer, the memorial prayer for the deceased, someone asked, when do we say it? So, obviously, as I mentioned, the first year, whenever someone from the family goes up to the Sefer, they will Terahamu, they will make the memorial prayer on the deceased, the Hashkabah, which is found on page 289 in the Kol Ya'akob, one for men, one for women.

Following that, the week of the date of the passing, anniversary of the passing, which is called the Ma'ad, or Ashkenazim say the yahrzeit, so that Shabbat someone will go for the family. But it's not limited to that week of the year. There's been a custom in our community for many, many years, way, way back, that during the high holidays or the Shalosh Regalim, someone goes up to the Sefer, they will make Hashkabot for family members who have deceased. In addition, if there's a farah in the family, I've seen many families have this custom, when there is a happy occasion in the family, they will the one, the Ba'al HaSimhah, when he goes up to the Sefer, will make Hashkabah if someone from the immediate family has passed away.

Now, it's also it's not limited to family members. People can make Hashkabot when they go up for somebody, a friend, someone they respected, someone they knew very well. It's not limited to family members. Anybody can make Hashkabot. And the another question came in: Do the family members stand up when Hashkabah? So, the immediate family does stand up when Hashkabah is being said for someone in their family. Beyond the immediate family, no, unless it's for a big Hakham, as we mentioned, someone who served the community in a rabbinical capacity, so they will say "VeHaHokhmah MeAyin Timmasse," in which case the entire Kahal will stand up.

The prayer is said, this Hashkabah prayer is said in a normal tone. It's not, you know, said in a very loud voice. It's a personal, solemn prayer that really has no it's not made for the Sibbur. So there's no reason for the Kore or the Somekh, whoever is making this, to say it in a very loud voice, as opposed to the Mi SheBerakh, which is done in a louder voice.

Before I get to the Mi SheBerakh, I'll talk about Mi SheBerakh for a Holeh. If someone needs, feels the need to someone was very ill in the family, after the he has had the Hashkabot, and then they will do Mi SheBerakh for a Holeh if he needs to, and they will add "Shabbat Hi MiLiz'ok URefuah Kerobah Labo."

Now, for the Mi SheBerakh, it's the custom is that the one gets an 'Aliyah will give a donation, right? And that's called the Mi SheBerakh. We say in Arabic, we use it as a verb, in shabberakh, to shabberakh somebody is to make them a Mi SheBerakh. So, generally, the amounts that they give, they can give Matenat Yado, which means they don't want to set a specific sum, and they'll give whatever they can, or they'll give a donation.

And many, many times you'll see the donations follow a pattern of like these symbolic numbers, like 18, Hai, the numerical value of the word Hai, or the numerical value of the word of the name of God, Yod-Ke-Vav-Ke, which is 26, and 52 would be two times that, or Eliyahu, 101, Mikha'el, and so on and so you'll see a lot of times these numbers are used for these symbolic reasons. The usually some synagogues will put a little plaque on the Tebah indicating a list of suggested donations: the synagogue, the Mikveh, Ma'ot LaEbyonim, Bikkur Holim, and so on. So someone wants to give, I remember when I was young in Shaare Zion, they had this plaque and somebody would someone would just say, let's say, 101 to all the Sedarim, to the whole list.

And it's important because the one there's somebody in the Kahal who's keeping record of the donations. And it's very important to keep record so we could bill the people properly, so they don't, Has VeShalom, are violating the this the Neder that they give. Even though some people say "Beli Neder," but nonetheless if someone makes a pledge, it's important that the synagogues keep track so they can bill them accordingly. So that's another reason why it has to be said out loud so a person could hear clearly and keep the records appropriately.

Now we say "Me'ah VeEhad" or "me'a wahed," we'll say it in Arabic, or 52, and we'll say "LaMikdash." Mikdash to the Temple. Now this, some Hakhamim said you know, you really shouldn't say the word LaMikdash, as it could be the Bet HaMikdash and inferences to that, but that's not, it's a concern for some Hakhamim, but our custom has always been to say LaMikdash, because meaning the synagogue, Mikdash Me'at. And that's the custom till today to say LaMikdash.

And then of course we'll say when they say his name, again we said his given name, his family name, and the Laqab, the nickname of the family. And it's very important that the Kore and or the Somekh, the one who's making the Mi SheBerakh, know that person very well, his family situation. So when he says "LeHayye," the life of, he could say "Abiv," "Immo," "Ishto," "Banav," he knows exactly the situation, and he does it properly. Kol Tub.

139.title: The Bar Missvah Speech
139.text:
SCA Minhag of the week, Lifecycles: Bar Missvah. As we mentioned in our last video, there are many aspects of various Halakhot and Minhagim associated with the Bar Missvah. One Minhag that has pretty much fallen to the wayside is the speech. Yes, people hear Bar Missvah speech and they begin to cringe. They have no idea what a Bar Missvah speech even is nowadays, and we have, thankfully, examples of what was actually done in our community.

A boy at his Bar Missvah would give a speech, and not just a speech talking about what people think about today, but rather an intricate, detailed speech dealing with Talet, Tefillin, with the Parashah, with a subject that permeates the Torah in specific detail, and it was done in Hebrew.

First, we have Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin talking about his Bar Missvah in Yerushalayim at the age of 12, where he gave a detailed, intricate Derashah in front of the Hakhamim of the city. But you'll say, okay, that's Minhag of Yerushalayim, but what about our Minhag? What about the Halabi Minhag? What about what was done here in the United States within the Halabi community?

So, thankfully, we have examples of that. Rabbi Ya'akob Malah, the father of the late Moe Malah, the many-year president of Magen David, in fact wrote a Bar Missvah speech for his son, for Moe Malah, in 1938, and he even published it. Seven detailed printed pages, a great speech, something that you would think a chief rabbi is making the speech.

You'll say, okay, that's an isolated case, but it's not an isolated case at all. The famed Hazzan, Hakham Moshe Ashear, Moses Ashear, who was the Hazzan of the community until his passing in 1941, wrote speeches for many, many Bar Missvah boys in the community, and recently the family has gathered them and prepared them for publication. There are scores of Bar Missvah speeches in here for so many people in the community that you know. Your own grandparents may have a Bar Missvah speech over here.

And we see detailed, beautiful speeches talking about the love of Torah and Missvot, and they would give these speeches in Hebrew to the entire Kahal. This was something that was done on the Shabbat of the Bar Missvah. It's a beautiful Minhag. It's a Minhag that unfortunately has fallen to the wayside. People don't seem to have the patience to wait and to listen and realize and understand, but it's something that connects the Bar Missvah to the Torah, it makes the day extra special for him, and it keeps him connected to the Torah, to Missvot, Ma'asim Tobim, which is the purpose of bringing the boy to fruition at the age of 13 years and one day.

140.title: Daytime Kiddush on Alcoholic Beverages
140.text:
According to Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, one may only use an alcoholic beverage other than wine for Kiddush on Shabbat day in a place where wine or grape juice is not available. However, the custom of many Ashkenazim is to be lenient and to use other alcoholic beverages for Kiddush on Shabbat day, even in a place where wine or grape juice is available.

This custom dates back to the 14th century, when the Agudah, a halakhic authority from Germany, was lenient with this. The custom was recorded by Mahari Weil in the 15th century in Germany. Furthermore, Ribbi Shelomo Luria, otherwise known as the Maharshal, used to recite Kiddush on other alcoholic beverages, even though wine was available, in Poland in the 16th century. The Nahalat Sebi, an authority from Ukraine in the 17th century, explained that since the obligation to recite Kiddush again during the day is rabbinical, they are lenient and recite it on other alcoholic beverages, even though wine is available.

The Magen Abraham, an authority from Poland during the 17th century, resolved the custom by explaining that since the daytime Kiddush is only a blessing on wine, and bread is also valid for Kiddush, so you also fulfill your obligation for Kiddush afterwards when you recite HaMossi, especially if you prefer the bread over the wine, and therefore the blessing beforehand on the drink is just so it won't look like you are eating without reciting Kiddush, and therefore it's okay to be lenient with the drink itself and use another alcoholic beverage other than wine.

The Mishnah Berurah quoted the Hayye Adam, an 18th-century authority from Poland, who wrote that in a place where people prefer other alcoholic beverages over wine, they may use the other beverages even to begin with for the daytime Kiddush.

Up until now, we have discussed the custom of the Ashkenazim, but what about the Syrian custom? Normally we follow the rulings of Maran, who in this case requires wine or grape juice for the daytime Kiddush, unless it's not available, in which case he permits using other alcoholic beverages. However, Hakham Yosef Yedid HaLevi, who was born in Halab in 1867 and later moved to Israel in 1890, wrote in his book Yeme Yosef Batra, "On Shabbat day, I always recite Kiddush on Shekhar, an alcoholic beverage, and then I eat something with it before beginning the meal."

Furthermore, Ribbi 'Amram Aburbeh, who was born in Morocco towards the end of the 19th century and moved to Israel at the age of 14, wrote in his book Netibe 'Am, "The custom of the Sefaradim in Jerusalem is to recite Kiddush on an alcoholic beverage, even though wine is available." And he explained that they did this because they made Kiddush after an early Minyan before a dairy breakfast, where they preferred an alcoholic beverage over wine.

Similarly, Ribbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that the elders that came from Halab to Argentina would recite Kiddush on arak, and that Hakham Yisshak Shahrabani, 'Alav HaShalom, used to recite Kiddush on beer and sometimes on whiskey. Hakham Yosef Sha'yo told me that his grandfather, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, 'Alav HaShalom, brought a silver vessel with him from Halab to Jerusalem in the year 1935 that they used to fill with arak for the daytime Kiddush, and they would pass the vessel around so that after everyone drank a little, it would add up to the minimum requirement of drinking a little more than an ounce and a half from the Kiddush cup. Likewise, Ribbi 'Amram Aburbeh specified that they filled a cup that held at least three ounces of liquid.

But there are some authorities that were even lenient with the size of the cup and the amount that they drank from the Kiddush cup on Shabbat day. This is based on the opinion of the Ture Zahab, a 17th-century authority from Ukraine, who wrote that with regards to reciting Bore Nefashot after a strong alcoholic beverage, that since people do not normally drink three ounces of a strong alcoholic beverage at once, that one should recite Bore Nefashot after the amount that one normally drinks of that type of beverage. So even though we don't follow that opinion with regards to reciting Bore Nefashot, since the other authorities disagree, and when there is a disagreement regarding reciting a blessing, we remain passive and do not recite it, but with regards to the daytime Kiddush, some were lenient to consider a small cup of a strong alcoholic beverage as the equivalent of three ounces of wine, and drink the amount that one normally drinks of that beverage, even though it's less than the normal requirement of more than an ounce and a half. They did this since the daytime Kiddush is a rabbinical obligation, and one can rely on a lenient opinion in for rabbinical obligations, when a custom developed like the lenient opinion.

The Peri Megadim, an 18th-century authority from Ukraine, wrote that based on the opinion of the Ture Zahab regarding reciting a blessing after a small quantity of a strong alcoholic beverage, that we can recite the daytime Kiddush on that smaller quantity. The Hatam Sofer, another 18th-century authority from Germany and Slovakia, followed the Peri Megadim in applying the opinion of the Ture Zahab to the daytime Kiddush. Both of these opinions were cited as the Halakhah by HaRab Sebi Pesah Frank, a Lithuanian authority who moved to Israel at the end of the 19th century, in his responsa Har Sebi. But the Mishnah Berurah quoted the Hayye Adam, who did require using at least 3 oz, even for a strong alcoholic beverage, and drinking more than an ounce and a half from the Kiddush cup, at the very least between several people.

So while Maran requires one to use wine or grape juice for the daytime Kiddush, unless it was not available, the custom of many Ashkenazim is to use other alcoholic beverages even if wine or grape juice is available. Similarly, in Syria, they would recite the daytime Kiddush on arak or other alcoholic beverages, and this custom continued in Argentina, New York, and in other Syrian Jewish communities around the world. This was also the custom of the Sefaradim in Jerusalem as well. Many were careful to use at least 3 oz, even when reciting Kiddush on a strong alcoholic beverage, and to drink more than an ounce and a half from the Kiddush cup, at least between several people. However, some were lenient to recite the daytime Kiddush even on less than 3 oz, and to drink the amount that one normally drinks of a strong alcoholic beverage, based on the opinion of several authorities. All these leniencies may only be applied to the daytime Kiddush. On Friday night, one may not recite Kiddush on alcoholic beverages other than wine. One must use at least 3 oz of wine or grape juice, and one person must drink more than an ounce and a half from the Kiddush cup.
