141.title: Standing for the Hakham's 'Aliyah
141.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are discussing the Minhagim relating to the reading of the Sefer Torah, Shabbat morning in the synagogue, and before we continue with the Musaf, we do want to address the questions, inquiries, concerns, comments that we've been receiving from our Kahal of listeners. Really, we very much appreciate it. Hazakim UBerukhim, Tizku LeMissvot. It gives us a lot of strength when you do comment and send in your questions.

One of the questions, actually, that a number of you requested that we state the custom in Brooklyn in the Halabi community is: Do we stand up for the 'Aliyah of the when the rabbi goes up to the Sefer? Does the Kahal all stand the way we would stand for a father, grandfather, uncle, as we discussed in previous videos? Now, before I state the custom, I did want to preface it by saying that Sefaradim in general and our community really in particular is very, very well known for the tremendous and well-deserved reverence and respect and honor and admiration we show our Hakhamim. It's a hallmark of the Syrian community. The Posekim, the Dayyanim, the Hakhamim, these are the light of our eyes, Me'or 'Enenu, and it's a very, very great practice and great feeling that we have towards our Hakhamim.

That being said, the custom was never for the Kahal to stand up during the 'Aliyah of the Hakham of the Kehillah or Hakham in general. It was not our custom as we do for father or grandfather. We've been blessed since we came to the shores of New York to have great, world-renowned Hakhamim serve our community in various capacities: Hakham 'Ezra Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, who came from Halab, and Hakham Moshe Sabbagh, and I won't list all the names, but certainly Hakham Matloub Abadi, one of our great Posekim, Zekher Saddik LiBrakhah, our great greatest of leaders, our Chief Rabbi Ya'akob Shaul Kassin, Zekher Saddik LiBrakhah, of course, the our great teacher and Posek, Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim, Zekher Saddik LiBrakhah, just to name some of the Hakhamim, but we never saw in any of the Kehillot that they served, in Shaare Zion or other Kehillot, when they went up to the Sefer, the Kahal did not stand up for the 'Aliyah. Of course, when they make their approach towards the Sefer, we would do the Hiddur Missvah as is required, and certainly, when they finish the 'Aliyah, the entire Kahal would go to up to them to shake their hand and tell them "Hazak UBarukh" and receive a blessing in return: "Hazak," "Hazak VeEmass," "Hizku VeImmesu." We did not have the custom to kiss their hands, but we would shake their hands, and that was the custom in our community from the day we landed on the shores, I would imagine that was the custom also in Halab.

Now, I did want to discuss two other customs which came up about a week and a half ago when we read Parashat Yitro, and it's relevant. There's a custom among some Kehillot, Ashkenaz mainly and but also some Kehillot Sefaradiyot, where they would stand up for the reading of the 'Aseret HaDibrot, the Ten Commandments, which we read in Parashat Yitro. The custom, Egyptian custom, Aleppian, Iraqi custom was not to stand up, and most Kehillot Sefaradiyot, certainly in Yerushalayim today where Minhag Yerushalayim is not to stand up, and it'd be very hard-pressed to find a Minyan of Sefaradim which do stand up for 'Aseret HaDibrot. Our custom is clear and well-known that we do not stand up. It's based on a Gemara in Berakhot that we don't show extra preference to the 'Aseret HaDibrot, so we don't open the door for misunderstanding of what came from Sinai. The whole Torah came from Sinai, so we don't want to show extra preference to the 'Aseret HaDibrot. Based on that Gemara, Rambam was emphatic, used very strong language to say we do not stand up for 'Aseret HaDibrot, and the Aleppian tradition, as I mentioned, is clear that we do not stand up.

Another tradition which is certainly our tradition as well, as well as many Kehillot Sefaradiyot, is that we send up the Hakham for this 'Aliyah. And this is not all Kehillot around the world, but certainly our Kahal and all the, most Sefaradi Kehillot do send up the rabbi for this 'Aliyah. So to review, we do not stand up for 'Aseret HaDibrot, and we do send up the Hakham. Now just to put it all together and to make a point regarding standing up for the rabbi, going back to my original question, certainly we don't need to have proof for it. You could ask anybody who's lived in our community, ask any of the elders. It's something which we did not see ever. We don't see it in Yerushalayim either, to stand up for the rabbi for the 'Aliyah. But I just want to make a point, again, not that we need a proof, but just to make a point that if it's so clear that the custom is not to stand up for 'Aseret HaDibrot, and if it's always the rabbi that goes up for 'Aseret HaDibrot, well, there you have it. That shows that we did not stand up for the 'Aliyah of the rabbi in general on any of the 'Aliyot. Kol Tub, LeHitraot.

142.title: Bar Missvah Talet and Tefillin
142.text:
SCA Minhag of the week, life cycles, Bar Missvah. So as we've been speaking about the Bar Missvah and reaching the age of 13, reading from the Torah, there's also the weekday morning ceremony, usually happening on a Monday or Thursday morning or even Rosh Hodesh morning, because people generally would like to do on the morning of Sefer Torah, but it of course can be done on any day of the week. What really happens that morning? It's the first morning that this Bar Missvah boy gets his new Talet, new Tefillin, he's putting them on for the first time in a public ceremony. So what exactly transpires?

So used to be that the Bar Missvah boy would receive a gorgeous, brand-new silk blue-and-white Talet, something that we don't really see often nowadays, usually nowadays we see more of a white woolen Talet, but back then the Talet was silk as we see in old pictures from Turkey, from Syria, from Egypt, from Iraq, from many other places. Even the Sissiyot, the strings, were silk. And it was a very, very special garment. It was exciting for everybody there.

So first the boy would put, before putting on the Talet, he would make the Berakhah of "LeHit'attef BeSissit," followed by the Berakhah of "Sheheheyanu," then he would wrap himself in the Talet. We get up to the Tefillin now. Tefillin, he'll be wearing them for the first time as well. He sits down, makes the Berakhah of "LeHani'ah Tefillin," knots that Tefillin to his forearm, or rather Tefillah to the forearm, and the Ressu'ot, the strap that he is supposed to wind around his arm, he doesn't do it himself, rather those are given out as honors.

Important people: grandfathers, father, older uncles, possibly the teacher who taught him and prepared him for the Bar Missvah, taught him the Te'amim, how to read the Sefer Torah, maybe some Hakhamim, depending on who the family has decided to give the honor to, and who happens to be there at the time. So each one of these seven straps is given out, like I said, grandfathers first, followed by father, and then others, and then finally he has to put on the Tefillah Shel Rosh, and that honor is given to the most senior and greatest of the Hakhamim, the Chief Rabbi usually if possible, or the rabbi of the Bet Keneset, or the family rabbi. He'll come and put on the Tefillin Shel Rosh, crowning him with this Missvah of Tefillin.

Finally, the boy wraps the Tefillin straps around his middle finger, says the Pesukim of "VeErastikh Li Le'Olam," and all this is done to make the Missvah of the Tefillin beloved to him, showing him, "Here, we are your elders, and we love this Missvah, and we are now welcoming you into our crowd. You're part of our circle, you're a man now, that you're going to be wearing Talet and Tefillin with us every day. We love it so much, we want you to love it so much. Welcome aboard." And this is how the start of the Bar Missvah day begins.

143.title: Minhah After Peleg Minhah
143.text:
The custom in the Syrian community is that whenever we recite Minhah after Peleg Minhah, we omit the additional supplications after reciting VaYa'abor, meaning we skip "Rahum VeHannun Hatanu Lefanekha," "LeDavid," and "Abinu Malkenu." But in other Middle Eastern communities, these paragraphs are recited in Minhah, even when Minhah is recited until sunset.

Peleg Minhah is 75 variable minutes before sunset, which is the earliest time that 'Arbit could be recited. I would like to point out that our custom is to call that time period Peleg Minhah, not Pelag Minhah. Peleg is also grammatically correct, like we say Melekh Yisrael. Melekh doesn't change to Melakh when it's together with Yisrael. Likewise, Peleg doesn't change to Pelag when it's together with Minhah.

In any case, our custom of omitting these paragraphs when Minhah is recited after Peleg Minhah was documented in the book Derekh Eress as the custom of Aleppo, quoting Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, 'Alav HaShalom, who reported that this custom was practiced with the approval of the leading rabbis of Halab, including Hakham 'Ezra Hamwey Kabbaz, Hakham Moshe Mizrahi, Hakham 'Ezra Abadi Sha'yo, and Hakham Moshe Tawil. Hakham Yisshak Zafrani explained that since according to one opinion in the Gemara, the opinion of Rabbi Yehudah, it's too late to recite Minhah after Peleg Minhah. Now even though we are not bound by that opinion, and we do still recite Minhah after Peleg Minhah, we only recite Minhah, which is obligatory, but we skip those penitential prayers, which halakhically speaking, are optional, since we apply the rule of "Sheb VeAl Ta'aseh 'Adif." In certain halakhic situations, it's preferable to remain passive. Here we are avoiding reciting a halakhically optional part of the Minhah prayer, since it's already too late to recite Minhah according to Rabbi Yehudah.

The fact that Nefilat Appayim, reciting LeDavid is optional, was quoted by the Tur in the name of Rab Natronai Gaon. The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer explained that according to the opinion that reciting LeDavid is optional, custom dictates when it is said or not said. Furthermore, according to Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, "En Nefilat Appayim BaLailah," LeDavid is not recited at night. Since we consider the time after Peleg Minhah is nighttime in some respects, as we would begin reciting 'Arbit after Peleg Minhah, we don't recite LeDavid at that time, again because we apply the rule of "Sheb VeAl Ta'aseh 'Adif," remain passive regarding reciting something that is not an actual obligation at a time when according to one opinion it should no longer be recited at all.

One last point: Peleg Minhah can either be calculated where the day begins at sunrise and ends at sunset, or where the day begins at dawn and ends at nightfall. The book Derekh Eress specified that the time of Peleg Minhah is one and a quarter hours before sunset. That is also the time that synagogues in our community begin praying 'Arbit, which is listed on the time charts as Peleg Minhah according to the HaGra, otherwise known as the Gaon from Vilna. This calculation of Peleg Minhah comes out earlier than if we begin the day at dawn and end at nightfall. Therefore, we already refrain from reciting LeDavid after the earlier calculation of Peleg Minhah.

All this is when we recite Minhah after Peleg, but when reciting Minhah before Peleg Minhah, we recite these paragraphs beginning with "Rahum VeHannun Hatanu," "LeDavid," and "Abinu Malkenu."

144.title: Blessings Recited by the Hakham
144.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the Minhagim dealing with the reading of the Sefer Torah and the Sibbur. We will now continue with the prayers. The Maftir, following the reading of the Haftarah and reciting of the Berakhot, does Hashkabot, Mi SheBerakh, he leaves the Tebah, and now generally it is the Rabbi of the Kahal, the Hakham, who will now approach the Tebah and begin a series of blessings, which is found in Kol Ya'akob, if you wish to follow, on page 290.

He begins with what we call the Berakhah LaMemshalah. It's a blessing for the head of state. In the case of the United States, it's the President of the United States and his advisors, that they should be protected, and they should succeed in their endeavors, and most importantly, they should look favorably upon the Jewish population and deal favorably with them. He will begin saying it in a clear voice, a loud voice, "HaNoten Teshu'ah LaMelakhim," and the Kahal will join in on the third line. When he says, "VeHaNoten BaYam Darekh," the Kahal will answer, "UMayim 'Azim Netibah!" And then he goes on to bless, "Yishmor VeYinssor." Here it says, "Rashe HaMemshalah VeYo'assehem." Obviously, in the case of the United States, it's "Nesi Arssot HaBerit." He doesn't necessarily have to mention the name, he's mentioning the office and the title. He can, is that is not required. Generally, if I recall, 'Alav HaShalom, Hakham Ya'akob Kassin, our esteemed Chief Rabbi, when he used to come and make these blessings, he did not generally mention the name, but "Nesi Arssot HaBerit" and blesses him, "Melekh Malkhe HaMelakhim," and so on. "VeKhen Yehi Rasson, VeNomar Amen."

Following the blessing of the government is the blessing to the Kahal, which is very, very important. The Kahal is quiet, they're listening to the blessing that the Hakham will say in a very loud and clear voice, "Mi SheBerakh Abotenu," on page 291: "Abraham, Yisshak VeYa'akob, Moshe VeAharon, David UShelomo." I've heard many Halabi Hakhamim who'll say "Moshe VeAharon, VeHaMelekh David, VeHaMelekh Shelomo." Just a little textual nuance, but that's the way we do it at Ades. And he blesses the entire Kahal, "Gedolim, Ketanim, Hem UBnehem UNshehem, VeTalmidehem," and it ends up "Yosef 'Alekhem KaKhem Elef Pe'amim," a beautiful blessing. "VeKhen Yehi Rasson, VeNomar Amen."

He continues with Birkat HaHodesh when the Shabbat precedes the week where Rosh Hodesh will fall out on. He begins a series of "Yehi Rasson." "Yehi Rasson LeHadesh Et Hayyenu," to protect us from calamities, to strengthen our Hakhamim, and to generally pray for good news, Besorot Tobot. Following that, he says "Mi She'asah Nissim LaAbotenu." He mentions the month in a Rosh Hodesh, Nisan, let's say, "BeYom Rishon." If it's two days, he will say "BeYom Rishon UMahorato BeYom Sheni." Following the mentioning of the days, the Kahal will join in and say, "BeSiman Tob!" Now, here, our custom, unlike other communities, our custom is to remain seated. The Kahal remains seated for the Birkat HaHodesh. Most other Kehillot in the world, from what I've witnessed, they stand up, like the Minhag is in Yerushalayim. The custom of the Halabi community is to remain seated.

If the final announcement he makes is that if there's a fast day coming up that week, Shib'ah 'Asar BeTammuz, 'Asarah BeTebet, he will say the prayer "Ahenu Bet Yisrael Shema'u," it's an announcement of when the fast is going to be, and a prayer that the fast, BeEzrat HaShem, BiMherah BeYamenu, should become days of festivities and joy. We will continue in our next video, beginning the Musaf, the Minhagim related to the Musaf prayer. Kol Tub.

145.title: Ana or Yehi Shem on Bar Missvah
145.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: life cycles, Bar Missvah. So as we know, the Bar Missvah day, that morning of prayers, is a very celebratory one. The question arises: do we say Ana or Yehi Shem? Do we say Tahanunim, supplications, or do we omit them? And this is a bit of a tricky question, because as we've mentioned in the past, the entire Bar Missvah celebration is something that is fairly new, only the last few centuries. And this question about omitting Tahanunim, not saying Ana, is something that only began to arise in the last 120 years or so, and we first see anybody writing about it in 1908, nothing prior to that.

So we have scanty information on this topic, but we do know what we actually practice. So in practice, the Minhag of our community here in the United States is that on the Bar Missvah day, whether the boy is fully 13 years and one day or even younger than that, like we mentioned earlier, we start anywhere from approximately 12 years and six months, anytime during that six-month period that the celebration of the Bar Missvah happens, we omit Ana, we say Yehi Shem on that day.

Now what is this based upon? So as we said, the earliest source we have is the 1908 book called Nehar Missrayim by Hakham Refael Aharon ben Shim'on, and he basically compares a Bar Missvah boy to a Hatan as well as to a Milah. And he says Hatan because on the Hatan the Pasuk says, "KeHatan Yekhahen Pe'er," the groom adorns himself with his ornamental headdress, and this word that used is used is Pe'er, and the Hakhamim say Pe'er is Tefillin, like the Pasuk says, "Pe'erkha Habush LeRoshekha," your ornamental headdress is attached to your head. And the Milah, because the Pasuk from Megillat Ester says, "LaYehudim Hayetah Orah VeSimhah VeSason ViKar," and the Gemara says Sason is Milah and Yekar is Tefillin, so once again putting Tefillin together with Milah. So therefore, since the Hatan Bar Missvah, the Bar Missvah boy, is like a Hatan as well as like Milah, we omit Ana on that day, we do not say Tahanunim, and we only say Yehi Shem.

But was this always the case, and is that the case of other Halabi communities? So we have an interesting testimony from Hakham Yisshak Alfiah. Hakham Yisshak Alfiah was one of the all-time Hakhamim of Halab who made 'Aliyah to Yerushalayim. In his book Siah Yisshak from 1923, he says, no, in fact this is a new question that's being posed whether to say Ana or not, and in fact the old custom at least here in Yerushalayim is that Ana is in fact said. And he doesn't say Halab, but he's hinting that in Halab it was said as well. Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya in his Yaskil 'Abdi also doesn't mention anything about Yehi Shem when being posed with this question, but he seems to say, look at what Rabbi Alfiah says, follow Rabbi Alfiah.

We know in fact that until the last Jew left Halab, they were still saying Ana on this day of the Bar Missvah. But here in Brooklyn, the custom is to in fact say Yehi Shem, it's based upon the chief rabbi of Israel, initially the Mishpete 'Uzi'el, Rabbi Ben Siyyon Meir Hai 'Uzi'el who wrote it in his Mishpete 'Uzi'el volume three in the 1940s, and then later on Hakham 'Obadia Yosef in his Yabia' Omer also wrote the same thing to say Yehi Shem, not Ana, on the day of the Bar Missvah. So even though as we mentioned, we know the Minhag of Halab, as recorded in the book Derekh Eress quoting Rabbi Nissim Zafrani says that Minhag of Halab was to say Ana, in our community we say Yehi Shem.

What about in other Halabi communities? So in Argentina they used to say Yehi Shem, and Hakham Yisshak Chehebar stopped them from saying it, because he only wanted them to say it if the boy was fully 13 years and one day. And since they weren't adhering to that, he said from now on, no more Yehi Shem for the Bar Missvah day, no matter how old he is, only Ana. Once again, our community, we say Yehi Shem, and that's correctly recorded in our Siddur Kol Ya'akob.

146.title: The Half Shekel Custom in Halab
146.text:
During the times of the Bet HaMikdash, males 13 and over were obligated to give a silver half shekel annually to the Bet HaMikdash. A half a shekel is the equivalent of nine grams of silver. The money paid for the public sacrifices and offerings that were made throughout the year. Since that time, a custom developed to give money to charity every year in memory of the half shekel that was obligatory during the times of the Bet HaMikdash. This custom goes back to at least the eighth century, as we find a reference to it in Masekhet Soferim, which was composed around the eighth century. It is also referred to in a responsa from the Geonim from the same time period.

Interestingly, there is no reference to this custom by HaRambam, or even by Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. But still and all, it was customary to give money in memory of the half shekel in Halab. Towards the end of the 18th century, the chief rabbi of Halab at that time, Ribbi Refael Shelomo Laniado, wrote in his book Bet Dino Shel Shelomo that in his opinion, one should not use money set aside for Ma'aser to fulfill the custom of giving money for the half shekel. And his son, Hakham Efrayim Laniado, who succeeded his father as the chief rabbi of Halab, wrote in his book Degel Mahaneh Efrayim that his father sent the Shamash to collect the half shekel from everyone, men, women, and for children of all ages, so that the charity donated would be an atonement for the entire community.

Hakham Abraham Antebi, who was the chief rabbi of Halab in the beginning of the 19th century, wrote in his book Ohel Yesharim that one is obligated to give money for the half shekel, and that the custom is like any other requirement. Based on the writing of Muram, an Ashkenazic authority from the 16th century, he said that they should really give more than was customary in order to fulfill the custom properly. Other Aleppian rabbis that refer to the giving of money for the half shekel include Hakham Mordekhai Abadi in his book Ma'ayan Ganim, Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his book He'anah Nafshenu, and Hakham Yisshak Alfiah in his book Kunteres HaYehieli.

In Halab, the money collected for the half shekel was used to buy Massot for the rabbis and anyone in need. This was documented by Hakham Yosef Sethon, who was born in Halab in the year 1813, in his book VaYimssa Yosef, and by Hakham Ya'akob Dwek, who was born in Halab in 1828, in his book She'erit Ya'akob. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, who was born in Halab in 1893, also wrote that the money was used to buy Massot for the rabbis and others that needed assistance. He also wrote that between Rosh Hodesh Adar and Purim, two rabbis sat in the Kenis every morning to collect money for the half shekel, and in every Minyan, the Shamash would announce, "Mahassit HaShekel," to encourage everyone to give. And if someone didn't give, they sent someone to collect from him. The amount that they gave was half a Mejidi per person. The Mejidi was a Turkish currency that was in use in Halab at that time. All of this was documented in his book on the customs of Aram Soba.

Giving half of the currency used in your location was documented as the custom by Ribbi Yehudah 'Ayash, an 18th-century authority from Algeria, in his book Mateh Yehudah. However, Ribbi Yosef David, an authority from Salonika in the 17th and 18th centuries, wrote that one should give the value of nine grams of silver. He wrote this in his book Bet David. Interestingly, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar instructed his community in Argentina to give the value of nine grams of silver. Rabbi Abraham Ades wrote that he heard from Hakham Yisshak Tawil that in his times, around the 1940s, they did not collect money for the half shekel in Halab, but they did collect money for his father's Yeshibah, Degel Torah, in the Kenis on the morning of Purim.

So we see that the custom of giving money in memory of the obligatory half shekel was first recorded in the eighth century, and was practiced in Halab at least since the 18th century. In Halab, they gave a half of their currency, and the money was used to buy Massot for the rabbis and others who needed assistance. Others give the value of nine grams of silver, which was adopted by Hakham Yisshak Chehebar when he was the rabbi of Argentina. In later times in Halab, they did not collect money for the half shekel, but they did collect money for the Yeshibah on the morning of Purim.

147.title: Returning the Sefer Before Musaf
147.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the various blessings given to the Kahal, the Mi SheBerakh, following the completion of the reading of the Sefer Torah, we're ready to begin Musaf. As I said, it's generally the Hakham who comes to give these Berakhot, the Mi SheBerakh to the Kahal, or Rosh Hodesh, what not. And now it's time for Musaf. I'm on page 293 in the Kol Ya'akob if you wish to follow.

The overview is: the Hazzan comes up, Yehi Hasdekha, Ashre, Barukh HaShem Asher Natan Menuhah, Yimlokh, Mizmor LeDavid, take back while we take back the Sefer, Shubah LiM'onakh, Kaddish, 'Amidah.

Now into more detail. The Hazzan, generally the Hazzan begins with the Yehi Hasdekha, the one who's invited to say Musaf. I have seen on occasion where the one who was at the Tebah, whether it be the Hakham or Hazzan who said the Mi SheBerakh, will continue Yehi Hasdekha and Ashre, and then the Hazzan will begin in Shubah LiM'onakh, but in Brooklyn, the prevailing custom is when you say Kabod Musaf, he comes up and he begins with Yehi Hasdekha.

Now which Maqam does he pray in? Which scale, liturgical scale does he use? Here is a couple of opinions: the prevailing custom, at least the last 30-40 years from my recollection, is that you will sing Musaf in the same scale as the following Shabbat's Maqam, the following scale of the following Shabbat's scale. So for instance, if let's say VaYiggash is Bayat, and VaYehi is the next Parashah is Hijaz, so you will say Musaf in Hijaz. That's the general custom.

There are, however, other opinions. One is, and Joey Mosseri was kind enough to share with me the notes of our esteemed Hazzan from the early part of the 20th century, Hakham Moshe Ashear, who has kept meticulous notes as to which scales he used and what tunes he used, and we see very interestingly he didn't follow this rule. He would say Musaf in different Maqamat without any connection to what's going to be said the following Shabbat. So that's opinion number two.

Finally, there's an interesting conversation that Joey Mosseri had with our famous Hazzan, 'Alav HaShalom, Beto Tawil. And he told Joey, he said, "Look, I, if the Shabbat is Bayat, I want Shahrit Bayat, I want Musaf Bayat, I want to leave the Kenis with that feeling for that Shabbat." So while that is rare to see, rare to find that a Hazzan will pray the same Maqam as Shahrit, this was his opinion, and it's an important opinion, so you have three opinions. Again, the prevailing custom is to say the Musaf with next week's Maqam.

So you will say Yehi Hasdekha, Barukh HaShem Asher Natan Menuhah, and he gets to Yimlokh. In Yimlokh, the Kahal will stand up because we're going to take back the Sefer. When do we begin taking back the Sefer? It all depends. Generally, when the Kahal sings Mizmor LeDavid, after they recite the Yimlokh twice, when the Sefer is on the Tebah, and then Mizmor LeDavid they will start taking it back. In the event where the Kenis is very large and takes a long time, you will find very often that they will begin Yimlokh, they will start taking the Sefer Torah back to the Hekhal.

Now, Yimlokh, unlike other communities, unlike the Egyptians or the in Yerushalayim certainly, we sing together both times the Yimlokh without having it sung and repeated. In other words, in Yerushalayim especially, they'll have or they'll have children come up, they will say Yimlokh, the Kahal will answer. They will say the second time, the Kahal will answer. That's not the custom of the Syrian community. We all sing it together twice, and we have a couple of basic tunes that we use: "Yimlokh Ad-onai Le'Olam," very famous tune. And one which is unique to, I think, the New York community is, "Yimlokh Ad-onai Le'Olam Elokayikh Siyyon." Now, I haven't heard that outside of the community ever, certainly not in Yerushalayim. Maybe it spread to Panama, Mexico by now, but it seemed that that may have been an American tune that was adapted to the Yimlokh. Of course, in Yerushalayim we sing a different tune: "Halleluyah Yimlokh Ad-onai Le'Olam Elokayikh Siyyon." That's the basic tune in Yerushalayim.

Following that, we have Mizmor LeDavid, which we all sing together. The Sefer Torah, as I mentioned in our video for Shahrit of the weekdays, the Sefer Torah, our custom is to bring it back while it is open to the Kahal. We do the reverse direction as when we brought it out. We bring it out to the right, and we go back, all right, the other side of the Kenis. So it makes sense, especially in a big Kenis, where you're showing the Sefer Torah to one side, you're putting it on the Hekhal. Now you go to the other side, you're showing it to the Hekhal. I know in many synagogues they've changed the custom, maybe based on Ben Ish Hai, but our custom was always to return it open.

Another point in the Yimlokh, we don't have a jedyad, what's called, what, are we, we call it just carrying the Sefer, but by the Egyptians, or even in Yerushalayim, while they're saying Yimlokh, the one who's carrying the Sefer will hold it up to the Kahal and turn it around, and then they'll set it down, and then they'll take it back for Mizmor LeDavid. We don't have that custom. We don't have the, as we mentioned when we took out the Sefer, and when we bring it back, that's not the custom, although other communities indeed do have that custom.

We'll continue next week with the Musaf prayer. Shalom UBerakhah.

148.title: Yehi Shem on the Bar Missvah Day
148.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: life cycles, Bar Missvah. This is a follow-up to my last episode, episode number 145, where I talked about Yehi Shem on the Bar Missvah day, Yehi Shem as opposed to Ana. Many people have come back to us and questioned us, how could it be that we are practicing here differently than what they did in Halab? I thought we're here to uphold our Halabi Minhagim. Yes, we are here to uphold our Halabi Minhagim, but some of those Minhagim developed differently. Let me explain.

So, we mentioned that in Halab, that on a Bar Missvah, they would say Ana, they would not say Yehi Shem. We also mentioned the practice in Argentina, where they used to say Yehi Shem, and then Hakham Yisshak Chehebar insisted that only if it's on the Bar Missvah day, the day that the boy turns 13 years and one day, do they say Yehi Shem, otherwise do Ana. And since he saw that people were not listening, and they were saying Yehi Shem no matter what day the Bar Missvah was, he laid out a blanket rule, from now on, every Bar Missvah is Ana, no matter what the day is. So, this clearly tells us that wasn't only in the United States where we were saying Yehi Shem, they were doing it in Argentina as well. That means there's something more to it, and something that has to go back to Halab, and something that the Hakhamim of the times have saw differently than what was going on in the past.

So, bring us back to Brooklyn. Hakham Leon Guindi, who was one of the Hakhamim in Halab, and is now currently one of the rabbis in our community in Brooklyn, recently told us that yes, the Minhag in Halab was to say Ana on the Bar Missvah day, but if it was the actual day of the Bar Missvah, 13 years and one day, even in Halab, they said Yehi Shem. So now this gives basis to the concept of Yehi Shem being said on the Bar Missvah day.

Let's go back now. Speaking to Rabbi Moshe Shammah of Sephardic, he mentioned that he recalls clearly in the 1940s Chief Rabbi Ya'akob Kassin coming to the kuttab and telling the boys that on his Bar Missvah in Jerusalem when he was a boy, they said Ana. He didn't recall though, speaking about Rabbi Shammah, did not recall what was going on in the community at the time in the 1940s, but from the 1950s forward, he clearly recalls every Bar Missvah being Yehi Shem and not Ana.

So what are the other rabbis telling us in the community? We have Rabbis Eli Ben-Haim and Rabbis Ya'akob Ben-Haim, the sons of Hakham Barukh, both telling us that the practice of their father, Hakham Barukh, was to always say Yehi Shem at every Bar Missvah, no matter if the boy was fully Bar Missvah, 13 years and one day, or celebrating prior to that. We also know that in 'Ateret Torah, Hakham Yosef Raful says to say Yehi Shem.

Interesting story that we recently found out about is that a community family traveled to Israel to celebrate their son's Bar Missvah in Jerusalem, this is about 35 or so years ago, and they were there celebrating, and they wanted to uphold the old custom of saying Ana since it wasn't the full Bar Missvah day of the boy. Present was Hakham Ben Siyyon Abba Shaul, and he said, "Absolutely not, you are not saying Ana, you are saying Yehi Shem." And he put his foot down that they say Yehi Shem. He said, "You're here to celebrate, you came here to celebrate, your family is excited, the boy is excited, this is a celebratory prayer, and you must say Yehi Shem."

So obviously based upon numerous sources and numerous Hakhamim, both from the Middle East, both and Halab, as well as Argentina, as well as New York, the established practice of saying Yehi Shem for a Bar Missvah day, no matter when it falls, is firmly ground. It is the practice of our community, as I mentioned, as clearly stated in the Kol Ya'akob Siddur, and another community Siddur, which did not mention it in the past, made no mention of the Bar Missvah, now tells us that in upcoming editions, they will add that to the instructions on days that you omit Tahanunim. So our community practice is to say Yehi Shem and not to say Ana on the Bar Missvah day.

Now, the next Halakhah deals with on the day of a Berit Milah. It is

149.title: Three Sifre Torah on Rosh Hodesh
149.text:
When Rosh Hodesh Nisan falls on Shabbat, like it does this year, we take out three Sifre Torah. We read the weekly Parashah from the first Sefer, the Rosh Hodesh portion is read from the second Sefer, and the special reading for Shabbat HaHodesh is read from the third Sefer.

According to Maran in the Bet Yosef, Kaddish is not recited after the first Sefer, because only six 'Olim are sent up to the first Sefer, which is less than the minimum amount of 'Olim for Shabbat morning. According to Maran, Kaddish is only recited after the second and third Sifre Torah. However, the custom in Halab was to send at least one extra 'Oleh to the first Sefer and to recite Kaddish after the first Sefer as well, for a total of three Kaddishim.

This custom was documented by Ribbi Refael Shelomo Laniado, the Chief Rabbi of Halab towards the end of the 18th century. In his book, Bet Dino Shel Shelomo, he wrote: "The custom of our city is to recite Kaddish between the first Sefer and the second Sefer on a day that three Sifre Torah are brought out. And the reason is because we always send up more than seven 'Olim to the first Sefer. The exception to this is Simhat Torah, when Kaddish is not recited after the first Sefer, based on Maran's second reason for not reciting Kaddish after the first Sefer on Simhat Torah, which is so it won't look like we don't want to begin Bereshit again. Therefore, we begin Bereshit immediately, with as little interruption as possible. And even though Maran's first reason of not saying Kaddish after the first Sefer on Simhat Torah is so that it will be similar to the Shabbatot when we take out three Sifre Torah, when Kaddish is not recited after the first Sefer, Rabbi Laniado explained that this reason only applies to a place that has a custom to send up six 'Olim to the first Sefer. But our custom is to send up at least seven 'Olim to the first Sefer, and we should maintain our custom," as Rabbi Laniado stated, "that anything that is dependent on custom should not be challenged or changed. We have our customs and others have theirs." And he continued saying that this custom of sending up at least seven 'Olim to the first Sefer was established by rabbis of previous generations in Halab, and therefore it would be improper for him to change it.

This custom of reciting Kaddish after each Sefer on a day that we take out three Sifre Torah was also documented by Hakham Abraham Antebi, who was the Chief Rabbi of Halab in the beginning of the 19th century. In his book, Hokhmah UMusar, he wrote: "On Rosh Hodesh Tebet that falls on Shabbat, when we also take out three Sifre Torah, a Kaddish is required after each Sefer Torah, according to our custom of sending up seven 'Olim to the first Sefer." According to the book, Derekh Eress, this custom of sending up at least seven 'Olim to the first Sefer and reciting Kaddish after each Sefer continued in Halab into the 1980s.

We take out three Sifre Torah when Rosh Hodesh Adar or Rosh Hodesh Nisan or Rosh Hodesh Tebet falls on Shabbat. In all these cases, we do not read the Haftarah for Rosh Hodesh. On Rosh Hodesh Adar, we read the Haftarah for Shekalim. On Rosh Hodesh Nisan, we read the Haftarah for HaHodesh. And on Rosh Hodesh Tebet, we read the Haftarah for Hanukkah.

In the Bet Yosef, Maran discusses two other cases when Rosh Hodesh falls on Shabbat, but the Haftarah for Rosh Hodesh is not read. One is Rosh Hodesh Ab, when we read the Haftarah for the Three Weeks, and the other is Rosh Hodesh Elul, which occurs during a series of seven Haftarot of comfort following Tish'ah BeAb. In those cases, Maran writes to add the first and last verse of the Rosh Hodesh Haftarah after the special Haftarah. However, our custom is not to add any verses from the Rosh Hodesh Haftarah. We only read the special Haftarah for that Shabbat without adding any additional verses.

Our custom was documented by Ribbi Yisshak Palachi in his book, Yafeh LaLeb. He explained that we don't read verses from different books of the Prophets in one Haftarah reading, as specified by Muram in his Hagahot: "En Medallegin MiNabi LeNabi," we don't jump from one book of the Prophets to another. So, since the Rosh Hodesh Haftarah is from the book of Yesha'yah, and the Haftarah for the special Shabbatot is usually from a different book of the Prophets, we don't add the verses from the Rosh Hodesh Haftarah. And even on Rosh Hodesh Elul, when the special Haftarah is also from the book of Yesha'yah, we still don't add the first and last verse from the Rosh Hodesh Haftarah.

Ribbi Yisshak Palachi recounted a story when he went up for Maftir on Rosh Hodesh Elul that fell on Shabbat. This was in front of many great rabbis, including his father, Ribbi Hayyim Palachi, and he did not add the verses from the Rosh Hodesh Haftarah, and nobody said a word. So he concluded that this verified the accepted custom not to add verses to the Haftarah. And he added that all the more so, we do not add the verses from the Haftarah of Mahar Hodesh for a special to a special Haftarah when Rosh Hodesh falls on Sunday for the months of Nisan, Tebet, Ab, Elul, or Adar. And this was always the custom in our community as well.

So when we take out three Sifre Torah, we send up at least seven 'Olim to the first Sefer, and recite Kaddish after each Sefer. And when we read the special Haftarah for that Shabbat, we don't add any verses from the Haftarah for Rosh Hodesh or from Mahar Hodesh. Similarly, when Rosh Hodesh Ab or Elul falls on Shabbat, we only read the special Haftarah without adding any verses from the Haftarah for Rosh Hodesh or from Mahar Hodesh.

150.title: Shubah LiM'onakh and Tikkanta Shabbat
150.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim, and in our last video we concluded with the return of the Sefer Torah to the Hekhal, and now the Hazzan is at the Tebah, and he's going to begin Shubah LiM'onakh, and we're going to discuss today some of the textual variants and the Minhagim concerning the Tefillat Musaf. We're on page 296 in the Kol Ya'akob if you wish to follow.

So I began by saying that the Hazzan will say Shubah LiM'onakh, Milra', as opposed to Shubah LiM'onakh, which in some Siddurim it's found that way, and there are some grammarians which insist that it should be Mil'el as in Shubah LiM'onakh. That is not our custom. We've, for all our lives and in Halab, we've always said Shubah LiM'onakh. I spoke to Hakham Abraham Shama, Dr. Abraham Shama, one of the top grammarians in Israel, a Halabi, who grew up in Ades, and he says Hakham Dwek, 'Alav HaShalom, and all the Hakhamim that he heard pray Musaf always said it Milra', Shubah, and there is no difference and no Hekhre'a, there's no definitive proof that it has to be one way or the other, and therefore we will just continue with the Minhag of our Hakhamim and Hazzanim, parents, and grandparents.

After the Shubah LiM'onakh, he says the Kaddish, and if it is Rosh Hodesh, then the Hazzan or a few people from the Kahal the way it is today will out loud before the beginning of the 'Amidah will say "Attah Yassarta 'Olamekha MiKedem," indicating and reminding the people that they should be reading from the Musaf of Shabbat and Rosh Hodesh as opposed to the regular Musaf.

Now, in the 'Amidah we'll continue. We have the first paragraph Tikkanta Shabbat on page 300, a paragraph which is written in the poetic form of Tashrak, it's the Alef-Bet backwards: "Tikkanta Shabbat Rassita Korbanoteha," and after the final word of Az, the Alef, you have "MiSinai Nisstavvu Sivvuyeha 'Aleha KaRa'uy," which is Otiyot Manssepakh, the letters in the Hebrew alphabet that have special a different form of the letter in the when it's written at the end of the word. So that's the formula, but it wasn't always like that.

If we go to earlier Nushaot, especially that of HaRambam, he doesn't have this entire paragraph. He writes "LeMoshe Sivvita 'Al Har Sinai," and it's found in some Siddurim till now, even Livorno. It's not our custom. It's generally not the custom of any of the Sefaradim. You may find it in some of the North African Kehillot. Our custom is to say Tikkanta Shabbat.

At the end of Tikkanta Shabbat, what we did find in many of the Musta'arabi and even in the Mahzor Aram Soba, is after "Sivvuyeha 'Aleha KaRa'uy," there's another sentence: "VeSivvanu Ad-onai Elokenu LeHakrib Bah Korban Musafin KeDinan KaRa'uy Lah." This is found in Mahzor Aram Soba. Again, we do not say it anymore. This Minhag dropped off. We do not say it. We end up with "Sivvuyeha 'Aleha KaRa'uy."

One more note on the Tikkanta Shabbat: there are earlier Nushaot, such as Mahzor Aram Soba, Rab Sa'adya Gaon, which have Tikkanta Shabbat with a Kof as opposed to Tikkanta Shabbat with a Kaf. Without getting into the meanings, Tikkanta would be BiLshon I guess Takkanah, to Takkanat Hakhamim, in this case Tikkanta Shabbat, Bore 'Olam Tikken the Korbanot and the Shabbat for 'Am Yisrael, and many grammarians feel that it evolved into a Tikkanta Shabbat, as many Pesukim means to establish like "Konen Eress." So we do say it and it's printed with Tikkanta, but just to let you know that there was an earlier Nusah with a Kof: Tikkanta Shabbat.

We'll continue with the couple of paragraphs after "Yismehu BeMalkhutakh Shomere Shabbat VeKore'e 'Oneg," which we're familiar because we say this paragraph Friday night, Shabbat morning, and Shabbat afternoon. The difference is Friday night and Shabbat Musaf, after "Hemdat Yamim Oto Karata," we'll say "Zekher LeMa'aseh Bereshit." It's we do not say it in Shahrit, we do say it in 'Arbit and in the Musaf. And this is also, this distinction is brought down also in the Aharonim.

Kol Tub, LeHitraot.

151.title: Barukh ShePetarani at a Bar Missvah
151.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: life cycles, Bar Missvah. So in this series of Bar Missvah, a number of people have written in asking about a custom that we're not familiar with, custom of making a Berakhah of "Barukh ShePetarani Me'onsho Shel Zeh." So what exactly is this and is it our custom? Where does it stem from?

So if one opens up the Shulhan 'Arukh in Orah Hayyim Siman Resh Kaf He, Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo is talking about the laws of Sheheheyanu. In the midst of that, Hagahah Muram, Rabbi Moshe Isserles, adds a gloss and says: "Yesh Omerim, Mi SheNa'asah Beno Bar Missvah, Yebarekh: Barukh Attah Ad-onai Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam ShePetarani Me'onsho Shel Zeh." So these are glosses written by Rabbi Moshe Isserles, who we know as Muram, and these are generally following Ashkenazi practice, and he says there are those who say that a person whose son becomes Bar Missvah should make the Berakhah of "Barukh Attah HaShem Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam ShePetarani Me'onsho Shel Zeh," who has exempted me from the punishment of this one's sins.

The question is, is that our Minhag? Is it not our Minhag? So it is not our Minhag, it's not something that we do, even though it seems that there may be some people in the community that may want to begin such a tradition, and we can prove that very easily. Obviously we can look around and we know we've never seen it, we've never heard it. But sometimes that's not enough.

So we have Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin. Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin in his Keter Shem Tob writes specifically about this. The book Keter Shem Tob was published in 1934 by Hakham Shem Tob Gagin, who came from a very long, distinguished line of Sephardic Hakhamim. Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin himself was from Yerushalayim, from there he traveled to Egypt and then to England, and in England he was the Rabbi of the Sephardic Jews both in London as well as Manchester.

And he writes on page 318: "Lo Ra'iti VeLo Shama'ti SheHaSefaradim Nahagu LeBarekh Birkat Barukh ShePetarani Me'onsho Shel Zeh KeSheHaBen Na'asah Bar Missvah, VeHaAshkenazim Nohagim LeOmrah Be'et SheHaBen 'Oleh LaTorah SheNa'asah Bar Missvah, VeOmerim Otah Beli Shem UMalkhut." He writes very, very clearly: "Lo Ra'iti VeLo Shama'ti," I've never seen, I've never heard that Sefaradim have a custom to make such a Berakhah of "Barukh ShePetarani Me'onsho Shel Zeh" when the boy becomes a Bar Missvah. This is an Ashkenazi practice that they say when the boy goes up to the Sefer Torah, and they say it without Shem UMalkhut. He tells it very clearly.

And he was familiar with Sefaradim: Sefaradim in Yerushalayim, Sefaradim in Egypt, and then in London and Amsterdam, and London, rather, and Manchester. He interacted with Sefaradim from all over the world, and in fact even held the post of the Rabbi of the Syrian Congregation in Manchester for a number of years. So obviously he was very familiar with Halabi traditions as well. And he documents for us what is and what is not our practice, and this should be very clear to everybody that we do not say "Barukh ShePetarani Me'onsho Shel Zeh."

152.title: Reading the Shirot on the Seventh Day of Pesah
152.text:
Hakham Abraham Hamwey, a rabbi from Halab in the 19th century, wrote the following regarding the seventh day of Pesah in his Pesah Mahzor, which he called Bet HaBehirah: "It is customary for the righteous and men of good deeds to study on this night and to talk about the acts of kindness that HaShem performed for His nation, as it is written in the book Keri'e Mo'ed. Go and take it from there. And in the early morning hours, they wake up and read Parashat BeShallah and the Shirah, standing and facing the east, until the end of the verse that concludes 'Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha.'"

From here, it sounds like the custom was practiced by pious individuals at home. However, in many Middle Eastern communities, the customary reading was conducted in the synagogue. In some places, they read after dinner before going to sleep. In other places, they would wake up after midnight or in the early morning pre-dawn hours to read from the book Keri'e Mo'ed.

In his book Mo'ed LeKhol Hai, Rabbi Hayyim Palachi wrote that one should be careful to wake up in the early pre-dawn hours to recite the songs, which refers to biblical songs such as Ha'azinu, the song of Deborah, the prayer of Hannah, the song of David, various Psalms, and Shir HaShirim, all of which are found in the Shirot section of the reading for the seventh day of Pesah in the book Keri'e Mo'ed that was also referenced by Hakham Abraham Hamwey. And Rabbi Palachi continued by saying that after reading those songs, Shirat HaYam is recited with a pleasant voice and great concentration by the congregation. And he continues by saying that one only stays home that morning if there are concerns about leaving the house at that hour.

The custom of waking up early and reading on the seventh day of Pesah was also mentioned by the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer. He supported the custom with a Gemara from Masekhet Sanhedrin that taught, "Kol HaKore Pasuk BiZmano Mebi Tobah La'Olam, SheNe'emar: Dabar Be'itto Mah Tob," "Anyone who reads a verse in its appropriate time brings goodness to the world, like the verse says: How good is a thing in its appropriate time." And he also quoted Masekhet Soferim where it says, "Kol HaMazkir Pasuk Be'onato Ma'aleh 'Alav KeIlu Boneh Mizbeah Hadash UMakrib 'Alav Korban," "Anyone who mentions a verse in its proper time is as one who builds a new altar and offers a sacrifice upon it."

In Brooklyn, several synagogues conduct an early-morning pre-dawn reading from the book Keri'e Mo'ed. Keri'e Mo'ed is the same book that's used for the all-night readings on Hosha'na Rabbah and Shabu'ot. On the morning of the seventh day of Pesah, we usually only read the Shirot, the biblical songs, followed by Parashat BeShallah until the end of the verse that concludes "Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha." Parashat BeShallah is usually read a little bit before dawn, and dawn is usually around 5:00 a.m. in Brooklyn on the seventh day of Pesah. It is not customary in our community to read the other pieces found in Keri'e Mo'ed for the seventh day of Pesah, such as the passages from the Tanakh found in the beginning of the reading, or the passages from the Talmud or the Zohar.

In episode 88, we discussed the custom of Halab of adding the verses that begin with "VaTikkah Miryam" in Shahrit on the seventh day of Pesah after Shirat HaYam. Beginning with VaYosha', the congregation recites Shirat HaYam in unison and continues until the end of the verse that concludes "Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha."

So the custom in Middle Eastern communities is to read from Keri'e Mo'ed on the night or in the early morning of the seventh day of Pesah. Some read at home, while others read together in the synagogue. In our community, we read the Shirot followed by Parashat BeShallah until after Shirat HaYam, concluding with the verse that ends "Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha." And then in Shahrit, we begin reading together from VaYosha' and add the verses that start with "VaTikkah Miryam" until the end of the verse that concludes "Ani Ad-onai Rofe'ekha."

153.title: Concluding Musaf of Shabbat
153.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. In our last video, we discussed the textual variants in the Musaf of Shabbat prayer, and we will continue with Minhagim of Musaf, conclude them, and continue with the Minhagim of Minhah of Shabbat.

So we the Hazzan is beginning the Hazarah on page 297 if you'd like to follow. There are no unique customs, Halabi customs for the Hazarah Musaf which we didn't find in Shahrit. The Keter is sung by the entirety of the Kahal with a tune that's initiated by the Hazzan. Kohanim as well, is generally said by, recited to the Kohanim by the Hazzan. It's not unusual for some synagogues to have the custom of inviting a different Hazzan to say the Kohanim, that's how we do it at Ades, but it could be said by the Hazzan, it generally is. And he concludes the prayer, the formal prayer ends with the, he's saying the Kaddish Titkabbal.

After Kaddish Titkabbal, he leaves the Tebah, and the custom is to have another Hazzan come to the Tebah to conclude the Kol Yisrael and the Rabbi Hananya, for the Ketoret. Not required, the Hazzan can stay on the Tebah and continue, but generally the custom what we find is that another Hazzan comes to the Tebah. He'll finish the Ketoret, the those who are required and obligated to say Kaddish will say Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, followed by Barekhu, and the Kahal will say 'Alenu LeShabbeah.

Following 'Alenu LeShabbeah, we do not have the custom to add a Mizmor and another Kaddish. You will find communities which have that custom, especially in Yerushalayim, they'll say Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat followed by another Kaddish. That's not our custom. After 'Alenu LeShabbeah, Tefillah is over.

154.title: The Bar Missvah Boy's 'Aliyah
154.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: life cycles, Bar Missvah. So, in our discussions regarding the Bar Missvah, the question has arisen as to the 'Aliyah that the Bar Missvah boy takes, goes up for, makes a Berakhah for, reads a Sefer Torah for on his particular day, and whether it's a weekday like a Monday or Thursday, or a Rosh Hodesh, or on a Shabbat. So, what is the common practice, what was done in the past, what's currently done, and are there differences of opinion?

So, in a nutshell, there is a Halakhah that talks about a Katan, a child, that means somebody under the age of thirteen years and one day, and if that person could go up to the Torah and have an 'Aliyah and read. And obviously, like everything else, there are various opinions, and our common practice is that a Katan does go up. But was that always practiced and to what degree?

So, speaking to old-timers, it seems that, going back to the '40s and '50s in this community, they would not on a Shabbat give this Bar Missvah boy a 'Aliyah at the beginning of the Parashah, but rather later on in the Parashah, usually after seven people already went up to the Sefer Torah, and now there are extra 'Aliyot, what we know as Rakkeh, and the boy would go up for a Rakkeh and read, or he would go up and read the Maftir, which is the final reading from the Torah. On a weekday, though, things were a little bit different.

But let's move forward to how that transpired. With the community growing and many more boys going up, they started to move the reading to the beginning of the Parashah as well, or to various 'Aliyot within the Parashah on a Shabbat. For a weekday, there were various opinions as well. Some would have the boy go up and read the Sefer Torah on Monday and Thursday, Monday or Thursday, rather, and he would not have an 'Aliyah, but rather his father would stand by him and have the 'Aliyah instead and have the boy read. And some would actually have the boy make the Berakhot and have the 'Aliyah. And this, again, is based upon various readings within the Halakhah and how the Halakhah transpired.

But by the 1960s and early '70s, it became common practice that the Bar Missvah boy definitely goes up on Monday and/or Thursday to read the Sefer, from the Sefer Torah, and has the 'Aliyah, and makes the Berakhot, and does everything. And that was the common practice, definitely in the days of Hakham Matloub Abadi in the 1960s. After his demise, there are those that wanted to come along and contest that, but the Minhag stayed pretty strong, and throughout the '70s, '80s, '90s, the Minhag persisted with almost all the rabbis in agreement, and that is still the common practice today, that the Bar Missvah boy in our community, as we've said in the past, who's generally younger than thirteen years and one day, usually some point after twelve years and six months, does go up, has the 'Aliyah, makes the Berakhot, and that would be on a weekday and, as well, on a Shabbat. And that is the common practice in our community today, both in the Halabi, Shami, Egyptian, Lebanese, all our synagogues, that's what's generally done.

155.title: Minhah After Pelag and 'Arbit Before Sunset
155.text:
In the Gemara, there's a difference of opinion between Rabbi Yehudah and the other rabbis. According to Rabbi Yehudah, one can only pray Minhah until the time of Pelag HaMinhah, which is 75 variable minutes before the end of the day. And from that time and on, it is the time of 'Arbit. But according to the rabbis, one can pray Minhah until the end of the day, and the earliest time for 'Arbit is from the beginning of the night. The conclusion of the Gemara is that one may follow either opinion.

In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that one must always follow one of the opinions. So if someone prays Minhah to the end of the day, he may not pray 'Arbit before sunset. But if he prays 'Arbit before sunset, he may not pray Minhah during the time of Pelag HaMinhah. And then he writes that now that it's customary to pray Minhah until nighttime, one should not pray 'Arbit before sunset. If one did pray 'Arbit before sunset, they fulfilled their obligation, so they don't have to pray again. And in a pressureful situation, one may pray 'Arbit before sunset after Pelag HaMinhah.

According to Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, one has to consistently follow one opinion. You can't pray Minhah right before sunset one day and 'Arbit before sunset on another day. So all the more so, Maran would not permit praying Minhah after Pelag HaMinhah and 'Arbit before sunset on the same day. However, in Maran's work, the Bet Yosef, which is the basis for his rulings in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran acknowledged that even in his times, the custom of the world is to be lenient, and when Minhah is recited after the beginning of Pelag HaMinhah, the congregations continue with 'Arbit before sunset, even though this is contradictory by simultaneously following both Rabbi Yehudah and the rabbis, who disagree with each other. Maran then suggests that this custom is based on the way that the Rosh explained Rabbenu Tam, who was lenient with regards to praying Minhah after Pelag HaMinhah, followed by 'Arbit before sunset. The Rosh explained that we are lenient with halakhic issues pertaining to the prayers.

Rabbi Yisrael Ya'akob Algazi, a Turkish rabbi from the beginning of the 18th century, who eventually became the Rishon LeSiyyon in the land of Israel, discussed this topic in his book Shalme Sibbur. And he added that the Arizal also would pray 'Arbit early and then repeat Shema again after nightfall. He wrote that according to the Ari, 'Arbit should be recited while it is still daytime or close to the daytime. This explains our custom of praying 'Arbit immediately after sunset in the wintertime, as opposed to many Ashkenazim, who wait until nightfall to recite 'Arbit. Sometimes they have a break between Minhah and 'Arbit, or they come back later for 'Arbit.

The Ben Ish Hai also wrote about this topic in his responsa Rab Pe'alim, stating that the custom of his city was to pray Minhah after Pelag HaMinhah and 'Arbit before sunset, based on the custom of the world that is recorded in the Bet Yosef and the opinion of Rabbenu Tam, as well as the opinion of the later authorities, including the Shalme Sibbur and the custom of the Arizal.

All of this is for weeknights, but on Friday night, even Maran writes that 'Arbit should be recited earlier than it is recited during the week in order to add time to Shabbat. And therefore, Maran wrote that after Pelag HaMinhah, one could accept Shabbat with 'Arbit and then make Kiddush and eat before sunset as well.

So even though Maran rules that one may not pray Minhah after Pelag HaMinhah and 'Arbit before sunset even on different days, our custom is to pray Minhah after Pelag HaMinhah and 'Arbit before sunset even on the same day. This is an example of maintaining a custom that existed before the ruling of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. In this case, Maran himself recorded the existing custom in his work known as the Bet Yosef. The custom was subsequently recorded by the Shalme Sibbur and the Ben Ish Hai, and continues as the accepted custom in our communities in New York and New Jersey. However, on Friday evening, even Maran advocates praying 'Arbit and accepting Shabbat before sunset.

156.title: Shabbat Minhah and UBa LeSiyyon
156.text:
We will now begin the customs for Tefilat Minhah. The timing for Minhah generally in our community was to begin 35 minutes, that's how it was in Shaare Zion in my days. Sometimes they have Kehillot that begin 40 minutes before, giving them that a little bit more time for Se'udah Shelishit. That is called Minhah Ketanah. We pray Minhah when the day is shorter, where there's less hours left in the day. 2 1/2 hours, relative hours, before sunset is the time for Minhah Ketanah.

There are those that prefer to pray Minhah Gedolah. You may have some synagogues which offer Minyanim for Minhah Gedolah, which is it's called Gedolah because the day is still great, the day is still "'Od HaYom Gadol." And that's done at 6 1/2 hours relative hours following sunrise, around 12:30, 1:00, depending on the time of the year, for those who prefer.

Tefilat Minhah is always said, Tefilat Minhah of Shabbat, always recited in the scale of Rast. This is our custom throughout all Syrian communities throughout the world. This is the custom to pray in Rast.

We'll finish the Ketoret, Ashre, becomes, and it comes to UBa LeSiyyon. Now here the custom is evolved in our community to sing UBa LeSiyyon in the tune that everybody's familiar with: "UBa LeSiyyon Go'el." Now this is not a Halabi tune at all. As a matter of fact, it's a Moroccan tune. When I came to Yerushalayim a few decades ago and there's no shortage of Moroccan synagogues, and it's exactly the same tune. It turns out it's a Moroccan tune, North African.

So the theory, actually it's more of an educated guess, probably accurate, that this tune was introduced to our community by the esteemed and famous Hakham Meir Vaknin, 'Alav HaShalom, who came and served in our community for a few years in the around the world time of World War I. And he was from the Vaknin family is Moroccan descent. And it seems that he introduced this tune to our community. It spread, took hold. As a matter of fact, it even spread to Mexico, and in some cases I was told that even in Argentina they would sing it on occasion.

In Ades, we don't sing it that way. UBa LeSiyyon, the Hazzan continues. Not sung at all by the Kahal. Continues with the Hazzan saying it as usual. He finishes the UBa LeSiyyon, gets says the Hassi Kaddish, and we sing VaAni Tefillati, which is we say it twice. It's sung by the entire Kahal before the Hekhal is opened. It is sung in, they'd have a couple of common tunes which the Kahal is all familiar with: VaAni Tefillati, the Pizmon Ribah Ribi, or VaAni Tefillati. Now, the Hazzan can get creative and do other tunes in Rast, but these are the tunes that are generally sung. The Kahal is familiar with them, and they sing it with enthusiasm.

Now we get to Petihat HaHekhal. In our next video, we'll discuss the Minhagim of Petihat HaHekhal and continue to the conclusion of the Minhah of Shabbat prayer. Kol Tub.

157.title: The Coracha
157.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: life cycles, Bar Missvah: the coracha. What is this word, coracha, that we have? It's a word. It means so much. It carries so much history and tradition with it, and we use it all so proudly, most people not having any idea whatsoever what it is, where it came from, what its origin is.

The word coracha is an old Spanish word, and it means small leather pouch. And that's what they used to keep their Tefillin in. And way back when, if you had a small silk-style Talet, you could also basically fold that up and put that there as well. But this coracha, this word that goes back to pre-Expulsion Spain, has lasted with us, has traveled with us from Spain to the Middle East, to Syria, to Lebanon, to Egypt. It has come back with us. It's come back to the other part of the world. It's here in New York, it's in New Jersey, it's in California, it's in Mexico, it's in Panama, it's in Brazil, it's in Argentina. We all use this word coracha.

Way back when, when the small leather pouch fell out of use, yes, they would embroider a small bag, silk, cotton, wool, whatever material they had, something small, something pretty, something that would protect the Talet and Tefillin, no great fanfare. Even here in the United States, originally they used some of those old bags, then it became the norm over here to use generally a velvet bag, usually blue velvet. It would be a plain blue velvet like this, or a plain blue velvet like this, simple stitching, simple embroidery on it. You'd go to the store, you'd buy it, nothing personal about it, everybody had the same one. You'd walk into Kenis, you look at the table, everybody had the exact same coracha, and you'd have to find a way to distinguish yours or just from the place where you placed it, you knew it was yours.

As time evolved, they got a little fancier, and by the '70s, coracha started looking like this, with the name on it and fancy imagery of lions and Ten Commandments and what have you. But now we've gone into a new world, and we've passed the '60s and the '70s and the '80s and the '90s, and once the century changed, we've came into the world of needlepoint, and everybody has a very unique coracha. And it hearkens back to the way a coracha used to be: a special family heirloom that was made by a mother, by a grandmother, for the grandson, for the great-grandson, something that he would carry with him throughout his life, something that would connect him to his past and make his ancestors proud of him that he's carrying on the tradition.

We have beautiful corachas today made by the ladies of our community, our wives, our mothers, our grandmothers. Look at the beautiful jobs they do, so many different shapes and colors and designs, and it really lends a lot to our expression coracha that we use with so much expression and so much fanfare and so much happiness and gusto. Everybody, take your coracha, be proud of it, and carry on this word and tradition for generations to come.

158.title: Staying Up All Night on Shabu'ot
158.text:
The custom of staying up all night and engaging in Torah study on the first night of Shabu'ot is observed by Jewish communities all over the world. This custom, which is based on the Zohar, is observed in both Middle Eastern and Ashkenazic communities. Hakham Abraham Antebi, the chief rabbi of Halab from the beginning of the 19th century, praised the custom in his book Ohel Yesharim. Similarly, Hakham Abraham Hamwey, a rabbi from Halab in the 19th century, considered the custom obligatory in his Mahzor for Shabu'ot, which is called Bet HaShem.

Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, who was born in Halab at the end of the 19th century, wrote about this custom in his book on the customs of Halab. He wrote that on the night of Shabu'ot, they gather in houses, synagogues, and study halls, and learn Seder HaLimud, the order of study, the entire night, and at dawn, the entire congregation would go to immerse themselves in a Mikveh that was rented for Shabu'ot by a community philanthropist. The custom of dipping in the Mikveh at the end of the night was also recorded by Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Shabu'ot Mahzor, Bet HaShem.

The Seder HaLimud mentioned by Rabbi Sha'yo refers to the order of study specified by Rabbi Hayyim Vital, the main student of Rabbi Yisshak Luria, otherwise known as the Arizal, in his work known as Sha'ar HaKavvanot from the end of the 16th century. This order of study, which is also known as Tikkun Lel Shabu'ot, can also be found in the book Keri'e Mo'ed, which is used by our community and in communities all over the world on the night of Shabu'ot. Keri'e Mo'ed also has readings for the night of Hosha'na Rabbah and the seventh of Adar, as well as a reading for the seventh day of Pesah.

The reading for Shabu'ot consists of portions from the beginning and end of each Parashah from the Torah, as well as from the beginning and end of each book of the Nebi'im and Ketubim. The reading also contains portions pertaining to the holiday of Shabu'ot, so the entire Ten Commandments from Yitro and VaEthannan are included, as well as the entire book of Rut. Keri'e Mo'ed also contains passages from the Mishnah. However, Rabbi Hayyim Palachi quoted HaRab Hayyim HaKohen MeAram Soba, an important student of Rabbi Hayyim Vital from the 17th century, who taught that Mishnayot should not be part of the reading on the night of Shabu'ot for mystical reasons. The general custom in our community is not to read the Mishnayot that night.

After reading the Tanakh passages, it is customary to read a passage from the Zohar on Parashat Naso, which is called the Idra Rabba, which means the great gathering. It contains secrets revealed by Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yohai to his students who gathered to hear his teachings. The custom of reading the Idra after the Tanakh passages was also documented by Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Shabu'ot Mahzor, Bet HaShem. Furthermore, it is not customary to read the list of the 613 commandments or the passage from Midrash Rabbah that is found in Keri'e Mo'ed for the night of Shabu'ot.

Similarly, Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that in Argentina, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, 'Alav HaShalom, participated in the reading on the night of Shabu'ot. They read the passages from the Tanakh and then the Idra from the Zohar. Rabbi Antebi wrote that they would read until approximately 2:00 a.m. and then they would go home to sleep. They didn't pray at sunrise, but rather at the regular holiday morning Minyan. Here in Brooklyn, some have the same custom. They read the Tanakh and the Zohar until approximately 3:00 a.m., and then they sleep and wake up for the regular holiday Minyan.

Interestingly, Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin, in his work Keter Shem Tob, wrote that the custom in the Middle East was to stay up all night on the first night of Shabu'ot, but the custom of Sefaradim and Ashkenazim in Europe was to stay up for half of the night. And he explained that the reason for not staying up all night was so that they could pray Shahrit and Musaf in the proper condition and with concentration. Likewise, Rabbi Hayyim Palachi wrote in his book Mo'ed LeKhol Hai that one who is not able to pray properly after staying up all night should sleep a little bit before praying.

Is it preferable to read the Tikkun or to study and have classes in other Torah subjects? According to the Hida, a major Middle Eastern authority from the 18th century, everyone is obligated to read the passages established by the Arizal. Therefore, the custom of Halab is to read the Tanakh passages and the Idra from the Zohar before studying anything else. Afterwards, some study the Sefer HaMissvot from HaRambam.

So the custom of staying up all night on the first night of Shabu'ot was practiced in Halab. They read the Tikkun all night, and then they went to dip in a Mikveh at dawn, and then prayed Shahrit and Musaf. In Brooklyn, many stay up all night. However, some stay up until they complete the Tanakh passages, others complete the Zohar passages as well, and then sleep a little bit, so that they could pray Shahrit and Musaf with the proper concentration. All should read the Tanakh passages before studying other Torah subjects, but the tradition is to read the Idra from the Zohar as well before studying other subjects on the night of Shabu'ot.

159.title: Taking Out the Sefer at Shabbat Minhah
159.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have been discussing the Minhagim of the prayers of Minhah of Shabbat in the synagogue. We have completed through VaAni Tefillati in our last video, and now we are on page 338 if you wish to follow in the Kol Ya'akob. We are ready to take the Sefer out in order to read the Torah on Minhah of Shabbat, and generally, the customs are the same in taking out the Sefer. The Mesader will invite someone for Petihah, for Gilyan to carry the Sefer open to the Tebah, and for the 'Aliyot.

There are a couple of small differences between taking the Sefer Torah out of in Shahrit and in Minhah. So if you notice in the Kol Ya'akob it says "BeMikssat Kehillot Omerim Kan," some congregations recite the Berikh Shemeh. Now, I understand that today most Kehillot, most Minyanim, do indeed say the Berikh Shemeh, but it is the scope and intent of this video series to bring you the Minhagim as they were in Halab and as they were in the early part of our history in Brooklyn. The Berikh Shemeh was not recited in Halab, and even growing up, I do not recall it being said on a consistent basis in most Kehillot. In fact, in the book Derekh Eress compiled by Hakham Abraham Ades, he brings down specifically that we do not say Berikh Shemeh during Minhah, and on my last trip to Deal, I had the opportunity to speak with Hakham Edmond Nahum, Yizzakher LaTob, and he confirmed to me that in Halab they did not say Berikh Shemeh in Minhah of Shabbat.

We take out the Sefer with "Se'enah URe'enah," "Barukh HaBa BeTorat Ad-onai," "VeZot HaTorah Asher Sam Moshe" until the Pasuk "Ad-onai Hafess LeMa'an Sidko Yagdil Torah VeYa'dir", while the one who has the Gilyan is carrying the Sefer to the Tebah.

Now, I did want to point out during the discussion of Minhah of Shabbat something which is a very, very important practice that was always done in our community, and it involves people who are receiving honors from the Mesader, whether it be Petihah, carrying the Sefer, or the 'Aliyot. They always wore a jacket. Now, usually in Shabbat morning it's not an issue, but the last number of years which I've been in New York I've noticed that there's a more casual attire being worn to Minhah of Shabbat, and I recall very, very clearly was a very pronounced Minhag that anybody who had an honor, if someone, let's say, was invited for an 'Aliyah and he didn't have a jacket, it was a scramble. People would take their jacket off and make sure he gets a jacket that fits him, and he goes up to the Sefer, and it was a beautiful display of reverence and the Kabod that we have for our holy Torah. And I think it's a beautiful custom, and it left a very big impression on me, and it's a custom which we should continue to do.

The after the third 'Oleh, he does not say Kaddish. Instead, the Hazzan will say "Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat." Following Mizmor Shir, the one who brought the Sefer out will now return the Sefer to the Hekhal open, as is our custom and as clear that that is our custom. The Kahal will say "Yehalelu Et Shem Ad-onai Ki Nisgab Shemo Lebaddo," a series of Pesukim on page 332, ending with "VaYira VaYomar Mah Nora HaMakom HaZeh En Zeh Ki Im Bet Elokim VeZeh Sha'ar HaShamayim". Kol Tub.

160.title: New World Bar Missvah Birthday Customs
160.text:
SCA Minhag of the week: life cycles, Bar Missvah. In this episode, I'd like to discuss two New World customs that equate the Bar Missvah with a birthday.

The first one is a present. We see nowadays at many a Bar Missvah celebration, whether it be on a weekday or on a Shabbat, that towards the end of the prayers, the rabbi will get up, congratulate the young man, and call him up to the podium, to the stage, to present him with a token of appreciation, a gift from the congregation to him, be it a Siddur, a Humash, a Tikkun, or possibly something else. And the rabbi in turn may also even invoke a blessing on the child. Now, obviously, this is something that is very new. It's not something that existed in the past. It's just a show of appreciation to the family, you know, and respect to the family for being a part of the congregation, for celebrating and having the celebration within the confines of that synagogue. So, in turn, we present the young man with this gift, which will hopefully encourage him to continue on his path of prayer and reading Torah and joining the congregation in the future. Again, this is strictly a new custom, something that did not exist anytime in the past or any place in the past.

Another even newer custom is we've all been to many a Bar Missvah party, grand reception, whether it be as a breakfast or as a night affair, and all of a sudden, there's a lavish cake with a candle-lighting ceremony. And for each one of the thirteen candles, a different family member is called up, you know, to hold the candle and light a candle on the cake and take a picture with the boy. This is something that is completely foreign to most people any place in the world. This is not one of our original customs.

This, in fact, after much, much research, I've discovered that this is a custom that was created by caterers, kosher caterers on the eastern shore of the United States of America, basically New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Washington, D.C. This is something that they created to give a birthday connection, as well as a concept of the people that are there coming to celebrate with the boy, this is their, quote-unquote, their 'Aliyah to the Sefer Torah. So the whole family, the aunt and the uncle and the cousin, for each one of these candles can come and have an 'Aliyah, have a coming up with the Bar Missvah boy, and each one gets honored with such a thing. This is something that even if you go to the West Coast, they're unfamiliar with. It's a nice gimmick. It's, you know, there's no harm in it, but you should know this is definitely not one of our original customs, nor is it anybody's original custom.
