161.title: Announcing Rosh Hodesh: Sitting or Standing
161.text:
It is customary to announce Rosh Hodesh on the Shabbat prior to Rosh Hodesh. This custom is found in the Mahzor Vitry, a prayer book with Halakhot from France that was compiled in the 11th and 12th centuries. The custom was also mentioned by Rabbi Sidkiyah Ben Abraham in his book Shibbole HaLeket in Italy in the 13th century, and by Rabbi David Abudarham in Spain in the 14th century.

Interestingly, in Mahzor Aram Soba, a prayer book that was made by the Jews of Aleppo in the year 1527, Rosh Hodesh was announced when taking out the Sefer Torah on Shabbat morning. That's also when they bless the congregation and announce fast days, according to Mahzor Aram Soba. And this custom continued into the 20th century in Halab.

In Hakham Salim Zafrani's description of the customs of the Great Synagogue of Aleppo, he also wrote that they bless the congregation and announce Rosh Hodesh or fasts while the Sefer Torah was carried, before it was brought to the Tebah. Hakham Salim Zafrani was born in Halab in 1891, and left Halab to move to Israel in the year 1959.

We find the same description by Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo in his book on the customs of Halab. The congregation was blessed, and Rosh Hodesh was announced while the Sefer Torah was carried, before it was placed down on the Tebah. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo was born in Halab in 1893, and moved to Israel in the year 1935.

All these sources, Mahzor Aram Soba and the writings of Hakham Salim Zafrani and Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, have a different textual version of the announcement of Rosh Hodesh than we have in our Siddurim. Their version is in Aramaic, and it is not preceded by a series of Yehi Rassons, as is found in the Siddurim that we use today.

It is important to note that there were two Jewish communities living in Halab. One community lived in Halab at least since the time period of the second Bet HaMikdash, and they were known as the Musta'arabim. The other community came to Halab from Spain in the beginning of the 16th century, and were known as the Sefaradim. Mahzor Aram Soba was composed by the Musta'arabim, and that tradition continued side-by-side with the Spanish traditions into the beginning of the 20th century. Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca suggested that perhaps the textual version of announcing Rosh Hodesh that we recite today, which is recited before Musaf, is based on the tradition of the Sefaradim.

If you announce Rosh Hodesh while the Sefer Torah is being carried, then the congregation would stand for the Sefer Torah. But what is our custom when we announce Rosh Hodesh before Musaf, when the Sefer Torah is on the Tebah? Do we sit, or should we stand up? According to the book Derekh Eress, the custom in Halab was to remain seated when announcing Rosh Hodesh.

There's a difference of opinion among the later authorities about sitting or standing when announcing Rosh Hodesh. According to the Magen Abraham, a famous authority from Poland in the 17th century, it is customary to stand, since he understood that the judges on the Bet Din were standing when they declared the new month. And the Ben Ish Hai wrote that as well. However, Rabbi 'Akiva Eiger, an authority from Hungary and Poland in the 18th and 19th centuries, understood that the judges on the Bet Din were sitting when they declared the new month.

In some Middle Eastern communities, they remain seated when Rosh Hodesh is announced, including in the communities in Algeria, Djerba, and Libya. But in other Middle Eastern communities, such as in Damascus, Egypt, and Baghdad, they stood for the announcing of Rosh Hodesh. In the Halabi community in Argentina, under the leadership of Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, they stood for the announcing of Rosh Hodesh. But Hakham Yisshak Chehebar did not allow anyone to come up to the Tebah and hold the Sefer Torah, which is customary in other communities. However, Hakham Ya'akob Attieh, a contemporary and consuegro of Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, is quoted as saying that the custom in Halab was to remain seated when announcing Rosh Hodesh.

The custom of Halabi Jews in New York has always been to remain seated when Rosh Hodesh is being announced. On one occasion, when they were announcing Rosh Hodesh in the Midrash in Shaare Zion, and everyone was sitting down, including Hakham Yom Tob Yedid 'Alav HaShalom. Afterwards, a young man approached Hakham Yom Tob and asked him why everyone was sitting while Rosh Hodesh was being announced. Hakham Yom Tob asked him, "Why not?" The young man then showed Hakham Yom Tob the Mishnah Berurah that cited the Magen Abraham, who wrote that it is customary to stand when announcing Rosh Hodesh. Rabbi Yedid closed the book, kissed it, and returned the book to the young man.

Since standing for the announcement of Rosh Hodesh is a custom that developed in some communities, and it is certainly not a halakhic obligation, each community could and should maintain their own custom. The prevalent custom in Halabi communities that announce Rosh Hodesh before Musaf is to remain seated when Rosh Hodesh is being announced, while in some other communities, they stand, based on the writings of the Magen Abraham, the Ben Ish Hai, and the Mishnah Berurah.

162.title: Minhah of Shabbat After the Torah Reading
162.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are discussing the Minhagim of Minhah of Shabbat. We have completed in our last video the reading of the Sefer Torah and returning the Sefer to the Hekhal. The Hazzan now will be at the Tebah and will say Kaddish before the 'Amidah.

Following the 'Amidah, we have Hazarah, and the Hazzan generally for Minhah of Shabbat, as I mentioned in a couple of videos ago, will sing in Maqam Rast, in the Rast scale. That's generally the custom. There may be an exception here or there, as Joey Mosseri indicated to me. We have now access to the notes of 'Alehem HaShalom our great Hazzanim, Hakham Moshe Ashear and Gabriel Shrem, and occasionally they would veer from Maqam Rast, but generally we say Minhah Maqam Rast. So the Kedushah will be sung as is appropriate for all the Tefilot on Shabbat.

Following the 'Amidah, we have the Tefilah of Sidkatekha KeHarere El. This is a few Pesukim which we say on days where the date would indicate that there are Tahanunim. It is said by the Hazzan, people will say to themselves seated, the Kahal will be seated, only the Hazzan is standing, the Kahal will be seated. This is unlike other communities, the Damascus community, the Egyptian community, Minhage Yerushalayim, where Sidkatekha is said standing up. The Halabi community, the custom is to sit down for Sidkatekha Sedek.

On days where there is no Tahanun, we don't say Sidkatekha, we go straight to Yehi Shem. Now, it's interesting that most days, on weekdays for instance, we will say Tahanun and it will be followed by Yehi Shem. Here, it's not the case. We say Sidkatekha and we don't say Yehi Shem, or we'll say Yehi Shem and we won't say Sidkatekha.

It's followed by Kaddish Titkabbal, and the Mizmor "Halleluyah, Odeh Ad-onai BeKhol Lebab, BeSod Yesharim Ve'Edah," it is said by the Hazzan. Unlike other communities such as the Egyptian community where the entire Kahal will sing it, the Halabi community, Kahal is seated and the Hazzan will say it by himself. Of course, the Kahal will say it to themselves, but there is no singing in unison.

On days where there is another Mizmor to be said, like Shabbat Hol HaMo'ed Sukkot, Hol HaMo'ed Pesah, we do not say two Mizmorim. We will say only the Mizmor of the holiday and not say the Mizmor Halleluyah. And this is followed by Kaddish Yehe Shelama for those who are required to say Kaddish, followed by 'Alenu LeShabbeah. Kol Tub.

163.title: The Bar Missvah in Syria and America
163.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles, Bar Missvah. In the last episode, we discussed American Minhagim of the Bar Missvah. People have come back to me and asked, what did they really do in Syria? What went on in Halab? What went on in Sham? What was the Bar Missvah like over there?

And simply put, pretty much nothing. It was very, very simple. The appointed day, the boy would be taken to Kenis, put on Tefillin, he'll have an 'Aliyah to the Sefer Torah, he'll read his portion, and that's basically it. On Shabbat, possibly another 'Aliyah and possibly a speech. No real fanfare. During the week, after the prayers, give out some Ka'ak, some Ma'amoul, some Mlabas, you know, and everybody goes about their, you know, their way and their day. On Shabbat, possibly a Sebet. Sebet we'll talk about in a future episode, but that's really the gist of it. Nothing else was really done, and over time it developed outside of Syria into a greater celebration.

We know what we've done here in America for the last century or so, what's going on now that people are picking up, leaving home, going to Israel, making even more lavish and extravagant affairs with parties every day of the week. That's something that was really unheard of, and until a couple of decades ago wasn't even a thought.

In any case, what else goes on here at the American Bar Missvah? What have we picked up, or what has become something that's really deeply associated with it? And believe it or not, it's the dress code. Everybody comes wearing a suit and tie, not only the Bar Missvah boy, but father, the grandfather, the uncles, the cousins, the guests. But what about the ladies? Of course our ladies always dress in very fine clothing, very elegant clothing, but it's the mother. The mother of the Bar Missvah boy stands out because she wears a hat, and not a simple hat, but a very, very fancy, opulent hat.

And this is something that developed in the United States based upon, believe it or not, the fashion trends of ladies here beginning from the 1920s, '30s, '40s, '50s, '60s. It was very commonplace for women to wear a fancy hat when attending, if you will, an elegant affair, when, if you want to show yourself that you're put together, you're wearing hat and gloves, you know, to attend whether, what do you want to call it, a wedding, or the opera, or a show, or what have you. We see black-and-white photos, we see color photos, we know how women dressed.

So even though this style and this fashion fell out of use by the late '60s with the trend in more freedom in dress and in habits, this is something that because of the connection to a woman wanting to cover her hair in a Makom Kadosh, in the Bet Keneset, it's a trend that stayed. Also I think maybe because people saw pictures of, you know, the Bar Missvah celebrations or the pre- or post-wedding celebrations in the Kenis, and they saw their mothers wearing hats, they wanted to continue with that trend. Until today, that's the trend.

But now that trend is going even further. Now it's not only the mother of the Bar Missvah boy that's wearing a fancy custom-made hat, it's sometimes also the sisters of the Bar Missvah boy, and it may be some other close female relatives as well. But mark my words, this is not something that was done in Halab. This is strictly a Western custom based upon female Western fashion trends.

Speaking of females, people have asked me, were there any Bat Missvah celebrations in Syria? Absolutely not. They didn't have such celebrations. Maybe other countries did, but in Syria it was never done. And as we know, the custom in our community is we do not have any true Bat Missvah celebrations, nor a Bat Missvah Se'udah, or anything of the such.

Nonetheless, as we know, the women of our community are very, very important, and their place in the Jewish home, in Jewish life, in the upbringing of our families is paramount to everything that we believe in. The Torah tells us that without the Jewish women, we would be nowhere today. So, it's not that we're neglecting them or pushing them aside, this is the way customs have developed, and this is our custom till today.

164.title: Adding 'Anenu in 'Arbit Before a Fast
164.text:
The Gemara in Masekhet Shabbat taught that a prayer for the fast day is added to the 'Amidah on fast days in the Shome'a Tefilah blessing, in 'Arbit, Shahrit, and Minhah. This is referring to the paragraph that begins with the word 'Anenu. And in Masekhet Ta'anit, Rab Huna taught that one who accepted a fast upon himself for the following day adds 'Anenu in 'Arbit, even though he's not fasting yet that night. This is based on a Baraita that taught, sometimes we don't add 'Anenu to the 'Amidah when we are fasting, like in 'Arbit after the fast, before we broke the fast; and sometimes we add 'Anenu to the 'Amidah when we are not fasting, like in 'Arbit on the night before a fast.

Based on these sources, many authorities ruled that 'Anenu is added to the 'Amidah in 'Arbit before a fast day, even though we don't actually begin fasting until the morning that begins at dawn. These authorities include Rab 'Amram Gaon, Rab Sa'adya Gaon, Rabbenu Hananel, the Rif, HaRambam in a responsa, the Rosh, the Ramban, and the Rashba.

However, Rabbenu Zerahyah HaLevi, a 12th-century authority from Spain and southern France, explained that 'Anenu is only added to the 'Amidah in 'Arbit on fasts that begin at night. But when the fast begins in the morning, 'Anenu is only added to the 'Amidah in Shahrit and Minhah. And the Rashba, who lived in Spain in the 13th century, wrote that the custom in his times was to add 'Anenu to the 'Amidah in Shahrit and Minhah on fasts that began at dawn, even though he believed that 'Anenu should be added to 'Arbit as well. Rashi quoted Geonim who wrote that the custom is only to add 'Anenu to the 'Amidah in Minhah on a fast day, since a person might become sick and will be unable to complete the fast. Therefore, they don't want to add 'Anenu to 'Arbit and Shahrit when they are not sure that they will be able to complete the fast.

In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that on the four fasts, meaning on the obligatory fast days, 'Anenu is included in all the 'Amidot, because even if one got sick and had to eat, one could still refer to the day as a fast day in the 'Amidah, since the rabbis instituted a fast on these days.

Still and all, not all Middle Eastern communities followed Maran regarding adding 'Anenu in 'Arbit, Shahrit, and Minhah on a fast day. The Hida wrote that their custom was only to add 'Anenu to the 'Amidah in Minhah on a fast day. And many wrote that their custom was to only add 'Anenu in Shahrit and Minhah. These authorities include Ribbi Hayyim Benveniste in 17th-century Turkey, the Shulhan Gaboah in 18th-century Greece, Ribbi Elisha Dangor in 19th-century Baghdad, and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef in 20th-century Jerusalem.

What was the custom in Halab? Mahzor Aram Soba, an Aleppo prayer book that was printed in the year 1527, includes instructions to add 'Anenu to the 'Amidah in the 'Arbit prayers of the 17th of Tammuz, of Som Gedalyah, and on 'Asarah BeTebet. And this custom continued in Halab at least until the end of the 18th century. Hakham Hayyim Attieh, who was born in Halab in 1751, wrote in his book Orhot HaHayyim: "Know that we have the custom here in Aram Soba to say 'Anenu in all of the prayers, and even in 'Arbit on the night that the fast comes in for the four fasts, like it says in Masekhet Shabbat." And then Hakham Hayyim Attieh continued, "And since I see many criticizing this custom, I'm going to expound and validate and maintain our custom that is founded upon the ancients and upon the law of the Talmud."

Hakham Hayyim Attieh passed away in 1795, and it appears that the custom changed in Halab sometime during the 19th century to only recite 'Anenu in Shahrit and Minhah on fast days that begin in the morning. However, adding 'Anenu on 'Arbit was not only the original custom in Halab, it was also the custom in Yemen, Tunisia, Djerba, Morocco, Libya, and in the city of Izmir in Turkey.

As we mentioned, adding 'Anenu in all of the prayers, including 'Arbit on the night before the fast, is based on the opinion of many authorities, including HaRambam and Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh.

165.title: Se'udah Shelishit and the Alfa Beta
165.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed in our last video the Minhagim of Minhah of Shabbat of the Sibbur, and before we get to 'Arbit, of course we want to discuss the Minhagim of Se'udah Shelishit.

So Se'udah Shelishit, approximately 25 minutes between the end of Minhah and the beginning of 'Arbit, the custom was that the synagogue will provide Berakhot, Mezonot, Ka'ak, cake, and sometimes fruit and drinks, so that people could fulfill the obligation of Se'udah Shelishit. This was, in all the synagogues it was only Mezonot. I guess in the last couple of decades there's been a trend towards people who want to be more particular and more stringent in their fulfillment of this great Missvah of Se'udah Shelishit, and they want to partake with bread and make Netilah and make Birkat HaMazon. Ashrehem Yisrael. So nowadays you have many, many synagogues that will provide that option for the Sibbur.

But, I wanted to discuss my experiences growing up in the Kahal in Brooklyn. So for instance, Shaare Zion in the '70s and '80s, the interesting things I used to observe: so many people would just go out to the hall, have their Mezonot, socialize. You always had a group that came back into the synagogue and they used to sing Pizmonim, which was very, very nice with the Hazzan and Ba'ale Batim which really enjoyed the Hazzanut and the Pizmonim. I remember in my days I used to see, 'Alav HaShalom, Joe Gindi used to always be at the forefront of this group and singing the more complicated Pizmonim. So this was nice.

In fact, in Ahaba, we do something similar, except we do it for a couple of hours between Minhah and 'Arbit, which we established roughly 45 years ago. It's called 'Oneg Shabbat, where we pray Minhah a little earlier and have two hours of singing Pizmonim, Bakashot and Pizmonim.

There was another group, a sizable group, that used to go to the terrace room downstairs, and Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim, Zikhrono LiBerakhah, our esteemed rabbi, used to give a Shi'ur, which was very popular, and many people would go and hear the Shi'ur during that to take advantage of that 20 minutes to study Torah.

The group that was most loyal to our customs of Halab would go up to the Midrash, I'm sure they still do, and they would read the Alfa Beta. This is what I wanted to discuss today. The Alfa Beta is a very, very old custom. In fact, it's printed in the Mahzor Aram Soba, which was printed at the beginning of the 16th century, and it consists of the Alfa Beta, which is Perek Kof-Yod-Tet of Tehillim, followed by all of the Shir HaMa'alot, and it continues with various Perakim from different parts of the Tehillim, culminating in the LaMnasseah BiNginot, which leads into the Pesukim "Ad-onai Seba'ot 'Imanu, Misgab Lanu Eloke Ya'akob Selah," which everybody sings in unison and in preparation for the 'Arbit prayer.

Now there are different customs, nuances, in the Alfa Beta. For instance, in even in Kol Ya'akob, I'm looking at on the Kol Ya'akob, the most recent printing, page 350. So we'll begin saying three Pesukim, "Lekhu Neranenah," it's customary before we begin saying Tehillim to say these Pesukim, and it's very sensible. "Lekhu Neranenah," we're going to embark on singing now Tehillim to Bore 'Olam, "Nari'ah LeSur Yish'enu," "Nekaddemah Fanav BeTodah," so these three Pesukim are found in the Kol Ya'akob, the current edition, although it was not in the original edition. And this is not by chance, there was a specific custom not to say these Pesukim, differences of opinion. It's not printed in the Mahzor Aram Soba, in fact they start with another few introductory Pesukim which we do not say today, although it is printed in the Argentinean Siddur. So you see it's very interesting the way things develop.

The way it is now we do say "Lekhu Neranenah," and we begin "Ashre Temime Derekh." It continues, as I said, with the Shir HaMa'alot, followed by two Perakim which are generally not said because there's no time: Mizmor LeAsaf and LiShlomo. It was to the point where this wasn't even these two Perakim weren't even printed in the original Kol Ya'akob. They are printed now, but as was told to me by many people who reside now in Brooklyn, they do not say those two Perakim. This is simply is no time. In fact, in the book Derekh Eress, bringing the customs in the last generation of Halabiyeh that were there in the '60s and '70s and '80s, they also would skip these two Perakim due to lack of time. It's followed by Mikhtam LeDavid and LeDavid Barukh Ad-onai Suri.

Now what's going to be interesting, what we'll do in our next video, is discuss the tunes that are used for these Perakim of Tehillim, because they're not the classical Tehillim Ta'amim singing that we're used to. Kol Tub.

166.title: The Bar Missvah Morning Prayers
166.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles: Bar Missvah prayer recap. What goes on that morning? Let's go through it. They come to the Kenis, the Bar Missvah puts on his Talet with the Berakhot of LeHit'attef and Sheheheyanu. Then we said about putting on the Tefillin. He does not put on the Tefillin himself, rather he is assisted with the winding of the straps, the Ressu'ot, around the arm with his father, his grandfather, uncles, Hakhamim, other respected men that may be there. The greatest Hakham in presence, let's say the chief rabbi, will put on the Tefillin Shel Rosh for the boy, and the prayers begin.

Now, normally the Hazzan says everything, but since this is a special day for the boy, for the Bar Missvah boy, he is given certain portions to say, and of course based upon his fluency, his expertise, his clarity, and obviously also his poise, you know, that would determine what he'll say. So generally he is given VaYedabber to say, which is technically Kadesh Li, one of the two of the Parashiyot that are written in the Tefillin and what we recite at the beginning of the prayers. So he'll say that out loud and clear.

When the Hazzan gets up to HaShem Melekh, he is going to sing HaShem Melekh, the congregants will respond to him in unison and sing to the same tune. The prayers continue like, say, a regular holiday atmosphere, singing of Barukh SheAmar, singing of "Halleluyah, Halelu El BeKodsho." One of the Halleluyot may be given to the Bar Missvah boy to recite as well. Possibly they'll give him VaYebarekh David or VaYosha' or Az Yashir. The Hazzan sings Kaddish, obviously the Hoda'ot and Kaddish.

They get up to the Shema. The Shema is given to the Bar Missvah boy once again. Sometimes they'll even invite the Bar Missvah boy to come up and stand at the Tebah with the Hazzan and say it from there, or he may say it from his seat depending on what the normal practice within that particular congregation is. They'll sing MiMissrayim, they get up to the Hazarah, say Nakdishakh, sing it together. Hazarah is over. As we mentioned in two episodes, in episode 145 and 148, we omit Tahanunim and we only say Yehi Shem.

Sefer Torah comes out. Before taking out the Sefer Torah, the appropriate members are invited from the family party, and the grandfather or the father will be doing Petihah, the Bar Missvah boy will be carrying the Sefer. They'll sing a Pizmon or two while carrying the Sefer. Before the Bar Missvah boy goes up for his 'Aliyah and for reading a portion of the Torah, they'll sing Pizmon, usually Yosser Adamah.

After the Sefer Torah is put back, at that point the rabbi in attendance or the Hakham of the Kenis will bestow blessings of congratulatory fashion on the boy and his family, give him possibly a Humash, a Tikkun, Siddur, some token of this momentous day, something to carry him forward with Torah and Missvot and prayers. The boy at that point may also make a speech, but if it's a weekday and it be considered a Torah Sibbur, a burden on the congregants, that speech would be left aside to be done on Shabbat when people are not rushing off to work.

But these are the basic celebrations associated with the Bar Missvah. This is what's done throughout the community. It's been pretty much the norm over the course, I'd say, of the last 60, 70 years, and it looks like it's only growing, becoming much more opulent, much more involved, more steps along the way, more introductions of more Dibre Torah and more Pizmonim and more singing, and you know, it's a beautiful celebration, and it's something that the family enjoys, and it's a way to bring the boy into, you know, manhood of the Yahadut, of Judaism, of following Torah, Missvot, Ma'asim Tobim for the remainder of his life.

167.title: Tish'ah BeAb Prayer Customs
167.text:
The book Derekh Eress documents the custom of Halab to sit on the floor on thin mats in the synagogue on Tish'ah BeAb. This custom is observed on both the night and morning of Tish'ah BeAb.

The custom in our community is not to recite Kaddish Titkabbal in 'Arbit on the night of Tish'ah BeAb. This custom was established by Hakham Matloub Abadi and is discussed in his book Magen Ba'adi. However, according to other sources, Kaddish Titkabbal was recited in Halab on the night of Tish'ah BeAb. These sources include Shulhan HaMelekh that was written by Ribbi Shemuel Laniado in the year 1804, Hakham Salim Zafrani's notes recording the customs of the Great Synagogue of Aleppo from the beginning of the 20th century, and Hakham Yisshak Chehebar's Siddur for Tish'ah BeAb also has Kaddish Titkabbal in 'Arbit for Tish'ah BeAb.

Our custom is not to recite the blessing of She'asah Li Kol Sorki on the mornings of Tish'ah BeAb and Yom Kippur, in accordance with the opinion of the Arizal. Our custom is recorded in the book Derekh Eress, quoting Hakham Yisshak Chehebar. On the morning of Tish'ah BeAb, we replace Az Yashir with Ha'azinu. This was also recorded by Hakham Salim Zafrani in his notes describing the customs of the Great Synagogue of Aleppo.

According to the book Derekh Eress, some added 'Anenu in 'Arbit of Tish'ah BeAb, while others did not. However, the prevalent custom in Halab was to only add Nahem to the 'Amidah in Minhah. This is based on Maran in the Bet Yosef, who described only adding in Nahem in Minhah as the Minhag Ha'Olam, the custom all over the world. Ribbi Hayyim Ben Asher Sethon also wrote that the custom of Sefat was to only add Nahem in Minhah. He wrote this in his book Eress Hayyim that was published in the year 1908, and this was also the custom in Baghdad as well.

Other changes to the prayers include replacing Sim Shalom with the shorter 'Oseh HaShalom that's found in the Siddur Arba' Ta'aniyot. This change is made in the 'Arbit and Shahrit 'Amidot, and was part of Hakham Shemuel Laniado's instructions for Tish'ah BeAb in his book Shulhan HaMelekh. However, in Magen Ba'adi, Hakham Matloub Abadi wrote that the regular version of Sim Shalom should be recited in all of the 'Amidot on Tish'ah BeAb.

The usual version of Nakdishakh VeNa'arissakh is replaced with Nekaddesh Et Shimkha in Shahrit, as found in the Siddur Arba' Ta'aniyot. This custom was already recorded in 14th century Spain by the Abudarham, and was the custom in Halab, according to the book Derekh Eress, quoting Hakham Sa'adeh Harari and Hakham Yisshak Zafrani.

According to Hakham Shemuel Laniado in Shulhan HaMelekh, Birkat Kohanim is not recited in Shahrit on Tish'ah BeAb, only in Minhah. This custom was also recorded by the Abudarham and the Shibbole HaLeket, an authority from Italy in the 13th century. This is consistent with our custom that a Kohen does not recite Birkat Kohanim during his seven-day mourning period, as we are all considered like mourners on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb.

We do not recite a Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb. There is no mention of a Haftarah in the instructions for Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb in the famous Mahzor Aram Soba that was published in the year 1527. Hakham Salim Zafrani specified that there is no Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb in his customs of the Great Synagogue of Aleppo. And Hakham Matloub Abadi also specified no Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb in his book Magen Ba'adi. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar does not have a Haftarah for Minhah in his Siddur for Tish'ah BeAb. Furthermore, the custom in our community was always not to recite a Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb.

What about breaking the fast? The book Derekh Eress quotes Hakham Yisshak Tawil and Hakham Abraham Zafrani, who said that in Halab, most broke the fast of Tish'ah BeAb with meat. This is based on the fact that in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran uses the words Minhag Kasher, literally a kosher custom, to describe the practice of not eating meat on the night and day after Tish'ah BeAb. These are words that are used to describe a stringency, not an actual halakhic prohibition, and therefore, the majority were not stringent upon themselves, and followed the actual law that does not prohibit meat right after Tish'ah BeAb.

However, the rabbis and their students were stringent upon themselves, and did not eat meat until the following night, meaning until the night of the 11th of Ab. This is also based on Maran, who applied the stringency of not eating meat or drinking wine to the night and day of the 10th of Ab. But if the fast day fell on Shabbat and was pushed to Sunday, like it does this year, then the rabbis and their students would eat meat and drink wine on the next day, meaning on Monday. They would still not eat meat or drink wine on the night after the fast, but they wouldn't wait until the next night, like they would when the fast was observed on the 9th. Furthermore, the Ben Ish Hai also wrote that the custom in Baghdad was to eat meat right after the fast of Tish'ah BeAb.

168.title: Singing the Alfa Beta with Morris Arking
168.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have the honor to be joined this video presentation with somebody you are very, very well familiar with, Mr. Morris Arking, from the Minhag of the Week series. He's in Yerushalayim, and I asked him to please join me and help me with this presentation in singing the Alfa Beta the way we are, the way it is customary in our community.

As I mentioned last week, between Minhah, Shabbat, and 'Arbit, very, very old custom to sing the Alfa Beta, Perakim of Tehillim. Alfa Beta is one part of it. It begins with Perek Kof-Yod-Tet of Tehillim, that's why it's called the Alfa Beta, even though it continues with Shir HaMa'alot, and many and a number of other Perakim following that. As I mentioned, we begin with the three Pesukim, "Lekhu Neranenah," that is the custom of Brooklyn. And we're going to begin, we're on page 350 in the Kol Ya'akob, if you would like to follow. Kabod, Morris.

"Lekhu Neranenah LaAd-onai, Nari'ah LeSur Yish'enu. Nekaddemah Fanav BeTodah, BiZmirot Nari'ah Lo. Ki El Gadol Ad-onai, UMelekh Gadol 'Al Kol Elohim."

"Ashre Temime Darekh, HaHolekhim BeTorat Ad-onai. Ashre Nossere 'Edotav, BeKhol Leb Yidreshuhu. Af Lo Fa'alu 'Avlah, BiDrakhav Halakhu."

And this is the tune throughout the Perakim of Alfa Beta, and we're going to do the first Perek of the Shir HaMa'alot, and that's on page 356.

"Shir HaMa'alot, El Ad-onai BaSaratah Li, Karati VaYa'aneni. Ad-onai, Hassilah Nafshi MiSfat Sheker, MiLashon Remiyah. Mah Yitten Lekha UMah Yosif Lakh, Lashon Remiyah. Hisse Gibbor Shenunim, 'Im Gahale Retamim. Oyah Li Ki Garti Meshekh, Shakhanti 'Im Ohale Kedar. Rabbat Shakhnah Lah Nafshi, 'Im Sone Shalom. Ani Shalom VeKhi Adabber, Hemah LaMilhamah."

Now, following the Shir HaMa'alot, as I mentioned in our last video, there are two Perakim which are only occasionally mentioned sung if there is time, and that's the Mizmor LeAsaf and LiShlomo. It's done in the same tune as Morris was singing now. So we'll go directly now to Mikhtam LeDavid, and that is on page 363, because this tune is a lot different than the previous tune he was singing. Kabod.

"Mikhtam LeDavid, Shomreni El Ki Hasiti Bakh. Amart LaAd-onai, Ad-onai Attah, Tobati Bal 'Alekha. LiKdoshim Asher BaAress Hemah, VeAddire Kol Hefssi Bam. Yirbu 'Assbotam Aher Maharu, Bal Asikh Niskehem MiDam, UBal Essa Et Shemotam 'Al Sefatai."

That Maqam, that tune continues till the end of Mikhtam, and now we begin LeDavid Barukh Ad-onai Suri, which is a completely different tune, and it has similarities to the tune of, but different, but similarities to the tune of Yerushalayim, and the tune of the Sefaradim, and the tune of the Shawam, and the Egyptians, and now we're going to sing it the way we sing it in the Brooklyn community, in the Halabi community.

"LeDavid Barukh Ad-onai Suri, HaMlammed Yadai LaKrab, Essbe'otai LaMilhamah. Hasdi UMessudati, Misgabi UMfalti Li, Magini UBo Hasiti, HaRoded 'Ammi Tahtai. Ad-onai Mah Adam VaTeda'ehu, Ben Enosh VaTehashebehu."

Now we will go to the last Pasuk, and then we'll continue LaMnasseah.

"...Zeh Ha'Am SheKakhah Lo, Ashre Ha'Am SheAd-onai Elokav."

"LaMnasseah BiNginot Mizmor Shir. Elokim Yehonenu ViYbarkhenu, Ya'er Panav Ittanu Selah. Lada'at BaAress Darkekha, BeKhol Goyim Yeshu'atekha."

And then we continue till Afse Aress and go into HaShem Seba'ot 'Imanu, which we're all familiar with it, so all the whole Kahal will sing in unison. So we'll say the last Pasuk: "Kol Afse Aress."

"Ad-onai Seba'ot 'Imanu, Misgab Lanu Eloke Ya'akob Selah. Ad-onai Seba'ot, Ashre Adam Boteah Bakh. Ad-onai Hoshi'ah, HaMelekh Ya'anenu BeYom Kor'enu. Mi Yitten MiSiyyon Yeshu'at Yisrael, BeShub Ad-onai Shebut 'Ammo, Yagel Ya'akob Yismah Yisrael."

And this is the tune for the... Now, and then the Hazzan will get up and sing the Kaddish, which we'll discuss in our next video. Kol Tub.

169.title: What Is a Sebet?
169.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA, Minhag of the Week, life cycles: the Sebet. We started off with birth, we moved on to Bar Missvah, and now before we get to engagements, weddings, etc., we must stop and deal with the Sebet.

So, first things first: Sebet, not a real word. We have Shabbat, and the Arabic word for Shabbat is sebt, S-A-B-T. Being in the United States for 100, 120 years, the word sebt got watered down, Anglicized, which is now Sebet, S-E-B-B-I-T, if you will, but the real word is sebt, and plenty of old-timers still call it Shabbat. And that's because this is a celebration that happens on Shabbat, and only on Shabbat, so you can only have a Sebet on Shabbat.

Now, what is a Sebet exactly? When does it take place? Why does it take place? Who's involved? What goes on? There are so many details, even though we all think we've been to them so many times and we know everything about them, there are a lot of fine details that we need to study, examine, share, so they do not be forgotten or be watered down.

So, first things first: we have to understand Syria as opposed to other places. Obviously we know on Shabbat, after prayers, Shabbat morning, family gets together to have Se'udat Shabbat, Shabbat lunch, sing Pizmonim, speak Dibre Torah, talk, have a good time, etc. So, what's the big deal? A Sebet is just an expanded, extended version of that.

But Syria is unique. Syria till today is unique in the food tradition of Syria. Syria different than other places, other places all have their unique dishes, but Syria is known for its mezze, for its various appetizers, hors d'oeuvres, finger foods, pick-me-ups, and having such a great variety helped to create the atmosphere of what we know as a Sebet.

Besides the food, the concept of music. In all countries, in all communities they like to sing, but Syria, and more particularly Aleppo, is known till today as a region where people in general love singing old, classical Arabic music, and that's basically the basis for our Pizmonim, which we sing at a Sebet.

So even though families were eating mezze and singing Pizmonim on every Shabbat, this was an event that due to a happy occasion, it gave due cause to make a grander Shabbat celebration, and that is our Sebet. So the Sebet only happens on Shabbat, it happens when there is a happy occasion, like a birth, a Bar Missvah, an engagement, a wedding, any other sort of reason to celebrate that's connected to a life cycle and to Shabbat, and it's always preceded by prayers in the synagogue, after which they move on from the synagogue to the home to have the Sebet, and only a recent phenomenon in the last 30 years approximately, where Sebets are being done outside the home in a synagogue, or catering hall, or what have you.

So over this next bunch of videos, we're going to discuss the Sebet, we're going to examine what it is, where it is, what songs are sung, who attends, the preliminaries leading up to the Sebet, in other words, what goes on in Kenis on Shabbat, the morning of the Sebet, and anything else connected to a Sebet. So please stay tuned, send in your questions, and I hope you enjoy the series.

170.title: Hatarah Before the High Holidays
170.text:
Hakham Abraham Hamwey wrote that in Halab the leading rabbis and judges came to the Kenis, the synagogue, to perform Hatarah for the congregation. He wrote about Hatarah in his Selihot book, Bet El, which was published in the year 1878. He explained that the reason that the leading rabbis and judges performed the Hatarah in Halab was because they also annulled various forms of excommunications along with the vows, which required rabbis who were proficient in annulments.

Hakham Abraham Hamwey wrote that Hatarah was done on 'Ereb Rosh Hodesh Elul, 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah, and 'Ereb Kippur. However, in the beginning of the 20th century, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that the first Hatarah was performed on the night of the 20th of Ab, which is 40 days before the holiday of Rosh HaShanah. This is based on the Zohar that taught that one who is guilty of improper speech, which includes unfulfilled vows, or one who has been excommunicated, will not have their prayers accepted for 40 days.

Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo also wrote that first the rabbi would address the congregation with words of rebuke, and then the rabbi would ask for Hatarah from the other rabbis, and they would recite the Hatarah declaration for him. And only after the rabbis performed Hatarah for each other, would they then perform Hatarah for the congregation.

The book Derekh Eress wrote that the first Hatarah was performed on the 19th of Ab, and even though it was performed during the month of Ab, it was referred to as Hatarat Elul. Derekh Eress also pointed out that at all the Hatarot, the first one on the 19th of Ab, as well as on the other two, on 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah and 'Ereb Kippur, they also annulled curses, in addition to annulling vows. Derekh Eress described the procedure as follows: One representative of the congregation read the request for Hatarah from 10 rabbis, and then the rabbis read the Hatarah declaration. Originally in Halab, the rabbis went from house to house to perform Hatarah for the women, but in later times, the rabbis went to the ladies' section in the Kenis to perform Hatarah for the women.

Here in Brooklyn, the custom developed to perform Hatarah on the Saturday night before the 19th of Ab, again on the Saturday night before Rosh HaShanah, and again on the Saturday night before Kippur, all in the Kenis. And it has always been customary for women to attend Hatarah as well.

A representative, usually the Hazzan, reads the request for Hatarah in front of the rabbis on behalf of the congregation. The congregation joins the representative for the last paragraph of the request. The rabbis then nullify the various types of vows, excommunications, and curses. Then the Hazzan and the congregation make an additional declaration regarding future vows, and add a short prayer asking HaShem to nullify all curses and excommunications, turning everything into a blessing. The rabbis then accept the declaration and conclude with the verse, "VeAttem HaDebekim BaAd-onai Elokekhem, Hayyim Kullekhem HaYom," which is a blessing for the congregation.

Our community never had the custom to annul vows by ourselves, without a tribunal of at least three rabbis or learned men who recite the Hatarah declaration, or without a representative making the request before the tribunal on behalf of the congregation. Our custom is based on how the custom was practiced in Halab, as described by Hakham Abraham Hamwey, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, and the book Derekh Eress.

171.title: 'Arbit of Mossa'e Shabbat
171.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will be discussing the Minhagim of 'Arbit of Mossa'e Shabbat in the synagogue. In our last video, we discussed the customs between Minhah and 'Arbit. One of them was the reciting of the Alfa Beta, Mizmor Kof-Yod-Tet in Tehillim, followed by the Shir HaMa'alot series, and then a few more Mizmorim at the end. Even if the Kahal does not say the entire Alfa Beta, at the very least a few minutes before they begin 'Arbit, they will sing the Mizmor of Tehillim, LeDavid Barukh Ad-onai Suri, followed by LaMnasseah BiNginot in the unique tune which we recited in our last video.

The time that they begin 'Arbit, when I was growing up in Brooklyn, Shaare Zion, other synagogues, they used to begin 18 minutes after sunset, they used to begin 'Arbit. So they finish around 35 minutes, 36 minutes, and that's where we have the saying, Shabbat ends Nusf U-Khamseh. Nusf being half plus five, 35 minutes after sunset Shabbat was over, so they used to start 18 minutes after. I know there are some Hakhamim today which want to push it up to 40 minutes, each according to their own understanding and Kahal, Ashrehem Yisrael.

Followed by the, excuse me, the Mizmorim, after LaMnasseah, "'Al Kol HaAress," they begin, the whole Kahal, "Ad-onai Seba'ot 'Imanu," which we also mentioned in our last video. And there are another few Pesukim which are unique to Mossa'e Shabbat, which are not said every evening, and that's "Mi Yitten MiSiyyon Yeshu'at Yisrael" until the last Pasuk, "Akh Saddikim Yodu LiShmekha, Yeshbu Yesharim Et Panekha."

And then the Hazzan will begin immediately the Kaddish. I say immediately because he does not repeat the final Pasuk of what the Kahal was singing, which he does do on the Shalosh Regalim, who repeat the last Pasuk of the Mizmor of the holiday before he begins Kaddish, not on Mossa'e Shabbat. They finish "Yeshbu Yesharim Et Panekha," immediately he will begin singing the Kaddish.

Now the Kaddish and the 'Arbit is sung in the scale of Bayat. That is the custom throughout most of the Kehillot, the Halabi communities. In Ades we have a different system, but we won't get into that now. This gives them the opportunity to use one of the tunes of Mossa'e Shabbat for the Ra'u Banim, because we know most of the Mossa'e Shabbat tunes are written in the scale of Bayat, which is probably why we sing Bayat for Mossa'e Shabbat.

He will begin Kaddish, Barekhu, Barekhu, begin the Berakhot of Keri'at Shema, and then he will recite the Keri'at Shema. Unlike Shahrit, where there is always the possibility that if there is a Hazzan, a guest, a Paytan, he will honor them with saying the Keri'at Shema, more times than not, generally speaking, 'Arbit, the Keri'at Shema belongs to the Hazzan, he doesn't give it out. It's followed by Emet VeEmunah, it goes all the way to Kayyam 'Alenu, and we mentioned that Ra'u Banim is also sung.

I remember when I was growing up in Brooklyn, you would hear the same Mossa'e Shabbat tunes for Ra'u Banim: Ramu Sayom Meruham, "Ra'u Banim Et Geburato," or Amar HaShem LeYa'akob, "Ra'u Banim Et Geburato," or "Ra'u Banim Et Geburato." So, you see, these tunes would repeat themselves, generally in Mossa'e Shabbat, the Ra'u Banim. Obviously, the Hazzan has the option to use any tune in Bayat he's comfortable with, but just giving you a little of my recollections.

It's followed by Kaddish and the 'Amidah. Of course, in the 'Amidah we say Attah Honantanu, and you'll always hear the first five or six people that get to Attah Honantanu will say it out loud, "Attah Honantanu," reminding the people who didn't get there yet not to forget to say it. In our next video, we will discuss the Minhagim following the 'Amidah. Kol Tub.

172.title: When Is a Sebet Made?
172.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA Minhag of the Week: Life cycles, the Sebet. So, we spoke in the introduction about Sebets, general terms of what a Sebet is. But now we're going to get into the details regarding the Sebet. So, first and foremost: When? When does a Sebet happen? Obviously, a Sebet, as we said, mentioned, happens on Shabbat. But for what occasions?

So, we know our general occasions we have: birth of a boy, birth of a girl, Bar Missvah, engagement, wedding. These are our generally accepted happy occasions. Do we have a Sebet for each of them? So, let's go through them one by one.

For a baby boy, most of the time, there is no Sebet because there will be a Berit Milah, and sometimes there's also a Pidyon as well, and to have an extra financial burden, if you will, with a Sebet sometimes can be too difficult. Plus, it's rushed because you're preparing for the Berit Milah, so generally a Sebet does not happen. For a baby girl, although in the past, okay, and it's sad, but in the past, the birth of a girl was not celebrated. Nowadays, thankfully so, it is celebrated, and usually there is a Sebet. For a Bar Missvah, as well, in the past, there was nothing, and nowadays, it's generally accepted to have a Sebet. For an engagement, there's usually not a Sebet because the family is looking forward to the wedding, but some families will make a Sebet for an engagement. And for the wedding, that is really the main time that a Sebet is always made. And it's agreed upon by all that that's really when Sebets began, with the wedding.

So now, when does the Sebet happen in all of these occasions? So, obviously, if you're dealing with the birth of a child, boy or girl, it would happen after the birth. With a Bar Missvah, the Sebet would happen on the Shabbat that the Bar Missvah boy is reading from the Parashah publicly in the Kenis, or on the Shabbat immediately following his weekday Bar Missvah celebration. For an engagement, if it happens, it would be immediately following the engagement.

And now for the wedding: Does it happen the Shabbat prior to the wedding or the Shabbat after the wedding? So, the original Minhag is the Shabbat after the wedding, and it would be a Shabbat Hatan, okay, Shabbat of the groom, obviously the groom and the bride. So, what happened? Why for many decades was the custom in our community to do the wedding Sebet the Shabbat prior to the wedding? That happened out of necessity. As people picked up on the custom of the honeymoon and leaving immediately after the wedding—and we'll get to that with the going-away outfits at the wedding, where they actually went away immediately afterwards, and they didn't come back for a week, two weeks, three weeks, a month, whatever the case may be—so the whole fanfare and excitement associated with the wedding was gone to do it have a Sebet after the wedding. So, the Sebet was pushed back and done the Shabbat prior to the wedding.

Now, as we see a return to the original way of things, where they didn't leave immediately after the ceremony right after the wedding, and people lingered around at least for a week, so now we're seeing the Sebet returning to the Shabbat after the wedding. So, these are our occasions of when we do the Sebet in association to the happy occasions. We will talk about when the Sebet happens on Shabbat in an upcoming video. Thank you.

173.title: The Rosh HaShanah Simanim
173.text:
One of the most notable customs on the holiday of Rosh HaShanah is the special foods that are served on the first night, and in some homes on both nights, of Rosh HaShanah. The book Derekh Eress quoted Hakham Yisshak Chehebar as specifying that the custom in Halab was to only serve these foods on the first night. Only serving the special foods on the first night was also recorded by the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer. Furthermore, according to Derekh Eress, most serve these foods after HaMossi, but some families have the custom to serve these foods after Kiddush, before washing their hands and reciting HaMossi.

The origin of this custom is the Gemara. In Masekhet Horayot, the Gemara writes that one should see these foods on Rosh HaShanah, but in Masekhet Keritot it says that one should eat them, and in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that one should eat these foods. The Gemara only lists five foods: the gourd, the black-eyed peas, the leek, Swiss chard, and dates. In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran added the head of a sheep, based on the writings of the Mordekhai, a 13th-century authority from Germany, quoting the Geonim of the Middle East from prior to the 11th century.

The custom of eating an apple was recorded by the Tur in the 14th century as the custom of the Ashkenazim. The custom of eating a pomegranate was recorded by the Abudarham, also in the 14th century, but in Spain. Even though Maran did not include the apple or the pomegranate in Shulhan 'Arukh, it was included by many later Middle Eastern authorities, including Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Mahzor for Rosh HaShanah, which he called Bet Din. We also find both the apple and the pomegranate in the writings of the Ben Ish Hai, the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef. Our community Mahzor, Shelom Yerushalayim, also lists both the apple and the pomegranate. Mahzor Shelom Yerushalayim is based on an earlier Mahzor known as Zekhor LeAbraham.

When checking the various sources, I noticed that each source presents the list of foods in a different order. One question is whether to begin with the dates or with the apples. When one is going to eat several different fruits that are all Bore Peri Ha'Ess, the Halakhah is, if you have one of the special fruits that is associated with the land of Israel, you should eat that one first in order to recite Ha'Ess on the special fruit. Dates and pomegranates are both one of those special fruits; apples are not. And regarding the special fruits themselves, dates take precedence over pomegranates, based on their position in the verse that lists the special fruits that are associated with the land of Israel. And therefore, some begin with the dates. The book Derekh Eress quoted Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, who began with dates.

However, the prevalent custom in our community is to begin with the apple. Hakham Abraham Hamwey began with the apple. The book Keter Shem Tob also begins with the apple, and both our community Mahzor, Shelom Yerushalayim, and the Mahzor Zekhor LeAbraham begin with the apple. According to the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer, the apples should be brought out before the dates, so that the dates won't be on the table when Ha'Ess is recited on the apple. Others would eat the dipped apple on a piece of bread in order to avoid reciting Ha'Ess on the apple, so that they could still recite Ha'Ess afterwards when they eat the date. Hakham Abraham Hamwey suggested reciting Ha'Ess on the pomegranate after Kiddush, before washing your hands for HaMossi. Then one would not recite Ha'Ess again on the apple or the date. But as we said, dates really take precedence over pomegranates.

Another option is to recite Ha'Ess on an olive, which also takes precedence over the date, after Kiddush. Then wash your hands, recite HaMossi, and after eating bread, you begin with the apple. Since you already recited Ha'Ess on the olive, you just recite the Yehi Rasson before eating the apple, and then continue, following the order of the Mahzor, reciting the appropriate Yehi Rasson before each food. The prevalent custom in our community is to recite the Yehi Rasson before tasting each food. However, according to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, the Yehi Rasson is recited after tasting each food.

The custom of eating an apple with the special foods on the night of Rosh HaShanah, as we said earlier, was originally an Ashkenazic custom. They ate an apple dipped in honey first in order to begin the year with something sweet. Eventually, this Ashkenazic custom was adopted by Middle Eastern Jews as well because of its Kabbalistic significance. The apple signifies a field of holy apples, which is a Kabbalistic expression that refers to the divine presence, and therefore, it's appropriate to begin with the food that symbolizes the divine presence. Our community custom of beginning with the apple is based on several sources.

While the original custom of the Ashkenazim was to dip the apple in honey, the prevalent custom in our community is to dip the apple in white sugar. Similarly, it is customary to dip the bread in white sugar as well, instead of salt, throughout the holiday of Rosh HaShanah.

174.title: After the 'Amidah on Mossa'e Shabbat
174.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed the 'Amidah of Mossa'e Shabbat and we will continue now with the prayers that follow the 'Amidah. In the Kol Ya'akob, I am on page 383. After the 'Amidah, he says the Hazzan will say Yehi Shem followed by Hassi Kaddish.

Now in the books on page 384, you'll see "Shubah Ad-onai 'Ad Matai, VeHinahem 'Al 'Abadekha," "Sabbe'enu BaBoker Hasdekha," there are four Pesukim preceding the final Pasuk "Vihi No'am Ad-onai Elokenu 'Alenu, UMa'aseh Yadenu Konenah 'Alenu, UMa'aseh Yadenu Konenehu," followed by Yosheb BeSeter 'Elyon, Orekh Yamim, VeAttah Kadosh.

The Minhag in Halab, Syrian custom, the Aleppo custom, was not to say the first four Pesukim, which is in the Mizmor preceding Yosheb BeSeter 'Elyon, which I think is number 90 if I'm not mistaken. We only begin with "Vihi No'am Ad-onai Elokenu 'Alenu, UMa'aseh Yadenu Konenah 'Alenu, UMa'aseh Yadenu Konenehu." That was the Halabi custom. That I think till today is the custom in most synagogues in Argentina. Rabbi Shammah and others verified that in 67th Street indeed they did not say Shubah Ad-onai 'Ad Matai, they began Vihi No'am, and then Yosheb BeSeter.

It must have been, if I have to guess, the introduction and the proliferation of the Mansour Iraqi books in our community maybe late '50s, early '60s, so it began to take hold. Maybe Hakhamim who came from Eress Yisrael also strengthened this custom. Today most synagogues, if not all, will say "Shubah Ad-onai 'Ad Matai, VeHinahem 'Al 'Abadekha," they will begin from there and not from Vihi No'am, which is the original custom of the Halabi community.

We say this, the custom in our community, the Halabi custom is to say this seated. We do not stand. Many other communities, Egyptian community, Yerushalmi, the Damascus community, they stand for Shubah Ad-onai 'Ad Matai, Yosheb BeSeter, Orekh Yamim, and then they will sit down for the VeAttah Kadosh. The Halabi custom is to sit down throughout.

Here it's also appropriate to mention that if Yom Tob is, if the Yom Tob falls during that week, we do not say Vihi No'am and we begin "Orekh Yamim Asbi'ehu," VeAttah Kadosh. The reason being is that "Ma'aseh Yadenu Konenah 'Alenu, UMa'aseh Yadenu Konenehu," there has to be a six-day workweek that week before the next Shabbat in order to say that Pasuk. That's the Ta'am, the reason that's brought by many of the Aharonim, "Ma'aseh Yadenu." So if there is a day during the week where it's forbidden to work, like a Yom Tob or even 'Ereb Pesah that falls out on a Friday, then we also would not say Vihi No'am.

Finally, around the time of the VeAttah Kadosh, the Shamash will have a few of the boys, a few of the young boys, go out to the entire Kahal with the Mazahar, the, those silver beautiful silver canisters of, the bottles, I don't know what you call them, of Besamim and they will give it out to all the people in preparation of the Habdalah. After the, we have the Kaddish Titkabbal, Shir HaMa'alot of course, and Kaddish Yehe Shelama, Barekhu, and 'Alenu LeShabbeah, and we have concluded 'Arbit of Mossa'e Shabbat, and we will begin discussing the Habdalah in our next video. Kol Tub.

175.title: Shabbat Morning in Kenis Before the Sebet
175.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles: The Sebet. So, we talked about when we have a Sebet, for what occasions. But now we also mentioned that the Sebet happens on Shabbat. So what goes on the morning of that Sebet, that Shabbat morning in the Kenis? Is anything going on that's special?

So firstly is that the family, the person that has the happy occasion, they come to the Kenis as usual, they generally go to the synagogue they generally pray in with their family. And depending on the makeup of the synagogue, they may sit in the front row or they may sit in their regular seats. In any case, people generally as they walk in, they will acknowledge their presence, especially if they know they had a happy occasion that week or something coming up, and they will Mabrook them. They'll either walk up to them to greet them, tell them "Shabbat Shalom, Mabrook," or they'll, from the entrance or from their own seat, they'll give them a hand gesture like that, acknowledging them and letting them know that they're wishing them well and they're happy for them.

Now, these people that have the happy occasion, whether let's talk about the Abi HaBen, the father of the child for example, or possibly the father of the Bar Missvah boy, or maybe the Bar Missvah boy himself, or maybe the Hatan, the groom, okay, they generally don't have a role of participating in the prayers, and they're not given anything to be said publicly unless, of course, they're well-versed, they're a regular as to part of the routine of what's being said in the Kenis, or they're a Hazzan, or amateur Hazzan even. Otherwise, they're sitting there as guests, and nothing is special going on.

Everything starts happening once it's time for the Sefer Torah to come out and for the 'Aliyot to happen. And as my dear friend Joey Harari discussed in his Minhag of the Week videos, depending on the makeup of the Kenis, and obviously with what the occasion is will determine who gets Petihah, who gets to carry the Sefer Torah, who has Gilyan in other words, who has an 'Aliyah, how many 'Aliyot are given out, is all determined based upon the social mores of the particular synagogue, and obviously on time constraints, especially if there is more than one Simhah, more than one Farah on that day. So that's really what's going on.

Now, the Sebet prayers, or the prayers prior to the Sebet, always happen in the main synagogue, or at least at the time that the main synagogue is praying. In other words, you would never hear of people praying in first Minyan, being out and done by 9:00, then everybody going on their way and coming back for a Sebet at 12:00 or 1:00 or 2:00. It's unheard of. Nowadays we see it, but it's not the true practice, the true custom.

Also, something that was beautiful that was always done in the past, and it's still done amongst many traditional families, but it's for some reason it's falling to the wayside, is that if you were invited to a Sebet, that means the family gave you the Kabod to invite you to their Sebet, you did not pray in your regular Kenis that morning. You went to pray with them. So let's say you generally prayed in Beth Torah, but you have a Sebet in Shaare Zion, and the family is praying in Shaare Zion, you went to pray with them in Shaare Zion, and you would sit together with them. So now this family of 4, 5, 6, 7 people now swells to 20 people, 30 people, 40 people, whatever happens, those are the people sitting with them: extended family, cousins, friends, neighbors, they're all sitting together, and that heightens and enhances the happiness of the day. And those people are there also want to get involved, they're given 'Aliyot as well, and it just increases the beauty and excitement of the day, and gives extra jubilation to all those involved.

So this is a wonderful Minhag that we also need to see come back. There are many other Minhagim associated with Semahot in the Bet Keneset, and each one we'll discuss as we get to it at its proper time.

176.title: Kapparot on 'Ereb Kippur
176.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote, that which is customary to make a Kapparah, an atonement on 'Ereb Kippur by slaughtering a chicken for each male and to recite some verses upon it, this custom should be stopped. In his longer work known as the Bet Yosef, Maran explained that this is based on the opinion of the Rashba, a 13th-century authority from Spain who followed his teacher, the Ramban, who prohibited this practice because he considered it an occult practice of the Amorites, which is forbidden by the Torah.

However, many still practice this custom, which was recorded by the Geonim of the Middle East between the 7th and 11th centuries. The custom was discussed by Rab Sheshna Gaon, Rab Natronai Gaon, and Rab Hai Gaon. Rab Hai Gaon described it as the custom of the majority in Babylonia during the 10th and 11th centuries. We also find the custom in the writings of the Tashbess, who was born in Spain in the 14th century. Eventually he moved to Algeria, where he passed away in the 15th century. Furthermore, the custom of slaughtering chickens for Kapparot was promoted by Rabbi Yisshak Luria, otherwise known as the Arizal, the master of Kabbalah from the 16th century.

In the 19th century, Hakham Abraham Hamwey devoted five pages to the custom of Kapparot in his Mahzor for Yom Kippur, which he called Bet HaKapporet. In his discussion, he mentions that it is preferable to use white chickens for Kapparot, and that the most appropriate time to slaughter the chickens is before sunrise on 'Ereb Kippur after reciting Selihot. While he does mention Maran's opposition to the custom, he also cites the opinions of Rab Natronai Gaon, the Tur, the Arizal, and Muram, all of whom were in favor of the custom. Although it's clear that Hakham Abraham Hamwey was also in favor of slaughtering chickens for Kapparot, he did write that one who does not have the custom of doing Kapparot with chickens should perform the custom by giving the monetary equivalent of a chicken to charity.

In the beginning of the 20th century, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that in Halab, they slaughtered the Kapparot at dawn on 'Ereb Kippur, but a small few did not slaughter chickens; they gave money to the poor for Kapparot instead. Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca quoted Hakham Nissim Levi, who reported that in Halab, the ritual slaughterers would go from courtyard to courtyard with white male chickens to slaughter on behalf of the men, and with white female chickens to slaughter on behalf of the women. Some ate the chickens themselves, but gave the monetary value of a chicken to the poor, while others gave the actual chickens that were slaughtered for Kapparot to the poor. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote that the custom is to slaughter male and female chickens for Kapparot, but that it's preferable not to give the actual chickens to the poor, but rather the monetary equivalent of the chicken should be given to the poor.

So even though Maran was against the custom of slaughtering chickens for Kapparot, the prevalent custom in Halab was to practice the custom with chickens, based on the opinion of other authorities, including the Arizal. The ritual is meant to inspire thoughts and feelings of repentance, while also providing food or money to the poor. As we mentioned, there were those that did not practice the custom with chickens; instead, they performed the custom of Kapparot with money, by giving the monetary equivalent of a chicken to charity for the poor.

177.title: Habdalah and Mossa'e Shabbat at Home
177.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have completed in our last video the Minhagim of 'Arbit of Mossa'e Shabbat in the synagogue. We will move on now and discuss the Minhagim of the Habdalah.

Now, as I mentioned in our last video, towards the end of the 'Arbit, Shamash will have a couple of young boys go around the synagogue with the Mazahar, the rose water in the nice decanter, the nice silver holders, distribute the Mazahar to the people who will hold it in their hands, the liquid, and then go until the time when the Hazzan will recite the Berakhah Bore Mine Besamim, they'll answer "Amen" and they'll smell it to fulfill their obligation.

It's interesting that when I spoke about the Minhagim of Friday night that were in the old days, they used to have the Shamash would stand at the door of the synagogue, and as the people exit Friday night, Lel Shabbat, they would, the Shamash would sprinkle them, would distribute Besamim on the way out, and they'll make the Berakhah Bore Mine Besamim. It's interesting we receive the Shabbat and we depart from the Shabbat with that same beautiful, fragrant Mazahar, which reminds us so much of the Kenis, the synagogue, and our Shabbat. It's very, very nice. And this is, by the way, the Minhag of in our community to use Besamim is the old Minhag, probably in Halab as well, as opposed to many Kehillot which use Hadas or some other fragrant green plant, which will say "'Asse Besamim" or "'Isbe Besamim." Our custom was always to do it on Mazahar and to say "Bore Mine Besamim."

Now we're going to talk about the Minhagim of the reciting of the Habdalah. There's always that lucky young boy that gets to hold the candle. Also, it's a nice custom to get the children involved, and it's a big thrill for them. Our custom throughout, certainly in my experiences, and I've seen it you know, countless synagogues, was that the Hazzan, who is usually standing at the podium near the Hekhal or in smaller synagogues maybe near on the Tebah, the Hazzan reciting the Habdalah would be standing up, holding the cup of wine. The people would be seated. It is our custom. I know there are those now that want to insist that the Hazzan, based on Pesakim of Gedole HaHakhamim, that the Hazzan also be seated. But the custom was always in front of great Hakhamim that the Hazzan would be standing and the people would be seated.

Now let's talk about the Nusah of the Habdalah, the actual wording of the Habdalah. Now here you'll find some variance among you know, variances among the Hazzanim. The Nusah that we use, you'll find it on page 392 in Kol Ya'akob. It was also similar, very similar, almost exact to the Nusah printed in 1915 in the Siddur in Halab, 'Olat HaShahar: "Rishon LeSiyyon," "Kos Yeshu'ot Essa," "Ana HaShem Hoshi'ah Na," "Ana HaShem Hasslihah Na," a couple of Pesukim about Simhah, "Orah VeSimhah VeSasson ViYkar," "VaYehi David," "Be'Ene Elokim VeAdam," "Sabri Maranan." It's concise.

You will find sometimes they will invite Hazzanim, especially from Israel, so they'll start "Kumi Ori Ki Ba Orekh" and many Pesukim which we may not be familiar with. Actually that it would be found in Mahzor Aram Soba from 500 years ago, but the Nusah which is accepted by the Halabi community is the Nusah printed in Kol Ya'akob without all the added Pesukim.

Following the Habdalah in the synagogue, there was a custom. Now it's brought down in Sefer Derekh Eress, a custom that is testified to by 'Alav HaShalom Hakham Yisshak Tawil and also Rabbi Hayyim Dayyan. They say that following the Habdalah, the Kahal would sing a number of the Pizmonim, the beautiful Pizmonim, which are very old by the way, they go date back way back to the Rishonim, and they would sing like Mossa'e Yom Menuhah, El Eliyahu, HaMabdil Ben Kodesh LeHol, and they would sing these Pizmonim in the synagogue. We know that in Halab in the earlier days, I'm talking about based on the Mahzor Aram Soba printed in the 16th century, that even has a Kaddish following these Piyyutim, so it's clear that it would be done in the synagogue. Today you don't find that as much following Habdalah, immediately HaMabdil Ben Kodesh LeHol, the Hazzan will drink and everybody disperses and goes home. But it is a nice custom. In Israel we do maybe a couple of Battim, a couple of verses.

There was a very interesting custom and a very important custom in our community that Mossa'e Shabbat, families would gather at the homes of the patriarch, matriarch of the families, the grandparents, all the siblings, the grandchildren would gather, they would say Habdalah together, followed by they would get around the table, the men, and they would say VeYitten Lekha Elokim. It's in our Kol Ya'akob, page 393. Beautiful Pesukim from the Torah, from the Nebi'im, from the Ketubim. Everybody would say a few Pesukim. That's also how they sharpened their skills with the Ta'amim when they were younger.

And following that, they would sing all of the songs of Mossa'e Shabbat: Agil VeEsmah BeKhol, Mossa'e 'Eden VeRavahah, Hadesh Sesoni. These are well-known songs. The entire families would sing them, following with the blessing that the grandfather would give to his children and grandchildren. It's also printed in the book, in the Siddur, in the whole Seder Mossa'e Shabbat. This was a really beautiful custom and inshallah we'll revive it, because it's important for the feeling of not leaving Shabbat right away. We let Shabbat linger a little bit with the songs of Mossa'e Shabbat. And it's also important for the families to come together for this beautiful custom. Shalom UBerakhah.

178.title: Flowers on the Rimmonim for a Sebet
178.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA Minhag of the Week: Life Cycles, the Sebet. So in previous episodes we spoke about that Shabbat morning in the Bet Keneset, the morning of the Sebet, what occasions a Sebet would be held for, the fanfare in the synagogue. What we didn't talk about yet are the flowers.

Yes, everybody knows a beautiful bouquet or rather an arrangement of flowers is sent to the Kenis before Shabbat. It'll sit up there near the Hekhal, you know, to adorn the Bet Keneset, to announce to anybody who walks in, "Oh, there's some sort of Farah today, there's a happy occasion today." You know, some people may walk up, you know, to the flowers, read the card, see who has the occasion, or just ask, "Oh, who has flowers today? What's going on?" you know. And it adds another layer of happiness to Shabbat.

But what else is going on with flowers? A beautiful, beautiful Minhag that unfortunately in the last few decades has fallen to the wayside. And this was the pride and joy of the women of the community, especially the mothers and grandmothers and great aunts of the person having the happy occasion. For example, if it was a groom, his mother and grandmother and aunts and great aunts would be involved. If there was a baby born and there was a Sebet for that, the grandmothers would be involved once again.

So what went on? On Friday, the day before the Sebet, they would arrange with the Shamash, the Shammosh of the Bet Keneset: "We need to come. We need to come to the Bet Keneset. We need to bring flowers." But not the arrangement of flowers that we all know, rather flowers to adorn the Rimmonim on the Sefer Torah. Yes, the women took pride in this. It was a beautiful thing. It was their opportunity to come to the Kenis, have a few private moments in front of the Hekhal, you know, say a short prayer. They would be handed the Rimmonim by the Shammosh, and they would do their work. They would buy simple flowers, not fancy flowers, less expensive flowers, but flowers that would survive the night, survive the day inside the Hekhal on the Rimmonim. They got simple metal, which you barely can see, thin metal twist ties, if you will, to attach flowers to the Rimmonim. And they did it with pride, they did it with joy. "Look at this! Look how nice!" And they would put these on top of the Sefer Torah.

The Sefer Torah would come out. Let's say the Abi HaBen, the father of the baby boy, or Abi HaBat, the father of the baby girl, or the Arus, or the Hatan, the groom, you know, the engaged person, is carrying the Sefer Torah, he's given that honor, and on top of that Sefer Torah he's carrying these beautifully decorated Rimmonim. And everybody would see them and they would know the women of the family were involved. And the women would be in the women's gallery, and they would see them, and they would take pride, you know, that they have a Farah today.

This was something that was very, very special. It really added so many different levels of excitement to the Sebet. It's something that was done for generations, and something that really should be brought back. Simple flowers, but they add a beautiful touch. They adorn the Rimmonim, which adorns the Sefer Torah, which is our pride and joy. Minhag for the women, and for the Kahal, everybody should enjoy it once again.

179.title: When Berikh Shemeh Is Recited
179.text:
The Zohar on Parashat VaYakhel quoted Rabbi Shim'on saying that when we take out the Sefer Torah to read it for a congregation, the gates of heaven of mercy open, and we arouse love on High, and it is required that a person say the following. And then the text of the Berikh Shemeh prayer that we are familiar with from our Siddurim is written in the Zohar.

In the Sha'ar HaKavvanot, a Kabbalistic work that was written by Rabbi Hayyim Vital, a student of the Arizal, it is reported that the Arizal used to recite Berikh Shemeh before taking out the Sefer Torah on Shabbat morning. According to some other Mekubbalim, including Rabbi Moshe Zacut, a 17th century Kabbalist who officiated in Italy and was known by the acronym Ramaz, the main time to recite Berikh Shemeh is in Minhah of Shabbat, and the Sha'ar HaKavvanot is only pointing out that the Arizal also used to say Berikh Shemeh on Shabbat morning as well.

The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer wrote that it is customary to recite Berikh Shemeh on Shabbat in Shahrit and Minhah, and on Yom Tob, Rosh HaShanah, and Yom Kippur in Shahrit. Interestingly, according to the Ben Ish Hai in his responsa Rab Pe'alim in the section entitled Sod Yesharim, Berikh Shemeh should also be recited on Rosh Hodesh.

What was the custom in Halab? According to the book Derekh Eress, the custom of Halab was to recite Berikh Shemeh in Shahrit on Shabbat and holidays. It was not recited in Minhah of Shabbat or on Rosh Hodesh. This is based on the straightforward reading of the Sha'ar HaKavvanot that reported that the Arizal used to say Berikh Shemeh in Shahrit on Shabbat, without any mention of Minhah or Rosh Hodesh. Similarly, in the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar that was printed in Halab in the year 1915, there is no mention of Berikh Shemeh in Minhah of Shabbat or on Rosh Hodesh, only in Shahrit of Shabbat. Likewise, the original community Siddur Tefilat Yeshurun does not mention Berikh Shemeh in Minhah of Shabbat or on Rosh Hodesh, again, only in Shahrit of Shabbat.

So the custom of Halab was not in accordance with the Ramaz and other Mekubbalim who considered Minhah of Shabbat as the main time to recite Berikh Shemeh, as there is no mention of this in the Zohar or in the Sha'ar HaKavvanot. Furthermore, the custom of Halab was not in accordance with the Ben Ish Hai who advocated reciting Berikh Shemeh on Rosh Hodesh. The custom was only to recite Berikh Shemeh in Shahrit on Shabbat and Yamim Tobim, including Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur, based on what is written about the Arizal in the Sha'ar HaKavvanot.
