180.title: Parashat Bereshit, Noah and Lekh Lekha
180.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. In our last video, we completed the customs of Mossa'e Shabbat, the Habdalah, the Pizmonim, and the prayers following the Habdalah. And with that, completed the customs of the prayers of the Sibbur, the Tefilah BeSibbur for Shabbat. However, we're not quite done yet. I do want to go back now and speak about customs which are specific to Parashiyot on Shabbat. So we're going to start with Parashat Bereshit and go through the entire Hamishah Humshe Torah to discuss the unique customs of each Parashah, and we will begin with Parashat Bereshit.

Now, Parashat Bereshit, the Hazzan will sing in Maqam Rast, Rast from the word Rosh, at least hinting to the word Rosh, which we begin Bereshit and Shemot and VaYikra, those Parashiyot in Maqam Rast. The rule doesn't apply to BeMidbar if it falls out before Shabu'ot, and Debarim, which is usually Shabbat Hazon, which we'll get to it when we discuss those Parashiyot. You can go to the website pizmonim.org, it's a wealth of information and recordings of our Pizmonim book, and there you could find, more often than not, there's quite reasonable explanations as to why we chose, the Hakhamim chose, the Paytanim, certain Maqamat for certain Parashiyot.

So Parashat Bereshit, we have two interesting customs. One is that the 'Aliyot are broken up based on the days of creation. So the Kohen will end "VaYehi 'Ereb VaYehi Boker Yom Ehad." The Levi will do the second day, Shelishi the third day, and so on until the Shishi concludes with "Bara Elokim La'asot," with the creation of the seventh day, the Shabbat. Now, the rest of the Parashah is broken up as many 'Aliyot as are required in each Minyan, and that's like until you get to the Samukh, Mashlim, and Maftir.

There is recently, I did want to point out a couple months ago, a Tikkun Soferim called Birkat Abraham, which was published in our community by just a group of people who really dedicated many years of research and Daikanut to prepare and present this Tikkun Soferim, where we break up all the 'Aliyot based on our customs, and there's other features which are very important. I urge all the Kehillot to get a copy and to use it so that we have a unified custom of the 'Aliyot throughout the community.

Another very interesting custom, Parashat Bereshit, being it's the first Parashah of the year, the Minhag, even from Halab, and it did carry on in Brooklyn in certain Kehillot, is to give 'Aliyot on this first Parashah of the year to those who are selflessly working on behalf of the Hebra Kaddisha, the burial society. It's a beautiful custom, and I know that it's still done in certain Kehillot. I know for certain Beth Torah makes sure to send up representatives from the Hebra Kaddisha in Parashat Bereshit.

Noah, there's a little bit of a difference of opinion as to the scale. In most Kehillot in New York, Argentina, and Mexico, they'll use Maqam Sigah. In Ades Kenis in Yerushalayim, we sang today actually Maqam Bayat. The Shishi of Parashat Noah is a beautiful blessing given to mankind by Bore 'Olam when Noah exits the Tebah, "VeSharssu BaAress UFeru URebu 'Al HaAress," to be fruitful and multiply on the land.

Parashat Lekh Lekha, as you know, is the Parashah that Missvat Berit Milah is given to Abraham and his household. It's our first introduction to this beautiful Missvah. And as you know, Maqam Saba is the Maqam for the Berit Milah, therefore it's the Maqam for Parashat Lekh Lekha. The Kedushah, the Nakdishakh, is sung worldwide in every Syrian community in the world to the tune of Attah Ahubi, the famous tune of the Berit Milah. It's on page 410 in the red books, the Pizmonim books.

In addition, there is a custom for the Kaddish and for the Nishmat, which is not widespread among all the Kehillot, but certainly in Ades, they're very particular about it. There's a Pizmon on page 409 called Ahallel VeAgilah. And again, if you go to pizmonim.org, you could find a beautiful rendition by our esteemed Hazzan Isaac Cabasso, who sings this, in addition Hakham Yosef Bozo, Hazzan of Kenis Ades, also sings it, and we do that for Nishmat.

For the Kaddish, it's very interesting. There's a Pizmon called Mekom Binah Efoh Nimssa. It was brought to Israel from Halab by the father of Hakham Yosef Bozo, Ya'akob Bozo, and it's a, you could find a rendition of this Pizmon by the Ustaz, the maestro, Daniel Binker Dweck from Argentina. You have to put a search because it's not in our Pizmonim book. You put Mekom Binah, and you'll have his recording come up. Now this tune was adapted to the words of, in Israel at least, in the community Syrian community in Israel, to the words of Yehi Shalom BeHelenu, and therefore it became the Kaddish of the Shabbat of Lekh Lekha, even though it's Huseini. It's a beautiful tune. As in fact, when I was showing to Joey Mosseri the tune, he says, "Wait, page 375, 'Elyon Ram. Go to pizmonim.org, you'll have a recording again by Isaac Cabasso. It's the same song." Even though you'll have other versions of the song, it's very, very interesting, and it's a beautiful Kaddish.

Shishi in Lekh Lekha is begins after the battle that Abraham joined, and it starts with "Malki Sedek Melekh Shalem Hossi Lehem VaYayin." It ends "VaYitten Lo Ma'aser MiKol." Kol Tub.

181.title: The Pizmon for the Ba'al Simhah
181.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles: The Sebet. So we're talking about the day of the Sebet, prayers going on in the synagogue. What else goes on in the synagogue prior to actually getting to the Sebet, to the festive meal after prayers? And there is an important issue of a Pizmon. And a Pizmon will be sung for the people that have happy occasions, whether there is a Sebet or there's no Sebet. Whether we're talking about a birth, we're talking about an engagement, talking about a Bar Missvah, we're talking about a wedding, for all these occasions, when the person that has a happy occasion is invited up to the Sefer Torah for an 'Aliyah, a Pizmon will be sung for them.

But it's just not a Pizmon is sung for them, it's announced. And that announcement itself wakes up and creates jubilation within the congregation. So the Mesadder, the person who gives out the 'Aliyot, okay, in some congregations they're known as a Gabbai, but according to our tradition it's known as the Mesadder, that Mesadder knows who he's giving out the 'Aliyot to. He'll approach the person, let's say, for example, the father of a baby girl, okay, and tell him, "Come on, you're going to go up next, but wait." Okay? And the prior 'Oleh will finish his 'Aliyah, he'll finish the Mi SheBerakh, they're waiting for the next guy to come up, and the Mesadder will, you know, scream out, "Abi HaBat!" And all of a sudden, that's a signal to the Hazzan and to those who sing along with the Hazzan—it could be designated people, it could be just people within the congregation itself who know the Pizmonim and enjoy singing—it's a, is a signal to the Hazzan, start Pizmon for Abi HaBat.

And generally, we have, let's say, two Pizmonim that are sung, one or the other for Abi HaBat. You have on page 144 in our Pizmon book, Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah, page 144, Navah Yafah Sebiyah, okay, or we have on page 240, Yefat 'Ayin Libbabtini. And automatically, the Hazzan is going to sing. Let's stay, say it's Navah Yafah Sebiyah: "Navah Yafah Sebiyah, Roni Sahali," etcetera, etcetera. He finishes, you know, that section of the Pizmon—he's not going to sing the entire Pizmon, but he'll sing one stanza of the Pizmon—and then he'll go into "Ya'amod Abi HaBat LiKhbod HaTorah, Yishmerehu El." And then the person who had the baby girl will go up to the Sefer Torah.

Same thing if you have an Arus, you have a person who got engaged: "Ani Ekra Dodi Arus," and then, you know, "Ya'amod," etcetera. You have a Hatan. A Hatan is not an Arus. A Hatan is somebody who already got married, an Arus is somebody who's going to get married. So for a Hatan, you have either Makhelot 'Am or Yeborakh HeHatan. For a Bar Missvah: Yosser Adamah or Shir VeShir Hedvah. For Abi HaBen: Attah Ahubi or Vihi Shalom BeHelenu. These are the standard songs that are sung that the Hazzan knows, that he could, that he would say them by heart. He doesn't have to fumble for a book when the Mesadder screams out that somebody's going up.

So we said we have Abi HaBen, or if the grandfather is present of the Abi HaBen as well, as we discussed in previous videos, then they would scream out, "Abi HaBen 'Ateret!" Okay? And they would sing for the Abi HaBen, for the Abi HaBat, for the father of a girl, Abi HaBat, for Bar Missvah, Hatan Bar Missvah, for an Arus, for an engaged person, Arus, for a person who just got married, Hatan. And for all, each one of these occasions, the indication to the Hazzan, the Hazzan knows the preset songs, the songs that I mentioned are the generally preset songs, and he'll sing it.

Now, because a special song is being sung for the person who has the occasion, we are very careful to not change the Maqam of the day, the tones of that Shabbat for the happy occasion, even if it's an important person in the Kahal, okay, let's say even if it's the president of the congregation, we don't change the Maqam of the day for that Ba'al Simhah, for the person who has the happy occasion. The Maqam of the day remains the Maqam of the day. So let's, for example, if Parashat Lekh Lekha is always Saba no matter what. Parashat Hayye Sarah is always Hijaz no matter what. You know, so we have a standard system of Maqam that's based upon the concepts within the Parashah or within the upcoming holiday, depending on the system and standards that are there as known to the Hazzanim who have studied this properly. And then we have a happy occasion and we sing specifically for the person who has a happy occasion prior to their 'Aliyah. It has no reflection on the Maqam of the day. But all in all, everybody gets a song and everybody is honored and everybody is happy, and inshallah, each and every one of you has happy occasions to enjoy and to celebrate.

182.title: Bread or Mezonot for Se'udah Shelishit
182.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran writes that one should be very careful to eat a third meal on Shabbat, and even if one feels full, they can fulfill the Missvah by eating two ounces. However, if one is so full that they can't eat at all, they're not obligated to make themselves suffer. However, one should plan accordingly when eating the second meal, and leave room for Se'udah Shelishit.

Maran also writes that one must have bread for Se'udah Shelishit. Maran then cites three more opinions, each one prefaced by "and some say." According to some, one can have any food from the five grains, like wheat or barley, including cake, cookies and crackers, for Se'udah Shelishit. Others say that one can have foods that are normally eaten with bread, like meat or fish, but they can't fulfill the Missvah by just having fruit or vegetables. And yet others say even just fruit or vegetables are sufficient. After presenting all of these opinions in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran concludes that the first opinion, requiring bread, is the main opinion, unless one is very full, in which case they may rely on the other opinions.

What was the custom in Halab? Ribbi Yisshak Harari, a prominent halakhic authority in Halab in the 18th century, discussed a case in his book Zekhor LeYisshak, where one had breakfast on Shabbat morning with foods that are Bore Mine Mezonot, as was the common practice at that time in Halab, and then they had another meal with bread in the afternoon. Ribbi Yisshak ruled that since the second meal on Shabbat must include bread, the breakfast, which was only with Mezonot, did not count as a Shabbat meal, and therefore, in his opinion, the afternoon meal with bread is considered his second Shabbat meal, even though he ate it in the afternoon, which is already the time for Se'udah Shelishit. So he writes that this person must recite Birkat HaMazon, and then have another meal afterwards for Se'udah Shelishit.

Now, even though Ribbi Yisshak acknowledged in this responsa that Maran requires bread for Se'udah Shelishit, he writes that after Birkat HaMazon, it would be sufficient for this person to eat other foods and fruits, in accordance to what they said the law is for Se'udah Shelishit, referring to the other opinions cited by Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. So from here, we see that even though the custom in Halab is normally in accordance with the opinion of Maran, with regards to Se'udah Shelishit, it was customary to rely on the other opinions quoted in Shulhan 'Arukh.

In the 20th century, Hakham Yisshak Tawil was quoted as saying that in Halab, some ate bread for Se'udah Shelishit, while others did not. Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that in Argentina, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar ate Ka'ak for Se'udah Shelishit, and that's what was served to his congregation. Here in Brooklyn in the 1980s, Shaare Zion served Ka'ak and cake for Se'udah Shelishit, and in other community synagogues, they served Mezonot with fruit and soft drinks. It was only in more recent times that community synagogues began offering bread for Se'udah Shelishit for those that want to fulfill the Missvah of Se'udah Shelishit, according to all of the Posekim, including Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh.

183.title: BeSimana Taba and the Maqamat of VaYera to Toledot
183.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We have begun last week to discuss specific customs relating to Parashiyot, and we started with Bereshit, and we went through Lekh Lekha, and before I continue, I did want to correct an omission. I failed to mention in Parashat Bereshit a very important custom that we have.

This custom is that when the first 'Oleh goes up to Sefer Bereshit, Parashat Bereshit, the Kore, before saying "Bereshit Bara Elokim," after the 'Oleh makes the Berakhot, he will begin "BeSimana Taba, Bereshit Bara Elokim." If the 'Oleh himself is reading, like we find often in Hatan Bereshit, then the 'Oleh will say the Berakhah of the Torah, and then he'll begin to read "BeSimana Taba, Bereshit Bara Elokim." This has always been the custom in our community throughout all the synagogues and all the countries wherever the Halabiyeh are. There are other communities which feel that it's not proper that the Hazzan stops before Bereshit with words that are not from the Torah, and they'll have the Somekh or a third party say "BeSimana Taba." It's not our custom. Our custom is clear that the Kore himself says "BeSimana Taba."

Moving on to Parashat Noah, I did mention that in Kenis Ades in Yerushalayim we stopped the Shishi at "UFeru URebu 'Al HaAress." I had some comments that in New York, in Argentina, they stop "VaYa'al 'Olot BaMizbeah," and that's fine, and that is the custom. I think it's a point to point out, and that was a good opportunity, that it's reflected also in the Tikkunim, great Tikkun they just put out, Birkat Abraham, that there are variations, and the variations they put them at the end of the Tikkun. But the point is different Hakhamim had different approaches and maybe chose a different Shishi, and it's all fine. It's not set in stone. The idea was that the Shishi would be of three Pesukim or four Pesukim and end with a Berakhah, and so the framework is that should be followed. In the particulars, they can vary, it's not the end of the world. Okay. Parashat Lekh Lekha we did.

Parashat VaYera, here I want to spend a moment on the Maqam of Parashat VaYera, which is Maqam Nawa. Unfortunately, in the last few decades, Maqam Nawa has been falling into disuse in the New York and Deal communities, and it's very, very sad. It's very sad. It's a beautiful Maqam with very classic tunes, and it's the Maqam that we use for Friday nights. Kabbalat Shabbat and 'Arbit, Lel Shabbat, is always Maqam Nawa, and I understand that that's even being discarded in favor of Nahawand, which is sad, because it's so unique to the Syrian community, and it should be continued. If the people are not familiar with the tunes, well, let's educate ourselves onto these tunes. If the Hazzanim are not familiar with praying that, maybe if they came from Israel, they're not used to praying Nawa, well, they have to teach themselves and practice, and to say you're singing it. When I was growing up, it was a pleasure to hear the Hazzanim sing all of the tunes in Maqam Nawa, and there's some of them are from the Bakashot, and others we have in the, the tunes are in the Pizmonim book. So I urge everybody to keep this beautiful custom alive. VaYera, the Shishi ends generally in "BeYom Higgamel Et Yisshak."

In Parashat Hayye Sarah is Maqam Hijaz, which is perceived as a sad Maqam, and the reason is that Abraham and Sarah both pass away in this Parashah, so we sing Maqam Hijaz. Now, even though some may feel, oh, this sad Maqam, it's not proper to sing it on the day that we have occasions in the synagogue, that's not the case. As Joey Mosseri mentioned in a very recent video, we do not change the scale under any circumstances, regardless of how many occasions there are on that, on Shabbat in the Kenis. The scale of the Parashah, there's a reason behind it, and we continue saying it. There's only one exception, and that is if there's a Berit Milah in the synagogue on that Shabbat, the scale of the Shabbat will be used, but in the Hazarah, they will change it right before Nakdishakh, so that they can sing Attah Ahubi, and then promptly go back to the Maqam of the week. Hayye Sarah, the Shishi is generally "'Asarah Zahab Mishkalam," when 'Ebed Abraham is giving the jewelry to Ribkah, that's generally the Shishi that is used.

Parashat Toledot is Maqam Mahur, which is a higher Rast, beautiful tunes that many people, most people are very familiar with, that we sing on this Shabbat. The Shishi or is the Pesukim that are the blessings that Yisshak is giving to Ya'akob thinking he is 'Esav, and it ends with "UMbarakhekha Barukh." Kol Tub.

184.title: Where the Sebet Was Held
184.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: the Sebet. So, we finished in the Kenis, we're going to the Sebet. Where is the Sebet? Who's invited to the Sebet? How many people? What's the setup there? What's going on?

So, the Sebet was generally done at home. It was not done outside. It was not done in a banquet hall or in a catering hall. It was not done in, you know, in the Kenis, in the ballroom. It was done at home, generally at the home of the groom in the case of a wedding, or in the home of the Bar Missvah, or the home of the Abi HaBen, whatever the case may have been. So, the Sebet's at home.

Now, people lived in modest homes, and even if you had a larger home, it wasn't a mansion. You didn't have so much room. So, what did people do? People emptied out as much furniture as possible. They got family members to join together: "Let's move the furniture. Let's take it upstairs. Let's take it downstairs. Let's take it to the, you know, to our neighbor next door. Let's move as much furniture as possible." And they would rent or borrow long, narrow tables, chairs, and maximize the space, as much space as possible to fit as many people. And even if you fit as many people as you wanted to, you weren't getting more than a hundred people into your typical home, and that's really cramming them in sardine-style.

But that's what a Sebet was. It was close family, some friends, but mainly family, all together sitting close by, enjoying, and once you're in your seat, you basically weren't moving. You were there to stay. So, you came in, you located a seat, you sat down, you knew, you know, you were there for the long haul. And everybody knew the same thing, except for the rabbi. Rabbi and possibly a Hazzan, but again, Hazzanim weren't invited in the past like they are today as hired help, but the Hazzan came as a guest if you were close with him. The rabbis came, again, as guests and as a courtesy to you, their congregant. They would come, they would stay a few minutes, okay, and they would, generally the rabbi would make the Kiddush, sometimes a Hazzan, but usually a rabbi would be there, he'd make Kiddush, stay a few minutes, maybe eat something, maybe not, get up, say maximum of two minutes of words of Torah, connecting the Parashah to the event of the day, the happy occasion, blessing, let's say for example, the happy couple, and put on his coat and out the door. And obviously, somebody's waiting to grab that seat as it becomes vacated.

But that was the typical setup of the Sebet, full of people, and the people that were there were generally close family, very close family. In other words, you went from grandparents to parents, to siblings, to children, then, if there was still room, some first cousins. As far as friends were concerned, generally the bride and groom would have a few friends each, but that was it. As far as men and women, it was mainly men, much greater percentage of men to women, let's say at least 65% men and 35% women. The men would be in the larger area, and the women would be usually in the back end of the house, in a smaller area, making sure everything is being handled properly. But that was the general setup of the Sebet.

185.title: Hanukkah Lights and the 12 Cups for the Nesi'im
185.text:
The custom of lighting Hanukkah candles in the synagogue was first documented in the 12th century in Provence, a region in southern France, in a book called Sefer Ha'Ittur, which was written by Rabbi Yisshak Ben Abba Mari. Since that time, the custom was also documented in many other sources, including by the Ribash, and also by Rabbi David Abudarham, both of whom lived in Spain in the 14th century. It was also documented by the Radbaz, who was the chief rabbi of Egypt in the 16th century. In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran ruled that Hanukkah candles are lit with blessings in the synagogue in order to publicize the miracle, and that in the synagogue, Hanukkah candles are lit before Habdalah is recited on Saturday night.

According to the book Derekh Eress, the custom of Halab was in accordance with the opinion of Maran, to light Hanukkah candles in the synagogue each night, and on Saturday night, they were lit before reciting Habdalah. However, Derekh Eress also writes that in Halab, in addition to lighting Hanukkah candles each night in the synagogue, 12 cups of oil were lit every night in honor of the Nesi'im, the princes that brought offerings to the Mishkan in the desert, which is what is read about from the Torah each morning of Hanukkah. These cups of oil were lit in every synagogue and Midrash, even in the small Midrashim that did not light Hanukkah candles because people were not there in the evening. And these cups of oil burned until the morning, and if they went out before the morning, it was customary to relight them.

Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo also documented the custom of lighting 12 candles each day in honor of the Nesi'im, but he writes that they were, that they lit them in the morning, in all of the synagogues and Batte Midrash. It was only on Shabbat that they were lit on Friday evening before sunset, and they lasted for 24 hours.

Interestingly, this custom was also documented by an Ashkenazic rabbi in the American Hebrew newspaper called HaDo'ar. In 1966, Rabbi Tovia Preschel wrote that Hakham Douba Abadi told him that he remembered that in his youth in Halab, that they lit 12 cups of oil in the synagogue each day of Hanukkah, in honor of the princes that we read about in the Torah readings for Hanukkah, and that the custom continued in the Halabi synagogue in New York. Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that this custom also continued in the Halabi community in Argentina. The Shamash set up 12 cups of oil before first Minyan in the morning, and they invited members of the congregation to light them as they arrived to pray in the morning.

So we see that in Halab, in addition to lighting Hanukkah candles each night in the synagogue, there was also a unique custom to light 12 cups of oil each day of Hanukkah in the synagogues and Batte Midrash, in honor of the princes that we read about in the Torah readings for Hanukkah. These cups of oil were either lit at night, after the Hanukkah candles, or in the morning before Shahrit, except for Shabbat, when they were lit before sunset on Friday evening. This custom was also continued by Halabi communities, both here in New York as well as in Argentina.

186.title: Parashat VaYesse, VaYishlah and VaYesheb
186.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will continue our series of videos discussing Minhagim which are particular to certain Shabbatot and Parashiyot. So we are up to Parashat VaYesse. VaYesse is sung in the scale of 'Ajam. 'Ajam, as you know, is the Maqam that we use for happy occasions, for weddings in particular. And the reason we do VaYesse in 'Ajam is this is the Parashah where Ya'akob gets married to both Leah and Rahel.

We do have a very unique custom among the Syrian Kehillot where for the Semehim BeSetam piece in Shahrit, we will shift to Maqam Saba, and the reason is, excuse me, that there is a Pizmon that was written by the famous Rabbi Yisrael Najara in the 16th century called Yedidi Ro'i Hakimi. It's found in the Pizmonim book, Shir UShbahah VeHallel VeZimrah, on page 417. And the reason we sing this song is because the last stanza, actually the Pizmon ends with the line, "Rahel Ba'ah 'Im HaSon," which is taken from our Parashah. So there is that custom. I understand that in maybe in recent decades in the New York communities not all Kehillot do it. It's certainly done in Argentina in a number of Kehillot, in Ades. It's a beautiful custom, and it's, you know, we have all the resources with the fantastic website pizmonim.org for those who want to familiarize themselves with the Pizmon and the customs. So I urge the Hazzanim to restore these beautiful customs and do the Yedidi Ro'i for Semehim.

The Shishi is "VaYomer Hinneni." Now, someone asked me, why do I mention always when the Shishi is? Well, the Shishi is perceived as the most important 'Aliyah, certainly 'Al Pi HaKabbalah in Kabbalistic tradition, and it's always been our custom to send a Hakham or an elder statesman or a learned man for Shishi to the Sefer. And it's usually a few Pesukim long ending with a beautiful Berakhah that's found in the Parashah. So all 'Aliyot will be affected by when the Shishi is. So we'll decide when the Shishi is, that's why I mention it, and then Shelishi, Rebi'i, Hamishi will be figured out after we know when the Shishi is. Again, to mention the beautiful Tikkun Kore'im, Birkat Abraham, printed by the Sephardic Heritage Foundation, where it lists all of the, has all of the stops based on our community's traditions, and at the end of the Sefer, there's a chart showing all the different versions and variances with the stops based on different Hakhamim and different communities.

We move on to Parashat VaYishlah. Parashat VaYishlah, here there's a difference of opinion as to what the Maqam is. In Israel, we do Bayat. In America and Argentina, they will do either Saba or Sigah, probably Sigah in most cases. The Shishi ends "VaYikra Lo El Eloke Yisrael."

We move on to Parashat VaYesheb. Parashat VaYesheb generally is the Shabbat before the holiday of Hanukkah. This is how it is most of the years. In the rare case where you have Hanukkah spanning two Shabbatot, so you'll have the first, you'll have VaYesheb and Mikkess, so VaYesheb will be the first day of Hanukkah. The reason I point this out is that usually before a holiday, we will incorporate tunes of the holiday into the prayer and occasionally even change the Maqam, as we do in Parashat BeMidbar because it falls out before Shabu'ot. We will change the Maqam to fit the pieces of the prayer that we have to do for the holiday.

Hanukkah, we have no particular tunes for the holiday. It's true that the entire Kehillah, I would say the entire world, Jewish world sings Ma'oz Sur when they light the Hanukkah, but it's obviously not an authentic Halabi tune, and it was never really incorporated into the Shahrit prayer of Shabbat before the holiday as other holidays are we are accustomed to see. Nonetheless, being that it's Parashat, excuse me, it's Parashat VaYesheb is Maqam Nawa, in America, as we discussed in Parashat VaYera, they, many shift it to Nahawand.

But at any rate, there is a tune that is found in the notes of Hakham Moshe Ashear 'Alav HaShalom, our great Hazzan from the early part of the 20th century, where he says that in Shav'at 'Aniyyim, he writes the Shabbat before Hanukkah, he was particular of using the tune on page 207, the Pizmon is called Neri VeOri. Let me pull it up in the Pizmon books. "LeNeri VeOri Ta'ir El Ram." Obviously, Ner and Or, reminding us of the Hanukkah holiday. It's a beautiful tune. Again, look it up in the pizmonim.org, if you're not familiar with the tune, or go to the Hazzanim and ask to be taught this wonderful tune. So, that's the custom for the Shahrit.

For the Shishi, there is a number of opinions, even in our community. Most stop when describing Yosef as "HaShem Massliah BeYado." There are a number of opinions, and again found in the Tikkun, where they'll stop a few Pesukim later, describing Yosef as "Yefeh To'ar ViYfeh Mar'eh." Kol Tub.

187.title: Yah Yahid Ram, the King of the Pizmonim
187.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA Minhag of the Week: life cycles, the Sebet. Pizmonim at a Sebet. What is the place of Pizmonim at a Sebet? What Pizmonim do we sing? Is there an order to the Pizmonim? Why are certain Pizmonim sung? So many questions arise and so many beautiful Minhagim in turn.

First and foremost, our Pizmon book, the red book, Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah. This is the compendium of the vast majority of our Pizmonim, Pizmonim composed by our Hakhamim, Hakham Raphael Antebi Tabbush and his prized student Hakham Moshe Ashear Cohen. Pizmonim in this book, for the most part, are the songs that we sing on every occasion, but especially at the Sebet.

And at the Sebet, we have the king of songs. The king of songs means the song, the Pizmon that every Sebet, no matter the occasion, must open with. There is no question, and that is on page 238 in this book, it's called Yah Yahid Ram. "Yah, Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam." This is the song. There's no question about it, there's no reason to start with any other song, and you can't start a Pizmon for a Sebet without using this song as your intro. This song introduces our connection, our connection to Bore 'Olam, to Bore 'Olam being our rock, our salvation, everything that we turn to in life is all coming from the Almighty Himself, and we're thanking Him for the situation that we're in, thanking for bringing us to this happy occasion, and we use this song, Yah Yahid Ram, as a segue to go into other Pizmonim for numerous occasions.

If we have, for example, the occasion that we're having a Sebet for is, for example, a baby girl, we just flip page to page 240 and we have Yefat 'Ayin. If it's a wedding, we flip a few more pages, we go to page 266 and we have El Me'od Na'alah. If it's a Bar Missvah, we flip a few more pages and we go to page 277, Yosser Adamah. All these Pizmonim are all within the same melodic scale, in this case what's known as Maqam Bayat. We'll talk about Maqamat briefly as we talk about other Pizmonim, but for the most part Joey Harari discussed Maqamat as we use them in the synagogue service on Shabbatot in his video presentations of the Minhagim.

But we need to know that we start every Sebet with Yah Yahid Ram. It's the king of the Pizmonim. From there we go on to other songs, and we'll discuss in upcoming videos how we move to other songs outside of this musical scale of Bayat. What are the songs that we sing? What are the top 10 songs, if you will, at a Sebet? And then how you go back to other songs? Are we singing the entire time? Are we eating in between? Are we drinking in between? What goes on? What happens? Who directs the show? Stay tuned, and you'll enjoy, and you'll know how to have a great Sebet.

188.title: Looking at the Fingernails at Habdalah
188.text:
It is customary to place one's fingernails in front of the light of the Habdalah candle when reciting the blessing of Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh. Our custom is to bend four fingers on your right hand with your fingernails facing you. Some, based on the teachings of the Mekubbalim, completely cover their thumb with their four fingers. You then shine the light of the candle on your fingernails and look at the light reflecting on your fingernails. Some also look at their fingers. According to Maran, you should also look at the palm of your hand. However, it is not our custom to open your hand or to look at the other side of your fingers. Our custom is just to hold your hand like this.

This custom is first found in Pirke DeRabbi Eli'ezer, which is attributed to the second-century Tanna, Rabbi Eli'ezer. Subsequently, this custom was mentioned by the Geonim of the Middle East in the ninth and tenth centuries, and in the eleventh century by Rabbi Yisshak Ibn Ghiyyat in Spain and by the Rif in North Africa. Many more authorities discuss this custom, including Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh.

According to the law, one only recites or fully participates in the blessing recited upon the candle if they are close enough to the candle to be able to use only the light of the candle to differentiate between coins from different countries. According to Pirke DeRabbi Eli'ezer and many other authorities, the custom is to use the light of the candle to differentiate between one's fingers and their fingernails. They explain that if one can differentiate between their fingers and their fingernails with the light of the Habdalah candle, then they would also be able to differentiate between coins from different countries with that light, which means that they are close enough to the candle to be able to recite or fully participate in the blessing that is recited upon the candle.

Based on this reason, many authorities, including the Shibbole HaLeket, the Orhot Hayyim, and the Kol Bo, wrote that one should shine the light of the candle on their fingernails before reciting the blessing of Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh. They also explain that this blessing is not a blessing that is recited upon enjoyment, like the blessings that are recited before eating or drinking, which must be recited prior to enjoyment. This blessing is a blessing of praise, like Birkat HaLebanah, the blessing that is recited upon seeing the new moon. With those blessings, first you see the object of praise, the new moon, or in our case, the light of the candle, and then you recite the blessing. In the case of the Habdalah candle, the law is "En Mebarekhin 'Al HaNer 'Ad SheYe'otu LeOro." The blessing on the candle is not recited until you enjoy its light. However, seeing the light of the candle shining on your fingernails is not a halakhic requirement. It is only a custom. The halakhic requirement is fulfilled by being close enough to the candle to be able to differentiate between coins from different countries.

Other authorities gave different reasons for the custom. According to the Geonim, the Rif, and Rabbi Yisshak Ibn Ghiyyat, we look at our fingernails with the light of the Habdalah candle because fingernails grow, which would be a good sign for a blessed week. The Meiri and the Mordekhai connect the custom to Adam HaRishon, who discovered fire on the first Saturday night. According to the Midrash, Adam HaRishon's entire body was hard like fingernails before he sinned. After the sin, his body turned into ordinary skin. When he discovered fire on Saturday night, he saw that he still had the hard nails on the ends of his fingers and toes, and that made him happy. The students of Rabbenu Yonah explain that we enjoy the light of the candle on our fingernails because it's an easy way to enjoy the light.

Based on these other reasons, it might not be necessary to see the light of the candle on one's fingernails before reciting the blessing. In fact, the Siddur of Rab Sa'adya Gaon from the tenth century specifies shining the light of the candle on your hands after reciting the blessing of Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh. Furthermore, when Purim falls on Saturday night, our custom is like those authorities that wrote that the blessing on the candle is recited before reading the Megillah in order to avoid enjoying light before reciting the blessing on the candle. Similarly, when Tish'ah BeAb falls on Saturday night, we recite the blessing on the candle before benefiting from light to recite the Kinot, and according to some authorities, the blessing on the candle is considered a blessing on enjoyment, which suggests that the blessing should be recited before enjoying the light of the candle. In the seventeenth century, Rabbi Abraham HaLevi, who was the chief rabbi of Cairo, Egypt, wrote in his book Ginat Veradim that the custom is to recite the blessing of Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh first and then to look at one's fingernails.

What was the custom in Halab? In the famous Mahzor Aram Soba that was printed in the year 1527, the instructions to look at one's fingernails is printed after the blessing of Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh. Likewise, when growing up in the community, the custom was always to look at the light of the candle on our fingernails after reciting the blessing of Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh.

So while many authorities wrote that one should look at the light of the Habdalah candle on their fingernails before reciting the blessing of Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh, our custom is to look at our fingernails after reciting the blessing. Our custom is based on the fact that even according to the opinion that the blessing is a blessing of praise, the law does not require one to actually use the light before reciting the blessing. It is sufficient to be close enough to the candle to be able to use the light to differentiate between coins from different countries before reciting the blessing. Therefore, we wait until after the blessing before actively using the light when shining it on our fingernails, just like we recite Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh before using and enjoying light to read the Megillah or to recite Kinot on a Saturday night. And as we said earlier, our custom of looking at our fingernails after the blessing is found in the Siddur of Rab Sa'adya Gaon, in Mahzor Aram Soba, and in the book Ginat Veradim.

189.title: Mikkess and Mi Lo Yira'akha with Three Sefarim
189.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Kahal Kadosh Aram Soba in Ra'anana. We have been discussing Minhagim which are unique to specific Parashiyot and Shabbatot, and we are up to Parashat Mikkess.

Now, Mikkess we will sing the Nishmat of Shahrit in Maqam Sigah. Maqam Sigah, as you know, is associated with Nerot of the Bet HaMikdash, the Menorah, 'Aliyah LaRegel, the pilgrimage. Anything having to do with the Bet HaMikdash we will sing in Maqam Sigah. That is why the three holidays Pesah, Shabu'ot, and Sukkot, the first day is always Maqam Sigah. That's why Parashat Mikkess, because it always falls out or generally falls out during Hanukkah, we sing Maqam Sigah. Parashat BeHa'alotekha, Parashat Tessaveh, the building of the Mishkan. So that was the reason for this Maqam this week.

Now, there is a possibility when it's Shabbat Hanukkah that it will also be Shabbat Hanukkah and Rosh Hodesh as it falls out in this current year. The possibility exists also for Parashat HaHodesh where we read it may fall out on Rosh Hodesh, and rarely, but it can happen on Parashat Shekalim as well, where you have Parashat Shekalim and Rosh Hodesh. It always happens every year, as you know, at Simhat Torah where we take out three Sefarim.

Now the taking out of three Sefarim, there is a very unique custom that was in the Bet Keneset HaNasi in Aram Soba. And what they did was when they had three Sefarim, they would, before they begin the procession around the Bet HaKeneset, the Hakham in a very awe-inspiring Tefilah would recite Pesukim from Yirmeyah, and the Kahal would answer. And this Minhag and the Pesukim begin with the words "Mi Lo Yira'akha Melekh HaGoyim," who will not fear You, the King of all nations.

Now, this was usually done with a lot of ceremony. It was told my grandfather, the Hakham Aharon Shwekey 'Alav HaShalom, he related to his children that this, he recalls speaking to people who were in Halab in Bet Keneset HaNasi when the famous Hakham Bashi, Hakham Mordekhai Labaton, Zikhrono LiBerakhah, would tremble when he said these prayers, and many of the local dignitaries, even the Goyim, were invited to witness this special prayer.

Now, this was done every week in the Kahal Kadosh of the Musta'arabim, in the Bet Keneset HaGadol, which is called on the name of Yo'ab Ben Seruyah. The last Hakham of that Kenis in the second half of the 20th century was Hakham Salim Zafrani, Zikhrono LiBerakhah, and he records the customs of the Musta'arabim. As we mentioned many times, the Musta'arabim were the local inhabitants of the Jewish community in Halab prior to the arrival of the Sefaradim in the 16th century. The Minhag of the Musta'arabim he writes was to say this Tefilah, "Mi Lo Yira'akha," every single Shabbat. However, that was only the Musta'arabim. The other Kehillot only did when there were three Sefarim, and we're not even sure if all the synagogues in Halab did this custom. Hakham Yisshak Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, in the years before he passed away a couple of years ago, he gave interviews regarding the Minhagim, and he said in the Jamiliyeh synagogue he was not sure if this was the custom.

More to our 'Inyan, in New York, in Argentina, in Panama, Mexico, the community did not continue this custom. We did however continue the custom in Bet Keneset Ades, and in fact I will attach a link to the reciting of this prayer by Hakham Yosef Chehebar, Zakhur LaTob, so you can get an idea of the tune that was used when we recited this prayer. Kol Tub.

190.title: The Bayat Pizmonim at a Sebet
190.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: life cycles, the Sebet. In the last episode we spoke about the king of all Pizmonim at a Sebet, the song that we must open up every Sebet with, and that's Yahid Ram that appears on page 238 in our Pizmon book Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah. 238, Yahid Ram, we sing it, everybody's happy, everybody knows the tune, it's in the musical scale known as Maqam Bayat.

Now, what else is sung immediately after this Pizmon? Well, it really depends on the occasion. Okay, if we have, for example, in many cases you have a baby girl, so you would go to page 240 and sing Yefat 'Ayin, "Yefat 'Ayin Libbabtini," and everybody knows that song, jumps right in. If we have, for example, a Bar Missvah, we have a whole slew of songs, and they're generally sung in order from the oldest of these Pizmonim, which is Yosser Adamah on page 277, "Yosser Adamah Bore Shamayim." From there they would jump right into Habu Godel on page 261, "Habu Godel LeElokenu," and to the following page, 262, Habu HaBanim Me'ehad, and then finally go to page 312, Shiru Shir Hen VaHod. So all these are all in the same musical scale. Everybody's head is focused in the same notes, in the same ideas, the same thoughts. It's a beautiful thing. But if you have a wedding, you go to El Me'od Na'alah on page 266, El Me'od Na'alah.

Well, this is very nice and well, but what about all so many other songs? This section of Bayat, okay, is close to 100 pages long, the largest section of Pizmonim in our book. So many people will stay in that Bayat mode and sing heavier songs, deeper songs, sometimes less well known, sometimes well known for their chorus, whereas the Hazzan is singing many solo portions of the song.

But now today we're seeing something else. We're seeing, especially amongst the younger crowd, they jump to two songs immediately: Ma'uzi on page 246 and Habibi on page 318A. Traditionally, neither one of these songs was ever sung. They were never sung at any Sebet. Okay, Ma'uzi is a song for Shalosh Regalim. It has certain connotations of sadness as well, never really fit into a Sebet, and Habibi is much more of a modern Israeli song. It's not even in Maqam Bayat, it's in a different musical scale. But for some reason these have become popular because they are very, very easy and people have fun with them. Go ahead, have fun, but don't forget the tradition. Don't forget the heritage. Sing what your fathers and forefathers have sung, and then go into the newer songs.

It's very important, and that's why we have this important compilation of Pizmonim called Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah. It's almost every Pizmon written by the great Hakham Raphael Tabbush and his prize student, Hakham Moshe Ashear. So let's adhere to the Pizmonim. In the following episode, we're going to talk about the other Pizmonim in the other Maqamat that are considered the most popular Sebet Pizmonim, we'll call them the top 10, and stay tuned, we'll share them with you.

191.title: Laughing and the Leftover Habdalah Wine
191.text:
When we recite Habdalah, the common practice in our community is to laugh after the blessing of Bore Peri HaGefen. Rabbi Shemtob Gaguine describes this as a custom of the land of Israel in his book Keter Shem Tob, which was published in the year 1934. He explains that we laugh for a good sign and a blessing.

What about the custom of those who dip their fingers in the leftover wine from Habdalah, and rub it on their eyes, behind their ears, on their forehead, and even in their pockets? In Pirke DeRibbi Eli'ezer, which is attributed to the second-century Tanna, Ribbi Eli'ezer, it says that after drinking the wine from Habdalah, that it was customary to add a little water to the cup and drink it, to show affection for the Missvah, and then to take some of the leftover water from the cup and rub it on your eyes, because in the Gemara it says, leftovers from a Missvah prevent troubles.

In the ninth century, Rab 'Amram Gaon describes the same custom, stating that he heard from his rabbis that practicing this custom is a Missvah, citing the teaching in the Gemara that leftovers from a Missvah prevent troubles. He goes on to say that they would take what was left in the cup on their hands and rub it on their face to show affection for the Missvah. This custom was recorded by others as well, including by Ribbi Yisshak Ben Ghiyyat, who lived in Spain in the 11th century. In the 18th century, the Hida mentions this custom in his book Birke Yosef, and in the 19th century, the Ben Ish Hai described the custom, specifying rubbing the water added to the cup after Habdalah on one's eyes and forehead.

What about also rubbing your pockets with the wine? Rabbi Gangi, Rabbi Gaguine mentions it in his book Keter Shem Tob, and says that he heard that this is done to bring about financial success, but he does not cite any written source for this. Similarly, Hakham David Yosef mentions putting some of the leftover wine in one's pants pockets in his book Halakhah Berurah, without mentioning any source at all.

Furthermore, in all the sources prior to the 20th century, the custom begins with adding water to the leftover wine in the cup used for Habdalah, drinking it, and then using what was left over from that to rub on your eyes, your face, and in some sources, on your forehead. However, Rabbi Gaguine in Keter Shem Tob does not mention adding water to the cup, only pouring the leftover wine itself into a plate and distributing it to the members of the congregation to dip their fingers in it and to rub it on their eyes, behind their ears, on the top of their spine, and in their pockets. Hakham David Yosef also first mentions using the wine itself, and then adds that some add water to the cup, drink it, and use what's left over to rub on their eyes, their forehead, and to put in their pockets.

So this custom of rubbing leftover Habdalah wine on various parts of your head is over a thousand years old. Originally, it was done to show affection for the Missvah with what was left over, which the Gemara taught protects one from troubles. It was only in more recent times that people began putting some of the wine in their pockets, hoping that it would bring about financial success. Similarly, according to Rabbi Gaguine in Keter Shem Tob, the more recent customs of putting some of the wine behind one's ears and on top of one's spine was done hoping to prevent sickness in one's ears and to strengthen the spine, enabling one to rise with the resurrection of the dead in messianic times.

192.title: Three Sefarim, the Haftarah, and VaYiggash and VaYehi
192.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Kahal Kadosh Aram Soba in Ra'anana. We will continue in our discussions of the Minhagim which are unique to specific Shabbatot and Parashiyot. In our last video, we discussed the taking out of three Sefarim, which can happen and it did happen this year on Shabbat, Hanukkah, and Rosh Hodesh. There are two very important Minhagim I wanted to discuss and to remind the Kahal what the custom of the Syrian community from Aleppo is.

The first custom deals with the Kaddish, the reciting of the Kaddish following each Sefer. Generally, the custom in the Halakhah is brought down that in the first Sefer, we read six 'Olim and we do not say Kaddish. The second Sefer, which is the Rosh Hodesh, we will recite Kaddish, that is, that's the Mashlim, and the Maftir from Hanukkah will also say Kaddish. If you do more than six 'Olim in the first Sefer, indeed you would say Kaddish after each Sefer. The custom in our community is that we insist on adding more than six 'Olim and have at least seven 'Olim in the first Sefer so that we specifically want to say Kaddish, and we say Kaddish after each Sefer. For more elaboration of this custom, it was discussed by my colleague Morris Arking in video number 149 where he goes into greater detail. But we do say Kaddish after each Sefer.

Another custom is the Haftarah. Now, we read the Haftarah of course of Hanukkah, even though it's Rosh Hodesh, we read the Haftarah of Hanukkah. There are communities that will read obviously the Haftarah of Hanukkah, but when they conclude that Haftarah, will read the first and last Pesukim from Rosh Hodesh, and in this case Mahar Hodesh because it's a two-day Rosh Hodesh, and it's done in other communities. That is not the custom of the Halabi community. Our custom is we read the Haftarah and we conclude the Haftarah of Hanukkah and we will say Go'alenu, we will, some add "Barukh Ad-onai Le'Olam Amen VeAmen" straight into the Berakhot of the Haftarah. We do not skip from one Nabi to the other Nabi, and even for one Pasuk or two Pesukim, we do not read from other Haftarot. This is the case not only on Hanukkah Rosh Hodesh, it's a case of a two-day Rosh Hodesh where the first day is Shabbat and the second day is Mahar Hodesh, so we do not read from any other Haftarah, only the Haftarah that we're dealing with. Again, Morris Arking deals with this issue as well in greater detail in video number 149.

The Shishi for Parashat Mikkess is "VaYasem Rebid HaZahab 'Al Savvaro," discussing when, speaking when with the procession of Yosef after being appointed viceroy. And that is how, where we stopped the Shishi. Pretty much unanimous in the consensus of all the Hakhamim and all the various Minhagim brought down in the Tikkun.

Shishi for Parashat VaYiggash, because we're going to go through Parashat VaYiggash and VaYehi, VaYiggash the Maqam is Bayat, and the Shishi there's a difference of opinion, pretty much split down the middle, whether it's "VaTehi Ruah Ya'akob Abihem" when he sees the chariots that Yosef sent to Kena'an, and that's where it's marked in the Tikkun, or a few Pesukim later, many, many have the custom as we do in Ades, "Ya'akob Ya'akob, VaYomer Hinneni."

Parashat VaYehi, we sing the Nishmat in Maqam Hijaz. It's the sad Maqam which we did also in Hayye Sarah, which the death of Sarah and Abraham are in that Parashah. Here it's the death of Ya'akob. We will use this sad Maqam in various Parashiyot which we will discuss when we get to them. And the Shishi is "LiShu'atekha Kivviti Ad-onai." That is the Pasuk in the middle of the Berakhot that Ya'akob is blessing his children. And it's again pretty unanimous that this is the Shishi for Parashat VaYehi. Kol Tub.

193.title: The Top Sebet Pizmonim
193.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA, Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles, the Sebet. This morning we had a Sebet. After the last episode, many have asked me, what are the top 10 songs at a Sebet? What are the main songs that are sung? What are the songs that have withstood the test of time that people are singing today, they sang 10 years ago, 20 years ago, 30, 40, 50 years ago, etc.? What are those songs? We want to sing them, we want to know them.

So, I made a short list, it's about, I don't know, approximately 15 songs in page order, and I'll give you the name, the page number, and I'll sing you the first few words, that way you could become familiar with them. These are the songs that really have given the shape to a Sebet, at least in my lifetime and in the lifetime of those that I've asked that are older than me.

Page 127, Ma'oz Yish'i: "Ma'oz Yish'i El Ram Na'alah."

Page 144, Navah Yafah Sebiyah: "Navah Yafah Sebiyah, Roni Simhi."

144A, "Anah Ya Habibi Limekbalak."

156, Bo'i BeRinah: "Bo'i BeRinah Ya 'Adinah."

168, "Melekh Rahman Shema' Na, Hogeh Nekha'im Lekha Yahel."

210, Attah El Kabir: "Attah El Kabir," followed by 213 immediately, "Ehezeh BeNo'am Panekha Nisbe'ah Ram."

Page 220, Melekh Ram: "Melekh Ram Yahid Hai Ve'Olam."

Page 260, El Me'od Na'alah.

Page 313, "Sur Yah El Melekh 'Olam."

376, "Yehalelu El Nora BeKhol Zimrah 'Am Hasideha, Halelu Halelu."

Page 458, "Nagilah Halleluyah Nagilah."

490, "Samah Nafshi Ya Suri."

And finally, 502A, "Mul Eli Bijmalo Yar'ani Fi Khulo."

What do we find common in all these songs? Almost all of them, 10 out of the 14 songs—I've counted now, there are 14 here—10 out of these 14 are general songs not related to any particular occasion. But more importantly, these are songs that everybody can sing together, that you don't have real soloist parts, that you don't need a Hazzan to carry you through, and the general person can sing them, enjoy them, and really they give the flavor and the shape to the Sebet.

And obviously you don't have to sing these in any particular order, and generally people will go from one of these songs, and if they have a crowd that likes heavier songs, or if you have a Hazzan over there that can enhance it with prettier melodies, they'll follow, you know, these, we'll call them lighter popular tunes, by a heavier Pizmon, a Pizmon that requires a Hazzan to lead and sing the solo verses while the people answer choral verses, or maybe a song that is more of a listening song where you have just one or two singers and the rest of the people are just listening and enjoying. But whatever it is, enhance your Sebet, make it beautiful, make it enjoyable, stick to the heritage, to tradition, and Mabrook on your Sebet.

194.title: HaMappil With or Without HaShem's Name
194.text:
According to the Gemara, one is required to recite the blessing of HaMappil Hable Shenah before going to sleep at night. After the blessing, Keri'at Shema is recited, followed by some Pesukim, all of which is found in our Siddurim. HaRambam specified that this blessing is recited with HaShem's Name, both at the beginning and end of the blessing. Mahzor Aram Soba, which was printed in the year 1527, also has HaShem's Name at both the beginning and end of the blessing. However, in more recent times, a custom developed among some to recite this blessing without HaShem's Name.

In the 19th century, Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, the Chief Rabbi of Izmir, Turkey, wrote that their custom was to recite this blessing without HaShem's Name, as was found in old Siddurim. The Ben Ish Hai wrote that even though the blessing of HaMappil was instituted with HaShem's Name, and that according to the Arizal, it should be recited with HaShem's Name, but since there are authorities that would consider it a blessing said in vain if one spoke before falling asleep, therefore, everyone should follow their custom, and those that recite the blessing with HaShem's Name should make a great effort not to speak between the blessing and falling asleep. He specified that his own custom and the custom of his father was to recite the blessing without HaShem's Name. The Ben Ish Hai also mentioned a correspondence that he received from Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, which reported that the majority of the pious people of Jerusalem do not recite this blessing with HaShem's Name, because they might have to speak after the blessing, and some say that if one speaks, then the blessing was recited in vain.

In the 19th century Siddur Bet 'Obed, which was very popular in the Middle East, including the city of Halab, this blessing has HaShem's Name in parentheses in both the beginning and at the end of the blessing. In the instructions before the blessing, it says, "Some recite the blessing without HaShem's Name, VeHakol Holekh Ahar HaMinhag, everything goes according to the custom." Interestingly, in the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar that was printed in Halab in 1915, the blessing is printed with HaShem's Name in both the beginning and end of the blessing, without any mention of a custom to recite the blessing without HaShem's Name. And that's how this blessing was printed in the Siddur Tefilat Yeshurun, which was very popular in our community from the 1930s until the 1960s.

However, Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya, an Aleppo-born rabbi who lived in Jerusalem from the beginning of the 20th century, wrote that the blessing should not be recited with HaShem's Name in his set of responsa entitled Yaskil 'Abdi. And in the book Yisshak Yeranen, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote, "Regarding the blessings of HaMappil, Tefilat HaDerekh, the blessing for thunder, and similar blessings, it is not our custom to recite these blessings with HaShem's Name." Hakham Yisshak Chehebar lived during the 20th century.

So, while none of the earlier authorities ever mentioned reciting the blessing of HaMappil without HaShem's Name, by the 19th century, the custom developed among some Middle Eastern rabbis to recite this blessing without HaShem's Name. This was done to avoid an interruption between the blessing and sleeping in a case where one needed to speak or to eat or drink something before going to sleep. From Rabbi Yisshak Chehebar, we see that this custom was eventually accepted in Halab as well.

195.title: Parashat Shemot, VaEra and Bo
195.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We will continue with our discussion regarding Minhagim that are unique to specific Parashiyot, when we are up to now Parashat Shemot.

So Parashat Shemot, generally the beginning of the Sefer, we do Maqam Rast. However, in Shemot, there is a little bit of a discussion. As a matter of fact, if you look at the Pizmonim book on page 565 where we have the list of the Maqamat for the Parashiyot, it says on Shemot: Rast or Bayat. Now, the general consensus today is that we do Maqam Rast for Parashat Shemot, although we do have notes from our legendary Hazzan, 'Alav HaShalom, Hakham Moshe Ashear in the late '30s. We have notes that are compiled and we can see them in the fantastic website pizmonim.org, organized by David Betesh, Zakhur LaTob. And in speaking to Joe Mosseri, he also noted that Hakham Moshe Ashear occasionally did do Bayat for Parashat Shemot. The Minhag in Ades in Eress Yisrael is to do Bayat for Parashat Shemot because of "VeKhol HaBat Tehayun," and in fact we'll do Nakdishakh to the tune of Yefat 'Ayin, the famous Pizmon that we sing for Abi HaBat, although it's not, it wasn't the case in the notes of Hakham Moshe Ashear. Nonetheless, there is either Rast or Bayat that is the consensus for Parashat Shemot. The Shishi, which now we have the advantage of having the Tikkun that we put out, the Shishi is ending in the Pasuk: "VaYomer Hinneni," "Moshe Moshe, VaYomer Hinneni." That is Parashat Shemot.

We'll move on to Parashat VaEra. Now, Parashat VaEra is interesting in that the also here, if you look at the Pizmonim book, it says Huseini or Rast. Obviously if you did Rast for Shemot, you wouldn't do Rast for VaEra, you'd do Huseini. The Minhag in Israel is to do Maqam Nawa. We do Maqam Nawa because that Maqam Nawa, many of the Pizmonim relate to the Pesah holiday on Maqam Nawa, particularly the Pizmon Mi Yemallel, which is on page 361, which speaks about, among other things, about the Makkot, the ten Makkot. And being that seven of the Makkot are in Parashat VaEra, we have the custom to do Nawa in Parashat VaEra, and the Kaddish will be to the tune of Mi Yemallel. Also we use the tune Beneh Li Zebul Mikdashi, and we'll do it either Semehim or Kedushah if we're doing Maqam Nawa, also found in page 361 in the Pizmonim book. The Shishi for Parashat VaEra is "VaYehi BeYom Dibber Ad-onai El Moshe BeEress Missrayim." There are alternatives, and that will be found at the end of the Tikkun, the chart which brings the different alternatives for Shishi.

Now Parashat Bo, in the Pizmonim book it's written Maqam Sigah, and on the website you can see it for Maqam Sigah, and Sigah always speaks about the holidays, as we know the laws of Korban Pesah, anything having to do with Korbanot and the Bet HaMikdash and 'Aliyah LaRegel would be Maqam Sigah as we mentioned in our last, in our recent videos. Hakham Moshe Ashear actually used to do sometimes Maqam Nawa for Parashat VaEra, for Parashat Bo, because of the same reason that we done it Parashat VaEra, because we're talking about the Makkot, and he would use Mi Yemallel as well.

It's written in the Pizmonim book, it's important that we familiarize ourselves with this monumental work, it also has a list of certain Shabbatot, which Pizmonim are unique to those Shabbatot. And if you look at page 572, it'll say Shir LeShabbat Bo, Mi Yemallel, and generally that is the tune that is sung, the Pizmon, sorry, not the tune, the Pizmon that is sung when we take the Sefer out. We will sing the Mi Yemallel. Here, the Shishi for Parashat, Shel Parashat Bo is "LeHok LeHok 'Olam 'Ad 'Olam," and in Israel we would either do that Shishi or "Ka'asher Sivvah HaShem Moshe VeAharon Ken 'Asu." So these are the customs which are unique to Parashiyot Shemot, VaEra, and Bo. Kol Tub.

196.title: What a Real Sebet Is About
196.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA Minhag of the Week: life cycles. We've been talking about the Sebet and Pizmonim, and I've touched upon a lot of very important aspects, and a lot of questions have come back, so I hope to clarify everything in this episode.

So in episode 187, I spoke about Yahid Ram. Yahid Ram being the Pizmon in our Pizmon book, Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah, the red book, on page 238. Yahid Ram is the opening song, and I showed how to segue from there into various Pizmonim, depending on what the occasion is. Then, in episode 190, spoke about Yahid Ram using it to deal with a wedding, or with a baby girl, or with a Bar Missvah, and how we have a compendium for each one of these occasions in this same melodic mode in what's known as Maqam Bayat. Finally, in 193, I spoke about the top 14 songs. I didn't mention Yahid Ram because I already dedicated, you know, a special place for that in 187 and again in 190. So I got to those additional songs in 193.

But don't think that that's it, we're limited to 14, 15 songs. We have this Pizmon book, which has over 600 Pizmonim, 600 Pizmonim, all from our great Hakhamim, our great poets. And why this book? People have asked. Because this book really is a true reflection of our community, of our style of Pizmonim, written by the great Hakham Raphael Antebi Tabbush and by his prized student Hakham Moshe Ashear. These are our Pizmonim. These are the Pizmonim that we sing.

And you go to any real Sebet, growing up going to a real Sebet, you had the feeling of Shabbat, and Pizmonim enthusiasts would sit and sing for hours on end. And everybody knew a good Sebet gave the feeling of Shabbat. Hence, if you go back to episode 169 where I talked about Sebet, and the name for a Sebet, and how people refer to it as a Shabbat, okay, because it gives you the feeling of Shabbat. That's what the Sebet is all about: good food and good Pizmonim, together, that gives you Shabbat. So, there are many, many Pizmonim, don't think they're confined to just those 14, but besides those 14, you have so many more to sing, and in each section of the book, we have different Maqamat, and we have different songs, different tunes, and each one is enjoyable for various reasons.

Now, what else is going on at the Sebet besides the Pizmonim and the food? We mentioned that at the beginning of the Sebet, usually after the first or second Pizmon, Hakham is present, and Hakham will get up and speak Dibre Torah, a few minutes, three, four, five minutes, you know, connecting the happy occasion to an idea in the Parashah of the week, and that's basically it. Otherwise, there's no talking going on in the Sebet.

Nowadays, we see a new phenomenon that they stop the singing after a few songs, maybe even after an hour if they're pushing it, and they go into speeches: the friends talking about the happy couple or about whatever the occasion may be. This is a very different concept, and it may be nice, and the couple may enjoy it, but it's not what a Sebet is. A Sebet is about the Pizmonim, about enjoying Shabbat, about praising Bore 'Olam, thanking Him with song. This is part of the 'Oneg of Shabbat. This is something that we need to really enrich our lives with, bring it back to our homes, bring it back to our families, and you'll see that the meaning of the Sebet will carry on and linger for not just the hours of the Sebet, but for the entire day, the entire week, and people will come back and talk, "Oh, wow, I remember that Sebet that you had, it was amazing, we had so much fun singing all those amazing songs." That's what the Sebet's about. So let's bring back the real Sebet, let's enjoy the Sebet the way it was, the way we had it for generations, and we'll bring it on to generations to come.

197.title: Women and Parashat Zakhor
197.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran quoted the opinion of those authorities that consider hearing the reading of Parashat Zakhor as an obligation from the Torah. However, Maran never addressed the question of whether women are also obligated to hear the reading as well.

According to Rabbi Meir Mazuz, the Rosh Yeshibah of Yeshibat Kisse Rahamim in Israel, it was not customary in Middle Eastern communities for women to come to the synagogue to hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor. He specified that in Tunisia, Djerba, Algeria, Libya, Morocco, Iraq, Egypt, and Yemen, it was not customary for any women to come hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor, even those who were more meticulous in observing Missvot. Interestingly, we don't find any mention of women being obligated to come hear Parashat Zakhor in the writings of the Middle Eastern authorities. So there is no mention of women being obligated to come hear Parashat Zakhor in the writings of the Hida, or Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, or the Ben Ish Hai.

Hakham Ben Siyyon Abba Shaul wrote that it was not customary for Sephardic women to come hear Parashat Zakhor, but he added that it's good if they make an effort to come if it's not difficult for them. Similarly, Hakham 'Obadia Yosef wrote that women may be lenient if they're not able to come, but that it's preferable for them to come hear the reading if they could. He also allowed taking out a Sefer Torah in the afternoon in order to read Parashat Zakhor for women without sending up an 'Oleh or reciting any Berakhot before or after the reading.

What was our custom in Halab? Hakham Yisshak Tawil said that women did not come to hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor in Halab because it was not required. They would hear Megillat Ester because they were required to do so, but they did not come hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor. Similarly, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar's son wrote that women did not come hear Parashat Zakhor while his father was the rabbi of Argentina, and that his father never mentioned that women should come.

There were some Ashkenazic authorities who wrote that women are obligated to hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor, including Rabbi Natan Adler, Rabbi Hayyim El'azar Shapira, and Rabbi Yisrael Eliyahu Yehoshua. However, other Ashkenazic authorities reported that it was not customary for women to come hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor, including Rabbi Shneur Zalman Fradkin in the 19th century.

So while it is customary for men to make sure to hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor based on the opinion quoted by Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh that considers hearing that reading an obligation from the Torah, it was not customary for women to come hear the reading in the Middle East. This was based on the fact that the Middle Eastern authorities did not mention a requirement for women to come hear the reading of Parashat Zakhor. Some Ashkenazic authorities required women to come hear the reading of Zakhor, but even in Europe, it was not always customary for women to come hear the reading. In more recent times, some of our Sephardic rabbis have encouraged women to come hear the reading of Zakhor if they were able to, but even those rabbis do not require women to come. Growing up, we never had the custom in our community to take out a Sefer Torah in order to read Zakhor to women in the afternoon. It's only very recently that some synagogues have begun that practice.

198.title: Shabbat Shirah and Ibtida Kalam
198.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim, and we continue with our series of videos discussing specific Minhagim associated with particular Shabbatot. We are up to Parashat BeShallah, the Parashah where Bene Yisrael sing the Shirah 'Al HaYam, and that therefore this Shabbat is also known as Shabbat Shirah, and there are a number of interesting Minhagim associated with this Shabbat.

We will begin with the Tefilah in the Zemirot. Every Shabbat, one of the Hazzanim will say the Az Yashir himself, and the people will quietly say to themselves. However, Shabbat Shirah, the entire Kahal, in unison, sing the Shirah beginning with VaYosha', with the Ta'amim. So "VaYosha' Ad-onai," and they will continue through the end of the Shirah, and not only that, they will continue following the end of the Shirah, and continue with "VaTikkah Miryam HaNebi'ah Ahot Aharon" until "Ki Ani HaShem Rofe'ekha." This is the custom in many Kehillot in New York, it's the custom of course in Ades, and in other Syrian Kehillot throughout the world. It is a Minhag which is from Halab, and for an in-depth discussion regarding this Minhag, it would be beneficial to see the beautiful video prepared by my colleague, Mr. Morris Arking, it's video number 88 discussing this particular Minhag.

Shahrit is in Maqam 'Ajam, a very festive Maqam, and because it is often that Tu BiShbat falls the week following the reading of Parashat BeShallah, when it does fall during the week, the Hazzan will often switch in Semehim from Maqam 'Ajam to Maqam Saba in order to be able to sing the Semehim to the tune of Yah El Gadol VeNehdar, which is a beautiful Pizmon, it's found actually twice in the Shir UShbahah, once on page 72 as part of the Bakashot, and once on page 391. It's based on the tune, the Arabic song associated with Tu BiShbat, and you'll find many Hazzanim who do that.

When we take out the Sefer Torah, there is usually, not always, but sometimes there is a Pizmon which is associated with the Parashah, and the Pizmon associated with Parashat BeShallah is Rahum Attah in Nahawand, a beautiful Pizmon, very familiar to all of you, it's on page 216. As a matter of fact, in the Pizmonim book, you will look at page 572, where you have a list of the Pizmonim which are associated with particular Shabbatot, and usually that's the Pizmon that we sing as we take out the Sefer Torah that week.

In the Keri'at Sefer Torah, and it happens throughout the Hamishah Humshe Torah, but many times prior to the Shirah and during the Shirah, there is a Ta'am at the end of the Pasuk, right before the Sof Pasuk, which is called Tarha Arukah, where the Kore will extend the Tarha, giving a more dramatic backdrop to the Pesukim. In this beautiful Tikkun that the Kehillah recently published, Birkat Abraham, the Sephardic Heritage Foundation, they created a special symbol to denote when that Tarha Arukah is to be said. It's a little triangle above the word that has the Tarha. I've seen it sung by the Kore, sometimes an extended Sigah, and sometimes it will go into the Huseini Maqam. Shishi, of course, is the Shirat HaYam.

Following the Shirat HaYam, the Parashah, we talk about, we discuss the, we read about the war with 'Amalek. Now, here, there is a practice which you'll find not only in our Kehillah, but in many, many other communities throughout the world, especially the Ashkenazim, where when they get to the word 'Amalek, people will bang lightly with their feet. Now, this is not, I can't elevate this to the status of a Minhag. It's not sourced anywhere. It's something that, growing up, I remember some people would do it, many wouldn't. So it's a practice, not a Minhag, and it's a practice, actually, the Hakhamim were concerned, and in certain Teshubot, were critical if this light banging became anything more than that, and became disruptive to the decorum and to the Kabod of the Bet HaKeneset, and the Kabod of the person banging, of course, and if it in any way disrupts the reader, then it's not looked upon favorably by the Hakhamim.

Finally, Minhah, of course we read Parashat Yitro, the Parashah which includes the 'Aseret HaDibrot. There is a beautiful custom in Halab that began in Halab that we read the 'Aseret HaDibrot with the Arabic Targum, the Ashir Kilmat, which means Ten Commandments. It's called Ibtida Kalam, that's on page 515 in the Pizmonim books. It's a beautiful custom, and Joey Mosseri said to me that he remembers that in Bnei Yosef, Yizzakher LaTob Abraham Dwek used to read it during Se'udah Shelishit. Once we read Parashat Yitro, now's the time where we could read Ibtida Kalam. Now, so he used to read during Se'udah Shelishit. Actually in Halab, and the way we used to do it in Israel, it's done, there's usually a big get-together Mossa'e Shabbat. They used to do it the Mossa'e Shabbat of Parashat BeShallah. They used to get together, very festive atmosphere. They used to read Ibtida Kalam. Now, in Halab, that I heard that they used to sell the Zekhut to read one of the 'Aseret HaDibrot, and it was a very big honor. So it's a beautiful custom, and I know that there are synagogues in New York that still keep, maintain this custom. I know with there's a Minyan of Hakham Joey Mizrahi in Beth Torah, which insist on singing Ibtida Kalam, has a very unique tune, and inshallah we should keep this great custom going. Kol Tub.

199.title: The Mezza at a Traditional Sebet
199.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Sebet. So, we've spoken about the Sebet, what goes on, what doesn't go on, who comes, who doesn't come, where we have the Sebet, but everybody's excited to know about the actual Sebet. Okay? Not just the Pizmonim that we've discussed, but about the food. Everybody loves food.

But without a drink, we can't really get into the Sebet to enjoy the food. So, at a typical Sebet, everybody pours himself a nice glass of arak. At times, it may have been Scotch, hot summer month, a nice ice-cold beer, but that was it. There was nothing else at the Sebet. It wasn't a drinking party. It was a party to sing, to eat homemade, delicious morsels, to enjoy.

But what are these morsels that we're enjoying at the Sebet? It's what we call today mezza. Mezza comes from the Arabic word mezze. Mezze coming from the Ottoman Turkish word, which came from the Persian, and it means a small, tasty snack. And this tasty snack is something that really is the showcase of our Sebet. Beautiful homemade foods, small pieces, dainty, that everybody enjoys.

Let's talk about these foods. Generally, you ask somebody about mezza, and what do they know? They know Kibbeh, they know Lahm Ba'ajeen. That, those are the quintessential Sebet foods. And we all know our typical Kibbeh. Here it is. Okay? Beautiful bulgur surrounding the meat inside. But the way it used to be made, and traditionally, it would have romman inside, which are pomegranate seeds, or it would have snobar inside, which are pine nuts. And I must thank Mrs. Nadia Mishanieh and SY Cuisine for preparing all these authentic Halabi dishes. She's from Halab, and she has transplanted these authentic recipes to SY Cuisine, and she makes them available to the entire community.

We have Lahm Ba'ajeen, also beautifully decorated with pine nuts, which give it an exquisite flavor. We have Sambusak, which is obviously not with cheese, but with meat inside. And besides your regular Sambusak, we have Pasteles, or Pastel, which is the same thing like a Sambusak. The meat is a little bit different, the dough is a little bit different, and it's shaped, on purpose, like a top and bottom, a lid and a pot. And it's to represent the Man, the Man that Bore 'Olam served to 'Am Yisrael in the desert, because every day when the Man was sent down, it had a layer of dew beneath it, a layer of dew above it, and therefore this is represented like this, and it's a special food for Shabbat.

Of course, everybody knows and loves Yebraq, prepared wonderfully with lemon and garlic. And these are the foods that we all know. We know the beautiful pickles of turnips and of cauliflower. We're aware of the Bazargan and the Tabbouleh salads. But we have three items here called Quaisat, which we rarely see at Sebets anymore. This is prepared with pistachio stuffed inside and a tomato sauce. This is egg inside with tomato sauce. And this is pistachio in a lemon sauce. And these were typically found at every Sebet. Very, very delicious items, very enjoyable to eat, that unfortunately we don't see anymore, because they've been taken over.

Taken over with chicken nuggets, thing, something that wasn't introduced to a Sebet until the early '80s, wontons, franks in blankets, cold cuts. All these different items have come in later on. Don't get me wrong, they're all delicious, but they're not traditional. At a traditional Sebet, more or less what you see in front of you today, these are the foods. So, keep it in mind. Try to stay authentic. Have a Sebet with real Pizmonim, real arak, real Kibbeh with snobar, and enjoy, and Mabrook.
