200.title: The Haftarah of Shabbat HaGadol
200.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that the Shabbat before Pesah is called Shabbat HaGadol. However, Maran did not mention reciting a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol. But we do find a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol in earlier sources. Rabbi Shelomo Yisshaki, more popularly known as Rashi, who lived in France in the 11th century, wrote that the Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol is Ve'Arebah, even when Pesah begins during the week, and all the more so when 'Ereb Pesah falls on Shabbat. Rashi wrote this in his book, Pardes HaGadol.

Since that time, the custom of reciting a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol was recorded by the Or Zarua', who lived in Austria in the 13th century, and was also quoted from the Maharshal, who lived in Poland in the 16th century. There were some Ashkenazim who only recited a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol when 'Ereb Pesah fell on Shabbat. This custom was recorded by the Ba'er Heteb, who lived in Poland in the 17th century.

Interestingly, only reciting the special Haftarah when 'Ereb Pesah fell on Shabbat was recorded as the custom in the Land of Israel by Rabbi Hayyim Ben 'Asis Sethon in his book, Eress Hayyim, which was published in the year 1908, and also by the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer, who lived in Jerusalem in the beginning of the 20th century. However, Rabbi Yisshak Alfiah, who was born in Halab in 1877 and moved to Jerusalem in 1890, wrote in his book, Siah Yisshak, that the custom in Jerusalem was not in accordance with what was documented by Rabbi Hayyim Ben 'Asis Sethon in Eress Hayyim. He wrote that they never recited a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol, even if 'Ereb Pesah fell on Shabbat, and he specified that in the year that he was writing this book, which was 1923, 'Ereb Pesah fell on Shabbat, and they read the regular Haftarah for Sav, not the Haftarah that others read for Shabbat HaGadol.

At the same time, HaRav Abraham HaLevi Prag, an Ashkenazic rabbi who was born in Jerusalem in the year 1870 and passed away there in the year 1921, wrote that the custom in almost every synagogue and Bet Midrash in Jerusalem was to read the special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol every year. Rabbi Yisshak Palachi, a rabbi in Izmir, Turkey in the 19th century, wrote in his book, Yefeh LaLeb, that they never recited the Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol even when 'Ereb Pesah fell on Shabbat. So we see that some had the custom to read a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol every year. Others only read the special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol if 'Ereb Pesah fell on Shabbat, while others never read a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol.

What was the custom in Halab? Hakham Yisshak Shahrabani wrote in his book, Ro'eh Ne'eman, that the Halabis never read the Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol even when 'Ereb Pesah falls on Shabbat. Similarly, Hakham Yom Tob Yedid wrote in his Humash, Me'ir Tob, that in Aram Soba, they never read the Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol. And Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that the Halabi community in Argentina never recited the Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol. I also remember Hakham David Tawil, here in Brooklyn, always reminding us that we never recite the Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol.

However, Hakham 'Ezra Ades, who was born in Jerusalem in the 1920s and was the son of Hakham Ya'akob Ades, was quoted as saying that the custom in Aleppo and Damascus was to recite the special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol when 'Ereb Pesah falls on Shabbat. Furthermore, in the 19th century, Hakham Abraham Hamwey wrote that it is customary to recite a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol only when 'Ereb Pesah falls on Shabbat. This was included in his supplementary notes for his Pesah Mahzor, Bet HaBehirah, that was printed at the end of Bet Simhah, which is his Mahzor for Sukkot. However, he did not specify that this was the custom in Halab, like he often did with regards to other customs in all of his writings.

So the custom of reciting a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol developed in France in the 11th century and was practiced in other Ashkenazic communities as well. In some Ashkenazic communities, the special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol was only read when 'Ereb Pesah falls on Shabbat. Some Middle Eastern communities adopted the custom of reading the special Haftarah when 'Ereb Pesah falls on Shabbat, while other Middle Eastern communities did not practice the custom of reading a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol at all. The prevalent custom of Halab was not to read the Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol, even when 'Ereb Pesah falls on Shabbat, and this custom was maintained by Halabi communities, both in New York and in Argentina. Our custom is based on Maran HaShulhan 'Arukh, who did not make any mention of reciting a special Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol.

201.title: Parashat Yitro, Mishpatim and Terumah
201.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our series of videos dealing with particular Minhagim for specific Shabbatot. We are up to Shabbat Parashat Yitro.

As we all know, Parashat Yitro is the Parashah which contains the 'Aseret HaDibrot. We read the Ten Commandments on Parashat Yitro, and therefore the Hazzan will sing the Nishmat and the entire Shahrit in Maqam Huseini. The reason is that there is the very well-known Pizmon Da'at UMezimmah, which is found on page 334 in the Pizmon book. And this Pizmon is sung, the tune is sung for Nakdishakh. All Halabiyeh, all Aleppian communities throughout the world, all sing the same Nakdishakh on this Parashah. Whenever we read the Ten Commandments, so it will also be sung in Parashat VaEthannan.

When we take the Sefer out, there is another Pizmon dealing with Mattan Torah, and this is called Ahallel VeAbi'a. It's on page 220, and we will sing that Pizmon generally when we take the Sefer out and we bring it to the Tebah. This is the Pizmon that is sung. As I mentioned in my previous videos, there's the list of unique Pizmonim for each Shabbat where it applies, it's on page 572 and 573 in the Pizmonim book.

The 'Aliyat Shishi, generally, most Halabiyeh communities, and it's reflected accurately in the Tikkun Kore'im Birkat Abraham, will do the Shishi of "'Al Mekomo Yabo BeShalom," and the 'Aseret HaDibrot will either be Samukh or Mashlim. We do differently in Ades, but most Kehillot, if not all, do the 'Aseret HaDibrot either Samukh or Mashlim. Our custom is always to send up the Hakham or one of the Hakhamim in the Kehillah for this 'Aliyah. It is also our custom, as well as most other Sefaradim and even some Ashkenazi communities, that we do not stand up for the reading of the 'Aseret HaDibrot. There are Ashkenazi communities which do stand up; our custom is not to stand up. Regarding standing up for the Hakham, I dealt with this extensively in video number 141. It's not our custom to stand throughout the whole 'Aliyah when the Hakham goes up to the Sefer, but for more information you can go to that video, page one video number 141.

It's followed by Parashat Mishpatim. Parashat Mishpatim, generally we will do Maqam Saba, because the Dam HaBerit which we read about at the end of the Parashah. Because of the Berit, we'll do Maqam Saba for Mishpatim. There is an exception: during those years where Parashat Mishpatim is Shabbat Shekalim, which happened to be this year, that's how it fell out, we will switch, and we will do Maqam Bayat Nawa for Mishpatim, and Terumah will then become Maqam Saba. The Shishi for Parashat Mishpatim, also from the, and here there is pretty much across the board, begins "Hinneh Anokhi Shole'ah Mal'akh LeFanekha" and it ends "VaHasiroti Mahalah MiKirbekha." That is the general consensus for the 'Aliyat Shishi in Parashat Mishpatim.

Parashat Terumah is generally, it could be Maqam Bayat, I think they have it in this, in the book here, and or Huseini. Again, we will keep it Huseini unless Mishpatim becomes Huseini, then Terumah will become Maqam Saba. Here, the Shishi is "BeTabnitam Asher Attah Mor'eh BaHar." There is maybe one or two other variances when it comes to Shishi, but the general consensus is "Asher Attah Mor'eh BaHar." Kol Tub.

202.title: Kiddush, Berakhot and Food at the Sebet
202.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: lifecycles, the Sebet. So we've been speaking about the Sebet. The last episode I did, I displayed various mazza, and that has caused a lot of questions to come flying in. People are asking all different things about the Sebet, some things that I've touched upon in previous episodes and things that I didn't touch upon because I didn't think they needed to be, but obviously people asking, we're here to answer.

So first and foremost, Kiddush. The Kiddush was always made after the host came to the Sebet. When the host arrived, either the Hakham or the Hazzan would be told to make Kiddush. Now, this Kiddush was one Kiddush made by the Hakham or the Hazzan, and nobody made their own private Kiddush. Also, not necessarily everybody having their own cup of wine, everybody relied upon his Kiddush. He knew who he was making Kiddush for everybody, he had everybody in mind, they had his Kiddush in mind, and immediately following Kiddush, everybody immediately generally said Mezonot. They took, picked up a Kibbeh and said Mezonot. So nobody was drinking a glass of wine or a shot of arak or anything else. That's the first thing. Obviously, there were small shot glasses of grape juice and the such, and some people partook of those.

When making Berakhot at a Sebet or at various other occasions, generally there was an order, and the order is you start with Mezonot, and then you go to Ha'Ess, then you go to HaAdamah, and then you go to SheHakol, and then you continue with everything that's on the table. You don't have to make any further Berakhot. So if you're going by in order: Mezonot, Ha'Ess, HaAdamah, SheHakol, you have, let's say, for example, you'll have a Kibbeh, then you'll have an olive, then you'll have a pickled turnip, and then you'll have a Quaisat, and you're covered.

Kids never sat down at the table, they always gave respect to the elders. The elders sat down, and maybe a kid would sit on somebody's lap, but more often than not, the kids would be, you know, playing outside and waiting for the Sebet to start emptying out before they could even come in. Even young men would not sit down until elders sat down. There was always this sense of Kabod, of respect and honor that was given to elders before anybody else sat down.

Now, what else was going on at the Sebet? Foods. People want to know what kind of foods besides the mazza foods that I showed. Obviously, you could put any other mazza foods on the table. You could put, you know, small meat Edjes on the table, many people had that. People had small Ka'ak on the table, of course you had bizr on the table, you had various other pickles and the such, like let's say pickled artichokes and things like that. So whatever was in season and whatever was to the liking of the family and to the ladies of the family that were doing the cooking and the preparation, that's what you found.

Now, obviously, other foods, foods that came out after the mazza: rice. Rice is a staple for people from the Middle East, and obviously rice was served. But what is the main dish that generally would appear at a Sebet, what we know of and we think of today immediately, we think of Kibbeh Mushroom. And Kibbeh Mushroom wasn't necessarily served in Syria. In Syria, mushrooms weren't as common as they are over here, and in Syria, they had something else: they had Kibbeh Kamay. Kamay is truffles. And the truffles from Syria are very, very different than the truffles from Europe, from Italy and France, Portugal. The Syrian truffles come from the desert and they have a different taste and a different texture than truffles the way we know of today. And also, they're a seasonal item that generally appear in March on the market, and they are considered a great delicacy, even till today. So when they weren't able to find these truffles here in America, they began substituting mushrooms for the truffles. But the real thing was Kibbeh with truffles. Obviously, all other foods appeared at the table. You even have, you know, you'd have Artichoke Medyas and you'd have different potatoes, and you'd have meat, and you have chicken, you have roast. Really, it depended on the family and the freedom to serve whatever they want.

Desserts, some people asked me about. Now, obviously, cakes and cookies and fruit, but what other things always appeared? The number one thing that was always there on the dessert table, even though most people couldn't get to the dessert table and you had to wait till dessert was possibly, you know, served to you on the men's table and, you know, sent down to you, was Almasiyeh. Almasiyeh, this, we'll call it a Syrian Jell-O if you will, okay, but it's nothing like it, it's more of a cornstarch Jell-O. It's white, it's shimmery, it's speckled with nuts and golden raisins. It's cool, it's refreshing, you know, it's the perfect dessert at a Sebet, especially, you know, after partaking of some alcoholic beverage and some different types of foods, you want to have something like that with, you know, with a small piece of watermelon or cantaloupe or honeydew. It was the perfect dessert, and it was something that everybody enjoyed, and we're seeing it less and less today, so it's definitely something to bring back and to partake of.

Any other questions related to food that have come up? I think that's basically it. Let me just take a look at some notes over here. Oh, another thing about food: somebody asked about Birkat HaMazon. Sebets, as I said, were cramped. There was no room to get up, so therefore there wasn't any bread, there was no way to get up to wash, and so they weren't serving bread, there was no HaMossi. No HaMossi means no Birkat, no Zimmun, and no Birkat HaMazon. And that was basically the way a Sebet was. So, Mabrook again, enjoy.

203.title: Tefilat HaDerekh, Singular or Plural
203.text:
Tefilat HaDerekh, the traveler's prayer, is recited when traveling from one city to another. In the fourth chapter of Masekhet Berakhot, Rab Hisda taught, "Kol HaYosse LaDerekh Sarikh LeHitpallel Tefilat HaDerekh," anyone who sets out on a journey must recite the traveler's prayer. And then the Gemara provides the wording of this prayer. At first, the Gemara writes the prayer in the singular: "SheTolikheni LeShalom," lead me in peace, "VeTass'ideni LeShalom," direct my steps to peace. But then the Gemara records the statement of Abaye, who specified that this prayer should always be recited in the plural: "SheTolikhenu LeShalom," lead us in peace, and so on and so forth. Furthermore, in this part of the Gemara, the prayer concludes with the blessing, "Barukh Attah HaShem, Shome'a Tefilah."

However, in the ninth chapter of Masekhet Berakhot, a shorter version of this prayer is recorded in a Baraita. This version is in the singular and does not have a blessing at the end. Interestingly, in the 10th chapter of the Laws of Blessings, HaRambam only brings the shorter singular version, without the blessing at the end, from the Baraita in the ninth chapter of Masekhet Berakhot. In the Bet Yosef, Maran is surprised that HaRambam omitted the blessing at the end of the prayer, and in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran specified that the traveler's prayer must be said in the plural. HaRambam is ruling like the Baraita in the ninth chapter of Masekhet Berakhot, whereas Maran is ruling like the Sugya in the fourth chapter of Masekhet Berakhot.

In Mahzor Aram Soba, the textual version more closely resembles the Sugya in the fourth chapter, but it is in the singular, not in the plural. However, it does have the blessing at the end with HaShem's name. This Mahzor was printed in the year 1527, 31 years before Maran published the Bet Yosef, and 39 years before Maran published Shulhan 'Arukh.

In the 19th century, the famous Middle Eastern Siddur, Bet 'Obed, which was also popular in Halab, has a much longer version of the traveler's prayer. The text of the prayer is in the singular, but the Halakhah in the Siddur states that one must recite this prayer in the plural in accordance with Maran's ruling in Shulhan 'Arukh, meaning the text of the prayer doesn't match the Halakhah printed before the prayer in the Siddur Bet 'Obed. Furthermore, the blessing at the end of the prayer is printed without HaShem's name in the Siddur Bet 'Obed.

In the book Yisshak Yeranen, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote that in Halab, it was not customary to recite the blessing at the end of the traveler's prayer with HaShem's name. According to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, this is based on HaRambam, who did not include a blessing at the end of the prayer, and also because of other halakhic doubts that could pertain to the traveler's prayer.

So even though, according to Maran, the traveler's prayer is said in the plural and with a blessing at the end, some still recite this prayer in the singular and without saying HaShem's name in the blessing at the end, in consideration of HaRambam's ruling in Mishneh Torah. In Halab, the blessing at the end was not recited with HaShem's name. The prayer concludes with "Barukh Shome'a Tefilah."

204.title: Parashat Tessaveh, Ki Tissa and VaYakhel-Pekude
204.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim, we are continuing with our series of videos that discuss unique Minhagim particular to specific Parashiyot. We are up to Parashat Tessaveh.

Parashat Tessaveh, the Hazzan will sing Shahrit in Maqam Sigah. As we mentioned a number of times, Sigah is associated with the building of the Mishkan, the Bet HaMikdash, the Menorah, the three Regalim, the 'Aliyah LaRegel, the pilgrimage to Yerushalayim on the three festivals. And so, being that Parashat Tessaveh deals with the Menorah and the Mishkan, we sing Maqam Sigah. There is another reason: generally speaking, many of the years Parashat Tessaveh will also be Shabbat Zakhor. That's where we take the Sefer Torah, special second Sefer Torah out, and we read the Parashah of 'Amalek at the end of Parashat Ki Tesse. And this Shabbat Zakhor always falls the week of Purim. And therefore, that's another reason to sing Maqam Sigah, because all of the Pizmonim that deal with the holiday of Purim are generally in the Sigah scale. In fact, when Parashat Zakhor comes out, we will sing most if not all of the tunes for the Nishmat, the Shebahot, and so on, with using the tunes, the melodies of Purim, the famous Pizmonim that we sing on Purim.

So, the Shishi in Parashat Tessaveh is, and I'm referring of course to the Tikkun Kore'im of Birkat Abraham, the Shishi begins with "VeAsita Et Me'il HaEfod Kelil Tekhelet" and ends "LeRasson Lahem Lifne Ad-onai," that's one option. The one that's actually printed in the, that's how we do in Israel, in Ades. The one that's actually printed in the majority opinion is "VeAsita Shete Mishbessot Zahab," beginning and ending "VeNasa Aharon Et Mishpat Bene Yisrael 'Al Libbo Lifne Ad-onai Tamid." That is the Shishi, and of course the Maftir would be Parashat Zakhor if it falls out this week. And regarding the banging for 'Amalek, you can refer to my comments in Parashat BeShallah, it's video number 198.

We move on to Parashat Ki Tissa. Parashat Ki Tissa is Maqam Hijaz, one of the few times that we sing Maqam Hijaz, and of course the reason being is that the 'Avon, the sin of the golden calf, of the 'Egel HaZahab, is read during this Parashat Ki Tissa, and so we do Maqam Hijaz. What's interesting is that the Kohen will go all the way till "Shabat VaYinnafash," right before the story of the 'Egel begins, and the Levi will continue and read the entirety of the story of the 'Egel. So, we'll go all the way until "Yehoshua Bin Nun Na'ar Lo Yamish MiTokh HaOhel," and that of course is symbolic as Shebet Levi did not participate in the 'Egel, and when Moshe Rabbenu called out "Mi LaHaShem Elai," so all of Shebet Levi gathered to follow the commandments of Moshe regarding how to deal with the situation. So, therefore the Levi, because they weren't part of the 'Egel, they will read the entirety of the 'Egel. Shishi is the Yod-Gimmel Middot, "El Rahum VeHannun." It starts with "Pesol Lekha," and it ends "Asher Ani 'Oseh 'Immakh."

The following week is usually combined the Parashiyot. I failed to mention that Parashat Ki Tissa often is Parashat Parah. Parashat Parah again involves a second Sefer where we will read from Parashat Hukkat and have a special Haftarah. And of course the Maftir, whenever you have two Sefarim, Maftir will also say Kaddish.

The following Parashiyot, VaYakhel-Pekude, are generally read together. There are years, especially if it's a Jewish leap year, where they will be read separately, but generally they are read together in conjunction with Parashat HaHodesh, that is the Shabbat before Rosh Hodesh Nisan. So, VaYakhel-Pekude, when they're separate, we'll do Huseini for VaYakhel and Nawa for Pekude. The end of the Sefarim are generally done in the scale of Nawa. When they're together, in the Syrian community in Brooklyn and in Deal they will do Maqam Bayat. In Israel we will do Maqam Nawa. The Shishi when it's combined is, begins "VaYa'asu Shete Mishbessot Zahab," and it ends at "Ka'asher Sivvah Ad-onai Et Moshe." There are a couple of minority opinions, but that is the general consensus, and that's what is printed also in the Birkat Abraham Tikkun. Kol Tub.

205.title: The Women Who Make the Sebet Happen
205.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Va'Ed."

SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. Today's episode dedicated to all the women of the community, all the wonderful wives and mothers that make a Sebet happen. What am I talking about? So, so many have asked for a recap: What is the woman's role at the Sebet? What does she do? How is she involved? And honestly, without her, nothing happens.

So, let's start. First and foremost, Sebet has to have food prep. In episode 199, spoke all about the mazza foods, the Sebet preparation, everything being homemade, every, you know, morsel being prepared with care and love. Then, we talk about the, for the Sebet day, the woman would go and set up flowers on the Rimmonim, okay, to beautify the Sefer Torah and to beautify the day.

Women tend to go to Kenis on that Shabbat morning of the Sebet, something that women generally will not go to Kenis, but because of a Sebet, they'll go for the occasion. They come dressed in a special fashion, and that particular woman whose occasion it is, let's talk about the bride, she'll be wearing a special, you know, beautiful hat, or let's say the mother of the Bar Missvah boy, she'll be wearing a beautiful hat, and that sets her apart from everybody else. The same way the men sit in a dedicated section so everybody knows they're having a Simhah that day, the women tend to sit in the front row, that front row in the ladies' section is left open for them. They sit there, the other women come, greet them, kiss them, congratulate them, etcetera.

When the men of the family have 'Aliyot to the Torah, there are some women they have the custom to stand, some who do not. My good friend Joey Harari discussed that Minhag in episode 129. While this is happening, some will throw Mlabas or other candy down, you know, in honor of that person standing either before the 'Aliyah or after the 'Aliyah. We rarely hear it, but once in a while you'll have a real old-timer that may do a—talking about old-timer from the women—may do a Zaghruta, which is that shrilling, ululation sound, you know, that's usually reserved for other occasions, but they may do it there as well.

Before the prayers end, usually after the speech or so in the Kenis, before Musaf, the women tend to leave the Kenis, get home, make sure everything is in perfect order, presentable and prepared and ready for when the men enter. And what happens now at the Sebet at home? Okay, the men are seated, they're taking up the bulk of the room. The women are still present, but further inside the house. They're greeting everybody who comes, they're making sure everything is set up properly, that everybody is enjoying themselves. And as the men tend to leave a little bit later, women come and sit also in that main section. Towards the end of the Sebet, it's basically the women sitting, listening to men singing Pizmonim, enjoying it. Those few women that may know the Pizmonim may join in as well or may, you know, bang on the table or may clap, you know, but they enjoy the sound, or as the old women say, you know, were enjoying the Bizmonim, okay? They didn't have that. In the old Arabic language there was no P, there was only a B, they would say Bizmonim or Bezmenu, okay, the men are singing Pizmonim, that's what it would mean in turning the word Pizmon and making it into a verb.

As far as, you know, any other women and where they're sitting at the Sebet, nowadays we see this common custom of the bride sitting next to the groom, you know, at the head table at a Sebet. Years back, that didn't happen. Also, as we said in previous episodes, years back the Sebet was usually done before the wedding because people tend to leave right away on a honeymoon, and now we're going back to an older custom where the Sebet is after the wedding because people aren't leaving as quickly. In those cases, the woman may or may not sit with her new husband at the Sebet, either to his right or to his left, and the new couple is flanked by the father of the groom to his right or left, depending where he's sitting, and the bride with her father to her side as well.

But other than that, there are no women sitting in the men's section, quote-unquote if you will, but the women are definitely present, they're definitely enjoying, they're definitely participating, and as the Sebet becomes much smaller and more homeier, obviously the families, husbands and wives and brothers and sisters tend to sit together and all enjoy in this wonderful day, and we wouldn't be able to have this wonderful Sebet without the women of our community. Thank you. Mabrook.

206.title: LeShem Yihud in Halab
206.text:
In some Siddurim, a paragraph beginning with the words LeShem Yihud is found before putting on the Talet, and again before putting on Tefillin. Some Siddurim also include a paragraph that begins with the words LeShem Yihud before each prayer, meaning before Shahrit, before Minhah, and before 'Arbit. And it is also customary for some to recite a paragraph that begins with the words LeShem Yihud before counting the 'Omer.

The origin of this custom is from the teachings of Rabbi Yisshak Luria, otherwise known as the Arizal, a master of Kabbalah, who lived in the Land of Israel in the 16th century. This practice was also promoted by Rabbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, who is commonly referred to as the Hida. The Hida was born in Jerusalem in the year 1724.

Was it customary to recite LeShem Yihud before prayers and Missvot in Halab? There is no mention of reciting LeShem Yihud by Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo in his book on the customs of Aram Soba. In fact, prior to putting on Tefillin, he specifies that the verse from Tehillim that begins "Vihi No'am" is recited. However, those that do recite LeShem Yihud recite it before reciting the verse that begins "Vihi No'am." Furthermore, in the book Yisshak Yeranen, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote that in Halab, it was not customary to recite LeShem Yihud before any Missvah, not before counting the 'Omer, and not before any other Missvah.

The reason for not saying it would be because it's based on mystical teachings that could only be properly understood by those that are proficient in Kabbalah. Literally, it refers to unifying HaShem's name, so to speak, with the performance of the Missvah after the recitation of LeShem Yihud. Since this paragraph is not intended literally, many would not consider it appropriate for one who is not knowledgeable in Kabbalah to recite it at all.

My rabbi and teacher, Hakham Shim'on Alouf, HaShem Yebarekhehu VeYishmerehu, recalled being together with a group of young rabbis over 40 years ago, together with Hakham Yosef Ades 'Alav HaShalom, who was born in Jerusalem in the early 1920s. It was time to pray Minhah, and one of the young rabbis stood up to be the Hazzan. He began by reciting LeShem Yihud. Hakham Yosef Ades, who was proficient in Kabbalah, immediately stopped the Hazzan, rhetorically asking him if he knows how to unify HaShem's name.

So, even though some communities have the custom to recite a paragraph beginning with the words LeShem Yihud before prayers and Missvot based on the teachings of the Arizal and the Hida, in Halab, it was not customary to recite this paragraph. This is based on the idea that it should only be recited by those that are truly knowledgeable in Kabbalistic teachings and understand the meaning of the paragraph properly. However, it was customary by many to recite the verse from Tehillim that begins "Vihi No'am" before prayers and practicing Missvot.

207.title: Parashat VaYikra, Sav and Shemini
207.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing in our discussions of specific Minhagim relating to particular Shabbatot and Parashiyot. We are up to Sefer VaYikra.

The first Parashah is Parashat VaYikra, and whenever possible, as is the Minhag, we, the scale that is sung for Parashat VaYikra is Maqam Rast. Many Hazzanim will go to a higher tone and do the Maqam of Mahur, which is the same family as Rast. The Shishi, as reflected in the Tikkun Kore'im, Birkat Abraham, begins "VeIm Zebah Shelamim Korbano," and ends "Isheh Reah Nihoah LaAd-onai," pretty much across the board. There may be a slight difference in Ades with the list that's used by Hakham Shaul, 'Alav HaShalom. At any rate, it's all in the Birkat Abraham Tikkun.

The following Shabbat is Parashat Sav. Now, more often than not, Parashat Sav will also be the Parashah that precedes the holiday of Pesah, and therefore is called Shabbat HaGadol. Shabbat HaGadol, we will use the tunes of Pesah, and therefore the scale that is used is Rahaw or Nawa. They're similar that they start at the same tone. Rahaw has more of a Bayat scale, and the reason we do a combination of these two scales is because the tunes that we use for the prayer are generally the tunes for the holiday of Pesah. So Kaddish may be Mi Yemallel, it's on page 361 in the Shire Tishbahah, MiMissrayim, or Kedushah could be Beneh Li Zebul Mikdashi, which is also on the same page.

It's very important that our custom is for Semehim, whenever you have a Shabbat that precedes a holiday, the defining tune for that holiday will be used for the Semehim piece in the Shahrit prayer. So in this case, we will sing the Pizmon Emunim, El Kon Shebah, a very famous and well-known Pizmon that we sing for Pesah, and many sing it during the Seder as well. And so this will, you will be used for the Semehim. Now, I understand there are many Hazzanim which may want to use it for Nakdishakh or for other parts of other pieces of the prayer, but the custom is that we use it for Semehim.

Regarding the Shishi, again here it's pretty much across the board, it begins "Kah Et Aharon VeEt Banav Itto VeEt HaBegadim," and it ends "Ka'asher Sivvah Ad-onai Et Moshe." It's also reflected accurately in the Birkat Abraham Tikkun.

Regarding the Haftarah on Parashat Sav when it is Shabbat HaGadol, a very important video was made by my colleague, Mr. Morris Arking, I think it's video number 200, in which he discusses the custom, the Syrian custom is not to recite the Haftarah of Shabbat HaGadol, which is recited in many many communities. Even if the Shabbat HaGadol is 'Ereb Pesah, we still read the regular Haftarah of that Parashah. Now, if Shabbat HaGadol, sometimes there are leap years, and Shabbat HaGadol is not Parashat Sav, whenever Shabbat HaGadol is, whatever Parashah, we will move the Maqam of Rahaw and Nawa to that Parashah, and again, we read the Haftarah of that particular Parashah and not the Haftarah of Shabbat HaGadol.

Moving on to Parashat Shemini, Parashat Shemini is sung in the scale of Huseini, and the Shishi, "Kehu Et HaMinhah," it ends "Ka'asher Sivvah Ad-onai," and again, that's generally the consensus. There is one dissension that's mentioned in the book, the Tikkun Kore'im, but generally, that is the stop for Shishi. Kol Tub.

208.title: Pizmonim Written for the Occasion
208.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam."

SCA, Minhag of the Week, life cycles. We've been speaking about the Sebet and different aspects of the Sebet, and one item that has come up again and again and so many people have continued to ask questions is about Pizmonim. And people want to know, besides the Pizmonim that we've mentioned that we sing at a Sebet, what about a special Pizmon? Are there any special Pizmonim being composed for the person that has the occasion, and if there are such Pizmonim, when are they debuted? So definitely.

We know that, as we've mentioned before, our red Pizmon book, Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah, is mainly a composition that is a compilation of Pizmonim from Hakham Raphael Tabbush and his prize student, Hakham Moshe Ashear, Rabbi Moses Ashear. Now, Hakham Moshe Ashear wrote his Pizmonim here in America, and almost every one of his Pizmonim that he wrote was for an occasion within the community. And even though he published his own first book of Pizmonim in 1928, he didn't stop writing. He continued to write and write and write, and all those Pizmonim, or the majority of them, are in this book, the Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah red Pizmon book.

But how did that come about? People want to know. A lot of people have a connection to a Pizmon. How did it get there? And simply put, sheets, sheets of songs. Rabbi Moshe Ashear worked for weeks and months to compose a proper Pizmon for the occasion, for the family, and he would allude to family names within the Pizmon, and he would highlight those names at times. And here, this Pizmon was written in 1934 for the Bar Missvah of Yisshak Yosef Shasho HaLevi. We have one over here for the wedding of the groom David Ya'akob Beda. And we have for the Samach family, we have for the Ashear family, we have for the Mishanieh family, we have for the Shams family, we have practically every family in the community that was connected to Hakham Moshe Ashear, Hakham Moshe Ashear wrote a Pizmon for their happy occasion, generally being for a Bar Missvah or a wedding, sometimes for a birth. So it's a fantastic heirloom.

But he didn't just compose a Pizmon, he had his own choir, he taught the Pizmon to the choir in advance, and on that Shabbat morning in Kenis, the morning of the Sebet, he would have the entire choir stand up and perform the song for the entire congregation. By that point, once you had an entire choir, a group of young men and boys that knew the Pizmon, they made sure that this Pizmon was taught to the rest of the congregation and to the rest of the community, and it was sung at the Sebet, and it was sung for weeks thereafter until it became a mainstay. It became one of our songs, our beloved songs in the Pizmon book. So many Pizmonim that we sing today are from these songs that Hakham Moshe Ashear composed.

Now, he passed away, Pizmon writing didn't stop. Hakham 'Ezra Mishanieh, 'Alav HaShalom, he continued with this practice and he wrote many Pizmonim, many of which are in the Pizmon book. And of course, the same way, with sheets that were given out to the congregation, taught the songs, everybody got to know them. Here's a Pizmon from 1950, another Pizmon over here from 1959, 1960. Later on, others wrote Pizmonim. May he live and be well, Mr. Albert Cohen Sabban, a Hazzan of the community, he wrote Pizmonim. Today we have Menahem Mustaki, a well-known Hazzan in the community, writes Pizmonim.

Many people write Pizmonim to perpetuate the special day. They teach the Pizmon, Pizmon gets carried over, gets included in the book, becomes part of our repertoire, and that's what makes our Sebetot even more special because we have a true strong hold and family connection that everybody can relate to. So once again, Mabrook.

209.title: Rut, Azharot and Mishle on Shabu'ot
209.text:
The custom of reading the book of Rut for Shabu'ot is first found in Masekhet Soferim, a tractate that was compiled by the Geonim in the eighth century. Since that time, many reasons have been given explaining why Rut is read on the holiday of Shabu'ot.

One reason is that Shabu'ot is celebrated during the harvest, and when the Torah commands us to observe the holiday of Shabu'ot, it also mentions the Missvot of leaving certain portions in the field for the poor. The book of Rut also takes place during the harvest, and in the story, Bo'az leaves those portions in the field and allows Rut to collect them. Another reason is that we celebrate receiving the Torah on Shabu'ot. Similarly, Rut accepted the Torah upon herself when she converted to Judaism. And another reason: the Torah is described as a Torat Hesed, a Torah of kindness, in the book of Mishle, and the book of Rut has many examples of performing kindness. In fact, the Midrash on Rut taught that the purpose of the book of Rut is to show how good the reward is for those that perform kindness. Yet another reason is that the book of Rut demonstrates the importance of the oral Torah, which taught that even though it's not permitted to marry a male Moabite convert, it is permitted to marry a female Moabite convert. That allowed Bo'az to marry Rut. The importance of the oral Torah is a relevant point to highlight on the day that we celebrate receiving the Torah. One more reason is that the end of the book of Rut shows how David HaMelekh descended from Rut, who according to our tradition was born and also passed away on the holiday of Shabu'ot.

The custom of the Ashkenazim is to read the book of Rut in the synagogue on Shabu'ot before the reading of the Torah. Some Ashkenazim even read Rut from a Kasher Megillah and recite a blessing before reading it. However, the custom of the Sefaradim is to read Megillat Rut informally from a printed book, and without reciting a blessing beforehand. The Sefaradim also recite Azharot, a poetic rendition of the 613 Missvot on Shabu'ot.

Regarding reciting Azharot, Hakham Abraham Hamwey wrote in his Mahzor for Shabu'ot, which he called Bet HaShem, that the custom in North Africa is to recite the Azharot of Ribbi Yisshak Ben Re'uben, but the custom in the Middle East and Spain is to recite the Azharot of Ribbi Shelomo Ibn Gabirol. In his book on the customs of Halab, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that on Shabu'ot it's customary to study the Azharot that were composed by Ribbi Shelomo Ibn Gabirol, Rut, and Mishle, each person in their house. Similarly, the book Derekh Eress quoted Hakham Edmond Cohen, who said that on the holiday of Shabu'ot they read Rut, Azharot, and part of the book of Mishle. Regarding the reading of the book of Mishle on Shabu'ot, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote in his book Yisshak Yeranen that the old custom of Halab was to teach the schoolchildren the book of Mishle with the Arabic explanation prior to the holiday of Shabu'ot, and it was read on the holiday at home, not in the synagogue.

The custom of reading Rut on Shabu'ot began 1,300 years ago and is observed by Jews all over the world. The custom of Middle Eastern and Spanish Jews is to also recite the Azharot that were composed in Spain in the 11th century by Ribbi Shelomo Ibn Gabirol. In Halab it was customary to recite the Azharot and Rut at home with the family in the afternoon on the days of Shabu'ot. In addition to reciting the Azharot and Rut, it was customary in Halab to also read from the book of Mishle at home on the afternoons of Shabu'ot.

On the first day of Shabu'ot, we begin by singing a poem about the Ten Commandments that begins "Amon Yom Zeh." It was composed in Spain in the 12th century by the poet David Ben El'azar Ibn Pakuda. Then we sing the Azharot for the positive commandments, followed by the first half of the book of Rut, which is read with Ta'amim. On the second day of Shabu'ot, we sing the Azharot for the negative commandments, followed by the second half of the book of Rut. After reading Rut, it was customary to read from the book of Mishle with Ta'amim on both days of Shabu'ot.

210.title: Tazria'-Tahor Before Yom Ha'Assma'ut
210.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our discussion of particular Minhagim that relate to specific Shabbatot. And we are up to HaParashah of Tazria'. And what we'll do is we'll do the Minhagim based on this year's calendar, which means Tazria' and Tahor are read together, two Parashiyot in the same week.

Now, I refer to the Parashah as Tahor. If you look at the Humashim, most Humashim, if not all, will say Messora'. That's the common name for the Parashah. However, our custom is not to use the negative connotation of the word Messora' and to use the word Tahor, Tahor, purity. And if that's the way it's referred to in the Tikkun of Birkat Abraham, if you look even in the old Pizmonim books, they all refer to this Parashah as Tahor. When the Halabiyeh, Aleppo community get together, they speak about Parashat Tahor. So, it's called Tazria' and Tahor.

The Maqam of the week: if it's Tazria' alone, of course, Saba, because you have "UBaYom HaShemini Yimmol Besar 'Orlato." That's what's written in the book as well, in the Pizmonim book, it says Saba or Bayat. Tahor is Nahawand or Sigah. But when they're Mehubbarot, it says to do Saba.

However, this year and many years, the Parashiyot Tazria' Tahor are read the Shabbat before Yom Ha'Assma'ut, the Independence Day of Israel. Now, as in all holidays, for instance, Pesah, the Shabbat before Pesah, Shabbat HaGadol, we will always do Maqam Nawa, because the tunes concerning the holiday of Pesah are generally written in that Maqam, that scale. Similarly, in Shabu'ot, we will switch to Huseini so we could do Sameah, "Yismah Libbi Me'ai." In Tu BiShbat, we don't change the Maqam. It's Maqam 'Ajam generally for Parashat BeShallah, but we will switch to Saba to do the famous tune of Tu BiShbat for Sameah. That's generally the policy of the Hazzanut and the Minhag of the Hazzanut of Aleppo.

So, similarly here, we will switch to, most, not all Kehillot, will switch to Nahawand when doing Tazria' Tahor because it's the week before Yom Ha'Assma'ut, and they will do all the tunes or as many tunes as possible in the Nahawand scale which are related to the State of Israel. As we know, HaTikvah, of course, is in Nahawand. We usually do that for Nakdishakh. I mentioned in my earlier videos of the Shabbat prayer that Hakham Moshe Ashear 'Alav HaShalom incorporated the HaTikvah into the way we sing Barukh SheAmar. And this was even pre-state. It was already the hymn of the Zionist Congress. So, that's very, very interesting, and the Hazzanim will generally do tunes, Yerushalayim Shel Zahab is in Nahawand, and other tunes that have been popularized in Israel are in Nahawand, and that's the tunes that they will use. When in their Mehubbarot, Tazria' Tahor, the Shishi is "VeHenif Otam Tenufah Lifne HaShem."

211.title: Sebet Questions and Answers
211.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam."

SCA Life Cycles Minhag of the Week. We've been talking about the Sebet, pretty much talked about everything regarding the Sebet, but so many of you have sent in questions. Some questions I've been able to answer privately because I've dealt with them in previous episodes, and some I think warrant a quick question and answer over here, so we'll go through them. And of course, if anybody has any more questions, please send them in before we move on to the next topic.

Is it true that the Bar Missvah boy or the groom says Shema' in Kenis on the morning of a Sebet? What about VaYosha'? No, it's not true. Generally, the Hazzan does his job. He says Shema', he says VaYosha', he says anything. The only thing you may see sometimes is definitely not given to a groom, of course unless he's a Hazzan of sorts, but the Bar Missvah boy many times if he knows how to read, you know, really loud and clear and properly, so he'll say the VaYedabber, the Kadesh Li when he puts on the Tefillin, and maybe Shema' as well, and that would be on the weekday morning, but on the Shabbat morning, it generally would not happen.

Two: I've seen the rabbi Mabrook the family at the pulpit on the day of the Sebet. Is that our custom? Is that not Torah Sibbur? So speeches of any sort were not done in the old country. Speeches at the pulpit is an American custom. They included it as part of the Shabbat morning prayers, but for the rabbi of the synagogue to get up and bestow a blessing in his name and the name of the congregation upon the people that have a happy occasion, that's not Torah Sibbur. Torah Sibbur meaning a burden on the congregation. It's not a burden on the congregation. This is part of the congregation, and you want to bring that blessing to one and all, and it all takes all of a few seconds, so it's definitely not problematic.

Three: How long do Sebets last? Is it longer in the summer than in the winter? How long do Sebets last really depends on the people that are there. Every family has a different dynamic. Every family and friends have different ways of singing and enjoying, and some Sebets could be as short as an hour, an hour and a half, and some Sebets can go practically all day long until Minhah. Are they longer in the summer than in the winter? Summer is a longer day, so it may last longer.

In the summer, are Sebets held outdoors? You want to put up a tent, the weather's nice, enjoy yourself, do it outside.

How were invitations sent out for Sebets? So in the old days, it was word of mouth. You would tell the people that you wanted to invite, or you would send the Shamash around to invite those people to you. With the advent of the telephone, people called those people that wanted to invite. Later on, some people actually sent out printed invitations. Nowadays it's done via text. Invite the people however you feel is proper and respectable.

The groom stands for all of the 'Aliyot that his uncles, siblings, father, grandfathers get. Does he also stand for his wife's relatives? So a person is to stand for their father and grandfather, and of course for older siblings and uncles. Once a person is already married, it is proper respect to do the same for those same members of his wife's family, yes.

Are we permitted to bang on the table in rhythm during Pizmonim at a Sebet? This is an issue of Halakhah. There are different opinions on it, and it's not a place for Minhag of the Week.

You mentioned that Yah Yahid Ram is the king of all Pizmonim starting off every Sebet. Is there a last song that is traditionally sung at every Sebet? No, there is no last song. There's always a first song, we don't look for an ending. We continue the happiness, and we don't end the happiness.

You spoke briefly about drinking at a Sebet in episode 198. Can you go a little more into which alcoholic beverages were served? Obviously, traditionally in the Middle East, arak is served. Scotch is well known throughout the world, Scotch is served as well. Here in America, especially on a very warm day, a nice ice-cold beer is served. But if you want to serve gin or vodka or tequila, go right ahead, there's nothing wrong.

Seeing today at Sebets Kippot with the Bar Missvah kid's name, couple's name, is that something new? Obviously it's something new. It's not something that ever existed before. A Sebet, as we said numerous times, was done immediately after Shabbat morning prayers. So you're wearing your Kippah for the Shabbat morning prayers, and you go with your head covered as it was, directly to the Sebet, whether it's in the home like it traditionally was, or in the banquet hall, a social hall of the synagogue or elsewhere, you're wearing your Kippah. So there was no need to make a new Kippah. Nowadays people just like to make more and more things with names on them.

What is the origin of the Sebet? Was it like a bachelor party, but in the Middle East? Is it just Syrian or all Sephardic communities? How far back does it go? Nobody can tell you the exact origin of a Sebet, but a Shabbat Hatan, a special Shabbat, as we referred to in earlier episodes that the Sebet is also known as a Shabbat, and traditionally is known as a Shabbat, so the Shabbat Hatan, the Sebet for the Hatan, for the groom, is something that is very old. It exists in all Sephardic communities. But as we showed, in the Syrian tradition, between the various special Pizmonim and the special foods, the mazza that we talked about, it was brought to a level much higher and much greater than in other communities, and that's why the Sebet is a key figure in the functions and in the festivities and in the merriment of the Syrian community whenever there is a joyous occasion. And therefore you see it as something special, but it was not a bachelor party or anything like that. It was something that existed in all Sephardic communities, and it was raised to a higher level in the Syrian community.

What is the proper attire to wear at a Sebet? It's Shabbat. You're dressed properly for Shabbat. You're coming from Kenis, you're dressed properly for Kenis, generally suit and tie, and you continue to wear those same clothing.

So in a nutshell, we've covered Sebets, we've covered everything pertaining to Sebets. Once again, enjoy, Mabrook, and by all good occasions by everybody.

212.title: Blessings on Thunder Without HaShem's Name
212.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that one recites a blessing upon seeing or hearing various natural occurrences, including hearing thunder and seeing lightning. The blessing for these occurrences is 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereshit, or one could recite SheKoho UGeburato Male 'Olam instead. According to Maran, these blessings are recited the way that a blessing is normally recited, with HaShem's Name.

However, several authorities wrote that these blessings are recited without HaShem's Name, meaning you just say "Barukh 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereshit" or "Barukh SheKoho UGeburato Male 'Olam" after hearing thunder or seeing lightning. One of the earliest authorities to write this was Ribbi Abraham Ben David, who is popularly referred to by the acronym Ra'abad. He lived in Provence, which is in southern France, in the 12th century. This was also the opinion of the Meiri, who lived in southern France in the 13th century.

In more recent times, it became customary to recite these blessings without HaShem's Name in the Middle East. This custom was documented by Ribbi Hayyim Pontremoli, who lived in Turkey in the 19th century, in his book Petah HaDebir. However, he concluded that one who is knowledgeable in Halakhah should recite these blessings with HaShem's Name. The custom of reciting these blessings without HaShem's Name was also recorded by Ribbi Refael Barukh Toledano, who was the head of the Bet Din in Meknes, Morocco, in the 20th century. Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya, who was born in Halab and then moved to Jerusalem, wrote that the custom of the Sefaradim is to recite these blessings only without HaShem's Name. He wrote this in his book of responsa that he called Yaskil 'Abdi, which was published in Jerusalem in the year 1931.

Similarly, the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer wrote that the custom of the world is to recite all the blessings in this part and the next part of Shulhan 'Arukh without HaShem's Name. Perhaps this is based on what Maran wrote in his note above. In Maran's note above, he wrote that some wrote that it's customary to be lenient with some blessings because they consider them optional. Based on the Kaf HaHayyim, it is also customary to recite the blessing upon seeing a comet or experiencing an earthquake or angry winds, which are also either 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereshit or SheKoho UGeburato Male 'Olam without HaShem's Name. The other blessings that are recited without HaShem's Name according to the Kaf HaHayyim is the blessing that is recited upon seeing the Mediterranean Sea or one of the four biblical rivers, like the Euphrates or the Tigris River. And the blessing recited upon seeing an unusual mountain or desert is also recited without HaShem's Name according to the Kaf HaHayyim.

What was the custom in Halab? In his book Yisshak Yeranen, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote that they did not say HaShem's Name in the blessing upon hearing thunder, or in similar blessings. He also quoted the Kaf HaHayyim, who wrote that it is customary not to recite any of the blessings mentioned in those two parts of Shulhan 'Arukh with HaShem's Name.

So even though Maran and the majority of halakhic authorities, including HaRambam, require one to recite the blessings for thunder, lightning, and other natural occurrences and wonders with HaShem's Name, the custom developed in several Middle Eastern communities to recite these blessings without HaShem's Name. And according to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, it was also customary in Halab to recite these blessings without HaShem's Name.

213.title: Aharei, Kedoshim and Emor
213.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our series of videos dealing with Minhagim which are particular to specific Shabbatot and Parashiyot. We are up to Parashat Aharei. This year, this year's calendar, we read together Aharei and Kedoshim, they were Mehubbarot.

So the Maqam of the week, had they been read separately, Maqam Hijaz would be used for Parashat Aharei, as the first Pasuk in this Parashah is "Aharei Mot Shene Bene Aharon," the tragedy of Nadab and Abihu, a very sad event, and therefore we will use the Maqam which reflects that sadness, as we did with the passing of Abraham and Sarah in Parashat Hayye Sarah, the passing of Ya'akob in Parashat VaYehi, Ki Tissa with the 'Egel, Shabbat Hazon, and so on. Kedoshim alone is Maqam Saba. When they are read together, Mehubbarot, in Ades, we still do Maqam Hijaz, and in the Pizmonim books, Shir UShbahah, Kol Rinah VeZimrah, it says if you look at Aharei Kedoshim, it says Bayat-Hijaz. So generally it's a Hijaz where the tunes that will be selected are tunes that have a little bit of Bayat or Muhayyar in them.

The Shishi for when they are Mehubbarot, there's two Shittot based on the Birkat Abraham Tikkun. The predominant view is "VeAhabta LeRe'akha Kamokha." That's one view, and in Ades we may also do with the alternative, which is "LeHosif Lakhem Tebu'ato Ani Ad-onai Elokekhem."

When it comes to the Haftarot, there are a number of Minhagim when it comes to the Haftarot of Parashat Aharei and Parashat Kedoshim. Certainly amongst the Ashkenazim who introduce in Parashat Aharei the Haftarah from 'Amos, "HaLo KiBne Kushiyim Attem Li," we do not have that custom. But even amongst the Sefaradim, we have differences in which Haftarah to use. Our custom is that in Parashat Aharei, we read from Yehezkel Perek Kaf-Bet, "HaTishpot HaTishpot Et 'Ir HaDamim," "Attah Ben Adam HaTishpot HaTishpot," and in Parashat Kedoshim, also Yehezkel Perek Kaf, "HaLidrosh Oti Attem Ba'im." When they are Mehubbarot, we will use the Haftarah of Kedoshim, "HaLidrosh Oti Attem Ba'im."

Now we move on to Parashat Emor. The content of Parashat Emor, among other things, are mentioning of all the holidays, the three festivals, and therefore, whenever festivals are mentioned, pilgrimage, the Bet HaMikdash, the Menorah, we mentioned a number of times, we will sing the Maqam in Maqam Sigah. We will sing this Parashat Emor in Maqam Sigah. Now, another reason to sing in Maqam Sigah this week is, generally speaking, Parashat Emor falls right before the week of where Lag Ba'Omer is celebrated. And as you know, the custom among the Halabi community is to sing the tune of Bar Yohai, who is associated with the holiday of Lag Ba'Omer. We use that tune for Kedushah, and that's another reason why we will sing this Parashat Emor in Maqam Sigah.

Shishi, we also have two predominant customs. In the Birkat Abraham, the main custom is the Shishi goes up when he begins the holidays, "Elleh Mo'ade Ad-onai Mikra'e Kodesh," and ends "BeKhol Moshbotekhem." Another option is to begin "USfartem Lakhem," ending with "Bikkurim LaAd-onai." Kol Tub.

214.title: How Matches Were Made in the Old Country
214.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Va'Ed."

SCA Minhag of the Week: life cycles, introduction to engagements. Engagements in the old country were very different than the way we know them today. We know today guy and a girl either know each other from school, or they met through friends, they date, they go out, they mingle, you know, they do whatever they do to get to that point where they determine that this is the right one for me. For some people, they go out for a short period of time, some people go out for a longer period of time, and basically among themselves they decide, obviously they'll get their parents' blessing before moving ahead with it, and they get engaged, they get married, we know how it all works, we've all been there, done that.

Thing is, in the Middle East and practically the entire world, a hundred-plus years ago, that wasn't the way things were. And especially not in the Middle East, not among the Jews, not among the Muslims, not among the Christians. And the way of arranging a marriage was practically unchanged for centuries. If it was time for a guy and a girl to get married, it was determined by the fathers. The fathers determined, "Okay, my daughter is of marriageable age, my son is of marriageable age, we need to find a suitable mate, let's call a matchmaker."

The matchmaker back then was referred to usually as a Dallal, as a broker, 'cause he brokered the deal between the fathers, between the families. And based upon what the fathers were looking for, and not only what they were looking for, but what he knew to be best for them, he would go out looking for appropriate families, families based upon heritage, based upon lineage, based upon religion, based upon social standing, based upon financial standing. Many, many factors came into play. And that's what determined who the matchmaker, the broker, the Dallal, would find as a suitable mate for the person that engaged his services.

And for example, I would say, "Okay, it's time for my daughter to get married, I need you to find her a suitable husband." He would go out, look for that right person, come back to me, "Okay, I think I have a great guy for you. Mr. XYZ has a son, he's this many years old, he has this kind of business, he does such and such with this person, with that person, he has a good name, the family we know their lineage going back for the last six generations, there haven't been any health concerns over there, and many other factors." If it's suitable to me, and I think it might be a possibility, I'll tell him, "Okay, go speak to her father and see if he's interested." If both fathers decide that they're interested, and it's a possible suitable match, then they'll talk further. They'll have the broker go back and forth between the fathers, discussing details, asking questions, answering questions, and what have you.

Now, not only was it the lineage of the family, sometimes it was, and not only the social standing of the family, sometimes it was even if this family is a Musta'arabi family, and I'm Musta'arabi, I only want Musta'arabi. If I'm Sefaradi, I only want Sefaradi. If I'm Franji, I only want Franji. As we know, in Halab there were three distinct communities, if you will, that sometimes married between one another, and sometimes didn't. Also among the Hakhamim, the Hakhamim would generally marry from a rabbinic family to a rabbinic family, but sometimes you may have a wealthy individual that would want his daughter to be married to a Hakham to therefore have grandchildren that turn out to be Hakhamim. So there were different conditions going back and forth.

At the same time, what happens next? There were many different factors, which we'll get to in the next video.

215.title: Moving or Standing Still During the 'Amidah
215.text:
There is a difference of opinion among the authorities regarding whether one should move their body back and forth or stand still during the 'Amidah. The Sefer Hasidim, which was written by HaRav Yehudah Ben Shemuel of Regensburg in Germany in the 12th century, wrote that one must move their body during the prayer in order to fulfill the verse in Tehillim that says, "Kol 'Assmotai Tomarnah, Ad-onai Mi Khamokha," "All my bones will say, HaShem, who is like You?" Other early authorities who wrote this include the Sefer HaManhig from southern France in the 12th century, the Shibbole HaLeket from Italy in the 13th century, and the Orhot Hayyim, who was originally from southern France in the 14th century.

However, HaRav Menahem 'Azaryah MiPano, who is more commonly known as HaRama' MiPano, wrote that one should not shake their body during the 'Amidah, and that one fulfills that verse from Tehillim when moving their body during other parts of the prayer. Rama' MiPano lived in Italy during the 16th century. Other authorities who were opposed to moving or shaking one's body during the 'Amidah include the Keneset HaGedolah from Turkey in the 17th century, the Shalme Sibbur from Turkey and Jerusalem in the 18th century, and the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer, who was from Baghdad and Jerusalem in the 19th and 20th centuries.

Even though the prevalent custom among Sephardic and Middle Eastern Jews is not to move their body during the 'Amidah, there were some Sephardic and Middle Eastern authorities who did advocate moving one's body during the 'Amidah, including HaRav Yisshak Aboab in his famous work Menorat HaMa'or, which he compiled in Spain in the 14th century. The Maharikash, a chief rabbi in Egypt in the 16th century, wrote that it's good to shake one's body when praying, without differentiating between the 'Amidah and other parts of the prayers. And the Peri Hadash, who lived in Italy and Jerusalem in the 17th century, specified that one may even move their body during the 'Amidah. Interestingly, the Hida wrote in his book Mahzik Berakhah that one may follow either opinion: to move one's body or to stand still, but he concluded that it's preferable not to move during the 'Amidah, since you should stand like you are standing before a king.

Now while it's a common practice among Ashkenazim to shake their body during the 'Amidah, we do find HaRav Menahem Mendel Auerbach prohibiting moving one's body during the 'Amidah in his work 'Ateret Zekenim, which he wrote in Austria in the 17th century.

In his book Ro'eh Ne'eman, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar quotes Shalme Sibbur, who wrote that moving during the 'Amidah detracts from one's concentration, and that standing still makes it easier to concentrate. But the Peri Megadim, who lived in Ukraine in the 18th century, and the Petah HaDebir, who lived in Turkey in the 19th century, both wrote that some concentrate better on the 'Amidah when they move their body back and forth, while others concentrate better if they stand still, and therefore, each person should pray in a manner that enhances their concentration.

As we said earlier, the prevalent custom among Sephardic and Middle Eastern Jews is to stand still during the 'Amidah. However, some Sephardic and Middle Eastern authorities did advocate moving one's body even during the 'Amidah, especially for one who finds it easier to concentrate on their prayers while they are moving their body back and forth. Generally speaking, those Sefaradim that do move their body during the 'Amidah usually move their body gently, as opposed to many Ashkenazim, who often move the upper part of their body with greater and quicker movement.

216.title: BeHar-BeHukkotai and the Tokhahot
216.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our series of videos that deal with specific Minhagim for particular Shabbatot. We are up to Parashat BeHar and Parashat BeHukkotai, which very often are read together. This is known as Mehubbarot.

So when they are read together, BeHar UBeHukkotai, as we did this year, if you look at the Pizmonim book, on page 565, in the series BeHar, it tells you which Maqam to do when they are separate, and which Maqam to do when they are together. It says Saba for BeHar, Nahawand for BeHukkotai, and when they are Mehubbarot, Saba. This is the way it's done in New York. In Israel, in Ades, whenever they are Mehubbarot at the end of the Sefer, the end of each Sefer, as it happens in Shemot, VaYakhel-Pekude, and VaYikra, BeHar-BeHukkotai, and BeMidbar, Mattot-Mas'e, and Debarim, Nissabim-VaYelekh, generally, when they are Mehubbarot, we will do Maqam Nawa, which Nawa is always for the end of the Sefer, just as Rast is in the beginning, we do Nawa at the end. Nawa has morphed into Nahawand in many communities in synagogues in New York. However, in Ades, we are very particular to do Maqam Nawa, which is a favorite among the Halabim. That's the Maqam used for Friday night, as well, and for Bakashot. It's very one of the very old scales.

In any rate, when we do it Mehubbarot, when we do two Parashiyot together, it's always the 'Aliyah Rebi'i which is going to connect the two Parashiyot, and this is not a custom particular to the Syrian community. Most, if not all, communities around the world, Sefaradim, Ashkenazim, follow this system. It's discussed in the early Aharonim as well.

In Parashat BeHukkotai, we have what's known as the Tokhahot or the Kelalot, what, God forbid, would happen if we don't follow the ways of Bore 'Olam, Bore 'Olam rebuking us, and the curses that follow, Has VeShalom. And this 'Aliyah is read generally after the Shishi. The Shishi will finish "VaOlekh Etkhem Komemiyut," and then you begin the next 'Aliyah. However, the 'Aliyah begins "VeIm Lo Tishme'u Li," and we don't begin with a negative, so the 'Aliyah, this 'Oleh would go back and the Hazzan would start, the Kore would start "VaAkhaltem Yashan Noshan." Now, the Pesukim of the Tokhahot are always read in a lower tone, and therefore the Kore will make sure that when he's reading "VaAkhaltem Yashan Noshan" to make it a higher tone so that he can lower his tone without, and still be heard. So that's the Tokhahot.

Now, before the 'Aliyah, before the 'Oleh goes up, and as to who goes up, I don't think there's a specific custom. In some other Kehillot, we will see maybe they will send the Shamash up to do this 'Aliyah, a custom probably better off without, as we don't want to give the impression that there are different types of 'Aliyot, better and not as good. That's not the case. This is Dibre Torah. They are all, all "Dibre Elokim Hayyim" and Debarim Kedoshim. And there's no difference, and so that custom, it's better if it's not perpetuated.

The Musta'arabi community in Halab, which the last rabbi of that community was the very, very outstanding scholar Hakham Salim Zafrani, Zekher Saddik LiBerakhah, and he recorded some of the customs of the Musta'arabi community. Musta'arabim, to remind you, are the Jews that from Halab before the Sefaradim came in the 15th, 16th century. Now, he has a custom that before the 'Oleh goes up, there are four Pesukim that are going to be recited by the Kore or by the Hakham, two from Mishle, two from Yirmeyah. We have "Musar Beni Al Tim'as," don't reject my Musar that I'm giving you because it's who God loves who He rebukes. "Refa'eni HaShem VeErafe," we follow, we ended up with two Pesukim from Yirmeyah. And it sort of give a, gives a comforting message to the Kahal before we go to read these difficult Tokhahot and Kelalot.

The voice of the Kore is restored to the regular tone, the last two Pesukim of this 'Aliyah, "VeAf Gam Zot BiHyotam BeEress Oyebehem Lo Me'astim VeLo Ge'altim LeKhallotam," that God will never forsake His people and eradicate them, Has VeShalom, and will always bring them back and remember the Berit that we have with Bore 'Olam. Kol Tub.

217.title: The Khattab, the Bazra and the Engagement Contract
217.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles, Introduction to Engagement, Part Two. So, we've been speaking about how engagements were in Halab or how they led up to engagements. I mentioned the broker, the Dallal, but I recalled another word that was even more commonly used in Halab particularly for these matchmaker brokers and that was Khattab. And it was generally always a male and a female. Sometimes they worked as a team, sometimes it was husband and wife, to be go-betweens, the male dealing with situations for the groom and the female for the potential bride.

In any case, this going back and forth, as we mentioned, speaking to father of the groom, going back speaking to father of bride, discussing terms and what have you, this was the true Bazra. The Bazra wasn't picking the girl, but the negotiation, making the sale, going back and forth and deciding on these terms. Once these terms were met, and they were in agreement, that's when they call together for the meeting of the family, and the meeting of the family was strictly the immediate family, in other words, the groom, his parents, his siblings, the girl, her parents, her siblings.

They met together with a Hakham present, and the Hakham is the one that would finalize these terms. He would sit with them, "Gentlemen, have you come to terms? We're going to write a contract." Instead of the Ketubah, or not instead, but in addition to the Ketubah that we know today that is prior to the wedding ceremony, there was a contract for the engagement, where the terms of the engagement were listed, who would be bringing what into the marriage, what would be expected from each side. And the Hakham would ask the father of the groom and the father of the bride, and in certain cases, they would tell the Hakham, "There's really nothing to discuss, Kol Ehad KeFi Kebodo, each person according to his honor, we know each other, we know each other well enough, we're men of well-standing in the community, our word is our word, and we're going to each do the utmost for this new couple." And so in some cases, that those were the terms: KeFi Kebodo.

But in most cases, details were listed: who's going to bring what into the new home, how much is going to go back and forth, what kind of dowry, if the dowry is going to be going from the guy to the girl or from the girl to the guy, depending on who was more desirable, how much money they really had coming their way, if you will, for lack of better terms. And this whole discussion and creating of this contract was called the 'Inyan, what we would call today Kinyan, or in more modern Hebrew would be called Tena'im. And in addition to that, the Hakham would ask the gentlemen, "What about the jehaz?" The jehaz was the trousseau. "Have you decided upon the trousseau? Who's doing what? What is it going to be? What is it going to include?" And at times, that would be included in this contract as well.

And this was the introduction to the engagement. At that point, once that was done, they were considered engaged, and then they could start going out. And they would go out under chaperone supervision. Going out wouldn't last long, it would be just for them to get to know each other. Obviously, if they really did not find favor in each other's eyes, the whole thing would be called off. In most cases though, they knew their parents had their best interests at heart, and most of the time they got along well. And, as we know, they had wonderful families. So, going forward, we're going to discuss how the engagement developed, how it changed here in the United States and elsewhere, and what we do today as part of the traditional engagement.

218.title: Hakham Matloub Abadi on Ekhah and the Tish'ah BeAb Haftarah
218.text:
Hakham Matloub Abadi was born in Aleppo in 1889, and he learned Torah there from Hakham 'Ezra Abadi Sha'yo. In the 1920s, he came to live in Brooklyn, New York, and became the leading Posek in our community. He passed away in Brooklyn on January 1st, 1970. A collection of his responsa was published in his book Magen Ba'adi.

One of the questions addressed in Magen Ba'adi is regarding the prayers on Tish'ah BeAb. Hakham Matloub responded to four questions that the community had about the Tish'ah BeAb prayers at that time.

The first question was: Should the Syrian community in Brooklyn maintain the custom of Aleppo to read Ekhah before 'Arbit, or can they change their custom and read Ekhah after 'Arbit, like the Ashkenazim, and in accordance with what is printed in all the Siddurim? Hakham Matloub answered that although from what the Posekim wrote, we see that they did recite 'Arbit before Ekhah, there is no doubt that the custom of Aleppo to read Ekhah before 'Arbit was established by the leading rabbis of the city. He also pointed out that Halab was known as a city of Hakhamim, and that the Jewish people of Halab did not veer to the right or to the left from how their teachers instructed them. Based on his investigation into this question, Hakham Matloub discovered that our custom of reading Ekhah before 'Arbit dates back to at least the beginning of the 16th century, as he found Ekhah before 'Arbit in Mahzor Aram Soba that was printed in the year 1527, approximately 50 years before Maran, the author of Shulhan 'Arukh, passed away. He then suggested two possible reasons for reading Ekhah before 'Arbit: one, it's so that latecomers will still be able to pray 'Arbit with the Minyan; and secondly, by reading Ekhah first, the congregation will be reciting Keri'at Shema' in its proper time, after nightfall. Therefore, Hakham Matloub concluded that Aleppian Jews in America are not permitted to change their custom, that they must maintain the tradition of their forefathers and read Ekhah before praying 'Arbit.

The second question that was posed to Hakham Matloub was regarding reciting a Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb. All the Siddurim for the fast days had a Haftarah for Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb. Should our community recite this Haftarah? Hakham Matloub answered that although several Posekim write that a Haftarah is recited in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb, the custom of the Aleppo community is never to recite a Haftarah in Minhah, except on Yom Kippur. And this is in accordance with the ruling of HaRambam in Mishneh Torah, who wrote that the only Haftarah that is recited on a public fast day is the Haftarah that is recited in Shahrit on Tish'ah BeAb. Hakham Matloub wrote that therefore, we cannot change our custom and read the Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb. Since we even refrain from reciting a blessing when there is a doubt about that blessing against the opinion of HaRambam, certainly we cannot recite the blessings before and after the Haftarah when HaRambam himself is the one who says not to recite this Haftarah or the blessings before and after. This is so especially in this case, where our custom is already in accordance with the ruling of HaRambam. So again, Hakham Matloub concluded that we should not move away from the custom of our forefathers that was also customary in other communities.

Hakham Matloub quoted the book Eress HaHayyim by Rabbi Hayyim Menashe Sethon, who wrote that the custom of native Middle Eastern Jews, who were known as the Musta'arabin, was not to read a Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb, and that was also the custom in Jerusalem at that time. Only later, the custom of Jerusalem changed to the custom of the Spanish Jews, who do read a Haftarah in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb.

Hakham Matloub's decisions in this responsa were accepted by the community and continue to be the standard practice in our communities in New York and New Jersey in our times: Ekhah is recited before 'Arbit, and the Haftarah is not recited in Minhah on Tish'ah BeAb. BeEzrat HaShem Yitbarakh, we will have the privilege to discuss the rest of this responsa in a future video. Tizku Lir'ot BeNehamat Siyyon UBeBinyan Yerushalayim BiMherah BeYamenu, Amen.

219.title: BeMidbar, Shabbat Kallah and Naso
219.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our series of videos that deal with customs which are particular to specific Shabbatot. And we are up to Sefer BeMidbar and Parashat BeMidbar. Now, even though the Pasuk says "BeMidbar Sinai," nonetheless we refer to the Sefer as BeMidbar and to the Parashah as BeMidbar.

As always, or generally, we try to do Rast for the beginning of the Parashiyot that begin the Sefer, as we did with Bereshit, as we do with Shemot, and VaYikra, and now BeMidbar. However, very often, this Parashah will fall out on the week before Shabu'ot, the week that Shabu'ot falls in. And therefore we refer to this Shabbat as Shabbat Kallah, Shabbat of the bride, Shabbat of the bride. Because Shabu'ot falls out during this week, we will tailor the tunes of the Nishmat to the upcoming holiday, as we do with all major holidays, and there's no exception. And because the most popular tunes of the holiday of Shabu'ot is the Azharot, "Amon Yom Zeh" the introduction, "Amon Yom Zeh," and the "Shemor Libbi Ma'aneh," which is the Azharot of Rabbi Shelomo Ibn Gabirol, "Shemor Libbi Ma'aneh." And that's what identifies really the tunes that we identify with Hag HaShabu'ot, and those are in Maqam Huseini, and therefore we will bypass Rast and do Huseini for this Shabbat, for the Nishmat.

Now, the way we incorporate these tunes, there are two different ways to incorporate "Amon Yom Zeh" and "Shemor Libbi Ma'aneh." The one most common is that Shav'at we will do "Amon Yom Zeh," and Semehim "Shemor Libbi Ma'aneh," that tune, "Semehim BeSetam." However, there's another way, which our Hazzan in Ades, Zikhro LeTob, Barukh Levi Mar'ashli, he says that he heard from Hakham Bosso and other Hazzanim that they would do both of these tunes in the Semehim. So you have the first two lines would be "Amon Yom Zeh," and we will go right into "Shemor Libbi Ma'aneh" tune for the last two lines of the "Semehim BeSetam."

The Shishi for this Parashah generally is "Elleh Hem Mishpehot HaLevi LeToldotam," and there is an approach that would take Shishi to "Rishonah Yissa'u." It's interesting in Ades we have a custom that's not common in most Syrian communities around the world, we will take the Kohen all the way until "Rishonah Yissa'u." Those are the Minhagim for Parashat BeMidbar.

Now we move along to Parashat Naso. Now, if we had Parashat BeMidbar Huseini because of Shabbat Kallah, then maybe we would do Naso Rast, or a Rast-Saba combination. If BeMidbar was Rast, then we would continue generally with Saba.

The Shishi, here there's a very specific custom in the Syrian community, which is unlike many other communities. The Minhag Yerushalayim, and a Minhag of other communities as well, is that the Kohen will read all the way until Birkat Kohanim. As we know, Birkat Kohanim is found in Parashat Naso. It's brought down in the Netibe 'Am and in many other Sefarim that this was the custom in Yerushalayim. However, the custom in Halab was to have the Birkat Kohanim Shishi. So I just wanted to point that out, that that's the custom, to do Shishi and not to take one long 'Aliyah for Kohen. In Ades we do like Minhag Yerushalayim with a twist. We don't stop at Birkat Kohanim, we actually continue going until the Korbanot of Nesi'im, and the Korban of the first Korban of Nahshon Ben 'Amminadab would be 'Aliyat Kohen, and then the second would be Levi, and the third would be Shelishi, and so on. Those are customs that are particular to Shabbat Parashat Naso. Kol Tub.
