220.title: Engagements in America
220.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: life cycles, engagements in America. Yes, in the last couple of episodes we spoke about engagements the way they were in the old country, but how much so have they remained the same here in the United States after being here for some families close to 120 years? How have they changed? What has been added? What has been taken away? What has been modified? We'll try to address that based upon so many questions that have come my way.

So let's talk about dating first. So obviously dating exists in the United States, it's the way people get to know each other and go out, but how often, you know, did people date? How many dates did people go on before it became to be thought of as something serious and we need to see where it's going? So generally the way it was, at least for myself when I was much younger and what I always heard, it's the magic number was three dates. Now, it wasn't always exactly three dates, it could be four dates, five dates, six dates, but generally it was a small amount of time before it got too serious.

But generally after three, four dates, okay, the guy coming over, ringing the bell, coming into the house, making, you know, some small chit-chat with the parents, picking up the girl, taking her out two, three, four times, okay, the parents are obviously concerned, interested, and want to know what's going on. The father will generally sit down the young man: "Tell me, what are your intentions? What are you up to? What are you doing for business? What are your plans for the future? What do you think about my daughter? You're going out, you know, and you keep going out." If the father is happy with the responses he receives, he gives the green light to let them continue to go, to continue to go out, but they don't go out forever, the courtships aren't, you know, for months upon months upon months, it's generally, you know, a few months.

Few months, they're comfortable, obviously his parents by that point have an idea of what's going on, they're, you know, his parents will then realize the ball is in their court. The groom's parents call up the bride's parents: "It's time for us to talk, let's get together, we're coming over." It used to be that the groom's parents would go over to the bride's parents, to their home, they would sit down, generally not necessarily have a meal, but have, you know, tea and tea or coffee and Syrian pastries, and get to know one another and talk about plans for the future. Nowadays, as we know, still the groom's parents call the bride's parents, but they go out usually to a restaurant far away from prying eyes, and they discuss whatever needs to be discussed. If all is well, they move forward, and this was basically in the old days, this was used to be the job of the matchmakers. So now it's been taken over by the parents, if you will, this portion of it.

We move forward to engagement. Person gets engaged. In the old country they may have gotten engaged with a necklace, or a bracelet, or another piece of jewelry. In the United States, as we all know, you get engaged with an engagement ring. A diamond engagement ring, it's the norm, it's what we all do, everybody expects it, and it's a beautiful symbol of the love and connection between the young couple.

What happens next? Engagement party, get-together, not get-together? Nowadays people say, "Oh, we have a LeHayyim, they got engaged." We don't have LeHayyims, we have a meet the family. The family gets to meet each other. Obviously the family already got to know each other, the immediate, the parents, now you get the siblings, you get the uncles, you get the grandparents, you get some cousins, maybe some friends, and they meet one another. They get together for a small family gathering, which of course can become bigger and bigger depending on the wants and needs of those involved, and it was traditionally done in the bride's home. Nowadays sometimes done an outside venue, but let's say we're still talking about the bride's home.

The groom's family would send over a lavish bouquet of always white flowers. Other family members would also send over flowers, and that's to heighten the excitement and the specialness of the moment and the occasion. When the guests would come, they would be served Sharab el-Loz, the original almond milk that was heavily sweetened and scented with either orange blossom water or rose water. It was another beautiful symbol of the whiteness, of the purity, of the happiness of the upcoming marriage.

Nowadays we see with the flowers people will put a poem from the groom's parents exalting the virtues of the bride-to-be. This is something that's very new, it's a fad, it's nothing that existed in the past. They really don't know the girl yet, they barely have met her to be able to write such a piece of poetry and attach it, but it's a cute idea nowadays that people like to do, but I really don't see it lasting much longer.

In any case, we move forward. People are there, they get to know each other. It was always with musical accompaniment, and the musical accompaniment was generally what was known in Syrian circles as a Nobe, a Nobe being a traditional small Arabic band, and they would play Arabic music for at least a few hours with a singer, sometimes even a little bit of dancing. Nowadays we don't see much of that anymore. That custom seems to have fallen to the wayside, I guess being in America for close to 120 years. For many families, they don't have that same affinity and closeness to the Arabic culture and the Arabic music, but it was definitely something that always heightened the engagement, and it was still something very popular until even a few decades ago.

As far as dowries, people keep asking, "Dowries, what happened to the dowries?" Dowries are very simple. The girl is paying for the wedding. There's your dowry money right there. Need I say more? In any case, Mabrook to all, and enjoy all your happy occasions.

221.title: Zedim or Minim in the Twelfth Blessing
221.text:
There's a difference of opinion about the last word of the twelfth blessing of the 'Amidah. The blessing begins, "LaMinim VeLaMalshinim," or an older version is, "LaMalshinim VeLaMinim." According to many sources, the last word of this blessing is Zedim, but according to some sources, the last word of this blessing is Minim. The blessing is a prayer to destroy our enemies and to subdue wicked people. Zedim means evil people, while Minim means heretics.

All of the early sources have Zedim. Zedim is what is found in the Talmud Yerushalmi, in the Siddur of Rab 'Amram Gaon in the ninth century, and in the Siddur of Rab Sa'adya Gaon in the tenth century. HaRambam has Zedim in his prayer text in Mishneh Torah. Furthermore, in the Yalkut Shim'oni, a Midrash that was compiled in approximately the thirteenth century, and in another Midrash quoted by Maran in the Bet Yosef, the blessing concludes with Zedim.

However, in the eighteenth century, the Hida wrote that the final word of this blessing should be Minim. He explained that since the blessing begins with Minim, and the beginning of a blessing and the conclusion of a blessing should be similar, the last word of this blessing should be Minim. He also supported his opinion with what he found in some Siddurim, including a Siddur based on the teachings of the Arizal that was printed in Ukraine.

What was the custom in Halab? The earliest source for Halab is Mahzor Aram Soba, which was printed in the year 1527, and that has Zedim. In the nineteenth century, Hakham Abraham Hamwey's Mahzor for Rosh HaShanah, which he called Bet Din, has Zedim in the 'Amidah for Som Gedalyah. However, this is not necessarily a reflection of the custom of Halab at that time, since his Mahzor was not made specifically for the Jews of Halab, and in general, he followed the textual version of the Siddurim printed in Livorno in the nineteenth century. On the other hand, Siddurim printed in Livorno were popular in Halab in the nineteenth century, and certainly had an impact on the accepted prayer texts in Halab at that time. Interestingly, the nineteenth-century Siddur Bet 'Obed, which was printed in Livorno and was popular in Halab, has Zedim followed by the word Minim in parentheses, and after the word Minim it says "VeKhen 'Ikkar," which means that is the main or more correct opinion.

In Halab, Hakham Yesha'yah Dayan, an important authority in the nineteenth century, wrote a short responsa regarding whether to say Zedim or Minim. In his opinion, Zedim is more correct. In his responsa, he does not mention what the custom of Halab was at that time. Perhaps he wrote the responsa because the custom of Halab at that time was not clear. This responsa was printed in the book Ginze Eress, a collection of writings by various Halabi rabbis.

In the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar, which was printed in Halab in 1915, it has Minim. And Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, who was born in Halab in 1912, wrote that the custom of Halab is to say Minim in accordance with the opinion of the Hida. He wrote this in his book Yisshak Yeranen. But in the book Derekh Eress, it says that the custom of Halab was to say Zedim. And Derekh Eress wrote this based on what he heard from Hakham Nissim Zafrani and Hakham Abraham Dwek, who both lived in Halab in the twentieth century.

So the original custom was to say Zedim, but since the nineteenth century, some switched to Minim, based on the opinion of the Hida. The Siddur Tefilat Yeshurun, which was very popular in the community in Brooklyn from the 1930s until the 1960s, also had Minim. But even in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, many maintained the original custom of saying Zedim, as we saw in the responsa of Hakham Yesha'yah Dayan and other relatively recent sources, including the book Derekh Eress.

222.title: BeHa'alotekha, Shelah and a Letter from Hakham Moshe Tawil
222.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our series of videos dealing with specific customs that pertain to particular Parashiyot and Shabbatot during the year. We are up to Parashat BeHa'alotekha and Shelah, that's what we will be doing today, but beforehand I wanted to make one correction and one comment on my previous video of BeMidbar and Naso.

In BeMidbar, I misspoke with the Shishi, it's from the "Mishpehot HaLevi," "LeBet Abotam" it ends. I said on mistake "Toledotam," it's "LeBet Abotam."

Now, regarding Parashat Naso, we discussed the Shishi, which our custom is the Birkat Kohanim is 'Aliyat Shishi and not like other communities where the Kohen will go up all the way through almost half the Parashah until Birkat Kohanim. So someone commented to me and said, "Well, maybe in Halab they didn't do it that way, but it's a nice custom, why don't we do it?" So I did want to read an excerpt from a letter just to clarify that they were aware of this custom in Halab. And in fact, Mr. Sam Catton, Sam Catton, 'Alav HaShalom, he inquired regarding this custom to the very famous Hakham Moshe Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, who was the chief rabbi in Halab in the 1950s. He was the Hakham and rabbi of Hakham Yom Tob Yedid HaLevi, 'Alav HaShalom. And he wrote a letter, he responded to Sam in a letter that I will translate, in 1972. And he writes: in the matter of reading Birkat Kohanim for 'Aliyat Kohen, he says: this is not our custom, Kelal Ve'Ikkar, absolutely not our custom in Halab from Dore Dorot, from way back. And only recently there were those who came from Europe and they wanted to incorporate this Minhag in Halab. However, the Hakhamim of the city Nazfu Bahem, they rebuked them. And he calls it a strange custom, Minhag Muzar Zeh, and it did not take hold in Halab, and actually they kept their original custom. So it's that they were aware of the custom, but rebuked it very strongly and continued with Minhag Abotehem.

We will continue now with Parashat BeHa'alotekha. BeHa'alotekha is Maqam Sigah, the Hazzan will recite Nishmat in this Maqam, and we mentioned many times, any time you're dealing with the Bet HaMikdash, Menorah, 'Aliyah LaRegel, the pilgrimage to the Bet HaMikdash, we generally sing it in Maqam Sigah. The Shishi, based on the Tikkun of Birkat Abraham, the Shishi is "'Aseh Lekha Shete Hassosserot Kesef" until "Rashe Alfe Yisrael." And the Haftarah: "Roni VeSimhi" from Zekharyah.

Now the next Parashah, Parashat Shelah, that's the Parashah of the Meraggelim. And here the custom is first of all there's difference of opinion as to which Maqam should be sung. In New York, they always sing Maqam Hijaz, which is associated with very sad and tragic events. Of course, the 'Avon of the Meraggelim, the sin of the spies, falls into this category, as the Pasuk says: "VaYibku Ha'Am BaLaylah HaHu," the nation cried, and know that this was the night of Tish'ah BeAb, and the Midrash speaks about that. And so they do Maqam Hijaz, which is associated with a sad scale of music. However, in Argentina and in Eress Yisrael, we sing this week in Maqam Nahawand. Now, take notice that we have Nawa during the year, and in New York generally when it's Nawa they will do Nahawand. In Israel we do not have Maqam Nahawand any time during the year except in Parashat Shelah, and the same generally for the Argentinean community.

Now the story of the Meraggelim, here there's a slight difference of opinion as to which 'Aliyah. We know we read the entire story in one 'Aliyah. So our custom based Hakham Kassin, and many of the references that are in back of this beautiful Tikkun, they have 'Aliyat Rebi'i as the 'Aliyah which will read this entire Parashah of the Meraggelim. There is, I know Ades we do Shelishi, but there is another custom to do it 'Aliyat Hamishi that was brought down by, 'Alav HaShalom, our great leader Mack Tawil in the name of Hakham 'Ezra Sha'yo, 'Alav HaShalom. And also in Argentina, based on Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, also the entire Parashah of the Meraggelim, the story is read in 'Aliyat Hamishi. The Shishi is "Yayin LaNesekh," and it ends "Takrib Reah Nihoah LaAd-onai." The Haftarah is of course the Meraggelim that Yehoshua sent, "VaYishlah Yehoshua Bin Nun," and that is from of course Sefer Yehoshua. Kol Tub.

223.title: The Swanee in Halab
223.text:
"VeErastikh Li Le'Olam, Le'Olam."

SCA Minhag of the Week, life cycles. Swanee, what is the Swanee? What does the word mean? Where does it come from? What's it tied into? Why do we do it?

So, first and foremost, the Swanee was a ritual associated with the Mikveh, the bride going to the Mikveh for the first time prior to her marriage. Swanee is a corruption of the word sawani. Sawani is the plural of the word sanieh. Sanieh is a tray, so sawani are trays. In the Halabi tradition, a day or two prior to the bride going to the Mikveh, the groom would send over three trays, specifically three trays.

Those three trays would correspond to the word VeErastikh. When men put on Tefillin every morning, they wrap the strap around the middle finger, saying two Pesukim from Hoshea': "VeErastikh Li Le'Olam, VeErastikh Li BeSedek UBeMishpat UBeHesed UBeRahamim, VeErastikh Li BeEmunah VeYada'at Et HaShem." VeErastikh, and I betroth, and I engage. So, here the man is showing what he does every day, he gets engaged. He's now showing the purity of his intentions in sending the three trays corresponding to the three VeErastikhs to his bride-to-be, that he's coming in with pure intentions to get engaged and get married. Even though they're already engaged, this is the final part of the engagement.

Why three trays besides the VeErastikh? Each tray had a different purpose. The first tray held a purse or a pocketbook, and that pocketbook had the money for the Mikveh. This purse was usually either silver or white or a combination of the two, the silver showing the extreme richness of the situation at hand, and what do you call it? And the richness the bride were bringing into the home, the white would show the purity. This purse had the money for the Mikveh, but not just for her, for the bride-to-be, but for the female family representatives that would join her, which included the mother, the mother-in-law, possibly some aunts, some sisters. It was an event, something that we don't have on the scale that it existed in the past, but it was definitely an event. And generally, there was a custom to have 101 coins in this purse.

Second tray would have what was needed in the bathhouse, if you will: robe, towel, slippers, and something called Bayloon Bel-Ward. Bayloon was a type of clay that was native to Halab, and it had a property of cleansing and moisturizing both the skin and the hair. So, this was also an important element of beautifying.

And finally, the third tray was a tray that had two different things on it: it had a sweet called Ka'ak Bel-Loz, was a type of Ka'ak made out of almond flour, and it had two different spices, if you will, or we'll call herbs. One was Habbat al-Barakah, black Nigella seeds, which Habbat al-Barakah meaning the seed of Berakhah, and the other one was henna. Henna, as you know, is like a red plant dye. And not that they had a henna party, but we'll talk about that in a second.

So, these were the three trays. These trays were also adorned with flowers. And these trays would be sent from the house of the groom to the house of the bride, and then they would be taken by the women from the house of the bride to the Mikveh. And that's where the Swanee was, and it was strictly for women, and it was only for women items that the man would give to his bride-to-be, and there was nothing in return, no Swanee for men that the woman would be giving to the man. That's something that's nonexistent, okay? Exists now, but didn't exist in the past.

Now, back to the trays. As we said, the first one had the money for the Mikveh, the second were the items that she needed for the Mikveh, for the hammam. And the third one had the Ka'ak Bel-Loz, which the woman would eat and enjoy, and it had these two things: the Habbat al-Barakah and the henna. Both items would be thrown into the water of the Mikveh. The Habbat al-Barakah, as we said, is the seed of Berakhah. Throwing that into the Mikveh water, the bride would be in there, would bring Berakhah to the union, and the henna was not to paint her palms or her soles, or her hair even, but rather it was to be thrown into the water. They looked at the word henna from the Hebrew root of Hen, Hen being charm, and by throwing some henna into the water, it would bring charm to the woman, so she would always find charm and her husband would see her as charming.

And this was a beautiful custom that they had in Halab, and this was the original Swanee custom. In the following episode, we'll talk about how the Swanee adapted and evolved here in America, how it has changed, what parts are connected to the past and what parts aren't. Mabrook to all.

224.title: Combining Korah and Hukkat in Halab
224.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our series of videos dealing with particular Minhagim of specific Shabbatot. We are up to Parashat Korah, but before we go into the details of Korah, Hukkat, and Balak, I wanted to give an overview of these three Parashiyot and discuss a very unique custom of the Halab community, which goes back way, way back to the time of the Musta'arabim, the original local Halabi community of 1,000 years ago.

We are generally accustomed, when there is a need to combine two Parashiyot, what we call Mehubbarot, generally because the eighth day of Pesah is on Shabbat, and so we don't read the regular Parashah, so in the Diaspora they have to realign the calendar in order so all the Shabbatot fall out at the right time, the Parashiyot. So we usually combine Hukkat and Balak. Indeed, most of the world, most of the communities in the world combine Hukkat and Balak. However, the custom in Halab was to combine Korah and Hukkat, not Hukkat and Balak.

We have very early written testimonies to this custom. A book about the calendar that was written in 1510, Tikkun Yissakhar, Yissakhar Ben Susan, who from Morocco went to Sefat, he writes about it, and he says HaRav Sa'adya Dayan Soba, and he could be referring to one of the Dayyanim in Aram Soba, or he could be referring to Mishpahat Dayan, the family of Dayan, which were very known Musta'arabim, which had their ancestors go back to David HaMelekh, which we call Bet, that way we call them Bet Nasi. He says in his name that he says, "VeHaMinhag Hayah LeHabber Korah VeHukkat." The Mahzor Aram Soba, which we have shown here many times, printed in 1527, in the section dealing with the 'Ibbur, he writes "Mehabberim Korah VeHukkat." And we know that this is the Nusah of the Musta'arabim, this Mahzor. In the famous book of She'elot UTeshubot Bet Dino Shel Shelomo, Rabbi Shelomo Laniado 'Alav HaShalom, he writes "Kegon Anan Bene Soba DeMehabberin Korah VeHukkat." So we see it's a very, very old custom. Of course, Hakham Ades, Zakhur LaTob, he brings it in Derekh Eress.

That is actually the custom today in the main synagogues in Argentina, in Buenos Aires, where they combine Korah and Hukkat, and Balak is always read alone, unlike the custom that we adopted in New York. Also according to Hakham Moshe Sutton, Zakhur LaTob, he says also in Mexico they read Korah and Hukkat until today.

Now, this is the custom. The reasons for the custom, we can give a number of reasons. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar 'Alav HaShalom, the Chief Rabbi of Argentina until his passing, he said that because the Targum of Hukkat is the beginning, "Zot Hukkat," "Da Gezerat," and Gezerat is not something you want to open up the Keri'ah, not something you want to open up the Parashah with. Another reason that Hakham Barukh 'Alav HaShalom, he was in a conversation he had with, Bela Tishveh, with Hakham Meir Mazuz, the Rosh Yeshibah of Kisse Rahamim, one of the Gedolim we have today, had a conversation with him, he records the conversation in his monthly publication years ago. He said told him that because he gave him that reason that Hakham Yisshak Chehebar gave, and also because Korah is associated with Mahloket, so we add to it Parashat Hukkat, although in New York we don't do it that way, we should do it that way.

In truth, the Ta'amim, the reasons, may be weak, because what happens if you don't have a reason to do Mehubbarot, to join two Parashiyot? So you're going to read Korah alone, Hukkat alone. So the reasons are weak. Nonetheless, this was a clear, clear custom. There are other reasons given, we're not going to go into the Derashot, but there are other very good reasons to be Mehabber Dor Abot and Dor Banim, that the Dor that came out of Egypt was until the end of Parashat Korah, the beginning of Hukkat, and Hukkat talks about the fortieth year in the Midbar, so you want to join the two. There are many reasons. That's secondary. The main thing is that this was our custom. It's a very unique custom. Again, it's not done in New York, but it's done in other communities, as we mentioned, in Buenos Aires and some synagogues in Mexico. Kol Tub.

225.title: HaMelekh HaMishpat, Going Back or Not
225.text:
During the ten days from Rosh HaShanah until Yom Kippur, there are many changes in the prayers, including several changes in the 'Amidah. One of those changes is the ending of the 11th blessing that begins "Hashibah Shofetenu." During the year, that blessing concludes with "Melekh Oheb Sedakah UMishpat," but during the days from Rosh HaShanah until Yom Kippur, we conclude that blessing with "HaMelekh HaMishpat."

There is a disagreement among the halakhic authorities regarding whether one must go back and correct themselves if they accidentally said Melekh Oheb Sedakah UMishpat instead of HaMelekh HaMishpat. According to most authorities, if one accidentally said Melekh Oheb Sedakah UMishpat and they do not correct themselves immediately, then they go back to Hashibah and repeat all of the blessings from thereon, unless they already completed the 'Amidah, in which case they must repeat the entire 'Amidah. These authorities include the Rif, HaRambam, the Rosh, and Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. The later authorities who concur with this opinion include the Hida, and Ribbi Hayyim Palachi, and also several authorities from Halab. This was the opinion of Ribbi Yisshak Harari, an 18th-century Halabi Posek who wrote this in his book Zekhor LeYisshak. This was also the opinion of Hakham Abraham Hamwey in the 19th century, and was recorded in his Selihot book that he called Bet El. Ribbi Yisshak Sasson, another Halabi Posek from the 19th century, wrote that one repeats if they did not say HaMelekh HaMishpat. He wrote this in his responsa Keneset Yisrael. Other Halabi rabbis who wrote that one repeats in order to say HaMelekh HaMishpat were Hakham Yosef Yedid in his book Birkat Yosef, and Hakham Hayyim Menashe Sethon in his book on the customs of the Land of Israel, which he called Eress Hayyim.

However, the students of Rabbenu Yonah, a Spanish rabbi from the 13th century, wrote that if one accidentally said Melekh Oheb Sedakah UMishpat instead of HaMelekh HaMishpat, that they do not go back and repeat, since Melekh Oheb Sedakah UMishpat includes the word Melekh, king, which is what we are emphasizing during these days. This was also the opinion of Ribbi Moshe Isserles, otherwise known as Muram or Rema, and that is the custom of the Ashkenazim.

So up until approximately 100 years ago, the Sefaradim followed Maran and went back to say HaMelekh HaMishpat if necessary, but Ashkenazim followed Muram and did not. But then the Ben Ish Hai wrote that even Sefaradim should not go back and repeat blessings in order to say HaMelekh HaMishpat. The Ben Ish Hai considered this a case of Safek Berakhot LeHakel: when there is a doubt regarding reciting a blessing or not, do not recite it. Here, the doubt is maybe the law is like the students of Rabbenu Yonah, and one does not repeat any blessings if they accidentally said Melekh Oheb Sedakah UMishpat on the days between Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur.

Interestingly, the book Derekh Eress writes that the more recent custom of Halab was not to go back and repeat to say HaMelekh HaMishpat. This was the opinion of Hakham Moshe Tawil, who was the chief rabbi of Halab in the 1930s. Therefore, his students, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar and Hakham Yom Tob Yedid, instructed their communities not to go back and repeat in order to say HaMelekh HaMishpat. Similarly, Hakham 'Ezra Attieh also did not repeat in order to say HaMelekh HaMishpat. Now, even though Hakham Matloub Abadi was of the opinion that we should follow the original custom and go back and repeat in order to say HaMelekh HaMishpat, our other community rabbis instructed the people not to go back and repeat based on the opinion of the Ben Ish Hai, and so eventually, the custom changed in our community as well.

The original custom of the Middle East in general, and in Halab in particular, was to go back and repeat if one accidentally said Melekh Oheb Sedakah UMishpat in the 'Amidah on the days between Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur. However, during the 20th century, Halabi rabbis accepted the ruling of the Ben Ish Hai to not go back and repeat if one made that mistake, and as a result, the custom changed in Halabi communities around the world.

When I present two opinions on a custom, I often get asked: So which opinion should we follow? I don't necessarily consider it my role to decide between two opinions. In this case, I personally follow the original custom and repeat if necessary, but the main purpose of these videos is to provide you with the background information about the customs and why in some cases there is more than one opinion regarding our custom. In general, you should consult with your rabbis when deciding which halakhic opinion to follow.

226.title: The Swanee, Part Two
226.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam." SCA Minhag of the Week: Life Cycles. Swanee, part two.

So in the last episode, I spoke about the Swanee, and I brought up what the Swanee was in the old days. And so many people have sent in texts and emails and seen me on the street questioning me, "What about the Swanee here in New York? How is it so different? What vestiges are the same? Why has it changed? How does it compare? How did this happen?" And I must tell you, the Swanee we have in New York is a mixture of different things that went on in Syria, and it became known as the Swanee in New York. As I said, the Swanee has to do with the trays, the trays with the Mikveh, and the items that are on each tray. But now we go to a Swanee today, and you see a grand display of women's furnishings, things that are all given by the groom and his family. That's not something that ever existed in Syria.

In Syria, as I spoke about in episode 217, there was the trousseau. The trousseau, or in Arabic, jehaz. Jehaz was what the bride brought into her marriage. Now people ask me about that as well, "What do you mean the bride brought into her marriage? If she brought something, it was private, it was just for her." But it wasn't just for her because we said that when the Hakham would sit with the two fathers, the father of the bride and the father of the groom, they had to detail what's coming into the marriage, who's bringing what. And these items had to, of course, be assessed. So the only way to be assessed is by being seen. And the bride would take pride in these things. These are things that she's been preparing from adolescence. She learned how to sew, she learned how to embroider, she learned how to stitch, she learned how to put, you know, different types of decor on the endings of certain things. And these are things that she was proud of. So she was bringing in— She would show her mother-in-law-to-be, "Here I am. I'm shatrah, okay? I'm very sharp, I'm very wise, I'm with it, and I'm a great bride for your son, and I'm going to be a great mother to your grandchildren." And this is why these things were shown.

I'm going to show you an example of some of these things. Look at this. You have gorgeous silk brocade, and you have hand-embroidered dresses, you have these special fabrics and the trimmings on the bottom, you had all different types of silk and lace and cotton and linen, embroidered pillowcases and things like that. These are all things that the bride would actually make herself. She didn't go to the store to buy them. She would make them, and she would display them with pride for her mother-in-law to see. So when the mother-in-law came with the Swanee, as I mentioned, a day or two before the wedding, the bride would have all this stuff on display for the mother-in-law to see.

What we see today at our Swanee today is technically a mixture of the Swanee and the jehaz, but it all falls now under the guise of the groom has to buy all this for the bride. Whereas in the past, it was the bride bringing it into the marriage. And as far as a Swanee for a man, never existed. Even here in the United States, it's only something that's a number of decades old, but it doesn't go back to the early days, not to the '20s, not to the '30s, not to the '40s. Just didn't exist. So this is all something new.

People have asked, "Well, what about jewelry?" Yes, of course. Jewelry was always given by the groom to the bride throughout the engagement period, at, you know, at the time of the engagement party as well, the shower, the, you know, the marriage. All these times were opportunities for the groom to shower his bride with gifts of jewelry and other things as well. But then they tell me, "Well, what about the watch?" There was no watch. There was no specific concept of giving the bride a watch or the bride giving the groom a watch. Again, a new concept, only exists for a number of decades. All these things are new.

If you think I'm making it up and we add nothing new, look, nowadays we have the quote-unquote Swanee dinner. That's also something new. It's not something that always existed. It's one of these new fads, and some of the fads stay, some of the fads go, but I'm sure in ten to twenty years we're still going to have vestiges of what the original Swanee was, but we're going to have changes depending on place and time. Nowadays we see furs being given at the Swanee. Furs weren't given in the past. We're seeing not just slippers, but you're seeing slippers, and you're seeing expensive sneakers, and you're seeing dress shoes, and you're seeing all types of things. You're seeing clothing being given: clothing for winter, clothing for summer, leather jackets, vacation wear, swimwear. Again, it all has to do with different fads and each person trying to one-up the next person, show more off.

But the way of our people has always been with modesty. Things were done in a very modest fashion, in a tasteful fashion, in a classic fashion, and these are things that we need to look up to and we need to revert to, return to these beautiful traditions of ours without going overboard. The traditions were beautiful, what they displayed was beautiful, and it was done in a very tasteful manner, and this is who we are. I wish all the brides and grooms out there a heartfelt Mabrook, and have a wonderful marriage and a wonderful life together.

227.title: Parashat Korah, Hukkat and Balak
227.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We're continuing in our series of videos discussing the particular Minhagim of specific Shabbatot and Parashiyot. We are up to Parashat Korah. We will deal today with Korah, Hukkat, and Balak, part two. Part one is our last video. We discussed the very unique custom of our, the Aleppo community, the Halabi community, to combine, when the calendar requires it, to combine the Parashiyot of Korah and Hukkat, as opposed to what we currently know and what we do in Brooklyn, we combine Hukkat and Balak. This interesting and very old custom, centuries and centuries old this custom is still practiced today in Argentina and some synagogues in Mexico. However in Brooklyn, like I said, we combine Hukkat and Balak, not Korah and Hukkat. We continue now discussing the particulars of this, of these Shabbatot.

So Parashat Korah, in the New York community, Deal communities, they will sing, the Hazzan will sing the Nishmat in Maqam Nahawand. As I mentioned a number of times, in Israel we do not use Maqam Nahawand throughout the year, only on Parashat Shelah, and in Parashat Korah at Ades, we do Maqam Huseini.

Now there is, interestingly enough, there's a Pizmon which is unique to Parashat Korah, which is mentioned in the Pizmonim book, the red book. It's Mah Na'avu Ragle Mebaser, it's on page 133, and because it mentions "Mattehu Yifrah" on the Matteh, the staff of Aharon which was Poreah, which gave flowers and the Shekedim and the almonds, we speak about that in this Pizmon. It's in Maqam Rast. And I urge all of you to look at this fabulous website, pizmonim.org, you could call up the Pizmon. It's a simple, but beautiful Pizmon. You could learn the Pizmon in five minutes. So that's Pizmon Mah Na'avu, which is for Parashat Korah.

The Shishi also talks about, it's consistent with the Pizmon, the Shishi is also about the flowering of the staff of Aharon, it ends "VaYir'u VaYikhu Ish Mattehu." That's pretty much consensus that that is the Shishi. There are some small variations you'll see in the Tikkun, Birkat Abraham. The Haftarah is "VaYomer Shemuel El Ha'Am," it's in Shemuel Alef and it's reminiscent of Moshe Rabbenu in our Parashah, and Shemuel speaking about after he was, after Sha'ul was crowned the king.

Parashat Hukkat, in the New York community they will do Huseini, and being that in Israel we did Huseini the previous week for Korah, so the Minhag in Ades is to do the Maqam Rast. The Shishi for Parashat Hukkat is the Shirah that Bene Yisrael did on the Be'er, "Az Yashir Yisrael Et HaShirah HaZot, 'Ali Be'er 'Enu Lah," ending with "VeNishkafah 'Al Pene HaYeshimon." Again, this is pretty much consensus, there's maybe a couple of Pesukim different differences in terms of where it starts, but basically that is the Shishi across the board. The Maftir is "VaYiftah HaGil'adi" from Sefer Shofetim.

And finally, to Parashat Balak. Balak, in New York they will do Mahur, which is a high Rast. If Hukkat and Balak are combined, they will default to the Maqam of Hukkat, which was Huseini. In Israel, Balak we will do Rast. Excuse me, Balak we'll do Bayat because for Hukkat we did Rast. And here, again, there's consensus across the board. The Shishi is the Berakhah that was given by Bil'am, "Mah Tobu Ohalekha Ya'akob, Mishkenotekha Yisrael," it ends "VeTinnase Malkhuto." There may be variances as to where we begin this 'Aliyah, but all of the opinions have this Berakhah as part of the 'Aliyah and ending in "VeTinnase Malkhuto." Kol Tub.

228.title: BeSimana Taba, Is It an Interruption?
228.text:
Whenever we read Parashat Bereshit, it's customary for the reader to say the words "BeSimana Taba" before beginning the reading. So after the 'Oleh completes the blessing, the reader says, "BeSimana Taba, Bereshit Bara Elokim Et HaShamayim VeEt HaAress." This is done when the Hatan Bereshit goes up on Simhat Torah, and again for both the weekday and Shabbat readings of Parashat Bereshit.

BeSimana Taba is Aramaic for with a good sign. It has become customary to mark various new beginnings with the words "BeSiman Tob," which means with a good sign in Hebrew. So when we announce Rosh Hodesh, the new month, it's customary to say "BeSiman Tob Yehe Lanu Rosh Hodesh" such-and-such. In Birkat HaLebanah, the new moon, we say "Siman Tob Yehe Lanu ULeKhol Yisrael." Similarly, many begin a wedding with the words "BeSiman Tob UBeMazal Tob," and many begin Habdalah, the new week, with the words "Shabua' Tob UMazal Tob VeSiman Tob." So too, when beginning the Sefer Torah, it's customary to begin with the words "BeSimana Taba."

However, since this is said between the blessing and the reading, some authorities consider this to be an interruption and objected to the custom. In the 19th century, in Izmir, Turkey, Rabbi Hayyim Palachi wrote the following in his book Mo'ed LeKhol Hai: "The Hatan who starts the Torah, meaning the Hatan Bereshit, should not say BeSimana Taba after the blessing, because it's an interruption. But if he wants, he could say BeSimana Taba first, and then recite the blessing."

However, Rabbenu Yosef Hayyim, who is more commonly known as the Ben Ish Hai, wrote about this custom in his responsa Rab Pe'alim. And after quoting Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, he wrote that since this custom is practiced in several communities, we must find support for this custom. And he wrote that even though the words are related to the reading, as they are a prayer for a good reading, it is normally not permissible to purposely interrupt in between the blessing and the reading even with something related to the reading. But if one did interrupt with something related to the reading, they do not repeat the blessing. But in this case, where many communities developed the custom to say these words before the reading, it has become considered a necessity by the congregation. And a situation where there is a necessity is more lenient, and is comparable to the case where one interrupted already with something related to the reading, which is considered acceptable. So here, the custom itself renders the situation to be more lenient than an ordinary case where one would not purposely interrupt even with something related to the reading.

The Ben Ish Hai also wrote a letter to his colleague Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, who attested to the fact that it was also customary in Hebron and Jerusalem to add the words BeSimana Taba before reading Parashat Bereshit. Rabbi Mani did mention that in the Kabbalistic synagogue Bet El, and in another famous Bet Midrash in Jerusalem known as Bet Ya'akob, it was customary for the Somekh to say the words "BeSimana Taba" in order to avoid an interruption by the reader himself. He also mentioned an opinion that it is only an interruption if the 'Oleh is reading his own 'Aliyah, because he's the one who actually recited the blessing. Now even though Rabbi Eliyahu Mani did not agree with this and felt that there's no difference if the 'Oleh was reading his own part or not, that it's still an interruption, but that it's customary to be lenient, the Ben Ish Hai did consider it only to be an interruption when the 'Oleh is reading his own part. And even then, it's customary to be lenient, as the Ben Ish Hai explained. But when the 'Oleh is not reading his own part, the Ben Ish Hai does not consider it to be an interruption at all.

So although some object to the custom of adding the words BeSimana Taba before reading Parashat Bereshit, the custom is to be lenient, as the Ben Ish Hai explained in his responsa Rab Pe'alim. This was not only the custom in Baghdad, it was also the custom in Hebron and Jerusalem in the 19th century. The Keter Shem Tob wrote that adding BeSimana Taba before reading Parashat Bereshit is a general Sephardic custom. Rabbi Moshe Suissa wrote that this custom was also practiced in Morocco and Libya, and it is also the original custom of our community as well.

229.title: Between the Swanee and the Wedding
229.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Life Cycles. So, we completed dating, and engagements, and Swanees, and we're ready for the wedding. But before the wedding, there is that time period between the Swanee and the wedding. What goes on? What doesn't go on? Is there anything special? Many people have asked me to speak about various customs or traditions or things that they see today, and they want to know if there are any origin to them.

First and foremost, everybody keeps asking me about hennas. It's not ours. Plain and simple. There are many Sephardic communities that have the custom of a henna, special party. It exists among the Moroccans, the Iraqis, the Yemenites, possibly others. It's not our custom. Never has been. Nothing to talk about. So, we'll move on from there.

Marriage classes. Marriage classes is something that didn't exist in the past, was something that was introduced by our late Chief Rabbi, Rabbi Dr. Jacob S. Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom, and he introduced it because he felt it was a great need to have especially the women learn the laws of family purity. In the old days, this is something that would be taught from mother to daughter. The Rabbi wanted to have it more uniform, and so he started teaching these classes on a small scale, and over the course of time, it escalated. It generally, originally was just one or two classes, you got the basics, you got the laws, maybe you got a little booklet with some more details, and the Rabbi's number if you had a question.

What else do we have? A custom that we talked about at length many times is Sebet. Sebet for different occasions. Now, there was a time period when everybody would go on their honeymoon immediately after the wedding. In those cases, the Sebet for the wedding was prior to the wedding, and not after the wedding. Prior to the wedding means that the bride and groom-to-be saw each other before the wedding, they spoke to each other before the wedding, they took pictures before the wedding, they did everything before the wedding. So, this newfangled custom that people think of today, that it's forbidden to speak to each other, or text each other, or talk to each other, or see each other in any place or occasion, you know, up to a week before the wedding, obviously was not the custom, because they were doing all that beforehand. Not a problem.

What else can we talk about prior to the wedding? Let's just get to the day of the wedding. Do we fast, or do we not fast? Our custom is not to fast. There may have been certain individuals that fasted, but as a general rule, it was the custom not to fast on the day of the wedding. I've recently heard about people buying books, and in the books it tells you that on that day you have to pray the Minhah of 'Ereb Kippur with Viddui in it. We never had such a tradition. It is not our custom. It is a happy day. It's not a day of saying Viddui for the Hatan or the Kallah. So, they would not say Minhah with Viddui, they would say regular Minhah, they would not add anything that would be said prior to Kippur either.

So, all these things are nice customs, but they're outside customs, customs that never belonged to our tradition, never belonged to our heritage. We have a very rich heritage. We have so many Minhagim that we've spoken about, and still more Minhagim regarding the wedding that we will be getting to very soon. So, let's take pride in who we are, in our traditions, in our heritage, in our culture, and let's enjoy it and pass it on from generation to generation. Mabrook once again to all the brides and grooms out there.

230.title: Fish on Shabbat
230.text:
Many Sefaradim and Ashkenazim have the custom to serve fish every Shabbat in honor of Shabbat. According to the book Tikkune Shabbat, which is based on the teachings of the Arizal and is attributed to his student Ribbi Abraham HaLevi Berukhim, fish should be served at all three Shabbat meals, on Friday night, and again at both the main meal and at Se'udah Shelishit on Shabbat day. On Friday night or at the main Shabbat day meal, it would typically be served right before, or even right after the meat dishes. However, Ribbi Hayyim Vital, a prominent student of the Arizal, only mentioned eating fish in Se'udah Shelishit in his book Peri 'Ess Hayyim.

The earliest mention of eating fish for Shabbat is in the Gemara. In Masekhet Shabbat, the Gemara asked, "What should you eat to fulfill your obligation of enjoying Shabbat?" The first answer included large fish. The second answer added, even just small fish. However, HaRambam made no mention of eating fish when he wrote about how one enjoys Shabbat in his work Mishneh Torah. This is because according to HaRambam, the Gemara was only giving an example of the type of important foods that one should have to enjoy Shabbat, but there is no halakhic requirement to have fish specifically in order to enjoy Shabbat. Similarly, Maran did not mention eating fish on Shabbat in Shulhan 'Arukh, even though he did write that one should eat and drink plentiful amounts of meat and wine on Shabbat in Shulhan 'Arukh.

Still and all, many Middle Eastern communities practice the custom of having fish for Shabbat. In the 19th century in Tripoli, Ribbi Ya'akob Rakah coined the popular adage, "Kol HaOkhel Dag BeYom Dag, Nissol MiDag." Whoever eats fish, which is Dag in Hebrew, on the day of Dag, meaning on Shabbat, since the numerical value of the word Dag is seven, is saved from Dag, which is the acronym for Din Gehinnam, which means from suffering in one's afterlife in the next world. And the Ben Ish Hai wrote that it's a Missvah to eat fish at all three Shabbat meals, and also provided a lengthy explanation as to why it is important to do so.

In Halab, many traditional delicacies were prepared in honor of Shabbat: Mahshi, Yebraq, Keftes, Kibbeh Hamda, Kibbeh Ba'ajeen, meat Sambusak, and more. But fish was not part of the traditional Shabbat menu in Halab. This is most probably due to the fact that fish was not considered a popular food in Halab in previous generations. It's not that fish was not available at all, but rather was not considered something as special or as enjoyable as the meat foods that were traditionally served for Shabbat.

So while according to the Mekubbalim, it is important to serve fish on Shabbat, at least for Se'udah Shelishit, in Halab it was not customary to serve fish at all on Shabbat. This is consistent with the rulings of both HaRambam and Maran, who did not mention eating fish as part of one's obligation to enjoy Shabbat. Likewise, growing up in the community in Brooklyn, it was not customary to serve fish at any of the Shabbat meals.

231.title: Pinhas, Mattot-Mas'e and Debarim
231.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Ra'anana. We will continue with our series of videos describing particular Minhagim which apply to specific Shabbatot and Parashiyot. We are up to Parashat Pinhas.

Parashat Pinhas is sung in Maqam Saba. Now the reason is clear, that the Berit is mentioned early, although it's a different type of Berit, not the Berit Milah, but the Berit is mentioned early on in the Parashah: "Hineni Noten Lo Et Beriti Shalom." And because of the association of Pinhas to Eliyahu, it's a tannaitic source in Pirke DeRabbi Eli'ezer, which compares the two, and later there's midrashic sources as well, that, who, Resh Lakish, "Hu Pinhas Hu Eliyahu." So we do have an association between the personality of Pinhas and Eliyahu, who we know is Mal'akh HaBerit.

And so, therefore, the custom is in Brooklyn that even though it's Maqam Saba, which is for the Berit, in Semehim we will shift to Bayat and sing the Pizmon that's on page 92, "Habib Allah Eliyahu," "Abinu Semehem BeSetam," which is a well-known tune. And in addition, which is not the custom in New York, though it's the custom in Kenis Ades in Yerushalayim, we will do similar tunes to what we did in Parashat Lekh Lekha when we spoke about the Berit of Abraham Abinu, the actual Berit Milah. So we will do Attah Ahubi for Nakdishakh, which is on page 410, Nakdishakh, very familiar tune to all of you. And as we mentioned in Lekh Lekha, in Ades we also, the Kaddish, we switch to Bayat Huseini, and we do this, the Pizmon called Bekho Mebinah, which is not in our Shir UShbahah, however a similar, almost the same tune is a Pizmon called 'Elyon Ram. It's on page 375. And you could go to pizmonim.org to get a beautiful rendition of this Pizmon. So we do that for the Kaddish.

Now another thing I found interesting, if we look at the list of course of the, on page 565, the Maqamat of the Parashiyot, I don't know if it's a rule or it's just a coincidence, is that Pinhas is the eighth Parashah of Sefer BeMidbar, and we know eight is the eighth day of the Berit Milah, and it's associated with the Berit in general, the number eight. And therefore in Sefer Bereshit, the eighth Parashah is VaYishlah, which is Maqam Saba. Shemot, it doesn't work, but in VaYikra, the eighth Parashah is Parashat Kedoshim, which is also Maqam Saba. So it works for three out of the five Humashim, which is pretty good.

The Shishi for Parashat Pinhas is "Ka'asher Dibber Ad-onai BeYad Moshe," it's almost unanimous based on all the sources in the Birkat Abraham Tikkun. And the Haftarah depends on whether we are reading Parashat Pinhas before Shib'ah 'Asar BeTammuz, in other words, before the Ben HaMessarim period between 17th day of Tammuz and Tish'ah BeAb, in which case you would have the three weeks of those difficult Tokhahot and Nebu'ot from Yesha'yah and Yirmeyah: "Dibre Yirmeyahu" and "Shim'u Debar HaShem," and finally Shabbat Hazon, which we'll speak about in another video or so. The Haftarah if Pinhas comes before is of course dealing with Eliyahu HaNabi, "VeYad HaShem Hayetah El Eliyahu."

If we're reading Parashat Pinhas after Shib'ah 'Asar BeTammuz, then the next Parashah, Mattot, is connected with Mas'e. They are Mehubbarot, Mattot and Mas'e, and the Parashiyot at the end of the Sefer based on the list is Nahawand, and in Israel we sing Maqam Nawa, which is at the end, and most of the Humashim, Maqam Nawa. The Haftarah, like we said, is "Shim'u Debar HaShem." Finally, we get to, and the Shishi is, again, almost unanimous when Mattot and Mas'e are Mehubbarot, ends "LeNahel Et Bene Yisrael BeEress Kena'an."

So we move on to Parashat Debarim, always must fall out the week before Tish'ah BeAb, because Shabbat Nahamu, which Parashat VaEthannan is always the week following Tish'ah BeAb. So that's why Debarim, this Parashah is known as Shabbat Hazon, because of the Haftarah, "Hazon Yesha'yah." Now, in addition I've heard it being called Shabbat Ekhah. Ekhah always associated with Megillat Ekhah, which speaks of the Hurban, but also in Parashat Debarim, where Moshe Rabbenu, the beginning of his Ne'um, of his speech to Bene Yisrael, "Ekhah Essa Lebaddi." So some call it Shabbat Ekhah, some call it Shabbat Hazon. Certainly we would sing only Maqam Hijaz in Parashat Debarim, as that is associated with the sadder Parashiyot of the Torah, like Hayye Sarah, VaYehi, and so on, Ki Tissa. The Haftarah, like we said, Shabbat Hazon. The Shishi for Parashat Debarim, again almost unanimous, is "VeRagezu VeHalu MiPanekha." Kol Tub.

232.title: Fasting on the Wedding Day
232.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Life Cycles. So we've been speaking about weddings and wedding preparation, and before we get to the actual wedding ceremony, there's a question that keeps coming up time and time again, and that's about the bride and groom fasting prior to the wedding. The day of the wedding, do the bride and groom fast? Is it our custom, is it our Minhag? The short answer: no. Absolutely not, it is not our custom to fast. Now let's talk about this custom, where it comes from, what are the reasons behind it, who does it, who doesn't do it.

So, keep in mind this custom is not mentioned in the Mishnah or in the Gemara, nor is mentioned by HaRambam, nor do we see it in Shulhan 'Arukh. We first really encounter it is in the writings of Muram in his Hagahot, his glosses to Shulhan 'Arukh in Eben Ha'Ezer Siman Samekh-Alef, and he says the custom is to fast.

Now, what are the reasons for this custom? And the reasons for this custom all come as well from Ashkenazi sources. The most common of the reasons given is the concern that the Hatan will become intoxicated that day. He'll drink too much, and because he drinks too much, he will not focus properly on the Berakhot of the wedding ceremony, thus invalidating the marriage. That's the first reason, and that's brought by Rabbi Moshe Mintz of Germany, 1420 to 1482. The second reason brought is that on this day, a person is entering into a new life and so entering a new life, you enter forgiven of all sins, and since you're being forgiven of sins, you fast on such a day, the same way as a king would fast on the day that he is being judged, he fasts that day. And this is the reason brought by Rabbi Yisrael Brona from Czechoslovakia, 1400 to 1480. And finally, there's a reason brought by the Rokeah, Rabbi El'azar of Worms from Germany, 1176 to 1238, and he says there was a custom among Rishonim that the day prior to a once-in-a-lifetime Missvah or a Missvah that only comes up once a year, to show Hibbub Missvah, an admiration and a love for the Missvah, you would fast the day beforehand to prepare yourself for it. So these are three reasons brought all by Ashkenazi sources, and this is a custom done by Ashkenazim.

Now, what are the comments to Muram's Hagahah? Immediately we have Birke Yosef, the Hida, Rabbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, and he says, absolutely not, it is not the custom of the Sefaradim to fast on the day of the wedding. He quotes numerous sources, the primary source being Rabbi Yeshu'ah Shababo Zal of Cairo, Egypt, who says it is custom not to fast, not in Egypt and not in all of Eress Yisrael. He also doesn't seem to care for the custom of fasting.

But regardless, let's look at other sources who say not to fast. The Keneset HaGedolah, Rabbi Hayyim Benvenisti of Istanbul, Turkey, says the custom is not to fast. Rabbi Yehudah 'Ayyash of Algiers says the custom is not to fast. The Rishon LeSiyyon, the chief rabbi of all of Eress Yisrael, Rabbi Meyuhas Bekhor Shemuel, writes the Minhag of Eress Yisrael and all the Sefaradim is not to fast. Rabbi Yisshak Palachi of Izmir, Turkey, goes one step further. He says not only do we not fast, it's Assur to fast, it's forbidden to fast! This is a Yom Tob. This is a holiday for the bride and groom. How could anybody consider fasting on their own personal holiday? No, no fasting whatsoever.

Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, what's his opinion? He writes that the custom of the Sefaradim is not to fast. That is the original custom, and that what was the common practice. And that some people want to fast nowadays, it's not that they don't have a source to rely upon, but we are not in a position to take upon ourselves extra stringencies, extra Humrot, to put things upon ourselves that we never had a custom to do. And even those that had the custom, the custom then was for weddings to be held either in the morning or in the afternoon, so if they were fasting, they were fasting at most for a few hours, and they would immediately break the fast at the end of the wedding ceremony, as opposed to nowadays. Nowadays, we see that people are up from early in the morning on the wedding day, preparing for the wedding, going for pictures, greeting people, it's a very emotional day, it's a very lengthy day, the ceremony doesn't usually happen until some point after sunset and even later than that, and to put somebody through that is not the intention of the Hakhamim. I've also heard that in recent years, some people have taken upon this custom, and in some cases, Hatzalah members have been called in because that bride and groom may have fainted during the celebrations after, during the reception, because they were dehydrated. Again, we don't hear about many of these cases because most people don't fast, but when it does happen, we do sometimes hear of such things.

Now, what about those Sefaradim that do fast? Yes, there are some communities that have that Minhag. The Ben Ish Hai, Ribbi Yosef Hayyim of Baghdad, Iraq, says the custom in Baghdad is that they do fast. In Djerba, an island off of Tunisia, even though in Tunisia they did not fast, but in Djerba, they did fast. In many cities in Morocco, they fasted as well. But even in all these places where they did fast, the custom was only for the groom to fast, never for the bride. All the sources that we've seen among Sefaradim all clearly say that it's only the groom that fasts and never the bride.

In any case, we have to go back to the words of Ribbi Shem Tob Gagin, who we've quoted in these Minhag of the Week segments many times. Ribbi Shem Tob Gagin writes very clearly, the Minhag of the Sefaradim in Eress Yisrael and in Syria and in Turkey and in Egypt is not to fast, and that is our custom, our custom is not to fast. I wish a Mabrook to all the brides and grooms out there, enjoy your wedding day, your wedding night, and your celebration. Mabrook.

233.title: The Blessing on Lahm Ba'ajeen
233.text:
Hakham Yosef Ben Abraham Sethon was born in Halab in the year 1813. He was the author of ten books. However, only three of those books were ever published. In the year 1881, he wrote a book called VaYleket Yosef, which speaks about foods that are prohibited if they are cooked by a non-Jew. In the year 1883, he wrote Birkot Shamayim, which discusses which blessing should be recited on various Syrian foods. And in the year 1915, Hakham Yosef Sethon's grandson, Hakham David Moshe Sethon, published VaYleket Yosef together with a shortened version of Birkot Shamayim. This book was published in Halab.

One of the foods that he discusses is Lahm Ba'ajeen. According to Hakham Yosef Sethon, the blessing before Lahm Ba'ajeen is Bore Mine Mezonot. He equates Lahm Ba'ajeen, which is dough baked with meat on top, to pocket-shaped dough baked with meat inside. There is a difference of opinion between the later authorities about Maran's opinion on pocket-shaped dough baked with meat or cheese or fish inside. According to the Magen Abraham, Maran would say HaMossi on pocket-shaped dough if the filling was meat or cheese or fish. But according to the Ture Zahab, Maran would say Mezonot on pocket-shaped dough, even if it was filled with meat or cheese or fish. According to Hakham Yosef Sethon, we should follow the Ture Zahab and say Mezonot.

However, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote in his book Yisshak Yeranen that Lahm Ba'ajeen is HaMossi. He explained that even though we follow the Ture Zahab, the Ture Zahab only said Mezonot on pocket-shaped dough, but Lahm Ba'ajeen is not pocket-shaped. The dough is flat and the meat is on top. And therefore, according to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, even the Ture Zahab would say HaMossi on Lahm Ba'ajeen. Hakham Chehebar also quoted Hakham Moshe Mizrahi, who was the Rosh Ab Bet Din, the head of the religious court in Halab until he passed away in 1955, who also ruled that the blessing on Lahm Ba'ajeen is HaMossi.

Interestingly, Hakham Shaul Kassin, who was the father and grandfather of our community's chief rabbis, Hakham Ya'akob Kassin and Hakham Shaul Kassin, 'Alehem HaShalom, he wrote in his book Peri Saddik that even dough that was filled with meat or cheese is HaMossi, unless the dough is kneaded with a significant amount of oil, in which case the blessing would then be Mezonot. Therefore, he would definitely consider Lahm Ba'ajeen HaMossi, unless the dough is kneaded with a significant amount of oil, which would make the blessing Mezonot.

So according to Hakham Yosef Sethon, the blessing on Lahm Ba'ajeen is Mezonot, but according to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, Hakham Moshe Mizrahi, and Hakham Shaul Kassin, the blessing before Lahm Ba'ajeen is HaMossi. But even those rabbis would say Mezonot on Lahm Ba'ajeen if the dough was kneaded with a significant amount of oil or another ingredient that modified the taste of the dough. In this case, we cannot say that there was a specific custom in Halab, since none of the rabbis cited the custom of Halab in their writing about the blessing before Lahm Ba'ajeen. But the majority of the rabbis whose opinion has been documented say that the blessing on Lahm Ba'ajeen is HaMossi. The exception was Hakham Yosef Sethon, who ruled that the blessing is Mezonot in his book Birkot Shamayim.

234.title: VaEthannan, 'Ekeb and Re'eh
234.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from the city of Ra'anana. We are continuing with our series of videos discussing particular Minhagim for specific Parashiyot and Shabbatot during the year. We are up to Parashat VaEthannan.

Parashat VaEthannan begins a series of seven Shabbatot where we are reading Haftarot which deal with comfort and consolation to Bene Yisrael. It's called the Sheba' DeNehamata, the seven Haftarot of Nehamah. It begins in Parashat VaEthannan with the Haftarah "Nahamu Nahamu 'Ammi," and therefore this Shabbat is referred to as Shabbat Nahamu.

Now in Parashat VaEthannan, we have the Ten Commandments already, the 'Aseret HaDibrot. This is the Shishi, and the custom has always been to give this to the Hakham of the Kahal. Now regarding the Minhagim of whether we stand or do not stand for a Hakham that goes up to the Sefer, you could refer back in detail to the video number 141, which we spoke about that we did not have the custom to stand for the entire 'Aliyah of the Hakham going up. It's also a very unique custom amongst Sefaradim, not amongst Ashkenazim, but the Sefaradim do not stand up at all for 'Aseret HaDibrot. We discussed this again in the video that I mentioned and in another video as well. You could refer back to that.

The Kedushah, whenever there is 'Aseret HaDibrot, we have it in Shabu'ot, we have it in Parashat Yitro, and now Parashat VaEthannan, we have a special Nakdishakh, which we sing to the tune of Da'at UMezimmah. It's in page 334 in the Shir UShbahah, and being that that is the Maqam Huseini, the entire Nishmat is sung in Maqam Huseini. This is unanimous amongst all the Halabiyeh all over the world, all the Syrian communities, they do Huseini and they do Da'at UMezimmah for Nakdishakh.

We move on to the next Parashah, which is 'Ekeb. In 'Ekeb, the Maqam is Sigah. No specific reason I could point out to. I have a theory that maybe because it's the third Parashah, and Sigah is on the third note, but that's, we won't go into that now. The Shishi is unanimous actually, the Shishi for Parashat 'Ekeb, "Ve'Attah Samekha HaShem Elokekha KeKhokhbe HaShamayim LaRob," and the Haftarah is "VaTomer Siyyon."

We continue to Parashat Re'eh. Now here, Parashat Re'eh, it's unclear what exactly the custom was regarding the Maqam. There's two predominant customs. In page 565, of course, as we refer a lot, actually it's 566, because Parashat Re'eh is the beginning of 566, in the Red Book it says Rast, and indeed many Kehillot do Rast, but there are many sources, including Hakham Moshe Ashear, 'Alav HaShalom, used to do Bayat. And the reason he used to do Bayat is because Parashat Re'eh is the Parashah which we bless the new month that's going to be that week, generally, and that's Rosh Hodesh Elul. Rosh Hodesh Elul, of course, we begin the Selihot. So, just as is the custom on all holidays or special upcoming events that we take the Semikhin, that tune for Semikhin and we apply it to the relevant tune for something, the holiday which is going to happen during the week, so Hakham Moshe Ashear, 'Alav HaShalom, used to like to do "Elekha HaShem Nasati 'Enai," which is in Bayat, the song that we sing at the end of the Selihot. So therefore we have two options for the Maqam of Re'eh, could be Rast or could be Bayat.

The Shishi, actually again there's a split down the middle, the Shishi in the Tikkun of Birkat Abraham for Parashat Re'eh, we have the Shishi as "LeMa'an Yebarekhekha Ad-onai Elokekha BeKhol Ma'aseh Yadekha Asher Ta'aseh," but you have just as many sources which begin the next one with "MiKess Sheba' Shanim Ta'aseh Shemittah," and ending "UMashalta BeGoyim Rabbim UBkha Lo Yimsholu." So those are two good choices and two sourced choices for the Shishi. The Haftarah is a continuation of Shib'ah DeNehamata, and we read the Haftarah: "'Aniyah So'arah Lo Nuhamah." Kol Tub.

235.title: The Ketubah Signing
235.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam," SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. We're up to the Ketubah. The Ketubah is the marriage contract. And what is that marriage contract exactly? Basically, it is a contract by the husband to his wife, promising to her that he will care for her, he will clothe her, he will feed her, he will put a roof over her head, he'll take care of her. And it's a promise that he will contractually fulfill these obligations, and if, God forbid, in the event of divorce, that he will pay her.

And let's deal with that amount of payment. Payment is a standard amount, and in this community has been for decades that amount was always in fives, generally let's say $5,555, for a wealthier person, $55,555, et cetera, in that manner. It was always a number in fives, and many other synagogues or communities that came from outside of Halab and joined the community here in New York have followed suit and do the same thing as well.

But now, the Ketubah, we think about it today as a major ceremony. You know, before the wedding ceremony, everybody is like, "Oh, what time's the Ketubah? What time's the Ketubah? You're going to be at the Ketubah? Are you going inside to see the Ketubah?" It was never like that before. The Ketubah was a very private issue. It was basically the Hakham, the rabbi, and the witnesses, which generally were other rabbis, together with the bride and groom, their parents, and the siblings of the bride and groom. And that was it. There was nobody else that was invited to come in. No friends, no aunts, no uncles, no marchers, you know, nobody was there. It wasn't done in the wedding hall or in the reception room, you know, with whole fanfare, and, you know, the rabbi standing up and explaining line by line, point by point. There was, you know, photographer or videographer making a whole big thing about it. There was no singing afterwards. It was a very, very simple thing, generally done in the rabbi's office, most of the time even done standing up, you know, and that was it. There was really not a big deal at all.

The Hakham would have a form of the Ketubah, he would fill in the blanks, as opposed to the old days where there was no pre-printed Ketubot and you had a special Sofer, a scribe of the Bet Din that would write up a specific and exact Ketubah at that time and place. Nowadays, there's a form that's been used already for the last almost 100 years where the Hakham would have everything, who would fill in the name of the city, which is by which body of water, fill in the names of the bride, the name of the groom, and the amount of money that was discussed. And at the end of it, the rabbi would basically contractually obligate the Hatan, the groom, by having him shake with a handkerchief per se or a pen or something that has some sort of value to it, and that would be called a Kinyan Sudar, and you'd have witnesses there, they would witness it, and they would sign that they witnessed the Hatan agreed to what was written in the Ketubah. And that was it. And in the old days, you didn't always have the Hatan sign the Ketubah. It was enough that the witnesses signed it that they witnessed this happen and he didn't have to sign. Nowadays, it's also become standard that the Hatan also signs the Ketubah. And like we said, it's just showing his obligations to his wife, and if, God forbid, in the case of divorce, it would have the amount of money that he would pay her.

Now we do see in many other communities, mainly Ashkenazi communities, they take the Ketubah and they frame it, they hang it up on the wall of the newlywed couple. This goes really against the grain of our beliefs. We have to try to bring positive energy and hope into our homes. So hanging up a Ketubah that talks about, you know, in very, very usually large numbers, okay, or larger fonts, if you will, on the Ketubah, how much he's going to pay her in the case of divorce is not a positive thing. So we don't hang it up, we basically hide it away. The Ketubah is generally given to the mother of the bride, put it away for safekeeping, and, God willing, it will never have to come out for any purpose whatsoever. We only wish congratulations and good will and good cheer, Mabrook to the bride, to the groom, and all the families involved. Mabrook.

236.title: Mourners Changing Seats on Shabbat
236.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that mourners do not come to pray in the synagogue on weekdays. However, they do come to pray in the synagogue on Shabbat. And then Maran added that those that have the custom that mourners do not change their seat in the synagogue on Shabbat are doing the right thing.

In the Bet Yosef, Maran quoted the opinion of Rabbi Yosef Ibn Habib, a Talmudic authority from Spain in the 14th and 15th centuries, who wrote that places that have the custom that mourners change their place in the synagogue if they come to pray on a weekday should also change their place when they come to pray on Shabbat, since changing one's place is not an actual mourning practice like sitting on the floor, and therefore it does not constitute a public display of mourning, which is not permitted on Shabbat. However, Maran did not agree with Rabbi Yosef Ibn Habib, who wrote this in his commentary which is known as the Nimmuke Yosef, and therefore, in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran supported the custom of those places where the mourner does not change his place on Shabbat.

The Radbaz, who was born in Spain towards the end of the 15th century and later became the Chief Rabbi of Egypt in the 16th century, disagreed with Maran and ruled like the Nimmuke Yosef, who did not consider changing seats a public display of mourning. Furthermore, Muram, an Ashkenazic authority from the 16th century, specified that their custom is that mourners do change their seat in the synagogue on Shabbat, and that the custom should not be changed.

In the 18th century, the Hida, in his book Mahzik Berakhah, wrote that there are places that have the custom that the mourners sit in a designated area on Shabbat, and that important members sit next to them for a short time, one group at a time. The Hida wrote that this custom has support from a Midrash that was quoted by the Ramban, and is also supported by the opinion of the Nimmuke Yosef and the ruling of the Radbaz. The Hida also quoted the Radbaz in his book Birke Yosef, but then continued with the opinion of the Arizal, who wrote that mourners should not change their place in the synagogue on Shabbat. The Hida's conclusion was that one should still follow the custom in a place where mourners do change their place in the synagogue on Shabbat, unless they are well known in that place as a pious person who conducts himself based on the teachings of the Arizal.

In the 20th century, Rabbi Hayyim Moshe Sethon, in his book on the customs of the land of Israel, which he called Eress Hayyim, recorded the custom of the land of Israel, which is that mourners do change their seat in the synagogue on Shabbat, and that this is an old custom dating back to before we accepted the rulings of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. The Keter Shem Tob also documented the custom of mourners changing their seats in the synagogue on Shabbat. He documented this as the custom of the land of Israel, the custom of Syria, Turkey, and Egypt, again based on the Nimmuke Yosef and the Radbaz.

What about the custom of Halab? Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that in Halab, the mourners attended the main synagogue on Shabbat and sat in a designated area which they called Shemaliyeh, which means the left side. Candles were placed in that area before Shabbat began, in honor of the mourners, and at various points in the prayers, friends and acquaintances from the congregation would stand near the mourners as a sign of comfort, either at "HaShem Melekh," or "Barukh SheAmar," or "VaYbarekh David," and then the congregants would return to their places. Afterwards, one of the mourners' relatives would receive an 'Aliyah to make a Hashkabah for the deceased, and after the prayers, the Hazzan would make another Hashkabah in front of the mourners.

The custom of mourners changing their seat in the synagogue on Shabbat was also practiced in Egypt and in North Africa, as was stated by Rabbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on in his book on the customs of Egypt, which he called Nehar Missrayim. There he explained that it's to make it known to the congregants that they should sit for a short time near the mourners as a sign of comfort. He also wrote that the congregants took turns sitting near the mourners before returning to their seats.

This custom also continued here, in Brooklyn, New York, as Meyer Safdieh, 'Alav HaShalom, wrote the following in his book on the customs of mourning, which is called Me'ir Ot: "The law in Shulhan 'Arukh is that the mourner sits in his regular seat in order not to make it known publicly that he is in mourning. Nevertheless, it is our custom that the mourner does not sit in his regular seat, but in the back row."

So even though, according to Maran and the Arizal, mourners should not change their seats in the synagogue on Shabbat, our custom is that the mourners do change their seats in the synagogue on Shabbat. In Halab, there was a designated spot for mourners on the left side of the synagogue, but here in Brooklyn, they sit in the back row. It's also customary for groups of congregants to take turns sitting near the mourners for a short period of time, and then returning to their places at various points in the prayers, such as Hodu, "HaShem Melekh," "Barukh SheAmar," and so on. Our custom is based on the opinions of the Nimmuke Yosef and the Radbaz, who did not consider sitting in a different seat an actual mourning practice. This custom was also practiced in the Land of Israel, in Egypt, and in North Africa. The Ben Ish Hai wrote in a responsa in his book Rab Pe'alim that the custom in Baghdad was that mourners change their seat in the synagogue on both weekdays and Shabbat during the 30-day mourning period. From all this, we see that the accepted custom in the Middle East, in North Africa, and among the Ashkenazim is that mourners do change their seat when they come to the synagogue on Shabbat, and this is also our custom in our community in our times.

237.title: Shofetim and the Month of Elul
237.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Yerushalayim. We are continuing with our series of videos dealing with Minhagim which are particular to specific Shabbatot and Parashiyot. We are up to Parashat Shofetim in Sefer Debarim. And as you know, this Parashah among other things deals with the appointment of a king and the laws concerning a king of Israel. And in fact, the Shelishi, also on weekdays and on Shabbat, ends with "LeMa'an Ya'arikh Yamim 'Al Mamlakhto Hu UBanav BeKereb Yisrael." A very festive occasion and national festivities, and therefore we will say Nishmat and Shahrit in Maqam 'Ajam, which is associated with very happy occasions. In fact, we say 'Ajam for a wedding, why? Because a Hatan Domeh LeMelekh, a Hatan we compare him to a king, and therefore for these occasions we sing Maqam 'Ajam.

It's interesting to note that in many countries, even Middle Eastern countries, even though 'Ajam is a very European scale, you will find the national anthem, we have for instance the Pizmon "Shir Agid" on page 167 which is "Salam el Malaki" in Egypt, it was the royal march and became the national anthem, Maqam 'Ajam.

For Nishmat we have a custom, brought down in the notes of Hakham Moshe Ashear 'Alav HaShalom, that the Pizmon they use for Nishmat is a Pizmon on page 203 which is called "Ya'arikh Yamim 'Al Mamlakhto." It's a beautiful, beautiful Pizmon, fits very nicely into the Nishmat. You can go to pizmonim.org to hear the renditions of this Pizmon and how it fits into the Nishmat from many of our Hazzanim, including our esteemed Hazzan, Mr. Isaac Cabasso, "Bore 'Olam Ya'arikh Yamav BaTob UShnotav BaNe'imim."

Shishi begins with "Ki HaGoyim HaElleh," and it ends "Hetibu Asher Dibberu." That's almost a consensus that that's where the Shishi ends. Because this is the seven weeks of Nehamah Haftarah, we don't change the Haftarah for any reason, and the Haftarah is "Anokhi Anokhi Hu Menahemkhem."

Another note is that Shofetim generally is the first week in Elul, generally speaking. And we have a Minhag that beginning with the Shabbat preceding the beginning of Selihot, which could very well possibly have been Parashat Re'eh, but certainly Shofetim, we will use a tune from the Selihot for Semehim, as usually is the case where you precede the upcoming week, the festival of the week, with the Semehim of the previous Shabbat. So here we will use the tunes from "Elekha HaShem," which is at the end of Selihot, and we know that there's many tunes that we could use for "Elekha HaShem," so we use in this case the one for 'Ajam: "Elekha Ad-onai Nasati 'Enai." So you do that for Semehim. And then every week, every Shabbat in Hodesh Elul, you will take the Maqam of that week and apply it to the Semehim using a tune from "Elekha HaShem."

Also, "VaAni Tefillati" in Hodesh Elul, we switch from the normal tunes that are used. We have four or five tunes in Rast that the Hazzanim have the option to choose whichever they want for "VaAni Tefillati," and in this case, Hodesh Elul, we switch the tune from "VaAni Tefillati" to the tune of the Selihot: "VaAni Tefillati." And that we will do that all the way through until Kippur. We will continue in our next video with the Parashiyot Ki Tesse and Ki Tabo. Kol Tub.
