238.title: When and Where the Wedding Was Held
238.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. We are talking about the wedding, and in the last episode I spoke about the Ketubah. Bringing up the Ketubah brought forward a lot of emails, a lot of questions. People want to know so many different things, and I'm happy to try to answer these questions and bring them to light and let people know what our Minhagim are.

So the main question that keeps coming up is when was the wedding done? Was it daytime? Was it nighttime? Where was it done? Was it done outdoors? Was it done indoors? Was it done in a home? Was it done in Kenis? Was it done in the rabbi's office? All different questions are coming up, all surrounding the wedding. Since we brought up the Ketubah and people associate, obviously, the Ketubah already, you know, wherever you're having the wedding, so they want to know about that first and foremost.

So first let's talk about the wedding in the sense that there was a Takkanah that you must have a Minyan, you must have ten men present to have a wedding. Without it, the wedding is invalid. That was something that was established by the Hakhamim of Halab, and we know about this from the writings of Rabbi Abulafia, one of the chief rabbis in Damascus who writes about it.

Was the wedding done daytime or nighttime? So there seems to be some sort of conflicting evidence, but I do know when I was very young and I spoke to our late chief rabbi, Rabbi Jacob S. Kassin, about weddings in general, he said when he arrived in this community, okay, approximately 1933 or so, says that the Minhag that they had was weddings were done at midnight. And he said that was the Minhag that they brought with them from Halab, and they continued to have weddings very, very late at night until slowly he was able to convince them to have it somewhat earlier. But the old Minhag was to have weddings very, very late, and he specified that it used to be at midnight.

Now, where was the wedding done? So in the old days, oh, let's talk about the new days first, okay? In modern times, it's done in the Kenis. Same way we like to do a wedding in the Kenis, in the Bet Keneset, in the synagogue, it was also done that way. And we're talking about indoors, not in the courtyard of the synagogue, not outdoors, you know, under the stars. No, inside the synagogue, like we would do it in Shaare Zion, for example.

But what was the custom in the old days? This is very interesting. As we know, nowadays, the bride's family is the one who basically pays for the wedding. And back in Halab, the wedding was actually in the home of the father of the bride. He had the wedding in his home. Everything would be prepared there, and then the Hatan, the groom, would arrive there. The wedding would actually happen in that home. After the ceremony was over, then the groom would leave. The bride would still stay with her family. The groom would leave. He would go home, he would go to his home and sit in an area that was designated to be called also the Huppah. So even though the ceremony is over, they had another designated area called Huppah in the house of the groom. He would sit down on an elevated area, like a podium, and he would wait for the Kallah, for his bride, to arrive. And when she would arrive, he would greet her by going down a step or two towards her. She would come up a step or two, and then he would help her up, and they would sit together, and the festivities would happen while they were seated. At least that's the way the festivities would start.

Also, when ceremony happened, again, back in the old days, as opposed to modern days where both the bride and groom are standing, in the old days, the groom would stand and the bride would sit. There would be a specially decorated chair, okay, like a throne, if you will, for the bride, and it would have like a crown of flowers on top of the bride, and everybody knew this was the bride's chair, and she sat there with pride, but the groom would stand to her side. The groom was always to the left of the bride. The bride was always to the right of the groom, and that's the way the weddings happen. As we get up to the wedding ceremony, we'll talk about more details about the wedding, but I hope that gives you a basic idea of where the wedding was, what time of day it was, and how things developed and changed over time. Mabrook.

239.title: The Berakhah on Mahshi and Yebraq
239.text:
In episode 233, we discussed the blessing one recites before eating Lahm Ba'ajeen, and we quoted from the book Birkat Shamayim, which was written in Halab at the end of the 19th century by Hakham Yosef Sethon, and we also quoted from the book Peri Saddik, which was written by Hakham Shaul Kassin, who was born in Halab in the year 1864, and who passed away in Jerusalem in the year 1917. Both books also discuss which blessing is recited before eating Mahshi and Yebraq. Mahshi is a vegetable, like an eggplant or squash, that is stuffed with a mixture of meat and rice.

In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote, based on the Gemara, that when a food is comprised of a combination or mixture of more than one food, that the blessing is recited on the main food in the mixture. In many cases, but not in all cases, the food which is the majority of the mixture is considered the main food.

In Hakham Yosef Sethon's description of Mahshi and Yebraq, he wrote that there is more meat than rice, but still and all he wrote that the main part of the food is the vegetable that holds the meat and rice together, and therefore in his opinion, one should recite the blessing of Bore Peri HaAdamah before eating Mahshi. Similarly, he wrote that one should recite Bore Peri HaAdamah on Yebraq, which is grape leaves rolled around a meat and rice mixture. He explained that even though grape leaves grow on a vine, and the fruit from the vine, namely grapes, is Bore Peri Ha'Ess, the leaves do not have the same status as the fruit, and therefore, the blessing on grape leaves is Bore Peri HaAdamah. He also considered the grape leaves that are holding the meat and rice mixture together to be the main part of the food, so in his opinion, one also recites Bore Peri HaAdamah before eating Yebraq. And according to Hakham Yosef Sethon, one also recites Bore Peri HaAdamah before eating Mahshi or Yebraq that was stuffed with rice and chickpeas, and which is usually cooked with butter.

However, Hakham Shaul Kassin disagreed and wrote that the main part of the Mahshi or Yebraq is the inside part. According to Hakham Shaul, if the majority of the meat and rice mixture is the meat, then you say SheHakol, but if the majority of the meat and rice mixture is the rice, then you say Mezonot. Furthermore, Hakham Shaul did not agree that the blessing on grape leaves is Bore Peri HaAdamah. He explained that since grape leaves are not eaten by themselves, but only as part of a dish that has other foods, therefore in his opinion, the blessing on grape leaves is SheHakol.

So according to Hakham Yosef Sethon, the blessing on Mahshi and Yebraq is Bore Peri HaAdamah, but according to Hakham Shaul Kassin, the blessing goes according to the majority of what's inside, and if one is not sure what the majority of the inside is, then you say SheHakol. Hakham Yosef Sethon also added that if one did say SheHakol or Mezonot on Mahshi or Yebraq, that they fulfilled their obligation, and they should not recite another blessing. Hakham Yosef Sethon also added that if you eat the outer vegetable and the inner meat and rice mixture separately, then you recite two blessings: HaAdamah on the vegetable, and SheHakol on the meat and rice mixture.

So with regards to the blessing on Mahshi and Yebraq, there is no universally accepted custom. There is a difference of opinion as to what the main part of the food is, and therefore, one fulfills their obligation whether they said HaAdamah, or SheHakol when the majority of the inside part is the meat, or Mezonot when the majority of the inside part is the rice.

240.title: Ki Tesse and Ki Tabo
240.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Rena’ana, we're on and on and we're continuing with our discussion of specific Minhagim that are done on particular Shabbatot. We're up to Shabbat Ki Tesse LaMilhamah in Sefer Debarim.

The Maqam for this week is Maqam Saba. Not sure exactly why. There are a couple of reasons offered in pizmonim.org. Maybe it has to do with the Saba as "Ki Tesse LaMilhamah," not quite sure, but it's Maqam Saba is used. But regardless, in Semehim, as we discussed in our last video, during the entire month of Elul, beginning with maybe Re'eh, it was before Rosh Hodesh, Shofetim, Ki Tesse, Ki Tabo, and till Rosh HaShanah and till Kippur, we do the tunes for Semehim from the Selihot, generally the some of the tunes we use for Elekha HaShem. So it's no different, as well as we mentioned also the "VaAni Tefillati Lekha HaShem 'Et Rasson" is done in the special tune for the Yamim Nora'im and for Hodesh Elul, VaAni Tefillati instead of the classic Rast, the other ones that we do.

The Shishi begins with "Ki Tiddor Neder," it ends "Asher Dibbarta BeFikha." The Haftarah, being that it's Shib'ah DeNehamata, is "Roni 'Akarah," it does not change.

There is a Pizmon associated with Parashat Ki Tesse. There's a Pizmon on page 389 in the Shire Shebahah of the Sefaradim. It's called Ya Eli Sur Misgabi. It's a very beautiful Pizmon, very simple, it repeats itself, simple to learn. Go to pizmonim.org and you will learn a very nice Pizmon in a short time. The reason it's connected to Parashat Ki Tesse as well as Parashat Zakhor is because there is a stanza dealing with "Zekher 'Amalek Timheh, Taf Ve'Olel," to erase all the memories of the nation of 'Amalek. And as you know, Parashat Ki Tesse, the Maftir, the end of the HaShelim is "Zakhor Et Asher 'Asah Lekha 'Amalek." And that's why we have this Pizmon, we'll sing it when we take out the Sefer.

We move on to Parashat Ki Tabo. "Ki Tabo El HaAress," it's "VeHayah Ki Tabo El HaAress," it's dealing with initially the Bikkurim that we bring our first fruit to Yerushalayim. Because anything associated with 'Aliyah LaRegel, with the pilgrimage to Yerushalayim which is done during the Shalosh Regalim, Pesah, Shabu'ot, Sukkot, we will sing Nishmat in Sigah. And it's not set in stone. We saw the notes of Hakham Moshe Ashear 'Alav HaShalom where he would sometimes do Nawa, sometimes do Saba, but our custom is to do Sigah as it has to do with the 'Aliyah LaRegel as we do for Pesah, Shabu'ot, excuse me, and Sukkot.

The Shishi begins "VaYessav Moshe," it ends "Ba'er Heteb." After the Shishi, we have the 'Aliyah of the Tokhahot and the Kelalot, the curses and the reprimands and the Musar, the Shebet Musar that we're being told what would happen, God forbid, if we don't follow in the ways of the Torah. And these 'Aliyot, it could either be 'Oleh 'Erki, an extra 'Oleh, or Samukh. It's done, it's after the Shishi.

There was a Minhag in the Kenis in Halab, Bet Keneset HaGadol, where they had Minyanim for the Sefaradim, the ones who came in the 15th-16th century, and for the Musta'arabim, the local Halabi community. And in that Minyan of the Musta'arabim, the second half of the 20th century was Hakham Salim Zafrani Zekher Saddik LiBerakhah, was the Hakham and the Hazzan for many decades in that synagogue. And he records, we have a recording of all the customs of the Minyan Musta'arabim from him, and in it he writes that in Shabbat BeHukkotai, where there's also Tokhahot, and in Ki Tabo, before the reader, the 'Oleh makes the blessing, the Hazzan says four Pesukim, two from Mishle and two from the Nabi Yirmeyah: "Musar HaShem Beni Al Tim'as, VeAl Takoss BeTokhahto, Ki Et Asher Ye'ehab HaShem Yokhiah, UKhe'Ab Et Ben Yirsseh," telling the Kahal, the person going up is, don't be, don't reject the Tokhahah and the punishments and the reproofs of Bore 'Olam, it's like a father raising his child and bringing him up. "Refa'eni Ad-onai VeErafe, Hoshi'eni VeIvvashe'ah Ki Tehillati Attah," "Yaserenni Ad-onai Akh BeMishpat, Al BeAppekha Pen Tam'iteni," praying to Bore 'Olam is to send us Refuah, and give us Yissurim, but with measure, so as not, "Al Tam'iteni," the Nabi writes.

So this custom is not found today in Brooklyn. It was the custom of the 'Arabiyeh, Musta'arabi community in Halab. We see it in some North African communities. It's not an unusual custom, although, again, we haven't seen it in Brooklyn. The Shishi, we mentioned, was Baerevtem, and the Haftarah is "Kumi Ori Ki Ba Orekh," one of the Shib'ah DeNehamata. Kol Tub.

241.title: The Wedding Ceremony in Halab
241.text:
"Yah Yahid Ram Le'Olam Le'Olam Yah."

SCA Minhag of the Week: life cycles, the wedding ceremony. So in the last episode, I spoke about the wedding the way it was in Halab, and people have asked me, when was it that way? Where did this information come from? And this is the way it was 150, 200 years ago, and is based upon the writings of Hakham Abraham Antebi. Rabbi Abraham Antebi was the chief rabbi of Halab, and he passed away in 1858. This is from a book of his called Ohel Yesharim, which he published in 1822. And we know from other sources that this is more or less the way weddings continued in Aleppo till around 1900 or so. But even by that time, things started changing, and they started having weddings in the Bet Keneset, in the synagogue. And that's the way the custom continued here in America, having the ceremony in the synagogue, differently than what way it was done prior, to have the ceremony in the home of the bride.

Now, many people think of weddings, probably all of us, and we think about the marchers, the bridesmaids, and the groomsmen. None of that existed in the past. This is something that developed later on. It is not an original custom. Even the Hazzan marching in and singing, and the rabbis marching in, none of that existed at all. In fact, there was basically one Hazzan and one rabbi for the wedding. The Hazzan's role was extremely limited, we'll talk about in a moment, and the rabbi said all the Berakhot. The Berakhot were never divvied up among various rabbis. Rabbi, rather one rabbi would say all the Berakhot, okay? Sometimes he may have another rabbi with him, and you'd let one rabbi would say the Birkat Erusin, in other words the first three Berakhot, and then the other one would say the Berakhot of the Kiddushin, which are the following seven Berakhot. There was no concept of a Hazzan saying the last Berakhah, like we see today.

So what did the Hazzan do at the ceremony? The Hazzan sang a traditional piece called Yif'atekh Tammah, and this ancient song, written by Rabbi Yisrael Najara, who was originally from Damascus, he wrote this very, very brief piece of poetry, and it was sung specifically in Aleppo, in Halab, by the Hazzan, prior to the seven Berakhot of the Kiddushin. And the only other thing the Hazzan would sing, or really get the people to sing, is after the, all the seven Berakhot were over, then he would commence the singing of "Yigdal Elokim Hai," and everybody would join in with him. That was the job of the Hazzan at the wedding. The rabbi, as we said, did the Berakhot. There are the initial three Berakhot, and then the following seven Berakhot done by the rabbi, sometimes two rabbis, one doing three, one doing seven, and that's it, like we said, not given out to other people.

But what else went on at the ceremony that was a little bit different? And we spoke in an earlier episode about the Ketubah. And nowadays we think of the Ketubah ceremony, as I mentioned there was no Ketubah ceremony in the past, when we think about a Ketubah ceremony, many of us have this image of the rabbi pulling out a handkerchief, and the groom and the rabbi shaking on this handkerchief, making a Kinyan. And the custom of the community, not only in Syria, but here in America, and I'd say even until the '70s, maybe even early '80s, it still existed that this Kinyan happened at the wedding ceremony itself.

Before making the Kiddushin, before the Hatan would tell the Kallah, "Hare At Mekuddeshet Li BeKhaspa Den KeDat Moshe VeYisrael," before saying that line of Kiddushin, okay, and handing her the coin, the rabbi would tell the groom, "Take out a handkerchief." They would hold the handkerchief together, and the Hakham would ask the groom, "Do you swear to upkeep everything that you signed to in the Ketubah prior?" And this is done in front of the witnesses under the Huppah. And if the groom says yes, they shake on that, and that is the Kinyan then and there. Okay, it happens then, and immediately after then he would say the "Hare At Mekuddeshet Li" and hand the coin to the bride.

So this is what's already shaping a little bit differently than what we've been used to today, to what was going on in our community it's only 50 years ago. So we're seeing a progression of the Minhagim of the wedding changing in the last 200 years from Aleppo, within Aleppo, and to United States, and we're still watching some changes nowadays, as we said, with the Hazzanim coming in with so many songs and we have the marchers and other things. But as we continue to talk about the Minhagim of the wedding, everything will become a little bit clearer. And please, if you have questions, you have concerns, you have things that aren't clear, send in your questions to the SCA, and we'll be more than glad to answer them. Mabrook.

242.title: Omitting Hoshi'enu on Fridays
242.text:
The Mishnah in Masekhet Tamid listed which Mizmor from Tehillim was recited by the Leviyyim in the Bet HaMikdash each day of the week. HaRambam wrote that some have the custom to recite the Mizmor that was recited that day in the Bet HaMikdash each morning in the prayers after reciting the supplications. HaRambam wrote this in the order of the prayers that is part of his book Mishneh Torah.

In the first Siddur printed in Spain in the year 1490, the verses that begin with Hoshi'enu are printed after the daily Mizmor. The verses that begin with Hoshi'enu are also found after the daily Mizmor in two old Italian Siddurim from the same time period. Interestingly, we do not find the daily Mizmor or Hoshi'enu in the famous Mahzor Aram Soba that was printed in the year 1527. In some old Italian Siddurim, the daily Mizmor is found without Hoshi'enu afterwards. Since that time, it has become customary to recite the daily Mizmor followed by Hoshi'enu.

Hoshi'enu begins with a prayer for the redemption. Ribbi Moshe Cordovero, a prominent Kabbalist who lived in the city of Sefat in Israel in the 16th century, explained that Hoshi'enu is recited after the daily Mizmor since we just recited the Mizmor that was recited in the Bet HaMikdash on that day, so it's appropriate to continue with a verse asking for the redemption, which would bring back the recitation of the daily Mizmor in the Bet HaMikdash once again.

According to some Siddurim, Hoshi'enu was recited every day after the Mizmor, including Friday. According to other Siddurim, Hoshi'enu was recited every day after the Mizmor except on Friday. According to the first Siddur printed in Spain, and an old Siddur printed in Italy, both of which were printed in the year 1490, Hoshi'enu is recited on Fridays. And according to the Siddur of the Rashash, and the Siddur of Ribbi Hayyim HaKohen MeAram Soba, and also according to the Siddur of Ribbi Moshe Zacut, Hoshi'enu is recited on Friday. However, there are other Siddurim that omit Hoshi'enu on Friday, including a Siddur printed in Venice in the year 1528, and by several Ashkenazic Siddurim that are based on the Nusah of the Arizal or on Nusah Sefarad.

In the book Keter Shem Tob, it says that the custom of the Sefaradim in Aram Soba and in all of Syria is to omit Hoshi'enu on 'Ereb Shabbat, meaning on Friday mornings, and on 'Ereb Yom Tob. He explained that since Hoshi'enu is a prayer for the redemption, and the Gemara in Masekhet 'Erubin taught that the Mashiah won't come on a Friday or on 'Ereb Yom Tob, since the Jewish people are busy preparing for Shabbat or for the holiday on those days, therefore, Hoshi'enu is not recited on 'Ereb Shabbat or on 'Ereb Yom Tob.

However, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo only mentioned the custom of not reciting Hoshi'enu on Fridays without any mention of omitting Hoshi'enu on 'Ereb Yom Tob as well. Similarly, the book Derekh Eress quoted Keter Shem Tob regarding the custom of omitting Hoshi'enu on both 'Ereb Shabbat and on 'Ereb Yom Tob, but then quoted Ribbi Nissim Zafrani and Hakham Edmond Cohen, who both said that Hoshi'enu is only omitted on Fridays, but that it is recited on 'Ereb Yom Tob.

Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi suggested that maybe we only omit Hoshi'enu on Friday as opposed to also omitting it on 'Ereb Yom Tob, since on Friday, we specify that the day is Friday, and then recite a Mizmor that is particular to Friday, so we don't add the prayer for Mashiah, who doesn't come on Friday. But on 'Ereb Yom Tob, we don't specify that it's 'Ereb Yom Tob, and we don't recite a Mizmor that's particular to 'Ereb Yom Tob, so we don't highlight the fact that Mashiah doesn't come on 'Ereb Yom Tob by omitting Hoshi'enu. Similarly, we don't omit other requests for the Mashiah in other parts of the prayer on Fridays, only Hoshi'enu, where we just specified that it's Friday, and recited a Mizmor that's particular to Friday.

Rabbi Antebi also offered another reason for omitting Hoshi'enu on Friday. The Mizmor on Friday concludes with the words "Le'Orekh Yamim," which means for a long time. If we would go right into Hoshi'enu after the words "Le'Orekh Yamim," it might sound like we're asking for the redemption in a long time from now. So we only omit Hoshi'enu on Fridays, when the Mizmor ends with the words "Le'Orekh Yamim," but on 'Ereb Yom Tob, that issue is not applicable.

So even though the custom in some communities is to recite Hoshi'enu after the daily Mizmor even on Fridays, the Syrian custom is to omit Hoshi'enu on Fridays. However, we do recite Hoshi'enu on 'Ereb Yom Tob, as was explained by Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi.

243.title: Nissabim, VaYelekh and Shabbat Teshubah
243.text:
Shalom UBerakhah to all of us. We are continuing with our series of videos discussing the particular Minhagim for specific Shabbatot. We are nearing the end of the Torah reading cycle for the year. We are up to Parashat Nissabim, which is followed by VaYelekh and Ha'azinu. VeZot HaBerakhah, the final Parashah of the Hamishah Humshe Torah, we will not discuss in this series because that will, we will be discussing when we speak about the holiday of Sukkot, since that is read on the final day of Sukkot, on Simhat Torah.

So, we're going to talk about Nissabim, which is often read together with Parashat VaYelekh. How do we know when we read it together and when we read it separately? So, Maran gives us a Remez, a nice Siman to remember. I think it's Shulhan 'Arukh Resh-Peh-Het, where he's discussing that we know that Ha'azinu has to be the final Parashah of the year, right? Because they're right before Sukkot, which means before Sukkot, you have to finish Parashat Ha'azinu. So, it all depends on how many Shabbatot there are between Rosh HaShanah and Sukkot. If there's one Shabbat only, of course that would be Ha'azinu, and that would be Shabbat Shubah, and Nissabim and VaYelekh would be read together before Rosh HaShanah. If, however, there are two Shabbatot remaining between Rosh HaShanah and Sukkot, one would be for Parashat VaYelekh and one would be for Parashat Ha'azinu. VaYelekh then would be Shabbat Shubah, and Nissabim would be read before Rosh HaShanah.

The Siman that he gives is "Bag HaMelekh Pat VaYelekh," based on a Pasuk in Daniel, "Patbag HaMelekh." He says when, the Siman is when Rosh HaShanah, which is referred to as HaMelekh, when Rosh HaShanah falls out on Bag, falls out on Monday or Tuesday, that means that you have two Shabbatot between Rosh HaShanah and Sukkot, so Pat VaYelekh, separate VaYelekh from Nissabim. Rosh HaShanah can also fall out on Thursday or Shabbat. In that case, there would only be one Shabbat between Rosh HaShanah and Sukkot. It would actually be Rosh HaShanah and Kippur, and that would be Parashat Ha'azinu, and therefore Nissabim and VaYelekh are read together before Rosh HaShanah. So, Monday, Tuesday, we split Nissabim before Rosh HaShanah, VaYelekh after. If Rosh HaShanah is Thursday or Shabbat, then we do Nissabim and VaYelekh together before Rosh HaShanah, and Ha'azinu at Shabbat Shubah.

Now, I wanted to, before we get into the Maqamat and the Minhagim of the tunes, I wanted to discuss the Shabbat, we, I mentioned I'll often refer now to Shabbat Teshubah or Shabbat Shubah. There seems to be two ways to pronounce this Shabbat which is between Rosh HaShanah and Kippur. One is based on the fact that it's 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah, so it would be Shabbat Teshubah, and that's the way it's recorded in the Kol Ya'akob Siddur. Or, it could be referring to the Haftarah, "Shubah Yisrael," and therefore would be Shabbat Shubah. It's tough to say exactly since we have references to both ways. It seems in today's world the Ashkenazim generally use Shabbat Shubah based on the Haftarah, and the Sefaradim basically use Shabbat Teshubah. So we'll refer to it as that, even though in the Kol Ya'akob it says Shabbat Shubah. Not Kol Ya'akob, the Pizmonim book. But it seems to be, I'm not 100% sure in Halab what they would say, it seems to be that the Shabbat Teshubah was the way they referred to it. We will discuss in our next video Nissabim and VaYelekh, the Maqamat, HaShishi, the tunes, when we use the tunes for holidays and whatnot, BeEzrat HaShem. Kol Tub.

244.title: The Five Conditions in the Halabi Ketubah
244.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week. Life Cycles. As we're talking about the marriage and we spoke about the Ketubah, we have to understand that the Ketubah is not a dry business contract of any sort. It is a living contract which has terms and stipulations in it, and there were differences from country to country, from city to city, community to community. And even though we're talking about Halab, even within Halab there were differences.

We need to understand that in Halab there were three distinct groups. You know, even though we look at Halab, Aleppo, and we think it was one community, there were three distinct communities within the community. There were the Musta'arabim, which are the ancient, indigenous, what we call Arab Jews, Jews that were there prior to the expulsion from Spain. You had the Sefaradim, those who arrived in Aleppo after the expulsions from Spain and Portugal, let's say around 1500 or so. And then you had the latest group, who were known as the Señores Francos, or plainly Francos, and later on as Frangi. They were Sefaradim, but European Sefaradim, meaning they came from Italy, mainly from Livorno and from Venice, and they arrived in Aleppo approximately between the years 1680 to 1740. Each one of these groups—the Musta'arabim, the Sefaradim, and the Francos—had their own distinct terms that they included in the Ketubah. And later on, all of these terms became the standard for the Ketubot of Aleppo. So let's see what these terms are.

The Musta'arabim had one Tenai, one condition that they had in the Ketubah. And what was that condition? The condition of the Musta'arabim that if the woman passed away without any offspring whatsoever, then the question is who inherits her portion of the Ketubah? And according to the term of the condition of the Musta'arabi community, it gets divided between the husband and her family. That's condition one.

Now we go to the Sefaradim. The Sefaradim had three conditions, three Tena'im that they put into the Ketubah. Condition one, that the man was not allowed to divorce the woman against her will. Okay? And he could only divorce once he got permission of the Bet Din. Condition two, that he could never marry a second wife while she was alive, unless he lived with her for 10 full years and she was never able to have a child. Condition number three, even if she says that she is willing to forego some of the benefits of her Ketubah—the amount of money that is coming her way or what is promised to her from his side—even if she said she's willing to forego that and she doesn't want it, she's not allowed, and he must give her everything that is stipulated in the Ketubah.

Finally, the fifth condition, and that's the condition of the Francos, that if he, the man, becomes sick with a life-threatening illness, he must immediately give her a divorce with a legal Get, and all the money stipulated in the Ketubah plus any additional moneys stipulated in the Ketubah, all must be given to her immediately before he passes away.

So now we had one condition of the Musta'arabim, three conditions of the Sefaradim, one condition of the Francos. Later on, let's say by about 1800 approximately, all of these five conditions became included in all Ketubot of the Halabi community, whether you were Musta'arabi origin, Sefaradi origin, or Franco origin. And this is what makes the Ketubah of Halab unique. Mabrook to all the brides and grooms out there.

245.title: Covering the Knives at Birkat HaMazon
245.text:
Sometimes Maran records customs in Shulhan 'Arukh, but not all these customs were necessarily observed in every Middle Eastern community. An example of this is with regards to Birkat HaMazon, when Maran wrote that it's customary to cover the knives during Birkat HaMazon, except on Shabbat and Yom Tob, when Birkat HaMazon is recited without covering the knives.

In the Bet Yosef, Maran cited the Rokeah, a 13th-century authority from Germany, the Shibbole HaLeket, a 13th-century authority from Italy, and the Rabbi David Abudarham, a 14th-century authority from Spain, as the sources for this custom. Both the Rokeah and the Abudarham provided a similar reason for this custom. The Gemara taught that a person's table serves as an atonement for him in place of an altar in times when there is no Bet HaMikdash. The Gemara learned this from a verse in the book of Yehezkel, when Yehezkel saw a vision of the altar in the future Bet HaMikdash. The verse describing the altar concluded with Yehezkel being told, "Zeh HaShulhan Asher Lifne Ad-onai," "This is the table in front of HaShem." Based on this verse that called the altar a table, the rabbis taught that our tables are like an altar that is used for atonement, and since the Torah taught that the altar may not be built with metal tools, it became customary to cover the knives after the meal while reciting Birkat HaMazon.

The Abudarham explained that since the table is like an altar that atones for sin and lengthens one's life, it's not appropriate for a knife, which could also be used as a weapon and shorten life, to be left on the table while the blessing is being recited. And according to the Abudarham and the Shibbole HaLeket, the custom is to remove the knives from the table before reciting Birkat HaMazon. However, on Shabbat and Yom Tob, when it's not permitted to build an altar, it was customary to leave the knives on the table uncovered.

Other sources provided different reasons for this custom. According to the Mekubbalim, knives must be removed from the table before Birkat HaMazon; covering them is not sufficient. And many Mekubbalim remove the knives from the table before reciting Birkat HaMazon on Shabbat and on holidays as well. However, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar wrote in his book, Yismah Yisshak VeYeranen, that it was not customary in Halab to remove knives from the table before reciting Birkat HaMazon.

So the custom of covering or removing knives from the table before Birkat HaMazon was first recorded in Germany and in Italy in the 13th century, and then in Spain in the 14th century. Maran included this custom in Shulhan 'Arukh in the 16th century, and this custom was also practiced by the Mekubbalim as well. However, the prevalent custom in Halab was to leave the knives on the table uncovered during Birkat HaMazon, whether it was a weekday, Shabbat, or a holiday. This is an example of a custom recorded by Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh that was customary in some places, but not necessarily customary in all places, and even after Maran included this custom in Shulhan 'Arukh, it did not become customary in Halab.

246.title: Nissabim, VaYelekh, Shabbat Shubah and Ha'azinu
246.text:
Shalom UBerakhah from Ra'anana, we are continuing with our series of videos discussing the particular Minhagim of specific Shabbatot. In our last video we spoke about the way to split up Nissabim VaYelekh, the times we do, the times we don't, and now we're going to talk about the specific liturgical Minhagim associated with whether we say it together or whether we say it as, we say these Parashiyot separately.

So if we are reading Nissabim VaYelekh together before Rosh HaShanah, in that case the Haftarah would be, of course, "Sos Asis," it would be the last of the seven Haftarot of Nehamah. The Maqam for the combination of Nissabim VaYelekh together is Maqam Nawa. Very often the end of each Sefer we do Maqam Nawa. Of course, when I always say Nawa, as I mentioned many times, in the New York communities that generally means they would say Nahawand. As a matter of fact, in the Shire Shebahot it's printed as Maqam Nahawand. In Israel and other communities they would say Maqam Nawa. Now this is the week before Rosh HaShanah, so we will do the Selihim in one of the tunes of the Selihot as we mentioned. The rest of the tunes are regular tunes of Nawa. The Shishi when Nissabim and VaYelekh are combined begins with "Ki Abi'ennu" and it ends by "Lammedah Et Bene Yisrael." There are other opinions, but that's the predominant opinion and the way it was printed in the Tikkun Birkat Abraham.

If we are saying, if we are reading only Nissabim, only Nissabim, and VaYelekh now becomes Shabbat Shubah, so Nissabim we would have the Haftarah of course would be "Sos Asis," and the Shishi now would be the end of Shishi "BeKhol Lebabekha UBeKhol Nafshekha," that's the predominant view. It begins with "VeNatan HaShem Elokekha." There is also another opinion which says you begin a little after, "Ki HaMissvah HaZot," and you end "BeFikha UBiLbabekha La'asoto." And again here the same applies, it would be Maqam Nawa because it is before Rosh HaShanah, and that's Nissabim alone, or Nahawand in New York.

If, however, so in that case Parashat VaYelekh now becomes Shabbat Shubah, so Parashat VaYelekh would become Maqam Muhayyar or Bayat, Huseini, that family of Maqamat associated with the High Holiday tunes, because Shabbat Shubah, all of the tunes are from the High Holidays, bar none, from Nishmat, Shav'at, El HaHoda'ot, Kaddish, across the board all of the tunes are High Holiday tunes. That is the predominant custom. There are some Hazzanim, very prominent Hazzanim, that are of the opinion that we shouldn't use the holiday tunes only on the holidays, but that BePo'al, practically, and what we've seen done for the last you know, 60, 70, 80 years, is that indeed the holiday tunes are used by a vast majority of the Hazzanim. Shabbat Shubah is actually all of the tunes, as we said. And here, of course, the Haftarah would be "Shubah Yisrael 'Ad HaShem." The, what's interesting is that Mossa'e Shabbat of Shabbat Shubah, Mossa'e Shabbat is the, not only are the tunes the holiday tunes, the Kaddish, but the entire prayer, including Barekhu, the entire prayer, 'Arbit, everything is done as if we are already in the High Holidays, it's the time between Rosh HaShanah and Kippur.

Now if there are, if we said, like we said, Nissabim and VaYelekh are separate, then Ha'azinu now is not Shabbat Shubah, it's the Shabbat before Sukkot, after Kippur, and the Maqam would be, according to the pizmonim.org and they claim, they say there that the Maqam would be Nahawand, which would make sense, Nawa, Nahawand, signifying the end of the Torah reading cycle. And in that case the Haftarah for Ha'azinu would be the song of David, and it would be "VaYedabber David LaAd-onai Et Dibre HaShirah HaZot," and that would be the Haftarah if Parashat Ha'azinu was read after Yom Kippur.

The Shishi of course and all the 'Aliyot in Parashat Ha'azinu is not dependent on Minhag; it's actually dependent on Halakhah Meforeshet. Haziv Lakh is the code, and so the Shishi for Parashat Ha'azinu would be across the board across all Jewish communities, "VeKhipper Admato 'Ammo." Another thing to mention is that the Monday and Thursday, the reading Monday, Thursday, Shabbat Minhah before Ha'azinu would also stick to the same breaks as on Shabbat. So it would be Ha'azinu until "Hu 'Asekha VaYkhonenekha," "Zekhor Yemot 'Olam" until "En 'Immo El Nekhar," and "Yarkibehu" until "VaTishkah," the way it's printed in the Kol Ya'akob. Not all communities have this custom. There are some communities, especially Ashkenazi communities, which the system of Haziv Lakh applies only on Shabbat, but we have it apply also on the Shabbat afternoon reading and the Monday and Thursday prior to Parashat Ha'azinu. Kol Tub.

247.title: The Wedding Day: Shomer and Prayers
247.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. The wedding day. What is special about the wedding day? Are there special Minhagim? Are there Minhagim that we're seeing today that were never really our Minhagim and we shouldn't be practicing them? Where did they come from, what's going on?

So, I've received quite a few texts, emails, verbal questions about the Shomer, okay? The person that watches, the guard for the Hatan and possibly for the Kallah. Do the bride and groom-to-be need somebody to watch them? Answer: no. Absolutely not. This was never our custom. It's not something that we're familiar with, and if you look at the sources, the sources all point to a watcher, a guard for the bride and groom after the wedding for that entire week.

Now, people have asked, "Well, what's going on? I've always been told that the bride needs to be watched because she's very emotional, the groom needs to be watched because he may get cold feet and run out and not show up for the wedding, and that's why we have a Shomer." That's 100% false. The sources are very clear that once a man and woman get married, they are like a king and a queen, and a king and a queen, okay, and they will remain a king and queen for that entire week, a king never goes out unescorted, never goes out without his entourage, same for the queen. And therefore, once they get married, during that week of wedding, the week of the Sheba', what we call today the week of Sheba' Berakhot, that's when they need their Shomer. That's when they need somebody to guard over them, to escort them, to be with them, to be part of their entourage. And again, it's only not for protection from themselves, rather it's protection from others who may be jealous of them and may want to hurt them. And that's where the custom comes from, but even then, we've never had such a custom. That's item number one.

Item number two: prayers on the wedding day. So, on the wedding day, as we've said in previous episode, we do not have a custom to fast, not the bride, not the groom. There may have been certain individuals, certain families who did it, but overall the custom of Sefaradim was not to fast outside of the Sefaradim of Amsterdam. Otherwise, all the Sefaradim of the Middle East have never really had this custom. And even if they did fast, they didn't change anything in their prayers. Going back to the custom of Amsterdam, as well as the custom of the Ashkenazim, those who fasted also said special prayers on that day. But what kind of special prayers? In the Minhah prayer of the day, they would add the Viddui of Yom Kippur, okay, the long Viddui. We do not have this custom. It has never been our custom. It's not something we've ever seen, not something we've ever heard of. That people tell you that that's what they do now, it's all from outside sources. It's not ours, we don't do it, there's no reason for it.

But it's a very special day for the bride and groom, and they should be praying for themselves. They should be praying to have a successful marriage, to be able to get along with one another, to be able to work things out, to be able to raise a proper family. And people should be praying on behalf of the bride and groom. And that's what always was, that prior to the wedding, you'd go to the elders of the family, you know, to get a Berakhah. You'd go to the Hakhamim of the family, the Hakhamim of the community to get a Berakhah. You'd have people bestow upon the bride and groom their well wishes.

What we see today is the exact opposite. We see people running, especially to the bride, and giving her lists of names: pray for this ill person, pray for that sick person, pray for this person who still didn't get married yet, pray for this person because she hasn't been able to have a child yet, pray for them. And instead of the bride and groom praying for themselves and taking in the glory and the specialness of that day, they end up being bogged down thinking about people's problems and trying to pray for others, instead of taking in the happiness and the Berakhot of their own day. So let's put aside these outside influences, let's focus that this day is for the Hatan and for the Kallah, and the people that care about them have to pray on their behalf, and they have to take it all in and enjoy and not be thinking about others, only be focused on themselves. And this is the day of the wedding prior to the wedding ceremony. Mabrook to all the happy couples.

248.title: Holding and Kissing the Sissit at Keri'at Shema
248.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that it's a Missvah to hold the Sissit in your left hand near your heart while reciting Keri'at Shema. This is based on a Midrash that taught that David HaMelekh would hold his Sissit in his left hand near his heart while he recited Keri'at Shema. There is also a statement in the Talmud Yerushalmi that said that one must educate their son in the Missvah of Sissit once their son knows how to hold the Sissit properly. Some understood this as referring to holding the Sissit in your hand during Keri'at Shema.

And even though the Bet Yosef quoted the opinion of Rab Natronai Gaon and Rab Moshe Gaon who objected to the custom of holding the Sissit on the grounds that it appears arrogant, since it was not a widely practiced custom in their times, Maran concluded that since it was more commonly practiced in his times, it is not considered arrogant, and therefore it is proper to hold the Sissiyot during Keri'at Shema.

In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran also mentioned the custom of looking at the Sissiyot when saying the words "UR'item Oto" in the last paragraph of Keri'at Shema, and then placing the Sissiyot over your eyes. Maran wrote that this is done to show our love for the Missvah of Sissit. And Rema also included the custom of kissing the Sissiyot after looking at them. According to Maran, you only hold two Sissiyot from the two corners that are in front of you.

However, many follow the teachings of the Arizal and gather all four Sissiyot at the end of the second blessing before Keri'at Shema when they say the words "Meherah Me'arba' Kanfot Kol HaAress," and they hold the Sissiyot in their left hand between their pinky and their ring finger, and they hold them near their heart. And when reciting the last paragraph of Keri'at Shema, which is about the Sissit, the Sissit strings are held with the right hand while the knots are still held with the left hand, and they look at the Sissit strings during the entire last paragraph of Keri'at Shema. And according to the Arizal, the Sissit strings are held continuously until the words "VeNehemadim La'ad," which is in the "Emet VeYassib" paragraph after Keri'at Shema. Furthermore, according to the Arizal, one should kiss the Sissit after placing them over their eyes at "UR'item Oto." And again, the Sissit are kissed when you say "Aharei Lebabkhem," and placed over your eyes when you say "VeAharei 'Enekhem." And according to the Arizal, the Sissit are kissed and placed over the eyes one more time when you say the words "VeNehemadim La'ad" in the "Emet VeYassib" section before letting them go.

The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer also recorded the common practice of kissing the Sissit every time the word Sissit is mentioned in the last paragraph of Keri'at Shema. The Kaf HaHayyim quoted this custom from the book Hesed LaAlafim, which was written by Rabbi Eli'ezer Papo, who lived in Bulgaria in the beginning of the 19th century.

The custom of holding the Sissit during Keri'at Shema is based on a Midrash and recorded in Shulhan 'Arukh, along with the custom of looking at the Sissit when saying "UR'item Oto" and then placing them over the eyes. However, many also observe the customs of the Arizal and kiss the Sissit after placing them over their eyes, and then kiss the Sissit and place them over their eyes again at "Aharei Lebabkhem," and then again before releasing them at "VeNehemadim La'ad" during the "Emet VeYassib" paragraph. Furthermore, some only hold Sissiyot from the front two corners of their Talet in accordance with Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh, while others hold the Sissiyot from all four corners of their Talet in accordance with the teachings of the Arizal. And lastly, it has also become customary to kiss the Sissiyot each time the word Sissit is mentioned in the last paragraph of Keri'at Shema, as recorded by the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer quoting Rabbi Eli'ezer Papo in his book Hesed LaAlafim.

249.title: The Huppah, the Talet and Yif'atekh Tammah
249.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Life Cycles, marriage. So, we've been speaking the last number of episodes about the marriage and many have asked, well, how similar or how different were wedding ceremonies in Halab or in Damascus as compared to what we're used to here in the United States? So, there's really not much different, but at the same time, there are things that are the same and things that are not the same.

So, first and foremost, the questions that have been posed to me is about marching. Obviously, marching was not anything as elaborate as we have today with so many people marching and the whole marching procedure taking a long time, or a Hazzan coming down the aisle singing. None of that existed. It was simple. You had the flower girls, if you will, throwing flowers before the bride. You had the groom marched with his parents. You had the bride marched with her parents. And that was basically it.

At the spot that the ceremony would be done, what we call today the Huppah, okay, we'll talk about that in a moment. The bride in Halab sat on a bridal throne while the groom stood. And that was generally the way the ceremony was done, with the groom standing and the bride sitting. In other places, the bride stood, but in Halab, the custom is clearly documented in many, many sources that she sat down for the ceremony. The bride was always to the right of the groom, never the opposite way, and never with anybody between them. They were always next to each other, the groom and the bride to his right. How did they face? Did they face the Hekhal with their backs to the people that were in attendance, or were they facing the people? And generally, based upon so many different pictures over a period of let's say the last 100 years or so, they faced the people.

What was the Huppah? The Huppah, interestingly enough, was, and I'll talk about what was done in Halab, what was done in Brooklyn, how things have changed in Brooklyn. So, what we know from numerous sources, what was done in Halab as opposed to other Sephardic communities where the Talet would be placed over the head of the bride and the groom after the Hatan, if the wedding was during the day, the Hatan would say the Berakhah of "LeHit'attef BaSissit." If it's a new Talet, to say Sheheheyanu, let's say make both those Berakhot. He'd wrap himself up in it and then cover the bride together with him. In Halab, weddings, as we said, were generally done at night, so only the Berakhah of Sheheheyanu would be said if it was a new Talet. But what was done in Halab was a little bit different. They had the Talet attached, all four corners, to poles. And this Talet attached to poles with four different men holding these poles and this Talet attached to the poles working as a canopy over the bride and groom.

And this is similar to what we grew up here in Brooklyn. In Brooklyn growing up, it was generally the Hatan would make the Berakhah of the Talet, let's say it was just Sheheheyanu because at night it was a new Talet, and then the father of the bride, the father of the groom, and usually, you know, either a brother or an uncle from each side would hold the corners of the Talet over the bride and groom, and it was not put down over the bride and groom's heads as we see commonly today. So, this Talet was held above the heads of the bride and groom as opposed to on top of the heads of the bride and groom. And this is the general way that it was. Sometimes you would have a double application with the bride and groom having a Talet over them as well as the additional Talet canopy above their head, but generally it was just the Talet canopy above their head. Here in Brooklyn, as I said, it used to be carried in four corners. In Halab it was attached to poles and carried that way. Approximately 1985, it started changing here in Brooklyn to the way we know it today, with it placed over the head of the bride and groom, and that was a custom that was done in many other communities, but not in the Syrian communities. In Damascus they also held it on top of the bride and groom, from the holding from four corners. And in fact, during the Berakhot, they would shake the Talet and not keep it stationary, and that was to lighten the mood and to make everybody, you know, there joyous and invite them to participate. Okay, I shook a little bit, you come and you grab the corner now and you get involved in the ceremony as well and shake the Talet a little bit to give a little bit of merriment and joy to the bride and groom.

Now, besides what we talked about, facing the bride facing the people as opposed to their backs to the people, and the way the Talet was placed, we have a Berakhah of Besamim. We have two different sets of Berakhot said at the wedding. We have the Berakhah of the, Berakhot rather, of the Erusin and of the Kiddushin. The Erusin are the first Berakhot before the Talet, and then the Kiddushin are the Berakhot after the Talet, or the Berakhot Nissu'in sometimes referred to. In any case, during those first two Berakhot, we add, in our community, a Berakhah of Besamim. After HaGefen, we make a Berakhah of Besamim, and it seems that this is a very old custom. It's mentioned by the Abudarham in the name of HaRambam. And if you look in the Yemenite sources, which are very, very scrupulous in upholding the practices of HaRambam, they also have this Berakhah of Besamim, but as opposed to doing it in the Erusin Berakhot, they do it after the HaGefen of the Kiddushin Berakhot.

Also, as we said, there was no singing per se during the ceremony except for this one ancient song, ancient approximately 500 years old we've now discovered, but still a very, very old song written by Rabbi Yisrael Najara. It's called "Yif'atekh Tammah." Here is a very, very old handwritten manuscript Pizmon book from Halab, written by Hakham Shaul Al-Abyad in Halab in the year 1866. And here we have the song "Yif'atekh Tammah." And this song has been reproduced in our Pizmon book, the Red Book, Shir UShbahah Hallel VeZimrah. And this was the only song that was sung at the ceremony itself, and it was sung before the Sheba' Berakhot. So in other words, after the Hatan would make the Berakhah of the Talet, and the Talet would either be put over his head or used as a canopy, the Hazzan would sing this one song called "Yif'atekh Tammah." And I'll sing just the first few words. "Yif'atekh Tammah Mebish Hammah Mahpir Yareah." It's a very, very old, ancient tune, but it awoke in the people and in the Hatan VeKhallah the glory and the Kedushah, the holiness of this moment. And that's what the Kiddushin is. It is, you're going into Kedushah, you're going into holiness. It's holy matrimony as referred to in American society, and according to the Torah, it is truly holy, and you feel the Kedushah with this beautiful ancient song. It's a song that was sung until very recent years in Halab, and it's something that we need to bring back, we need to uphold, and we need to pass down to future generations as well. Mabrook to all the happy couples.

250.title: Banging for Haman at the Megillah
250.text:
In the Bet Yosef, Maran quoted the Orhot Hayyim, which was written in Provence, a region in southern France in the early part of the 14th century. Orhot Hayyim recorded the custom in France that children would bang rocks or pieces of wood with Haman and his children's names written on them whenever Haman's name was mentioned during the reading of the Megillah. They did this to erase Haman and his children's names, meaning the names that they wrote on the rocks or wood would get erased by repeatedly banging them together. This custom is based on a Midrash on the verse about wiping out the memory of 'Amalek, which taught that their memory should even be erased from wood and from stones.

In 14th-century Spain, Ribbi David Abudarham also recorded this as the custom in France. However, he quoted an earlier source known as Sefer HaManhig, which was written in Provence in the 12th century. Both the Sefer HaManhig and the Orhot Hayyim also supported this custom with the verse in Mishle, "VeShem Resha'im Yirkab," the name of wicked people shall rot. Interestingly, in the Bet Yosef, Maran added that one should not make fun of customs, since they were not established without reason. And this custom of France is based on the verse "VeShem Resha'im Yirkab" from the book of Mishle.

In Italy in the 13th century, the book Shibbole HaLeket described the custom as banging their feet, or banging two rocks, or even banging pots when Haman or Zeresh were mentioned. Later in the 16th century in Poland, Muram suggested that originally rocks or pieces of wood with Haman's image or name written on them were banged together by the children to erase Haman, but not during the reading of the Megillah. However, eventually, due to confusion, the custom evolved to banging the wood or the rocks during the reading of the Megillah.

There were also authorities who opposed the custom of banging during the reading of the Megillah because it prevents people from hearing every word of the Megillah and properly fulfilling their obligation to hear the reading of the Megillah. These authorities included Ribbi Yisrael Ya'akob Algazi from Izmir, Turkey in the 18th century, Ribbi Abraham Palachi from Izmir, Turkey in the 19th century, and Ribbi Refael Meir Panigel, who was the Rishon LeSiyyon in Jerusalem at the end of the 19th century.

In the beginning of the 20th century, Ribbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on, who was the Chief Rabbi of Egypt, reported that the custom in Egypt was that the children only banged when the reader read the ten sons of Haman. And after they finished banging, the reader would repeat the ten sons of Haman in one breath. And the only other time that the children banged was after the Megillah reading, when they said "Arur Haman," and that was it. This was recorded in his book on the customs of Egypt, Nehar Missrayim.

The book Keter Shem Tob said that the custom was for both adults and children to bang when the reader read "Haman HaRa' HaZeh," a second time for the ten sons of Haman, and then a third time after the reading of the Megillah for "Arur Haman." According to the Keter Shem Tob, the custom in the Middle East was that the children used wooden noisemakers, the adults banged with their feet, and the elderly would bang the wooden piece that holds the Megillah.

What was the custom in Halab? Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca quoted Hakham Yisshak Tawil saying that in Halab, they only banged with their feet, and they didn't use any noisemakers or anything else to bang. Similarly, in Hakham Yisshak Chehebar's times in Argentina, they would bang lightly with their feet both when 'Amalek was read from the Torah and when Haman was read from the Megillah. And even for Haman, they didn't bang every time Haman's name was read, only the first three or four times. And again, it was only banging with their feet. They did not use any other types of noisemakers.

So the custom of banging during the reading of the Megillah began in France around the 12th century and was practiced by the children. Eventually, the custom spread to other places, including to Middle Eastern communities. In some places, adults also participated in the custom by banging their feet or even the wooden holder of their Megillah. In Halab, the custom was only to bang with their feet and in a manner that was not so disruptive, allowing everyone to properly fulfill their obligation of hearing the reading of the Megillah.

251.title: Consecrating the Marriage with a Silver Coin
251.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. We're on the marriage ceremony, we're up to the consecration of the marriage. So after the initial first three Berakhot, the Seder Erusin, the betrothal, you have HaGefen, and Besamim, and the Berakhah of "Mekaddesh 'Ammo Yisrael 'Al Yede Huppah VeKiddushin." After that point, we have the point where the groom consecrates the marriage, okay, by telling the bride, "Hare At Mekuddeshet Li," "Behold, you are sanctified unto me." This sanctification, this consecration, how was it done? What was used? What was said?

So, overall, the Jewish world, both Ashkenazim and Sefaradim, use a ring, usually a silver ring or a gold ring, depending on different customs. According to the Zohar, it needs to be a ring, it needs to be a silver ring, it has to be round, there's all different things. But if you go back to earlier sources, if you go back to the Mishnah, to the Gemara, to the Rishonim, we see early on that the initial custom, this consecration was done with silver, and not just silver, but with a silver coin.

And this is still, in fact, the Minhag of the Halabi community. It was the Minhag in Halab, as attested to by various manuscript documents, and it was the Minhag that was carried from Aleppo to the shores of the United States by those Aleppian immigrants. It's a custom that remained here, and it's the only Halabi community that has held on to this custom of using a silver coin. If you go to Mexico, to Argentina, or Panama, or Yerushalayim, or any place where there's a Halabi community, they're not as strict as doing the wedding ceremony with a coin. The Halabi community in Brooklyn has held on to it, and he would use a silver coin.

This is a 1922 American silver peace dollar. This is typical of what would be used in the community for many, many years. Obviously, older coins or newer coins, but something that has value to it, that immediately upon seeing it, you could tell that it has worth and value to it. And the custom, as we said, in Halab, instead of saying "Hare At Mekuddeshet Li BeTaba'at Zo," okay, with this ring, rather they would say "Hare At Mekuddeshet Li BeKhaspa Haden," with this silver coin.

Now, as we know, when we say this formula at the wedding ceremony today, we translate it: "Hare," "Hare," "At," "At," okay, the Hakham will tell the words to the groom to say it, and then once he says it in the Hebrew-Aramaic mix, he will then repeat it in the lingua franca. In the United States it would be English, in the Middle East it was done in Arabic, whatever language the bride would understand.

Something also that we see nowadays is the changing of this language. Growing up, it was, "Behold, you are sanctified unto me with this coin according to the law of Moses and Israel." Later on, it started making some changes based upon various rabbis that joined the community, and now we're more or less at the version of, "Behold, you are sanctified unto me with the silver of this coin according to the law of Moshe and Yisrael." So even though the wording has changed in English, the meaning is still the same. But it remains a coin: "BeKhaspa Haden."

Also what we see nowadays at weddings, and this is already going on for at least 30 years, maybe a little bit longer, before he does this consecration, you hear the rabbis whispering among themselves, "Shaveh Perutah? Shaveh Perutah? Shaveh Perutah?" Is it worth a Perutah? Does it have the value of a Perutah? A Perutah is about three cents in today's American monetary system. So that's why a well-known silver coin, the monetary value is well-known, and when it's an older coin, you know it's worth more than the actual dollar that it is, there was no question that it's Shaveh Perutah, and that question was never asked in the past. It was always known: he has a silver coin, he showed it to the Hakham before the wedding ceremony, everybody knows that the value was there, and that's what was used, and so you didn't hear anybody saying, "Shaveh Perutah? Shaveh Perutah? Yes, Shaveh Perutah." No, it would just automatically take the coin, "Hare At Mekuddeshet Li BeKhaspa Haden KeDat Moshe VeYisrael," say it in English, it was handed to her, placed in the palm of her hand.

Ceremony of the consecration of the sanctification is done, and that is our custom here in the community, it's been going on long and strong in the United States for 120 plus years, and inshallah all the people that get married this way will have beautiful weddings. Mabrook.

252.title: Pouring Wine for the Ten Plagues
252.text:
When reading the Haggadah, it has become customary to pour out a drop of wine for each one of the ten plagues. The one who is leading the reading of the Haggadah begins pouring out drops of wine from his cup into a bowl or a pot just before reading the ten plagues, in the paragraph that ends: "Dam, VaEsh, VeTimrot 'Ashan." He pours out one drop for each, meaning three drops. And then, when reading the ten plagues, he pours out another drop for each: "Dam, Sefarde'a, Kinim, 'Arob, Deber, Shehin, Barad, Arbeh, Hoshekh, Makkat Bekhorot." And then three more drops for each part of the acronym: "Dessakh, 'Adash, Be'ahab," for a total of 16 drops.

It is customary to pour the entire cup of wine for the 16 drops, and then discard the wine either by pouring it down the drain or even by flushing it down the toilet, and the cup itself is rinsed out as well.

The custom was originally practiced in Germany in the 12th century and recorded by Rabbi El'azar MiGarmeiza in his book Sefer HaRokeah. The original custom was to flick drops of wine with your finger. Some used their pinky, others used their ring finger, while others used their pointer to flick drops of wine. That's how the custom was recorded by Muram as well, in his notes that are appended to Shulhan 'Arukh, and that is still the prevalent custom among most Ashkenazim.

Middle Eastern Jews adopted the custom after it was embraced by the Mekubbalim, including Rabbi Hayyim Vital, a student of the Arizal, who lived in the 16th century. The custom of Middle Eastern Jews is to pour drops of wine from a cup, as opposed to flicking drops of wine with their finger. This is also based on the teachings of the Mekubbalim. Some have the custom to bring a separate cup in order to pour the 16 drops, while others use their own cup and just refill it after rinsing it out.

Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi wrote that some families have the custom to say "Rahmana Lisslan," which means "HaShem save us," after each plague, including the three at the beginning and the three acronyms at the end, and that it was more common for the women to say "Rahmana Lisslan" than it was for the men.

What is the reason for this custom? Some explain that the 16 drops allude to an angel who is the spiritual equivalent of a 16-pronged sword that HaShem used to punish the Egyptians, and that pouring wine, which represents salvation, is a symbolic way to ask HaShem for protection from these kinds of plagues for the Jewish nation.

This custom of pouring drops of wine for each plague is based on the original Ashkenazic practice of flicking drops of wine with your finger. Subsequently, the Mekubbalim taught that the drops of wine should be poured from a cup, and that's how the custom was adopted by Middle Eastern Jewry. Since the wine that was poured is associated with the plagues, it has become customary to dispose of the wine completely after pouring out an entire cup of wine for the 16 drops.

253.title: Speeches, Birkat Kohanim, Songs and Prayers
253.text:
SCA, Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. Continuing with the wedding ceremony, many people have asked about four specific topics, and they are speeches, Birkat Kohanim, songs, and prayers.

So speeches, traditionally, speeches were never made at a wedding ceremony. Speeches were generally done by the Hatan Bar Missvah at his Bar Missvah on Shabbat in the Bet Keneset, but they were traditionally never made at a wedding ceremony. Speeches at a wedding ceremony in our community exists for over half a century here in the United States, but just keep in mind they were never traditionally done in the old country. As far as new custom that we're seeing today that various rabbis, or more than one rabbi I should say, are making a speech as well as possibly father of the bride or father of the groom, this is something we've never heard of before. And at times it can become one-sided, and sometimes too much praise is thrown on one side and the other side is forgotten about, so keep those things in mind.

Let's go to Birkat Kohanim. Birkat Kohanim, we see it frequently at the end of the wedding ceremony. Birkat Kohanim was never done in Halab, nor was it done in almost every Middle Eastern Sephardic community, Birkat Kohanim was not done at the wedding ceremony. The one exception is the Moroccan community. The Moroccan community would say Birkat Kohanim prior to the reading of the Ketubah, but it was not our custom. How it got into our community, when it got into our community, I've yet to figure out.

Also the recitation of the Pasuk from Rut, "Yitten Ad-onai Et HaIshah HaBa'ah El Betekha," etc., never concludes the entire Pasuk, but rather they end with the two words "Va'Aseh Hayil." And sometimes you'll hear certain people saying "Va'Asu Hayil," but the Pasuk is "Va'Aseh Hayil."

Also we're seeing them call people up, various Kohanim that are related to either side, calling them up from the crowd to come up to say Birkat Kohanim. Growing up, we didn't see anybody being called up. The Hakhamim themselves, the rabbis, would recite Birkat Kohanim for the bride and the groom, and that would be sufficient. And if there was a Kohen there, so he'd also put his hands up, but you wouldn't hear him because many times possibly a regular family member or friend is not proficient in the words and can make a mistake. The rabbis that know the words of the Berakhah, they make the Berakhah clearly, pronouncing each and every letter properly without any mistakes, the same thing for the Pasuk from Rut. And that's the way it should be done, if at all.

As far as Pizmonim, as I mentioned in episode 249, the only traditional Pizmon said at the wedding in Halab was Yif'atekh Tammah, no other songs. Nowadays, we hear all different types of songs. We not only hear songs, we're hearing Israeli love songs, and sometimes we even see guest singers, not even Hazzanim, but singers are brought in from the outside to sing a song and to turn it into a love fest, if you will. The wedding is Kedushah, it's Birkat Kiddushin, and we have to keep that holiness of the Bet Keneset and of the wedding ceremony. So the songs should be appropriate to the Kiddushin.

Finally, prayers. As I've said before, prayers were never recited by the bride and groom as the ceremony would be going on. They had to pay close attention to the Berakhot. But nowadays, not only is the bride and/or the groom saying prayers and they're swaying back and forth and shaking and really not paying attention to the wedding ceremony, but even they have cards out for the guests sitting in their seats to also say an array of various prayers for all different types of situations. This is something we never heard of before, something that we've never seen before, don't know where it came from and how it infiltrated our community. There's a time and place for everything, and keep that in mind. Prayer is for time and place of praying, and a wedding is time and place for a wedding. Don't mix up the two, they don't really go hand in hand with one another.

Keep our weddings traditional, keep them beautiful, give them the Kedushah, give them the holiness and sanctity they deserve and the proper respect and decorum, and Mabrook to all the happy couples.

254.title: Slanted or Straight Mezuzot in Halab
254.text:
There is a difference of opinion between Rashi and Rabbenu Tam regarding the positioning of a Mezuzah on a doorpost. According to Rashi, the Mezuzah is affixed standing straight on the doorpost, like this. According to Rabbenu Tam, the Mezuzah is affixed horizontally to the doorpost, like this. HaRambam's ruling concurs with Rashi, that the Mezuzah should be affixed vertically to the doorpost. And in Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran ruled like HaRambam and Rashi, that the Mezuzah is affixed in a straight, upright position on the doorpost. However, Muram quoted the opinion that those that are meticulous affix the Mezuzah in a slanted position in order to fulfill their obligation according to both opinions.

Normally, the Sephardic and Middle Eastern custom is to follow Maran, which in this case would be to affix the Mezuzah to the doorpost in a straight, upright position, and the Ashkenazic custom would be to follow Muram and affix the Mezuzah in a slanted position. And in this case, the Ben Ish Hai and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alehem HaShalom, both wrote that the Mezuzah should be affixed vertically in the upright position. And the common practice among Ashkenazim today is to affix the Mezuzah in a slanted position.

However, Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi asked Hakham Yisshak Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, about the custom in Halab regarding the positioning of the Mezuzah, and Hakham Yisshak told him, "Mezuzot BaAlakhson, Kakhah Hayah BeHalab." Mezuzot were slanted, that's how it was in Halab.

Similarly, Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya, a rabbi who was born in Halab at the end of the 19th century and later moved to Jerusalem, wrote in his responsa Yaskil 'Abdi regarding whether the Mezuzah should be straight or slanted, the custom is to put it slanted in order to fulfill your obligation according to all opinions in accordance with the words of Rama. Rabbi Hedaya was referring to the notes appended to Shulhan 'Arukh by Rabbi Moshe Isserles, who lived in Poland in the 16th century.

Interestingly, another rabbi, Rabbi Yisshak Alfiah, who was also born in Halab and then moved to Jerusalem, wrote the following in his book, Kunteres HaYehi'eli: "and Mezuzot are affixed straight, on a slant, and on a diagonal, with the top of the Mezuzah, which is Shema, tilting inwards, and the bottom of the Mezuzah tilting outwards." So he mentions both options, straight and slanted, without specifying exactly who observes which custom.

Based on the sources that we mentioned earlier, it seems some Middle Eastern Jews followed Maran and put it up in the straight position, while other Middle Eastern Jews put it up on a slant in accordance with what was added by Muram. In fact, in some places, there were those who put it up straight and others who put it up slanted, meaning in some places there was not one custom practiced by the entire city. Other Middle Eastern sources that record the custom of affixing the Mezuzah on a slant include the Ma'aseh Rokeah, who lived in the 18th century in Izmir, Turkey, and later in Tripoli; the Nehar Missrayim, who was the chief rabbi of Egypt at the beginning of the 20th century; and the book Keter Shem Tob, which recorded and discussed Middle Eastern customs in the 20th century.

Growing up in the community, the common practice was to put Mezuzot up in the slanted position. It only became common to put Mezuzot up in the straight position during the last 30 or 40 years. I clearly remember visiting our former chief rabbi, Hakham Shaul Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom, and even until the very end of his life, the Mezuzot were always in the slanted position. This is consistent with Hakham Yisshak Tawil's account of the custom in Halab.

So while the general rule in Halab was to follow Maran, there were exceptional cases where they did not follow Maran. In this case, the custom developed in accordance with the opinion cited by Muram.

255.title: Breaking the Glass
255.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. The end of the wedding ceremony. At the end of the wedding ceremony, we have a practice of breaking a glass, or breaking a cup, or breaking something. What's going on, what is broken, why is it broken, where does it come from, etc.?

So, at this heightened moment of joy, where a man and woman are coming together, as happy as they are, something is still lacking, and what is lacking is Yerushalayim, Jerusalem rebuilt in its entirety with the Bet HaMikdash. And no matter how happy we are, we still are mournful over the incompleteness of Jerusalem today. Therefore, at the end of this wedding ceremony, so we don't think that our celebration's complete, we break a glass.

Now there are those that have had the custom in the past to break something less expensive, like think of it as a small earthenware Turkish coffee cup, and that was in fact the custom in Baghdad, Iraq, like the Ben Ish Hai tells us, but that's not our custom. Our custom is to use glass. And usually it would be the glass that was used to make the Berakhot on the wine at the wedding ceremony. Nowadays, we know we have caterers, and a glass is set up beforehand, it's wrapped up in a napkin so no shards get, you know, strewn around when the glass is broken, or it doesn't go, God forbid, into the person's shoe, through, you know, through his shoe to his foot. So, that's already set up, laid aside, and ready to be broken, but it still remains as glass, and that's what we use.

And when the groom is ready to break that glass, he says the words of the two Pesukim in Tehillim. He says: "Im Eshkahekh Yerushalayim Tishkah Yemini, Tidbak Leshoni LeHikki Im Lo Ezkerekhi, Im Lo A'aleh Et Yerushalayim 'Al Rosh Simhati." Now, since many do not know all those words by heart, so the rabbi will say a couple of words, the groom will repeat after him, etc., etc., until the entire two verses are said. When he completes them, he will break the glass with his right foot.

Now, as we said, this is to remind us of our mournful feeling for Yerushalayim. The problem is, is that people don't realize it, and immediately when he breaks this glass, people start yelling, and screaming, and cheering, "Mazal Tob," "Siman Tob," "Mabrook," and you see everybody's glowing and radiant. Whereas, the ancient custom, and not so ancient, it was still going on in Yerushalayim less than a hundred years ago, that when the Hatan, the groom would finish those Pesukim and he would break the glass, those in attendance would also say "Im Eshkahekh Yerushalayim Tishkah Yemini," okay? They would also say it, and repeat it, and remind themselves. Obviously, they're going to tell the guy, and the, you know, the bride and the groom, they're going to tell them "Mabrook" after, and they're happy for them, but at that moment, that solemn feeling was in the air.

Nowadays, we see even more than this, and it's become a problem where we have Hazzanim, we have singers, we have guest appearances, you know, of performers coming in to sing Im Eshkahekh with special tunes, and music, and what have you, and in fact, it turns, it flips the whole meaning of saying Im Eshkahekh to something that it's not meant to be, and it turned into a joyous occasion, and as people are walking out of the ceremony, "Wow, did you hear that performance? Did you hear what he did? What an incredible music!" According to many sources, we're not even allowed to listen to music at all since the destruction of Yerushalayim, and so here we're combining the destruction of Yerushalayim, the remembrance of it with breaking glass, but we're using music, and we're using song, so it's basically one confusion of emotions and thoughts. So our custom was to never to have Im Eshkahekh sung by anyone at all. The, just the verses were said by the groom, he'd break it, and they'd walk out.

Nowadays, on top of that, it seems that this broken glass has turned into some sort of memento, or for some others, into a magical potion where they have to keep it, and they have to hide it, and they have to gather it, and some people use it as a good luck charm to put it under a single woman's bed to bring her good luck to get married, while others take it and they turn it into a Mezuzah to hang up in the bride and groom's new home or apartment, some will turn it into a decorative piece to put it on their bookshelf. We never had any of these customs.

In fact, looking at the sources, after this cup was broken, it would be buried, so we could take this memento of the destroyed Yerushalayim and we could bury it under the ground and leave it there with the, what you call, the pieces of Yerushalayim, which are also destroyed and buried under the ground. And so, God willing, BiMherah BeYamenu, speedily in our days, we will see the rebuilding of Yerushalayim and the Bet HaMikdash, and all couples and all families will only know joy and happiness. Mabrook.
