256.title: Birkat Kohanim in Parashat Naso
256.text:
The custom in many Middle Eastern communities is to read until the end of the verses of Birkat Kohanim, the priestly blessing, for 'Aliyat Kohen, when reading Parashat Naso, on Shabbat. This makes the first 'Aliyah of Parashat Naso a total of 87 Pesukim. This was documented as a custom of the land of Israel by Rabbi Hayyim Ben Minasheh Setihon, in his book Eress Hayyim, in the year 1908. This was also recorded as a custom of Safed and Gibraltar by the Keter Shem Tob. Other places that practice this custom include Morocco, Tunisia, Baghdad, Egypt, and Damascus.

What about Halab? Was it also customary to read 'Aliyat Kohen until the end of the verses of Birkat Kohanim in Halab? In the year 1974, Mr. Sam Catton, 'Alav HaShalom, an important community leader at that time, sent a letter to Hakham Moshe Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, who had been the Chief Rabbi of Halab in the 1930s, and later went to live in Israel. In his letter, Mr. Catton inquired about the custom of Halab with regards to reading 'Aliyat Kohen until the end of Birkat Kohanim in Parashat Naso.

Here is a copy of the letter that Mr. Catton received in response from Hakham Moshe Tawil. The letter is dated the 28th of Sivan in the year 5734, which is June 18th, 1974 on the secular calendar. Hakham Tawil responded that reading Kohen until the end of Birkat Kohanim was never the custom in Halab at all, and that their custom goes back for many generations. He then added that new teachers who came to Halab in recent times from Europe tried to introduce that custom, but the rabbis rejected the change and maintained their original custom.

So if Birkat Kohanim is not part of 'Aliyat Kohen, which 'Aliyah was it read for in Halab? If you look at the relatively new community Tikkun, Birkat Abraham, which marks the 'Aliyah stops in accordance with the traditions of Halab, you will see that the verses of Birkat Kohanim are read for 'Aliyat Shishi. In fact, the verses of Birkat Kohanim is all that is read for 'Aliyat Shishi according to the tradition of Halab. And if you look in the back of the Tikkun, you will find a chart which shows how the 'Aliyot were broken up for each Parashah by various Halabi rabbis. If you look in Parashat Naso, you will find that reading Birkat Kohanim as 'Aliyat Shishi, is based on the 'Aliyah stops of Hakham Ya'akob Kassin, Hakham 'Ezra Mishanieh, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, and Hakham Yom Tob Yedid, 'Alehem HaShalom.

This is consistent with the custom of Halab of selecting a very important part of the Parashah for 'Aliyat Shishi, as 'Aliyat Shishi is considered the most important 'Aliyah according to the teachings of the Mekubbalim. And when we read Birkat Kohanim for 'Aliyat Shishi, it is not necessary to only send up a Kohen for that 'Aliyah. As we said, 'Aliyat Shishi is considered an important 'Aliyah, and therefore it is always customary to send up an important person for 'Aliyat Shishi. Similarly, with Parashat Naso, we send up an important person for 'Aliyat Shishi, but not necessarily a Kohen, even though Birkat Kohanim is being read.

So even though many, if not most Middle Eastern communities read the verses of Birkat Kohanim as part of 'Aliyat Kohen in Parashat Naso, the custom in Halab was to read the verses of Birkat Kohanim for 'Aliyat Shishi. This custom was continued by our community in New York by Hakham Ya'akob Kassin and Hakham 'Ezra Mishanieh, and in Argentina by Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, and most recently this custom was perpetuated by our new community Tikkun, Birkat Abraham.

257.title: Defending ULe'Alme in Kaddish
257.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, special edition. This edition is regarding defending our traditions. "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya Yitbarakh."

Recently, a video came out based upon a book from Israel talking about the custom of Aleppo in the words of Kaddish. According to the Mekubbalim, those seven words, "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya," have to have a total of 28 letters. Now the question came up as to how to spell the words to have 28 letters, and there are two words in question: Shemeh, the second word, and ULe'Alme, the sixth word. If you put a Yod in Shemeh, then you cannot put ULe'Alme, you have to put Le'Alme. But if you omit the Yod from Shemeh, the second word, then you make the sixth word with a Vav, ULe'Alme. The prevalent custom in our community, and I will show that is a custom going back a very long time, is ULe'Alme with the Vav, and therefore Shemeh without a Yod, which has its sources within the Tanakh, within our Bible. But according to Mekubbalim, certain kabbalists, Shemeh must have a Yod, and therefore we have to omit the Vav from Le'Alme, from ULe'Alme and make it Le'Alme.

So let's talk first about the word ULe'Alme. We know that we say the Pasuk in Az Yashir, "Ad-onai Yimlokh Le'Olam Va'Ed," and immediately afterwards, we have the Targum, the Aramaic translation that says "Ad-onai Malkhuteh Ka'em Le'Alam ULe'Alme 'Almaya." So we know based upon the Aramaic Targum, the Aramaic translation, it's ULe'Alme.

If we look throughout the book of Daniel, the book of Daniel is the source for our knowledge of the Aramaic language outside of the Targum. It shows us the words, it shows us usage, it shows us grammar. We know that words throughout that are similar to Shemeh or like Shemeh, and there are many of them like them, for example we have Ukashreh, LeBeteh, Shemeh, 'Ammeh, Rasheh, Rumeh, Hakimeh, Malkhuteh, Shulkhaneh, etc., all of them, without exception, are written throughout the book of Daniel without a Yod. So therefore, according to the laws of the Aramaic language, we know Shemeh should not have a Yod, and ULe'Alme should have a Vav. And therefore, the text that I have above the line, these two lines over here, are our text in the majority of our Siddurim, and this is our prevalent custom. Whereas according to Mekubbalim and many Siddurim coming out of Israel, you will see the text this way with the added Yod over here and without the Vav over there.

So what's our custom? What's it based upon? Is it really our custom? Is it not our custom? Where did the custom develop from to have the Yod in Shemeh and to remove or omit the Vav from ULe'Alme and say Le'Alme? So the main proponents of the kabbalistic movement in the Kaddish over here are three people, mainly Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, Rabbi Yosef Hayyim the Ben Ish Hai, and Rabbi Ya'akob Hayyim Sofer the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer. These three sources, and these are very important Sephardic sources, all say to follow the Kabbalah and omit ULe'Alme and say Le'Alme, and therefore you're making Shemeh with a Yod. But according to Shulhan 'Arukh, Shulhan 'Arukh is very, very clear: we do not change the custom, and the custom is, and he's talking about all Sefaradim, is to say ULe'Alme.

Now, what do the ancient Siddurim say? We have the Siddurim of the Geonim, Rab 'Amram Gaon, Rab Sa'adya Gaon, and Rabbi Shelomo Sajilmasi, and the Siddur of HaRambam. All these older Siddurim that we have, the oldest Siddurim in fact, all have it as ULe'Alme. Now, given Mahzor Aram Soba, the old Mahzor of Aram Soba from 1527 does have it Le'Alme, but the older Siddurim, the Siddurim that predate it, as well as the Aramaic sources, show that it should be otherwise.

Now, let's move forward. What was the actual custom based upon the Halabi sources that we have? This applies, of course, to other communities as well, but I'm gonna single out Halab, and I'll show you why later on. We have numerous sources from Halabi Hakhamim, or even printed in Halab.

So what do we have? In this book from Israel that came out, it mentioned Hakham Abraham Hamwey. So Hakham Abraham Hamwey printed numerous books, and, in fact, in his books, this is, for example, his Mahzor for Rosh HaShanah, called Bet Din, he has it over here: "Le'Alam ULe'Alme." So he has ULe'Alme. In his Selihot book, published in 1878, he also has "Le'Alam ULe'Alme." In his Bet HaKapporet, his book for Yom Kippur, he has it "Le'Alam ULe'Alme." So Rabbi Abraham Hamwey in at least three of his Mahzorim has it "Le'Alam ULe'Alme."

But that's not the only source we have. We have Hakham Yisshak Moshe Mordekhai Dayan, who was from Halab, as it says on the title page. I made a photocopy from a friend of mine who had this book. And he published Selihot book in Yerushalayim in 1885. And what does he have? And this follows the Minhagim of Aram Soba. He even has Viddui HaGadol in it, so we know it's authentic. And he has "Le'Alam ULe'Alme." So, once again, "Le'Alam ULe'Alme."

But we have, in fact, the only two prayer books published in Aleppo, we have Siddur 'Olat Tamid by Hakham Yesha'yah Dayan, who was also mentioned in this book from Israel. Hakham Yesha'yah Dayan, in his Siddur for Minhah-'Arbit, says it over here, and it's in small print, but you could definitely see it: "ULe'Alme." It's there. And the only other Siddur published in Aleppo was published in 1915 by 'Ezra Djoudjati. Again, "Le'Alam ULe'Alme." So we have "Le'Alam ULe'Alme."

If you want to say, "Well, maybe the Mekubbalim of Halab said different," so Hakham Yisshak Alfiah, who was a famous Mekubbal from Halab, moved to Yerushalayim. He published a book called Siah Yisshak. In his Siah Yisshak, he also has it as—this was published in Yerushalayim in 1923, and he has it over here: "Le'Alam ULe'Alme." So all these sources that are either from Hakhamim of Halab or published in Halab, all have it as ULe'Alme. And this was basically the case among almost all Sefaradim.

Now, the book from Israel also contends that, well, in Halab they used Siddur Bet 'Obed. Bet 'Obed was the most common Siddur in Halab. Well, true and not true. It was common, but it wasn't the most common. The most common Siddurim in Halab all came from Livorno like Bet 'Obed did, but the common Siddur used by the masses was Tefilat HaHodesh. Bet 'Obed was used by more learned people, okay? But the most common person had the Tefilat HaHodesh. Granted, both Tefilat HaHodesh and Bet 'Obed were published in Livorno, and they did not have ULe'Alme; they had Le'Alme. And that's because they were based upon the Mekubbalim and writings of the Hida, etc.

What else did this book from Israel say? It said that based upon Hakham Yesha'yah Dayan. So, we showed you Hakham Yesha'yah Dayan in his 'Olat Tamid had it ULe'Alme. He has a book called Zeh Ketab Yadi, and in Zeh Ketab Yadi, he talked about the subject, and he showed the importance and more than the importance, that there is definitely a place, and possibly a prominent place for saying Le'Alam, but he didn't say it to change the Minhag, and he didn't say that's the Minhag of Halab.

One more. What was the Minhag in our community? Okay? Community is here for 120 years. What's the Minhag of the community? So, we didn't start printing our own Siddurim until 1974. In 1974, Gabriel Shrem, who was a Hazzan in the community for over 45 years, from about 1941 till about 1986, he published the first community Siddur, called Bet Yosef VeOhel Abraham. It has the approbation of Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim. I'm bringing him up because his name was brought up in the video as well. So, we have the approbation of Hakham Barukh. And he based his Siddur on a book from Israel called Tefilat Yesharim. Tefilat Yesharim, based upon Mekubbalim, does not have it as ULe'Alme; it has Le'Alme. Gabriel Shrem insisted that the printer insert the Vav throughout the Siddur to make it ULe'Alme, once again showing what the custom of our community.

Just in case we're mistaken, I checked with the Halabi community in Argentina. I checked with the main Hazzan and upkeeper of the Minhagim, Ustaz Daniel Binker, and I checked with Hakham Shelomo Antebi Sa’ah, what is the Minhag over there, and both of them unequivocally stated that the Halabi Minhag, "Le'Alam ULe'Alme." So we know this is the Minhag, this is what we do. Not that there was no person in Halab saying "Le'Alam Le'Alme." No, Le'Alme also existed, but to come and discredit those who say ULe'Alme is a problem.

Now, the biggest problem is that this booklet from Israel that came out in English talked specifically about our community, and it singled out the Kol Ya'akob Siddur. Said the Kol Ya'akob Siddur, let's give the exact words, it said: "The popular prayer book, Kol Ya'akob, used by Syrian Jews in the United States, has the text of ULe'Alme 'Almaya. Apparently, this is an oversight." It's not an oversight. It's done on purpose, and it's based upon numerous sources, as I've just shown.

Now, obviously, not everything in the Kol Ya'akob is perfect, and the original editors and founders of the Kol Ya'akob Siddur, Rabbi David Sutton, Hakham Shim'on Alouf, Mr. Sam Kassin, Mr. Dennis Werber, Hakham David Tawil, these were upstanding leaders of the community, people that were familiar with Halakhah, familiar with Dikduk, familiar with the Hakhamim, familiar with the Minhagim. They knew what they were doing. But the Kol Ya'akob Siddur is constantly under review, and any time something comes up, if it has a solid basis, so corrections are made. But to come out from nowhere and say that this is an oversight to have it as "Le'Alam ULe'Alme," I'm sorry, that's inappropriate.

The custom of the community has been for a very long time to say "Le'Alam ULe'Alme," and it has many solid sources going back from the Tanakh through the Rishonim, through the Aharonim, through the Hazzanim of the community, and this is what we do. So please, before knocking Siddur, look into it, find out what's going on, "She'al Abikha VeYaggedkha, Zekenekha VeYomeru Lakh," ask the elders, find out the true Minhagim. Enjoy your Tefilot. May HaShem accept all our prayers "BeAhabah UBRasson," Amen.

258.title: The Kapseh Superstition
258.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. We've been speaking about the wedding, the wedding ceremony, everything connected to weddings. And fair warning, I'm going to bring up something now that is not part of the regular customs, but it's part of the superstitions and a superstitious custom. And this is because so many people have asked about it, it was felt that it's very important to bring it up so people have clarity as to what this is.

And this custom basically goes like this: there is a bride, she's about to get married, and she has a guest that's coming to the wedding. And this guest has either recently got married or has recently given birth to a child, recently generally meaning thirty to forty days in either case, whether we're talking about a woman who got married or one who gave birth. It is considered an ill omen for this new bride or new mother to come to the wedding unless something transpires between the bride-to-be and this guest. What is this that has to transpire? And this is referred to as the superstition of the kapseh.

What's a kapseh? Kapseh is an old Syrian word for a hairpin. And this hairpin, okay, what we know today in America more or less as a bobby pin, but there are hairpins as well that are a little wider, as we know. In any case, what's going on over here?

So basically the order of this superstitious ceremony is the bride-to-be will be called outdoors, yes, outdoors, okay? And as we spoke in earlier ceremonies, wedding ceremonies in Syria, particularly in Aleppo, in Halab, were done at night. So basically, you're outside at night. There she'll meet the woman who has recently got married or recently had a child, and they will exchange bobby pins, the guest removing a bobby pin from her hair, and the bride-to-be removing a bobby pin from her hair, and they will exchange them, give them to one another and replace the one that they've taken out of their own hair.

What's going on over here? So you have a few factors: you're looking to ward off any sort of evil. Nighttime is a time of evil, so these evil spirits, if you will, are outdoors. They're surrounding these women who just are either entering into a happy situation or have just, you know, had a happy situation. So you have these evil spirits around, these Mazzikin, if you will. And metal is used as a general tool to ward off these evil spirits. This according to many Hakhamim, especially Mekubbalim, having metal with you basically wards them off. But more than that over here, you're taking something that is pointy, if you will, okay? So it's spear-like. So when you're removing it from the hair and placing it in the hair again, you're basically spearing it, and you're stopping it. But not just stopping it in its tracks, okay? The kapseh means also to squeeze together, to bring together and put pressure on, so it can no longer do its work, okay? And you're stopping it in such a sense.

Take it for what it is. This is something that has been carried on by women in the Syrian community for many generations. We don't know the origin of it, we don't know how long it goes back, but we do know that it is still practiced. In any case, this is what the custom is.

And why does this custom go on? Okay, it's not just to stop this evil spirit, and why is it an ill omen? It's because the woman who is getting married, okay, like any new bride, can be nervous. And she may think that this woman who just, you know, got married or just had a child, you know, is stealing away, you know, the limelight from her that night, and therefore causing her difficulty in consummating her marriage, in being able to get pregnant, in being able to have a happy marriage. So, by the women meeting with each other and exchanging this hairpin, it's as if they've become one, and by them it's like them telling one another, "No, I'm here for you. I'm part of you, and part of your ceremony, and part of your celebration, and I, too, am here for you and want you to be as part of my celebration, and I want you to be here, and I know that you're here to be with me." And therefore, by them doing this, it basically calms them down emotionally, psychologically, so they know that there is no one out there that would possibly be looking for their, for evil interests for them, but rather it's all good, and they're here to celebrate together, and be happy.

So, this is the ceremony, if you will, of the kapseh. It's a superstitious ceremony. It's not something that we generally talk about with our Minhagim or Minhag of the Week, but since so many people have asked about it, people have questions about it, how it's done, when it's done, where it's done, why it's done, we felt was important to bring it up. We wish you all lots of good luck, great celebrations, happy marriages, and good times.

259.title: Sitting or Standing for Tefillin Shel Yad
259.text:
There is a difference of opinion among the authorities about whether one should sit or stand when putting the Tefillin Shel Yad on their arm. Maran wrote that some put the Tefillin on their arm while sitting and the Tefillin on their head while standing, but the Ashkenazic custom is to put both the Tefillin on their arm and the Tefillin on the head while standing. The common practice among most Middle Eastern Jews is to put the Tefillin on the arm while sitting, based on the teachings of the Arizal that was recorded in both the Sha'ar HaKavvanot and the Peri 'Ess Hayyim.

However, there is also a difference of opinion regarding whether the blessing for wearing Tefillin is recited while sitting or while standing. The Ben Ish Hai wrote that most of the halakhic authorities taught that the blessing for Tefillin is recited while standing, but some taught that the blessing is recited while sitting, and the Mekubbalim recite the blessing while sitting. And the custom of Baghdad was in accordance with the teachings of the Mekubbalim, who recite the blessing while sitting. However, the Siddur Bet 'Obed wrote that one should recite the blessing for Tefillin while standing, and then sit down to tighten the strap and wrap it around the arm.

Interestingly, my friend David Catton told me that his grandfather, Sam Catton, 'Alav HaShalom, used to recite the blessing for Tefillin while standing, and then sit down to tighten the strap and wrap it around his arm, like it says in the Siddur Bet 'Obed. However, most people in our community do not stand to recite the blessing before wearing Tefillin.

Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo, who was born in Halab in 1893, wrote the blessing for Tefillin should be recited while leaning forward, not standing and not sitting, meaning you lift yourself up a little bit like some people do when they answer Barekhu or when a rabbi walks in. This is a compromise between sitting and standing. He only wrote this regarding reciting the blessing, but tightening the strap should be done while sitting, in accordance with the teachings of the Arizal. I've been told that in the 1950s, it was common in our community to see men reciting the blessing before wearing Tefillin while leaning forward, as described by Hakham Yosef Sha'yo in his book on the customs of Halab. Furthermore, Hakham Yosef Sha'yo wrote that one covers their arm with their Talet when they tighten and wrap the Tefillin strap on their arm. This is also based on the teachings of the Arizal and was recorded by the Hida and also quoted in the Siddur Bet 'Obed.

So there is a difference of opinion about whether Tefillin Shel Yad, the Tefillin that we wear on our arm, is put on while sitting or while standing. The prevalent custom in our community is to put it on while sitting. There is also a difference of opinion about sitting or standing when reciting the blessing before wearing Tefillin. Many also sit for the blessing, while others stand for the blessing and then sit down to tighten and wrap the Tefillin strap on their arm. But Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo recorded the custom of Halab as to lean forward a little bit, so you are not sitting or standing when reciting the blessing for wearing Tefillin, and then sitting to tighten and wrap the Tefillin strap on your arm. All this is for the Tefillin on your arm, but the Tefillin on your head is put on while standing, and the wrapping of the Tefillin strap on your finger is also done while standing.

260.title: After the Breaking of the Glass
260.text:
SCA, Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles: The end of the wedding ceremony. So we spoke about the wedding and all the steps of the wedding, and now we finally reach the end, as we discussed in episode 255, the breaking of the glass. What happens now after the breaking of the glass?

What we see nowadays is that immediately after the breaking of the glass, throngs of people come rushing up to the bride and groom, they surround them, they dance around them, they basically march them out of the wedding hall or out of the synagogue where the wedding took place, the actual ceremony took place, and in the process, they're basically trampling so many guests that are also trying to move around or to get out of their seats or to get up and get out. This wasn't always the way. This is only something that started about 40 years ago. It started among more, we'll call quote-unquote a religious, Yeshivish mindset type of group that picked up this concept of dancing around the bride and groom from their Ashkenazi counterparts. But this is not something that we've ever known in our community prior to that.

We have obviously people that have told us, you know, that how their weddings were in earlier days. We've seen pictures, we even have videos from the 50s, the 60s, even the 70s where after the ceremony the bride and groom walked out, they marched out of the synagogue. Everybody, you know, stood to the side, watched them walk out. After the bride and groom would walk out, their parents would follow, the Hakhamim would follow, and the bride and groom would basically stand in the lobby outside the synagogue, okay, and as the guests walked out after them, each of the guests walked up to the bride and groom to Mabrook them, to congratulate them, to shake their hands, to kiss them. And it was done in a very, very beautiful, orderly, dignified, refined fashion. And this was even the way it was done in earlier days, and even people that I spoke to, old-timers from, you know, from Syria, from Egypt, from Lebanon, they all told me that it was always done in a very dignified way and not the commotion that we see nowadays, where everybody goes rushing either to get out of the room right away to go get a seat, you know, for the reception or what do you call it, or to just, you know, crowd around the bride and groom or to run up to the, you know, to the stage where the ceremony was held. It was very, very different and, like I said, it was much more dignified. There were a lot more manners involved and it was a very nice thing.

Also, what we see today, a lavish catered event, a tremendous meal, also is something that was only introduced into the community beginning in the 1950s. Prior to that, the guests would leave with a memento. What was that memento? It's what people today, you know, reminisce about a mlebbes wedding. Mlebbes wedding, the bride and groom or their parents, you know, would have arranged to have handed out to all their guests a memento, a token of appreciation for coming, that would remind the people of the wedding as well. It was a small porcelain dish wrapped with lace or tulle and a ribbon. It had some mlebbes, you know, in it, and that was given out to each guest, and that was your party favor, if you will, and you went home with that. And that was it. There was no lavish meal, there was no dancing, there was nothing. All the big parties that we know today, all began in the 1950s. And once Shaare Zion was built in 1960 and obviously they built a, you know, a tremendous reception hall, a catering hall, they had a caterer on staff, so obviously more and more people, you know, picked up on the idea and it became what we know today. But that wasn't done in the past.

If we want to talk about what was done in Halab once upon a time, even in Halab they would give out something like the mlebbes, okay, and they called it dayfat. They gave it to each guest, they got what they got, dayfat, they got these little dishes, if you will, of candy, of raha, of some sort of sweet, and they went home with it. There was no lavish meal for the guests. Even the bride and groom went directly to the home of the parents of the groom, they had a small meal over there, there wasn't even Sheba' Berakhot done that night, that's something that we'll talk about in a upcoming episode. The main wedding meal and party was held on the following night. Again, we'll talk about that in the future, but weddings were very different than what we're used to today.

In any case, Mabrook and best of luck to all the families and all the brides and grooms. Mabrook.

261.title: Hakham Matloub on the Kaddishim of Tish'ah BeAb Night
261.text:
In episode 218, we discussed the first two questions that Hakham Matloub Abadi addressed in his responsa on the prayers for Tish'ah BeAb in his book Magen Ba'adi. In that episode, we said that Hakham Matloub required the community to maintain their custom of reading Ekhah before praying 'Arbit on the night of Tish'ah BeAb, as opposed to praying 'Arbit first. We also said that Hakham Matloub required the community to maintain their custom of not reciting the Haftarah in Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb, even though a Haftarah is read in Minhah in many other communities.

The third question that Hakham Matloub addressed in this responsa is how many Kaddishim are recited after the 'Amidah on the night of Tish'ah BeAb, and is Kaddish Titkabbal recited at all on that night? According to Hakham Matloub, our custom is to recite three Kaddishim after the 'Amidah on the night of Tish'ah BeAb. The first one is Hassi Kaddish, which is recited right after the 'Amidah. The second Kaddish is a Kaddish that we recite on Tish'ah BeAb, which includes the part that begins "DeHu 'Atid LeHaddata," which is recited right after VeAttah Kadosh. And the third Kaddish after the 'Amidah that night is Kaddish Yehe Shelama, which is recited right before 'Alenu. According to this order of Kaddishim, we do not recite Kaddish Titkabbal at all on the night of Tish'ah BeAb.

Hakham Matloub gave several reasons for this order of Kaddishim. One: we never say four Kaddishim after the 'Amidah in 'Arbit on any other night of the year, and there is no source that mentions the night of Tish'ah BeAb as being exceptional in this regard.

His second reason: it would not be proper to say a Kaddish after the Kinot without saying VeAttah Kadosh first. This is because according to HaRambam, Kaddish is only recited after an actual prayer that was established by the rabbis, not after prayers that were composed after the talmudic period, and the Kinot that we recite were composed even later than that, after the geonic period. Furthermore, Hakham Matloub cited the Hida, who wrote that it's not proper to add extra Kaddishim.

Hakham Matloub's third reason: reciting four Kaddishim after the 'Amidah on the night of Tish'ah BeAb is against the tradition of our ancestors from Halab, and we should not change our traditions. Here, Hakham Matloub recalled his education in Halab, where he had the privilege of attending to the great rabbis in the study halls and synagogues of Aleppo. He singled out Bet Nasi, where the religious court of Halab issued rulings and they also prayed there. He also mentioned the Midrash of 'Obadia Harari, where great rabbis and proficient halakhic authorities, including his own rabbis and teachers, studied and prayed. The Midrash of 'Obadia Harari also had a group of rabbis who were proficient in Kabbalah and engaged in mystical studies the entire day. This group included Ribbi Mikhael Mishan and Ribbi 'Obadia Laniado. Hakham Matloub went on to say that from the days of his youth, he would regularly pray with these religious judges and Kabbalists on the night of Tish'ah BeAb, and wherever he prayed, they only recited three Kaddishim after the 'Amidah, never four. And therefore, we should not change their custom, since they certainly knew what was proper, both according to the halakhic authorities and also according to the Ari, the authoritative master of Kabbalah. Hakham Matloub added that this is also what they had been doing for many years in Brooklyn since he came to the community. Furthermore, some later authorities also mentioned the custom of not reciting Kaddish Titkabbal on the night of Tish'ah BeAb, including the Bet David and the Maharikash.

Hakham Matloub's fourth reason: according to many authorities, Titkabbal is not recited after reading Megillat Ekhah at night because Ekhah includes the phrase, "Satam Tefillati," "He closed off my prayer." Many of these authorities had the custom to pray 'Arbit before Ekhah at night, and therefore they recited Titkabbal at night, but not the next morning in Shahrit. But since the custom of Halab was to read Ekhah before 'Arbit, according to Hakham Matloub, they did not recite Kaddish Titkabbal at night, but they did recite Titkabbal the next morning in Shahrit. Hakham Matloub explained, "MeEkhah 'Ad Ekhah En Kaddish Titkabbal," meaning the custom is not to recite Titkabbal in between the night reading and the day reading of Megillat Ekhah, but after the reading of Ekhah in the morning, the sad elegies have been concluded, and then Kaddish Titkabbal may be recited.

Hakham Matloub also supported his position with the fact that the famous Mahzor Aram Soba from the year 1527 had no mention of Kaddish Titkabbal for the prayers on the night of Tish'ah BeAb, but did specify reciting Kaddish Titkabbal in Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb.

But before concluding his discussion regarding not reciting Kaddish Titkabbal on the night of Tish'ah BeAb, Hakham Matloub expressed his surprise in finding Kaddish Titkabbal listed in the order of the prayers on the night of Tish'ah BeAb by Hakham Shemuel Laniado in his book Shulhan HaMelekh, which was written in Halab in the year 1804, but was not published until 1923. Rabbi Laniado also only had three Kaddishim after the 'Amidah, because he omitted the Hassi Kaddish after the 'Amidah. However, Hakham Matloub dismissed this source as not necessarily reflecting the custom of Aleppo, but rather just a summary of Shulhan 'Arukh and some of the comments appended to Shulhan 'Arukh by Muram, or perhaps Titkabbal was recited in his synagogue, but not in the other synagogues in Aleppo.

Hakham Matloub also disagreed with Rabbi Laniado regarding replacing Sim Shalom with a shorter version that begins "'Oseh HaShalom," that is found in some Tish'ah BeAb Siddurim like Arba' Ta'aniyot, on the night and morning of Tish'ah BeAb. According to Hakham Matloub, we should recite the usual Sim Shalom in all of the 'Amidot of Tish'ah BeAb, which is in accordance with the teachings of the Arizal.

Hakham Matloub then summarized the order of the prayers on the night of Tish'ah BeAb according to the custom of Aleppo. We begin with Ha'azinu, then Megillat Ekhah, followed by the Mizmor that begins "'Al Naharot Babel," then Hassi Kaddish, Barekhu, and 'Arbit. After the 'Amidah, Hassi Kaddish, and if it's Saturday night, Bore Me'ore Ha'Esh is recited on a candle. Then the lights are dimmed, and the Kinot are recited, beginning with A'azot Espedah. Then we go down on the floor and count the years since the destruction of the Bet HaMikdash, and cry about the length of the exile. After that, we recite verses of comfort, including "'Ad Anah Bekhiyah BeSiyyon" and "'Urah Na Yeminekha Ramah," and then go right into VeAttah Kadosh, which is followed by the Kaddish Targum that is recited on Tish'ah BeAb. Then "Shir HaMa'alot BeShub HaShem Et Shibat Siyyon," followed by Kaddish Yehe Shelama, Barekhu, and 'Alenu.

BeEzrat HaShem, in a future video, we will discuss the fourth and final question that Hakham Matloub addressed in his responsa on the prayers for Tish'ah BeAb. Tizku Kulkhem LeNehamat Siyyon UBeBinyan Yerushalayim BiMherah BeYamenu, Amen.

262.title: Yihud Rooms, Mezinke and Going-Away Outfits
262.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles, more wedding practices. So, many people send in questions and queries regarding various things that they see nowadays or things that they've heard about.

One of them is Yihud room. Is it our custom to have a Yihud room, a room where the bride and groom go and separate themselves alone immediately after the wedding ceremony that is watched by two witnesses to make sure nobody enters or exits that room? So, no, we do not have such a practice. This is not the practice of the Sefaradim. The Sefaradi Hakhamim consider the ceremony where the Talet is spread over the heads of the bride and groom, and the seven Berakhot of the wedding itself, to be considered as complete marriage, and therefore a Yihud room is not necessary. Among Ashkenazim and Yemenites and possibly some specific communities, there is a concept of a Yihud room where they do not consider the wedding complete until the bride and groom avail themselves of this privacy in a room that is guarded over, and they're in there for at least 15 minutes or so, and that is considered a Yihud room where the wedding is considered completely finished and they are fully married. We do not have such a concept whatsoever.

Now, we do see that after the ceremony, the bride and groom go to a room. Yes, they go to the bridal room. It was a long, trying day for the bride and groom, especially with hours of pictures and pressure on them. So, they need a few minutes to compose themselves, to talk, to relax. Usually, the caterer will bring them some food in there because they know they're going to be dancing for hours on end, and they need some sort of nourishment beforehand. So, it's not that they're going into a Yihud room because of Yihud, but rather they're going in there for practical reasons. And many a time, we know that the mother of the bride or the sister of the bride will knock and go inside the room, and it's all very normal. So, that's Yihud room.

Number two: dancing. Yes, we have plenty of dancing, but people ask about something called Mezinke dance, when the last child of either the parents of the bride or the parents of the groom get married, do we have this custom? Absolutely not! The Mezinke dance is a Yiddish custom, custom of Ashkenazim, mainly from Eastern Europe. And this is a dance where they're celebrating the emptying of their home. And if you notice in the real Mezinke dance tradition, there are brooms involved where they're sweeping away, and they sweep away their children. This is very, very different than Sefaradim. When our children get married, we want to bring them closer to home. We bring back our daughter together with the new son-in-law, or we bring our son together with the new daughter-in-law, and we bring their children and hopefully their children after them, and we become one big extended, tremendous, happy family. We never push people away. Rather, we bring closer, and this custom of the Mezinke dance where people celebrate and dance around, you know, these parents who have emptied their home and are sweeping away their children does not exist among Sefaradim whatsoever.

Next custom that has come up is going-away outfits. No, it's not a Sephardic custom to have going-away outfits. So, people say, "Well, why do we have it? Why do people do it? We're the only community that has such a thing as going-away outfits." So, let me explain very simply. In the time or at the time when people got married and immediately after the wedding went on their honeymoon, that was going away. The whole reception, the party ended, the music, the dancing, everything ended, and they got into the limousine and went straight to the airport to go away on their honeymoon. Nowadays, we think about going on a flight, we think about putting on something comfortable, you know, sweats, sneakers, Uggs, slippers, whatever it may be. But when flight first started and it was considered a very fancy thing and people got dressed up to go onto a flight wherever they were going. And so here you go: going-away outfit. You got dressed up, you removed your wedding gown and your tuxedo, and you put on your going-away outfit. You put on nice, fancy clothing to get on the flight, and that is your going-away outfit. As far as a hat for the woman, yeah, that was the mode of the time. In the '50s and the '60s, it was very commonplace for a woman to go out wearing some sort of hat, so that tradition continued in the going-away outfit.

Finally, a very new custom is that the bride and groom, after the entire wedding is over and the night is finished, they start giving blessings out to friends and family, especially to single young men and young women, wishing them and blessing them a upcoming marriage soon. We have no such custom. Bride and grooms do not give out blessings. They are not Hakhamim to give out blessings. They have no such power, they have no frame of mind even to do such a thing, and it's never been our tradition, it's not something that we do.

So, we talked about four things: Yihud, Mezinke, going-away outfits, and giving out blessings. I think we pretty much clarified them, and that concludes the wedding ceremony, reception, and party. Mabrook to all the happy brides and grooms.

263.title: The Father's Blessing at the Berit Milah
263.text:
There are several blessings that are recited at a Berit Milah ceremony, and we find a difference of opinion among the authorities regarding whether the father of the baby recites the blessing of "LeHakhniso BiBrito Shel Abraham Abinu" before or after the Berit Milah.

In the Bet Yosef, Maran discussed the opinion of Rashbam, who wrote that this blessing is recited before the Berit Milah, because he considered it a Birkat HaMissvah, which should be recited before the performance of the Missvah, which in this case is the Berit Milah. Maran also discussed the opinion of Rabbenu Tam, who based on their custom, held that this blessing should be recited after the Berit Milah. Rabbenu Tam explained, one only recites the blessing for a Missvah before the Missvah when they themselves are performing the Missvah, but in this case, since the Mohel is the one performing the Missvah, the father should wait until after the Missvah was performed before reciting his blessing. Yet others explained that the father's blessing is not a Birkat HaMissvah, but rather a Birkat HaShebah, a blessing of praise, which does not have to be recited before the performance of the Missvah.

In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran ruled in accordance with the opinion of the Rosh, who recited this blessing in between the Milah and the Peri'ah. The Peri'ah is the peeling back of a thin tissue that is found underneath the foreskin. Since Peri'ah is required in order to complete the circumcision, reciting this blessing before the Peri'ah is considered reciting the blessing before the Missvah is completed, which is a compromise between reciting the blessing before or after the Berit Milah.

The general rule in Halab and other Middle Eastern communities was to follow Maran, but this is an exceptional case. In the end of the 18th century, Hakham Eliyahu Shamah HaLevi published a book on the laws of Berit Milah, which he called Makhshire Milah. In this book, he wrote that the custom in Aleppo and Damascus and Iraq and other places was to recite the blessing of LeHakhniso before the Berit Milah. He then addressed the question of not following Shulhan 'Arukh like we usually do, and he wrote that the custom is based on the opinions of the Rif and HaRambam, who lived several centuries before Maran wrote Shulhan 'Arukh. So even after Maran wrote that it should be recited in between the Milah and the Peri'ah, the custom in Syria and Iraq did not change. They continued with their earlier custom of reciting it before the Berit Milah.

Hakham Eliyahu Shamah also quoted the book Shulhan Gaboah, who wrote that even though the custom in Salonica was to recite the blessing in between the Milah and the Peri'ah, the custom in Jerusalem was to recite the blessing before the Berit Milah. Interestingly, Rabbi Hayyim Menashe Sethon cited Makhshire Milah in his book Eress Hayyim, but he also noted that the custom in Sefat, his city in northern Israel, was in accordance with the ruling of Maran in Shulhan 'Arukh. Rabbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on also quoted Makhshire Milah in his book Nehar Missrayim on the customs of Egypt, and he affirmed that the custom of Egypt was like the custom in Syria and other places, to recite the blessing of LeHakhniso before the Berit Milah. He also added that this is the custom in North African communities and many other places. The book Keter Shem Tob also quoted Makhshire Milah, and then he wrote that the custom in the Land of Israel, Iraq, Syria, and Egypt was to recite the blessing of LeHakhniso before the Berit Milah.

So we see that even though Maran wrote that the blessing of LeHakhniso should be recited in between the Berit Milah and the Peri'ah, the custom in Syria, Egypt, Jerusalem, and Iraq was to recite this blessing before the Berit Milah. And this was the custom in North African communities as well. Although the general rule is to follow Shulhan 'Arukh, there are exceptional cases. This is a case of a custom that predated Shulhan 'Arukh and remained in effect even after the general acceptance of Shulhan 'Arukh.

Now the last blessing recited at a Berit Milah is the blessing of "Asher Kiddesh Yedid MiBeten." Included in this blessing is the phrase of "'Al Ken BiSkhar Zot," referring to the reward for performing the Missvah of Berit Milah. Many Siddurim have changed the word from "Zot" to "Zo." However, Hakham Eliyahu Shamah recorded the exact wording of this blessing in his book Makhshire Milah, and he has "Zot," as we find in our printings of the Gemara, Rambam, and the Tur. Interestingly, the use of the word "Zot" is a reference to a Pasuk that is found at the end of Parashat Lekh Lekha, which describes the Berit Milah with "Zot Beriti." So we see from Hakham Eliyahu Shamah that it was customary to say "BiSkhar Zot" in Halab, at least since the end of the 18th century, as opposed to "Zo," which is found in many Siddurim.

264.title: Ne'ilah Customs in Halab
264.text:
It's customary to begin Ne'ilah by singing the famous Piyyut El Nora 'Alilah. It's important to note that the tune for El Nora 'Alilah is not the same tune as the Pizmon Mippi El. There's a voice note attached to this video with El Nora 'Alilah being sung the Halabi way.

Hakham Salim Zafrani documented the customs of the Great Synagogue of Aleppo in the first half of the 20th century. In his notes he wrote that they sang the Piyyut Hon Tahon before the 'Amidah in Ne'ilah. This was also recorded by Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo in his book on the customs of Aleppo. However, in the book Derekh Eress it is noted that in later times they did not sing Hon Tahon in Ne'ilah in Halab. Furthermore, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that they sang 'Et Sha'are Rasson before singing El Nora 'Alilah. Now in our community, 'Et Sha'are Rasson is sung at the beginning of Minhah on Yom Kippur, and Hon Tahon is sung on the holiday of Rosh HaShanah.

One of the notable customs in Ne'ilah is that the Kohanim wash their hands with orange blossom water before reciting Birkat Kohanim. This was recorded as the custom in Halab in the book Derekh Eress. I've heard that the reason for this custom is so that the fragrance will rejuvenate the Kohanim as they might feel faint towards the end of the fast day, and this will help them recite the priestly blessing with greater concentration and a stronger feeling of love. The book Keter Shem Tob recorded the custom of the Kohanim washing with fragrant water on Yom Kippur as a custom in the Land of Israel and in Egypt. And he also wrote that women who had difficulty getting pregnant donated the fragrant water for the Kohanim to wash their hands with, and then after the fast, they would drink from that water and believe that it would help them get pregnant and have a child. In Damascus, it was customary to use orange blossom water or rosewater. The Kohanim would wash their hands with this water over a bowl, and then the water that was left over in the bowl was used to cure aches and pains.

Interestingly, some Ashkenazic authorities discuss a custom of Kohanim washing their hands with fragrant water on Yom Tob, and several authorities objected to the custom, as they considered it a violation of the prohibition of being Molid Reah, creating a fragrance, so to speak. But there are Middle Eastern authorities who permitted it, such as Ribbi Abraham HaLevi in his book Ginat Veradim. He lived in Egypt during the 17th century. And the Hida in his book Birke Yosef in the 18th century. They wrote that one should not mix the fragrance in water on Shabbat or Yom Tob, but if it was mixed before Shabbat, they can wash with it on Shabbat and Yom Tob. Similarly, Hakham Abraham Antebi wrote in his book Hokhmah UMusar that in Halab it was customary to sprinkle rosewater on each other on Simhat Torah, or when there was a groom or a father of a new baby boy on Shabbat, or even when visiting friends and relatives on Shabbat and Yom Tob, and that they relied on the authorities that permitted this. And the book Keter Shem Tob wrote that in the famous Kabbalistic synagogue Bet El in Jerusalem, rosewater was given to the rabbis, which they rubbed on their hands, faces, and beards on Simhat Torah, and also on Shabbat when celebrating with a groom or the father of a new baby boy.

There is also a difference of opinion about whether the Kohanim only wash their fingers on Yom Kippur, like everyone does on Kippur when waking up in the morning or after using the bathroom, or if they wash their entire hands before reciting Birkat Kohanim. Hakham Leon Guindi told me that they washed their entire hands.

Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that the Hekhal is left open during Ne'ilah until after the Hazarah. Here in our community, it is left open until the end of the entire Ne'ilah prayer. Hakham Yosef Sha'yo does not mention anything about going up to the Hekhal to recite personal prayers during Ne'ilah, but he did mention that custom for after 'Arbit on the night of Yom Kippur. He wrote that in the Great Synagogue of Aleppo, they would enter one of seven small rooms where they stored the Sifre Torah. Each room had between 20 and 30 Sifre Torah. They would enter barefoot and kiss the Sifre Torah, and then make personal requests from HaShem.

Now even though the old Mahzorim have "Bedil VaYa'abor" in Ne'ilah, like in the other prayers for Yom Kippur, the custom has developed to answer "Amen" instead of "Bedil VaYa'abor" in Ne'ilah. This was the custom in both Aleppo and Damascus and in Egypt as well. Furthermore, the book VaYikra Abraham documented this as the custom of the northern Israeli city, Safed.

There's another custom, which is particular to Halab. And that's the loud recitation of the verse from Tehillim that begins with the word "Eshme'ah." In Mahzor Aram Soba, which was printed in the year 1527, the Hazzan recited the entire verse at the end of each prayer before Kaddish Titkabbal on both Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur. The book Derekh Eress wrote that in more recent times, in the Great Synagogue of Aleppo, it was recited before Kaddish Titkabbal in Musaf of Rosh HaShanah and before Kaddish Titkabbal in every prayer on Yom Kippur. In the synagogue Bet Nasi, they also recited it before the 'Amidah in Musaf of Rosh HaShanah, but eventually it was only said before Kaddish Titkabbal in Ne'ilah on Yom Kippur.

The book Derekh Eress quoted Hakham Yisshak Zafrani 'Alav HaShalom, who said that someone with a strong voice recited the first part of the verse, "Eshme'ah Mah Yedabber HaEl Ad-onai," and then the congregation answered the continuation of the verse, "Ki Yedabber Shalom El 'Ammo VeEl Hasidav VeAl Yashubu LeKhislah," and then the Hazzan repeated the first part of the verse again, and the congregation again responded with the continuation of the verse, but eventually the custom changed, and the congregation answered by repeating the first part of the verse again. So the Hazzan said it, and the congregation repeated it. This was done two times. Here in our community, some still practice this custom at the end of the Ne'ilah prayer. The beginning of the verse is recited and repeated by the congregation. This is done two times in a loud voice right before Kaddish Titkabbal.

265.title: The Week of Se'udot for the Hatan and Kallah
265.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. So the wedding ceremony is over. We now move into the week of joy, of happiness for the bride and groom. And this week of joy is funny in a way because it parallels the exact opposite. This is a week of happiness where the Hatan VeKhallah, bride and groom, used to be in their Bet Hatnut, in their home of marriage, where basically everything would go on: the prayers for the entire week, their meals for the entire week, festivities for the entire week. People would come to see them there, they would never leave. Basically all this is akin to, Bar Minan, the Bet Abel, the mourning house, where over there people would gather, people would pray, people would eat. Okay? One hand, there's the house of Simhah for the Hatan VeKhallah, for happiness, and the other house is a house of mourning. But in both these places, that's where everything went on.

We still have the house of mourning where everything goes on. We no longer really have a house of marriage where things go on. People don't get married in that in the house, the Huppah doesn't stay up in the entire house the entire week, the bride and groom don't stay in this confined area for an entire week with all their meals and all their prayers going on over there. Rather the bride and groom are out and about. Part of the bride and groom going out is the groom going to Kenis for Shahrit, for Minhah, and as he goes, he of course does not say any Ana or any Tahanunim. It's a day of happiness for him, he will say Yehi Shem, and therefore all those that pray with him in the Minyan also don't say Ana, they don't say Tahanunim. It's a time of Yehi Shem.

What else goes on during this week that everybody's familiar with? It is currently known as Sheba' Berakhot. Now, this term, Sheba' Berakhot, is of course referring to the Berakhot said at the conclusion of the meal, but referring to the meal as a Sheba' Berakhot meal was not what our Hakhamim referred to it as. They used to refer to it as Se'udat Hatan or Se'udat Hatan VeKhallah or Se'udat Nissu'in. And these are the way our Hakhamim and our people knew these meals.

Now, these meals, if you will, fell out. They were pushed aside, forgotten about. I wouldn't call abandoned, but they just, you know, were neglected, if you will, because the concept of a honeymoon became very popular. And it's not something that became popular just here on these American shores; it was already popular in the Middle East. And already in the Middle East, you know, in Syria, in Lebanon, in Egypt, and in other places, people weren't really staying home after the wedding for a week of these Se'udot, okay? As time progressed, as far as I know, here on these American shores, when certain young men of the community started going to institutes of higher learning of Torah, of Yeshibot outside of the community post-high school in the late '50s, in the early '60s, they started picking up on this concept and reinstituted it and brought it back to the community. And slowly over time, it really crept back into the community and has a very prominent place and role in the wedding celebration today.

Now, as far as these Se'udot Hatan VeKhallah, these Sheba' Berakhot, it cannot occur unless certain conditions are met. You have to have a Minyan of men, 10 men must be there. They all must eat bread. The bride and groom must eat bread. A very important factor over here is that you have to have Panim Hadashot, new faces. New faces meaning people that weren't at the actual wedding ceremony and are now present at these special Se'udot. Nowadays, people invite friends, invite neighbors, people that they forgot to invite, people that they invited but just couldn't make it. But how was it in the old days? You'd invite over 'Aniyyim, poor, impoverished people. You're giving them a chance to eat a meal and bring a smile to their face. You'd invite over Hakhamim. Hakhamim would come and bestow their Berakhot upon you, their Berakhot of good wishes, and they would give Dibre Torah 'Al HaShulhan, they would speak Dibre Torah at the table before the Berakhot would be made. So this was a Se'udah of the highest caliber.

The Hakhamim refer to this as the best Se'udat Missvah because you have the happiness that you're giving to the Hatan VeKhallah, you have the happiness that you're giving to the 'Aniyyim, you have the Hakhamim that are coming and bestowing their Berakhot and their Dibre Torah upon everybody there, and it's a joyous moment, and anybody who has opportunity to participate and to join a Se'udat Missvah, a Se'udat Hatan VeKhallah is considered very, very lucky and very esteemed. In the next video, we're going to talk about the Se'udah itself briefly, and get into the Berakhot.

266.title: The Congregation Reciting Nakdishakh Aloud
266.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that the congregation is not supposed to recite Nakdishakh along with the Hazzan. According to Maran, the Hazzan says Nakdishakh by himself, while the congregation listens quietly until the Hazzan gets up to "VeKara Zeh El Zeh VeAmar," and then the congregation answers with the verse "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh." According to the Arizal, the congregation is supposed to recite Nakdishakh along with the Hazzan. But even according to the Arizal, the congregation only says the first two words, "Nakdishakh VeNa'arissakh," out loud, but the rest should only be recited out loud by the Hazzan, while the congregation continues reciting it in a whisper until they get to the verse that begins with "Kadosh Kadosh," which is recited out loud by the congregation.

So what about the common practice today in our community and other communities, where the congregation recites the entire Nakdishakh out loud along with the Hazzan? Not only that, on Shabbat and holidays, it has become customary for the entire congregation to sing Nakdishakh in loud voices along with the Hazzan.

This exact question was posed to Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, 'Alav HaShalom, by his student, Ribbi Moshe Hadid, and the question and answer were printed in Hakham Yisshak Chehebar's book, Ro'e Ne'eman, which was printed in the year 2020 by the Sephardic Heritage Museum. Ribbi Chehebar cited the opinions of some later authorities, such as the Ture Zahab, who lived in Europe near Ukraine in the 17th century, who said individuals can say the entire Nakdishakh together with the Hazzan. And even Maran has a case in Shulhan 'Arukh about one who is beginning his silent 'Amidah together with the Hazzan's recitation of the Hazarah. In that case, Maran writes that the person reciting his silent 'Amidah says the entire Nakdishakh along with the Hazzan. Some explained that since in that case the individual is saying his 'Amidah with the Hazzan's Hazarah, he is supposed to say exactly what the Hazzan says, including the full Nakdishakh. Ribbi Chehebar also quoted HaGaon Ribbi Zalman, the founder of Habad Hasidut, who lived in Europe in the 18th century. He wrote that the entire congregation may recite the entire Nakdishakh if they want to.

Ribbi Chehebar went on to say that in Halab, the Mezammerim, who were a group of men in the synagogue who knew all of the tunes and played an important role in leading the tunes during the prayers, also used to sing Kaddish with the Hazzan from the beginning of the Kaddish until the congregation answered "Yehe Shemeh Rabba Mebarakh," and so on. Ribbi Chehebar pointed out that the Mezammerim did this in the presence of the rabbis and religious judges of the city, and no one objected at all.

Then Ribbi Chehebar explained that sometimes we have customs that are against Maran because the custom was already established before Maran issued his rulings in Shulhan 'Arukh, and afterwards they didn't want to eliminate the custom. In those cases, we apply the rule that's found in the Talmud Yerushalmi that says "Minhag Mebattel Halakhah"; in some cases, the custom supersedes the law.

So while Maran wrote that one only recites Nakdishakh with the Hazzan when reciting the silent 'Amidah along with the Hazzan's Hazarah, the custom is that the entire congregation always recites the entire Nakdishakh along with the Hazzan. And even though the Arizal specified that only the first two words, "Nakdishakh VeNa'arissakh," are said out loud by the congregation, but the rest of it is recited in a whisper, the common practice is not exactly in accordance with the instructions of the Arizal. Our custom is that the congregation recites the entire Nakdishakh out loud, especially when we sing it together on Shabbat and Yom Tob. Furthermore, it is also customary for the congregation to recite "Le'ummatam Meshabbehim VeOmerim" and "UBeDibre Kodshekha Katub Lemor" out loud, in addition to the entire verses of "Kadosh Kadosh," "Barukh Kebod," and "Yimlokh," which are all recited out loud as well.

267.title: Sheba' Berakhot with Two Cups
267.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles. In the last video, we began speaking about Se'udot of the Hatan and Kallah during the seven-day period of merriment post the wedding. We're talking about the Se'udot themselves, and these Se'udot have become known as Se'udah of Sheba' Berakhot. What are the Sheba' Berakhot? They are the wedding Berakhot which are recited after the meal. Let's talk about this because this seems to be something that people have a lot of questions about. They want to know what we do, how we do it, and it's quite simple, it's not a difficult thing.

What we do need to discuss first is how many cups to use, okay? And this seems to be a major topic. If you look at Shulhan 'Arukh, Shulhan 'Arukh talks about the opinion of using just one cup and the opinion of using two cups, and he seems to go with just using one cup, and the Ashkenazim follow the opinion of using two cups. But we know from many sources that even in Sephardic communities, two cups were used. At the very least, we know from various sources that two cups were used in Eress Yisrael as well as in Egypt. As far as one cup, we know one cup was definitely used in Morocco and other North African communities, as well as in Turkey. We don't have concrete evidence on every locale.

As far as Halab is concerned, it's interesting because, as we mentioned in the previous video, people were already not doing Sheba' Berakhot already back in the '30s and '40s. In Halab, they weren't doing it. So, it's hard to find actual testimony from people. But Hakham Yisshak Tawil, 'Alav HaShalom, said even though in his day in Halab they weren't doing Sheba' Berakhot, he has a recollection of knowing, of hearing that they would only use one cup. Here in the United States, we generally use two cups. Both opinions are valid. You could do either one, and we'll talk about both of them and the Minhagim associated with them.

So, let's say we're doing two cups. First we talk about the Se'udah, people eat, then you have Dibre Torah, then you go into Birkat HaMazon. And you should try to do this as close to one another as possible. You don't want to have a tremendous break from when you finish eating the meal to when you finally start Birkat HaMazon. You want to move things right along. Therefore, you show that Birkat HaMazon and the happiness of the Hatan and Kallah and their Se'udah are all connected to each other.

So, we get to Birkat HaMazon, we're going to have a cup for the person saying Birkat HaMazon. We'll have two cups for now, okay? Let's imagine one glass, we'll call it cup A for Birkat HaMazon, and cup B we're going to call the wedding Berakhot, okay? Obviously, they'd be filled with wine; these are only half full with water. So, you have person saying Birkat HaMazon, he says the Zimmun. Now, when he does the Zimmun for a wedding Se'udah, he adds words to the Zimmun. He says, "Barukh Elokenu SheHasimhah Bim'ono SheAkhalnu MiShello." He has these extra words. And the people answer, okay, "Barukh Elokenu SheHasimhah Bim'ono SheAkhalnu MiShello." So, "Simhah Bim'ono" are the two extra words added to the Zimmun.

He then says the entire Birkat HaMazon, okay, he says it out loud. Obviously, the other people are saying Birkat HaMazon quietly. He says the Birkat HaMazon out loud. When he gets to the end of Birkat HaMazon, finishes "'Oseh Shalom BiMromav Hu BeRahamav HaRabbim Ya'aseh Shalom 'Alenu Ve'Al Kol 'Ammo Yisrael VeImru Amen," you would think he'd immediately pick up the cup and say "Kos Yeshu'ot Essa," "Sabri Maranan," and "Bore Peri HaGefen," but he does not. He stops, he pauses, he continues to hold his cup, his cup marked cup Birkat HaMazon.

Then this second cup, both of these cups were filled with wine prior to Birkat HaMazon. They're both on the table, one is being held by the person saying Birkat HaMazon, and the other one is on the table next to him. Birkat HaMazon is concluded, takes this second cup, and it's handed off to the person who is going to say the first Berakhah. From that person to the second Berakhah, to the next Berakhah, we have six Berakhot which are said. The first one being "SheHakol Bara LiKhbodo," the second one is "Yosser HaAdam," the third one is a different "Yosser HaAdam," the fourth is "Mesammeah Siyyon BeBaneha," the fifth is "Mesammeah Hatan VeKhallah," and finally the sixth is the long Berakhah, "Mesammeah HaHatan 'Im HaKallah." All six Berakhot are said, they could be said by one person, they could be said by two people, by three, but up to six people, each one making a Berakhah. They make the Berakhah and they pass the cup on, nobody's drinking anything yet.

Once they conclude all of those Berakhot, then the person who said the Birkat HaMazon, okay, he's referred to as the Mezammen, he lifts his cup up, says "Kos Yeshu'ot Essa UBeShem HaShem Ekra," "Sabri Maranan," everybody answers "LeHayyim," he says the Berakhah of "Barukh Attah HaShem Elokenu Melekh Ha'Olam Bore Peri HaGefen." Then he drinks from this cup of his, he drinks approximately half the glass, okay, then the two cups are brought together, and we share the wine from one to another, okay? Remember, his cup is half empty, so you take from this cup that the wedding Berakhot was said on, you pour some of it into his cup, then he pours some of it back into the other cup. The cups now have approximately the same amount of wine in each, okay?

Then the cup of Birkat HaMazon is given to the attendees, to the people that are enjoying the meal with the Hatan VeKhallah to drink from, and this cup, okay, the one that the Sheba' Berakhot, the six Berakhot really, were said upon is given to the bride and groom. The groom drinks first, and then the bride drinks from it. After that, she'll usually give it to her friends, to her single friends, to drink from, and it's considered as a good omen for her to drink from that cup. And this basically is what goes on at Se'udot of Hatan VeKhallah. Mabrook to all the happy couples.

268.title: Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit on Hanukkah
268.text:
One question that comes up regarding the prayers on the holiday of Hanukkah is at what point is "Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid" recited during Shahrit? In his book on the customs of Halab, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that it is recited when taking out the Sefer Torah, before placing the Sefer Torah down on the Tebah. Similarly, the book Derekh Eress quoted Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, who said that on all eight days of Hanukkah, the Mizmor for Hanukkah is recited while carrying the Sefer Torah, after the verses that are normally recited when taking out the Sefer. The book Derekh Eress also quoted Rabbi Nissim Zafrani and Hayyim Dayah, who attested to the fact that this custom continued in Halab until the very last days that a Jewish community remained there.

However, Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that the Halabi community in Argentina recites the Mizmor for Hanukkah when returning the Sefer Torah. Rabbi Antebi brought support for their custom from the Siddur Bet 'Obed that wrote that after Kaddish Titkabbal, the Torah is returned to its place, and Yehalelu is said, followed by the Mizmor for Hanukkah. In any case, it is not our custom to recite the Mizmor for Hanukkah towards the end of the prayers after Hoshi'enu. Here in Brooklyn, we should recite it when taking out the Sefer Torah.

Now, with regards to the fact that every morning in Shahrit, the Mizmor for Hanukkah is recited all year round right before HaShem Melekh, without the first verse of "Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid." All year round, we start this Mizmor with the second verse that begins "Aromimkha." But what about on the eight days of Hanukkah? Should we add the first Pasuk to this Mizmor and begin with "Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid"? According to several sources, this verse should not be added. Since later in the prayers, we recite the entire Mizmor for Hanukkah, and at this point in the prayers, we are only reciting it as part of our normal daily prayers when we don't normally include the first verse. If we add the first verse now, it will be unnecessary to repeat the entire Mizmor again afterwards. This was the opinion of Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, the Ben Ish Hai, and Hakham 'Obadia Yosef.

What was the custom in Halab? According to some sources, this verse was added on the eight days of Hanukkah. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote regarding the custom of Halab on Hanukkah, "Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid, Aromimkha HaShem" is recited, followed by singing HaShem Melekh with a tune. Furthermore, the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar, which was printed in Halab in the year 1915, includes an instruction to add the verse "Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid" to "Aromimkha" on Hanukkah. Interestingly, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo would have been living in Halab at the age of 22 when the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar was printed there. And the Siddurim Bet 'Obed and Tefilat HaHodesh also include the same instruction to add the verse of "Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid" to "Aromimkha" on the days of Hanukkah. Both of these Siddurim were also used in Halab.

However, the book Derekh Eress quoted Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, who said that the custom of Halab is not to add the first verse of the Mizmor to "Aromimkha" on Hanukkah. Furthermore, Rabbi Shelomo Antebi Sacca wrote that the Halabi community in Argentina does not add the first verse of the Mizmor to "Aromimkha" on Hanukkah. And he also cited the book Keter Shem Tob, who wrote that the custom in the Land of Israel and Syria is not to add the first verse of the Mizmor when reciting "Aromimkha" before HaShem Melekh on Hanukkah.

So it seems that in Halab, some did add the first verse to "Aromimkha" on Hanukkah, while others did not. But with regards to reciting the entire Mizmor later in Shahrit, the prevalent custom in Halab was to recite it while taking out the Sefer Torah.

269.title: Tefillin at Minhah on a Friday 'Asarah BeTebet
269.text:
This year the fast of 'Asarah BeTebet falls out on a Friday once again. In a previous video, episode number 83, we discussed the community custom of wearing Tefillin in Minhah, even when the fast of 'Asarah BeTebet falls out on a Friday. In that video, we referenced a letter from Rabbi Eliyahu Ashkenazi, a rabbi from our community in Deal, New Jersey, who wrote that in the year 1994, Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim 'Alav HaShalom told him that the custom in our community is to wear Tefillin in Minhah, even when 'Asarah BeTebet falls out on a Friday.

Since that time, a recording of Hakham Barukh himself discussing this topic was found and posted on the internet. A link to that recording is attached to this video. In that recording, Hakham Barukh attested to the fact that although there are Kabbalists who objected to wearing Tefillin in Minhah on Friday afternoon, he always instructed our community to wear Tefillin when the fast fell on Friday based on the Peshat, meaning the Halakhah according to the Gemara and the Posekim. He also said that in his opinion, it is preferable to pray Minhah earlier that day, before Minhah Ketanah, around 2:00, with Tefillin, but that he also instructed the regular Minyan to wear Tefillin as long as it was not Shabbat yet.

Still and all, there are some rabbis in our community who object to wearing Tefillin in Minhah when the fast falls on a Friday, especially in the regular Minyan, which ends right before sunset. Here are some important points to consider: even though there are many Mekubbalim who object to Tefillin in Minhah on Friday, our custom is not necessarily in accordance with those Mekubbalim. We have the book Sedek VeShalom, which was written by Rabbi Eliyahu Mishan, an important Mekubbal in Halab in the 19th century. He discusses the question of whether the Mekubbalim should wear Tefillin in Minhah on 'Asarah BeTebet when the fast falls on Friday. The fact that this question is being addressed is a strong indication that the common practice in the city was to wear Tefillin in Minhah when the fast fell on Friday. Otherwise, why would he ask about whether the Mekubbalim should wear them or not? His conclusion was that the Mekubbalim should not wear them, but he never suggests that others should not wear them as well.

Furthermore, HaRab Hayyim HaKohen MeAram Soba, an important Mekubbal from the 17th century, who is a student of Rabbi Hayyim Vital, used to wear Tefillin every Friday afternoon. So refraining from wearing Tefillin on Friday afternoon is not agreed upon even by all of the Mekubbalim. Furthermore, everyone should be clear that according to the Gemara and Posekim, there is no problem whatsoever with wearing Tefillin on Friday afternoon as long as you take them off before sunset. The suggestion that Hakham 'Obadia Yosef and his son Hakham David Yosef, who wrote that Tefillin are not worn in Minhah when the fast falls on Friday, that they wrote that based on Halakhah, is not accurate.

Another question: what do we know from Hakham Abraham Hamwey, a 19th-century rabbi from Halab, about wearing Tefillin in Minhah? From his book Bet Din, we know that it was the custom in Halab to wear Tefillin in Minhah on fast days. We also know this from other written sources as well, all of which we quoted in episode number 32. In his Mahzor Bet HaKapporet, he also mentions wearing Tefillin in Minhah when 'Ereb Kippur falls on Friday. We don't have anything from Hakham Abraham Hamwey regarding Tefillin in Minhah of a fast day that falls on a Friday.

So to summarize: the original custom of Halab was to wear Tefillin in Minhah on fast days. Even though that custom changed in Halab, and after around 1930 they no longer wore Tefillin in Minhah on a fast day, our community preserved the original custom of Halab here in New York and New Jersey. Our community also practices this custom when 'Asarah BeTebet falls on a Friday, and this was most probably the custom of Halab as well. When Hakham Yisshak Zafrani 'Alav HaShalom was asked if we also wear Tefillin in Minhah when the fast day falls on a Friday, he said that we do. Again, this custom is not problematic halakhically; it is only a matter of disagreement among the Mekubbalim. The vast majority in our community who are not Mekubbalim should maintain our community custom that was recorded by Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim 'Alav HaShalom and wear Tefillin in Minhah, even in the Minyanim that finish Minhah right before sunset.

270.title: Sheba' Berakhot with One Cup
270.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Life Cycles, Sheba' Berakhot, Part Two. So in episode 267, we spoke about the methodology of how to do Sheba' Berakhot with two cups. We also mentioned that Hakham Yisshak Tawil, whose father Hakham Moshe Tawil was Chief Rabbi of Halab, said he had a recollection of in Halab them only using one cup, even though he wasn't 100% sure. So from last video till now, I was informed by our dear friend Mr. Hayyim Sha'yo that he heard directly from Hakham Ya'akob Attieh, 'Alav HaShalom, that in Halab they definitely only used one cup.

And so what is the methodology when you only use one cup? We said when we use the two-cup method, you have two people or two separate cups. First cup is held by the person who is the Mezammen, the person who starts the Zimmun for Birkat HaMazon, and he holds that cup the entire time whilst saying Birkat HaMazon. He concludes Birkat HaMazon, then the second cup goes around to those people making the Berakhot. When they finish all the Berakhot of the Huppah, then he, the Mezammen, person who said Birkat HaMazon, will then say Birkat HaGefen on that first cup that he had in his hand.

But now for doing the one-cup method. The one-cup method is different in that the person saying Birkat HaMazon, immediately after Birkat HaMazon, says "Kos Yeshu'ot Essa UBeShem HaShem Ekra," "Sabri Maranan," everybody answers "LeHayyim," and he says the Berakhah of "Bore Peri HaGefen." After that Berakhah of "Bore Peri HaGefen," then that same cup that he just said HaGefen on goes around to the other people that are going to make a Berakhah, the Berakhot of the Huppah and the Kiddushin, and they'll make those various Berakhot. He, the Mezammen, could also say one of those Berakhot as well, okay? But it's all done on one cup. When that is all said and done and finished, he takes the first sip from that cup that all the Berakhot was said on, the HaGefen plus the six additional Berakhot, and then he gives it to the bride and groom to drink from, then of course they can give it to others to drink from as well. So that's the one-cup methodology, obviously a lot easier than using two cups, and that was the Minhag in Halab as attested to by Mr. Hayyim Sha'yo from Hakham Ya'akob Attieh and as we knew from Hakham Yisshak Tawil.

Also, question came up, do we make only two Berakhot, or do we do all Sheba' Berakhot, all seven Berakhot, even if it's not the home of the Hatan VeKhallah? Because as we know, Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, 'Alav HaShalom, is of the opinion to only do two Berakhot if it's not in the exact home of the bride and groom, whereas the common practice today is to do all seven Berakhot, whether it's in somebody else's house or even in a restaurant. So the same Mr. Hayyim Sha'yo has told us that in Mexico, Hakham Sa’ad Harari, 'Alav HaShalom, who was the chief rabbi of the Halabi community, had them do all seven Berakhot. We also know from informants here in New York, my dear friend Morris Arking went and asked around about this for a while, that in the '60s, Hakham Matloub, if given the cup, would make a Berakhah, Chief Rabbi Hakham Ya'akob Kassin would make a Berakhah, Hakham Barukh would make a Berakhah. All these Hakhamim of the community, 'Alehem HaShalom, would make Berakhot, all seven of the Berakhot, not in the Bet Hatan VeKhallah. So even though Hakham 'Obadia Yosef is the opinion of two Berakhot only, and it seems that his teacher Hakham 'Ezra Attieh was of the same opinion, the practice in our community here for the most part is to do all seven Berakhot even not in the home of the Hatan VeKhallah.

Other than that, people asked about Damascus. So speaking to informants from Damascus, we found out that they would only do Sheba' Berakhot on Leil Shabbat. Friday night would be the time that they would gather the families and the friends together and do Sheba' Berakhot, do all the Berakhot, all seven Berakhot as well, and we were unable to find out for sure if they used one cup or two cups, but they would only do it on Friday night, not on any other night of the week.

So, this concludes Sheba' Berakhot. Of course, if there are any questions, send them along, we'll be more than glad to research and respond. Mabrook to all the happy couples.
