271.title: The Hatan and VeAbraham Zaken
271.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week. Life Cycles. So we just completed the wedding ceremony, we completed the Se'udot of the Hatan and Kallah. Now on Shabbat, the first time the Hatan goes up to the Sefer Torah in Kenis on Shabbat, what is special about it? What is special about it is there is a special reading for the Hatan from Parashat VeAbraham Zaken.

This is just seven Pesukim from Sefer Bereshit that talk about Abraham choosing a wife for his son Yisshak when he tells his male servant, "Go and get a wife for my son, for Yisshak." And these are basically a notification to the congregation that when you go out, find a good wife. Don't look for money, don't look for fame, don't look for prestige, don't look for looks. Look for a good family, like Abraham went out to find a good girl from a good family for his son. This is what you need to find. You need to find a good wife for your son. And this is a Berakhah, obviously, for the Hatan and for all the members of the Kahal.

So what is this Parashah and how is it done? Our custom, the custom throughout the Middle East, meaning Eress Yisrael, all of Syria, all of Lebanon, all of Egypt, all of Iraq, Iran, is that these Pesukim are read out of a Humash, as opposed to the Minhag of Turkey, of Tunisia, of Libya, and some other places where they actually took out a special Sefer Torah. Besides the regular reading of the Parashah of the week, they also had the Hatan take out a special Sefer Torah from the Hekhal to read these Pesukim from.

Now, these Pesukim are not read by the Hatan; rather, they are read by others. Others meaning what? What's our custom? The custom of the community is that you have the Pesukim are read, and the Targum, the Aramaic translation, is also read. They are read by two different people. Generally, the Pesukim of the Torah are read by the person who reads the Sefer Torah or, in some congregations, by the rabbi, by the Hakham, and the Targum, the Aramaic translation of it, is read by the Somekh. The Somekh is the person who stands next to the Kore BaTorah to help him along, and he would read that.

In some congregations it's done very loud fanfare, but in Syrian congregations, especially in Halabi congregation, it's done very, you know, quick and simple and easy, with no real hullabaloo. It's, after he finishes the Berakhot of the Torah, before Mi SheBerakh, they'll do the VeAbraham Zaken Pesukim. Like I said, it's only seven Pesukim: Pasuk, Targum, Pasuk, Targum, etc. After the Targum of the final Pasuk, they'll read the Pasuk again, and then Mi SheBerakh. And of course, the usual Mabrooks and Hazak UBarukh, etc.

Now, this is only done on Shabbat. Could be Yom Tob as well, but generally Shabbat. It is never done on a weekday. On a weekday would be considered Torah Sibbur. It's a burden on the people. People have to go, they have to get to work, they have things to do, so it's never done on a weekday. It's only done on a Shabbat. So the first Shabbat that the Hatan goes up to the Sefer Torah after his marriage is when they do this.

Now, in the days when people used to go away on their honeymoon immediately after the wedding or extended honeymoons, I clearly recall that a person could be coming back to the community, you know, to the Kenis six weeks, possibly, after his wedding, and that's when they did the VeAbraham Zaken for him. But it was always done. This is something that was always done.

Now, you will see in some Siddurim and even in Pizmonim books, there is an extra line before VeAbraham Zaken that says "BiRshut El Hai Amid VeAshib Abo Etargem Parashat VeAbraham Sib." This was not said in Halab. This was not a Halabi Minhag. In most other communities it was said, and it's still said, but in the Halabi tradition it is not said. They just immediately begin "VeAbraham Zaken Ba BaYamim." And this is the tradition of VeAbraham Zaken. Once again, Mabrook to the Hatan, Mabrook to the Kallah, Mabrook to all the wonderful families.

272.title: Wrapping the Talet the Halabi Way
272.text:
Even though one is not obligated to throw all four corners of their Talet over their left shoulder after reciting the blessing on the Talet, many have the custom to do so based on the writing of Rabbi Hayyim Vital in his book Sha'ar HaKavvanot, where he referred to what the Gemara described as 'Atifat Yishma'elim, the manner in which Arabs wrap themselves, and he reported that his teacher, the Arizal, used to wrap himself in that manner after reciting the blessing on the Talet.

Interestingly, there are some variations in the specifics of 'Atifat Yishma'elim among those that have the custom to wrap themselves in that manner when putting on their Talet. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo briefly described the manner in which it was customary to wrap the Talet in Halab in his book on the customs of Aram Soba. In his description, he wrote that the four corners of the Talet are gathered and thrown over the left shoulder, and left there for the amount of time that it takes to walk four Ammot, which is a few seconds.

In the commentary on this, which is called Mehkere Eress, and was written by Hakham Rahamim Moshe Sha'yo, who was Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo's grandson, he reported that he saw his grandfather put on his Talet, and that his grandfather did not wrap the Talet only on his head at first, as instructed by the Ben Ish Hai. His grandfather placed the Talet on his head, and let it drape down over his body, and then gathered all four corners of the Talet at once, and threw them over his left shoulder. This is also unlike the instructions of the Ben Ish Hai, where it says to first throw the two corners of the Talet on the right side over the left shoulder, wait a few seconds, and then to throw the two corners of the Talet on the left side over the left shoulder, and to wait a few more seconds.

Hakham Rahamim Sha'yo also wrote that his grandfather's custom of letting the Talet drape down over his body when he put it on his head was also the custom in the famous kabbalistic synagogue Bet El, which was in Jerusalem, as recorded by the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer in his commentary on Shulhan 'Arukh. And the Kaf HaHayyim also quoted Rabbi Yisrael Ya'akob Algazi, who lived in Turkey and Jerusalem at the beginning of the 18th century, and he wrote that the Talet should be worn over one's head and body from behind immediately after reciting the blessing on the Talet. He wrote this in his book Shalme Sibbur. Furthermore, our good friend Mr. Joseph Mosseri, in a recorded class, recalled seeing Hakham Ya'akob Kassin 'Alav HaShalom, our former chief rabbi, place the Talet over his head and body after reciting the blessing on the Talet.

Now for a demonstration. So, first I'm going to demonstrate the Halabi custom. So, after reciting the blessing on the Talet, you place the Talet over your head and let it drape down over your body, and then all four corners are gathered at once and placed over the left shoulder for a few seconds. This is unlike the instructions of the Ben Ish Hai, where first you gather the Talet in a way so that you can put it over your head only, and then while it's over your head only, first from the right side over the left shoulder, and then the left side over the left shoulder.

So, there are two differences in the manner of wrapping yourself in a Talet between the custom of Halab and the instructions found in the Ben Ish Hai. One difference is that the Halabi custom is not to wrap your head only at first, but rather to place the Talet over your head and let it drape down over your body. Secondly, the Halabi custom is to gather all four corners of the Talet at once and throw them over your left shoulder for a few seconds, as opposed to throwing the two corners from your right side over your left shoulder first, waiting a few seconds, and then throwing the two corners on your left side over your shoulder, and waiting a few more seconds.

273.title: Purim on the 15th of Adar in Halab
273.text:
Most places celebrate Purim on the 14th of Adar. However, cities that were enclosed with walls in the days of Yehoshua Bin Nun celebrate the holiday of Purim on the 15th of Adar. Therefore, the city of Jerusalem observes the holiday of Purim on the 15th of Adar. There are also several cities that are not sure if they were enclosed with walls during the times of Yehoshua Bin Nun. These cities include Teberyah, Hebron, Safed, 'Akko, Yafo, Lod, Be'er Sheba', and Haifa. In these cities, the Megillah is read on the 14th of Adar with Berakhot, and again on the 15th of Adar without reciting Berakhot.

According to Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, these cities should not read the Torah again for Purim on the 15th of Adar, but they should add 'Al HaNissim in the 'Amidah and Birkat HaMazon on both the 14th and 15th of Adar. And it is recommended to be stringent in those cities, and to give Mishloah Manot and Mattanot LaEbyonim again on the 15th of Adar, and also to have another festive meal on the 15th of Adar.

What was the custom in Halab? Mahzor Aram Soba, which was printed in the year 1527, includes instructions for the second night and second day of Purim. These instructions say that the prayers are exactly the same as the first day of Purim, except that the Megillah is read without Berakhot. From here we see that Halab was also considered a city that might have been enclosed with walls in the days of Yehoshua Bin Nun, and therefore in Halab, Purim was celebrated on both the 14th and 15th of Adar.

It is important to note that from the 16th century on, there were two separate Jewish communities in Halab: there were the Musta'arabim, who were the Jews who were living in Halab for centuries, at least since the times of the second Bet HaMikdash, and then there were the Sefaradim, the Spanish Jews who came to live in Halab in the 16th century. Mahzor Aram Soba was made by the Musta'arabi Jews, but what was the custom of the Sefaradim on the 15th of Adar?

From several sources, it appears that the main differences in practice between the Musta'arabim and the Sefaradim on the 15th of Adar was that the Musta'arabim read the Torah for Purim and added 'Al HaNissim in the 'Amidah and in Birkat HaMazon on the 15th of Adar, just like they did on the 14th of Adar, but that the Sefaradim did not. In Shulhan HaMelekh, that was written by Hakham Shemuel Laniado in the year 1804, it says that the Sefaradim only read the Torah for Purim on the 14th of Adar, but that the Musta'arabim read the Torah for Purim on both the 14th and 15th of Adar. In the first part of the 19th century, Hakham Abraham Antebi wrote in his book Hokhmah UMusar that the Musta'arabim also add 'Al HaNissim on the 15th of Adar, but that the Sefaradim did not.

In the beginning of the 20th century, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote in his book on the customs of Halab that when the 15th of Adar fell on a weekday, that the Sefaradim and the Musta'arabim would pray together and read the Torah for Purim. But when the 15th of Adar fell on Shabbat, the Musta'arabim and the Sefaradim prayed separately. The Musta'arabim took out two Sifre Torah and read the Purim reading from the second Sefer, and repeated the Haftarah from Parashat Zakhor, but that the Sefaradim only read the Torah for Purim on the 14th of Adar. Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo also specified that the Musta'arabim added 'Al HaNissim on the 15th of Adar, but that the Sefaradim did not.

The book Derekh Eress wrote that in more recent times in Halab, they did not add 'Al HaNissim or read the Torah for Purim on the 15th of Adar, but they did maintain the custom of reading the Megillah on the 15th of Adar without Berakhot. Furthermore, the book Derekh Eress specified that they did not give Mishloah Manot and Mattanot LaEbyonim again on the 15th of Adar, and that they did not eat another festive meal on the 15th of Adar, either.

So Halab was considered a city that might have been enclosed with walls in the times of Yehoshua Bin Nun. Therefore, they celebrated Purim on the 14th of Adar, but they read the Megillah again on the night and day of the 15th without reciting any Berakhot before or after the reading on the 15th. With regards to adding 'Al HaNissim and reading the Torah for Purim, this was practiced on both the 14th and 15th of Adar by the Musta'arabim, but only on the 14th of Adar by the Sefaradim. But eventually, everyone in Halab only added 'Al HaNissim and read the Torah for Purim on the 14th of Adar. It was only the Megillah that was read on both days. On the 14th, the Megillah was read with Berakhot, and on the fifteenth, the Megillah was read without reciting Berakhot.

274.title: Legumes and Rice on Pesah
274.text:
The original custom of Aleppo was not to eat dried legumes, such as beans, lentils, and chickpeas on Pesah. Therefore, foods such as Fasoulyeh, Mujadara, hummus, and tahineh were not served on Pesah in Halab. This custom was mentioned by Hakham Abraham Hamwey, who was born in Halab in the 19th century, in his Mahzor Bet HaBehirah, and it was also discussed in the book Derekh Eress. However, the book Derekh Eress noted that the custom of Halab changed during World War I when there were food shortages and the rabbis permitted all dried legumes for Pesah.

The reason for this custom is because it was common to grow, process, package, and sell dried legumes alongside wheat flour and other grains, which could become Hamess. Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi quoted Hakham Yisshak Tawil 'Alav HaShalom, who said that the reason for not having hummus on Pesah is not because the word hummus sounds like Hamess, but rather because hummus is a dried legume, and it is included in the custom of not eating dried legumes on Pesah.

In Halab, the custom of not eating dried legumes on Pesah did not extend to fresh legumes and vegetables, such as peas and string beans. Based on that, fresh corn would not be included in the custom to be stringent, but dried corn, such as popcorn, would not be eaten.

But it was customary to eat rice on Pesah in Halab. In the 19th century, Hakham Mordekhai Abadi wrote the following in his book Ashre Ha'Am: "And here in Aram Soba, everyone eats rice. No one is stringent, but they check it six or seven times very well until they wouldn't find any more wheat in the rice, even once in 50 years." Hakham Mordekhai Abadi was Hakham Douba Abadi's grandfather. Hakham Abraham Hamwey also wrote that the custom of Aleppo was to eat rice on Pesah in his Mahzor Bet HaBehirah. However, in the 20th century, it became customary to check the rice three times, as recorded by Hakham Yisshak Chehebar in his book Ro'eh Ne'eman.

What was the custom with regards to legumes and rice in other Middle Eastern and North African communities? In the beginning of the 20th century, in his book Eress Hayyim, Ribbi Hayyim Ben Asher Sethon wrote that the custom of the Sefaradim in Sefat, a city in northern Israel, was not to eat legumes on Pesah, with the exception of fresh beans that were moist, and that that was also the custom in Salonica, Greece.

Similarly, Ribbi Moshe Suissa documented the custom of Morocco in his book 'Ateret Abot of not eating dried legumes on Pesah, but they did eat fresh ones. He added that some Moroccans do not eat hummus on Pesah, but others do. He also wrote that most Moroccans do not eat rice on Pesah, but some did check the rice and eat it.

In the 19th century, in Baghdad, the Ben Ish Hai wrote in his book Rab Pe'alim that some were stringent and did not eat rice on Pesah, but that most people in Baghdad ate rice on Pesah after checking it three or four times. He also wrote that they were not stringent with legumes on Pesah, but they did not eat hummus on Pesah because the hummus was imported in sacks that were also used for flour, and that sometimes actual Hamess got stuck on the chickpeas. The Ben Ish Hai also noted the custom of Izmir, Turkey, of not eating rice on Pesah.

In the beginning of the 20th century, Ribbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on described the custom of Jerusalem in his book Sha'ar HaMifkad: among the Sefaradim, the rabbis and pious people were stringent and did not eat rice on Pesah, while others, especially those with limited means, were lenient. They were also lenient with the children and fed them rice on Pesah, and all were lenient with legumes and ate them on Pesah.

Interestingly, we find a difference in custom between Tunisia and Djerba, which is an island off the coast of Tunisia, with regards to eating legumes on Pesah. In Djerba, they ate rice and legumes, including hummus, but in Tunisia, they did not eat any legumes, but they did eat rice. The reason why they didn't eat hummus in Tunisia was because sometimes the chickpeas were roasted with Hamess. All this was recorded by Ribbi Moshe Khalfon HaKohen in his book Berit Kehunah, which was published in the year 1943.

So the original custom of Halab was to refrain from eating dried legumes on Pesah. The custom changed in Halab during World War I due to food shortages. Therefore, the custom is unknown to the families who came to our community from Halab in the 1990s. Furthermore, this custom was not preserved in the Halabi community in Argentina, under the leadership of Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, who was born in Halab in the year 1912, and grew up after the custom had already been changed in Halab. But here in New York, many families have preserved the custom, and still do not eat foods like Fasoulyeh, Mujadara, hummus, or tahineh on Pesah. However, it was always customary to eat rice on Pesah, after carefully checking the rice to make sure no wheat kernels were mixed in with the rice.

275.title: Forgotten Minhagim of Shabu'ot
275.text:
Shabu'ot, the holiday of Shabu'ot, a holiday whose Minhagim are being forgotten. Year after year, more and more Minhagim are being forgotten, they are being pushed aside, and I'd like to bring some of these Minhagim to light.

First and foremost, the synagogue, not the synagogue itself, but certain aspects of the synagogue are decorated with flowers and greenery. We've spoken in the past about when people have happy occasions, they would attach flowers to the Rimmonim of the Sefer Torah. This is the holiday of the giving of the Torah, so obviously, on this holiday of Shabu'ot, yes, flowers would be attached to the Rimmonim, but not just to the Rimmonim. The stairs going up to the Tebah, where the Hazzan or the Hakham would read the Sefer Torah, the stairs, the banister would also be adorned in greenery and flowers, as well as the entire guardrail around the Tebah where the Hazzan stands, where the Torah is placed, that would all be wrapped in greenery and flowers, sweet-smelling things.

And it was done because, based upon the Midrash and various commentaries by the Hakhamim, that when HaShem gave us the Torah, upon the utterances of each one of the Ten Commandments, the entire world would be filled with sweet-smelling fragrances of various flowers. That's one reason, but an even more connected reason to the holiday of Shabu'ot, Shabu'ot is known as Hag HaBikkurim. In the days of the Torah, the days of the Bet HaMikdash, it was the holiday of bringing of the first fruits. Obviously, the first fruits come from growth, and that growth starts with the budding of a flower, and those flowers are brought into the Bet Keneset to remind us another aspect of Hag HaShabu'ot that we can no longer do now, but it's a major part of the holiday as Hag HaBikkurim, and that is the flowers, the greenery, the growth. So, that's Minhag number one, decorating the Sefer Torah and the areas where the Sefer Torah is read with flowers and greenery.

We have another Minhag on Hag HaShabu'ot that the Torah is compared to water, "HaTorah Nimshelah LaMayim," and therefore, on the holiday of Shabu'ot, in other communities, like the Moroccan community, people would actually throw water on one another on this holiday. In Syria, it wasn't thrown, but rather sprinkled in a more gentle fashion, and not only water, but Mazahar and Maward as well, orange blossom water and rose water, to bring that sweet-smelling fragrance upon one another, and to bring the water aspect of it as well, which is comparable to water, as the Hakhamim tell us, the same way the water quenches your thirst, the Torah as well quenches your spiritual thirst.

Another Minhag that is forgotten is the Ketubah of Hag HaShabu'ot. It has been, in fact, removed from our Mahzorim. You open up the holiday Mahzor for Shabu'ot, and it's not even there anymore, whereas in the old Mahzorim, we had something called Ketubah LeHag HaShabu'ot. Here's an old Mahzor, as you can tell, it's pretty old, and here's the Ketubah LeHag HaShabu'ot. And it had a special tune. In the Halabi tradition, it was said at the Hekhal itself, and in the Shami tradition, it was said once the Torah was brought to the Tebah before commencing the reading of the Torah.

And it would go like this. It would also be in Maqam Huseini, as we've discussed in previous Shabu'ot videos, the whole theme of Shabu'ot is Maqam Huseini, Megillat Rut is in Maqam Huseini, the Azharot is in Maqam Huseini, the Ketubah itself also is in Maqam Huseini. "Yarad Dodi LeGanno La'Arugat Besamo LeHit'ales 'Im Bat Nedibim VeLifros 'Aleha Sukkat Shelomo," and then the entire congregation would respond, "Appiryon 'Asah Lo HaMelekh Shelomo," and it would continue like this for the entire Ketubah, which is about three pages long, so obviously lengthening the holiday prayers.

Not only that, the beauty of the holiday was in bringing the messages of the holiday to the masses. As we know, living in Arabic-speaking countries for centuries, the vernacular was Arabic, and therefore they wanted to bring the message home not only to the men and to the children, but to the women as well. So at home the Azharot would be read, and it would be read not only in Hebrew, but in Arabic as well. Here we have Azharot printed in Aleppo with Hebrew and Arabic, Judeo-Arabic.

The 'Aseret HaDibberot, or as some people know it, Ibtida Kalamna, that is said prior to Mattan Torah, usually on Shabbat Yitro, was also said in many homes in Halab and in Sham, because it explained the 'Aseret HaDibberot, the Ten Commandments, and the women could listen, and they could understand, and they could appreciate the beauty of Hag HaShabu'ot. So even if you look at the 'Aseret HaDibberot that was printed in Halab, it tells you Shabbat Mattan Torah. So they connected this Shabbat Mattan Torah to the Shabbat prior to Shabu'ot, which was called Shabbat Kallah, as well as on Shabu'ot, and they would read it then.

Not only that, but as my friend Morris Arking mentioned in one of his videos, he talked about that in Halab they not only read the Azharot, and not only read Rut, and did them both in Hebrew and in Arabic, but Mishle as well was studied. And here we go, this is Mishle that was translated into Judeo-Arabic as well for the people to be able to read and understand. And all these things were done either published in Halab, or published by Halabi rabbis in Yerushalayim.

So these are all ancient things that were done, and they filled up the entire day of Shabu'ot with Torah, with understanding for men, for women in the vernacular, the things that we're lacking today, okay? We don't, obviously, the majority of the people don't know Arabic today to understand it, but these things should be done publicly in our homes in English, or in whatever language is understood, to bring home the message of Hag HaShabu'ot, of Mattan Torah, of the Berakhah that Bore 'Olam has showered upon us. Have a wonderful holiday, Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

276.title: Verses from Tehillim When Putting on the Talet
276.text:
The custom has developed, based on the teachings of the students of the Arizal, to recite six verses from the book of Tehillim when putting on the Talet Gadol in the morning. The first two verses are from the beginning of Mizmor 104, which is the same Mizmor that is recited for Rosh Hodesh. These verses are: "Barekhi Nafshi Et Ad-onai, Ad-onai Elokai Gadalta Me'od, Hod VeHadar Labashta," followed by the next verse, "'Oteh Or KaSalmah, Noteh Shamayim KaYeri'ah."

According to the Siddur Bet 'Obed, these two verses are recited before reciting the blessing on the Talet, and then the other four verses, which are found in the middle of Mizmor 36, are recited after reciting the blessing and wrapping oneself with the Talet. These instructions are also found in the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer. The four verses are: "Mah Yakar Hasdekha Elokim, UBne Adam BeSel Kenafekha Yehesayun," "Yirveyun MiDeshen Betekha, VeNahal 'Adanekha Tashkem," "Ki 'Imekha Mekor Hayyim, BeOrekha Nir'eh Or," and "Meshokh Hasdekha LeYode'ekha, VeSidkatekha LeYishre Leb."

However, from Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo's book on the customs of Halab, it seems like all six verses were recited together after reciting the blessing and putting the Talet on your head and body, but before throwing all four corners of the Talet over your left shoulder.

Let me demonstrate. You would begin by holding the Talet and reciting the Berakhah of "LeHit'attef BeSissit." Then you put the Talet over your head and let it hang down over your body. At this point, you would recite the six verses from Tehillim, and then take all four corners, throw it over your left shoulder, hold it like this for a few seconds, and then lower the Talet onto your shoulders and wrap yourself.

Furthermore, the Siddur 'Olat HaShahar that was printed in Halab in the year 1915 only has the four verses from Mizmor 36, and it instructs you to say them after you recited the blessing for the Talet and wrapped the Talet on your head for a few seconds. While the Talet is still on your head, say the four verses beginning with "Mah Yakar Hasdekha Elokim." The Siddur Tefilat Yeshurun, which was very popular in our community from the 1930s through the 1960s, has all six verses. The first two appear before reciting the blessing, and the last four after the blessing.

So it seems that there are some variations regarding the reciting of the verses from Tehillim when putting on the Talet. The sources from Halab indicate that the verses were recited right after reciting the blessing and wearing the Talet, but before throwing the corners of the Talet over your left shoulder and wrapping it on your body. In any case, the verses should not be recited in between the blessing and wearing the Talet on your head and body. That would be an interruption between the blessing and the performance of the Missvah. Lastly, from all the sources, at least the four verses from Mizmor 36 were recited while wearing the Talet, not before wearing it.

277.title: Blowing the Shofar at a Funeral
277.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Blowing the Shofar at a Funeral. Blowing the Shofar at a funeral. Is it our Minhag? Is it not our Minhag? Is it something that was picked up here in America or did it really come from Aleppo? So, yes, it came from Aleppo. It did not come from the Spanish-Portuguese who have a Minhag to blow Shofar for their chief rabbi. It did not come from the Moroccans, even though we had prominent and important Moroccans involved in our Hebra, notably Ya'akob Arama and Rabbi Lankry. This is a Minhag that is an authentic Halabi Minhag. It came from Aleppo.

We know this because it's attested to by Hakham Abraham Shalom Hai Hamwey in his Dabek Me'ah, as well as Hakham Yosef Sha'yo in his book of Minhagim, as well as it was done at the funeral of the chief rabbi of the Halabi community of Argentina, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar when he passed away, it was done over there as well. So therefore, we know from these three sources it is a true Halabi custom.

Now, what do these Hakhamim write about the custom? Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Dabek Me'ah writes that when they would be preparing the body, washing the body and preparing it for burial, they would only blow the Shofar for a person that was well known as being Yere Shamayim, God-fearing, or for a Haber, Haber being a member of the Hebra Kaddisha, a member of the burial society. Only for these people would the Shofar be blown. And obviously it was not done in public at the funeral, but rather only when the Hebra would be preparing the body for burial.

But later on, we see that Hakham Yosef Sha'yo tells us that the Shofar was blown at the funeral, but only blown for who? For a Talmid Hakham. And when was it blown? It would be blown after the speeches were completed, then they would say Kaddish, and only after Kaddish would the Shofar be blown before taking the body out for burial.

Now, who would blow the Shofar? It would be a member of the Hebra Kaddisha, member of the burial society. In our community for many decades, who blew the Shofar? Either Mickey Kairey 'Alav HaShalom or Rabbi Lankry 'Alav HaShalom. Now with the passing of these two great men, some people think it's a free-for-all, and you'll notice various people come with Shofar in their jacket pocket, they want to blow the Shofar. It's up to members of the Hebra who blows, or if the family has a request, they can approach the rabbi that's officiating at the funeral as to who's going to blow, but should be only one person blowing, that's the proper way to do things.

Now, why is the Shofar blown? So we have various testimony to the Shofar being blown. In the Gemara, in Masekhet Megillah, we are told that the Shofar was blown for a Hakham. Why? Because when the Torah was given to 'Am Yisrael, Shofar was blown, the Hassosrot were blown, there was a lot of pomp and fanfare. And so they say, "KeNetinatah Kakh Netilatah," the same way the Torah was given, same way when the Torah is going away. So this person was a Talmid Hakham, and he toiled his entire life in studying the Torah, he cannot just leave the world without that same fanfare. He has to leave the same way the Torah was given, with the blowing of the Shofar, so he leaves the world with the blowing of the Shofar.

But elsewhere in the Gemara, in Masekhet Mo'ed Katan, it says that anytime a person would pass away, they would alert the members of the city, members of the town, members of the neighborhood by blowing the Shofar. That was an indication somebody has passed away, and people get ready, you know, for a funeral.

Hakham Shem Tob Gagin tells us that in other sources of the Mekubbalim, the reason for blowing the Shofar is that when a person passes away negative spiritual elements cling to the body, and the only way to get rid of them, according to the Mekubbalim, is to blow the Shofar, and the blast of the Shofar would basically push away these negative spiritual particles.

But now later on if we look at the Zohar in Parashat VaYakhel, it tells us that the early Hakhamim established the blowing of the Shofar at a funeral not for the Kabod, not for the honor of the deceased, but rather for the sake of the living. Meaning what? Meaning that those people that are alive that are coming to the funeral, okay, usually there's a lot of people, and since there is a body of a deceased, that means Mal'akh HaMavet, the angel of death, is hovering around. When this angel of death, according to the Zohar, sees so many people, he wants to take more people, okay? So to prevent a quote-unquote premature death for any of the people at the funeral, we blow the Shofar so the sound of the Shofar works as a Zekhut, as a merit for these people up in the Shamayim, and up in Shamayim, in the heavens, the heavenly court prevents the Mal'akh HaMavet from harming any of the people that are at the funeral.

So according to that reasoning, maybe the Shofar can be blown for anybody at any funeral, but the custom is that is blown for a Hakham, somebody that's Yir'e Shamayim, somebody that's a member of the Hebra Kaddisha, definitely only blown for men, never heard of it being blown for women, and based upon the sources, nothing indicates that it was blown for women. Even according to the Spanish-Portuguese Minhag, it's only blown for the chief rabbi, according for the, according to the Moroccan Minhag, it's only blown for a Talmid Hakham, for a rabbi. So it's really reserved in that sense.

We know that the blowing is done by a member of the Hebra, we've given reasons for it. How many times is the Shofar blown is finally the question that everybody asks. And the Halabi Minhag is 'Asarah Kolot, 10 sounds, meaning Tashrat, Tashat, Tarat. Okay? And for those who blow Shofar, they understand what that means. And we don't blow anymore. The Minhag of the Moroccans is different, the Minhag of the Spanish-Portuguese is different, but the Halabi Minhag: Tashrat, Tashat, Tarat. And that is conclusion of blowing Shofar at a funeral.

278.title: Kaddish Before the Haftarah on Tish'ah BeAb
278.text:
In two previous videos, I discussed Hakham Matloub Abadi's Responsum on the prayers for Tish'ah BeAb from his book Magen Ba'adi. In episode 218, I discussed Hakham Matloub's instructions to maintain the original customs of Halab, which are to read Ekhah before reciting 'Arbit, and not to recite a Haftarah in Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb. In episode 261, I discussed Hakham Matloub's instruction of not reciting Kaddish Titkabbal on the night of Tish'ah BeAb. And in this episode, I will discuss the fourth and final question that Hakham Matloub addressed in that Responsum, which is if the third 'Oleh recites Kaddish before the Haftarah in Shahrit of Tish'ah BeAb, or if he should recite the Kaddish after the Haftarah instead.

The question posed to Hakham Matloub was based on the custom of Egypt that was recorded by Ribbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on in his book on the customs of Egypt, which he called Nehar Missrayim. The custom of Egypt was that the third 'Oleh did not recite Kaddish until after reading the Haftarah in Shahrit on Tish'ah BeAb. According to Ribbi Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on, their custom was correct since the Kaddish would be an interruption between the Torah reading and the Haftarah.

However, Hakham Matloub disagreed, since the custom in other places was to recite Kaddish right after the Torah reading, before reading the Haftarah. Hakham Matloub supported his position by quoting the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer, who quoted several authorities that specified that the Kaddish is recited right after the reading of the Sefer Torah.

Furthermore, Hakham Matloub argued that Kaddish is only an interruption between the 'Olim. Meaning, if you recited Kaddish before sending up the minimum amount of 'Olim, the 'Olim that went up after the Kaddish do not combine with the 'Olim sent up before the Kaddish. But Kaddish is not considered an interruption between the Torah reading and the Haftarah. Hakham Matloub wrote that he found this argument in the book Yaskil 'Abdi, which was written by Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya. Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya supported this argument with our practice of reciting Kaddish after a second or third Sefer Torah on special Shabbatot and holidays before reading the Haftarah. And Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya also cited the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer and the authorities quoted there.

And lastly, Hakham Matloub quoted the book Bet Dino Shel Shelomo that was written by the Chief Rabbi of Halab, Ribbi Refael Shelomo Laniado, towards the end of the 18th century. He wrote that the custom is not to recite Kaddish after the Torah reading in Minhah of Yom Kippur, but they do recite Kaddish between the Torah reading and the Haftarah in Shahrit of Tish'ah BeAb, even though the Maftir is one of the required 'Olim of the day, meaning the third 'Oleh. So Hakham Matloub concluded that our custom of reciting Kaddish after the Torah reading before reciting the Haftarah in Shahrit of Tish'ah BeAb is both in accordance with the law and it's the Minhag Kadum, the earlier custom.

So to briefly summarize, Hakham Matloub supported all the original customs of Halab in his Responsum on the prayers of Tish'ah BeAb. He instructed our community to read Ekhah before praying 'Arbit, not to recite Kaddish Titkabbal on the night of Tish'ah BeAb, to recite Kaddish after the Torah reading in Shahrit before reading the Haftarah, and not to read a Haftarah in Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb. Tizku Lir'ot BeNehamat Siyyon UBeBinyan Yerushalayim BiMherah BeYamenu, Amen.

279.title: No Birkat Kohanim on Tish'ah BeAb Morning
279.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week, Tish'ah BeAb Birkat Kohanim. The question is, on Tish'ah BeAb morning in Shahrit, do we do Birkat Kohanim? Simple answer, our Minhag is definitely not. But let's explain what's going on, and let's understand why I'm bringing up this question.

So as we've known for centuries, the custom of almost every Sephardic community is not to do Birkat Kohanim on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb, rather it is only done during Minhah of Tish'ah BeAb. And this was the custom throughout Syria, Lebanon, Egypt, Iraq, Turkey, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Greece, Bulgaria, no matter where there was a Sephardic community, this was the custom. Question is, why has it changed? Or why is it on the verge of change? And this is due to the writings of Hakhamim from Yerushalayim 'Ir HaKodesh. In Yerushalayim, the Minhag is otherwise. The Minhag in Yerushalayim is to do Birkat Kohanim on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb. And rabbis from Yerushalayim who frequent our community, they visit our community, they write books, they teach members of our community, and they have a different custom there. And it seems that in the last decade or so, there are some Minyanim in our community that have instituted doing Birkat Kohanim based upon these teachings. And it's not that they wanted to usurp our Minhag, they were unfamiliar with our Minhag.

So, what is our Minhag based upon, and why should we uphold it? There are a number of Hakhamim that have dealt with the issue of Birkat Kohanim on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb. In a nutshell, they have likened it to a mourner in a house of mourning, a mourner who's a Kohen in a house of mourning. So, on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb, there is no question, we are all, the entire Jewish nation is in a state of mourning. Whether you're a Kohen, you're a Levi, Yisrael, we're all mourning, we're all very sad, we're sorrowful, we're not in the frame of mind to do Birkat Kohanim or to accept Birkat Kohanim.

How does this come into play? In a house of mourning, the mourner is very sad. He has no Shalom, she has no Shalom, there is no peace for these people. And to come with Birkat Kohanim, which is a Berakhah of Shalom, of peace, it concludes with the words "VeYasem Lekha Shalom," is not befitting. And if the Kohen himself is a mourner, he cannot go up to do Birkat Kohanim and repeat those words and bless the people. On the morning of Tish'ah BeAb, we ourselves are mourners. And so any Kohen among us cannot go up and say those words, so it doesn't fit in.

Now, this is not something that, you know, it's a nice connection, but rather these are big Hakhamim that have written about this. This goes back, it seems, the earlier sources we know about them from Italy, where the Shibbole HaLeket and the Tanya Rabbati, they write about it. And then we also have later on in Spain, we have Rabbi David Abudarham, then in Turkey, in Istanbul, we have Hakham Hayyim Ben Benveniste in his Keneset HaGedolah, and they all talk about this.

So some talk about the connection of 'Am Yisrael as mourners, and since mourners don't bless, all of us cannot bless on the morning of Tish'ah BeAb. There are those that say that there's the issue of Shalom and the Birkat Kohanim, and there are those that bring another Pasuk, a Pasuk from Yesha'yah. And the Pasuk in Yesha'yah says, "UBefarisekhem Kappekhem A'lim 'Enai Mikkem." "When you spread forth your arms, your hands, I will hide my eyes from you." And the Hakhamim explain this Pasuk to mean, at a time when you are full of sins among your fellow man, you have shed blood—doesn't have to necessarily be that you were a murderer of real blood, but you embarrassed a person, you humiliated a person—at that point, you need to rectify yourself first before HaShem wants to hear from you. So, how could you then, on a day that we're mourning, and we're talking about the concept of Sin'at Hinnam, how could we come and lift our hands to do Birkat Kohanim when we know God is turning His eyes away from us? So, it's another concept that some of the Hakhamim point out.

So, even though this was a custom in Jerusalem, and still is a custom in Jerusalem to do Birkat Kohanim on Yom Tish'ah BeAb Shahrit, our custom, like I said, the custom of our community, and it's clearly detailed to us. We know we have three different versions of the Tish'ah BeAb morning prayers. We have that put out by Young Shaare Zion, we have that put out by Rabbi Cherba in Sha'are Rahamim, and we have that put out by Tebah Publications. All three of them for the Syrian community, all clearly indicate not to do Birkat Kohanim in Shahrit, and that is the custom. We also have the Tish'ah BeAb prayer book from the Syrian community in Argentina, which also says we do not do Birkat Kohanim. We also have the Tish'ah BeAb book of the Egyptian community here in Brooklyn, which also says no Birkat Kohanim.

This is a very, very clear custom. It's written about in many places. Some people want to say, "Well, the Ben Ish Hai says to say Birkat Kohanim." Ben Ish Hai, in fact, in Parashat Tessaveh, says do not do Birkat Kohanim, and that is the custom in Baghdad even, not to do Birkat Kohanim. So, this is our custom, it's a custom to uphold, and hopefully we will have Shalom, we have Shalom as we're ending the fast, during Minhah, we say Birkat Kohanim, and hopefully this will be the end of Tish'ah BeAb as a mournful, sorrowful day.

280.title: Eating Nuts on Rosh HaShanah
280.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Can we eat nuts on Rosh HaShanah? Yes, we can. Let's explain what's going on. In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo brings down the list of symbolic foods eaten on the night of Rosh HaShanah. Afterwards, Muram, Rabbi Moshe Isserles in his Hagahot, in his glosses to Shulhan 'Arukh, writes: "Yesh Medakdekim SheLo Le'ekhol Egozim." There are those that are scrupulous to not eat walnuts. And nowadays due to social media, people think this is either a law or a custom, and it is neither. It is not a law, and it's definitely not our custom. Let me explain.

What is the source of this statement by Muram? The source is Maharil. Maharil was a rabbi from Germany from the 14th century, and he writes very clearly: "Kol Dabar HaMebi Kihah VeNi'ah Asur Le'ekhol BeRosh HaShanah, UMitta'am Zeh Yesh Nizharim MiLe'ekhol Egozim BeRosh HaShanah Kodem HaTeki'ot Mishum DeMarbim Lehah." Anything that can cause a person to have excess phlegm, mucus, coughing, etc., is forbidden to be eaten on Rosh HaShanah, and due to this reason, there are those that are careful to not eat walnuts on Rosh HaShanah before the blowing of the Shofar, because it causes this extra wetness, which is of obviously would cause a person to cough or to be constantly clearing their throat.

Now, plain and simple, we don't eat while we're praying, we don't eat before blowing of the Shofar, and his concern over here is that either the person blowing the Shofar is going to not be able to blow properly because he's going to have that excess mucus, or the person that's supposed to be listening is going to be clearing his throat or coughing and not hear properly, or he's going to be interrupting the person next to him due to his constantly clearing his throat. That's point number one. Point number two, we know now scientifically that this is completely untrue, that walnuts do not cause mucus, they do not cause phlegm, they do not cause a person to cough, unless of course the person has an allergy to walnuts or other nuts, and then they could cause such a reaction. That's point number one.

Point number two, later on a different reason was attached to not eating walnuts, and they said Egoz in Gimatriya, the numerical value of Egoz, which is 17, is equivalent to the word Het, sin. Technically, also incorrect because the word Het technically equals 18. They tell you, "Well, the word Het has a silent Alef, so we look at it as if it's 17 and not 18." The word Egoz equals 17. 17 equals Tob. Tob is good. And therefore, there is nothing wrong with Egoz. Egoz is good.

Now, we need to realize that the Hida, Rabbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, a great Sefaradi Hakham who traveled the world and lived in the 17th and 18th centuries and wrote extensively—he wrote close to 70 books on all aspects of the Torah—and throughout Shulhan 'Arukh he added his own glosses as well, he mentions nothing about a custom of not eating nuts on Rosh HaShanah. He talks about not eating salty foods, or overly spicy foods, or sour foods, or lemony foods, or vinegary foods, or very dark-looking foods, but he mentions nothing about not eating nuts.

In fact, in his commentary on Sefer Hasidim, he writes about how Shir HaShirim Rabbah, the Midrash on Shir HaShirim which has a Pasuk "El Ginat Egoz Yaradti," comparing 'Am Yisrael to the walnut, and how even though all the different types of spiritual adversaries come up against Yisrael, Yisrael is like a walnut: it has a hard outer shell, we're resilient, we're able to be, you know, we take the abuse, but then we're able to wash off these 'Avonot, wash off all the sins, and we come out following the Torah and Missvot. So there's nothing wrong connecting Egoz over here to 'Am Yisrael.

Also, the concept of saying, well, we don't, we want to avoid the word Egoz on Rosh HaShanah because it's like the word Het. Also, you know, in the same section where Muram is putting his Hagahot about not eating walnuts, he talks about doing Seder VeTashlikh. And Seder VeTashlikh is about what? Throwing away the sins, like the Pasuk says, "VeTashlikh BiMessulot Yam Kol Hattotam," throwing out into the depths of the sea all our sins. So the word sins are mentioned in the same paragraph, and we are not attaching ourself to sins by eating nuts, we're attaching ourselves to good, and showing how we are the good aspect of the walnut.

Now, in all these books that you see behind me in each and every episode, these are books of our Sephardic communities, of their Minhagim, and no community has a custom of not eating walnuts on Rosh HaShanah. We eat walnuts, we eat almonds, we eat pistachios, we have no problem whatsoever with this. So enjoy the holiday, enjoy your foods, Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

281.title: How the Talet Is Worn During Prayers
281.text:
In Episode 272, we discussed how to wrap ourselves with a Talet after reciting the blessing. And in Episode 276, we talked about the verses recited when putting on a Talet. In this episode, we will talk about the manner in which a Talet is worn during the prayers.

If you look at how most people in our community today wear their Talet, you will find that they fold the front corners over each shoulder, like this. This manner of wearing the Talet is actually recorded in Shulhan 'Arukh. Maran wrote that one should wear their Talet with two Sissiyot in front of them and two Sissiyot behind them, in order to be surrounded with Missvot. In the Bet Yosef, Maran attributed this practice to the Ba'al Ha'Ittur, which was written in France in the 12th century, and to the Sefer HaRokeah, which was written in Germany around the beginning of the 13th century. Maran also quoted the Hagahot Maimoniyot, which was also written in Germany in the 13th century.

However, this manner of wearing the Talet was not the common practice in the Middle East and North Africa. In his responsa Mayim Hayyim, Hakham Yosef Messas discussed the custom of the world to wear a Talet with all four corners of the Talet in front, like this. Rabbi Messas was a rabbi from Morocco who came to Israel in the 1960s, where he eventually became the chief rabbi of Haifa.

Rabbi Messas made the following points: The general custom is to gather all four corners of the Talet in front of you, like this, before Keri'at Shema. Whereas according to Maran, you only hold the two Sissiyot that are in front of you during Keri'at Shema. This shows that the custom with regards to the position of the Talet corners is not in accordance with the opinion of Maran. Furthermore, we are already surrounded with Missvot when we wear a Talet Katan under our clothing or with the knot on the back of our head from the Tefillin Shel Rosh. Lastly, he points out that even according to Maran, one does not have to wear their Talet with two corners in the front and two corners in the back in order to fulfill the Missvah of Sissit. It is only a nice practice in order to be surrounded with Missvot.

What was the custom in Halab? Rabbi Moshe Perez from Mexico quoted Hakham Shelomo, the son of Hakham Abraham Zafrani, as saying that most people in Halab wrapped their upper body with the Talet with all four corners in front of them, in between their hands and their bodies. This is identical to how Rabbi Messas described the customary way to wear a Talet. However, the rabbis in Halab did wear their Talet with two corners in the front and two corners in the back, in order to follow what Maran wrote in Shulhan 'Arukh.

Rabbi Perez also quoted HaRab Ya'akob Hayyim, who is the Ben Ish Hai's son, who wrote in the book Yede Hayyim that one fulfills the Missvah of Sissit in any manner that they wear their Talet. So while Maran wrote that it's proper to wear a Talet with two corners in the front and two corners in the back, this is not a halakhic requirement in order to fulfill the Missvah of Sissit, and therefore many Middle Eastern and North African Jews had the custom to wrap themselves in a Talet with all four corners in the front. What is not proper is to wear the Talet while it's still folded or rolled up on your neck like a scarf, like this. But if the Talet is unfolded, you can wrap yourself in various ways.

The prevalent custom in Halab and in Brooklyn in previous generations was to wrap the upper body with all four corners in the front. However, the rabbis would follow Maran's instruction in Shulhan 'Arukh and wear their Talet with two corners in the front and two corners in the back, like this.

282.title: Tefillin of Rabbenu Tam
282.text:
SCA Minhag of the Week: Tefillin of Rabbenu Tam. So as we know, every morning we wear Tefillin, and our Tefillin are generally referred to as Rashi. And there is another pair of Tefillin called Rabbenu Tam. Let me explain.

There is in the Rosh, in the head of the Tefillin, there are four compartments, and in each compartment there is a chapter of the Torah that has to be there. So there's an order as to what goes in the first compartment, second compartment, third compartment, fourth compartment. Based upon the understanding of Rashi, which is also the understanding of Rambam, the order has to be first Kadesh Li, then VeHayah Ki Yebi'akha, and then Shema' Yisrael, and then VeHayah Im Shamoa'. And this is the standard practice of all Jews, Sefaradim and Ashkenazim, and it's currently referred to as Tefillin of Rashi.

There is another opinion, there are many other opinions, but another famous opinion, and that is the opinion of Rabbenu Tam, who happened to have been the grandson of Rashi, and his opinion was no, you have to have the two VeHayahs, the VeHayah Ki Yebi'akha and the VeHayah Im Shamoa', as the two middle compartments, flanked by Kadesh Li on one side and Shema' Yisrael on the other side. As we know, we follow plain Halakhah with the Tefillin of Rashi, Rambam, and that's what we pray with.

In recent times, and very recent times I should say, we're seeing many, many, many men that are wearing two Tefillin. And what are they doing? They're taking off their Tefillin after they finish the 'Amidah, they're taking off the Rashi Tefillin, and they're putting on Rabbenu Tam Tefillin. And while after they put it on, they recite the Parashiyot of VaYedabber and VeHayah Ki Yebi'akha and Shema' and VeHayah Im Shamoa', and then they'll continue their prayers with them and then remove them. Why didn't we see this before? What's going on? Is this our custom? Is it not our custom?

So the custom is, and this is very clear, that only the greatest of rabbis wore both types of Tefillin, and they had very small Tefillin, and they wore them together. Well known for this was our first chief rabbi, Chief Rabbi Dr. Jacob S. Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom. He wore two Tefillin together. And his son, chief rabbi after him, Rabbi Shaul Kassin, also wore two Tefillin together. And there were a few other great rabbis that did this. But everybody else, nobody wore another pair of Tefillin. They only wore the Rashi Tefillin, and nothing else.

What is the Halakhah? The Halakhah tells you, Maran Shulhan 'Arukh in Siman Lamed-Dalet, and we don't generally like to touch Halakhah in Minhag of the Week, but we have to to understand what's going on. So he tells us the Minhag of the world is to wear the Tefillin of Rashi or Rambam, whatever we want to call it. And he says, but because of the other opinion, you know, it's good to fulfill the other opinion. But then he tells us: "Lo Ya'aseh Khen Ella Mi SheMuhzak UMfursam BaHasidut." This is not for everybody to do! The only person or the only people that should be doing this, wearing two Tefillin, are those individuals that are well known to be extremely pious. In other words, great Hakhamim. It's not for the average person. But nowadays we see the average person doing this. And also if you look at Shulhan 'Arukh carefully, and you look at all the Sephardic sources carefully, they all talk about wearing the two Tefillin together, not one after the other. Again, they had small Tefillin.

Now, what was the Minhag in Aleppo? Everybody keeps asking me, did people do this? So yes, there were times where there were Hakhamim who wore two Tefillin together. Looking at the writings of Hakham Abraham Antebi in his Ohel Yesharim, he was the chief rabbi of Halab in the 1800s, yes, he talks about people who wore two Tefillin together. Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Bet HaKapporet also talks about it, okay, but neither one mentions it as a common custom, just that there were those who did it.

Let's move to our more modern times, to the 20th century. So Hakham Yisshak Chehebar in his Yisshak Yeranen was asked the question, do we wear two Tefillin? And he writes very, very clearly that only Talmide Hakhamim, only the rabbis, would wear two Tefillin. Some wore it together, and some prayed only with the Rashi Tefillin in Kenis, and only after that they went home and privately put on their Rabbenu Tam Tefillin and recited the four Parashiyot with the Rabbenu Tam Tefillin on at home, not in the Bet Keneset.

And we have the testimony of Hakham Yisshak Tawil regarding his father, Hakham Moshe Tawil, who was the chief rabbi of Aleppo, and he said that my father never wore two Tefillin together in the Bet Keneset. Only once he finished praying with the Rashi Tefillin in the Bet Keneset, he would go home and privately put it on. And most people never knew that he did this. This was a private matter. This was not something that was done by the common folk, and nowadays that we're seeing everybody doing it, and they are not Muhzak BeHasidut, they are not known as being, you know, scrupulous, religious, pious individuals, they should not be doing it based upon the traditions that we have upheld based upon Shulhan 'Arukh. And that is our Minhag.

283.title: The Talet Katan in Halab
283.text:
According to the law, one is only obligated to wear Sissit if they are wearing a four-cornered garment, but one is not obligated to wear a four-cornered garment. Still and all, the custom has developed to wear a Talet with Sissit when praying Shahrit in the morning, and a Talet Katan under one's clothing during the day.

In Mishneh Torah, HaRambam wrote that a pious person should always make an effort to be wrapped in a garment that requires Sissit in order to fulfill that Missvah, and when one is praying, one should be most careful to do so. So while HaRambam is not referring to the type of garment that we call a Talet Katan, or as was commonly referred to as Arba' Kanfot, he encouraged wearing a Talet all day, or at the very least when praying.

In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote, it is good and proper for everyone to be careful and wear a Talet Katan all day in order to remember the Missvot every minute, and then he concluded, at least be careful to wear Sissit when praying. So Maran refers to the Talet Katan that is worn today and suggests that everyone should wear it all day. So we see the concept of wearing Sissit all day is already mentioned by HaRambam, and later on, Maran specifically referred to the Talet Katan, recommending it for everyone.

Later, we see various discussions about wearing a Talet Katan by the rabbis of Halab. In the 19th century, Hakham Mordekhai Abadi wrote the following in his book Kishre Ha'Am: "Here in Aram Soba, our custom is not to recite a blessing on the Talet Katan, except when it's worn on Friday evening. And every night we sleep with it, we don't take it off. And when we recite the blessing in the synagogue on the Talet Gadol, we have it in mind to cover the Talet Katan." However, Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi wrote that the custom of the Halabi community in Argentina is never to recite a blessing on the Talet Katan. Similarly, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar writes about having the Talet Katan in mind when reciting the blessing on the Talet Gadol. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote about the Sefaradi custom of wearing both the garment and the Sissiyot of the Talet Katan under one's clothing, even though Maran writes to wear it on top of our clothing in Shulhan 'Arukh.

Furthermore, Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi quoted a letter from Hakham Sa'adeh Harari that was recorded in the book Magen Shelomo by Rabbi Shelomo Tawil that stated it is customary to wrap 39 loops with the Sissiyot on each corner of the Talet Gadol and 26 loops on each corner of the Arba' Kanfot, which, as we said, is referring to a Talet Katan. However, the book Derekh Eress plainly stated that they put 26 loops on Sissit, and Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi quoted Hakham Yisshak Tawil, who told him that it was 26 loops on both a Talet Gadol and on a Talet Katan. But Hakham Mordekhai Abadi wrote that the custom of Aleppo is 39 loops on the Sissit. It's noteworthy to mention that Hakham Mordekhai Abadi was Hakham Matloub Abadi's grandfather, and Hakham Matloub Abadi was, of course, a prominent Posek in our community from the 1920s until he passed away on the first day of January in 1970.

So we see discussions among the rabbis of Halab in the 19th and 20th centuries about various questions regarding a Talet Katan. From their writings, it's clear that it was customary to wear a Talet Katan in Halab. This is based on what Maran wrote in Shulhan 'Arukh.

The prevalent custom today is to cover the Talet Katan with a blessing on the Talet Gadol, to wear the Talet Katan and the Sissiyot under our clothing, and to wind 39 loops on each corner. Still and all, one can still maintain the custom of 26 loops. As we said previously, even in Halab, some wrapped 39 loops, while others wrapped 26 loops. When wrapping 39, the first section of the knots gets seven loops, the second section gets eight loops, the third section gets 11 loops, and the fourth section gets 13 loops. When wrapping 26 loops, it's based on the name Yod-Keh-Vav-Keh, so the first section is 10 loops, the second section is five loops, the third section is six loops, and the fourth and final section would get five loops.

284.title: Customs of a Siyum Masekhta
284.text:
Siyum, customs associated with a Siyum Masekhta. What is a Siyum exactly? So there are 63 volumes of Mishnah. On the Mishnah, there is the Gemara, and the Gemara is the explanation of the Mishnah. From these 63 volumes of Mishnah, there are 37 volumes of the Gemara from the Talmud Babli, the Babylonian Talmud, or 39 Masekhtot from Talmud Yerushalmi, from the Jerusalem Talmud. Generally when we refer to a Siyum, for most people a Siyum is the completion of a volume of one of the volumes of the Talmud Babli, of the Babylonian Talmud, so that's one of the 37 volumes.

What goes on? So basically after intensive study and learning, it's a very, very happy occasion, and a Siyum occurs. What is the source of this? The source of this is a statement by Abaye in Masekhet Shabbat, where he says, "Teti Li DeKhi Hazena Surba MiDeRabbanan DeShalim Masekhteh 'Abidna Yoma Taba LeRabbanan." He goes, "It was my practice anytime I would see the rabbinical students complete a tractate, a volume of Gemara, I would make it into a holiday for them, to a party and a holiday for them." And this became a very big thing that became a tradition in the Jewish nation for many generations and centuries, in fact, to our present day.

While this was not something that was commonly known in our communities, and for most people when they hear Siyum, they think of the Fast of the Firstborn on 'Ereb Pesah, it is nonetheless a practice of those who study Gemara, and even in the old country it was those who study the Zohar, they would have a Siyum on Zohar and conduct a festive event. In any case, let's talk about Siyum Masekhet of Gemara, because that's the most common thing today.

What customs are involved with it? First of all, when we finish the Gemara, there is a prayer at the end called the Hadran 'Alakh. And this is basically a prayer that we say saying that Gemara, we studied you, but we're not neglecting you going forward. We're going to keep repeating you, we're going to come back to you and study you again, and we're going to keep repeating you again and learning you again.

And followed by that, we say a prayer where numerous members of the Rab Pappa family are mentioned. Specifically, 10 sons of Rab Pappa. Rab Pappa is one of the important Hakhamim in the Gemara, and 10 sons are mentioned. There are various reasons as to why these sons are mentioned. The two most common reasons are that these 10 sons were very, very generous and very wealthy and very generous, and anytime there was a Siyum, they would go and donate for the Siyum and put out a big party, a big spread. And therefore in their memory, we would always remember them at a Siyum Masekhta. Another explanation is that these 10 sons were all murdered on one day by the Persians, and therefore as a memorial prayer to them at the end of the Gemara, we mention their names in remembrance of them, followed by Kaddish.

We're saying Kaddish afterwards. Which Kaddish is said? If we look at the older printings of the Gemara, okay, let's start with the first printing of the Gemara which was published in Venice between the years of 1510 and 1513, we just see regular Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, what we know as Kaddish DeRabbanan. We don't see a different type of Kaddish. In most Masekhtot of Gemara printed throughout the world, we only see this same Kaddish. It's only in the last century, century and a half, the Gemarot coming out of Poland started printing a different Kaddish, a Kaddish that we know as among Sefaradim we know it as Kaddish Targum or Kaddish DeHu 'Atid LeHaddata 'Alma, which we generally only recite on Tish'ah BeAb, or among certain Sephardic communities it's recited at the burial of the deceased. It is not our custom to say this Kaddish at a Siyum Masekhet. And we know this, obviously we know this from oral tradition, but it's clearly written in Keter Shem Tob of Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin, who records our Halakhot and Minhagim, and it's written in various other places as well that we do not say that Kaddish at a Siyum Masekhet, regular—we, rather, we say the regular Kaddish 'Al Yisrael, as it was printed in the older Gemarot.

There are those who have asked, are there any certain Pizmonim that are associated with a Siyum? In fact, there are Pizmonim for a Siyum. We don't have them printed in any one place, but I have a old 1921 Pizmon book from Hakham 'Ezra Mishanieh, and Hakham 'Ezra Mishanieh in the table of contents actually wrote down which Pizmonim are for a Siyum. There aren't many of them. I could just name a few of them quickly. You have Refa Siri, we have El Ram Berikh, Man'ime Hatan, Ram Ben 'Amram, Ram DeHasdakh, Hanun VeRahem, and a few others. All in all, about 10 or 12 Pizmonim that are specifically marked by Hakham 'Ezra Mishanieh for a Siyum. Obviously that was tradition that he had, that he brought over from Halab with him.

Others have asked, on a day that somebody's making a Siyum, is it Yehi Shem, is it Ana? So this is not something we find in the older Siddurim or the older compilations of Halakhah, but in newer Siddurim, books published in the last 10, 20 years, you do see that it mentions a Siyum among issues that are considered a Se'udat Missvah, like a Pidyon HaBen or a Berit Milah or a groom, and says that if a Siyum is happening immediately before a prayer or immediately after a prayer, and those involved in the Siyum are there at the prayer, so in that prayer you would omit Tahanunim, you would omit supplications and confession, and only say Yehi Shem. That would apply whether we're talking about Shahrit or Minhah.

As far as Kiddush, some people have asked, do you need a cup of wine and to say Kiddush? So because it's a Se'udat Missvah, as we mentioned, if it's a wedding, which is a Se'udat Missvah, or a Berit Milah, Se'udat Missvah, or Pidyon HaBen, Se'udat Missvah, we consider Siyum Masekhet also Se'udat Missvah, and the same way we have a cup and we make Kiddush, we say Sabri Maranan and Berakhah, Bore Peri HaGefen at all these occasions, we do the same thing at the Siyum Masekhet. And these are the Minhagim associated with Siyum Masekhta.

285.title: Blessing Before or After Shabbat Candles
285.text:
The Gemara, Masekhet Pesahim, taught: "Kol HaMissvot Mebarekh 'Alehen 'Ober La'Asiyatan." The blessing recited when performing all of the Missvot is recited immediately prior to performing the Missvah. Based on that principle, HaRambam wrote regarding lighting candles for Shabbat: "VeHayyab LeBarekh Kodem Hadlakah," and one is obligated to recite the blessing before lighting. Just to clarify, when I say candles, I am not referring specifically to wax candles, as traditionally we lit cups of oil in honor of Shabbat and holidays.

Now, Rabbi Moshe Isserles, a halakhic authority from Poland in the 16th century, who we commonly refer to as Muram, wrote in a note appended to Shulhan 'Arukh that some recite the blessing on Shabbat candles before lighting, and there is one who says to recite the blessing after lighting, and they do not enjoy the light until after reciting the blessing, and therefore they place a hand in front of the candles after lighting, and then recite the blessing, and then move their hand away so the blessing is recited before enjoying the light, and that's the custom.

This custom of reciting the blessing after lighting is based on a concern that perhaps the law is in accordance with the opinion of the Ba'al Halakhot Gedolot, a Babylonian halakhic authority from the 8th century, who ruled that one automatically accepts Shabbat when lighting the Shabbat candles, and there are some who explain that the acceptance takes effect when the blessing is recited; therefore, they light the candles before reciting the blessing. However, according to Maran, one is only obligated to accept Shabbat when lighting Shabbat candles if they're lighting the Shabbat candles more than 30 minutes before sunset. Furthermore, according to Maran, one only accepts Shabbat when lighting Shabbat candles after they completed lighting, not after reciting the blessing.

Still in all, the custom of lighting Shabbat candles before reciting the blessing spread to many Middle Eastern communities. Lighting before reciting the blessing was supported by the Hida in his book Mahzik Berakhah, and by Ribbi Hayyim Palachi in his book Hayyim LaRosh. Furthermore, according to the Ben Ish Hai, the woman recites the blessing with her hand over her closed eyes after lighting the candles, and reciting the blessing after lighting was also practiced in Morocco and Djerba.

What was the custom in Halab? In the book Shulhan HaMelekh, which was written in Halab in the year 1804 by Ribbi Shemuel Laniado, it says that there is a difference of opinion about reciting the blessing before or after lighting, and the Hida agreed to recite the blessing after lighting in his book Mahzik Berakhah. So while Rabbi Laniado doesn't record what the prevalent custom of Halab was in his time, he did lend support to lighting before reciting the blessing. And in the book 'Aba 'Ezra, which records the writings of Hakham 'Ezra Attieh and his students, it says the custom of the Sefaradim in most places is to light before reciting the blessing.

There is also a story that is recorded in the book Abir HaRo'im, which is a biography of Hakham 'Obadia Yosef that was written by his grandson, Ya'akob Sasson. Hakham 'Obadia was visiting Hakham 'Ezra Attieh in his home and persuading him that lighting before reciting the blessing was incorrect. When Hakham 'Ezra Attieh agreed with Hakham 'Obadia, Hakham 'Obadia Yosef suggested that Hakham 'Ezra Attieh tell his wife to change her custom and start reciting the blessing before lighting from now on. Hakham 'Ezra called his wife over and told her that Hakham 'Obadia said that she should start reciting the blessing before lighting the Shabbat candles, but she politely declined to change what she was already accustomed to doing. So there definitely were Halabi families that practiced the custom of lighting before reciting the blessing for Shabbat candles.

However, the book Derekh Eress quoted Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, who said that the custom of Halab was to recite the blessing before lighting. And Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote in his book Yisshak Yeranen that the custom of Halab was to recite the blessing before lighting the Shabbat candles. Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi quoted both those who lit before reciting the blessing, like Hakham Ya'akob Attieh and Hakham 'Obadia Hedaya and Hakham Abraham Harari-Raful, and he also quoted the custom of those that recited the blessing first, including Hakham Yisshak Chehebar and other knowledgeable members of the Halabi community in Argentina. Lastly, he quoted Ribbi Hayyim HaKohen from Aram Soba, who was a student of Ribbi Hayyim Vital, who started the blessing before lighting, and then lit while reciting the last three words of the blessing. So from here we see that in Halab, some families lit before reciting the blessing, while others lit after reciting the blessing.

From a halakhic standpoint, Sefaradim are not obligated to accept Shabbat when lighting Shabbat candles, unless we are lighting more than 30 minutes before sunset, and even then, we don't accept Shabbat until we are finished lighting. And reciting the blessing after lighting is problematic, because we can only recite a blessing after performing a Missvah, if we are still performing the Missvah when we recite the blessing. Like, if we are still wearing a Talet, we could still recite the blessing, or we're still wearing our Tefillin, we could still recite the blessing, or if we still—or if we are still sitting in the Sukkah, we could still recite the blessing. But with regards to lighting the candles, after the act of lighting, you are not still performing the Missvah. So reciting the blessing afterwards would be considered a blessing said in vain. So if one does not have a clear family custom to light first, the blessing should be recited before lighting the Shabbat candles.

286.title: One Berakhah, Then Lighting the Hanukkah Candles
286.text:
An interesting Hanukkah custom that was very commonplace up to about 20 years ago has been disappearing. What is that custom? I'm going to read from Keter Shem Tob, Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin, who mentioned many times before. He writes as this: "UBeEress Yisrael, BeSuryah, VeTogarmah, Missrayim, Ve'Are HaMa'arab, VeHidlik Ahar SheBerakh LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah, UBe'Od SheHolekh UMadlik, Mebarekh HaBerakhot HaAharonot."

On the nights of Hanukkah when you light, you first say the Berakhah of LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah, and then you immediately begin lighting. And as you are lighting, you continue and say the rest of the Berakhot, meaning She'asah Nissim, or on the first night She'asah Nissim and Sheheheyanu. And then obviously afterwards you would continue with HaNerot Hallalu and Mizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid.

In recent years we see that people have abandoned this Minhag. I think it's more that they've forgotten the Minhag, because many books of Halakhah say to say all three Berakhot or all two Berakhot, depending what night it is, prior to lighting, and they have forgotten their custom or they haven't paid attention to it. This custom, as we see, is well-documented in Keter Shem Tob. Rabbi 'Obadia Hedaya in his De'ah VeHaskel, volume seven, item number 17 discusses over there as well. This is based upon the Rashash, meaning based upon the Mekubbalim, and the Mekubbalim say that that is the proper way, and that was the Minhag in Yeshibat Bet El of Yerushalayim, as attested to in the book Dibre Shalom.

Now, there are those who say, "Well, what was the Minhag in Halab?" So we just saw that Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin tells us that this was the custom in Israel, in Syria, in Turkey, in Egypt, in North Africa, in other words, right the gamut of the Middle East and North Africa this was the custom. But was it everybody's custom? No, it probably wasn't everybody's custom. There were those who did otherwise, and we have testimony in Shulhan HaMelekh of Rabbi Laniado from Halab, where he doesn't tell us the exact custom, but he does quote Muram, okay, which basically is usually the Ashkenazi practices of lighting after all the Berakhot, and he brings that over there, something he generally doesn't do. So that may be an indication that was the Minhag in Halab. Later on the Ben Ish Hai from Baghdad, Iraq wrote to say the Berakhah after all three Berakhot. In later years, especially, you know, in the '40s, '50s, and '60s, the Ben Ish Hai became very popular in Halab, and we see in the writings of Rabbi Yisshak Chehebar, who was the rabbi of the Halabi community in Argentina, he writes in his writings that the Minhag is to make the all three Berakhot and then light. So we see even in Halab there may have been two Minhagim.

Why do I know that at least we did the Minhag, the first Minhag, as that quoted by Keter Shem Tob of doing one Berakhah and then lighting? Because that was the common practice throughout the community. In every synagogue, you would see when they would light, first Berakhah would be said and then lighting would begin. This morning in fact, a number of people came up to me and said, "I remember my father always said the first Berakhah and then he lit." And these are all mainstream families, families that you know, and this was the custom, the prevalent custom.

Now, this is not a custom that's only based upon Kabbalah. In fact, we could trace it all the way as far back as Masekhet Soferim, which was written in the eighth century Eress Yisrael, where they write over there that the practice is to make the Berakhah of LeHadlik Ner Hanukkah and to light. And after that, listen to this, after the first Berakhah and lighting, then say HaNerot Hallalu, then say Sheheheyanu, and then finally say She'asah Nissim La'Abotenu. So obviously they don't seem that we have to connect the Berakhot of Sheheheyanu and She'asah Nissim directly to the lighting, rather the lighting and then HaNerot Hallalu.

So therefore our practice, and the common practice of making the Berakhah of the Hadlakat Ner Hanukkah, and then immediately lighting, and then continuing with the other Berakhot followed by HaNerot Hallalu UMizmor Shir Hanukkat HaBayit LeDavid, is very, very well-established and very, very old, based upon both the Peshat, the simple rendition of the Halakhah, as well as the Sod, the Kabbalah, the mystical rendition. Happy Hanukkah.
