287.title: The Fasts of Shobabim
287.text:
When we think of fast days, we think of Kippur, Tish'ah BeAb, and then the minor fasts: Som Gedalyah, 'Asarah BeTebet, Shib'ah 'Asar BeTammuz, Ta'anit Ester, and that's it. We don't think there are any other fast days. But in fact, in Syria, in Egypt, in Tunisia, in Libya, in Eress Yisrael, and many other Sephardic communities, there were other fasts. In fact, those fasts were called Shobabim. Shobabim is an acronym for the Parashiyot Shemot, VaEra, Bo, Beshallah, Yitro, Mishpatim. And during those six weeks, from beginning of Shemot till the end of Mishpatim, many, many people fasted. There were those that fasted just on Mondays and Thursdays, some just on Thursdays, some for entire week at a time, in other words from Mossa'e Shabbat until Shabbat started again. And there were those that would fast just two days straight, including both day and night, or three days straight, day and night.

Let me explain. According to the writings of the HaAri through his student Rabbi Hayyim Vital, Maharhu, we know that there is a great need to fast for certain sins, and they basically said this is the time to fast, during these weeks from Shemot through Mishpatim. What it's based on is another story, but it seems to be very kabbalistically based. It's something we only first know about beginning from around the year 1350, about 150 years before the HaAri, and then through the writings of the HaAri through his students we get to know about it, and our Hakhamim in our Sephardic communities talked about it at length.

So during these weeks of Shobabim, let's talk about Halab, for example. We know Hakham Abraham Antebi, who was chief rabbi of Halab, he passed away in 1858. He wrote numerous books, but in his books Hokhmah UMusar and Ohel Yesharim, which were his last two books that he wrote, he brings up the subject of Shobabim. Here's a copy of Hokhmah UMusar and Ohel Yesharim. He talks about these things and he says in the generation before him it was very, very common. So we're talking about basically 200 years ago from where we are today. And he talks about how almost a large segment of the community in Halab fasted during Shobabim. There were those that fasted just Mondays and Thursdays, those that fasted the entire week, and those that fasted for periods of two days or three days.

Why two days or three days? According to the kabbalists, fasting two days straight, in other words not eating for a full 48-hour period, is the equivalent of fasting 27 fasts. Or if you do a three-day fast, okay again, we're talking about 72 hours straight, no eating or drinking at all, that's equivalent to 40 days of fasting. For certain 'Avonot, they say that we need 84 fasts. So they would fast three days straight, take a break, another three days or one week three days, the next week three days, and then do four individual one-day normal fasts to get those 84 fasts in.

But not only that, he said even though not everybody did it, there were many, many people that did it, and those that did not do it encouraged those that were doing it and in fact came to pray with them. Nowadays, when we hear there's going to be longer prayers, we generally tend to run away. But in these cases, for Minhah, they would have an extra lengthy Minhah with extra prayers, with extra Tehillim including extra Mizmorim, with Selihot, with Bedil VaYa'abor, with everything, and he said the majority of the community, the majority of the congregation would show up to the Bet Keneset to join those that were in these Ta'aniyot, in these fasts of these Shobabim days, to join them for Minhah because they knew this was a Kapparah on not only them, but the entire community.

And Hakham Abraham Antebi specifically continues to write, he goes, in those days when they did these fasts, the community never knew of any misgivings, of any ill, any sorrow. He goes, even financially, people were better off. Even if they weren't making a lot of money, money seemed to go a lot further and they were able to get a lot more for their dollar. So he saw a lot of positive in these fasts of Shobabim.

We see it in the writings, as I said, of Hakham Abraham Antebi. He's not the only rabbi from Halab who wrote about it. Many other rabbis wrote about it, but he wrote about it at length. We know about from Egypt, in Nehar Missrayim he talks about it. We know about it from Tunisia, from 'Ale Hadas. In fact, there was a special book, prayer book, for Shobabim, printed in Livorno, called Tikkun HaShobabim, and these are all the prayers and the extra prayers for Minhah, including Viddui HaGadol. So this was a very, very big thing in the Middle East at the time. It was a big thing, according to the Hida, in Italy as well.

Nowadays, we've basically let it slide, go to the wayside. In Israel, there are some places where they still do it. But coming up in the next video, we're going to talk about in what way these fasts have been replaced with Ta'anit Dibbur, also through a Hakham from Halab, Hakham Yisshak Alfiah. Stay tuned for the next video.

288.title: Non-Jewish Milk in Halab
288.text:
In the early 1880s, Hakham Yosef Sethon, who was born in Halab in the year 1813, wrote a book called VaYelaket Yosef. This book was published by his grandson, Hakham David Moshe Sethon, in the year 1915. In this book, Hakham Yosef Sethon discussed the permissibility of buying certain dairy products from non-Jews because of the prohibition of drinking milk that was milked by a non-Jew without a Jewish person watching and making sure that the milk was from a kosher animal. When this happens, the milk is commonly referred to as Halab 'Akum, or non-Jewish milk, but when a Jewish person is watching, the milk is commonly referred to as Halab Yisrael.

One dairy product that he discussed was Sahlab, which interestingly he noted that when he wrote this book was something that had just become available in Halab approximately 10 years earlier. At that time, Jewish people started buying Sahlab from non-Jews, and Hakham Yosef Sethon concluded that it was not permissible to do so, even though the people claimed that unkosher milk was not available in Halab at that time.

Then in another discussion in the same book, he discussed ice cream that was flavored with fruit juices and milk and was called Anbar Buz. This ice cream had also become available recently, and Jews were also buying this from non-Jews. And Hakham Yosef Sethon cited an anonymous rabbi who permitted the ice cream, since unkosher milk was not available in Halab at that time. This rabbi was relying on the ruling of the Peri Hadash, a 17th-century authority who was born in Italy and later lived in Jerusalem. However, Hakham Yosef Sethon argued that the leniency of the Peri Hadash, who allowed milk milked by a non-Jew without a Jewish person watching in a place where unkosher milk was either unavailable or much more expensive, did not apply to Halab, since there were camels in Halab and in the surrounding villages. So Hakham Yosef Sethon concluded that it was not permissible to eat this ice cream either. However, the publisher, Hakham David Moshe Sethon, who was Hakham Yosef Sethon's grandson, added his own comment that the rabbi who permitted it would defend his position based on the fact that since the camel milk was not available, it would be much more expensive than the kosher milk, and the Peri Hadash also allowed non-Jewish milk in places where unkosher milk was significantly more expensive than the kosher milk.

In any case, decades later, in the year 1919, Rabbi Suleiman Mani, who was the rabbi of Hebron at that time, received a question from Halab regarding the permissibility of metal containers of cooked milk that came from Europe. In his response to them, he noted that the custom of the majority of the Jews of Halab was to drink milk that was not milked in front of a Jew based on the rulings of the Tashbess and the Peri Hadash. Additionally, the Hida wrote that if the custom of a city where unkosher milk is not available is to buy milk from a non-Jew in a pot, the custom does not have to be stopped, since they are relying on great authorities who permit this. In the end, Rabbi Mani also permitted the milk from Europe, since unkosher milk was also significantly more expensive in Europe, and the rabbis of America had also permitted it. All this was printed in the book Ma'aseh Eliyahu that was published decades later in the year 1978.

So we see that Hakham Yosef Sethon's position did not become so accepted, since most of the Jews of Halab applied the leniency of the Peri Hadash to their city, since unkosher milk was not available there. It seems that even though there were camels in Halab, they did not milk them. Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote about non-Jewish milk in his book Ro'eh Ne'eman. He noted that the same Hakham David Moshe Sethon, who published his grandfather's book VaYelaket Yosef, would drink non-Jewish milk in Argentina based on the ruling of the Peri Hadash, as well as Rabbi Moshe Feinstein's ruling that allowed non-Jewish milk in a place where the government did not allow unkosher milk to be sold as regular milk, and also due to the difficulty of acquiring Jewish milk in his city. Furthermore, Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi cited a written source that stated that in New York, Rabbi Jacob Kassin completely permitted non-Jewish milk. He wrote this in his not-yet-published book, Ma'agale Eress. But it seems that they were only lenient when they were buying ready-made dairy products, as Hakham Yisshak Chehebar also wrote that in Halab, the non-Jews would come up to their homes to sell them milk with their flock of animals, and they would be careful to watch the non-Jew milk the goats in front of them.

So we see that when certain dairy products became commercially available in Halab in the 19th century, the custom developed among the majority to be lenient and buy these products from non-Jews because unkosher milk was not available in their city, which is in accordance with the ruling of the Peri Hadash. This practice was also accepted by the rabbis of the Halabi communities in both Argentina and in New York. However, some were stringent, like Hakham Yosef Sethon, who prohibited buying the Sahlab and the ice cream from non-Jews in Halab. All of this was with regards to ready-made dairy products, but when they bought milk from a non-Jew who was milking the animal on the spot, they were careful to watch the milking process to make sure that the non-Jew was in fact milking a kosher animal. And just to clarify, the leniency in Halab was only regarding Halab Yisrael, but when a dairy product had other Kashrut concerns, of course it requires reliable rabbinic supervision.

289.title: Hakham Yisshak Alfiah and the Ta'anit Dibbur
289.text:
In the previous episode talking about the custom of fasting during the weeks of Shobabim, Shobabim again being those weeks, those six weeks of Shemot, VaEra, Bo, Beshallah, Yitro, Mishpatim, I mentioned that there were those who fasted every Monday and Thursday, those who fasted two days in a row, three days in a row, and each thing equaled something else. And these were people that were fasting to correct various 'Avonot, to do Teshubah, and I mentioned that this has been forgotten, and it has been replaced. And many have reached out to me, what am I talking about? How could a Minhag be replaced with another Minhag?

And this is something very, very unique, and we have to credit one man, one man alone, a great Hakham, a very, very pious individual, his name was Hakham Yisshak Alfiah. This is a picture of Hakham Yisshak Alfiah. He was born in Halab in 1878. He made 'Aliyah to Eress Yisrael, to Yerushalayim, with his father and grandfather at a young age. He passed away in 1955. He was well known for his piety and for his deep love and care of the people. He wanted people to be able to follow Torah UMissvot easily, he wanted them to be able to make Teshubah easily, and he saw people were having great difficulty with this.

He understood the importance of fasting during Shobabim, and, in fact, he says people can't do it anymore. He first talks about the concept of these fasts and the difficulty in his book Siah Yisshak. This is Siah Yisshak, published in Yerushalayim in 1923, and he really gets into it in his book HaKunteres HaYehi'eli that was published in Yerushalayim, it's old, falling apart, but it's an amazing book, published in 1928, and he writes, "Ve'Attah BiZmanenu Zeh SheHaGufot Nehelshu Ba'Avonotenu HaRabbim," and he continues. He says, nowadays the human body is weak, it can no longer withstand these fasts, these fasts that people were able to do and it was so easy for them, you know, people can't do it today. And even if they think they can do it, they have to understand that they have to be extra careful during these fasts to watch out of doing any 'Avon. And how could a man who's going to work, you know, watch his mouth from not saying something wrong, or talking about his products, you know, in a way that is incorrect, or possibly tipping the scale a little bit and stealing from himself or from the customer? Because there are so many sins that a person may be doing while they're fasting from—they're abstaining from food, but they're doing so many other sins, so their entire fast was worthless and doesn't mean anything. And we need to come up with a solution.

And in all his study and all his research, he came up with the concept of Ta'anit Dibbur, a one-day Ta'anit Dibbur, which would be the equivalent of fasting an entire week from, as—or as he writes, from Shabbat till Shabbat, in other words, from Saturday night, Mossa'e Shabbat, when Shabbat ends, until Friday night, when Shabbat begins. And he goes, and that is the equivalent of 65,600 fasts! Imagine that! You could do a one-day Ta'anit Dibbur that's the equivalent of fasting 65,600 days.

And he was doing this in Yerushalayim with a small group of people, and they were publicizing it, you know, in their inner circle and among friends and neighbors and things like that. When he passed away, his core group of people decided we need to publicize this, and they started publishing broadsides and plastering all over Yerushalayim and other cities, and then they decided to start sending them out around the world. And this is something that went on and something that we witnessed here in Brooklyn and in many other places that the association created by Hakham Yisshak Alfiah called Or Hadash VeSemah Saddik had a general one-day Ta'anit Dibbur every year, and it was always the—or almost always, I should say, the first Tuesday of the month of Shebat. And in his Kunteres HaYehi'eli, Hakham Yisshak Alfiah explains why that's the time it has to be, and he does all different calculations to come with that day and why it's that day and how it works, etc.

But regardless, this is an example of the broadside, the poster that went out to every community in the world. And they used to send stacks of these to Chief Rabbi Jacob S. Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom, followed by his son, Chief Rabbi Shaul Kassin, 'Alehem HaShalom, and they would give it to all the rabbis of the synagogues of the community to publicize this. And because they knew that the people of the community could not do a Ta'anit Dibbur on a Tuesday, they amended it here in Brooklyn to be on a, on the Sunday, usually the Sunday following the Tuesday that they did the fast in Israel. And it was a special order of reading Tehillim three times, not allowed to speak at all, not even Dibre Torah, not even to say hello to anybody, reading Tehillim three times, followed by other Mizmorim and other Pesukim, followed by a Minhah that included Viddui HaGadol and other prayers, and it was a very, very special day. And this went on in Shaare Zion, in Ahi'ezer, in Ahaba VeAhva, in Bnei Yosef, and many other community synagogues.

And this is something that existed for years and years from 1956 onward to our time. It's an amazing way of continuing the fasting of the days of Shobabim without actually having to fast so many days, whether it be Mondays and Thursdays for six weeks or more days than that. One day, Ta'anit Dibbur HaKelali established by Hakham Yisshak Alfiah, Zekhuto Yagen 'Alenu Amen.

290.title: The Berakhah on Mlabas
290.text:
When one thinks of Berakhot on food, one thinks of Halakhah, not of Minhag. But even though it's generally a Halakhah issue, Minhag also comes into play. A food that people don't think of often usually creates even more issues. Today's subject: Mlabas. We all know Mlabas, commonly known in the United States as Jordan almonds. They are almonds, whole almonds, that are candy-coated. What is the Berakhah?

I recently witnessed a couple of people discussing this and arguing, and they weren't sure what the Berakhah is. One of them went over to the bookshelf and pulled out a book very, very famously known as the Ben Ish Hai, written by Rabbi Yosef Hayyim of Baghdad, which was first published in Jerusalem in 1898. And in this particular book, the Hakham writes, and I'll just read it in translation for you, "Whole almonds that are covered in sugar, it was the custom of my father to separate them, separate the sugar from the almond. He would make a Berakhah of Ha'Ess on the almond and then Berakhah of SheHakol on the sugar. But the custom of the people of my city, that being Baghdad, is to make the Berakhah of SheHakol and not to separate them." And that's where he left it. He talked about other sources, he talked about some Ashkenazi sources that said you should just make Ha'Ess on it, but he left it at his father would separate them and make two separate Berakhot, and the Minhag of Baghdad was to say SheHakol.

Now, a person would think, "Okay, from Baghdad to Aleppo, on the centuries-old caravan route, about 500 miles, there was a lot of interaction between the people, between the Hakhamim, same Middle East region, same item that they're eating, same Mlabas, so okay, Berakhah is going to also be Minhag of Halab to also be SheHakol." But that's not the case.

We have a book called Peri Saddik by Hakham Shaul Kassin. He's the father of our original chief rabbi of our community here in Brooklyn, of Rabbi Jacob S. Kassin, Hakham Shaul Kassin. He passed away in 1915. The book was published in 1938 by his son, Hakham Shaul Kassin, who passed away in 1982. In this particular book, what does the Hakham write? He says that "Shekedim HaMehuppim BeSukar," almonds that are coated in sugar, the Berakhah is—and he writes in Arabic, "SheKorin Otam Ba'Arabi Mlabas," that's what we call Mlabas, so you have no doubt what he's talking about—saying the Berakhah is Bore Peri Ha'Ess. So here we go, different opinion now.

In the footnotes on the bottom, his son, Hakham Shaul, writes that, "I heard of different Minhagim, and I heard regarding the custom of those from Aleppo"—because they were already living in Jerusalem, so he asked those from Aleppo—"there are those that say Ha'Ess and there are those that separate them, like the Ben Ish Hai's father, to make two separate Berakhot." Okay, but nothing about the Berakhah being SheHakol, except that he heard in Yerushalayim, he's seen some people say the Berakhah of SheHakol. So we will leave it at that.

Question: is it Ha'Ess? Is it SheHakol? Or two separate Berakhot? We go back in time. We go back to Hakham Shemuel Laniado, who lived in the 18th century, and he wrote a book called the Shulhan HaMelekh. Shulhan HaMelekh, he writes the Berakhot of some of the foods, and he writes explicitly, he writes "Mlabas Mebarekh Ha'Ess." Okay? He wrote the introduction to this in 1804. The book wasn't published until 1923. Obviously, he was long gone by then, but obviously, he wrote this early on.

We would think, okay, maybe there is an opinion to say Ha'Ess, but we have the most recent publishing of Ro'eh Ne'eman, from the writings of Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, who was born in Aleppo, 1911, passed away in Argentina 1990, he was the chief rabbi in Argentina, and he also writes in his book Ro'eh Ne'eman that was published by the Sephardic Heritage Museum, the Berakhah is Ha'Ess. So we have a clear definition that the Minhag of Aleppo, the Berakhah of Mlabas is Ha'Ess, and that's a Minhag, as opposed to the Ben Ish Hai, who gives us an opinion to do two Berakhot, tells you the Minhag in his city of SheHakol, and he even quotes other sources to say it's only Ha'Ess. So, the Minhag of Aleppo for Mlabas is Ha'Ess, not SheHakol, and not to separate the two items.

291.title: Mizmorim for Purim and Fast Days
291.text:
The custom of reciting the 22nd chapter of Tehillim in honor of the holiday of Purim was already documented in the 14th century in Spain by David Abudarham. This Mizmor starts with "LaMnasseah 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar." Ayyelet is a female deer, and the Gemara compared Queen Ester to a female deer, since she was as beloved to Ahashverosh as a female deer is to her mate. The Abudarham also pointed to the acronym of Haman in this Mizmor, when it said, "Hassilah MeHereb Nafshi," which refers to HaShem saving one's life from a sword.

The Abudarham also mentioned reciting the 124th chapter of Tehillim, which begins "Shir HaMa'alot," and has the verse, "Lule HaShem SheHayah Lanu BeKum 'Alenu Adam," "Were it not for HaShem who was with us when a man rose up against us." The Gemara Masekhet Megillah explained that the man in that verse is Haman.

However, according to the Abudarham, these psalms are recited on the morning of Purim, towards the end of Shahrit. He has the Shir HaMa'alot while returning the Sefer Torah, and the LaMnasseah 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar right after Kaddish Titkabbal. And even in more recent times, we find the Mizmor of 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar on the morning of Purim, after returning the Sefer Torah, in the famous 19th-century Siddur, Bet 'Obed, and in the 20th-century Siddur, Tefilat Yeshurun.

But the custom of Halab was only to recite the Mizmor of 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar on the night of Purim, right before 'Arbit, and the Shir HaMa'alot is recited at the end of 'Arbit, instead of the usual Shir LaMa'alot, before Kaddish and 'Alenu. The Shir HaMa'alot is recited again the next day in Minhah, instead of LaMnasseah BiNginot, again before Kaddish and 'Alenu.

In his book Ro'eh Ne'eman, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar recorded the order of the prayers for 'Arbit and Shahrit on Purim. He has the Mizmor of 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar to start 'Arbit, and the Shir HaMa'alot at the end of 'Arbit, before Kaddish and 'Alenu. And in his instructions for Shahrit, he specified that the Mizmor of 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar is not recited. The book Derekh Eress also noted that the Mizmor of 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar is recited before 'Arbit, but not at all in Shahrit. And Derekh Eress also recorded the custom of saying the Shir HaMa'alot in 'Arbit and Minhat Purim, instead of the usual Shir LaMa'alot and LaMnasseah BiNginot that are recited on weekdays.

Now, the Abudarham also wrote that the Mizmor of 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar is recited on Ta'anit Ester after Kaddish Titkabbal in Shahrit. He also has another Mizmor that is recited on Som Gedalyah and on 'Asarah BeTebet, as well as a third Mizmor for Shib'ah 'Asar BeTammuz. However, we do not recite 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar on Ta'anit Ester, or the other Mizmorim on the other fast days.

The not yet published Ma'agale Eress by Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi states that according to Hakham Yisshak Tawil, the custom of Halab is not to recite a Mizmor for any fast day in any of the prayers. And this is also the custom in the Yesod HaDat congregation in Argentina, and this was also the original custom of the Halabi community in New York.

The only time a Mizmor is added at the end of Shahrit is in a Bet Abel, a house of mourning, when the 49th chapter of Tehillim is recited. That Mizmor starts with "LaMnasseah LiBne Korah Mizmor." Interestingly, Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo wrote that it's said before Kavveh in Shahrit, but in our community, it is usually recited right after Hoshi'enu, before Kaddish.

So our custom is to only recite the Mizmor of 'Al Ayyelet HaShahar once, right before 'Arbit on the night of Purim. We don't recite it in Shahrit on Purim, or at all on Ta'anit Ester. Furthermore, we don't ever recite a Mizmor for a fast day in any of the prayers. The only Mizmor that we ever add after Hoshi'enu in Shahrit is the Mizmor for a Bet Abel, in a house of mourning. But we do have another Mizmor for Purim that starts "Shir HaMa'alot," which is recited towards the end of 'Arbit and Minhah on the holiday of Purim.

292.title: Reading the Megillah at Home
292.text:
The holiday of Purim, Purim, we immediately think of Megillat Ester. And what about Megillat Ester? It's the story of Haman convincing Ahashverosh to annihilate the Jews. They're a different people, they're separated, they're scattered, and he easily convinced him to sign a decree to annihilate them. And as we know, HaShem saved us.

So why do I bring this up? I bring this up because of this salvation, we are told by the Hakhamim that it's important to praise God in public, in a multitude, and to thank Him among all the people so everybody hears about this wonderful salvation.

Why do I bring this up again? Because Hakham Abraham Antebi, Rabbi Abraham Antebi, who was the chief rabbi of Aleppo from 1817 till 1858, in his book Ohel Yesharim, in the section called Sha'ar HaNes, Musar for Shabbat Zakhor, he tells us that he doesn't understand what's going on. If this is such a tremendous Missvah, proclaiming this miracle, it behooves him and bewilders him and astonishes him, he says. What's going on that people are making small Minyanim in their homes and they create excuses why not to go to the synagogue to hear the reading of the Megillah? And it has reached a point in his day where almost half of the congregation no longer shows up to the Bet Keneset on Purim to hear the Megillah, but rather they have private Minyanim at home. And how could it be that they are ignoring the words of the Hakhamim and specifically of Rabbenu Nissim that tells us it's a Missvah to do this Kebod HaRabbim for Bore 'Olam in public in the Bet Keneset? Therefore, he reprimands the people and tells them, "Don't do it anymore. And you must come to the Kenis." And he was able to put a stop to it and get the people to go again to the Bet Keneset for Mikra Megillah.

As opposed to what we're seeing nowadays in the last decade or so, we're seeing people have reverted to this old style of making private Minyanim and creating excuses why not to go. We have the writings of our Hakhamim that tell us they encountered this situation before and they were able to put a stop to it and bring back the glory to Bore 'Olam, the glory to 'Am Yisrael, and to show the world and to show ourselves that we're not "'Am Mefuzar UMforad." We're not a people that are separated and scattered, but rather we are unified.

Now, of course, there's going to be situations where you have to read the Megillah at home. You have, you know, a woman at home that's tending to a child, you have an elderly person, you have an ill person, and there's going to be situations where you have to read at home. Now, if you're going home, you heard the Megillah already in Bet Keneset and you're going home to read for women, do you make Berakhot on the Megillah? Do you make opening Berakhot? Do you make closing Berakhot? Do you make no Berakhot? Do you make all the Berakhot? What's the law?

So we know Hakham 'Obadia Yosef is very clear that even a person that has heard the reading of the Megillah in the Bet Keneset goes home to read for his wife and his children, he would still make the Berakhot of the Megillah, or the opening Berakhah of the Megillah, "'Al Mikra Megillah." Now, does everybody agree to that? Is that the custom?

So we have to look first at Hakham 'Obadia Yosef. What does he base himself upon? He's basing himself upon the Minhag of Yerushalayim, as attested to by Rabbi Algazi, by Rabbi Yisrael, by the Hida, and others that say the Minhag of Yerushalayim is that when reading at home for ladies, you would say the Berakhah of "'Al Mikra Megillah." And this is also the custom in other places like Algeria, like Libya, like Tunisia, like Salonica.

But what about other places? So many other places had different Minhagim: like Istanbul and Izmir in Turkey, like Bulgaria, like Morocco, like the city of Hebron, like Baghdad, Iraq, like the island of Djerba. They would not make a Berakhah of "'Al Mikra Megillah." And obviously, if you're not making a Berakhah in the beginning, you're not making a Berakhah at the end either.

What about Halab? The Minhag in Halab, as attested to by Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, and Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, as he also wrote in his book Ro'eh Ne'eman, and by the last Rabbi of Halab, Hakham Edmond Cohen, the Minhag in Halab: do not make a Berakhah when going home to read for the ladies. That is the Minhag. It's well attested to, it's well documented, it has a lot of sources in many of the Posekim. So even though Hakham 'Obadia Yosef writes to make a Berakhah for ladies when reading at home, the Minhag of Aram Soba is otherwise. Happy holiday!

293.title: Amen After the Haftarah Blessings
293.text:
In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that one does not answer Amen after their own blessings, unless it's after the end of a series of two or more blessings. Then Maran added that it's customary to say Amen at the end of Yehallelukha, which is the blessing that is recited at the conclusion of Hallel, and also after Yishtabbah, which is the conclusion of the Pesuke DeZimrah.

In the Bet Yosef, Maran quoted Ribbi Levi Ibn Habib, who was the chief rabbi of Jerusalem during Maran's lifetime, who explained that the custom of saying Amen after Hallel and also saying Amen after Yishtabbah is based on the opinion of Rabbenu Asher, who is more commonly known as the Rosh. According to the Rosh, one answers Amen after a blessing even if it's not right after the first blessing, as long as it's not permitted to speak in between the two blessings. Ribbi Levi Ibn Habib also noted that it's not customary to say Amen after Ga'al Yisrael in Shahrit, based on what's written in the Zohar.

From this passage in the Bet Yosef and the language in Shulhan 'Arukh, we see that what was customary played an important role in determining whether or not we actually add the word Amen after a series of two or more blessings.

In his book Birke Yosef, the Hida wrote that based on this ruling in Shulhan 'Arukh, one should say Amen after reciting the blessings after the Haftarah. And then the Hida added, "VeKhen Nohagim Kessat," this is the custom of a few people. Similarly, the Hida wrote, "Yesh Mi SheNahag," there are individuals who have the custom to add Amen after the Haftarah blessings. He wrote this in his book LeDavid Emet. From the Hida, it's clear that only some people added Amen after the blessings after the Haftarah in his times. The Hida lived in Jerusalem, Hebron, and later in Italy during the 18th century.

Furthermore, Ribbi Abraham Alkalai, a Bulgarian rabbi who was born in Salonika in the 18th century, wrote that they did not have the custom to add Amen at the end of the Haftarah blessings. He wrote this in his book Zekhor LeAbraham. And in the 20th century, the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer wrote that in his times he did not see anyone that said Amen at the end of their Haftarah blessings. However, the Ben Ish Hai wrote that one does say Amen at the end of their Haftarah blessings, and this was also the opinion of Hakham 'Obadia Yosef.

What was the custom in Halab? If you look at Mahzor Aram Soba, which was published in the year 1527, the word Amen does not appear at the end of the blessings after the Haftarah. In more recent times, Ribbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi quoted the book Hedvat HaShabbat in his not yet published Ma'agale Sedek, which quoted Hakham Ya'akob Attieh, who said that the custom in Halab was not to say Amen after reciting the final blessing after reading the Haftarah. Ribbi Antebi added that this was also the custom in the Yesod HaDat congregation in Argentina, and that no one ever heard Hakham Yisshak Chehebar say Amen when he finished reciting the blessings after reading the Haftarah.

The book Derekh Eress also quoted Hakham Ya'akob Attieh, who reported that Amen is not added at the end of the blessings after the Haftarah, but Hakham Yisshak Zafrani remembered that some added Amen at the end of the blessings after the Haftarah, but others did not.

So while based on Shulhan 'Arukh one should say Amen after they finish reciting the blessings after the Haftarah, many Middle Eastern Jews do not have the custom to do so. Here in our community in Brooklyn, it was never customary to add Amen after reciting the blessings after the Haftarah. And based on our sources, it seems that the prevalent custom in Halab was to conclude the blessings after the Haftarah with "Mekaddesh HaShabbat" without adding the word Amen afterwards.

294.title: Reciting the Nesi'im in Nisan
294.text:
Rosh Hodesh Nisan brings with it the custom, the practice of reciting the Nesi'im each day for the first 12 days of the month plus another reading for the 13th day of the month. What are these readings? You'll popularly hear of them today called Nesi'im, Nesi'im. All of a sudden after 'Alenu LeShabbeah, somebody jumps up and starts reading six Pesukim of the Nasi of the day. They may follow it with a Mizmor of Tehillim, they may not, and people will jump to say Kaddish, and, "Oh, everybody did Nesi'im together," you know, and it's become a common spectacle, if you will, in many community synagogues and Minyanim.

And this was never the practice. Correct, this was never the practice. This was a practice of individuals. It was never done as part of the prayer service, never done with the entire congregation, never done with Kaddish. This wasn't the way it was.

This practice of the Nesi'im is done Rosh Hodesh Nisan and beginning those days for the 12, 13 days as we said, because on Rosh Hodesh Nisan the Mishkan, the tabernacle was erected. And when it was erected, on each day the prince, the leader of each tribe brought his gifts to the Mishkan. And so we read them to recognize it as if we're reenacting those gifts and to show that we are connected to all the Shebatim and we ourselves, even though we don't have the Mishkan, it's as if we are bringing our gifts and reenacting and reliving the building of the Mishkan.

Now, the old books, whether we're looking at Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his 1880 Bet HaBehirah, if we're looking at the famous Hukkat HaPesah from 1855, or if we're looking at the even more famous and older Sekhiyot HaHemdah that was published 12, maybe 15 times beginning in 1734 and onward, they all talk about this custom. Now, all these books are not Siddurim. These Nesi'im did not appear in the Siddurim. It wasn't part of the regular prayer service. They only appeared in special books for Pesah, either special holiday Mahzorim that included extra readings as well as Halakhot, or they appeared in Haggadot that also had extra things, not just the Haggadah.

And all these books say the same thing: "Yesh LeAnshe Ma'aseh Lilmod BeYom Rosh Hodesh Nisan Miyad Ahar Tefilah BeFarashat Hakamat HaMishkan Zekher LaMishkan SheHukam Bo BaYom." This was something that was done by Anshe Ma'aseh. And as we know the Gemara talks about Hasidim VeAnshe Ma'aseh. These are special people, extra pious, extra religious, extra scrupulous in their practice of Torah and Missvot and in extra readings, things that are above and beyond. And that's the way it's referred to in Hukkat HaPesah, in Sekhiyot HaHemdah, in Bet HaBehirah, in the Hida in his writings, and Hayyim Palachi in his writings.

This was not something for the common folk. Rather, after the regular people finished praying, we know the prayers end after 'Alenu LeShabbeah and nothing is added to the prayer after that, then certain Anshe Ma'aseh would say other things privately. They would spend 5, 10, 15, 20 minutes reading this order of the Nesi'im.

The first day was the longest of the days because you had to include all the reading from Parashat Pekude of the establishment and erection of the Mishkan, then you go into Parashat Naso and you read the whole section leading up to the first Nasi, Nahshon Ben 'Amminadab, bringing his Korbanot. And only after that, there's still more to come! It doesn't end over there. Then they go into Yehezkel, there's a section from the Nebi'im to read. After you finish with the Nebi'im, then you go to Tehillim and you read Mizmor Kof-Kaf-Bet, 122. After you read that Mizmor, then you, what do you call it, you say a special prayer for the Nasi and for the entire Shebet, for the entire tribe. Then you have a section of Zohar to read. After you read that section of Zohar, then there's a prayer for the elevation of the Neshamot of all those people that died from the beginning of time, especially if you, the reader, had a parent that you lost, it would be very important for you to read it to help elevate those souls and to connect them back with the rest of the nation.

So this was a procedure that was done. It was done with a lot of thought, with a lot of reverence, and it wasn't something that used to rush through six Pesukim and said Kaddish and ran out, "Haha, I said Nesi'im today." No, this was something that was really adhered to by special people, you know, by the Zekenim, if you will, by the Hakhamim, if you will, but not by everybody. If everybody wants to do it, it's beautiful, but go back to the old format. Look into the old books. See how it was.

Like I said, it wasn't published in the Siddurim. The famous Siddurim that they used throughout the Middle East and all the Sephardic communities, like Bet 'Obed and Bet Menuhah and Tefilat HaHodesh, none of them had Nesi'im in it, because it wasn't something that was said by everybody on a regular basis, even the month of Nisan, but it was printed in special books for Pesah and for the Haggadah, and those Anshe Ma'aseh would take them out and read them at their appropriate time and do it properly, and they would pass this heritage on, if you will, this custom, this tradition on to those who would learn from them, to those who they would teach and let them carry this baton on.

But if everybody wants to do it, it's beautiful. Let's go back, let's do it the old way, let's give it the proper reverence that it deserves. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

295.title: The 1897 Aleppo Haggadah
295.text:
In the year 1897, a Haggadah was printed in Halab. This Haggadah included an Arabic translation of the Haggadah in Hebrew letters. Here is a photocopy of that printing. Then in the year 2004, the World Center for Aleppo Jews' Traditional Culture printed an enlarged offset of the original printing and added color pictures. Since this Haggadah was printed right before our ancestors began moving to New York, it is a good source regarding the textual version of the Haggadah that was customary in the formative years of the Syrian community in America.

Here are a few examples of wording and pronunciation that are found in this Haggadah. Even though the Haggadah that was printed in Mahzor Aram Soba in the year 1527 has the more common textual version of "Ha Lahma 'Anya," the 1897 Haggadah has "Keha Lahma 'Anya." The additional Kaf before "Ha" suggests that our Massah is like the poor man's bread that our forefathers ate in Egypt; it is not the actual bread that they ate. Some of our community Haggadot also printed "Keha," based on the 1897 Aleppo printing, including the Young Shaare Zion Haggadah that was printed in the year 1988, and the Shalom Yerushalayim Haggadah that was printed in 1997.

Throughout the Four Questions, and in 'Abadim Hayinu, the word is "Anu," not "Anahnu." We also find that in the Mahzor Aram Soba Haggadah.

In the Arabic translation, the 'Abadim Hayinu paragraph begins with "Hada il-Jawab," this is the answer. Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi documented the custom of adding these words in Arabic before reading the paragraph of 'Abadim Hayinu in Hebrew. It is sung in the tune of the Haggadah: "Hada il-Jawab, 'Abadim Hayinu LeFar'oh BeMissrayim."

Furthermore, in accordance with our traditional pronunciation all year long, the Haggadah says "Keri'at Shema Shel Shahrit," with a Sheva under the Het in Shahrit, as opposed to others who regularly call the prayer Shahrit.

The last of the four sons is described as "SheEno Yode'a Lish'al," as opposed to "Lish'ol." Both mean to ask. However, Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi quoted the Hazzan Daniel Binker Dweck, who said that "Lish'al" is preferred since it doesn't sound like She'ol, which is associated with death.

The final portion of Massah is called Afikomin, not Afikoman or Afikomen.

The paragraph that begins "Barukh Shomer HaBtahato" has the word "Mehashev Et HaKess" in the present tense, meaning HaShem is always planning the salvation at the end, as opposed to "Hishev Et HaKess" in the past tense, which only applies to the salvation from Egypt. And the next paragraph begins "Hi She'Amdah," as opposed to "VeHi She'Amdah."

One more example: in the paragraph that begins "VeEt 'Amassenu," the 1897 Haggadah has "Zeh HaDahak," as opposed to "HaDehak" or "HaDohak."

What about Mish'arotam? Did they print the questions in Arabic? Unfortunately, they did not document the custom of Mish'arotam in the 1897 Aleppo Haggadah. This is because it is not formally part of the Haggadah. So while the custom of reciting Mish'arotam and asking questions undoubtedly was customary in Halab at that time, it was not printed in the Haggadah.

Now, all of the textual versions that we highlighted just now were reprinted in the Young Shaare Zion Haggadah, based on the 1897 printing from Halab. May we continue preserving our customs and read the Haggadah in accordance with the traditional texts of our ancestors. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

296.title: Pesah Sheni and Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes
296.text:
Pesah Sheni. Pesah Sheni, as we know, is a holiday instituted in the Torah for those who were unable, due to reasons of impurity and defilement, to bring the Korban Pesah on the original date of the 14th of Nisan, so they had a makeup day on the 14th of the month of Iyyar. In later generations, this became a minor holiday, a holiday where Tahanunim, Ana, is not said, and it's a Yehi Shem day.

But there's another very interesting custom associated with Pesah Sheni. First of all, our later Hakhamim, the Aharonim of the Sefaradim, specifically the Hida, Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, and Rabbi Yosef Hayyim, the Ben Ish Hai, all refer to Pesah Sheni as a holy day. They say "Ki Kadosh HaYom," it's a holy day, and therefore you have to increase your happiness on such a day, and as such some people would have certain Se'udot.

Nowadays we hear about a custom of eating a piece of Massah on Pesah Sheni. This was never our custom. Among Sefaradim in general, this didn't exist. It only existed among Jews in parts of Djerba and Tunisia, but otherwise it was unknown among Sefaradim.

But an interesting custom that did come up is the association between Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes and Pesah Sheni. Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes, as we know from the Mishnah and from Midrashim, was a very holy, saintly Hakham of old, and his passing became associated with the 14th of Iyyar. The funny thing is that this wasn't known until 1867. Around 1867, the rabbis of Tiberias, of Teberyah, decided to rebuild his tomb, his sanctuary, and associate the 14th of Iyyar. As such, this became something widespread over time in various communities, both among Sefaradim and Ashkenazim, and people would go there on their way to Meron. They would go to Meron for the Lag Ba'Omer, for the 18th of Iyyar, so a few days before on their trek to get to Meron, they had to pass by Tiberias.

The Hakhamim of Tiberias had the people stop in Tiberias, in Teberyah, at the Siyyun of Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes and elicit prayers over there, a special reading of prayers, okay, associated with the readings and the mentions of Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes was what was called Me'ir Bat 'Ayin. It was first published in Jerusalem in 1892, then in 1898 in Tunis, then in 1905 in Baghdad, and from there it spread out throughout the Sephardic world. And so even in Halab, where they weren't necessarily making the trek to go to Tiberias, they would be reading from this book. It wasn't a widespread custom. It was done among certain Hakhamim, certain pious, saintly individuals would do it. Obviously, people would go to Eress Yisrael. There was a very strong connection between the rabbis of Syria and Israel and those that would make that, you know, that visit, if you will, to Tiberias as well as to Meron.

But this connection to Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes was a strong connection to the Hakhamim of Halab and to the people of Halab because they used to give Sedakot, they used to give charity to what was known as the Kuppah of Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes. And even though the rabbis of Tiberias claimed that money should be going to them, this became an ensuing, you know, battle, if you will. This is not related to Pesah Sheni. This is not related now to Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes directly, but it became a big thing among the Hakhamim of Halab. They had this Kuppah of Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes, and the moneys they would use for the Hakhamim of Halab, for buying books for the Batte Midrash, for taking care of poor people in the city.

And as people started making 'Aliyah and started moving to Eress Yisrael in the 1940s and the 1950s, the rabbis of Tiberias said, "Well, you're collecting this money. You now have to send it to Tiberias," you know, and the Hakhamim of Halab got together, those that were living in Eress Yisrael, they had basically a gathering of all these rabbis of Halab in Israel, and they put together a halakhic ruling, which is pretty much unknown, and they put this together in 1954 saying, we are still an independent community even though we may be not living in Halab and we're living divided, and even though we call our Kuppah the Kuppah DeRabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes, we still give it to our own people and to our own Yeshibot, and in this ruling they specifically mention which Yeshibot they give it to, what kind of situations they give it to.

So even though they had a strong connection to Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes, and they would connect him with Pesah Sheni, post-1867, and especially post-1892 when these books started being published and some people were reading from them, they still had this independent feeling. So today's Minhag of the week has to do with both tradition as well as history. Have a beautiful holiday, and as the Hakhamim say, "Yarbeh Simhah BeYom HaKadosh HaZeh."

297.title: Tikkun Lel Shabu'ot and Praying at Sunrise
297.text:
Tikkun Lel Shabu'ot, what is it? It's the reading, the all-night reading of Shabu'ot. And what is it? It's Torah, Nebi'im, Ketubim, followed by the Idra Rabba, which is the Zohar. And this is what was done in our communities for centuries. It was done by all of our rabbis here in the community. It was followed by Chief Rabbi Jacob S. Kassin, 'Alav HaShalom, then by his son Hakham Shaul Kassin, by his son-in-law Hakham Barukh Ben-Haim, in Ahi'ezer by Rabbi Maslaton, in Ahabat Ahvah by Hakham Halfon Safdieh, all the rabbis of the community, this is what they did. As well as in Porat Yosef in Yerushalayim, this was done by Hakham 'Ezra Attieh and by all his students: Hakham 'Obadia Yosef, Hakham 'Ezra Sha'yo, Hakham David Shaloush, Hakham Hayyim David HaLevi, Hakham Siyyon Levi. All the Hakhamim did the same thing. Nobody deviated and said, "No, I'm going to learn Gemara tonight. I'm going to learn something else tonight." No, everybody adhered to what was printed in the book Keri'e Mo'ed.

Keri'e Mo'ed, here's an example of one printed in 1870. They had the order of the reading of the night, which was Torah, Nebi'im, Ketubim, the beginning of each Parashah, followed by the beginning and end of each of the books of the Nebi'im, Ketubim. It would also include sections pertaining to Hag HaShabu'ot like the 'Aseret HaDibrot in Parashiyot Yitro and VaEthannan as well as all of Megillat Rut. Then you would go into the Idra Rabba, which is the great gathering of the secrets of the Torah. You would spend about two and a half hours reading from Torah, Nebi'im, Ketubim, from the Tanakh, and then another two and a half hours reading from Zohar, and that would be your entire night.

If there was still time afterwards, there were those individuals who would set aside time to read through all Taryag Missvot, all 613 Missvot based upon the counting of the Rambam, of Maimonides. Even though we're going to read during the daytime the Azharot, which includes all the Missvot, that order does not follow the order of HaRambam, and therefore there were those that would make sure to read it on the night of Shabu'ot, but only if there was time at the end. In fact, in the old books of Keri'e Mo'ed, the counting of the Missvot is not even there. It only appears in the newer books that are published, you know, in our modern day and age.

Now, after the reading of the Torah, Nebi'im, Ketubim and after the reading of the Idra Rabba, there's no time for any classes. So if somebody tells you, "Oh, what class did you have tonight?" or, "Who were you learning with?", you weren't. This was the learning. Reading was considered learning, and that was the way it was. In fact, when you tell somebody today, "Oh, we have 'Arayat," 'Arayat people think of, "Oh, we're going to read Tehillim for somebody." But the reading of the all-night of Shabu'ot was also called the 'Arayat, and it was the 'Arayat of the all-night reading. That was the reading. And the reading was the studying. It was a reading to connect you with the words of Torah SheBikhtab as well as Torah SheBe'al Peh, connect us to a tradition of our fathers and forefathers going all the way back to the beginning of time, to creation.

Now, besides this reading, and nothing else was done, as we said, this was what all the Hakhamim did, we moved from that realm into nowadays people asking about classes. Study the Torah throughout the year, and the night of Shabu'ot is a review of all your Torah learning.

Moving on from there, you finished the night, you're tired, should you pray early or not pray early? And there was no tradition of praying prior to sunrise. At dawn, the prayers would begin so they could get to the 'Amidah at sunrise. And we have this tradition. We know it. We witnessed it as children. And even though there were those who wanted to make early Minyanim, and some of them did succeed, the established custom was to pray at Vatikin. And we know in Argentina, for example, Hakham Yisshak Chehebar, who was from Halab, would not allow any Minyanim prior to sunrise on Shabu'ot morning in the Halabi and Shami communities of Argentina.

What about here in Brooklyn? Yes, it was the same thing. In fact, our very own Rosh Ab Bet Din, the head of our Bet Din of the community from before World War I until about 1937 when he made 'Aliyah LeEress Yisrael, Hakham Hayyim Tawil, in his book Masa Hayyim, where he records the sermons that he gave here in Brooklyn to the community, says in his sermon to Shabbat Kallah, which is the Shabbat prior to Hag HaShabu'ot, that do not mess up your entire night of studying Torah by trying to rush the prayers early before the appointed time. Make sure you adhere to the tradition of praying with sunrise. So this was documented, it was done here in the community. Growing up, that's what we saw, and this is what it is.

This is what the night is: Torah, Nebi'im, Ketubim, Idra Rabba. At this time, go into the Missvot, and from the Missvot, you begin the prayers not before dawn. And at dawn, you begin the prayers. You have the 'Amidah at sunrise approximately, and then you continue with the holiday after that. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

298.title: Hallel in a House of Mourning
298.text:
We find different customs with regards to reciting Hallel in a Bet Abel, in a house of mourning. In some places, Hallel is never recited in a Bet Abel, not on Hanukkah, and not on Rosh Hodesh. In other places, Hallel is recited in a Bet Abel on Hanukkah, but not on Rosh Hodesh. And there are also places where Hallel is recited in a Bet Abel on both Hanukkah and on Rosh Hodesh.

The Siddur Bet 'Obed at first quoted the opinion of the Peri Hadash from the 17th century, who wrote that Hallel is never recited in a Bet Abel, whether it's Rosh Hodesh or Hanukkah. But he acknowledged that some places do have the custom to recite Hallel in a house of mourning, and their custom does not have to be changed. Then the Siddur Bet 'Obed quoted the opinion of the Hida from the 18th century, from his book Mahzik Berakhah, who wrote that Hallel is recited in a Bet Abel on Hanukkah. The Bet 'Obed did not say more than that.

Similarly, the Ben Ish Hai differentiated between Hanukkah, when there is a halakhic obligation to recite Hallel, and Rosh Hodesh, when it's only customary to recite Hallel. And therefore the Ben Ish Hai also concluded that Hallel is recited in a Bet Abel on Hanukkah, but not on Rosh Hodesh.

The Kaf HaHayyim Sofer also discussed the various opinions regarding reciting Hallel in the Bet Abel, and he concluded that Hallel is recited in a Bet Abel on Hanukkah, and the mourners also recite Hallel on Hanukkah. But Hallel is not recited on Rosh Hodesh in a Bet Abel, except in a place that has the custom to do so. The Kaf HaHayyim also wrote that in places where it is not customary to recite Hallel on Rosh Hodesh in a Bet Abel, the people who prayed that day in the Bet Abel should recite Hallel afterwards in their own homes. According to Keter Shem Tob, the custom in Jerusalem was that the congregants would walk out of the Bet Abel in order to recite Hallel, and then go back inside to complete the prayers.

Hakham 'Obadia Yosef wrote that on Rosh Hodesh, the people recite Hallel in the Bet Abel in another room, without the mourners, who do not recite Hallel on Rosh Hodesh. But on Hanukkah, Hallel is recited in the Bet Abel in the main room, and the mourners also recite Hallel on Hanukkah.

In Yalkut Yosef, Hakham Yisshak Yosef also wrote that on Rosh Hodesh, the people go into another room in the Bet Abel to recite Hallel. But he added that if the other room is too small to fit the people, then the mourners go into the other room, while the people recite Hallel in the main room. Hakham Yisshak Yosef also differentiated between when the deceased passed away in the house of mourning, when Hallel should not be recited in the main room of the Bet Abel, and when the deceased passed away elsewhere, in which case Hallel can be recited in the main room of the Bet Abel, but only the mourners refrain from reciting Hallel. This is based on the idea that the deceased's soul is still present in the house of mourning for the seven-day mourning period when the deceased passed away in that house. In such a case, it's not appropriate to recite a happy prayer like Hallel that includes the verse "Zeh HaYom 'Asah Ad-onai Nagilah VeNismehah Bo," This is the day that HaShem made for rejoicing and happiness. It's also not appropriate to recite the verse "Lo HaMetim Yehallelu Yah," which says that the deceased are unable to praise HaShem. This is insensitive to the deceased's soul, who just lost their ability to praise HaShem. However, most do not differentiate between where the deceased was when they passed away, and do not find it appropriate to recite these verses in a Bet Abel, at least on Rosh Hodesh, when there is no actual halakhic obligation to recite Hallel.

What was the custom in Halab? According to Hakham Siyyon Guindi, Hallel was only recited in a Bet Abel on Hanukkah, not on Rosh Hodesh, which is in accordance with the opinions of the Hida and the Ben Ish Hai. However, here in Brooklyn, many follow the custom of Jerusalem, and also recite Hallel in a Bet Abel on Rosh Hodesh. Mr. Meyer Safdieh, 'Alav HaShalom, wrote in his book Me'ir Ot, that we recite Hallel in a Bet Abel on both Rosh Hodesh and Hanukkah. On Rosh Hodesh, the mourners do not say Hallel with the rest of the people, but on Hanukkah they do. And even though he did not make any mention of the mourners leaving the room when Hallel is recited on Rosh Hodesh, the mourners usually do leave the room when Hallel is recited.

So the custom of Halab is only to recite Hallel in a Bet Abel on Hanukkah, and in that case the mourners also recite Hallel. But Hallel was not recited in the Bet Abel on Rosh Hodesh. In our community, many adopted the custom of Jerusalem and also recite Hallel in the Bet Abel on Rosh Hodesh, but the mourners do not recite Hallel on Rosh Hodesh, and it's customary for them to leave the room when the people are reciting Hallel.

299.title: Hinukh HaBayit, Part One
299.text:
Hinukh HaBayit. Hinukh HaBayit is the dedication of a new home. When a person builds a new home or buys a new home, they do something called Hinukh HaBayit, the dedication of the home. It is also referred to as Hanukkat HaBayit, but traditionally we refer to it as Hinukh HaBayit.

And this is based upon the Pasuk in Debarim, when people would be called to go out to war, the general or the person in charge, or the Kohen, would ask, "Mi HaIsh Asher Banah Bayit Hadash VeLo Hanakho, Yelekh VeYashob LeBeto." Who is the person that has built a new home and has not yet dedicated it properly? Let him go back, let him return to his home, he is exempt from the draft. And it's very, very important that a person whose mind was set on his new home that he's yet to go live in, that he's yet to dedicate it properly with Torah and Missvot and his family and with meals and with the way people normally would live, he's not going to be fighting on the front lines or even, you know, on the back end properly. He's going to be concerned with his home, and he's going to desert. He's going to desert the war front, and because he's going to run away, he may cause others to run away, and it could destroy the morality of the people and destroy the concept of the nation winning the war. So those people that have to dedicate their home are exempt from the war.

Now, the Hakhamim talk about this custom, and they say that it's a very, very old custom of Hinukh HaBayit. We definitely know about it at least going back to the, I don't know, 13th century in Spain, but probably much longer than that, based upon so many other sources. There are allusions to it in certain older Midrashim, in the Tanhuma, in the She'iltot of the Geonim, and other things like that. But it wasn't until the Hida, Rabbi Hayyim Yosef David Azulai, who lived from 1724 to 1806, actually put together a set order of the learning for Hinukh HaBayit. He put it together in a special book that he created and published in 1797 called Kerem Hemer. Kerem Hemer, Hemer, Het Mem Resh, three letters Het Mem Resh, Het for Hinukh, Mem for Milah, and Resh for Refu'ah, and that's what he writes exactly in the introduction and on the title page of the book. So, over there he put together all the special prayers for Hinukh HaBayit.

And the Hinukh HaBayit is talked about not only by the Hida, it's talked about by many Hakhamim, most famously by the Hida, then by Rabbi Hayyim Palachi, and then by Rabbi Yosef Hayyim, better known as the Ben Ish Hai. And all these great Hakhamim wrote about it, they attested to, you know, this being a custom in among all the people.

But more than that, we have Rabbi Yisshak Alfiah, Hakham Yisshak Alfiah, which I've mentioned many times in many of these videos. He was born in Aleppo in 1878. He wrote about many, many topics. And this topic, Hinukh HaBayit, he writes about at length in his book HaKunteres HaYehi'eli, and he goes on for scores of pages writing about the importance of this custom and connecting it to the building of the Bet HaMikdash, and connecting it to our lack of the Bet HaMikdash today, and therefore we have to make a dedication of our home, so it's like a mini Bet HaMikdash in a sense.

He talks about the importance of the Hinukh HaBayit, and says that it has three major principles. They are Torah, Se'udah, and Sedakah. You have to have learning of Torah, you have to have a meal, and you have to have charity. And he breaks it down even further, talks that you have to have a Minyan, and you have to have Hakhamim, and you have to have Dibre Torah, not just the reading of the Torah, but also Dibre Torah given by those Hakhamim. You have to have a meal, which also works as charity for the Hakhamim, who, in the past, were not as well-off as they are today, much more destitute, and they needed to have that Se'udah. There was also singing involved, there was also adhering a Mezuzah to the doorway, also Berakhah of Sheheheyanu, which is based upon Shulhan 'Arukh in Orah Hayyim, Siman Resh-Kaf-Gimmel, talks about a person who builds a new home has to make Berakhah of Sheheheyanu, we'll talk about that when we get to that point.

But he also talks about three other factors as to why the concept of Hinukh HaBayit is extremely important, and he says, first and foremost, thanking HaShem. We are thanking God that we were able to build a home, thanking God that we were able to buy a home, thanking God that we have a roof over our head. It's Hakarat HaTob, we have to give that thanks to HaShem. And number two, that we start off this home on the right notes of having Torah and Missvot in the home immediately as upon we enter the home before we start living in it, we start the home on Torah and Missvot. And thirdly, because this Se'udah is involved, this Se'udah connects us to Shelomo HaMelekh, to King Solomon, when he built the first temple, the Bet HaMikdash HaRishon, he made a tremendous, lavish Se'udah for the dedication of the Bet HaMikdash, and therefore, we do the same when we build our home. This is just part one of Hinukh HaBayit. Stay tuned for part two.

300.title: Food and Shehitah at the Hinukh HaBayit
300.text:
At the Hinukh HaBayit, while the reading is going on, basic items are put on the table for those reading to be able to make Berakhot and eat from them. Basic things like Ka'ak for Mezonot, raisins for Ha'Ess, small little chickpeas or peanuts for HaAdamah, and cold drinks for SheHakol. And after the traditional reading is complete, then a regular meal is served. And even though not everybody serves this meal anymore, it is definitely part of the tradition and it should be done.

And why is it done? Food is served to the guest, okay, not just pastries and sweets, because you want the guest to bless you and your home, so you sweeten them up by giving them tasty items to enjoy. And this is learned from the Pasuk in the Torah, when Yisshak Abinu wanted to bless 'Esav, he told him, "Va'Aseh Li Mat'ammim Ka'Asher Ahabti VeHabi'ah Li VeOkhelah Ba'Abur Tebarekhkha Nafshi." Go, prepare for me tasty morsels, bring them to me and I'll eat, and once I'm satiated and satisfied, then I'm going to be in the right frame of mind to bless you. And this is something that was traditionally done. But what kind of foods? That's really up to you, what foods you would want to serve.

But some people have asked me in connection to foods, "Well, do we serve chicken?" I go, "Why are you asking specifically about chicken?" "Well, we heard that some people bring a Shohet to the house and do Shehitah like it's a Kapparah, and they put blood on the doorpost, so what's going on with that?"

So Rabbi Shem Tob Gagin in his Keter Shem Tob clearly mentions Syria, and he writes, in the cities of Syria, the custom is when somebody goes to live in a new house, a week prior they bring hens and roosters into the house to live in the house for an entire week. Together, they put a bottle of olive oil on the windowsill as well as a container of flour. And after the week is over, they remove these items from the house, they get a Shohet to do Shehitah on the fowl, on the chicken, and they give it to 'Aniyim to eat from. They also give them the olive oil as well as the flour. That way they have basic necessities of life, and they view this as a Kapparah, as you will, because this is a new house, we want to do Kapparah on it, just in case something may have befallen us. Okay, so now it's happening to the chickens instead, and we're giving it to 'Aniyim, so this is looked as a Sedakah and as a Hesed, and all is fine as well.

Was this done in our community? So speaking to people, nobody remembers any sort of Shehitah in the past. But wait, in here, people say, "Yeah, we've been seeing it, you know, in the last 30 or 40 years. People have come from Syria in recent years and they bring a Shohet and they do a Shehitah on a chicken, and they spread blood on the doorposts, and they even put some blood on the forehead of the members of the household, but we don't remember anything from the past."

But I spoke recently to Mr. Ezra Ashkenazi, Ezra C. Ashkenazi. His grandfather was Hakham Salim Ashkenazi. He was a rabbi and a Shohet in the community, and he clearly told me, "Yes, in fact, I know from my grandfather that in 1930 Mr. Jacob M. Hidary built a home and they did Shehitah." Let me tell you, this home, I looked into it, was at 1537 West 12th Street. It's on West 12th between Bay Parkway and Avenue P, right across the street from the park, for those who know it. And he built his home in 1930. He called Hakham Salim Ashkenazi. Hakham Salim brought a sheep, a lamb to the house. They did Shehitah on the lamb. Yes, they did put blood, from what some people have told me when I asked around about it, but not only that, they took this animal that they did Shehitah on and they did barbecue that night and served those in attendance, they served them fresh barbecued lamb.

So they did Shehitah as a Kapparah for the home. It was done actually here in Brooklyn close to a hundred years ago, even though this custom has fallen out here in Brooklyn, it's still going on among the Halabi community in Argentina as well. So Mabrook to all, those of you with a new home.

301.title: The Final Meal Before Tish'ah BeAb
301.text:
When the fast of Tish'ah BeAb falls out on a Tuesday or on a Thursday, one may only have one cooked dish for their final meal before the fast. Rabbi Shelomo Sacca Antebi wrote that in Halab, many ate Mejadra, which is rice cooked with lentils, as their one cooked dish before the fast of Tish'ah BeAb. Others ate a hard-boiled egg, but did not dip it in salt as a sign of mourning for the destruction of the Bet HaMikdash.

In Shulhan 'Arukh, Maran wrote that it is customary to eat this final meal while sitting on the floor. In Mishneh Torah, in the fifth chapter of the laws of fasts, Rambam wrote that most people eat a cooked dish before Tish'ah BeAb, but those that are very pious would just eat stale bread with salt, and dip it in water, and then they would drink more water afterwards. Rambam added that the wise people should also do that, or something close to it, and he also wrote that he himself never ate a cooked dish, not even lentils, before Tish'ah BeAb when the final meal was eaten on a weekday.

However, according to the law, only the final meal itself is limited to one cooked dish. Technically, one could eat a large meal with several cooked dishes, even in the later part of the day, as long as they are going to eat another meal before the fast that will be limited to one cooked dish. Based on this, Muram wrote that the custom developed among the Ashkenazim to eat a larger meal before Minhah so that the fast won't be dangerous, and then after Minhah, they would eat the final meal that was limited to one cooked dish.

But several Ashkenazic authorities objected to this custom. In Poland, in the 16th century, Rabbi Shelomo Luria wrote that those that eat delicacies on the day before Tish'ah BeAb, including fried foods, are in the category of the stomach of the wicked, since they eat all that they need to eat with pleasurable foods, and then afterwards, they casually eat something, meaning for their official final meal. And this objection is found in other Ashkenazic authorities as well, as quoted by the Kaf HaHayyim Sofer.

Now, this custom of eating a larger meal with several cooked dishes before Minhah, and then a small meal right before the fast, was always only an Ashkenazic custom. Sefaradim always ate as they normally would eat on a weekday on the day before Tish'ah BeAb, and then at the end of the day, we eat a final meal that is limited to one cooked dish. Also note that one may eat a large quantity of that one cooked dish if they need to. Furthermore, one can eat bread and/or other baked items like crackers, as well as raw fruits and vegetables, in addition to the one cooked dish if they need to. So one can maintain our custom of only eating a meal that conforms to the requirements of the Se'udat Mafseket, the final meal before Tish'ah BeAb, and still have enough food to be able to fast.

Although the larger meal late in the day right before Minhah is technically allowed since you will eat another meal before sunset, it is not what our rabbis had in mind when they limited the final meal before Tish'ah BeAb to one cooked dish. Therefore, the Bayit Hadash, another authority from Poland in the 16th and 17th centuries, wrote that those that want to maintain the Ashkenazic custom should eat that larger meal earlier in the day, before halakhic midday, which is before 1:00 p.m. But as we said, eating a large meal on the day before Tish'ah BeAb was never our custom. We eat normally during the day on the day before Tish'ah BeAb, with a final meal that is limited to one cooked dish right before the fast begins.

302.title: The Order of the Hinukh HaBayit Reading
302.text:
Returning to the subject of Hinukh HaBayit, many have asked, what is the order of the reading? Many seem to be confused and they think that the reading of the Zohar for a Berit Milah is the same reading as for that of the Hinukh HaBayit. And the reason people are confused is because the books that are used for this and for that are the same book. It's a small book, usually called Berit 'Olam, Berit Shalom, or Seder HaMissvot, different names it goes by, but it generally has the reading for both items, for the Zohar for Berit Milah as well as Hinukh HaBayit. So for Hinukh HaBayit, it's a different reading. It is really not based upon reading section of Zohar after Zohar after Zohar, but it's more based upon Mishnayot.

Let me go through the order with you. So first and foremost, there are some basic Pesukim to say when entering the house, followed by a Mizmor from Tehillim, Mizmor Sadi-Alef, Yosheb BeSeter 'Elyon. And after Yosheb BeSeter 'Elyon is said, then there's Ana BeKhoah, which is a special prayer encompassing many of HaShem's names. Following that, immediately jump into the traditional reading of the Yehi Rasson, which is a prayer for the members of the household.

Then everybody sits down, and the reading begins from the Mishnayot. We read all of the Mishnah, the Mishnayot of Masekhet Berakhot, Masekhet Yom Tob, which is more commonly known as Masekhet Bessah, and Masekhet Tamid. So Berakhot, Yom Tob, and Tamid, Bet, Yod, and Tav spell out the word Bayit. And these are read in order. It's not we divvy up the pieces and everybody says a piece and we finish this entire reading in 15-20 minutes, it doesn't work that way. There is a set order, and it has to be read in order. You go around the table in clockwise order, okay? Basically you're running around from left to right, if you will, and that's the normal reading of the night. Either a person would read one Mishnah or two Mishnah and give it to the next person, or you want to read an entire Perek and go to the next person to read the next Perek. Whatever is chosen, or based upon the reading capabilities of the people involved, that's what is done. But it is not broken up beforehand, okay, you read page one to 10, and you read page 10 to 20, and you read page 20 to 30, and we finish it all up in a few minutes, rather we go around and read it in order, everybody listening and paying attention.

So after we read all these Masekhtot, the three Masekhtot of Mishnayot, Berakhot, and Yom Tob, and Tamid, then we read two small sections of Zohar, about a page or two each. After those two small sections of Zohar, there is an even smaller section of Gemara that is read. After that small section of Gemara, then we go into Rambam. Yes, into Maimonides, and there's a section read from Hilkhot De'ot, from the laws of knowledge if you will, followed by Hilkhot Bet HaBehirah, the laws of the Bet HaMikdash.

After all this reading is done, the preliminary Pesukim, and Mizmor Tehillim, and Ana BeKhoah, and all of the three Masekhtot of Mishnah, and the Zohar, and the Gemara, and the sections of Rambam, then we automatically jump. From that section, we go to the applying of the Mezuzah. There is, the homeowner comes, his special prayer is said prior to placing the Mezuzah on the main doorway, usually the main doorway, it could be a different doorway if that's what the homeowner has decided to, you know, to place the Mezuzah that night, or that day depending when they're doing Hinukh HaBayit. He says a Berakhah of Likbo'a Mezuzah before affixing the Mezuzah to the doorpost, then the Berakhah of Sheheheyanu is said.

Now, technically it's a new house, and you have new furnishings in the home as well, so Berakhah of Sheheheyanu is appropriate. According to Shulhan 'Arukh in Siman Resh-Kaf-Gimmel, Se'if Gimmel, "Kanah Bayit Hadash" or "Banah Bayit Hadash Mebarekh Sheheheyanu," and that's the law. But now it has become commonplace that we do not just rely upon the home and its furnishings to say Sheheheyanu, rather we tell the homeowner to wear a new piece of clothing, a new suit, a new sports jacket, something, you know, that gives him a lot of pleasure, and say Sheheheyanu on that while having in mind the new home as well as the new furnishings in the home. But if not, obviously you follow the Halakhah in Shulhan 'Arukh which is based upon the Gemara that if you have a new home you can make the Berakhah of Sheheheyanu.

After the Mezuzah, you make Berakhah of Sheheheyanu. After that Berakhah of Sheheheyanu, then there's another Yehi Rasson to be said, which is a blessing for the home and for the people that are dwelling in the home. After that, Ribbi Hananya and Kaddish 'Al Yisrael are said, and after that singing is done. The primary Pizmon for a new home is called 'Al Bayit Zeh VeYoshbehu. And after that, other Pizmonim can be sung, a Se'udah is brought forth afterwards, a festive meal, and that basically concludes the order of Hinukh HaBayit.

Now, some people have asked me, you know, home is very expensive today, and many people rent. They get married and they rent a home or an apartment or a condo for a year, two years, three years, four years, etc., you know, is there nothing to be said? Yes, there definitely is something to be said. I've been involved in those type of special readings. Most people don't know they exist, it's not well-publicized, it doesn't appear in the regular normal books, it is something set apart for us by HaHakham Yisshak Alfiah, as we've mentioned again in episode 299, and there's a special reading for people who are renting apartments. If anybody's interested, you could contact me privately, and I'll help you out with attaining the materials that are needed for that reading or give you the list of that reading. But there definitely is something, and it brings Berakhah to the dwelling as well as Berakhah to the inhabitants of the home. So Mabrook to all of you who are moving into a new home or a new apartment, may it bring you a lot of Berakhah.
