303.title: Selihot, Shofar and LeDavid in Elul
303.text:
Minhagim of the month of Elul. Generally when we think of Elul, we immediately think of Hatarat Nedarim, we think of Selihot. We don't really think of many other things. But this past week, a community rabbi, a rabbi of Halabi descent giving a brief class in a Halabi synagogue got up and said Shulhan 'Arukh says, "Nohagim Lakum BeAshmoret HaBoker Lomar Selihot," which we know the custom is to arise pre-dawn to say Selihot. But then he continued and he said, "But there are other Minhagim besides Selihot."

So first let's talk about the Selihot and then I'll tell you what else he said. So Selihot, as Shulhan 'Arukh says, the custom is to get up BeAshmoret HaBoker, in the pre-dawn hours to say Selihot, basically from that point or from dawn until sunrise. It was never done after sunrise. Selihot was one Minyan only, extra, extra early, before the day broke, if you will. And that's when the people who wanted to say Selihot, people who wanted to upkeep the custom and do it properly. And as we know, the custom today, and it has been for hundreds of years, as attested to us from Hakhamim who wrote in Spain, that Selihot is said the entire month of Elul, as well as 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah, for this 40-day period, excluding Shabbat, excluding Rosh HaShanah, and excluding Yom Kippur. So it ends up being 30 days within the 40-day period.

But if we go back to Mahzor Aram Soba, the old prayers of Aram Soba, of Halab, that was published in 1527, and this is a testimony to the original customs of Aleppo before the Spanish exiles arrived there and brought their customs and eventually changed the customs of Halab from being Musta'arabi to being more Sefaradi. The Mahzor Aram Soba says: "MiRosh Hodesh Elul 'Ad Yom HaKippurim Nohagim Lakum BeAshmoret HaBoker BeSheni UBaHamishi UBShabbatot Lomar Selihot." So also get up at Ashmoret HaBoker, get up at the pre-dawn hours to say Selihot, beginning from Rosh Hodesh Elul, but when? Not every day. On Mondays, on Thursdays, and on Shabbat! Yes, Selihot on Shabbat. That was the old custom of Aleppo. They would say Selihot three days a week: Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat, as well as on Rosh HaShanah, and Som Gedalyah, and Shabbat Teshubah, and Yom Kippur. So you had all different types of periods that they would say, and they had special Selihot for each one of these weeks. Each week had its own special Selihot. So Parashat Re'eh, Shofetim, Ki Tesse, Ki Tabo, etc., had its own special Selihot. So that's regarding Selihot. But everybody agrees Selihot was done at pre-dawn, dawn, concluding by sunrise.

Now, this rabbi got up and said, "Yes, I know that our custom was to blow Shofar during Elul." And a bunch of people in the room started looking at him, "What do you mean? We don't blow Shofar during Elul! That's not our custom. Yes, it's the custom of Ashkenazim. They blow the Shofar after Shahrit, some maybe even after Minhah or 'Arbit. Sefaradim don't do that. There are Sefaradim who blow Shofar during Selihot, but it is not the Aleppo custom to blow Shofar during Selihot. It never was. And we know our traditions, we know our customs, and it's even attested to by Hakham Shem Tob Gagin in his Keter Shem Tob volume six on page 11. He says it very clearly: the custom of Aram Soba is not to blow Shofar whatsoever until Rosh HaShanah." So even though some people have a recollection, which is really not really a true recollection of the Minhag, that at one point they were blowing Shofar on 67th Street and the Italian neighbors told them to stop, maybe one day somebody did it or, you know, or maybe some rabbi came to the community and tried to introduce it, but it was not the Minhag of the community, it was definitely not the Minhag in Halab.

Thirdly, this rabbi brought up another Minhag of saying after the prayers another Mizmor, Mizmor Kaf-Zayin from Tehillim, Psalm number 27 from Tehillim, "LeDavid Ad-onai Ori VeYish'i Mimi Ira." This is also a custom that was followed and practiced by individuals, but never on a communal level. Saying it on a communal level is something that was done by Hasidim and by Ashkenazim in general, and I think a lot of people picked it up from the Mishnah Berurah. The Mishnah Berurah, quoting that same section of Shulhan 'Arukh the rabbi quoted, says that it is their custom that they say this Mizmor, "VeNohagim BiMdinotenu MeRosh Hodesh Elul 'Ad Yom Kippurim Lomar BeKhol Yom Ahar Gemar Tefilah Mizmor LeDavid Ad-onai Ori, Boker Va'Ereb." So they have this custom, and so people picked up on it, and on the insistence of some of these people, it was then printed in one of the newer editions of Kol Ya'akob, but at least the instruction is very clear: the Syrian custom is not to say anything after 'Alenu LeShabbeah, but in Hodesh Elul, some say this Mizmor, meaning that some individuals may choose to say this Mizmor, but it is not the custom of the community, and it's not a communal custom. It's beautiful to do private Minhagim, but we have to distinguish between private Minhagim and communal Minhagim.

So as far as Selihot, our current practice is Selihot is supposed to be upheld prior to sunrise during the entire forty-day period from Rosh Hodesh Elul until Kippur. We do not blow Shofar except on Rosh HaShanah and the end of Kippur, and as far as saying an extra Mizmor after 'Alenu LeShabbeah, there are those that say it individually, privately after Shahrit, but it is not done in a communal level, it is not done with the Minyan or with Kaddish afterwards. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

304.title: When to Say Seder VeTashlikh
304.text:
My good friend Morris Arking explained the Minhag of Seder VeTashlikh in episode 119, and I don't want to repeat what he has said. But many have asked, when should Seder VeTashlikh be said? When is the proper time for it on Rosh HaShanah? Is it the first day? Is it the second day? What do we do if it's Shabbat? Can we do it in the morning after we finish Musaf? Can it be before Minhah? Does it have to be after Minhah? What's going on? What, and people seem to be confused about this, and understandably so. This is a Minhag. It is not a law, and many aspects of it are shrouded in mystery because it's connected to the Mekubbalim. And because of that, people that are not familiar with terms of Kabbalah are obviously unaware as to what are the best times of day to do things.

So first of all, the Minhag is always to do Seder VeTashlikh on the first day of Rosh HaShanah, and we'll explain that. Also, when? After Minhah, late in the day. We'll explain that as well. What about Shabbat? What are the concerns with that? And we're going to explain that as well.

So, the first day of Rosh HaShanah, according to the Gemara and according to the Midrashim, is the day that Adam HaRishon, Adam, the first man, was created. The Gemara also talks about him sinning on that day around the 10th hour of the day. The Midrash refers to him being expunged and cleared of all charges at the 12th hour. So that's according to the Hebrew or the Jewish way of looking at the day, with your day starting at approximately at sunrise or at dawn and ending at sunset or a little bit after sunset, that would be your 12-hour window. So basically towards the end of the day is when his judgment was cleared. The Midrash continues and says that you, Adam, you were judged and cleared on this day at this time, and so will all your offspring, in other words, all mankind, all humankind, forever and ever. So therefore, the Hakhamim see this late time of the day as being the best time to do Seder VeTashlikh because we're trying to get rid of these sins and having them expunged and having our cases dismissed, as the Gemara says, as the Midrash says, "Yassa BeDimos." BeDimos is dismissed.

Also, and we talking about Shabbat, what's the proper thing? All the more so on Shabbat. We know Shabbat Minhah time is called 'Et Rasson. And according to the Mekubbalim, there's a concept of Messah HaRasson. This is a time that is very, very opportune, where your prayers are not only preferable, but they're actually wanted and they're accepted much more readily, with all types of sins that are holding them back and hindering them being pushed aside. So all the more so that we want to do the custom of Seder VeTashlikh on Shabbat late in the day after Minhah. So after Minhah on the first day is always the right time, and Shabbat is the right time as well.

Well, what about Minhag? What's our Minhag? You talked about, you know, the Midrash and the Gemara. Yes, the Minhag is very clear. We have oral testimony from Hakham Yisshak Chehebar from Halab, who became the rabbi in Argentina, and he writes very clearly that our Minhag always has been to do it even if the first day falls out on Shabbat, to do it on Shabbat. We know from Egypt, Hakham Refael Aharon Ben Shim'on in Nehar Missrayim writes, "first day, Shabbat." Neveh Shalom, Alexandria, "first day, Shabbat." Sha'ar HaMifkad talks about the Minhagim of Yerushalayim, "first day, Shabbat to do it." The Ben Ish Hai, Ribbi Yosef Hayyim, writes the custom in Baghdad, in Iraq, again, to do it on the first day, Shabbat. Many of the Moroccan sources talk about doing it even if the first day of Rosh HaShanah falls out on Shabbat. Most communities continue to follow the custom of doing it on Shabbat at this late time of the day, because according to the sources that we have mentioned as well as other sources, that is the most opportune time for our prayers to be accepted and for these sins to be dismissed.

So, therefore, in a case where we do not have to worry about taking books or pamphlets out into a public area that may not have an 'Erub, so then absolutely do it on Shabbat. If you're in an area that has no 'Erub whatsoever, don't worry about saying the whole formula. Go to the body of water, just say those Pesukim of "Mi El Kamokha," which everybody knows by heart anyway, that mention Tashlikh. So, say those Pesukim three times. Say the other prayers, the preceding prayers from the Idra, from the Zohar, as well as the prayer that comes afterwards that was written by the Hida. You could say them elsewhere, in any building. As long as you said those Pesukim at the body of water at the proper time, you could say the other prayer before you go out to the body of water and when you return from the body of water, and continue to say the Seder Tashlikh on the first day of Rosh HaShanah even if it falls out on Shabbat. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

305.title: Yag Middot Before Taking Out the Torah
305.text:
Some have the custom of reciting the Yag Middot, the 13 attributes, which begin "Ad-onai, Ad-onai," before taking out the Sefer Torah on Rosh HaShanah and on Yom Kippur. According to the Mekubbalim, the Yag Middot should be recited not only on Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur, but also on the holidays of Pesah, Shabu'ot, and Sukkot before taking out the Sefer Torah.

What was the custom in Halab? According to the book Derekh Eress, the Yag Middot were not recited at Petihat HaHekhal in Halab, even on Rosh HaShanah or on Yom Kippur. This was based on reports from Hakham Ya'akob Attieh, Hakham Mordekhai Abbasso, Nissim Zafrani, Jack Sasson, Eliyahu Guindi, and Dr. Hayyim Dayan. This was also reported by Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, as well as by Hakham Yisshak Tawil.

In the year 1961, the Halabi community in Brazil opened their first official Kenis on Rosh HaShanah. When they opened the Hekhal, the Hazzan began to recite the Yag Middot. Hakham Yisshak Dayan was there, and he stopped him. He insisted that it was against our tradition and we are obligated to maintain our traditions. This was the prevalent custom in Halab.

However, there were those in Halab that did recite Yag Middot before taking out the Torah on Rosh HaShanah and on Yom Kippur. We find that in the Nusah of Hakham Yosef Abadi Sha'yo for Rosh HaShanah. Furthermore, in a letter written in the year 1986 from Hakham Sa'adeh Harari from Mexico to Mr. Sam Catton regarding the Mahzor Shalom Yerushalayim, Hakham Sa'adeh only objected to reciting Yag Middot at Petihat HaHekhal on the night of Yom Kippur. He did not mention anything about the mornings of Rosh HaShanah or Yom Kippur.

So, as we said, the prevalent custom of Halab was not to recite Yag Middot before taking out the Torah, even on Rosh HaShanah and on Yom Kippur. Only some recited it. Now, according to the Mekubbalim, Yag Middot is recited on Rosh HaShanah, Yom Kippur, and on Pesah, Shabu'ot, and Sukkot before taking out the Torah, but according to others, it's never recited then. So reciting Yag Middot on Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur before taking out the Torah, but not reciting it on other holidays, is inconsistent. Therefore, in my Minyan, we do not recite it on Rosh HaShanah or on Yom Kippur, based on the tradition of Hakham Yisshak Zafrani, Hakham Yisshak Tawil, Hakham Ya'akob Attieh, and Hakham Yisshak Dayan, 'Alehem HaShalom.

306.title: Visiting the Cemetery Before the Holidays
306.text:
In episode 19, I quickly mentioned the Minhag of visiting the cemetery before Yom Kippur. Since then, many years have passed. People have asked questions. They'd like to know what the reasons for visiting the cemetery are and when exactly can a person visit the cemetery? Must it be strictly on 'Ereb Kippur or is there a larger window of time?

So first of all, this custom is a custom that we have for 5 to 600 years, probably not longer than that. It has Ashkenazi origin, but it is a custom that is done by all Sephardic communities, including the Yemenite communities which generally don't pick up on Minhagim that have been phased in through Ashkenazim. So there must be some earlier origin that we have yet to discover. In any case, this is an old custom, it's a prominent custom, and it's a very, very revered custom of visiting the cemetery. The question is, is it to be done 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah or 'Ereb Kippur or during 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah? And what is the reason behind it?

So the reasons behind it, simply put, number one, to break us down, to make us more humble. When you enter a cemetery and you see the Saddikim that are buried there, you see your relatives that are buried there, you see friends that are buried there, you see all types of people, you instantaneously move down a notch, probably more than that. You go into a humble state of mind. And when you're in a humble state of mind, it puts things into perspective, you're able to seek forgiveness from God, you're able to change your ways, you're able to pray with much more concentration and with much more truthfulness and honesty. It helps you break yourself down and change your ways. And that is one of the main reasons the Hakhamim instituted going to the cemetery. Because once you're in that humble state of mind, then obviously the prayers can be much more readily accepted by HaShem.

There's another explanation, and saying these supplications at the cemetery in the presence of all these righteous souls that are buried there, also those Saddikim may hear your supplications and may help lift your prayers up.

There's another reason that's brought by Rabbi Yehudah Ashkenazi in the Ba'er Heteb and it's quoted by Hakham Abraham Hamwey. Hakham Abraham Hamwey was a great sage from Halab. He wrote many, many books. Only about 15 of them were published, but he has a book called Bet El. His Bet El is his book on the Selihot. And in there, he brings all the laws having to do with visiting the cemetery because it's something that is done at the end of the Selihot season, more or less. And he says that the cemetery is a very, very holy place because the Saddikim are buried there. And since it's a holy place, your prayers are much more likely to be accepted because of this. Because prayers offered there, it's like you're offering them, for example, not exactly, but for example, like a holy place in Israel, and therefore can be more readily accepted.

There are more reasons brought by Hakham Abraham Hamwey in his Bet El. He brings a number of reasons. He has a very, very interesting reason. He says when a person prays at the graves of the righteous, God bestows benefits on the person in the merit of the righteous person that is buried there, even though you yourself may not be worry of, may not be worthy of those benefits, because we're hoping to be granted a year full of blessings, it's advantageous to pray at the graves of the righteous to assist in granting these blessings, having a successful year. Also, because of the upcoming judgment, the souls of the departed pray to God to have mercy on the living, so it's very, very auspicious to pray at the, at these graves.

That being the case, Rosh HaShanah is Yom HaDin, and if you go and pray there prior to Rosh HaShanah, there is a statement in the Zohar that says that at the end of Rosh HaShanah, the souls go up to listen to the judgments that God is making, and at times, a soul can hear a judgment and can possibly go down in a dream to let the person know this is what's going on. If the judgment is not a favorable one, and this soul comes to you in a dream, you have 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah, the ten days of repentance, to change your ways prior to Yom Kippur. So, according to many sources, it is better to go to the cemetery 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah, but not prior to that.

There are those who say, "No, the custom is 'Ereb Kippur." We do it right before Kippur, so we can pray to HaShem on behalf of the deceased whose fate may still be hanging in the shadows, so and they can't pray, so we pray for them to allow them to have a favorable judgment still on Yom Kippur and possibly lessen their time of being in this state of limbo.

Either way, the custom was both to pray at the cemeteries both on 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah as well as 'Ereb Kippur. And we know this because of a booklet, a booklet that was published in Aleppo in 1929. K? See it? It's Tefilat Bet 'Almin, and it tells you, "Nohagim LeOmram 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah VeYom Kippurim." They're said on 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah and 'Ereb Kippur. And on the inside, it tells you, even if you want to say, "Well, it's not referring to that on the outside," on the inside it says it clearly: "Tefilot SheNohagim LeHitpallel 'Al Bet HaKebarot BiFrat 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah UBe'Ereb Yom HaKippurim." So, these are prayers that can be said either 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah or 'Ereb Kippur.

Nowadays, because of time constraints, and difficulties, and traffic, and what have you, people use the entire 'Aseret Yeme Teshubah to say these prayers. But the most opportune times are 'Ereb Rosh HaShanah and 'Ereb Kippur. May HaShem accept all our prayers willingly. May we all have a blessed year. Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.

307.title: Seven Sets of Hakafot in Halab
307.text:
Simhat Torah. On Simhat Torah, we do Hakafot with the Sefer Torah, means we dance around with the Sefer Torah and we encircle the Tebah on which a Sefer Torah is placed, and we dance with the Sefer Torah around the Sefer Torah that's there, and everybody participates. If you look at the order of the Hakafot, there are seven Hakafot to make. We go around the Tebah a total of seven times. Each time we'll sing, we'll dance around, we'll say a prayer, and we have seven of these prayers until we put the Sefer Torah back.

There are communities that do this just once on Simhat Torah, some do it twice, some even do it three times. Let's take for example in Damascus, it generally was not done the night of Simhat Torah, but it was done on the morning of Simhat Torah after Musaf. In Egypt it was done mainly at night, but also in the morning, hardly ever in the afternoon. In Aleppo communities, it was done morning, afternoon, and night. Other communities did morning and night, others did only night, some others did only morning.

But these Hakafot, these dancing and circling the Tebah each time for a total of seven times only is known to us from the writings of the Mekubbalim from Safed, beginning at the end of the sixteenth century. There were other Minhagim in Germany, in Poland, even in Spain and Provence, of taking out the Sefer Torah out of the Hekhal on the night or the morning of Simhat Torah, but nothing about doing Hakafot. Hakafot only came to us through the Mekubbalim, and we'll now focus specifically on Aleppo, where the transmission of this custom went from the Ari to his main student Rabbi Hayyim Vital, and from Rabbi Hayyim Vital to one of his main students, Rabbi Hayyim Kohen, who became known as Rabbi Hayyim Kohen of Aram Soba, even though he was originally from Cairo, he became a major Hakham in Aleppo, and he became known through all his writings, mainly Tur Bareket, as Rabbi Hayyim Kohen of Aram Soba, of Halab.

Now, what is the Halabi Minhag regarding Hakafot? Now this may surprise you, but in Halab the Minhag was to do seven sets of seven Hakafot. Yes, seven times! Now you're going to look at me and say, "How seven? When are they going to do seven different times?" They considered both days of the holiday as Simhat Torah, both days of Shemini 'Asseret, Day 1 and Day 2, they considered them both as Shemini 'Asseret and they considered them both as Simhat Torah. And as such, they incorporated all the customs into both days.

Let's talk about the old synagogue, Kenis Kbireh, that was in the old section of Halab, in the Bahsita, that was there, according to tradition from the days of Yo'ab Ben Seruyah, according to historians, at least there for many, many hundreds of years. And when did they do Hakafot over there? On the night of Shemini 'Asseret, they would do it after 'Arbit. The morning of the first day of Shemini 'Asseret, they would do it before Shahrit, then again after Musaf, then again after Minhah. Then on the night of Simhat Torah, they would do it again after 'Arbit, the day of Simhat Torah after Musaf, and at the end of the holiday, once the holiday was over, okay, Mossa'e all the holidays of the Tishri season, they would do Hakafot again, and that would be a total of seven times. In Bet Nasi, which is a very important synagogue in Aleppo, they did it exactly the same way, except they didn't do the Hakafot at the end of the holiday, instead they also did a set on the morning of Simhat Torah before Shahrit.

Growing up in Brooklyn, many vestiges of this existed. If we look at the notes of Hakham Moshe Ashear regarding the prayers of these days, he actually prayed 'Ajam, which we would normally pray on Simhat Torah day, he prayed it on the first day, on Shemini 'Asseret, showing us that they already began the happiness of the dancing and joyousness with the Sefer Torah on that first day. But how do we know it even better? Growing up, I clearly remember doing Hakafot before Shahrit on Simhat Torah. There are many synagogues even prior to that, on Shemini 'Asseret they'll do it before Minhah even. So we still have this, so many synagogues in the community today, till today. For example, Shaare Zion, Beth Torah, still do it on Shemini 'Asseret before Minhah, sometimes after Minhah. There are many first Minyanim that still do it today in the community before Shahrit, as well as doing it after 'Arbit, and after Musaf, you know? So these things exist. We have in a, in the community today, if you want to go and do it as many times as possible, you could easily do at least four or five sets of Hakafot. Definitely during Minhah is still a very, very big time on Simhat Torah day.

So this is a custom that for the rest, for the entire world was once, twice, or even three times of doing seven sets, but for Aleppo, it was a custom of doing seven sets of seven. That's how much they enjoyed the Torah, and they rejoiced with the Torah, and they embraced the Torah. Tizku LeMissvot, Tizku LeShanim Rabbot, Ne'imot VeTobot.
